It would be easier to inform Canadians about a streamlined ten-digit to three-digit number than a completely new one,
even if it is already being implemented in the United States. 456 would represent the continuance of its longer
predecessor, carrying the positive impact it has made nationwide whilst starting a further legacy towards better mental
health support when this idea, and others, are implemented and continue to be put in place across the country. While
456 is not an "easily recognizable code" marked by two latter digits of the same number, 456 runs adjacent from left to
right on a phone's keypad, essentially running through the middle and can also be considered quite simple to
remember. Both such aforementioned factors can thus make it an easily recognizable code for Canadians and those
needing or having needed mental health support.
I hope that the discussion about this new shorter hotline doesn't forget that there has been a longer number before it.
What should come from it is a better way of contact that considers being streamlined as a way of making more
effective what formerly was in being there for people. Making a shorter, easier to remember number is one way of
that, and perhaps making it connected to its current, longer form is also a good way of supporting that effort. After all,
it is probably very likely that this new hotline will draw from the same pool of resources that is currently used by
Canada's ten-digit 24-hour hotline for suicide prevention. Let's draw from its legacy of help to continue doing better
for those who need it most.

HELP PLEASE (for me and all Quebeckers who are suffering mentally)

None of you knows anything about what’s really going on in our streets. And in people’s heads.
In Quebec, the mentally ill are being beaten up on the street, abused, insulted and marginalized,
and people often call the police on them instead of offering real help. (I’m not saying Quebec
mistreats the most vulnerable, but it does let everybody pick on them and their illnesses…) We
should be protecting these people from everybody else and from our own institutions. We
should be putting them safely into centres where they will feel comfortable and be taken care of
for once, instead of leaving the mentally ill out in the streets, open to exploitation by all and
sundry.

Where have our social services gone? What are our social services doing?

If social services won’t look after these people, who will? (No one.) It’s not their responsibility.
The social workers aren’t responsible. Responsible for psychologically integrating our citizens.

Quebec is gambling with people’s mental health, and that’s a dangerous game to play. It’s
gambling with the mental stability of alienated, mentally ill people. It’s thrusting them into
unimaginable situations where they may not be able to take care of themselves… And no one is
coming to help them pick themselves up and get back on track.

In Quebec, we are setting mentally ill people loose in the woods, figuratively speaking, and
leaving them to fend for themselves.
We are leaving them to live in their own worlds, without ever trying to bring them back to reality.

Even if that means they end up lost in the deep, dark woods all alone.

Without trying to get back in touch with reality.

Without having people from real life around, just to break the heavy, empty silence of their
anguish.

Right now, it is police officers and the police who are picking up the slack and doing their job for
them.
We’ve sort of replaced social work with policing.
Unfortunately, police officers don’t get special training in social work.

But what if we gave our police officers a break and made Quebec’s social workers do their own
job? In the field they actually studied in.

In the field they actually studied in.

What if we trained a community police officer? (Even though that means involving the police)

What if we made our resources more accessible instead of closing them off?

Quebec would be a very different place today.
Ultimately, Quebeckers’ mental health would be better off.

A sickness that continues to grow.

QUEBEC’S SOCIAL SERVICES ARE CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT.
WHERE ARE THEY?
WHAT ARE OUR SOCIAL SERVICES DOING? (for people who don’t need them)
Is there no one with a heart in those services anymore?
Where has Quebec’s sense of humanity gone?
Things can’t go on like this.
Somebody somewhere needs to do something.
The Quebec government needs to step up and carry out social and community interventions for
all these people who need support.

For all these people in distress on our streets.
For all these cases of community and intimate partner violence.
And all these drug addicts who face stigma.
Are you waiting for a sign from God before reacting?
Do we actually have any social services in Quebec, or are those just words written on a
building? That’s the question I’m asking myself, and you, given what’s happening in the streets,
because it often gets crazy.

Tell me, have you noticed that Quebeckers’ mental health is deteriorating severely in community
organizations and everywhere in the streets, especially since the pandemic started? In fact, that
reality is nothing new. (There have been many failings in the area of mental health in Quebec,
where the situation is far worse than I believed and also than you thought you believed, not
knowing about everything that can be seen around us just out on the streets.

It’s obvious that nobody knows what to do anymore to help all these people.

Where are the social workers when we really need them, when people are grappling with
serious crises and mental distress?

What are social services doing at a time when Quebeckers’ mental health is at an all-time low
and our children’s isolation merits attention in society as a whole? (Both young and older
children.

(What’s really missing? Is it the patient or the resources?)

Is it the patient or the resources?)

WHAT ARE THEY DOING TO GET OUT IN THE FIELD MORE to identify needs and shortfalls
in the community… instead of staying in their offices, waiting for people to come see them and
show up for their appointments. (Thinking it over with our high-level degrees, we come to the

clear realization that the way social services operates is not very wise or smart. Conscientious
workers are basically stuck in their offices instead of out meeting the needs of people who are
falling through holes in the social safety net. And those holes are only getting bigger as our
social services get defunded They are plainly underfunded.

Have we over-centralized social services and mental health services instead of creating
services for the homeless! Mobile mental health services. Intervention services available 24
hours a day and in the event of emergencies, crises and psycho-social distress.

Where are the psychologists, given that wait lists are getting longer and longer and the wait time
to see a psychologist and receive treatment is over eight months and ALSO IS NOT
AVAILABLE to everyone free of charge… (All Quebeckers should have access to a psychologist
free of charge, without having to wait.)

People who are alone should never be condemned to stay alone with their thoughts and
problems. We should be providing them with support and help, and if they don’t want to see us
and receive our services, we should be even more courteous and patient and find more
engaging methods, regardless of which method of approach seems most appropriate.

Do social workers have all the agency, power and discretion they need, or are they getting
tangled up in the strings and cogs of bureaucracy, like puppets on a string?

Where are the psychologists, therapists and mental health networks when people need
services? What are they doing to adapt to this reality… Is it the patient who’s refusing care, or
care that’s being refused to them?
In the end, is it they who are rejecting reality and the lifestyle of this modern world in these
services?

In the end, is it they who are rejecting reality and the lifestyle of this modern world in these
services?

WHAT ARE SOCIAL SERVICES DOING to help people fight off their delusions and overcome
their psychosis… What are they doing to restore them to sanity and soothe their minds back to
a more logical state?

WHAT are social services doing?

(They are doing nothing.) They are just LEAVING vulnerable people ALL ALONE, so now
everybody has to cope with the distress of the world around them, and nobody is reacting or
doing anything. ANYTHING WHATSOEVER.

They are leaving people to suffer in a terrible, lamentable state of mind, to face the prejudice
and violence, both physical and verbal, perpetrated against poor souls who are not fully
responsible for their words and actions, by marginalizing them even more through shocking
indifference. AS UNFEELING as an iron door and the restraints and foundations of the
psychiatric ward at an insane asylum.

No equivalent or equivalence for the human side in society.

No responsibility for these individuals, who have no caregivers and who have been abandoned
by their own families.

WHO IS LISTENING TO AND SUPPORTING these people in everyday life and giving them a
hand when things go wrong and they really need help?

Are we trying to shut them up in the long silence of death?

Are we really listening to them, or are we just hearing their words and delusions, without trying
to get at the hidden message?

What are social services doing, besides paying for medications and degrees for psychiatrists to
hand out pills that end up being taken like legal drugs?

Just to give you an idea of how bad these medications are and how wrong this approach is…

Mix up sick patients’ medications in a psychiatric hospital sometime, and then you’ll see the
BAD TRIP and mass psychotic breakdown that that will create. That will show you just how
harmful these medications are to most people. These drugs are powerful, and they do not and
will never replace psychology, both psychoanalysis and the essential social work that should be
done from the outset and long before that point is reached.

These drugs are powerful, and they do not and
will never replace psychology, both psychoanalysis and the essential social work that should be
done from the outset and long before that point is reached.

Where are social services? I don’t know. Ask them, because even if I told you what I’ve seen
when people broke down and their mental health deteriorated… EVEN IF I TOLD YOU. YOU
WOULDN’T EVEN BELIEVE ME IF I TOLD YOU THAT OUR STREETS ARE THE NEW
PSYCH WARD NOWADAYS and that people who are sick and have mental disorders are
ending up abandoned and let down by the system that’s supposed to support them and save
them from a terrible collapse that could hurt their already severely damaged minds and mental
integrity.

People’s mental health is important, and it’s wrong to gamble with their brains as if it weren’t a
dangerous game.

As if there were no risk to the mind and to society in letting illness take an even stronger hold
without offering genuine comfort. A possible solution.

It’s time to make people who have mental disorders safe and protect them from the rest of the
world’s prejudice, such as mistreatment, including on the streets and while homeless.

There is a misguided belief, caused by fear of the unknown and their reactions, that they (the
people you say are crazy) need to be protected, but in fact, WHAT THEY NEED TO BE

PROTECTED FROM IS YOU. Sick people need to be shielded from mistreatment by society,
and fast.

They also need to be shielded from rejection due to discrimination and from psychological
violence stemming from a belief that they’re not smart enough to understand and that this can’t
affect them… (Even though we’re dead wrong about them) They understand more than we
realize… And it’s idiotic of us… To think that they’re so stupid…
People are being treated like criminals over nothing, when they’re not responsible for their own
actions. How can we have reached this point and this principle of abuse by authorities when it is
social services that are responsible for them and responsible for their actions? These people
are not responsible for themselves. You’re asking far too much of them. YOU are asking the
impossible by demanding that they do something they will never be capable of doing or maybe
even understanding or realizing on their own without help.

YOU are asking the
impossible by demanding that they do something they will never be capable of doing or maybe
even understanding or realizing on their own without help.

Who is taking responsibility for these individuals?
Where have their supports gone?
Why are social services in such chaos…
The government is letting Quebeckers grow sicker instead of fostering their shared well-being,
and our social services have totally lost their calling.

IT’S TANTAMOUNT TO ABUSE.

For real.

Érick Tremblay Dionne.

HESA: Submit a Brief – The Standing Committee on Health
National Three-Digit Suicide Prevention Hotline (988)
To the Standing Committee on Health (HESA) members:

The Mental Health Commission of Canada (MHCC) is strongly in favour of any measures that offer timely
mental health and suicide prevention support. A three-digit mental health crisis and suicide prevention
number will give more people easy access to the help they need when they need it, at a time when this
need has never been greater.

This brief provides information to support the HESA study relating to the National Three-Digit Suicide
Prevention Hotline (988).

On May 9, 2022, the MHCC and the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction released Mental
Health and Substance Use During COVID-19: Spotlight on Suicidal Ideation and Substance Use. The
report’s findings highlight the importance of having the three-digit hotline:
•
Of those surveyed, 7.9% reported seriously contemplating suicide.
•
About 1 in 3 people with a history of substance use disorders reported suicidal ideation during
the pandemic (30.2% of women and 35.7% of men).
•
About 1 in 6 people with current substance use concerns reported suicidal ideation during the
pandemic (17.4% of women and 16.4% of men).
•
Rates of suicidal ideation have been high among youth (16.6%) and Black respondents (15%).
•
People who were unemployed, either prior to (15.3%) or during the pandemic (16.3%), were
more likely to report suicidal ideation compared with people who were employed (7.9%).

One of the MHCC’s central projects in suicide prevention is Roots of Hope, a community-led evidenceinformed model that supports populations across Canada to reduce the impact of suicide in local
contexts. The program is built on the use of community expertise to implement suicide prevention and
life promotion interventions.

Considerations for Implementing a Three-Digit Suicide Prevention Number in Canada (attached), which
the MHCC developed in collaboration with Crisis Services Canada, the Centre for Addiction and Mental
Health, and the Canadian Mental Health Association (National), outlines considerations for policy
makers in the areas of accessibility as well as visibility of a three-digit number; the capacity of crisis
centres, training, and staffing standardization; funding and operating costs; and the recommendation of
a three-digit number.

MHCC developed in collaboration with Crisis Services Canada, the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, and the Canadian Mental Health Association (National), outlines considerations for policy makers in the areas of accessibility as well as visibility of a three-digit number; the capacity of crisis centres, training, and staffing standardization; funding and operating costs; and the recommendation of a three-digit number.

The MHCC firmly believes that a three-digit mental health crisis and suicide prevention number will save
lives. We would be pleased to appear before the committee to provide further details on the evidencebased work the MHCC is undertaking in suicide prevention, which can contribute to the current HESA
study and inform Canadian public policy.

Submission to the Standing
Committee on Health Study
on the Treatment and
Prevention of Cancer
December 9, 2024

Introduction
The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC) represents more than 3 million workers, bringing
together Canada’s national and international unions, along with provincial and territorial
Federations of Labour and more than 100 district Labour Councils. Our members work
in practically all sectors of the economy, in all occupations, in all parts of Canada. We
are pleased to offer our position as it pertains to the treatment and prevention of cancer.
Regardless of the approach taken by government, we submit that it should embody the
determinants of health, and account for the realities and needs of equity-deserving
groups, including women, racialized and Indigenous workers, and workers with
disabilities.

An Ounce of Prevention and the Right to Know

The right of workers to know of hazards in their workplace is fundamental. The CLC has
long taken the position that an “ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure” with
respect to cancer, including those that are acquired on the job (occupational cancer). To
this end, the fundamental right to know of hazards in the workplace must be adhered to,
not only for known carcinogens, but also, employing the precautionary principle, for
potential carcinogens. As such, all chemicals must be assessed utilizing a hazardsbased approach utilizing the hierarchy of controls; this means that, wherever possible,
known or potentially carcinogenic chemicals must be avoided. If this is not possible,
these chemicals must be substituted to reduce the potential for exposure, and
therefore, harm before other controls are used. In addition, Safety Data Sheets must be
regularly audited to ensure that carcinogens are properly disclosed in English and in
French, and accurate labelling must be assured. Finally, inherent to the right to know is
the right to refuse unsafe work – which workers cannot do if they do not know of
hazards in the first place.

Finally, inherent to the right to know is
the right to refuse unsafe work – which workers cannot do if they do not know of
hazards in the first place.

Canada must also employ stronger chemicals management with a focus to
 the use of chemicals for whom the long-term impacts of exposure are not yet known.
For example, there has been increased awareness of the harms posed Per- and
polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS); while there is stronger regulation of PFAS now than
in recent years, it would have been far preferable to limit their exposure to date, hence
the need for a regime that is nimble in responding to emerging research and trends.
In addition, we submit that the public would benefit from enhanced public awareness
campaigns related to carcinogens in the workplace and more broadly. Such campaigns
must also ensure that workers are informed of their right to refuse unsafe work and
understand the right to be free from reprisals if and when they refuse unsafe work.

Better Tracking of Occupational Exposures

Tracking of occupational exposures to carcinogens in the workplace is essential to not
only provide data on exposures per se but also to provide appropriate interventions to
support exposed workers where applicable.

Enhanced Access to Workers Compensation

Cancer diagnoses can wreak havoc on the finances of workers and their families,
especially where workers die, and survivor benefits can be a determining factor
between economic survival and poverty. Under existing workers' compensation
regimes, cancer diagnoses are presumed for specific occupational categories; these
should be reviewed and expanded regularly; occupational registries can be instrumental
in this respect.

Consumer Chemicals and the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information
System (WHMIS)

When WHMIS was first introduced in 1988, the existing exclusion of consumer chemical
products (such as cleaning products) from the WHMIS regime was intended to be
temporary. This exclusion was erroneously predicated, in our view, that chemicals in
consumer products pose little to no harm to consumers who use them for short periods
of time. Notwithstanding that rationale, the reality is that chemical products are used all
the time in the workplace. While employers have a general obligation to ensure the
health and safety of workers, this cannot be done if workers do not have the information
by way of Safety Data Sheets to know how to protect themselves prior to and after
exposure.

Enhanced Access to Publicly Funded and Administered Health Care

Enhanced Access to Publicly Funded and Administered Health Care

Existing challenges1 for Canadians finding a family doctor or for accessing specialists
only further exacerbate prevention and treatment. Without access to early screening,
many workers receive diagnoses at later stages, thereby posing real risks to their health
– and their lives. With respect to treatment, coverage should be expanded outside of
hospitals and physicians’ offices to include the provision of medications that may be
administered at home, at no cost to the patient. Furthermore, integrated care models
should also be expanded to provide access to necessary psychological and
rehabilitative supports. Such care should not be paid for out of pocket for those with the
means to access it.

All-of-Government Approach to Address Climate-Related Hazards

As our planet warms, risk factors for cancer are increasing.2 With a view to prevention,
Canada must meet its international obligations under the Paris Agreement. Good,

23.

unionized jobs in high-carbon industries are key; the Sustainable Jobs Act provides a
tripartite forum to achieve exactly this. In addition, governments must also recognize the
value of sustainable jobs in building and sustaining critical infrastructure as a means of
climate mitigation. Finally, we reiterate our position that emerging hazards must be
addressed in a timely manner, in consultation with workers and their representatives.
Conclusion
In sum, it is our position that prevention is preferred over treatment, and that where
treatment is required, that it be provided by our public healthcare system, along with
enhanced access to worker’s compensation. In a similar vein, we believe that a more
preventative approach with respect to chemicals management is required and that the
right to know should be employed for all known and potential carcinogens. Finally, the
government must be forward-looking with respect to addressing climate-related
hazards, including continued support for the development of good, unionized
sustainable jobs.

Brief to the House of Commons Standing
Committee on Health
Parliament of Canada: Cancer
Prevention Among Young People
Submitted by:
Marie Laberge, PhD
Jena Webb, PhD
Sami Fettah, PhD
Sabrina Gravel, PhD
Joseph-Omer Dyer, PhD
Sylvain Letscher, PhD
Nadielda Pastor-Bédard, MSc erg.

Hélène Sultan-Taïeb, PhD

Introduction
We are a team of researchers associated with the Canada Research Chair in Adolescent
Work Disability Prevention led by Marie Laberge. For the past two years, we have been
conducting research intended to develop a program for early prevention of occupational
cancers among adolescents with low qualifications and several vulnerabilities.
We are submitting this brief to encourage the government to apply the precautionary
principle when making decisions related to exposure to potentially toxic materials and
environments. Both external factors and lack of experience make it more difficult to limit
exposure among young people, and applying the precautionary principle would protect
their health. Our objective is to prevent occupational cancers early on. It is estimated
that between 4% and 8% of cancers are work-related,1 but this figure is probably an
underestimate due to the difficulty in establishing causal links.2 In 2011 in Canada,
roughly $4.4 billion in medical care costs, lost productivity and loss of quality of life3 are
attributable to occupational cancers. In 2010, research in France estimated that the cost
of a particular group of cancers (lung, laryngeal, etc.) for the French government was
between €960 million and €1.866 billion.4 More investment into prevention as soon as
possible is essential for alleviating the suffering of people with cancer and their families,
as well as reducing the economic burden of cancer. Prevention efforts must focus on the
overall environment and workplaces, and must not rely solely on young workers
adopting healthy behaviours. Making health and safety a priority in the workplace can
improve the health and quality of life of many people. Our health can no longer be
dissociated from the natural and built environments we’re a part of.
Overview
We work with high school students enrolled in co-op programs in Quebec. For many
reasons, these young people are particularly vulnerable to the risk of exposure to
carcinogens. First, research has shown that new workers—by definition inexperienced
because they’re just beginning their careers—are more likely to be exposed to harmful
environments to their health.5 Second, these young workers gravitate toward this type
of academic program because they’ve fallen behind in school for a variety of reasons,
including having a specific learning disability or an adjustment disorder. Learning,
communication and adjustment disorders/disabilities are recognized as an additional

risk factor that can contribute to difficulties functioning at work and susceptibility to
occupational health hazards.6,7 Third, disadvantaged young people are overrepresented
in this population, meaning that their ability to navigate toxic exposure in the workplace
could be compromised by their lack of both cognitive and material resources. Finally,
many of the jobs they will have throughout their lives involve manual labour. These
types of jobs pose significant exposure risks,7,8 specifically to heavy metals found in
electronic equipment; wood, metal or concrete dust; pesticides, organic solvents and
paint.9
Putting the burden of prevention on young workers is not only ineffective, but also
unethical. The time and cost requirements of educating them on prevention, individually
or in the classroom, is enormous. Several studies have demonstrated that traditional
approaches to teaching decontextualized safety protocols are not effective enough in
preventing occupational health hazards.10 This does not mean that traditional
approaches are completely useless; however, they must be paired with much stronger,
systemic measures and must include all stakeholders involved with young workers to
eliminate sources of danger.
We commend the government for recently adopting Bill C-226, which aims to develop a
national strategy to assess, prevent and address environmental racism and to advance
environmental justice. First- and second-generation immigrants are overrepresented
among students with learning disabilities who are enrolled in co-op programs.11,12 Their
exposure to carcinogens in the workplace is therefore an environmental justice issue.
The concept of environmental justice can also be extended to the gender division of
labour in Canada. We observed that students continue to choose internships for jobs
typically associated with their gender. Furthermore, it is well established that women’s
occupational health and safety risks are underestimated and invisibilized.13,14 It is

important to pay particular attention to “invisible” toxic exposures in jobs generally

In addition, we welcome the new Strengthening Environmental Protection for a Healthier
Canada Act, which is the first time a Canadian legislation has recognized the right to a
healthy environment for all members of society. This change holds the government
accountable for ensuring that Canadian workplaces are safe and healthy. The lack of
measures to protect the environment and public from the use of toxic materials in the
workplace is therefore contrary to this Act.
In addition to this environmental act, the new Act respecting the regulation of work by
children in Quebec aims at restricting certain tasks and jobs to make sure young people
are not exposed to excessive dangers, given that they are still developing physically,
cognitively, psychologically and socially, and that they may be negatively affected by
early exposure.15 However, regulations are still needed to define the protective
measures and ensure their efficiency.
Recommendations
As demonstrated in the previous section, young people enrolled in high school co-op
programs are particularly at risk to toxic exposure and require specific prevention
strategies. We recommend an ecosystem approach to protect them against occupational
cancers that:
1. Requires best practices for ventilation in the workplace.
2. Integrates cancer risk awareness into workplace training (e.g., explain the
hierarchy of controls, establish an adapted approach for teaching workers the
symbols for hazardous materials).
3. Integrates cancer prevention into workplace inspections, especially for femaledominated jobs that may appear to be safe (e.g., hair salon, florist, animal care).
4. Raises all individuals’ awareness (from the moment they are hired or trained) of
hazards, risks and means of prevention.
5. Implements health monitoring programs for workers exposed to risk factors.
6. Implements the precautionary principle. This means taking action before health
problems occur by taking into account the risks associated with various
exposures in the workplace, such as to chemicals or airborne particles. It is
essential to introduce collective measures that limit the use of materials that
appear to be safe but could have unknown long-term effects. Based on a
systemic approach, these actions will help create a safer work environment and
protect the health of future generations.

7. Implements rigorous assessment protocols for chemicals prior to use.
8. Replaces toxic substances with less toxic products that have less of an impact,
and introduces procedures that encourage sourcing, production and use of these
materials.
9. Reinforces the principles of environmental justice, human rights, employer
responsibility and non-regression (i.e., continuous improvement of
environmental protections) by improving Bill C-226 to apply specifically in the
workplace.
10. Enforces the new right to a healthy environment, as recognized in the
Strengthening Environmental Protection for a Healthy Canada Act.
11. Prohibits substances that are known to be carcinogenic, mutagenic, reprotoxic or
that present other risks of equal concern, where there is an alternative.
12. Funds research to better understand how environmental and occupational
cancers develop and how to prevent them. Such research must prioritize
potentially toxic substances that are still on the market and generated by human
activity in Canada, as well as also those that are often ordered online from other
countries.
13. Establishes and invests in training programs on prevention.
Conclusion
Young workers are particularly likely to occupy jobs that expose them to carcinogenic
substances in the workplace. Young workers are at greater risk of developing cancers,
since they are exposed to these substances from the beginning of their careers. They’re
also at risk of long-term exposure because they often occupy this type of employment
for a large portion of their professional lives. Occupational cancers represent an
underestimated and invisibilized risk that significantly impacts the quality of life for
Canadians and result in significant economic burden. It is important to use all possible
means and measures to limit the exposure of young workers to carcinogenic substances.
The government is responsible for legislating and enforcing current laws based on the
precautionary principle, as these laws help limit the use and presence of toxic
substances in work environments. Educating young workers and other stakeholders is an
important way to limit exposure to these substances. We recommend that the
government support initiatives to develop substance-related education programs that
target young workers, as well as research on carcinogenic substances and their presence
in our living and professional environments.

Submission to
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Study on: Treatment and Prevention of Cancer
November 2024
www.ac2orn.com
Keith McIntosh

Ac2orn (Advocacy for Canadian Childhood Oncology Research Network), is pleased to
provide the following comments to support the Committee’s study on the treatment and
prevention of cancer in Canada. It is important for the Committee to allocate specific time
to hear and consider the distinct issues faced by children and young people with cancer.
Children are not small adults, and there are unique challenges to treating and conducting
research on childhood, adolescent, and young adult cancers. When a young person is
diagnosed with cancer it has profound long-term physical, emotional, and financial impacts
on the individual and their family.
Ac2orn was founded in 2014 to advocate for translational research and effective treatments
to support the goal of curing childhood, adolescent, and young adult (CAYA) cancers. It is
made up of parents from across Canada, who have children with different types of cancer,
and the desire to help improve pediatric oncology research and outcomes. Ac2orn works to
achieve its mission by connecting with CAYA health advocacy groups across Canada;
identifying and addressing barriers that exist in accessing treatments and cancer clinical
trials, and educating policy makers, industry, and others about the issues facing the CAYA
cancer community.
Summary
Cancer that affects children and young people is different.
• The types of cancer are different
• Treatment considerations are different
• Treatments are different
• Research is different
• Government planning is different.
• The lifetime of long-term effects from treatment is different.
Recommendations
1) Funding of a minimum $150 million over 7 years to ACCESS (formerly Canadian
Pediatric Cancer Consortium). 4% of planned spending on research and cancer
strategy is a modest request to support the unique challenges and wide-ranging
impacts associated with cancer in children and young people in Canada.
2) Federal government support and coordination to establish a national vision for
proton radiation and other complex, high-capital cost cancer treatments like CAR Tcell therapy and radiopharmaceuticals.
3) Direction to federal and pan-Canadian agencies to adapt processes and procedures
to better accommodate the unique needs, considerations, and treatments for
children with cancer (e.g., from clinical trial approval to drug approval and
reimbursement).

Cancer that affects children and young people is different.
9 in 10 cancers are expected to be diagnosed in Canadians aged 50 years and older1. Every
system, strategy, program, research stream and decision-making algorithm is designed with
this in mind.
For Canadian children under 14, cancer is the leading disease cause of death2. Cancer is
responsible for 6 times more child deaths than the next ranked disease.
Approximately 1,500 children and young people are diagnosed with cancer each year. Each
diagnosis affects a family unit, with serious consequences for the sick child; parents; and
his or her siblings. In most cases one or both parents must reduce hours of work, or leave
their jobs while their child is in cancer treatment.
For young adults, a cancer diagnosis comes at a critical time in life when they are asserting
independence (social, financial, etc.), and they have to leave school and/or their jobs, often
moving back home during treatment.
Approximately 150 children and young people die every year due to cancer. This represents
11,000 lost potential years of life – each and every year3. The significant lost productivity of
bereaved parents and caregivers has never been properly quantified or understood.
The types of cancer are different
Children do not get the kinds of cancer typically seen in adults. Leukemias and Central
Nervous System tumours (brain and spinal) represent almost 50% of pediatric cancers but
don’t even register in the top 10 of any other age group in Canada. The most common
cancers in adults, breast, prostate, lung, and colorectal, are generally not seen in children4.
Treatment considerations are different
Children are not small adults, and there are unique challenges to treating and conducting
research on cancers in children and young people.
Cancer treatments kill human cells. Children are still growing and developing, so as a result,
cancer treatments have devastating impacts on their bodies, resulting in serious long-term
effects. These can include hearing loss, vision loss, mobility challenges, neuro-cognitive
effects, organ damage, infertility, secondary cancers, and more.

More than 95% of childhood cancer survivors will have a significant health related issue by
the time they are 45 years of age; these health-related issues are side-effects directly
attributed to the treatment they received.s.a
Treatments are different
Since 2000 Health Canada has issued upwards of 1000 approvals for drugs and indications
to treat cancer in adults. Roughly 12 have been approved for use for cancer in children. Even
this short list of medicines is not universally reimbursed for Canadian children.
Children with cancer did not benefit from the explosion of new drugs approved in the 1990s
and 2000s. It has taken many years and much effort to conduct follow-on research and find
how these drugs work in children, often led by academic clinicians — not industry or
government. 20 years later we are finally seeing an increase in approvals of medicines for
cancer in children. The pan-Canadian systems for reviewing drugs for reimbursement
decisions are ill-equipped to consider these drugs.
Canada lags far behind the rest of the world in proton radiation therapy5. Proton beam
therapy is an alternative type of radiation treatment that reduces damage to healthy cells.
Children are more susceptible to late effects of radiation, and as a result have the most to
gain from access to proton radiation, and the best evidence of benefits. There are no
confirmed plans in Canada for a proton radiation facility, and we cannot anticipate a
publicly funded proton center for at least 5 years. Across the G7 there are more than 75
proton centers and around the world there are more than 160 proton centres in 30 countries.
Canada needs better planning and capacity for delivering complex, high-capital cost cancer
treatments like proton radiation, CAR-T cell therapy and radiopharmaceutical production.
Research is different
More than $520 million is spent on cancer research every year in Canada6. Only a small
fraction of this spending is dedicated to cancer in children and young people. Even after the
Federal Government provided $30 million over 2 years to fund the Canadian Pediatric
Consortium7 (now ACCESS) there is a need for a sustained increase in funding for pediatric
cancer research.
For many children with cancer, the only treatment options are in the context of a clinical
trial. Without sustained funding and support, young Canadians will be left behind.

For example, as of November 2024, there are 68 enrolling CAR T-cell clinical trials for
children with cancer in the USA; however, in Canada, there are only 3 enrolling CAR T-cell
clinical trials for children with cancer.
Canada has been slow to open CAR T-cell clinical trials, with the USA significantly outpacing
Canada in the development of this promising treatment. CAR T-cell therapy was first
created for blood-based cancers such as leukemia and lymphoma and, work has been
progressing on utilizing CAR T-cell therapy for solid tumours and brain cancers in children
and adults. The USA opened their first CAR T-cell clinical trial for children with cancerous
brain tumours in Seattle in 2018 while Canada opened their first CAR T-cell clinical trial for
children with brain tumours in 2024. 44% of the USA’s current enrolling CAR T-cell clinical
trials are for cancers other blood cancers and include sarcomas, rare brain tumours,
neuroblastoma, and other solid tumours. In addition, even though Canada is involved in
many North American consortiums focused on the development of innovative
immunotherapy and CAR T-cell clinical trials, we are about 5-7 years behind in getting
access to these therapies.
Some of these trials, available in the USA, but lagging in Canada are offering meaningful
treatment options for childhood cancers that have universally fatal prognoses8.
Government planning is different.
Since 2007 the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer has received $885 million9 to develop
and execute a Canadian Strategy for Cancer Control. When it comes to childhood cancer,
the current Strategy10 focuses on enabling smoother transitions of childhood cancer
survivors to adult care and encourages greater supports for families and caregivers.
Unfortunately, childhood cancers do not develop from lifestyle choices or environmental
exposures and can not benefit from a preventative approach.
Most provincial governments have established Cancer Strategies to set goals and objectives
for improving cancer care for their citizens. Most – but not all - of these strategies
acknowledge that children and young people get cancer. Few have tangible goals. Only
Ontario has a comprehensive cancer strategy dedicated to improving care and treatment of
cancer for children and young people. Without inclusion in these plans, these patients are
effectively invisible to the cancer systems.

To: House of Commons, Standing Committee on Health (HESA) via [CONTACT]
From: Environmental Health Association of Manitoba

RE: The HESA study on Cancer Treatment and Prevention
Subject: Urgent need for a dedicated HESA study reviewing Health Canada’s exposure limits for
radiofrequency frequencies now used for 5G telecommunication and information technologies.
Lack of evidence is not proof of safety.
----------------------
5G wireless technologies such as smart phones, tablets, virtual headsets and wearables are being marketed and
purchased across Canada, with enthusiasm. Millions of Canadians are being exposed to the non-ionizing
radiofrequency electromagnetic fields that these devices emit in order to work. What most don’t realize is that
the emissions from these technologies have not been safety-tested for health outcomes such as cancer.

How do we know this? It is in a Health Canada 5G report that is available to the public upon request.

In 2011, radiofrequency radiation, such as emitted by cell phones, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and 5G technologies, was
classified as a Group 2B, possible carcinogen, by the World Health Organization’s International Agency for
Research on Cancer.1 IARC then noted particularly the need for studies in animals. In 2018, the U.S. National
Toxicology Program concluded from its multimillion-dollar animal studies, 2 that cell phone type exposures,
conducted under non-heating (non-thermal) conditions, caused cancer.3 Later in 2018, the Ramazzini Institute in
Italy published similar findings for cell tower level exposures.4 This and subsequent evidence from human,
animal and tissue studies, published in peer-reviewed journals, support reclassification to a Group 1 known
human carcinogen,5 6 alongside asbestos and cigarette smoke.

Health Canada’s Safety Code 6 sets out guidelines which recommend limits for safe human exposure to
radiofrequency electromagnetic radiation in the 3 kHz to 300 GHz range.7 This includes the radiofrequencies
used for telecommunications and information technologies. In 2021, without public consultation and not in
keeping with a HESA 2015 recommendation,8 Health Canada announced less restrictive guideline limits for 5G
technologies held close to the body (localized limits), in a webpage posting. 9 Health Canada refers to the
revised limits as a “Complement to Safety Code 6”. Part of the posting included an abstract from a document
with an “analysis” and rationale for these revised limits but there is no link to the full document.
A member of EHA-MB obtained it through a request to Health Canada.
On page 32 of the “analysis” document10 Health Canada states:
“No human studies were identified that assessed endpoints such as cancer,
ocular effects, reproductive system effects, cognitive effects, impacts on the immune
system, non-specific symptoms or any other adverse health outcomes in response to
exposure to RFEMF in the 6-300 GHz frequency range.”

In effect, limits for radiofrequency radiation emissions by 5G technologies held close to the body were loosened,
despite lack of any safety testing for health outcomes such as cancer.

In effect, limits for radiofrequency radiation emissions by 5G technologies held close to the body were loosened,
despite lack of any safety testing for health outcomes such as cancer.

The loosening of the limits was based on 10 human studies; there were fewer than 100 subjects in total, most of
the literature was more than 10 years old, and the brief exposures (from several seconds to 30 minutes) covered
only a few frequencies. The studies were published in 1960 (1), 1997 (1), 1999 (1), 2000 (1), 2002 (1), 2003 (2),
2004 (1), 2005 (1) and 2017 (1). A total of six frequencies were tested (it is well documented in scientific
literature that different frequencies can exert different effects) and no combinations with other relevant
frequencies were tested (in real-life conditions 5G technologies do not function on only one frequency).
Concerns about adverse health effects of 5G radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF) have been
expressed by scientists worldwide.
Two examples:
1. Declaration to officials of the European Commission demanding a moratorium on 5G proliferation.
"We the undersigned, more than 180 scientists and doctors from 35 countries, recommend a moratorium
on the roll-out of the fifth generation, 5G, for telecommunication until potential hazards for human
health and the environment have been fully investigated by scientists independent from industry. 5G
will substantially increase exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF) on top of the 2G,
3G, 4G, Wi-Fi, etc. for telecommunications already in place. RF-EMF has been proven to be harmful for
humans and the environment."
As of July 4, 2024, 266 EMF scientists from 44 nations and 15 Supporting Scientists from 11 nations have signed
the Appeal.
The press release, the declaration and a list of signatories can be found at http://www.5gappeal.eu
This and other appeals are available on a website by Dr. Joel Moskowitz, Director, School of Public Health,
University of California Berkeley. 11
2. Declaration that current standards are not protective of human health
Canadian and international scientists have stated that current guidelines/standards such as Health Canada's
Safety Code 6 are not adequate and precautionary measures are warranted.
 Statement signed by over 220 scientists from 41 nations, who have published peer-reviewed papers on the
biological or health effects of non-ionizing radiation:
“These findings justify our appeal to the United Nations (UN) and, all member States in the world, to encourage
the World Health Organization (WHO) to exert strong leadership in fostering the development of more protective
EMF guidelines, encouraging precautionary measures, and educating the public about health risks, particularly
risk to children and fetal development. By not taking action, the WHO is failing to fulfill its role as the preeminent
international public health agency." 12
The Government of Canada has raised billions of dollars13 within the last few years selling and leasing
radiofrequencies for telecommunications; however, none of this is going to high quality studies on cancer and
other health outcomes (only consequences of short-term over-heating). We know from a request from the
Parliamentary Library by a sitting Member of Parliament that as of April 2020, Health Canada had conducted no
laboratory or epidemiological cancer-related studies on any frequencies covered by Safety Code 6 or the
“Complement” to Safety Code 6. Recent searches by our members of PubMed14 and EMF Portal,15 databases
routinely used by Health Canada, did not find any original cancer-related research conducted by Health Canada
on frequencies above 6 GHz.
The warnings are here that exposure to radiofrequency radiation at ambient levels under certain conditions
causes cancer, and there are significant knowledge gaps in the setting of guidelines for Canadians. Lack of
evidence is not proof of safety. It is the position of EHA-MB that proactive, precautionary measures can be taken
for the prevention of cancer with regard to exposure to 5G and other wireless technologies. We urge HESA not
to delay investigating this issue further. We are especially concerned about children who are particularly
vulnerable because of their sensitive development and growing bodies, being immersed in this possible
carcinogenic agent not experienced by previous generations.

We are especially concerned about children who are particularly
vulnerable because of their sensitive development and growing bodies, being immersed in this possible
carcinogenic agent not experienced by previous generations.

EHA-MB recommends that HESA:
1. Undertake a study, with witness testimony, to review the scientific evidence and knowledge gaps on
5G frequencies of 6 GHz to 300 GHz with the goal of updating the “Complement to Safety Code 6”;
and
2. Provide recommendations on epidemiological and laboratory studies to be conducted by Health
Canada and by scientists who are independent of industry influence.
Ideally, roll-out of 5G technologies should be suspended until studies are conducted, upon which to base
appropriate guidelines. Given that this is highly unlikely, at the least, robust epidemiological and laboratory
studies should be conducted. Meanwhile, Canadians need to be informed about the potential hazards of
exposure to this possibly carcinogenic agent. Recommendations regarding awareness programs were made by
HESA in 201016 and in 2015.17 A future HESA study should include reviewing those recommendations and
assessing progress implementing them.

I would appreciate an invitation to present to the HESA Cancer Treatment and Prevention study to elaborate and
respond to questions on the material I have presented above.

Submission to Parliament of Canada House of Commons Standing Committee on Health (HESA),
RF-EMR is an Environmental co-factor of Childhood Cancers
Oct. 12, 2024
The national non-profit Canadian Educators for Safe Technology (CE4ST) respectfully submits, there is
mounting evidence and concern that radiofrequency electromagnetic radiation (RF-EMR) represents a
serious environmental contributor to cancer requiring recognition, rigorous independent assessment, and
public health attention to encourage families to practice safe tech when using wireless (e.g., RF-EMR
microwave frequency) technology.
I’m a retired teacher and Director of CE4ST. We work with families of children, and teachers, injured by
wireless RF-EMR. Children and school staff currently suffer chronic or debilitating adverse effects, including
cancers, caused by continuous and cumulative RF-EMR in schools, playgrounds, and daycares. It is
unnecessary to expose children to harmful radiation; safer wired technologies exist.
Cancer prevention is far more effective and humane, and less costly for children, families, and society than
treatment. While early detection has value, reduction of toxic exposures at homes and school environments
should be paramount.
We are deeply concerned that the escalating use of wireless devices and infrastructure (cell towers and
antennas) intensifies RF-EMR exposures in educational settings. A substantial body of scientific evidence
shows RF-EMR can cause biological effects linked to serious health issues, including cancers.
Although the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified
RF radiation as a possible carcinogen (Group 2B) in 2011, a cancer epidemiology update demonstrates a
clearer link between electromagnetic radiation and cancer.1
Adverse effects of wireless exposures are becoming globally recognized in medical, scientific, and legal
practices. Cell tower induced cancer clusters have posed costly consequences for children, young families,
and communities. Cell tower proximity to daycares, schools, playgrounds, or splashpads can pose a
serious threat to students. In Ripon, California, 12 students and staff plus 100 neighbours battled cancer
within 500 meters of a monopole before it was removed from school property. Eight students and four
teachers were diagnosed with breast, kidney, brain, or liver cancers. One student, Mason, had seven years

One student, Mason, had seven years

of surgeries and treatments that resulted in brain necrosis, nerve pain and paralysis, bone degradation,
loss of hearing, loss of vision; and the brain and spine cancers continued to return.2 Mason passed 7/18/24.
https://www.facebook.com/100057482588129/videos/685540363143983
Numerous studies highlight cancer risks associated with low-intensity wireless radiation, with Levitt and
Lai’s review (2010) highlighting increased cancer risk, among other biological effects.3 Several studies
report higher incidences of cancer in populations living near mobile phone base stations and in higher RFEMR exposure areas. Studies show significant increases in cancer within 500 meters of cell towers.4 An
Israeli study found the risk of cancer quadrupled among people living within 350 meters and a 10-year
Municipal Health Study in Brazil showed increased cancer mortality.5
Wireless devices are increasing, without rigorous pre-market testing. Pregnant women use microwaveemitting devices on their belly to monitor fetal growth. Baby monitors emit microwaves. Microwaveequipped diapers alert parents when their baby wets. 5G antennas are installed too close to schools and
children’s bedroom windows. Last year 18 Toronto teachers refused work due to cell tower-induced
injuries. https://preventcancernow.ca/educators-refusing-work-aside-powerful-cell-tower-north-york-toronto/
Manufacturers must be incentivized to create safer cell phones: Children often use cell phones against
their head, place the phone under their pillow or in a pocket or bra, stream microwave frequency with
devices against their abdomen and gonads. Colorectal cancer has increased in those 20 to 44 years of
age. Recently Brenner et al. report increasing colorectal cancer in males and females younger than 50
years, “It appears that primary prevention should be the highest priority to reduce the number of younger
adults developing [colorectal cancer] in the future.”6,7
Research indicates that federal regulations inadequately protect health,8,9 and cumulative lifetime
exposures to RF-EMR need consideration (e.g., Balmori's (2022) study, which links cell tower radiation to
cancer). Evidence supporting this concern includes a landmark review by Levitt and Lai (2010), which
examined biological effects of low-intensity wireless radiation, including increased cancer risk, cellular
damage, and genetic mutations.7
Wireless RF-EMR pollutants disproportionately impact children due to their rapid development and
they may be especially vulnerable to environmental factors that increase their risk of cancers. According to
leading epidemiologists and toxicologists, RF-EMR penetrates proportionally deeper into children’s critical
brain regions and developing nervous system.10,11 Children are smaller, have thinner skulls, higherconductivity tissues,10 and more active stem cells that are sensitive to RF-EMR.8 Their rapidly dividing cells
make them more susceptible to the potential carcinogenic effects of RF-EMR. Children will receive
significantly more cumulative lifetime exposure than today’s adults.12,13
Health Canada (HC) reminds cell phone users of practical measures they can take to reduce RF exposure
and encourages parents to reduce children's RF exposure from cell phones, since children “are typically
more sensitive to a variety of environmental agents.” HC offered “Practical Advice on safe Cell Phone Use”
to reduce RF exposures (Oct. 4, 2011). This is contradicted by other statements regarding lack of evidence.

This is contradicted by other statements regarding lack of evidence.

It is not ethical to await conclusive proof of harms before shifting to safer options. An international
group of lawyers, physicians, physicists, epidemiologists, and other children’s health experts endorsed an
International Declaration intended to raise public awareness of fundamental rights of children, who are not
adequately being protected. This Declaration calls on authorities to apply legal principles to protect children
from wireless pollutants: https://www.thechildrensdeclaration.org/.14
The NRC-associated Canadian Committee on Indoor Air Quality published Indoor Environmental Quality
(IEQ) and Productivity in Workplaces/Achievement in Schools (Module 14). This report recommends
essential research topics, focusing on effects on biochemistry, membrane permeability, DNA, human
reproduction, early development, chronic conditions, and CANCER “that occur at commonly encountered
radiofrequency exposure levels.” Additionally, the report recommends implementing Best Practices such as

Brief to the Standing Committee on Health
Study: Treatment and Prevention of Cancer
Dear Members of the Standing Committee on Health,
Thank you for conducting this study.
This brief refers to decades of inequity in Canada regarding access to highly specialized brain
radiation treatments. Depending on their postal code, Canadians are offered or denied access to
specialized brain radiation.
In 2002, Canadian Premiers agreed on equitable access to specialized treatments performed in
centres of excellence. BC Standing Committee on Health issued the report “Patients First 2002:
The Path to Reform” (1). It states:
Sites of Excellence For High Risk - Low Volume Surgery
In 2002, the Premiers of the provinces agreed to cooperate on consolidating high-risk, low
volume surgery in a few designated centres across the country. The decision came from
increasing research evidence, including the coroner inquest into the deaths of 12 children in
Winnipeg’s pediatric cardiac surgery program, that large population densities are needed to
safely deliver rare, high-risk surgery. Pediatric cardiac surgery, rarer organ transplants, and
gamma knife radiation neurosurgery are examples of the advanced techniques that require
specialized equipment and a highly experienced and trained team of health care providers. They
should therefore be concentrated in a few centres in Canada.
Details of the Sites of Excellence for low volume surgery are still being worked out. B.C. will
likely be a centre for one or two of the specialized surgeries, such as pediatric cardiac surgery,
where we have established a safe and reliable track record. Patients needing services not
performed here would be sent out of province to the nearest sites of excellence location, such
as Edmonton or Toronto. The Premiers all agree that this coordinated plan will build on
established expertise and will result in saved lives, better patient care and a wiser, more focused
use of limited resources.”
BC is not a centre of excellence for gamma knife and dishonors the Premiers’ agreement.
For the same evidence, same diagnosis and prognosis, similar taxation and provincial GDP, per
capita Health Transfer, a patient in BC is denied access to gamma knife, while the same patient
in another province receives gamma knife treatment with urgency and compassion, in the public
system. This situation may occur in other jurisdictions, however as a BC resident, I am aware of
the BC status only.

This situation may occur in other jurisdictions, however as a BC resident, I am aware of
the BC status only.

Gamma knife was invented in the 1960s, by Professor Lars Leksell, neurosurgeon at Karolinska
Institute in Stockholm. He emphasized “The tools used by the surgeon must be adapted to the
task and where the human brain is concerned, they cannot be too refined”.
Gamma knife provides non-invasive focal radiation for malignant and non-malignant brain
conditions, while sparing precious normal brain tissue.
The first Canadian gamma knife unit had been installed in Manitoba in 2003 (2). Today, gamma
knife units operate in Alberta, Quebec, and Ontario. All centres of excellence receive patients
from other provinces and territories, in the true spirit of federalism. However, not all Canadians
needing treatment are referred to gamma knife centres of excellence.
As Canadians, we are proud of the brain centre in Edmonton (3), which includes a gamma knife
unit. We are proud of scientists at Sunnybrook in Toronto that have championed specialized
radiation technologies like gamma knife for brain treatments (4). It is humbling to learn about the
meticulous work conducted by oncologists at Sunnybrook in treating patients with brain
conditions and always doing the right thing (5).
By contrast, BC employs radiation machines called linear accelerators (linacs), used for
irradiating body and brain. They are not specialized machines and come from a single supplier.
Similar Canadian tertiary centres use multiple suppliers for radiation machines. Disclosure
statements show BC directors receive grants from the single supplier and select linear
accelerators for BC Cancer. This situation erodes the public trust.
Focal treatment to brain is rarely employed in BC, because of technicalities and limitations of the
existing linacs, as per BC Cancer. Statistics show that only about 1% or less of the yearly
radiation courses in BC are focal radiation to brain (stereotactic radio surgery - SRS). However,
20%-40% of patients with cancer develop brain metastases during their lifetime.
Sadly, BC families are devastated to learn that specialized brain radiation is forbidden by their
province. Policies for brain radiation are revealed to patients as they experience illness.
However, accountability requires that accurate information be widely available. In BC one would
spend years to uncover practices, policies, statistics, research. Patients with brain metastases do
not have the luxury of time. They are in a vulnerable position and experience a harmful
imbalance of power. Patients’ only right is to suffer and die in silence, under the eyes of their
loved ones. BC leaders and members of legislature and parliament refuse dialogue with BC
citizens rising these issues.
Unwritten policies in BC prohibit cancer patients to access gamma knife in Canada and force
them out of country for self pay treatment and into financial toxicity for generations. Patients are
told “we do not pay for gamma knife, it has to be self pay”.
The written policy states that radiation treatments out of province will be approved only if a
clinically equivalent treatment cannot be performed by BC Cancer. However, without specialized
brain equipment, BC Cancer do not offer clinical equivalence.

However, without specialized
brain equipment, BC Cancer do not offer clinical equivalence.

Moreover, existing lengthy pre-authorization processes ending in denials cause irreversible harm
via progression in the brain. Timely access to brain treatment is essential for survival.
According to BC Cancer, five patients are sent yearly for gamma knife treatment in other
provinces (6). Hundreds with same characteristics are denied access to gamma knife.
Simultaneously, Toronto’s Sunnybrook treat seven hundred patients yearly for intracranial
metastatic disease (5), on gamma knife specialized equipment. Please note that Ontario operates
multiple gamma knife units.
In BC between 1996-2016 patients with brain metastases from lung cancer had a median time of
3.5 months from the first brain radiation therapy to death (7). Outcomes in BC are directly
related to the lack of specialized brain treatment and delayed diagnosis. The treatment of choice
in BC is whole brain radiation, an invasive treatment used to palliate symptoms in poor
prognosis patients, with short term effectiveness, irreversible neurotoxicity, risk of dementia, and
few indications today. It was first mentioned circa 1931 (8).
Doctors in BC advise patients to move out of province to obtain gamma knife radiation. Doctors’
referrals for gamma knife are ignored by directors. Doctors’ professional judgement is
disregarded. They are prevented from helping patients and face moral injuries.
The BC ten years cancer plan 2023 contains no reference to specialized brain radiation in or out
the province. Accordingly, the plan in BC is to continue denying life improving, life extending
specialized brain radiation.
A clinical trial offering gamma knife treatment exists in Canada (9), but is a missed opportunity
for BC people because they are not informed of it. A trial like this, for complex presentations, is
very rare, if not unique in the world. Through this research, scientists at Sunnybrook recognize
the moral status of patients with brain metastases. They innovate, advance the field, and honor
the human brain, the only source of human experience.
Several thousand Canadians benefit from gamma knife treatment each year (10).
Denied access to specialized brain treatment is a systemic issue in BC and possibly in other
jurisdictions. It is therefore a matter of public interest. Healthcare in Canada is a shared
responsibility between all levels of government. The autonomy offered to provinces and
territories in managing their individual healthcare systems should have never been used as a free
pass to abandon and harm vulnerable cancer patients by denying them equal access to health
services available in their own country.
The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires that state parties shall
prevent discriminatory denial of health services on the basis of disability. When we deny access
to gamma knife we place Canada in violation of the Convention.
The Convention is reflected in human rights legislation in Canada.
The prohibition of access to specialized brain radiation is a tragedy happening right here in
Canada, not in a underdeveloped corner of the world, and we allowed it for very long.

The prohibition of access to specialized brain radiation is a tragedy happening right here in
Canada, not in a underdeveloped corner of the world, and we allowed it for very long.

People are degraded to second class citizens, undeserving and inferior to Canadians with access
to specialized brain radiation in the public system.
The Government of Canada state that “CHT payments are made on an equal per capita basis to
provide comparable treatment for all Canadians, regardless of where they live”. In BC, CHT and
provincial funds are not allocated to specialized intracranial treatment in centres of excellence.
Patients contributed to funds through taxation but are denied access to specialized treatment, in
time of need.
The denial of access to gamma knife relates to an arbitrary exclusion from the out-of-province
program for a group of vulnerable patients that can’t be treated in BC because of lack of
specialized equipment. The exclusion is arbitrary because it undercuts the purpose of the
program, to offer treatment available in Canada when the local equipment cannot yield
comparable treatment. This exclusion is inconsistent with the principle of equality. The
distinction placed on BC patients with brain disease denies them equal human worth and dignity.
BC allows for the perpetuation of pre-existing disadvantage through unequal treatment.
Patients who experienced abandonment in Canada should receive compensation.
Recommendation:
Canada shall guarantee equal access to treatments in centres of excellence, with a referral
from a physician and without pre-authorization from their home province.
Canada shall restore the rights and dignity of Canadians who were denied access to
specialized brain radiation out-of-province and provide redress.
Thank you for your consideration.

Health Canada’s Safety Code 62 sets out guidelines for the human exposure limits for wireless radiation
such as from cell phones, cell towers and Wi-Fi. Safety Code 6 was revised in 2015, 2013 and 2009 and is
overdue for an update.
Radiofrequency/microwave/Wi-Fi radiation was classified as a Group 2B, possible human carcinogen in 2011
by the International Agency for Research on Cancer.3
Much evidence has accumulated since 2015 indicating harms from these types of emissions under
“non-thermal” conditions (that do not over-heat tissues), well below Safety Code 6 limits. Particularly
relevant are high-quality animal studies conducted in the USA4 5 6 and in Italy7 showing that wireless
radiation is carcinogenic. There is also additional evidence from studies on people 8 9 10 11 12 13 14 that must
be incorporated into Safety Code 6 limits for guidelines to be truly protective.

This is urgent because of rapidly increasing levels of radiofrequency radiation from the ongoing rollout of
tens of thousands of cell network antennas across Canada, and because vulnerable populations such as
children are being exposed from uses of wireless devices in homes, schools and elsewhere, at
unprecedented levels.

Cancer treatment and prevention
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
September 13, 2024 - updated: October 8, 2024
Prevent Cancer Now (PCN) respectfully submits that primary cancer prevention, addressing root
contributors to the disease process, merits the highest priority, to prevent cancer before it starts.
Screening is secondary prevention, hopefully averting the worst with earlier treatment.
We are scientists, medical experts and other volunteers, focusing diverse knowledge of environmental
health, medicine, chemistry and scientific approaches on cancer. Here, we summarize why and how to
“make least-toxic the norm” for cancer prevention.
When PCN was established in 2007, heart disease was Canada’s #1 cause of death. Today, more
Canadians die from cancer than any other single cause, and aggressive cancers are developing everearlier in life. Costs associated with screening, diagnoses, treatment and follow-up are unsustainable;
lost wages are substantial; and patients’ and families’ pain and losses must not be under-estimated.
Cancer trends
We join many scientists stressing urgency to identify and address underlying cancer risk factors. While
long-term Canadian data is lacking, we know that similar to American data, cancer diagnoses and deaths
are increasing, particularly at younger ages.1,2 Cancer incidence is also increasing in younger Canadians,3
with the highest rates among White and Indigenous populations.
•
Liver and intrahepatic bile duct cancer, kidney cancer, melanoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma are
increasing in younger Canadians.4
•
Colorectal cancer has increased in those 20 to 44 years of age.5 Recently, with colorectal cancer
rates increasing in both females and males younger than 50 years, Brenner et al. stated, “[I]t appears
that primary prevention should be the highest priority to reduce the number of younger adults
developing [colorectal cancer] in the future.”6
Why are cancers increasing at younger ages?
Recent cancer trends relate directly to harmful exposures. Health Canada and major cancer
organizations offer limited prevention advice, addressing adiposity, activity, dietary choices, alcohol,
smoking, sun protection, radon, inhaled (but not ingested) asbestos, and occupational health and safety.
For example, some chemicals affect metabolism, and signals of hunger and satiety, resulting in obesity.7
These “obesogens”7 or endocrine disruptors8 in plastics, pesticides and numerous everyday products
affect or mimic hormones and drive cancers.8 High body mass and associated cancers are symptoms of
endocrine disruption, that hinder diet and lifestyle efforts, in part resulting in “blaming the victim”.7
Multiple factors in concert cause cancers, early deaths, and poorer quality of life.9 Across Canada,
increasing toxic exposures are contributing to cancers, such as pesticides,10 plastics and additives,11
proximity to wastes,12 pollution from resource extraction and industries,13,14 and electromagnetic
radiation.15,16
