Inadequacy of regulatory procedures
Rates of cancer are lower among Immigrants,3 indicating the elevated carcinogenicity associated with life
in Canada, and inadequacies of current regulatory processes.
While a limited number of “complete carcinogen” chemicals are recognized under the Canadian
Environmental Protection Act, and pesticides under the Pest Control Products Act, these are a small
subset of long-known toxic substances. Regulatory processes are not responsive to emerging research,
and use outdated frameworks that ignore multiplicity of effects of environmental agents. Scientific
hazard and risk assessments do not recognize contributors to cancer such as inflammation, intestinal
distress, endocrine disruption, and genetic damage, that should necessitate prompt actions.17
PCN has observed shortcomings in pesticides regulation, as we follow peer-reviewed science and have
inspected confidential test data. Toxicities in regulatory animal studies (e.g., bladder, brain,
gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver, thyroid, prostate, ovaries and uterus) may be omitted or dismissed,
even when an observed effect is increasing in humans. For example, dysbiosis was observed in animal
studies of glyphosate—an omnipresent herbicide that impacts microbial populations. The Pest
Management Regulatory Agency (PMRA) deemed this not “adverse.” Nevertheless, dysbiosis can lead to
inflammatory bowel disease18,19 (IBD, increasing in Canadian children at 7% per year 20) and colorectal
cancer (CRC, increasing at a similar rate in Canadian adolescents and young adults21)—a trend consistent
with increasing use of glyphosate.
PMRA relies on the adequacy of data from proponents. During examination of confidential test data and
followup, PCN discovered that PMRA accepts unusable images of large datasets rather than requiring
spreadsheets. Thus, Health Canada did not, and could not confirm proponents’ favourable conclusions,
yet registered the pesticide. This systemic abdication throws into doubt present registrations. PMRA
addressed re-analyzable data in recent proposed regulatory amendments, but solutions are not in place.
Pesticides remain registered until eventually re-evaluated.
Multi- and inter-generational effects
Endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) interfere with hormone-mediated effects, increasing cancer risks
in exposed populations. As well, exposures of previous generations can affect eggs and sperm, change
genetic expression in the foetus and offspring, and cause cancers.22,23 For example, breast cancer is
caused by the endocrine-disrupting insecticide dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane (DDT), is more likely in
daughters, and may be more likely in granddaughters of women exposed to DDT.24
A distinct hypothesis, submitted by Michael Gilbertson to this study,25 is that chemicals may affect eggs
(oocytes) maturing in the ovary, and initiate pre-conception, eventual adverse outcomes in the
offspring. The birth cohort (up to early 60 years of age) following introduction of the birth-control pill is
experiencing increased cancers, and this was delayed where the Pill was introduced later. This
mechanism could itself increase cancers, and might also sensitize many people to effects of other
harmful exposures, discussed below. Effectively, a heavy thumb of hormone-active substances may be
tipping the scales towards developing cancers, with dire implications for future generations.

Effectively, a heavy thumb of hormone-active substances may be
tipping the scales towards developing cancers, with dire implications for future generations.

Electromagnetic fields
Electromagnetic fields (EMFs) have biological effects, and some frequencies can cause cancer. For
example, ultraviolet light causes sunburn and skin cancer,26 and artificial light affects circadian rhythm,
melatonin and sleep (potentially affecting cancer development and treatment).27,28
Electrification and wireless communications introduced powerline and pulsed radiofrequency radiation
(RFR) into lower frequency, previously dark regions of the spectrum. Decades of scientific research and
hundreds of peer-reviewed studies (including sophisticated modelling, laboratory biology, and studies of
humans and wildlife) demonstrate effects on children, and physiological changes and pathologies,
including cancers.29 These exposures are increasing rapidly, despite availability of inherently safer
options.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer found in 2013 that RFR was a 2B “possibly carcinogenic
to humans” hazard, based on human epidemiology.30 This certainty has been strengthened with large
animal studies using signals comparable to WiFi,31 and in rats32 and mice33 with exposures comparable to
cellphones.34 Recent reviews summarize evidence of adverse effects on human health35 and
carcinogenicity.36
Environmental effects of ambient RFR37 include impairing animals’ navigation,38 disrupting frog
reproduction,39 compromising health of trees and other vegetation,40 and harming insects.41,42 A 2020
Environment and Climate Change Canada review supported calls for research and precaution for biota.43
Environmental justice—cancer affecting equity denied populations
Cancer disproportionately affects communities impacted by industrial emissions, with contaminated
environments, air, water and food. Recent passage of Bill C-226, to develop a national strategy to assess,
prevent and address environmental racism and to advance environmental justice,44 recognizes
responsibilities and opens opportunities for redress. An Indigenous-led health study was announced for
residents of Fort Chipewyan downstream of bitumen extraction, who harvested deformed fish from the
Athabasca River and suffer disproportionate numbers of cancers.45 Many communities are surrounded
by or downstream from industries (e.g., Aamjinaang, Sarnia), or impacted by persistent carcinogenic
pollutants from resource extraction, the Distant Early Warning system (DEW line), or mercury emerging
from old pulp and paper mills, lands flooded for hydro-electric developments or melting tundra.
Climate
Atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations are rising, as are petrochemical emissions including organic
pollutants, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide, oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, and heavy metals.
Wildfires from warming-caused droughts release particulates (e.g., PM2.5) laced with arsenic and heavy
metals. These toxicants cause cancers, diseases of the lungs and other organs, and undermine
innumerable life forms with air and surface water pollution. Indeed, this affects the life trajectory of
children—even those yet to be conceived.
Healthy food and water are at risk from heat waves and droughts. Resilient, sustainable organic
agriculture, fostering biodiversity, must be central to adaptation and ongoing healthy food supplies.
Most burning of fossil fuels must halt, within a decade. On our current trajectory, within 15 years a
climate tipping point could bring further irreversible, rapid warming, risking a global catastrophe. A war
footing is needed, to blunt the climate crisis, with rapid use and emission reductions, and worldwide
deployment of renewable energy technologies. Expensive delays and distractions from available,
effective solutions include nuclear power and carbon capture.

Expensive delays and distractions from available,
effective solutions include nuclear power and carbon capture.

Next Steps
The solution to environmental exposures linked to cancer is to restrict substances and technologies to
safest options, rather than permitting all-comers until belatedly proven harmful.
Substitution is the framework to identify least-toxic, lowest impact, most effective and efficient options:
-
to carry out processes, to create, manufacture, distribute and use products; and
-
to extend and manage product “end of life”.
Clear problem definition and focus on least-toxic solutions are necessary to cut through complexity.
“Essentiality”—a misappropriated concept that should be applied to solutions
One strategy of industries and proponents, to maintain carcinogens on the market, is to label substances
and technologies “essential.” Integral to this strategy is to ignore, dispute and minimize safer
alternatives. Thus, various technologies, pesticides, flame retardants, water proofing and plastics-related
substances, have remained available for extended periods, without rigorous scrutiny and action on
potential substitutes (including doing without—i.e., the “null alternative”).
The numbers and volumes of pesticides in use continue to mount, despite Canada’s commitment to
halve pesticides risks by 2030 to protect biodiversity. The magnitude of necessary data makes rigorous
assessment impossible. “Lack of proof of harm,” when proof is not feasible in a timely fashion, is
translating into continued manufacturing, use and dispersal of toxic substances.
Essentiality should be the path to least-toxic solutions. Use of materials that inherently resist flame or
water, farming organically, and many other less-toxic options exist. The existence of a preferable solution
should be grounds to “ban the bad” and to require better.
Measuring what we propose to manage. Early detection and investigation of environmentally linked
diseases requires relevant health data, exposure data, and the means to link the two. The CANUE
(Canadian Urban Environments) research program (disbanded when five-year funding expired)
developed geospatial methodologies. Potential exposure data sources include personal and occupational
histories, and air, water and food quality monitoring programs. Conveniently, related data is essential to
track international commitments regarding climate, biodiversity and pollution; e.g., plastics. Medical
records may be expanded to include exposure data (e.g., diet), and/or combined with local or regional
pollution data.
Getting on-track, with best choices. When an agent has adverse characteristics and is not essential, or
inherently safer options are available, it is not ethical or practical to delay shifting to safer options. This is
the essence of the Precautionary Principle,46 operationalized by the Substitution Principle.47 Health
Canada’s standard of “consistent, convincing evidence” regarding plausible, probable harms before
taking action (e.g., as applied to drinking asbestos), is not aligned with the Precautionary Principle.
Focusing on least-toxic approaches, and essential ends,
could prevent cancer, improve health and inform public safety

Focusing on least-toxic approaches, and essential ends,
could prevent cancer, improve health and inform public safety

Conclusion: Solutions for cancer prevention
In the search for “the cure,” the answer to cancer is prevention. Cancers are increasing in younger
Canadians, and while survival statistics are improving, cancer care is increasingly costly financially, and to
families and society. Progress may be made on some specifics such as cigarettes, but evident mounting
disease in younger generations requires attention and actions. Many cancer-focused organizations, such
as CAREX and the Canadian Cancer Society, advance a narrower scope regarding contributors to cancer.
Neither do they, nor the government of Canada, apply independent science.
Cancer prevention could be greatly advanced by mandating clearly safer choices when there is emerging,
credible evidence linking certain common exposures with adverse health effects. PCN has a unique,
highly-informed expert perspective that we hope will be of assistance to the Committee. Please do not
hesitate to reach out for further information and discussion.

Cancer Action Now’s Recommendations to the Standing Committee on Health on the
Study on Prevention and Treatment of Cancer
Cancer remains the leading cause of death in Canada. An estimated 2 in 5 people living in
Canada will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime and about 1 in 4 will die from cancer. In
2024, 247,100 people living in Canada are estimated to be diagnosed.1 With an ageing
population, the number of people diagnosed with cancer and cancer mortality is projected to rise
significantly in the coming decades. While our health care system is pushed to the brink, people
living with cancer continue to face barriers at every step of their cancer journey.
The reality is people in Canada living with cancer are dying while they wait for care. Many are
faced with the impossible choice of putting food on the table or taking on significant debt as they
struggle to afford the out-of-pocket costs associated with a cancer diagnosis, such as, drugs
and treatments, medical transportation and accommodation and loss of pay due to inability to
work, among other costs. For underserved and equity-deserving populations in Canada, these
challenges are even greater.
CANA’s recommendations are intended to guide action that will promote better health and better
outcomes for all people living with cancer in Canada. We urge the Standing Committee on
Health to consider the issues presented here and incorporate our recommendations during your
discussion on the study on the treatment and prevention of cancer.
Ensure investments are made in measurable value-based patient outcomes in cancer.
This may be achieved through the implementation of the pan-Canadian cancer data strategy to
support the development of publicly available dashboards that regularly report on important
cancer care metrics, as well as strengthening pan-Canadian oncology federated data networks.
We cannot fix what we cannot measure. We do not know if the public dollars invested in our
care systems are having the desired impact unless we have data to measure that.
The pan-Canadian cancer data strategy outlines three areas for investment and focus:
•
Increase the efficiency and ease of data access to cancer data that is currently collected,
while improving the timeliness of data capture and availability, and build on guidelines
and standards, including data quality indicators.
•
Modernize and sustain infrastructure for cancer data interoperability, making diagnostic
and treatment data, primary care data and genomic data accessible and linkable.
•
Fill gaps that exist in current data collection, specifically, investments in data collection
on social determinants of health, patient-reported outcomes and experience,
survivorship, palliative and end-of-life care.

Having better data will help to improve cancer prevention, access to care and outcomes –
making cancer care in Canada better and more equitable – because it will focus cancer
research and inform policy decisions.
Canada’s care systems continue to lag in their ability to quickly and rapidly use existing
research and evidence to improve the health of the populations they serve, in ways that are
affordable, patient centered, financially sustainable, and equitable. To add to this challenge, our
care systems are pushed to the brink and siloed.
Strengthening cancer data collection, access and linkages will lead to a learning health system
that incorporates research within cancer care delivery, informed by quality improvement and
care, to speed up evidence use and impact.
Establish the practice of ensuring an equity lens is applied to all federal decisions related
to cancer care funding.
With cancer on the rise in Canada, the Canadian government must ensure an equitable
approach is taken any time decisions are made in relation to cancer care. Greater systematic
equity requires a better understanding of socio-economic barriers faced by all segments of
Canadian society.
During this time of economic uncertainty, with affordability top of mind for many Canadians, a
cancer diagnosis only adds additional financial pressure. A 2024 study shows cancer costs –
including medication, transportation to and from appointments, and caregiver expenses – can
range from an average of $253 to as much as $550 per month.2 The costs relating to cancer in
Canada such as direct healthcare system costs and out-of-pocket expenses was an estimated
$26.2 billion in 2021 with patients and their families being responsible for 30% of these costs.3
The added cost of a cancer diagnosis leaves some patients with no choice but to go without the
care and treatments they need.
With the ongoing affordability crisis, Canadians should not have to manage both a cancer
diagnosis and the costs associated with cancer treatment.
For individuals living in rural and remote communities, access to healthcare is an ongoing issue,
especially for those living with life-threatening conditions such as cancer. People in rural in
remote areas are more likely to die from cancer,4 as a consequence of having to travel to

Inequality relating to gender and cancer is an increasingly highlighted issue in Canada.
Currently, government policy around early detection is a barrier for women. A recent study
shows how rates of breast cancer in women under the age of 50 are rising in Canada due to
women being diagnosed at later stages, when the cancer is more aggressive. This worrying
phenomenon is occurring because women not being regularly screened. 6 There is a clear
barrier around diagnosis and treatment of Canada among women and the government must
apply an equity lens when allocating funding.
Understanding the financial burden associated with a cancer diagnosis and the impact on
groups facing barriers such as individuals living in rural and remote communities, and racialized
groups and gender inequality is critical. This is why we are asking the federal government to
apply an equity lens to all decision making for funding cancer care in Canada and support a
better understanding of the current inequities that exist.
Reduce the cost of cancer drugs, foster a research ecosystem of innovation, and
continue to provide safeguards to existing access to drugs that are already available to
patients
On average, Canadians wait two years for access to new medicines through public drug plans
following drug approval from Health Canada. This is double the average time reported in several
other high-income OECD countries. According to a report from the Conference Board of Canada
in 2022, it took a minimum of 28 months for life-saving treatments and drugs to reach 50 per
cent of public plan beneficiaries.
People in Canada living with cancer are waiting for far too long to get the treatments they need.
We need action to streamline processes and explore an expedited review and approval pathway
for novel and innovative cancer treatments. The Government of Canada can also play a key role
in supporting provinces and territories in ensuring equitable access to these treatments for
people in Canada living with cancer.
Additionally, as countries around the world accelerate their genome-based testing readiness,
Canada's health systems cannot afford to fall behind. Improved access to genomic testing can
ensure patients, care providers and the health system can benefit from where science and
innovation is today and where it is headed in the future. Ultimately, while provincial and territorial
governments need to address the gaps in their current infrastructure to foster an environment
for improved adoption and access to genome-based testing, the Government of Canada can
play a key role in supporting and driving this momentum.
Conclusion:

Conclusion:

Canadians participate in a lottery every time they have a brush with the cancer care system.
Addressing this inequity will require concerted action from federal, provincial and territorial
governments, informed by the experiences of health care providers across the cancer care
continuum, patients, caregivers, and equity-deserving groups that are navigating the cancer
care system in different parts of the country.
More silos will only make these challenges worse. The federal government working with
jurisdictions can tackle important priorities to improve cancer care in Canada, with particular
attention on strengthening cancer data systems, improving timeliness and access to treatments
and ensuring an equity lens is applied to all decision-making in cancer care.
Cancer Action Now encourages the Standing Committee on Health to consider these
recommendations during the Study on Treatment and Prevention of Cancer and we look forward
to working together to improve the lives of Canadians living with cancer.

Hypothesis on the Global Pandemic of the Early Onset of Cancers
Michael Gilbertson, PhD
Brief to the Parliament of Canada House of Commons Health Committee
3 September, 2024

Hypothesis on the Global Pandemic of the Early Onset of Cancers
Michael Gilbertson, PhD
Brief to the Parliament of Canada House of Commons Health Committee
3 September, 2024

I am Michael Gilbertson and I am an independent researcher. I have a Doctor of Philosophy degree in
occupational and environmental health from the University of Stirling, in Scotland. In 2004, I retired
after thirty-four years with the Government of Canada. In the 1970s, I was part of the organization
charged with implementing the Environmental Contaminants Act (1975) and I worked as the Early
Warning Coordinator identifying sentinel biological events from exposures to chemicals in the
environment. My final years of service were with the International Joint Commission where I specialized
in inferring the causal relations between the biological effects observed in fish, wildlife and human
populations exposed to persistent toxic chemicals in Great Lakes food webs.
Following my retirement from public service, I co-chaired the Halifax Project, an initiative involving 350
cancer scientists from 31 countries, half of whom were focused on the potential role of low-dose,
biologically disruptive, common environmental chemicals that might be acting in concert with one
another and contributing to various aspects of carcinogenesis. I was a co-author in this project and the
results of the work were published in a series of articles in a special issue of Carcinogenesis, a journal of
Oxford University Press, and which was also discussed in Environmental Health Perspectives, another
peer reviewed journal with a high impact factor.
In this brief to Parliament, I want to offer commentary on an important public health issue that has not
previously been resolved. During the past three decades, the incidence of and mortality from early
onset cancers has increased throughout the world (Zhao et al. 2023). For example, in Canada, the rate of
colorectal cancer in Canadians under 50 years of age has been increasing (O’Sullivan et al. 2020). In
contrast, the rates in those over 50 years of age have been decreasing, probably as a result of screening
with colonoscopies and associated polypectomy (Helsingen and Kalager 2022, World Health Organization
2023). Early-onset colorectal cancer is clinically, pathologically and molecularly distinct from traditional
colorectal cancer and is characteristically aggressive, diagnosed at a later stage and genomically different
(Yeo, et al. 2017). There is consensus that this sentinel event represents a birth cohort phenomenon
that corresponds to a sudden onset starting in 1960. There is further consensus that the cause is
unknown (De Vera et al. 2022, Gupta et al. 2024).
Based on the available evidence, the causal agent is likely a substance of modernity that is biologically
potent, was suddenly introduced on a global basis in 1960 and has been in increasing and continuous
use ever since. One agent of modernity that corresponds with all the known evidence, is the
contraceptive pill containing ethinyl estradiol and progestogen, and is here hypothesized as the causal
factor for the global pandemic of early onset colorectal cancer and possibly other cancers. The
contraceptive pill was approved in 1960 and sales of this biologically potent agent have continuously
increased globally (International Agency for Research on Cancer 1999).
The putative mechanism of action is likely not the traditional prenatal transplacental exposure of
embryos and fetuses to endocrine disrupting chemicals because the post conception uterus, by
definition, will likely be clear of the contraceptive. Instead, it is posited that the maternal exposure
results in transgenerational effects from exposure of oocytes, prior to fertilization by sperm to form a
zygote (Rizzi et al. 2023). For a long time, there have been concerns in assisted reproduction clinics
about the possibility of long term, delayed effects of exposures of oocytes to potent hormonal
substances used to stimulate oocyte maturation and ovulation (Hajj and Haaf. 2013, McGraw and
Trasler. 2013, Dvoran et al. 2022). The possibility that this effect may have occurred 64 years ago with
the 1960 introduction of the contraceptive pill, is a novel hypothesis for a new mode of injurious action.

The possibility that this effect may have occurred 64 years ago with
the 1960 introduction of the contraceptive pill, is a novel hypothesis for a new mode of injurious action.

Oocytes undergo profound epigenetic reorganization during oocyte maturation (Mani et al. 2020), with
removal and restoration of epigenetic markers. Thus, it is biologically plausible that a potent hormone
active compound, such as ethinyl estradiol and/or progestogens, designed to prevent ovulation could
alter the epigenetic organization of oocytes. With this exposure history, the resulting phenotype from
subsequent fertilization of the affected oocytes and development of the zygote, experiences a lifelong
predisposition to development of diseases and disorders, including cancers. By analogy, bisphenol A is
another potent estrogenic substance that has similar epigenetic effects on oocytes (Sabry et al. 2023)
thereby establishing coherence for the hypothesis with existing biological facts.
There is an interesting epidemiological “control” population in which the onset of the increase in the
early onset colorectal cancer was delayed by 20 years (Ullah et. 2018). Between 1935 and 1980, the Irish
Parliament proscribed all form of contraception (Kelly 2023). There is no doubt that the contraceptive
pill was smuggled into the Republic of Ireland in the 1960s and 1970s, but the large increase in early
onset of colorectal cancer did not occur in Ireland until it later manifested in the 1980s birth cohorts.
The annual percentage increase in colorectal cancer in these birth cohorts was 9.7 (di Martino et al.
2022) which was among the highest ever recorded.
The putative relationship between exposures of oocytes to potent hormonal compounds and the
subsequent development of early onset colorectal cancer may represent a novel model of carcinogenesis
that may be applicable not only to early onset of other cancers (Zhao et al. 2022, Rosenberg and
Miranda-Filho. 2024), but also to other biologically potent compounds of modernity. Of priority concern
are maternal cancer deaths in young families that annually leave more than a million children motherless
(Guida et al. 2022).
This hypothesis indicates that early onset colorectal cancer represents a challenge of modernity that has
been called a “wicked problem” and that has the following four distinct characteristics (Funtowicz and
Ravetz. 1993). First, despite this new hypothesis, there is uncertainty and there will be contestation
about the cause, and secondly, the stakes are very high because so many people, exposed during
preconception, were born in the past 64 years since the contraceptive pill was introduced. The third
wicked characteristic is that there will be disputes about what is signified and what to do about it
because of different value systems within and between different societies, and finally, there is a need for
urgent decisions to be made before new generations are conceived. For example, any suggestion that
the contraceptive pill containing ethinyl estradiol/ progestogen should be removed from the market to
safeguard the epigenetics of the next generation would be contested because, over the past six decades,
the pill has empowered women around the world to control their reproduction. I am bringing this issue
to the attention of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health because the alarming rise in the
incidence of, and mortality from, early onset colorectal cancers and other cancers, is an important
transgenerational public health issue that needs to be addressed.
Recommendations
Parliament should undertake the following immediate precautionary actions: -

Recommendations
Parliament should undertake the following immediate precautionary actions: -

1. Issue clear and comprehensive health warnings about the transgenerational risks associated
with the contraceptive pill while educating the public on the risks and benefits of contraceptive
methods;
2. Establish nationwide screening programs for those who have been exposed, focusing on early
detection of cancer;
3. Set up a compensation fund for those affected;
4. Reform regulatory processes to prevent similar incidents in the future;
5. Review and strengthen ethical guidelines for pharmaceutical research, development, and
approval processes;
6. Initiate a research program to investigate the variety of early onset cancers that have occurred as
a result of maternal consumption of the contraceptive pill
7. Launch long-term epidemiological studies to monitor the health outcomes of those exposed
8. Fund research to better understand the mechanisms behind the epigenetic effects, and public
health effects, of pharmaceuticals and other chemical products;
9. Inform the World Health Organization to ensure a coordinated global response and ensure
harmonization of pharmaceutical regulations across countries;

text:
Brief to the House of Commons Committee on Health from The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada

1. Introduction
The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada (GOC) is a professional organization dedicated to the improvement
of care for women with gynecologic cancers. Since our establishment in 1979, our mission has been to promote
excellence in the care of women with gynecologic cancers through education, research, and advocacy. We are
submitting this brief to support the Coalition for Responsible Healthcare Guidelines in their call for a review and
urgent remedy of the current guidelines on Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) screening. Our mission to improve the care
of women with or at risk of gynecologic cancer by raising standards of practice, encouraging ongoing research,
promoting innovation in prevention, care, and discovery, and advancing awareness. GOC also seeks to disseminate
knowledge to practitioners, patients and the general public on gynecologic cancer as well as cooperate with other
organizations committed to women’s health care, oncology, and related fields.

org: The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada
text:
GOC also seeks to disseminate
knowledge to practitioners, patients and the general public on gynecologic cancer as well as cooperate with other
organizations committed to women’s health care, oncology, and related fields.

2. Overview of the Issue
In 2013, the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care published cervical cancer screening guidelines that
stated the evidence supporting HPV testing as the primary method of cervical screening was not robust and required
further analysis. This was despite the preliminary results of our own Canadian HPV FOCAL trial, the largest North
American trial, were published 3 years previous that supported HPV testing and had improved cost-effectiveness and
outcomes compared to standard PAP screening. Ongoing results from this trial and other international trials
published over the following 5 years continued to strongly support HPV testing as the primary, cost-effective method
of cervical cancer screening. There were repeated calls from Canadian experts to push for Canada to change to HPV
testing but as of early 2024, the Canadian Task Force on Preventative Health Care guideline on cervical screening has
not been revised. As a result, Canada lags behind other countries like Australia, the Netherlands, and the U.K., which
began HPV screening as early as 2017. Australia's successful HPV screening and vaccination program is leading it
towards becoming the first country to eradicate cervical cancer, while Canada's outdated guidelines continue to
contribute to preventable cases of cervical cancer. In fact, cervical cancer has been identified as the fastest growing
cancer in women, with incidence rising at a rate of 3.7% per year since 2015.

3. The Goals of the Coalition for Responsible Healthcare Guidelines

3.1. Review Overall Processes and Philosophy
Practical Application: Guidelines should be designed to preserve Canadians’ health using resources wisely, with a
practical understanding of the topics involved.
Expertise and Bias: Conflicts of interest should be acknowledged, but expertise should be prioritized to ensure the
highest quality of care.
Diverse Representation: Evidence selection and committee compositions should reflect Canada’s diverse group of
experts.
Outcomes Focus: Guideline quality should prioritize safety and patient outcomes, with transparency and public
funding practices upheld.
Cost Evaluation: Screening costs should consider downstream savings and the patient/family costs related to laterstage diagnoses.

3.2. Urgent Remedy of Existing Guidelines

org: The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada
text:
Urgent Remedy of Existing Guidelines

Interim Guidelines: Suspend inappropriate guidelines and replace them with expert-recommended guidelines.
Expert Leadership: Guidelines should be led by content experts with methodologists in support roles, ensuring
specialty societies' approval to avoid conflicting guidance.
Neutral Knowledge Translation: Tools should be unbiased, presenting both relative and absolute harms and benefits.
Regular Revisions: Guidelines should be promptly updated based on significant new studies, with content experts
alerting bodies to breakthroughs.

3.3. Reform the Task Force
Governance and Accountability: The Task Force should have robust governance, with outcomes monitored and
deteriorating outcomes addressed quickly.
Ethical Involvement: Ethicists should be involved in restructuring and guideline development, with the Precautionary
Principle prioritized.
Patient Involvement: Patients should be partners at every level, provided with adequate training and support.
Transparency: Full disclosure of panel members' credentials should be required, with modernization of methodology
using updated concepts.

4. Recommendations
Immediate Action: Suspend current HPV screening guidelines and adopt interim guidelines based on expert
recommendations such as the 2023 Canadian Guideline on the Management of a Positive Human Papillomavirus
Test and Guidance for Specific Populations.
Expert-Led Development: Ensure guidelines are developed and led by field experts, with regular and prompt
updates.
Enhanced Transparency: Increase transparency in the guideline development process and involve diverse
populations and patient partners.

5. Conclusion
The Society of Gynecologic Oncology of Canada strongly supports the Coalition for Responsible Healthcare
Guidelines' call for a review and urgent update of the HPV screening guidelines with expert-led development. It is
imperative for the health and safety of Canadian women that these guidelines be revised to reflect current scientific
evidence and global best practices and remain up to date in a timelier fashion.

A Paradigm Change in Mental Health Care
Dealing with the Growing Mental Health, Addiction and Overdose Crisis.
Submission to the HESA Standing Committee on Health
Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
November 22, 2024
Axel Dorscht
[CONTACT]
Substance use, abuse, addiction and overdose death, the opioid epidemic and the
toxic drug crisis are the results of mental health problems. They provide an escape
from persisting and growing mental problems.
Mental health problems, addiction, and overdose deaths are out of control, and the
crisis is worsening. The evidence is everywhere around us. The statistics tell the story.
For decades, there has been a constant increase in the numbers, with no end in sight.
What is required is a rethinking, a different approach, a paradigm change in mental
health care.
The root causes of the persistence and growth of the problems lie in the limits and
shortcomings of conventional wisdom and established practices dealing with mental
health problems, addiction, and overdose deaths. What is required is a rethinking, a
different approach, and a paradigm change in mental health care. Mental health care
must be based on a new and different conceptual foundation. It requires education

It requires education

and training in mental development and growth. Develop the knowledge,
understanding, and mental faculties to understand and deal with the mind on the
inside as the place where we consciously exist and act, our role and responsibility. It is
where the inner mental life takes place, and the mental self, the conscious and aware
self, are active. We all know this, experience it, are aware of it, and must deal with it
daily. We have yet to put into words, and express in a clear picture and detailed
understanding.
What follows is based on long-term advanced, ground-breaking, and paradigmchanging research and study.
Millions are being spent on institutional and organizational development to manage
mental health care, addiction and overdose death. For example, at the federal and
provincial levels, the establishment of separate mental health and addiction
departments. But the problems keep growing. A point noted publicly some time ago by
the then-president of the Mental Health Commission of Canada.
It appears that mental health problems have become institutionalized and accepted as
an inevitable reality. They appear to have been translated into institutional and
financial issues. The focus is now on institutional, organizational, and financial issues
and concerns rather than individual mental problems.
More fundamentally, the mind, mental problems and how to deal with them are
misunderstood at a basic level.
Traditionally, in the science of the mind, such as psychiatry, psychology, behaviourism,
cognitive science, and neuroscience, the mind is understood indirectly from the
outside in the abstract. It is understood as either a human organ, a physical-biological
part of the human being, a thinking substance, a set of psychological faculties or
functions, an information processing mechanism, or, predominantly today, an
epiphenomenon, a reflection of what takes place in the brain in neurological and
biochemical processes.
Reality is, the mind is where we consciously exist and act, and we must be actively
engaged. It is where our inner mental life takes place and where we, the conscious
and aware self, are active. We consider and deal with experiences, perceptions,
sensations, feelings, thoughts, and ideas in the mind. It is where we make choices and
decisions, define goals and objectives, consider and manage behaviour and actions.
We all know and experience it individually; we are aware of it and must deal with it
daily.
Mental health problems are regarded as medical illnesses or disorders. Illnesses of
the mental organ, the physical-biological part of the human being, the thinking
substance, the psychological faculties or functions, the information processing
mechanism, or the neurological or biochemical processes of the brain. They are

org: Institute for Human Conceptual and Mental Development

text:
They are

treated either from outside through talk therapy, Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT),
internally through psychiatric medication, or through creating the right social conditions
externally.
Mental problems, in factual reality, are difficult mental conditions and states of the
mental self: disorder and instability, doubt and confusion, uncertainty and insecurity,
fear, stress, anxiety, frustration, and depression. They are not medical illnesses. They
result from failing to establish and maintain the necessary internal mental conditions:
order and stability, clarity of mind and understanding, certainty, security, and
confidence in what we do and engage in. The causes are lacking the required
knowledge, understanding, and mental faculties. This, in turn, results from missing the
necessary education and training in mental development and growth.
It is important to recognize the difference between mental problems and mental
disabilities. Mental disabilities are the consequences in the mind of neurological or
biochemical issues of the brain, where they must be dealt with. Mental problems must
be addressed and prevented from developing where they occur in the mind through
active mental engagement, mental work and effort.
External developments, such as COVID-19, social disorder and instability, ecological
crisis, and so on, are not causes of mental problems as conventional wisdom has it.
Instead, they show how mentally unprepared we are to deal with the changing
conditions, demands, and challenges of life and existence. They reveal the lack of
education and training in mental development and growth.
Mental problems are the most serious and fundamental problems we face today. The
officially recognized problems are only the tip of the iceberg. Mental problems affect
everything we do and engage in, in all areas of human activity, private and public life,
all sectors and levels of society, government, business, health care, education,
training, etc. It is difficult, if not impossible, to act, make considered choices and
decisions, define necessary goals and objectives, consider and manage required
behaviour and actions from mental disorder and instability, doubt and confusion,
uncertainty and insecurity.
What is required is a rethinking, a different approach, a paradigm change, and putting
mental health care on a different conceptual foundation. A change in focus and priority
from treatment to prevention is required. It is important to prevent problems from
developing instead of waiting for them to occur. The focus needs to shift from treating
symptoms and consequences to addressing underlying causes and developments.
Empowering the individual mentally to establish and maintain the necessary internal
mental conditions and state of the mental self is essential. Establish and maintain
order and stability, clarity of mind and understanding, certainty, security and
confidence in everything we do and engage in. Decentralize mental health care to the
individual where mental problems occur and must be dealt with. It is important for
individuals not to view themselves as helpless victims but as active agents. Empower

Empower

the individual mentally to cope with the changing conditions, demands, and challenges
of living in a constantly changing and transforming world.
Mental health care requires education and training in mental development and growth.
Not being educated and trained to recognize symptoms of mental health problems, as
currently is the case. Instead, education and training to develop the knowledge,
understanding and mental faculties to understand and deal with the mind on the
inside, as the place where we consciously exist and act, where the inner mental life
takes place and the mental self, the conscious and aware self, are active. Education
and training not only to deal with mental problems but, more importantly, to prevent
them from developing.
Develop the knowledge, understanding and mental faculties to understand and deal
with the mind directly, on the inside, as the place where we consciously exist and act,
where the inner mental life takes place, and the mental self, the conscious and aware
self, are active. It is where we are in charge and in control, we must actively engage
and take responsibility for what we do and engage in. The mind is where we
experience and become aware, and we must consider the conditions of existence and
how to deal with them. It is where we make choices and decisions, define goals and
objectives, consider and manage behaviour and actions, Problems, difficulties,
failures, errors and mistakes in what we do and engage in have their roots and
beginnings in the mind. And it is where the answers and solutions must begin.
Education and training to understand the fundamentals and essentials, the nature,
elements, and processes, the conditions, needs, demands, and challenges of the
mind, the inner mental life and the mental self, and our role and responsibility.
Establish and maintain the necessary internal mental conditions, order and stability,
clarity of mind and understanding, certainty, security and confidence in everything we
do and engage in. Mental order and stability about what takes place, what enters, and
what we do in the mind. Establish clarity of mind and understanding about what we
face and how to deal with it. Establish and maintain certainty, security and confidence

Establish and maintain certainty, security and confidence

errors and mistakes in what we do and engage in, reconsider the choices and
decisions we make and how we make them, the goals and objectives we pursue and
how we define them, the behaviour and actions in which we engage and how we
consider and manage them.
A paradigm change and a different conceptual foundation in mental health care will
reduce mental health problems, prevent them from developing, and reduce the costs
of mental health care. Education and training in mental development and growth will
not only reduce mental problems but, more importantly, prevent their development.
The costs of dealing with mental problems and their consequences, including
addiction and overdose deaths, will be reduced.
Mental development and growth education and training will address more than just
mental problems. It will address problems and difficulties in many areas of human
activities and engagement, in both private and public life, in all sectors and levels of
society, in government, business, health care, education, training, and so on. It is
difficult, if not impossible, as mentioned earlier, to act, make considered choices and
decisions, define necessary goals and objectives, and engage in the required
behaviour and actions from mental disorder and instability, doubt and confusion,
uncertainty and insecurity, fear, stress, anxiety, frustration or depression.
Mental development and growth are the entry point to necessary change and
transformation. Change and transformation in how we understand and manage human
existence and development, to understand and manage them in a constantly changing
and transforming world. To understand and manage them in an ecologically
sustainable, socially equitable, individually secure, and peaceful way within the natural
parameters, boundaries and limits of existence set by nature. They provide the
conceptual foundation of mental order, stability, clarity of mind, certainty, security, and
confidence to deal with today's human, social, and environmental problems and
crises.
The need for education and training in mental development and growth should be
raised, considered and discussed by the government, specifically the Federal
Government. The public looks to the government to lead. When the government
speaks, the public takes notice. The Federal Government has the cloud, the weight,
and the credibility the issue requires. It can raise the issue nationally with the mental
health community, institutions, organizations, agencies, and across the political
landscape from the federal to the provincial and municipal levels. Furthermore, it can
raise the issue globally, beyond Canada. It can publicize the issue by advocating,
promoting, and facilitating it within its own ranks. This will improve the credibility of
politics and government in the eyes of the public.

text:
Brief on the Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis
Families for Addiction Recovery (FAR)

A Plea for Balance and Nuance
Families for Addiction Recovery (FAR) is a Canadian charity founded in 2016 by parents of teenagers who
developed substance use disorder (SUD) in their teens. FAR was founded because the needs of our
families are not being met. We provide free peer support services across Canada to family members of
those struggling with SUD. FAR provides one-on-one and group support, as well as a live phone support
line. All of our volunteers are trained in the Invitation to Change Approach, which is a combination of
Community Reinforcement and Family Training (CRAFT), Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)
and Motivational Interviewing (MI). It is a non-confrontational, compassionate and evidence-based
approach.

We also educate about SUD and advocate for protective health laws and protective drug policies. FAR
participated in the work of the Standards Council of Canada to develop the Mental Health and Substance
Use Health Standardization Roadmap 1, as well as the work of Toronto Public Health to develop a
decriminalization model for Toronto. As such, FAR may be uniquely positioned to make recommendations
as we support decriminalization and modernizing our mental health acts, both of which are necessary if
we are to treat substance use and SUD as a health issue and protect the safety of all.

This brief is being submitted in the hopes of providing balance and nuance to the issues. It has been
concerning to see an increase in the polarization and politicization of these issues over time rather than
unification through widespread common ground.

FAR endorses all of the recommendations submitted to HESA by the Canadian Society of Addiction
Medicine (CSAM) and Children’s Healthcare Canada. FAR supports decriminalization as well as
involuntary treatment as part of a continuum of care and in certain circumstances. While it is recognized
that involuntary treatment is within provincial/territorial jurisdiction, much has been said about it during the
HESA Committee hearings to the detriment of families that have been advocating for long before the opioid
epidemic and toxic drug crisis. FAR also has recommendations in addition to the CSAM and Children’s
Healthcare Canada recommendations.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
FAR also has recommendations in addition to the CSAM and Children’s
Healthcare Canada recommendations.

1. Treating all substance use as a health issue means the decriminalization of drugs for personal
use
Both the medical community and law enforcement support decriminalization of drugs for personal use.
Much can be learned from the efforts at decriminalization in foreign jurisdictions and in BC. Aspects of
any model may need to be altered to ensure public safety and continued societal support.

It is important to keep in mind that the main purpose of criminal law is to protect people from other people,
not to protect them from themselves. It is our provincial and territorial mental health acts that are
supposed to keep people safe from themselves. There is nothing inherently criminal in possessing or
using substances. There is no harm to others in those activities alone although there could be harm to
self. While substance use can result in harm to others, those harms (for example driving impaired,
assault, theft, trafficking) are already illegal.
1 https://scc-ccn.ca/resources/publications/mental-health-and-substance-use-healthstandardization-roadmap

By way of analogy, prior to 1972 it was illegal in Canada to attempt suicide, the ultimate form of selfharm. We realized that self-harm is better dealt with through our mental health laws and we need to do
the same now for SUD. Labelling everyone who possesses a drug for personal use as a criminal is
harmful. Better strategies can be used to prevent/delay/deter the use of illegal substances that do not
stigmatize and harm people.

FAR supports the CSAM recommendation on decriminalization.
2. Treating all substance use as a health issue means ensuring that the protections of the mental
health acts and health care consent acts apply to those with SUD
Alcohol is the drug that has the greatest costs and harms in Canada, including costs to the criminal justice
system. Alcohol is the only substance where harm to others exceeds harm to self. Yet because alcohol
is legal, we are not having conversations about how to keep those with alcohol use disorder (AUD) or
binge drinkers out of the criminal justice system.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Yet because alcohol
is legal, we are not having conversations about how to keep those with alcohol use disorder (AUD) or
binge drinkers out of the criminal justice system.

The CCSA found:
“The total cost of policing crimes resulting from substance use or substance-related legislation
was $5.3 billion in 2020 (the latest year for which data are available). Alcohol accounted for $2.2
billion in policing costs for all offences, while all other substances accounted for $3.1 billion in 2020.
Nearly half of the costs due to alcohol use ($977 million) were related to violent crimes, such as
homicide and assault. In contrast, a larger proportion of policing costs attributable to other
substances, including opioids, cocaine and other stimulants ($1.8 billion) were related to non-violent
crimes, such as theft and arson.” (CSUCH)2.

Similarly, a recent study, Prevalence and correlates of alcohol and drug harms to others: Findings from
the 2020 U.S. National Alcohol Survey3 found that one-third of Americans (113 million) will suffer harms
during their lifetime from another person’s drinking versus 46 million from another person’s drug use.

Yet, as pointed out in Substance use as a public health issue: A critical review of the Canadian literature,
1896-20204, drug policy in Canada is leaning towards more criminalization for illegal substances and
more commercialization for legal substances, which is the opposite of a public health approach in each
case.
Decriminalization is not enough

The current model for decriminalization in BC will not ensure those with SUD who are at risk of harming
others stay out of the criminal justice system. Yet this is key to treating SUD as a health condition. Our
current models for decriminalization are based on the false assumption that the main reason people are
not seeking treatment is due to the stigma which decriminalization is intended to alleviate. However, a
2 elink.clickdimensions.com
3 https://www.phi.org/press/new-study-alcohol-and-drug-use-cause-significant-harms-that-gobeyond-the-individual/
4 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955395924003189?via%3Dihub

2017 survey of people in recovery5 conducted by the CCSA found that the main barrier to treatment was
that people were not ready, did not believe that they had a problem or that their problem was severe
enough to warrant treatment. According to the BC Coroners Service Death Review Panel6, 75% of those
who died from drug toxicity were not seeking treatment (although not all those who died had an SUD).

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
According to the BC Coroners Service Death Review Panel6, 75% of those
who died from drug toxicity were not seeking treatment (although not all those who died had an SUD).

To keep people out of the criminal justice system and ensure everyone’s safety, we need
treatment on demand and to ensure that the protections of the mental health acts and health care
consent acts apply to those with SUD. This is the case regardless of whether the substances
involved are legal or illegal.
Treatment on Demand

The State of Mental Health in Canada 2024 7 recently released by The Canadian Mental Health
Association, states that “no province or territory is spending enough on mental health, in part because
they’re not obliged to.” On average, they are spending 6.3% of their overall health budgets on mental
health whereas they should be spending 12%. This must be urgently rectified. Bad things happen when
people wait for treatment. They can change their mind about getting treatment, die by suicide, become
incarcerated or homeless, or suffer serious harms from their substance use including death.
Applying health law protections to SUD is part of the solution

While health laws are a matter of provincial/territorial jurisdiction, they are relevant to the federal
government. As explained in The Mentally Ill: How They Became Enmeshed in the Criminal Justice System
and How We Might Get Them Out 8 , commissioned by the Ministry of Justice Canada, if the
provinces/territories do not catch people upstream in the mental health system, the federal government
may well be catching them downstream in the criminal justice system:
“It is recognized that health care is constitutionally a provincial/territorial domain but
solutions, given that the problem of the over-representation of mentally ill individuals in the
criminal justice system is largely one of “transinstitutionalization”, must involve main stream
civil mental health care.”

Transinstitutionalization refers to the process by which the deinstitutionalization of those with mental health
conditions in reality often results in them being admitted to another institution, such as prisons or longterm care homes.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Transinstitutionalization refers to the process by which the deinstitutionalization of those with mental health
conditions in reality often results in them being admitted to another institution, such as prisons or longterm care homes.

The purpose of provincial/territorial mental health acts is to ensure the safety of all. While these laws vary
from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, generally they provide an ability to detain people with a mental disorder
who are at serious risk of harm to themselves or others and who are not seeking treatment. Further, our
health laws regarding informed consent generally ensure that a substitute decision maker can make
treatment decisions on behalf of someone who is incapable of making treatment decisions. These laws
are intended to be protective in nature.
5 https://www.ccsa.ca/life-recovery-addiction-canada-technical-report
6 https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/birth-adoption-death-marriage-anddivorce/deaths/coroners-service/death-reviewpanel/review_of_illicit_drug_toxicity_deaths_2022.pdf
7 https://cmha.ca/what-we-do/policy-research/state-of-mental-health-in-canada/#documents
8 https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/rp-pr/jr/mental/mental.pdf

Remarkably, there is good evidence that these health laws are significantly underutilized when it comes
to protecting those with SUD and those around them. The question isn’t whether the protections of our
mental health acts should apply to SUD, but rather why we have not historically extended these protections
to those with SUD even where in many jurisdictions they clearly do apply. A Commentary9 in the Canadian
Journal of Emergency Medicine by physicians and lawyers questions whether this is due to “therapeutic
nihilism, or worse, stigma”.

Further, recent research10 conducted by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) is evidence
that those with severe addiction are not being assessed to determine if they have capacity to make
treatment decisions with respect to their SUD. It states, “Individuals may be unable to consent to lifesaving OAT [Opioid Agonist Therapy for Opioid Addiction], and discontinuation of (or failure to
start) OAT, particularly in a controlled hospital environment, may represent the greatest immediate
threat to these patients’ morbidity and mortality with an extremely toxic unregulated drug supply.”

Many of the common concerns regarding involuntary treatment for SUD are addressed in Involuntary
treatment for severe addiction is better than doing nothing11.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Many of the common concerns regarding involuntary treatment for SUD are addressed in Involuntary
treatment for severe addiction is better than doing nothing11.

It is often argued that involuntary treatment is a violation of rights. However, a person’s rights can conflict.
This is explained in The Final Report of the Select Committee on Mental Health and Addictions (Ontario,
2010)12:
“The Select Committee believes, however, that the right to autonomy must be balanced
with the right to be well. The Select Committee also believes that our present laws tie the
hands of health professionals and families and have contributed to the criminalization of
mental illness, where individuals need to be arrested in order to receive care. While
Ontario undoubtedly needs better access to community supports and hospital beds, some
people will not avail themselves of such services because it is the nature of their condition
to deny that they are ill.”

Finally, it is also often argued that those seeking treatment voluntarily cannot access it and therefore
involuntary treatment should only be provided once there is treatment on demand. This is mental health
triage. It is the same thing as saying we will not apply the protections of our mental health acts to SUD
even though they apply, and we will not allow substitute decision makers to choose treatment for their
incapable loved ones. While many question the legality and ethics of intervening, the legality and ethics of
not intervening in these circumstances are of greater concern.
A common scenario for family caregivers

We have permission to share the following case of one of the mothers receiving support through FAR’s
programs. Her son has bipolar disorder and is addicted to methamphetamine. He was recently released
from jail to homelessness in a manic state with no medication or prescriptions. He cannot reside with her

He cannot reside with her

as he has previously destroyed her property and has physically assaulted her and another family member.
The following statements were made while she was crying and gasping for breath:
"Why can't I get him help? It's ridiculous. We look after our animals better. Physicians
aren't helpful. They are the ones who should get it. They say they can't force meds. But
we should be able to if they are a harm to themselves or others to keep everyone safe.
Once he is on his meds he is a normal person in society and can function. If not, he can't
function. He is, like, possessed…"

Though she fears for his safety and those around him, she doesn't call the police. Based on previous
experience, the police will take him to the hospital for an assessment, but he will be released. He will know
she spoke with the police and she fears for her own safety.

To summarize, involuntary treatment, done right, is not about prohibition or punishment. It is about
protecting those who cannot protect themselves due to untreated SUD and other mental health conditions.
It is also less expensive than the common alternatives, being revolving door incarcerations, hospital visits
and homelessness.

3. Update prescribed alternatives programs

There are valid concerns regarding current safer supply programs, including the risk of diversion. Most
concerns can be mitigated by ensuring prescribed alternatives are necessary for stabilization purposes,
are part of a treatment plan, and that precautions are taken to avoid and monitor diversion, including more
options for alternatives that better match tolerance levels.
4. Compliance with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC)

Drug toxicity is the leading or one of the leading causes of death of youth in Canada. Research by
ODPRN13 shows that while opioid related toxicities significantly increased for adolescents (15-17) and
young adults (18-24) in Ontario during the pandemic, treatment with OAT significantly decreased for young
adults and remained low and stable for adolescents. There was a fourfold decrease in residential treatment.

The word “neglect” has been used to describe the state of care in Canada for those with mental health
conditions including SUD.1415 This is particularly true for youth who often face longer waitlists for treatment.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
The word “neglect” has been used to describe the state of care in Canada for those with mental health
conditions including SUD.1415 This is particularly true for youth who often face longer waitlists for treatment.

Canada is a signatory to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC). Canada
could be considered to be in breach of three provisions of the UNCRC:
•
Article 3 which provides that all of our laws must be drafted in accordance with the best interests
of the child.
•
Article 12 that provides that children have a right to healthcare.
13 https://odprn.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Opioids-among-Adolescents-and-Young-AdultsInfographic.pdf
14 https://www.theglobeandmail.com/opinion/article-a-crisis-of-neglect-how-society-can-helpthose-with-mental-illness/
15 https://cmha.ca/what-we-do/policy-research/state-of-mental-health-in-canada/#documents

•
Article 33 which provides that children have a right to be protected from illegal drugs and the illegal
drug trade.
Aside from the fact youth are, at times, waiting more than a year for treatment for mental health conditions
including residential treatment for SUD, if they are not seeking treatment our laws, as drafted and/or
applied, usually prevent parents in Canada from intervening where their child is refusing treatment for SUD.
A Commentary16 in the CMAJ discussed the protection of minors under the UNCRC:
“Read as a whole, the sensible interpretation of the UNCRC is that addicted minors, in their best
interests, should receive treatment, regardless of their refusal, so they can recover, instead of being
harmed by criminalization or untreated and progressive addiction. This conclusion is supported in a
2009 report10 from a conference held at the University of Toronto, which concluded the following:
•
putting the best interest of the child first would require substantial changes in current
models of formal health care;
•
strategies are required to keep young people out of the criminal justice system;
•
codes of conduct by the colleges of health professionals on the best interests of the child
are required.”

5. Support family caregivers

The toxic drug supply and SUDs are destroying families. Canada is facing an unprecedented shortage of
healthcare providers, especially in the area of mental health and substance use health. Family caregivers
often act as first responders, default case managers and provide the bulk of support to their loved ones
with little support from service providers. They are the most motivated and least expensive form of care
and support. They need education, resources and support in their own right. Some will become caregivers
to their child for life. The oldest caregivers supported by FAR were in their late 80’s and early 90’s.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
The oldest caregivers supported by FAR were in their late 80’s and early 90’s.

Sometimes single elderly parents, usually mothers, are living with their child who has SUD and/or other
mental health conditions in unsafe environments. They will not evict their child and are willing to suffer
mental, financial and sometimes physical abuse to avoid their child becoming homeless. This is described
as a public health crisis in the U.S. by Judith Smith in her book, Difficult: Mothering Challenging Adult
Children Through Conflict and Change. These caregivers should not have to choose between their own
safety and that of their child.
Summary of Recommendations
FAR endorses all recommendations of CSAM and Children’s Healthcare Canada and, in addition,
recommends:

1. The federal government dedicate a minimum of 12% of the overall health care budget for mental health
and substance use health care and take all steps necessary to ensure that each province/territory does
the same.
16https://www.cmaj.ca/content/192/5/E121#:~:text=Letters-,Secure%20care%3A%20a%20questi
on%20of%20capacity%2C%20autonomy%20and%20the,best%20interests%20of%20the%20child

2. The federal government update prescribed alternatives programs to ensure that prescribed
alternatives are necessary for stabilization purposes, are part of a treatment plan, and that precautions
are taken to avoid and monitor diversion, including more options for alternatives to better match
tolerance levels.

3. The federal government ensure that all levels of government comply with the UNCRC with respect to
adequate funding for mental health and substance use health for children and youth, and ensure that
all health laws and policies are drafted and implemented in the best interest of the child.

4. The HESA Committee accept the offer of Children’s Healthcare Canada to convene leading child
experts to testify and provide further insights on the pressing needs of children and youth in the context
of the crisis if the Committee has not already done so. Ideally, this would include their views on
decriminalization as well as harm reduction, safer supply and involuntary treatment for children and
youth.

5. The federal and provincial/territorial governments collaborate to provide the resources and policies
necessary to incorporate family caregivers into the healthcare system as partners in care and provide
education, counselling, training and peer support to them in order to maximize the quality and quantity
of support they can provide to their loved ones with SUD and other mental health conditions and reduce
the possibility of homelessness.

Nasal Naloxone vs Needle-based Naloxone delivery by Non-Healthcare Professionals
Introduction
Since the Opioid Crisis began in North America (circa 2013) and spread across the USA, finding
itself in Canada in 2014/15, death rates have climbed steadily, year-on-year. In almost every illicit
“street-drug” available across North America, Opioids are mixed, or blended into these drugs to
increase addiction, dependence, and potency. Countries, governments, municipalities and nonprofit frontline organizations have worked diligently to reduce mortality and morbidity. These efforts
and initiatives focus on education, testing of drugs to confirm Opioid presence, and the global
training of non-healthcare providers to deliver life-saving naloxone to suspected opioid overdosed
individuals, prior to the arrival of EMS, and related Emergency agencies such as Fire-Rescue and
Law-Enforcement.
Terminology
Opioids – are synthetic drugs that are not naturally-derived from the sap of the poppy plant.
Opiates – are drugs made from the sap of the poppy plant, and may include some Opioids, deeming
them to be semi-synthetic.
Concentration
It is important to create a “spectrum of concentration” when discussing Opiates and Opioids. For
reference we will use morphine as our base drug and assign it a concentration of “1”.
As morphine is designated with a concentration of 1, the spectrum begins less than one in
fractional concentrations, and escalates into the tens of thousands.
Of interest, synthetic Opioids are easier to manufacture illegally than methamphetamine for
example. It does not produce noxious dangerous vapours compared to Opioids and requires
little electricity that would warrant a “red-flag” in the law-enforcement community.
