A brief example of this would be:
Morphine (1) – Oxycontin, Vicodin, Percocet (3-5), Methadone (7), Buprenorphine (40), Heroin (50).
It is important to note that Heroin is 50x more potent than Morphine. It is also noteworthy that
Heroin is the most potent drug that can be formulated from the sap of the poppy plant. Thus it is the
most potent opiate available.
Once we escalate in potency beyond Heroin (50), we enter the realm of the Opioids (synthetics).
This begins with Fentanyl and its analogues. Fentanyl manufactured by pharmaceutical companies
is 100x more potent than Morphine (1). It is currently the most widely used synthetic Opioid being
mixed with illicit street-drugs, and is also currently available and sold in its pure form. It is
important to note that Fentanyl is being manufactured illegally across the world, and its purity and
concentration are dynamic, without the closely monitored practices of the Pharma Industry.
Fentanyl (100) – Analogues of Fentanyl (100-1000) – Carfentanil (10000)
The Difference in First Response Care betwixt HealthCare Providers, and Non-Healthcare
Providers
Terminology
Healthcare Providers (HCP) for the purpose of this document refers to members of professional
colleges, associations, and healthcare teams such as Emergency Medical Services, Hospitals,
Community Clinics, etc. HCP personnel are typically registered with their specific college of
practice, such as Nursing, Paramedicine, Medicine, etc., and ultimately “answer” to those colleges
on their professional conduct and competency whilst working in their profession.
As a registered Paramedic myself, I must conduct myself in accordance with my professional
college. As a registered member I also work under (practice) the off-line or on-line supervision of a
Medical Director (MD). These medical directors are responsible for our patient care and write our
practices out in protocols, or medical control guidelines. This is the framework of all HCP’s
practicing in Canada, and varies slightly between Provinces, Territories and other regions.
Non-Healthcare Providers (Non-HCP) includes virtually every member of society that does not
belong to the category of HCP listed above. It may be Family members, co-workers, friends, clergy,
and others that come across an Opioid overdose “person in crisis”, in their day-to-day routines. In
Canada, members in this group can acquire Naloxone kits provided by government free of charge to
assist in the current Opioid overdose crisis. Training is available in many forms; a few moments with
a pharmacist, online training, and scheduled professional first-response training. Naloxone is
available to every Canadian through approved pharmacies and other agencies approved to
dispense.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Naloxone is
available to every Canadian through approved pharmacies and other agencies approved to
dispense.

Targeted Non-Healthcare Providers includes individuals that do not belong to a professional
healthcare college but work in primary first-response organizations such as law-enforcement, firerescue, non-profit – street level teams, social services, security agents, and other volunteer
agencies devoted and focused on reducing mortality and morbidity from Opioid overdose.
Individuals in this group of targeted responders are better trained, and much more likely to
encounter Opioid overdose “persons in crisis” - often once to several times per day in their regular
duties. Fire-Rescue personnel in many municipalities have provided medical support to EMS on
calls that required additional resources such as motor-vehicle collisions, chemical spills, fire, and
also medical calls that require strength in numbers such as cardiac arrest calls, bariatric patients
that require assistance in lifting and moving, etc. Since the Opioid crisis entered Canada, FireRescue personnel have been carrying the burden of first response and are providing critical lifesaving care to Opioid overdoses across the county. It would be safe to say that Fire-Rescue
personnel in Opioid infested regions of the country have provided more Naloxone, CPR, and lifesaving interventions than any other responder in the country. Our mortality and morbidity rates
across Canada and the USA would be considerably higher without the rapid response of FireRescue personnel.
How do Opiates and Opioids affect us
It is important to understand the basics of opioid effects on our bodies. It is also important to note
that opiates and opioids are used constantly in our communities, healthcare facilities, and EMS
units - in a therapeutic setting with positive and appropriate results. EMS Advanced Care
Paramedics use Opiates and Opioids for pain control and sedation procedures on a regular basis,
without “unwanted” effects. It is essential that we do not develop a “tossing the baby out with the
bathwater” approach, as the role of Opiates and Opioids are critically important. In the community,
Opiates and Opioids are used primarily for pain control in individuals suffering from chronic
medical conditions, cancer, and in the management of palliative (end-of-life) considerations.
Opioid receptors in the Body
When a person receives Opiates or Opioids, whether intentionally or unintentionally, they can
access our body through four routes: inhalation, injection, ingestion, or contact with the skin and
mucosa (mouth, eyes). Once the drug enters the body it finds its way into our bloodstream. As it
enters the bloodstream it is ultimately attracted to, and then attaches to opioid receptors located
throughout the body. The most noteworthy opioid receptors in our body are in the brain. As Opiates
and Opioids attach to these receptors, they have either a beneficial (therapeutic) effect, or an
unwanted and dangerous effect (overdose). Medications, simply put have the following effects:
Underdose –-> Therapeutic dose –-> Overdose
Opioid receptors in our brain fall into two basic camps:
1. Receptors that produce euphoria, the release of Dopamine, ultimately producing the “high”.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Receptors that produce euphoria, the release of Dopamine, ultimately producing the “high”.

2. Receptors around the brainstem that suppress breathing rate, depth, suppression of the
cough reflex, and even cardiac depression.
Depending on the “dose” of the Opiates or Opioids, the effects can be minimal, or devastating
within seconds of exposure. In fact, some doses are so significant, it produces death within
minutes of exposure. The role of all first responders is to reverse the effects on the opioid receptors
by administering naloxone. Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist. It works by taking space on
the receptor sites in the body, not allowing the Opiates or Opioids circulating in the bloodstream to
attach themselves. Naloxone is the only true defense available to first responders that can produce
this effect. Naloxone can be delivered to the body via injection (needle-based kits) or nasal delivery
via a nasal mist (needle-free kits). The majority of naloxone provided to members of the public is the
“low dose” naloxone via needle injections. In the hands of non-Healthcare Providers, these needlebased kits pose a biohazard risk (needle-stick injury to rescuer/bystander), and an “often lower than
needed” dose of naloxone. This is the primary purpose of this paper to your Standing
Committee.
Needle-based Naloxone Kits
These kits have been available in North America to the public at staggered times since shortly after
the Opioid epidemic began in 2014. As governments and municipalities began to struggle with
overdose deaths, they also began to allow untrained members of the public to carry and administer
naloxone by intramuscular (IM) needle-injection. These kits were cobbled together as the epidemic
was growing in severity, and they included two or three syringe/needle combo units; two or three
vials of injectable naloxone, usually 0.4 mg/1 ml vials (total naloxone per kit 1.2 mg) LOW-DOSE.
Some kits included two or three 1mg/1 ml vials (total naloxone per kit 3.0 mg) MODERATE DOSE.
NARCAN® Nasal Spray Kits
Nasal naloxone (Registered brand name NARCAN® Nasal Spray) kits have also been available since
2014 and differ significantly from their needle-based counterparts. In list form for clarity:
1. No needle in the system (decreased risk of needle stick injury to first responder) and
decrease in time of possible overdose recognition to actual delivery of naloxone to the
person in crisis. Ultimately this leads to earlier resuscitation, decreases in both mortality
and morbidity. Anecdotally, this may lead to less brain damage (hypoxic/anoxic brain injury),
due to prolonged periods of time without oxygen to the brain and potentially less individuals
on long-term brain injury care. https://ottawacitizen.com/feature/opioid-crisis-braininjury-epidemic#comments-area
2. High-Dose naloxone of 4mg/0.1 ml per nasal spray. Prior to the Opioid crisis (circa 2014)
opiate overdoses that were considered serious involved Heroin. As mentioned earlier in this
paper Heroin is the strongest natural Opiate from the sap of the poppy, at 50X concentration
to morphine. Despite its high concentration, it typically responded to low-dose naloxone
ranging from 0.4-2.0 mg in the care of the Heroin overdose person. In fact, prior to 2014 it
was uncommon to require greater than 2.0 mg naloxone to manage an Opiate overdose.
Today, with the introduction of the Opioids (synthetics) and the high concentrations ranging
from 100x – 10000x stronger than morphine, we soon realised that “old-school” dosing of
0.4-2.0 mg was not effective in reversing Opioid overdose, particularly with Fentanyl being

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Today, with the introduction of the Opioids (synthetics) and the high concentrations ranging
from 100x – 10000x stronger than morphine, we soon realised that “old-school” dosing of
0.4-2.0 mg was not effective in reversing Opioid overdose, particularly with Fentanyl being

the dominant toxin in the drug-supply. Nasal naloxone (NARCAN® Nasal Spray) delivers 4.0
mg per nasal spray, with most kits containing 2 nasal spray units for a total dose available of
8 mg. This would have been considered very high dose prior to 2014. Today with Fentanyl
and Carfentanil in the drug supply, often 8 mg of naloxone is not enough.

3. Educational competency – to use a needle-based kit is daunting and often frightening to
non-healthcare members of society. As Canadians we are not routinely trained in providing
injections to ourselves or others. Many societies around the world are more familiar with
this competency. In the current needle-based kits in Canada we are provided with three
syringe/needles some of which have a safety feature built in to reduce the risk of a needlestick injury to the first responder.
a. This safety-system requires training, practice, and review to maintain even a
functional level of competency.
b. In discussions with many people that have used these kits, they expressed concerns
over the time it took to recall how to draw the naloxone from the vial.
c. There is also the general fear and reluctance to inject another human being, fearing
that they could hurt them further.

I have personally trained thousands of individuals in Opioid Emergency Response, and we
have had many discussions about the overdose patients that they encounter in their daily
work. Without the Nasal naloxone (NARCAN® Nasal Spray) kits they carry daily; the
outcomes would have been much worse. Statements from responders (non-healthcare
providers) have been:

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Statements from responders (non-healthcare
providers) have been:

1. “I was able to remove the nasal naloxone from the NARCAN® kit and administer it in less
than 15 seconds”.
2. “We are able to provide the nasal naloxone (NARCAN®) while we are actively providing
CPR compressions”.
3. “I was able to provide myself with nasal naloxone (NARCAN®) after I inhaled Fentanyl
from the victim at the scene”.
4. “I don’t have to worry about getting “stuck with a contaminated needle” as most drug
users we encounter have infectious diseases”.
Public Access to Intramuscular naloxone and Intranasal naloxone Across Canada
All provinces and territories have Take Home naloxone programs that provide access to
intramuscular naloxone.
Only Ontario, Quebec, Yukon, and Northwest Territories provide public access to intranasal
naloxone through these programs.
Through this paper, I am proposing to the Standing Committee that there be equitable public
access to easier-to-use intranasal naloxone. Most times someone is found to be suffering
from an accidental opioid poisoning, it is a bystander from the public who administers the
first dose of naloxone while waiting for First Responders to arrive. Making intranasal naloxone

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Making intranasal naloxone

available for the public will increase the number of people who are able to help save a life
when the time comes and remove the fear, hesitancy and low-dose of using needles.
Interestingly, in the USA, intramuscular naloxone is not approved for use by members of the
public. It is reserved for First Responders and health care practitioners. Intranasal naloxone
is available over the counter for easy public access.
Timeline and Summary
Major timelines in North America are focused in three main frames:
1. Prior to 2014 (Pre-Opioid Epidemic) Most overdoses requiring Naloxone at this time were
for pharmaceutical overdose on pills, patches, and unintentional injection from healthcare
providers causing overdose. Almost all overdoses prior to the Opioid epidemic would
respond favourably to low-dose naloxone of 0.4 – 2.0 mg. Recall that almost all overdoses
were from the naturally derived opiates, from the poppy plant, or semisynthetic pills.
2. 2014 to 2020 – (Opioid Epidemic) The most significant factor is the introduction of Fentanyl
into the illicit drug supply in North America. In approximately the first six years 2014-2020
the majority of Fentanyl was obtained illegally, coming from China, north through Mexico,
and into the illegal supply. Ironically, the best thing about these particular batches of
Fentanyl was their quality and potency. This was, for the most part, pharmaceutical-grade
Fentanyl and it had a predictable concentration of 100x.
3. COVID restricted years – When the personal, corporate, and border lockdowns occurred,
this led to a significant rise of intergang related turmoil. The Fentanyl supply from Mexico
was being restricted, and gangs fought each other for supply to mix into their illegal drugs.
This inability to acquire illegal Fentanyl forced these gangs to find alternate sources. Many
gangs began to produce their own Fentanyl, a relatively easy process if you can get the
precursors (ingredients). The most significant issue in this lockdown phase, until our
present day is the purity and controls surrounding illegally-made Fentanyl. It lacks the
cleanliness of the pharmaceutical grade Fentanyl and may include other agents, and most
importantly, it is often much more concentrated and potent compared to the pre-lockdown
Fentanyl.
Final Points
•
The higher the concentration of Opioids in the drug supply require higher doses of naloxone
to reverse life-threatening overdose.
•
Nasal naloxone (NARCAN®® Nasal Spray) meets the need for higher concentration/dose
Naloxone with speed of administration, ease of use, no risk of needle-stick injury, and less
responder-reluctance to administer the nasal spray compared to sticking another person
with a needle.
•
Training and competency are simplified with the delivery of Nasal naloxone (NARCAN®®
Nasal Spray) compared to training for use of needle-based naloxone.
•
There is a better chance of naloxone entering the bloodstream if it is sprayed in the nasal

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Submitted by:
Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine – La société médicale canadienne sur l’addiction (CSAM-SMCA)
Brief Submitted to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Re: “Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada”
November 4th, 2024

Background
The Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine (CSAM) applauds the House of Commons Standing Committee
on Health undertaking a study of the Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada. As has already been
expressed by the variety of briefs and witnesses, this is a complex and tragic public health emergency with
multiple viewpoints and considerations. It is also a topic of great urgency to Canadians, with over 47,000
lives lost to opioid-related toxicity since 20161.
CSAM is eager to support a submission from the national perspective of addiction medicine providers.
Evidence-based policy requires expert and specialist points of view along with the added insight of the
etiology and epidemiology of those at risk of, or living with, substance use disorders (SUDs).
SUDs are best understood as chronic medical conditions, with multiple biopsychosocial factors underlying
their development, often in adolescence or early adulthood, not through a moral failing or a criminal justice
lens. A previous estimate of lifetime prevalence of a SUD2 in Canada is shockingly high, at 21%, or over 1 in
5 Canadians. Additionally, according to CIHI3, SUDs were the 5th most common cause of hospitalization in
2021-2022, reflecting a substantial impact on an already taxed medical system. Despite this, the CCSA
Canadian Life in Recovery Survey4 reported over 50% of those in recovery have never destabilized, which has
been seen in similar surveys of individuals in recovery in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia.
We know that treatment access is key to helping those living with SUDs recover while reducing the burden
and cost to the healthcare system. Although Canada’s healthcare system is purported to be universal, the
Canada Health Act only covers hospitals and doctors, a small part of the treatment pathway. Additionally,
there is substantial variability in the extent to which evidence-based interventions are funded and supported
across the country.
1.
Decriminalization

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Decriminalization

There is consensus that substance use should be treated as a health issue and many would agree5 this includes
the decriminalization of the possession of drugs for personal use. It is important to distinguish between
legalization and decriminalization. Legalization means the sale of the drug is legal and the government controls
sales through regulation. Decriminalization of possession for personal use means it is still illegal to sell the
substance but it is legal to possess a small amount for personal use, thereby removing the punitive and
stigmatizing approach to people who use drugs.
1 https://health-infobase.canada.ca/substance-related-harms/opioids-stimulants/
2 https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/pub/82-624-x/2013001/article/11855-eng.pdf?st=K51HASFu
3 https://www.cihi.ca/en/hospital-stays-in-canada-2021-2022
4 https://www.ccsa.ca/life-recovery-addiction-canada-technical-report
5 https://angusreid.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/2021.02.24_Opioid_Dependence.pdf

It is significant that both the medical community (including CSAM, CMA, CFPC, CAEP) and law enforcement
(CACP) support decriminalization to deal with the harms of substance use. Many lessons can be learned from
the efforts of decriminalization in Oregon and British Columbia, and successful implementations
internationally. Simply focusing on one piece of drug policy without access to treatment, without enforcement,
and without prevention may be more harmful than beneficial. That does not mean it will not work, but rather
we need to take a systemic approach and implement all safeguards and processes to create a system of care
for all to access, based on the four pillars of substance use policy: prevention, harm reduction, treatment and
enforcement.

The reasons for Oregon6 repealing decriminalization and BC7 making significant changes were primarily
concerns about public drug use and public safety. CSAM strongly supports decriminalization of drug possession
for personal use and eliminating the criminalization of addiction in the setting of a robust prevention program,
accessible harm reduction services, enforcement, and a treatment system of care available to all Canadians.

We recommend that the federal government work with provinces/territories to pursue decriminalization,
modifying approaches as necessary to balance the safety concerns of consumers, families and society. We
further recommend that the federal and/or provincial/territorial governments should ensure that they enact
legislation prior to decriminalization to restrict the use of currently illegal drugs in public places, similar to
existing legislation prohibiting public use of legal substances.
2.
Prevent/Delay use

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Prevent/Delay use

SUD is a pediatric onset illness, with up to 90% of the cases developing during adolescence and early adult
years. About 50% of the risk is genetic. Many youths with SUD have other mental health symptoms. Those who
initiate use before 15 years of age are six times more likely to go on to develop an SUD compared to those who
initiate use over 21 years of age.

We recommend that the federal government support public health and school programs to prevent/delay
initiation of substance use. Age-appropriate education should not be limited to education about the toxic drug
supply and harm reduction, but should include education about SUDs to reduce stigma and raise awareness
regarding when students, or their loved ones, may be at risk. We also advocate for more mental health
resilience training so that our schools become supportive environments that promote mental health and wellbeing, empowering young people to overcome challenges and thrive in their personal lives. Further, we
recommend rollout of programs to identify at-risk youth and provide them targeted interventions including
social supports and programming known to protect against substance use, similar to those in other
jurisdictions (e.g. Icelandic model, Preventure).
6https://www.opb.org/article/2024/09/01/oregon-starts-drug-possessionrecriminalization/#:~:text=Oregon%20has%20ended%20its%20experiment,again%20considered%20a%20misdeme
anor%20crime.
7 https://news.gov.bc.ca/releases/2024PREM0021-000643

3.
Update the Canada Health Act

Following our colleagues from the Canadian Mental Health Association8, we agree it would “simply be
inaccurate to call our health system universal, or comprehensive”. The Canada Health Act only covers
treatment for those with chronic complex illnesses, including SUDs, via doctors or hospitals. This means that
many first-line, evidence-based treatments are not covered under the Act. This is leaving our most vulnerable
lacking access to skilled professionals (including psychology, social work, physiotherapy, occupational therapy,
peer support, nursing), programs and supports that have been shown to aid recovery.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This is leaving our most vulnerable
lacking access to skilled professionals (including psychology, social work, physiotherapy, occupational therapy,
peer support, nursing), programs and supports that have been shown to aid recovery.

We recommend that the federal government update the Canada Health Act to cover the healthcare needs of
people with SUDs and other mental health conditions to provide a truly universal healthcare system for
Canada, or create a new act in order to do so.
4.
National Pharmacare Program Coverage
We applaud the work of the federal government as we agree all Canadians should have access to medications
that can save lives, especially our most vulnerable and marginalized. The best evidence for reducing death for
those living with an opioid use disorder and/or at risk of a toxic drug overdose are medications for opioid use
disorder9. Access to medications can be a significant barrier to treatment for this vulnerable and marginalized
population, and coverage varies across jurisdictions.
While there are several medications that can be beneficial for reducing substance related harms, we
recommend the federal government add, at a minimum, first-line medications for Opioid Use Disorder to the
national Pharmacare formulary including buprenorphine (including sublingual tablets, film, and injectable
extended-release formulations) and methadone. Further, we recommend the federal government address
barriers preventing the Health Canada approval of long-acting injectable naltrexone as an alternate treatment
option; once available, injectable naltrexone should be added to the national Pharmacare formulary.
5.
Canadian Mental Health and Substance Use Health (MHSUH) Task Force
Following the internationally recognized Canadian Pain Task Force10, we recommend that the federal
government build on and expedite the implementation of The MHSUH Standardization Roadmap11 by
establishing a Canadian MHSUH Task Force to provide advice regarding evidence and best practices for the
prevention and management of SUDs in Canada. The Task Force will develop and enact a national action plan

9https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2760032#:~:text=In%20a%20national%20cohort

10https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/corporate/about-health-canada/public-engagement/externaladvisory-bodies/canadian-pain-task-force.html

text:
The Task Force will develop and enact a national action plan

for funding and treatment of SUDs that includes regional/provincial representation of experts. The Task Force
would be mandated to:
●
Ensure integration and alignment between health services that are federally and provincially funded, thus
avoiding gaps in care provided in Indigenous communities;
●
Assess how addiction is currently addressed throughout Canada;
●
Conduct national consultations with experts, people living in recovery and people with lived and living
experience, and families of those affected by SUDs and review available evidence to identify best and
leading practices, potential areas for improvement, and elements of an improved approach to the
prevention and treatment of SUD in Canada;
●
Provide recommendations for the federal government to collaborate with provincial/territorial/municipal
governments to ensure the establishment of accessible treatment-on-demand (ie. benchmarks for wait
times to initiation of service) including withdrawal management services and flexible-length bed-based
and community-based treatment services that are trauma informed, culturally relevant and evidencebased;
●
Provide recommendations to ensure wide accessibility across Canada to evidence-based interventions
shown to reduce harms related to substance use, including drug use supplies (e.g. needles, sterile water),
intranasal naloxone, services (including supervised consumption sites, overdose prevention sites, drug
checking, testing and treatment of blood borne pathogens); and
●
Develop a framework, including research reporting standards, to support robust evaluation of innovations
to address the toxic drug crisis.

Summary:
Thank you for your attention to the information provided in this brief. Most of our membership work with
people impacted by SUDs on a daily basis. As such we have seen and continue to see first-hand the harms
caused by the opioid epidemic and toxic drug supply. While a comprehensive plan to address this crisis will
require a multi-pronged approach, we feel strongly that any successful response requires a coordinated
addiction strategy addressing all four pillars of prevention, harm reduction, treatment and enforcement. We
look forward to presenting to the HESA committee to provide further input and answer any questions that
arise from this brief.
Description of organization:
CSAM (https://csam-smca.org/) was founded in 1989 by a group of physicians, scientists, and researchers
who saw a need for a professional association that would represent the medical profession in the area of
substance use disorders. Originally called the Canadian Medical Society on Alcohol and Other Drugs, it has
evolved into a national organization of medical professionals, allied health workers, and scientists who are
committed to helping Canadians understand, endure, and overcome SUDs.
Recommendations Summary:
1. Decriminalization- The federal government should work with provinces/territories to pursue
decriminalization, modifying approaches as necessary to balance the safety concerns of consumers,
families and society.
2. Prevent/delay use- The federal government should work with provinces/territories to support public
health and school programs to prevent/delay initiation of substance use including mental health
resilience training as part of curriculums. Further, the government should support the rollout of
programs to identify at-risk youth and provide them targeted interventions known to protect against
substance use.
3. Update the Canada Health Act- The federal government should update the Canada Health Act to
cover the healthcare needs of people with SUDs and other mental health conditions to provide a
truly universal healthcare system for Canada, or create a new act in order to do so.
4. National Pharmacare Program Coverage- The federal government should add, at a minimum, firstline medications for Opioid Use Disorder to the national Pharmacare formulary including
buprenorphine (including sublingual tablets, film, and injectable extended-release formulations) and
methadone, and work toward Health Canada approval and subsequent Pharmacare inclusion of longacting injectable naltrexone.
5. MHSUH Task Force- The federal government should build on and expedite the implementation of
The MHSUH Standardization Roadmap by establishing a Canadian MHSUH Task Force, whose
mandate would include increasing access to evidence-based treatment for substance use disorders.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Over the Influence Brief to the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health
The Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis
As the opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis take deeper roots in Canada, youth have become a
largely affected population with little to no support. According to the Government of Canada
(2024), nearly 20% of total apparent opioid toxicity deaths were youth aged 0-to-29 years old. The
impact on young people in Canada is profound and multifaceted, as the crisis impacts their health,
wellbeing, and prospects. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC),
youth who engage in substance misuse are more likely to experience physical and sexual dating
violence and are more susceptible to mental health and suicide risk (Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention, 2020). This epidemic has far-reaching effects on the youth demographic and is
disrupting the lives and futures of our future leaders.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This epidemic has far-reaching effects on the youth demographic and is
disrupting the lives and futures of our future leaders.

As opioid-related poisonings and deaths escalate, there has been an uptake in interest around
interventions. However, even though Canadians are being introduced to opioids and addiction at an
earlier age, most interventions are based around the adult (25+) experience. According to Corace et
al. (2018), a majority of the related research is in reference to adults, even though youth were 3-4
times more likely than adults 25 and older to report harm related to substance use in their physical
health, social and work/study, legal, and housing problems. These interventions cannot adopt a
one-size-fits-all approach—youth have unique needs that require specialized prevention,
treatment, and support. Despite this need, systems designed for youth grappling with opioid
misuse and addiction are sorely lacking. At a youth summit ran in 2022, youth voiced that there is a
lack of information about opioids available to them (Nairn et al., 2022). Educational programming in
schools is non-existent, insufficient, or inconsistently implemented. Further, there are limited
youth-specific rehabilitation and treatment centers available. Moreover, access to mental health
services, which are crucial for addressing the underlying issues related to substance use, remains
inadequate for many young people. The time for change is now; we cannot afford to continue losing
young Canadians because of a focus on ineffective downstream approaches.
Background of Over the Influence
Over the Influence (OTI): Tackling the Opioid Crisis is a two-year, national initiative working to
amplify youth voices in combatting the opioid epidemic in Canada. OTI equips youth with the tools
to influence their communities by making informed choices and promoting harm reduction
techniques. OTI acknowledges the role that young people play in influencing and shaping their
environments and recognizes that peer-led efforts can have a profound impact on addressing
substance use issues.

OTI’s youth influencers are a diverse group of individuals aged 14-24 who have lived experience
and/or face heightened risks related to opioid use. These young people come from various regions
across Canada, including Ontario, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, British Columbia, Québec,

Nova Scotia, and the Yukon. Each of these regions presents unique challenges and contexts that
contribute to the opioid epidemic, impacting youth differently based on their local environments.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Each of these regions presents unique challenges and contexts that
contribute to the opioid epidemic, impacting youth differently based on their local environments.

Through weekly meetings, OTI provides a safer2 space for youth to have open and honest
discussions about the realities of substance use in their lives and communities. Meetings foster a
sense of community and support, allowing young people to share their experiences in a nonjudgmental environment and find pathways for change. Grounding our discussions in evidence, we
provide educational resources that explore the full spectrum of issues related to opioid use, from
understanding the science of addiction to exploring the social and economic factors that
contribute to the crisis. Youth influencers are then able to make choices based on a thorough
understanding of the facts and feel confident to advocate for evidence-based approaches within
their communities.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Youth influencers are then able to make choices based on a thorough
understanding of the facts and feel confident to advocate for evidence-based approaches within
their communities.

Through social media campaigns, youth conferences, and comprehensive educational programs,
OTI amplifies youth voice and engagement in the opioid epidemic. By partnering with youth
organizations and supporting youth-led initiatives, young voices are heard and engaged
Additionally, youth are involved in policy advocacy through forums with policymakers and highlight
their stories and experiences via social media. These efforts ensure that youth perspectives are not
only heard but also have a significant influence on shaping change, such as policy development.
OTI is fostering a new generation of advocates who are committed to creating safer, healthier
communities.
Call to Action
“By listening to youth voices you’re looking at a lifelong solution.”— This is how one of our OTI youth
influencers aptly captured how youth fit into the solution. As youth in Canada who have been
deeply affected by the epidemic, we appreciate the opportunity to share our experiences on the
ongoing opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis and how we, together, can take fresh approaches to
combat them. Youth influencers have described the impact on their families, friends, and
communities, saying:
“There [are] lots of issues of opioid use and [opioid poisoning] at school but it’s
still not talked about”.
“My city is getting hit a lot more by [the] opioid crisis – resources [are] limited
because funding is getting cut. It impacts [the] community; those who rely on
these resources, those who live, work, and visit.”
It is crucial that our experiences and what we’ve learned through OTI are centered in the proposed
solutions to the opioid epidemic. Youth have direct exposure and vulnerability to opioids through
2 “Safer”, as opposed to safe spaces, acknowledges safety as an always evolving goal-in-progress, requiring
intentionality and alertness to individual responses within the group dynamic. A space that is safe for some might not be
safe for all.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
A space that is safe for some might not be
safe for all.

social settings and peer pressure. They face significant mental health challenges and stressors,
increasing the risk of substance misuse as a coping mechanism. We are facing unprecedented
challenges that require immediate action, and we urge the House of Commons to listen attentively
to our perspectives and to recognize and act on the urgency of our asks
Recommendations
The following recommendations, brought forth by youth peer influencers from the OTI group are
organized at the individual, social, and system levels. On the individual level, our recommendations
speak to one-on-one interactions between adults and youth, aiming to address the opioid epidemic
and toxic drug crisis through intervention, response, and prevention.
At the broader, systemic level, these recommendations connect to provincial and national policies
that build out support and capacity for addressing the crisis. The House of Commons serves as a
critical conduit, working to bring these policies into communities, helping to foster collaboration
across all levels of society. This upstream approach tackles the opioid epidemic at its roots by
addressing the problem through coordinated efforts involving individuals, communities, and
governing bodies.

Individual Level Recommendations:
•
Seek out opportunities to add to your education and awareness: At a personal level, all
adults who interact with youth—whether as parents, educators, healthcare providers, or
community members—can benefit from increasing their knowledge of opioids, substance
misuse, and the stigma surrounding these topics. Listen to the experiences of young people
and use language that highlights systemic failures rather than blaming individuals for their
choices.
•
Be an adult ally: As an adult who influences youth—whether through personal
relationships or professional roles—actively support their journeys. Help them develop
healthy coping mechanisms, set personal boundaries, and foster compassion and open
communication. Your role as an ally can be instrumental in their wellbeing.
•
Get Naloxone4 training: As someone who engages with youth, it’s essential to learn about
Naloxone, understand how it works, how to administer it, and where to get it. Keep a
Naloxone kit in spaces where you interact with youth, such as homes, workplaces, or
recreational areas. Help young people access Naloxone if they face barriers to obtaining it.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Help young people access Naloxone if they face barriers to obtaining it.

Social Level Recommendations:
•
Invest in and design more community-led support programs: Invest funds into the
community-led organizations that are already doing intervention work and increase access
to youth programming to support upstream prevention approaches.
•
Create school-based prevention programs: Work with schools to create educational
programming on opioids, the opioid epidemic, and substance use in general. Create
4 Naloxone is a medication that can temporarily reverse the effects of an opioid overdose and allow
time for medical help to arrive.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Create
4 Naloxone is a medication that can temporarily reverse the effects of an opioid overdose and allow
time for medical help to arrive.

consistent and engaging programming to help youth develop their decision-making skills
and critical thinking.
•
Encourage stigma reduction: Have open conversations about substance misuse,
addiction, and recovery. Avoid using stigmatizing terms such as “addict” or “junkie” and call
people in when they use these terms. Avoid using fear tactics and give youth all the
information they need to make their own decisions.
•
Put informative posters in public spaces: Advertise addiction services/resources in the
bathrooms of schools, community spaces, malls, and bars/clubs.
System Level Recommendations:
•
Implement follow-ups, check-ins, and referrals for individuals accessing detox and
treatment centres: Have effective follow-up care to ensure long-term recovery and prevent
relapse. Support individuals in accessing additional supports, such as peer-to-peer
mentorship, mental health services, or post-recovery programming. In addition, these
centres should have a liaison who follows-up with individuals after their first overdose.
•
Increase funding and access to culturally competent and holistic spaces for healing:
Cultural connectedness and identity can help those struggling with addiction and should be
included in treatment plans. This is especially important for people who are First Nations,
Inuit, or Métis, as the implications of colonialism and intergenerational trauma highly
impacts Indigenous communities. By using approaches that address the physical, mental,
emotional, and spiritual components of recovery, you create a more comprehensive healing
journey.
•
Create follow-ups plans after injuries or accidents: Healthcare providers, such as
physicians and hospital staff, in collaboration with community health organizations, should
be responsible for developing comprehensive follow-up plans for individuals who are
prescribed opioids after an injury or accident. These follow-up plans should include regular
check-ins, alternative pain management options, and mental health support to prevent the
onset of substance dependency. At the system level, this requires coordination between
healthcare institutions, policymakers, and insurers to ensure that follow-up care is
standardized and accessible to all patients, particularly those at higher risk of developing
an addiction.
Conclusion
Over the Influence (OTI) is a vital initiative that amplifies youth voice in addressing the opioid crisis
in Canada. By providing a platform for young people to share their experiences, engage in open
discussions, and advocate for change, OTI empowers youth to become active participants in
creating safer, healthier communities. The program's recommendations, which span individual,
social, and system levels, reflect a comprehensive approach to tackling the opioid epidemic and
toxic drug crisis at its roots. By listening to and investing in youth, we not only address current
challenges more effectively but also pave the way for long-term solutions that will benefit future
generations.

Appendix: Youth’s Perspective on the Issue
The following recommendations have been brought forth by youth directly, and include quotes with
their thoughts and perspectives:

Invest in the future generation:
Investing in and listening to youth voices is essential because they represent the future of our
society. As the upcoming generation, their ideas, perspectives, and well-being will shape the world
to come. Ignoring their input is not only inequitable but also impractical: By taking into
consideration our upstream recommendations, there will be less harm to youth in the long-run. It’s
estimated that addressing issues at the source could prevent third-to-half of mental health struggles
from forming among young people (Colizzi et al., 2020). Their inclusion decreases the possibility of
long –term usage and addiction and they will be able to put their time, energy, and fresh perspective
into contributions to the country as a whole. It is crucial to take their perspectives into
consideration and ensure they are active participants in creating solutions for issues that impact
them.

“Youth are the future, we should be investing in them and listening to them.”
“Youth are affected by it so why wouldn’t you take [them] into consideration.”
"There's a need to have these conversations and have these programs. As someone who has been
in the OTI youth influencer, it's a lot of wishing and hoping that the words we share are taken
seriously.”
Build a comprehensive understanding:
Addressing critical issues requires a comprehensive approach and consideration of all dimensions
and impacts. Youth perspectives are especially crucial when the stakes are as high as life and
death. By focusing on the adult experience and leaving out the youth experiences, there are gaps
that can undermine the overall effectiveness of the approach.
“If you really want to be open to discussing how it looks to face the issue, you have to discuss the
issue at all the levels.”
“As morbid as it is, it is life or death, and we don’t want [youth] dying.”
“You can’t solve anything if you only solve half of it.”
“I feel like [adults] understand it's a crisis (maybe some don't) but the big thing is that nobody is
including youth voice in anything related to the opioid crisis. Interventions are for adults, kids aren't
learning anything in school, nobody is asking them.”

Listening to youth voices is crucial for developing lifelong solutions to the challenges they face.
When young people feel heard, they are more likely to engage actively and contribute their unique
perspectives and innovative ideas. This sense of being valued encourages them to care more about
the issues at hand and to participate in meaningful ways, such as sharing perspective, insight, and
ideas for solutions. By fostering an environment where youth input is genuinely considered, we not
only address current problems more effectively but also empower the next generation to continue
finding and implementing solutions throughout their lives.
“If youth know they’re being listened to they’ll be more inclined to speak up…they’ll care more…”
“From my perspective adults don't care about youth voice, [they think] that they don't have anything
to share, that their voice isn't valid…youth influencers are very smart, they're the ones being
affected, they want to make change. They need other people to connect to so they can be like ‘you
have power, you need to do this.”

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Joint Brief to the Standing Committee on Health
Study on the Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
Montreal Public Health – Toronto Public Health – Vancouver Coastal Health
Submitted by Dr. Mark Lysyshyn, Deputy Chief Medical health Officer, Vancouver Coastal Health
On behalf of
•
Dr. Mylène Drouin, Directrice régionale, Direction régionale de santé publique de Montréal
(Montreal Public Health)
•
Dr. Eileen Devilla, Medical Officer of Health, Toronto Public Health
•
Dr. Patty Daly, Chief Medical Health Officer, Vancouver Coastal Health
Importance of evidence-based harm reduction in response to the toxic drug crisis
A. Context and trends in the toxic drug crisis.
The toxic drug crisis continues to worsen in Canada’s largest urban centres, with the unregulated drug
supply becoming increasingly more toxic and deadly, ending more lives and causing life-altering harm to
many people who survive poisoning events (commonly called “overdoses”).1 As the Authorities
responsible for public health in the country’s three largest cities, we share the observation that Canada
is in the throes of a national emergency, and that government leadership at all levels is needed to
address this crisis. In all three of our jurisdictions, drug poisoning deaths have significantly increased
since 2019. In Montreal, toxic drug deaths increased from 137 in 2019 to 172 in 2022 and 182 in 2023; in
Toronto, suspect drug-related deaths increased from 495 in 2019 to 740 in 2022 and 733 in 2023; 2,3 and
in Vancouver, deaths increased from 250 in 2019 to 578 in 2022 and 652 in 2023.4 In addition to these
deaths, toxic drug poisonings are also having significant impacts on housing service providers, first
responders, emergency departments and hospitals.
Alarming and rapid changes in the drug supply have occurred in each of our jurisdictions, worsening
since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Increasingly toxic analogs of contaminants – such as
fentanyl, carfentanil, benzodiazepines (benzos), and nitazenes, as well as xylazine and medetomidine,
both tranquilizers approved only for use on animals – are regularly appearing in the street supply. All
three of our jurisdictions have also witnessed a significant change in consumption patterns of
1 In this brief, we may use the term “drug poisoning” rather than overdose, because in the context of a highly
contaminated drug supply, people don’t know the potency or even the substances they are consuming. Thus, they
are not misjudging dosage and overdosing, but being harmed by poisoned substances.
2 Office of the Chief Coroner, Ontario, extracted April 2024.
3 Suspect drug-related deaths are based on a syndromic surveillance approach and include deaths where the
coroner indicated that they suspect the death may be drug-related based on preliminary investigation.
4 BC Coroners Service (2024), “Unregulated Drug Deaths in BC,” Statistical Report.

org: Direction régionale de santé publique de Montréal / Toronto Public Health / Vancouver Coastal Health
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
and overdosing, but being harmed by poisoned substances. 2 Office of the Chief Coroner, Ontario, extracted April 2024. 3 Suspect drug-related deaths are based on a syndromic surveillance approach and include deaths where the coroner indicated that they suspect the death may be drug-related based on preliminary investigation. 4 BC Coroners Service (2024), “Unregulated Drug Deaths in BC,” Statistical Report.

unregulated drugs over the past few years, from predominantly injection to significantly or
predominantly inhalation. The crisis has touched so many people in Canada, with some of the most
marginalized communities contending with the intersecting crises of mental health issues,
homelessness, poverty, and lack of affordability in our urban centres. In Montreal, and Vancouver, more
than three quarters of drug poisoning deaths are occurring in private or other residences, which include
social housing, single room occupancy hotels and shelters. In Toronto, in 2022, close to two-thirds of
opioid poisoning deaths occurred in private residences.5 In all three jurisdictions, at least half of those
who died were using substances alone.5,6 Finally, many people who are dying from toxic drugs are using
drugs occasionally or may even be newer to substance use.
The increasingly toxic mix of substances in the unregulated supply is the primary driver of drug
poisoning deaths. We anticipate that the current toxicity of the supply will persist – if not worsen – until
people are able to access programs offering prescribed medications as alternatives to the poisoned drug
supply.
Canada’s historical experience of drug regulation indicates that we are not going to arrest our way out
of this crisis. For all the effort and considerable expense spanning decades, drug enforcement has not
succeeded at significantly reducing the availability of illegal drugs or the prevalence of substance use
itself. Rather, enforcement measures can put substance users at greater risk of death. Drug makers and
dealers have been incentivized to use more and more potent substances to avoid detection by law
enforcement agencies. There is also evidence that police seizures create perturbations in the
unregulated opioid market, which can result in greater uncertainty of the supply’s potency, and that
drug seizures are associated with higher rates of drug poisoning mortality.7
B. Providing an appropriate balance between harm reduction and treatment approaches.
As we respond to the toxic drug emergency that is occurring across Canada, we see a critical need for
the federal government to work closely with other levels of government to ensure health systems can
implement a comprehensive suite of culturally safe health services. From a public health perspective,
deepening the national resolve to confront this crisis is especially necessary in the face of growing and
often misinformed public opposition to evidence-based interventions that have been shown to save
lives.
Harm reduction measures, which aim to reduce harm associated with substance use without requiring
reduction or cessation of use, and addiction treatment services, which aim to reduce or eliminate use,
are both medically necessary health services that enable people who use substances in harmful ways to
survive and, when they are ready, to change their patterns of drug use. Both treatment and harm
reduction are pillars of a serious response to our worsening drug toxicity crisis; neither should be
prioritized to the exclusion of the other. Broader societal supports are also needed to wrap around
these point-of-care responses. For example, in Vancouver, an overdose outreach team follows up with

6 In 2022, in Toronto, 50% of confirmed opioid poisoning deaths occurred without the presence of another
individual who could intervene at the time of overdose; however, this information was missing in 40% of cases.
7 Cano, Manuel, et al. (2024), “A Scoping Review of Law Enforcement Drug Seizures and Overdose Mortality in the
United States,” International Journal of Drug Policy 124: 104321.

in Toronto, 50% of confirmed opioid poisoning deaths occurred without the presence of another individual who could intervene at the time of overdose; however, this information was missing in 40% of cases. 7 Cano, Manuel, et al. (2024), “A Scoping Review of Law Enforcement Drug Seizures and Overdose Mortality in the United States,” International Journal of Drug Policy 124: 104321.

every person seen in local emergency departments for drug poisoning to try to connect them to harm
reduction, addiction treatment or other health and social services after they have been discharged. But
most significantly, we need to ensure that those who are using unregulated drugs and are at high risk of
drug toxicity have access to stable and affordable housing, mental health services, and employment
opportunities.
Prevention of problematic substance use must also be central to our response. Acting on the social
determinants of health, supporting early childhood development, working with Indigenous people and
communities, supporting people affected by chronic pain, and programs for vulnerable groups such as
at-risk youth or workers in the construction and trades sectors are examples of promising prevention
approaches.8
We, therefore, encourage the federal government to recognize and communicate the necessity of harm
reduction approaches – concomitant with prevention and treatment approaches – clearly and
consistently to the public. We hope that the Standing Committee on Health will recognize that
expanding addiction treatment alone will not be sufficient to respond to the crisis, for the following
reasons:
● There are often delays in and barriers to accessing treatment services, and we want to make
sure that people do not die while they are waiting for treatment. Wait times need to be
eliminated, but we understand that access to treatment will often not be immediate,
necessitating other layers of protection for people who use substances.
● Treatment for addiction, a chronic relapsing illness, does not work for everyone. While some
people are not yet ready for treatment services, many who do seek treatment return to using
substances, and this will happen repeatedly for some. Unsuccessful withdrawal management
(detox) and treatment also carry risks. Those who relapse are at a greater risk of dying from
poisoned drugs because their tolerance declined during detox or treatment – yet many resume
using at the same level with which they were previously familiar. The risk of drug poisoning
because of reduced tolerance is particularly high for people who are released from correctional
institutions.
● Effective pharmacological addiction treatments are not available for all drugs at risk of
contamination, such as cocaine and methamphetamines. Even for treatment of opioid use
disorder, the available pharmaceutical options are limited and not universally effective. There is
an urgent need for expanded treatment options to better meet people’s diverse health needs.
Expanding the range of treatment options would provide more tailored and effective support for
those facing addiction and enhance the effectiveness of the public response to the toxic drug
crisis.
C. Evidence on public health measures that are saving lives and reducing harm.
● Supervised consumption
Supervised consumption sites are spaces where people can use drugs under the supervision of
trained responders who can assist in the event of an overdose. An exemption to the Controlled
8 Public Health Agency of Canada (2018), “Preventing problematic substance use in youth”, Report.

org: Direction régionale de santé publique de Montréal / Toronto Public Health / Vancouver Coastal Health
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
An exemption to the Controlled
8 Public Health Agency of Canada (2018), “Preventing problematic substance use in youth”, Report.

Drugs and Substances Act is required to operate a supervised consumption site in Canada.
Overdose prevention sites, implemented as emergency responses to the drug toxicity crisis, are
lower-barrier sites offering supervised consumption and other harm reduction services, where
overdose response is typically provided by people with lived or living experience of substance
use. Provinces and Territories can obtain a class exemption to the Controlled Drugs and
Substance Act to operate overdose prevention sites as urgent public health needs sites. In
British Columbia overdose prevention sites are authorized under a provincial Ministerial Order.
Over 25 supervised consumption sites and/or overdose prevention sites have been
implemented in our three jurisdictions.
At Insite in Vancouver, Canada’s first supervised consumption site, there has never been an
overdose death after more than 20 years of operation. Recent research has found that
implementing multiple supervised consumption sites in Toronto significantly decreased fatal
overdoses in the neighbourhoods surrounding the sites.9 A recent scoping review into the past
decade of global research on the impacts of supervised consumption sites found that these sites
were associated with reduced rates of drug-related infections and disease transmission, reduced
risk of non-fatal overdoses, and increased access to treatment and other health services.10 The
review also confirmed that supervised consumption sites were not associated with a significant
increase in drug use or increased rates of drug-related crime.
While evidence of the individual and social benefits of supervised consumption is strong, it is
important to recognize that patterns of drug use have changed since this harm reduction
intervention was first implemented in Canada, and that the focus on supervised injection at
most established sites may not meet the needs of a population that is increasingly inhaling
substances. We have, for example, seen people inhaling drugs directly outside of supervised
injection sites and other harm reduction services so that staff can respond to drug poisoning
events should they occur because of inhalation. More broadly, the gap in inhalation services is
likely contributing to more substance use outdoors, which may be creating a perception of
increased public drug use. The lack of supervised inhalation services may also be contributing to
a higher number of deaths, even though inhalation has a lower risk than injection as a mode of
consumption. Many jurisdictions are struggling to offer supervised inhalation services due to the
difficulty in offering these services indoors, and the challenges of finding appropriate sites for
outdoor services in dense urban environments. Our health systems must increase access to
supervised inhalation services, but it is also important that existing supervised injection services
remain in place.
● Naloxone and harm reduction supply distribution
Naloxone and harm reduction supplies, including those for inhalation, are pivotal components of
evidence-based public health measures that are crucial for saving lives and reducing harm
9 Rammohan, Indhu, et al. (2024), “Overdose Mortality Incidence and Supervised Consumption Services in Toronto,
Canada: An Ecological Study and Spatial Analysis,” The Lancet Public Health 9(2): E70-E87.
10 Dow-Fleisner, Sarah, et al. (2022), “Impact of Safe Consumption Facilities on Individual and Community
Outcomes: A Scoping Review of the Past Decade of Research,” Emerging Trends in Drugs, Addictions, and Health 2:
100046.

text:
Indhu, et al. (2022), “Impact of Safe Consumption Facilities on Individual and Community Outcomes: A Scoping Review of the Past Decade of Research,” Emerging Trends in Drugs, Addictions, and Health 2: 100046.

among drug users. Take-Home Naloxone (THN) programs empower individuals and communities
by providing access to naloxone, a life-saving medication that reverses opioid overdoses,
alongside training on its administration. Evidence consistently shows that increased accessibility
to naloxone significantly reduces fatalities associated with opioid overdoses. With the increased
potency of unregulated drugs due to newer adulterants such as nitazenes, however, greater
doses of naloxone are often required to reverse drug poisoning events.
Similarly, the distribution of harm reduction supplies, including sterile needles and syringes,
plays a vital role in preventing the transmission of infectious diseases such as HIV and hepatitis C
among people who use drugs. These interventions not only benefit the individuals who directly
use the services by promoting safer drug consumption practices and enhancing their health
outcomes but also confer broader community benefits. In addition to sterile needles and
syringes, the distribution of inhalation equipment has become increasingly important. This is in
response to the emergence of inhalation as a preferred method for consuming drugs,
particularly opioids. Providing inhalation equipment also aims to reduce the transition to
injection drug use. Naloxone and drug equipment distribution contribute to public health by
reducing the spread of infectious diseases and decreasing the burden on emergency medical
services and healthcare systems.
● Drug checking
In each of our jurisdictions, drug checking has become an essential service for people who use
unregulated drugs to understand the risks in the drugs they are planning to use and an
important tool for health authorities to understand the constantly changing risks in the drug
supply. Various technologies can be used but test strips, spectrometers and more advanced
laboratory methods are now all being used as part of community drug checking programs in
many jurisdictions. Drug checking has also become a common harm reduction measure at music
festivals and other large events in our jurisdictions. Health authorities and community
organizations can use information derived from drug checking programs to distribute toxic drug
alerts to warn people who use drugs, service providers and others about risks in the drug supply
as the information emerges in real time. While evidence to support drug checking is still
emerging, the intervention is a promising harm reduction approach.
● Prescribed medications as alternatives to the toxic drug supply
The toxic unregulated drug supply is the cause of this crisis. Overdose deaths will continue
unless we can separate people from exposure to the toxic drug supply. People who undergo
treatment and have “recovered” from addiction remain at risk of overdose and death if they
relapse and are re-exposed to the toxic drug supply. Medications such as methadone and
buprenorphine/naloxone, referred to as opioid agonist treatment (OAT), are prescribed
pharmaceutical alternatives to the toxic opioid drug supply. They have been shown to reduce
withdrawal symptoms, decrease use of unregulated opioids and other drugs and significantly
reduce the risk of overdose and death in those who take them. Injectable medications such as
diacetylmorphine (heroin) and hydromorphone, referred to as injectable opioid agonist
treatment (iOAT), have similarly been shown to reduce the risk of overdose and death, as well as

org: Direction régionale de santé publique de Montréal / Toronto Public Health / Vancouver Coastal Health
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Injectable medications such as
diacetylmorphine (heroin) and hydromorphone, referred to as injectable opioid agonist
treatment (iOAT), have similarly been shown to reduce the risk of overdose and death, as well as

reduce criminal activity, in those who take them.11 In addition to OAT which is available in all
three jurisdictions, iOAT programs exist in Toronto and Vancouver, and are being implemented
in many jurisdictions across Canada. OAT and iOAT can work for some people if the treatment is
effective for the drugs to which they are addicted – but only so long as people remain on
treatment (referred to as treatment retention). However, retention has been a challenge given
the strict conditions under which these medications must currently be dispensed, and because
OAT is not effective for many of the drugs people are now consuming. For instance, in
Vancouver, only about 4,500 people are on OAT as of March 2024 while it is estimated that over
three times as many people have an opioid use disorder.12
In our jurisdictions, because traditional OAT has proven less effective in the context of the
increase in fentanyl and other contaminants to the unregulated drug supply, there has also been
an expansion of Health Canada-supported programs that prescribe other pharmaceutical
alternatives to people at high risk of drug poisoning, accompanied by other health and social
services. While evidence that these interventions improve health and mortality outcomes is still
somewhat limited and based on small cohort studies, some research suggests that these
programs are associated with fewer hospital admissions and emergency department visits and
lower mortality rates.13 We believe that research must be conducted into expanding the options
for other pharmaceutical alternatives, including fentanyl and alternatives to stimulant drugs
such as cocaine and crystal methamphetamine. Research is also needed to examine alternative
controlled models for providing pharmaceutical alternatives to those at risk so that medications
can help the greatest number of people while minimizing harm to others if the medications are
diverted. Ensuring these models are culturally safe must also be a priority as data from First
Nations Health Authority in British Columbia shows that First Nations people are
disproportionally affected by this crisis.14
We understand that there are concerns among Standing Committee members that prescribed
hydromorphone is being diverted and being consumed by youth, and that this could lead to
young people developing addiction. Currently, in our three jurisdictions, there is no evidence
that hydromorphone is contributing to increased rates of opioid addiction or toxic drug
poisoning among youth. For example, there has not been an increase in new diagnoses of opioid
use disorder among young people under 25 years in BC since the province introduced its
prescribed safer supply policy in 2020; rather, the rate of new cases among youth 19-24 years
11 Oviedo-Joekes, Eugenia, et al. (2009), “Diacetylmorphine versus Methadone for the Treatment of Opioid
Addiction,” New England Journal of Medicine 316: 777-86.
12 British Columbia Centre for Disease Control (2024), “Unregulated drug poisoning emergency dashboard”,
Dashboard. OUD population estimate from Nosyk et al (2021).
13 Gomes, Tara, et al. (2022), “Clinical Outcomes and Health Care Costs among People Entering a Safer Opioid
Supply Program in Ontario,” Canadian Medical Association Journal 194(36): E1233-E1242; Slaunwhite, Amanda, et
al. (2023), “Effect of Risk Mitigation Guidance for Opioid and Stimulant Dispensations on Mortality and Acute Care
Visits during Dual Public Health Emergencies: Retrospective Cohort Study,” BMJ 384: E076336; Ledlie, Shaleesa, et
al. (2024), “Prescribed Safer Opioid Supply: A Scoping Review of the Evidence,” International Journal of Drug Policy
125: 104339.

(2024), “Prescribed Safer Opioid Supply: A Scoping Review of the Evidence,” International Journal of Drug Policy 125: 104339. 14 First Nations Health Authority (2024), “Community Situation Report: January 2024”, Situation Report.

has been decreasing since 2017 and has remained low and stable for youth under 19 between
2010 and 2022.15
D. Reducing stigma through harm reduction public policies.
The stigmatization of people who use drugs is a pervasive issue that significantly impacts their health,
well-being, and access to care. This societal stigma manifests through negative stereotypes and
prejudices, often portraying drug users as morally flawed or criminal, rather than individuals facing a
health issue. Such stigmatization not only marginalizes people who use drugs, pushing them further to
the peripheries of society but also discourages them from seeking help for fear of judgment,
discrimination, or legal repercussions.16 The consequences are profound, exacerbating the challenges of
addiction and hindering efforts towards recovery and harm reduction. Stigma affects not just the
individual's mental and physical health but also their social connections, employment opportunities, and
housing stability17. Breaking down this stigma is essential for creating an environment where people feel
safe to access the support and services they need, ultimately facilitating a more compassionate,
effective approach to drug use and its related complexities. The Standing Committee on Health should
recognize the need for the implementation of harm reduction policies, as advocated by the Canadian
Public Health Association, to promote a health-focused approach that prioritizes public health and
human rights over punitive measures, thereby reducing stigma and discrimination, while supporting
those affected by drug use.18
E. Recommendations
Cities across Canada are facing complex and unprecedented challenges related to the drug poisoning
crisis. A comprehensive response to this crisis must include culturally safe actions across the four pillars
of the Canadian Drugs and Substances Strategy: prevention, harm reduction, treatment, and
enforcement.
As the leaders responsible for public health in Canada’s three largest cities, we call on the Government
of Canada to provide support that is commensurate with the scale of the crisis and the degree of impact
on the health of Canadians.
We recommend that the Government of Canada:
1. Modernize the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act to reflect a public health perspective,
and, in the shorter term, simplify the process for health authorities and community agencies
to apply for and receive Section 56.1 exemptions to provide lifesaving supervised
consumption, overdose prevention, and drug-checking services.
15 BC Centre for Disease Control (2023), “Opioid Use Disorder among Youth in BC”, Infographic.
16 National Institute on Drug Abuse (n.d.), “Stigma and discrimination”, Website.
17 Public Health Agency of Canada (2022), “A primer to reduce substance use stigma in the Canadian health
system”, Report.
18 Canadian Public Health Association (2024), “Framework for a Public Health Approach to Substance Use,” Position
Statement.

2. Enhance access to evidence-based and culturally safe treatment for opioid use disorder, such
as OAT and iOAT, that reduce exposure to the toxic drug supply and decrease the risk of toxic
drug death.
3. Reduce the administrative and regulatory barriers to developing and implementing new harm
reduction and addiction treatment services.
4. Fund programs, research, surveillance, monitoring and evaluation to explore controlled
models for the distribution of a broader range of pharmaceutical alternatives to the toxic drug
supply to people at highest risk of toxic drug poisoning, including those that regularly use
fentanyl and those with stimulant use disorder.
5. Expand programs and research on harm reduction, including Take-Home Naloxone and harm

prevention of problematic substance use, including investment in the social determinants of
health, early childhood development, support for Indigenous people and communities, and
programs for at-risk youth.
