developing and implementing public policy and practices that enhance the health of individuals,
communities and the entire city
Vancouver Coastal Health (VCH) is one of five regional health authorities in British Columbia working in
partnership with the Ministry of Health to provide high quality, appropriate and timely health services to
British Columbians.
Guided by our core values of we care for everyone, we are always learning and we strive for better
results, we deliver community and acute care services to more than 1.25 million people—25 per cent of
the province’s population—including First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples living in the region.
Under B.C.’s Public Health Act, Medical Health Officers provide leadership for Public Health programs
that assess and monitor the health of our communities, and address the social, environmental and
structural factors, largely outside the health-care system, that impact population health.
We build collaborative partnerships, address conditions that create health inequities, consider the needs
of vulnerable groups, and focus on creating supportive environments for everyone in the VCH region to
achieve positive health outcomes.
Expert staff that support this work include public health nurses, environmental health officers, licensing
officers, tobacco reduction coordinators, epidemiologists and surveillance analysts, policy analysts,
speech-language pathologists, dental staff, harm reduction experts, and many others.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Brief Submission: Transforming the Response to BC’s Toxic drug crisis: A First Nations Health Authority
Perspective
Between April 2016 and April 2024, the toxic drug crisis has claimed over 14,500 lives in British Columbia (BC) (1).
Despite the increase of various mainstream harm-reduction initiatives, First Nations Peoples have continued to
experience disproportionate negative impacts, including toxic drug-poisoning events and deaths (2). In 2023,
17.8% of all deaths from toxic drugs in BC were First Nations, while we only represent 3.4% of the BC population
(2,3).
Prior to the toxic drug crisis being declared a public health emergency in 2016, the First Nations Health Authority
(FNHA) was already on the frontlines addressing this crisis, as substance use by First Nations people, along with its
consequences, is related to the systemic inequities and health disparities caused by colonialism that the FNHA
works to change. We were the first health authority in BC to develop a “Framework for Action” to address the toxic
drug crisis.
Our role is to engage with communities and expand our public health response to the toxic drug crisis in
collaboration with our health governance partners.
This submission offers an overview of the toxic drug crisis from a First Nations perspective, emphasizing the unique
challenges faced by First Nations communities and individuals, and addressing the negative impact of policies such
as involuntary treatment and restricting decriminalization on First Nations communities. The FNHA calls upon the
Standing Commitee on Health (HESA) to include a First Nations perspective in its study on the opioid epidemic and
toxic drug crisis that highlights culturally safe, stigma-free, trauma-informed, and community-led solutions to
address the crisis effectively and in a timely manner.
The Scope of the Toxic Drug Crisis
The toll of the toxic drug crisis on First Nations communities is alarming. In 2023, 448 First Nations people died due
to toxic drugs, a 10.3% increase from 2022. In the first part of 2024 (January 1, 2024 – July 31, 2024) (4), there
were 248 First Nations deaths due to toxic drug poisoning. These numbers reveal a deepening disparity, as First
Nations people in 2024 continue to die at rates 6.4 times higher than other BC residents. First Nations women and
young people are also disproportionately affected, with First Nations women representing 40.3% of toxic drug
deaths so far in 2024, compared to 23.5% for other female residents. In 2023, 37.3% of First Nations toxic drug
deaths were among females -- i.e., FN females are 11.7 times more likely to die of a toxic drug poisoning when
compared with other females in BC.
Particularly concerning is the impact of the toxic drug crisis on First Nations youth. Young people face unique
challenges, including the compounded effects of intergenerational trauma, mental health challenges, and limited
access to appropriate substance-use services. The toxic drug crisis exacerbates existing inequalities in housing,
education, health care access, and other social determinants of health for First Nations, especially First Nations
youth.
The combination of the recent COVID 19 pandemic and the toxic drug crisis has contributed to a sharp decline in
life expectancy for First Nations people in BC, which fell by 7.1 years between 2015 and 2021 (5). This decline
underscores the need for urgent, culturally safe interventions that prioritize the well-being of First Nations.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This decline
underscores the need for urgent, culturally safe interventions that prioritize the well-being of First Nations.

The FNHA’s Approach and Response
The FNHA’s response to date has been rooted in cultural safety, First Nations self-determination, community
engagement, and innovative approaches gathered from shared learnings across FNHA’s five regions. The FNHA
takes an approach that is community-driven and Nation-based, and that supports a continuum of care that meets
people where they are at on their wellness journey. Key initiatives developed or supported by the FNHA include:
•
Culturally Safe Harm-Reduction Services: The FNHA has developed and funded culturally safe,
community-based harm-reduction programs, such as expanding access to opioid agonist therapy (OAT),
establishing peer support groups and outreach teams, funding First Nations-led overdose-prevention
sites, and increasing availability of harm-reduction supplies in communities.
•
Public Education and Awareness: The FNHA has launched targeted communications campaigns and
public education and awareness training programs like the Not Just Naloxone program to increase
awareness of overdose prevention and response.
•
Youth-Focused Initiatives: The FNHA has prioritized youth-specific harm-reduction programs, recognizing
the need for culturally safe spaces where young people can access support without fear of stigma or
judgment. Our programs and support toolkits are designed to assist youth in having supportive
conversations with one another about substances, and to integrate traditional knowledge and land-based
healing. They have been particularly effective in engaging youth.
•
Cultural Programming and Land-Based Healing: The FNHA has expanded cultural programming,
incorporating traditional knowledge, land-based healing, and community-led initiatives to address
substance-use-related harms in a more holistic and effective manner.
•
Access to Treatment and Healing: The FNHA has supported rapid access to treatment, including funding
treatment and healing centres that integrate culturally safe practices to ensure trauma-informed care, as
well as expanded treatment access via a variety of virtual health care services to First Nations people in BC
who have limited access to health care services in their communities
Indigenous Harm-Reduction Model
The FNHA approaches substance use from a health perspective and takes a harm-reduction approach to addiction
and substance use.
Harm reduction is a well-researched and evidence-based public health approach that saves lives by minimizing
harm and potential danger. In 2021, FNHA launched the Indigenizing Harm Reduction (IHR) Study (6), aimed at
creating a First-Nations-specific harm-reduction model that reflects Indigenous knowledge and values. The study
identified four key aspects of harm reduction for First Nations:
1. Relational Practice: First Nations harm reduction is rooted in relationship, connection, and love. A relational
approach to care helps to build trust and create a sense of safety for our relatives who use substances.
2. Wholistic Health: First Nations approaches to harm reduction are wholistic and rooted in culture. This means
providing care that wraps around the person to support their physical, spiritual, mental, and emotional
wellness on their healing journey.
3. Strengths-Based Approaches: First Nations approaches to harm-reduction care draw on the ancestral
strengths of culture, community, and kinship to provide unconditional and inclusive care for all community
members. This includes honouring the expertise and experience of Elders and Peers in delivering harmreduction programs and services.
4. Person-Centered Care: First Nations approaches to harm reduction are grounded in person-centered care,
which respects an individual’s needs, priorities, and autonomy in determining their care plan and allows
flexibility to meet the unique needs of the individual.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Person-Centered Care: First Nations approaches to harm reduction are grounded in person-centered care,
which respects an individual’s needs, priorities, and autonomy in determining their care plan and allows
flexibility to meet the unique needs of the individual.

Barriers and Challenges
The numbers do not tell the full story of the lives lost or the resulting impacts to the families, friends, communities,
and nations. While the FNHA and its systems partners continue the good work to provide culturally safe programs
and services to support those who use substances, it is clearly not enough. First Nations communities and
individuals continue to face significant barriers in addressing the toxic drug crisis. These include:
•
Service Inaccessibility: Rural and remote First Nations communities face limited access to harm-reduction
services and treatment options, including long wait times and restrictive criteria for accessing culturally
safe programs.
•
Anti-Indigenous Racism and Colonial Legacy: Mainstream health systems oŌen lack cultural safety and
fail to recognize the compounding effects of colonialism and intergenerational trauma on substance use
among First Nations people. Racism and discrimination further marginalize those who seek care.
•
Stigma: The stigma surrounding substance use continues to prevent many individuals from accessing lifesaving services, especially in smaller communities where people fear judgment from peers.
•
Funding and Capacity: lack of long-term, sustained, and flexible funding for culturally relevant services,
combined with high levels of staff burnout, pose challenges to maintaining effective programs.
The Politicization of the Toxic drug crisis
The toxic drug crisis has provided a stark backdrop for the implementation of various policy initiatives including the
decriminalization pilot program and safer alternatives to the toxic drug supply.
BC’s decriminalization model, implemented in 2023, has shown promise in reducing the criminalization of people
who use drugs. According to the BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addiction’s May 2024 report (7), there was a
96% decrease in personal-use drug seizures under the 2.5-gram threshold in the first year of decriminalization.
However, following moral panic around this harm-reduction initiative, in April the provincial government
recriminalized drug use in public spaces including parks, public transit and hospitals.
Similarly, the Province’s recent push towards secure involuntary treatment facilities for those who use substances
raises significant concerns for First Nations communities. Research (8,9,10) has shown that involuntary treatment
may exacerbate trauma and lead to negative outcomes, including increased risk of relapse, overdose, and
disengagement from care. This approach further stigmatizes substance use and is counterproductive to the
principles of self-determination and cultural safety.
Forced treatment, particularly in institutional or correctional-like settings, risks retraumatizing individuals with
histories of colonial violence, such as Residential Schools and the Sixties’ Scoop. There is litle evidence supporting
the effectiveness of involuntary care, with studies indicating higher risks of distress and toxic drug poisoning postdischarge. First Nations communities have called for voluntary, culturally safe, and trauma-informed care systems
as more effective and humane approaches to addressing the toxic drug crisis.
Also recently, BC’s prescribed safer supply programs (PSS) which provide prescription alternatives to the toxic,
unregulated drugs, have faced unwarranted scrutiny due to widespread misinformation. Despite clear evidence
(11) supporting the effectiveness of safer supply, the provincial government has continued to reject expansion
further feeding into the backlash against PSS. This backlash has led to the deprescribing of PSS by some service
providers, which research shows encourages individuals back into the unregulated toxic drug supply with lower
opioid tolerance and decrease trust in healthcare services.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This backlash has led to the deprescribing of PSS by some service
providers, which research shows encourages individuals back into the unregulated toxic drug supply with lower
opioid tolerance and decrease trust in healthcare services.

The politicization of the toxic drug crisis threatens progress, especially as the backlash against proven, evidencebased harm-reduction measures that save lives hits First Nations people the hardest, deepening existing inequities.
Path Forward - Wise Practices and Recommendations
To effectively combat the toxic drug crisis and protect the health and well-being of First Nations communities, the
FNHA proposes the following recommendations:
1. Expand Culturally Safe Services: Increase and sustain funding and access to culturally safe, communitybased harm-reduction programs, with a particular focus on specific populations like youth and women
and those in rural and remote communities. This includes expanding OAT, detox services, and overdoseprevention sites, as well as creating targeted initiatives that incorporate traditional knowledge and
cultural practices.
2. Reject Involuntary Treatment Models: Prioritize the development of compassionate, voluntary, traumainformed care systems that include cultural supports and land-based healing. Any involuntary care
measures must be limited to exceptional cases and accompanied by safeguards, transparency, and
accountability in collaboration with First Nations leaders and communities.
3. Invest in wholistic and wraparound Care: Provide ongoing care that addresses the broader social
determinants of health, such as housing, food security, and transportation, while ensuring that services
are culturally safe and trauma-informed.
4. Promote Harm-Reduction and Safer-Supply Programs: Increase access to harm-reduction and safersupply programs that offer alternatives to the toxic unregulated drug supply, especially for First Nations in
rural and remote areas.
5. Strengthen Community Support: Build community capacity by investing in First Nations health services,
reducing stigma, and increasing public awareness about the toxic drug crisis. Peer support programs and
community-led initiatives can foster trust and engagement with care.
6. Cultural Programming and Land-Based Healing: Continue to fund and support land-based healing
initiatives and other cultural programs that provide First Nations people with opportunities to reconnect
with their cultural identity and support their wellness journeys.
Conclusion
The Toxic drug crisis of 2024 is more deadly than it was nine years ago; the major driver of deaths is due to the
increasingly unpredictable, dangerous, and potentially lethal unregulated drug supply. Every loss is of course felt
deeply by families and communities, and the FNHA calls upon the HESA to lead policy efforts to implement timely
solutions that are First Nations-led, culturally safe, trauma-informed, and appropriately funded. We must create a
climate of hope. We can build hope by stepping up our efforts and by changing how we think about, talk about,
and treat people who use substances.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Submission to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health (HESA): Prioritizing a
Child and Youth Lens in the Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis Study

Children’s Healthcare Canada (CHC), along with our members, urges the Standing Committee
on Health (HESA) to include a child and youth-centered perspective in its study on the opioid
epidemic and toxic drug crisis. Through extensive consultation with our member organizations,
health providers, and leading child health experts, we recognize that this crisis has deep and
far-reaching impacts on Canada’s youngest citizens—impacts that are too often overlooked in
favor of adult-focused interventions. Addressing these gaps is essential, as children and youth
face distinct challenges, vulnerabilities, and barriers when it comes to mental health, substance
use, and addiction.

We respectfully submit this brief to advocate for the inclusion of a comprehensive, evidencebased approach to children’s mental health and substance use in HESA’s study. Children’s
Healthcare Canada would also be honored to convene leading child health experts to testify
before the committee and provide direct insights into the unique needs of children and youth in
this critical study.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Children’s
Healthcare Canada would also be honored to convene leading child health experts to testify
before the committee and provide direct insights into the unique needs of children and youth in
this critical study.

The Urgency of Action for Children and Youth:
From our consultation with children’s healthcare providers, a clear and consistent message
emerged: the current systems of care are failing children and youth. Among the primary
concerns:
Rising Mental Health Pathology in Children: Children and youth are particularly vulnerable in
the current opioid and toxic drug crisis. Data from Statistics Canada's 2022-2023 Canadian
Health Survey on Children and Youth (CHSCY) underscores this vulnerability: 24% of children
and youth aged 5 to 17 reported challenges with their mental health, while only 41% received
the care they needed. Moreover, rates of substance use among youth are climbing, with 13% of
youth aged 12 to 17 reporting cannabis use in the past year. Alarmingly, this survey found that
more children are grappling with serious mental health challenges today than in previous
generations. i
Growing evidence reveals the increasing intersection of mental health disorders and substance
use among children and youth. Early childhood exposure to adverse experiences, including
trauma and family substance misuse, increases the likelihood of youth developing substance
use disorders later in life. Despite these clear correlations, Canada’s healthcare system is
largely unprepared to meet the complex and unique developmental needs of children and youth
caught in the opioid crisis. Their needs demand tailored, age-appropriate, and coordinated
interventions—yet this remains largely absent from the current response.ii

Fragmentation and Inequity in Care: Children and youth in Canada face a fragmented, siloed
system that is failing to meet their complex needs. There is no unified national framework to
ensure consistent, integrated care. Services for mental health and addiction are spread across
disjointed systems with little coordination, resulting in inconsistent care across provinces and

territories. This lack of national integration creates significant gaps, particularly for rural and
Indigenous youth, where geographic isolation exacerbates access issues. In Saskatchewan, for
example, youth suicide rates are alarmingly high due to a combination of inter-generational
trauma, substance use, and isolation, yet services remain scattered and underfunded .

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In Saskatchewan, for
example, youth suicide rates are alarmingly high due to a combination of inter-generational
trauma, substance use, and isolation, yet services remain scattered and underfunded .

The system is siloed between provinces, resulting in inefficiencies in the delivery of support to
children and youth. Research from the Child Health Policy Centre at Simon Fraser University,
details that mental health services for children and youth are often reactive and delayed, failing
to address the early stages of substance use. ii

Systemic Barriers and Stigma: Stigma continues to be one of the greatest barriers preventing
young people from accessing the care they need. Only 41% of children and youth who
experience mental health challenges receive professional support, leaving the majority without
the care they require. i The stigmatization of youth struggling with substance use, compounded
by systemic failures, ensures that young people fall through the cracks of a system not designed
for them. This is especially true for marginalized communities—racialized, Indigenous, and
economically disadvantaged youth who face even greater barriers to accessing equitable care.

Marketing and Substance Use Influences: Marketing and easy access to substances such as
alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis are increasingly targeting youth. In Nova Scotia, alcohol
marketing has contributed to increased substance use among youth, as provincial regulations
are insufficient without a unified federal alcohol act. Data from the CHSCY study also reveals
concerning trends in youth cannabis use, with 13% of youth aged 12 to 17 reporting cannabis
use within the past year. i This, combined with other substance exposures, raises risks for early
addiction and mental health challenges.

Family and Community Involvement: Substance abuse in youth often exists within complex
family dynamics, requiring a family-centered approach. Despite this, many youth are assessed
and treated without involving their families, which undermines the potential for long-term
recovery. In particular, children with caregivers who misuse substances face compounded risks.
Successful programs like the Substance Abuse Program for African-Canadian Youth at CAMH
demonstrate the importance of community-based models that engage families and use culturally
informed care. It is also critical to address the maternal and neonatal impacts of toxic drug use,
ensuring that pregnant individuals and newborns receive appropriate, comprehensive care to
mitigate long-term health consequences and break the cycle of substance use across
generations.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
It is also critical to address the maternal and neonatal impacts of toxic drug use,
ensuring that pregnant individuals and newborns receive appropriate, comprehensive care to
mitigate long-term health consequences and break the cycle of substance use across
generations.

Geographic and Economic Disparities: Rural and remote areas face severe shortages in
mental health and substance abuse services. CHSCY data highlights that youth in rural areas
are more likely to experience unmet mental health needs than those in urban settings.i

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
CHSCY data highlights that youth in rural areas
are more likely to experience unmet mental health needs than those in urban settings.i

Recommendations for HESA’s Consideration
1. Embed a Child and Youth Lens into National Strategies: Children are not small
adults—yet our current approach to the opioid crisis largely borrows from adult-focused
models, ignoring the developmental, emotional, and social realities of childhood and
adolescence. We call on the federal government to incorporate a child and youth lens
into all aspects of the national opioid strategy. This lens must be embedded in the
planning, implementation, and evaluation of interventions and policies aimed at
mitigating the opioid and toxic drug crisis. Without doing so, we risk perpetuating a
system that fails to protect our youngest and most vulnerable.
2. Integrate Services and Care Models for Youth: Children and youth are often
underserved by care models that fail to address their unique developmental needs. We
urge the federal government to incorporate a child and youth-specific lens into all
strategies for addressing mental health and substance use. Integrated "Youth Wellness
Hub" models, emerging in several provinces, should be expanded and adopted
nationally to provide comprehensive, coordinated care that reflects the interconnected
nature of mental health and substance use in children and adolescents. This model
would bridge critical service gaps across systems, ensuring that care is both accessible
and developmentally appropriate for Canada’s youngest populations. Without this focus,
interventions risk failing the children and youth they aim to protect.
3. Invest in Prevention and Early Intervention: We must shift from a reactive model of
care to a proactive one. Early intervention and prevention are critical to stemming the
tide of addiction and mental health disorders. Programs such as PreVenture, which
target early signs of substance use, have shown promising results in reducing substance
abuse among at-risk youth. The federal government should significantly increase
investments in early childhood programs, mental health services, and substance use
prevention strategies, ensuring that these services are universally accessible and
attuned to the needs of youth.
4. Build Integrated, Family-Centered Care Models: Children do not live in isolation; their
experiences are deeply connected to their families and communities. It is essential that
we move towards integrated care models that place families at the center of treatment.
We strongly recommend that the government incentivize the development of codesigned, family-centered models, ensuring that services work collaboratively with
families rather than in isolation.
5. Address Geographic and Socio-Economic Disparities: Youth in rural and remote
areas are at particular risk due to the scarcity of services in these regions. We urge the
government to prioritize equitable access to care for all children and youth, regardless of
their geographic location or socio-economic status. This includes expanding telehealth
and virtual care models that can bridge the gap for rural communities and providing
targeted funding to Indigenous health services to address the needs of youth in these
communities.
6. Invest in Child and Youth Mental Health and Substance Use Research: The federal
government should invest in research focused on the unique mental health and
substance use challenges faced by children and youth. This investment will help build a

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This investment will help build a

robust body of evidence to inform best practices, improve care, and address gaps in the
current system. Research should prioritize early intervention, the impact of trauma,
culturally responsive care, and harm reduction strategies tailored to youth, ensuring that
interventions are informed by the specific needs of diverse communities.
7. Develop a National Standard of Care for Youth Substance Use: The federal
government should develop and implement a national standard of care for youth-specific
mental health and substance use services. Such a standard should be evidence-based,
trauma-informed, and culturally sensitive, with particular attention to marginalized
populations. This would ensure consistency in service delivery across the country, and
hold provinces and territories accountable for providing equitable care to all children and
youth.

The opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis is a multifaceted and urgent issue that requires
immediate attention, particularly from the perspective of Canada’s children and youth. Our
healthcare system is currently failing to meet the needs of these vulnerable populations. We
urge HESA to recognize the importance of including a dedicated child and youth-focused lens in
its study, ensuring that federal policy decisions reflect the realities faced by young Canadians.

Children’s Healthcare Canada stands ready to assist the Committee by convening leading child
health experts to testify and provide further insights on the pressing needs of children and youth
in the context of this crisis. By taking a proactive, integrated, and equitable approach, we can
save young lives and secure a healthier future for all Canadians.

Evidence-based Drug Prevention.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Upstream solutions for Canada’s Opioid Overdose Crisis:
Evidence-based Drug Prevention.

Submitted on September 23, 2024
by Patricia J. Conrod, PhD, Clinical Psychologist
Professor of Psychiatry and Addiction, Université de Montréal, Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in
Preventive Mental Health and Addiction, Research Chair in Social and Community
Pediatrics, Fondation Julien/Marcelle et Jean Coutu, Centre de Recherche, CHU Ste-Justine
Despite having made some strides with respect to reducing adolescent drinking rates, illicit
substance use and substance use disorders (SUDs) remain significantly above national targets for
health promotion and disease prevention in Canada and the United States (1-3). There is also evidence
of increasing morbidity and mortality due to opioids among those aged 15-29 in Canada (2). The wide
scale delivery of effective prevention will help to address an emerging crisis of non-medical
prescription drug use (NMPDU) and opioid overdose deaths amongst youth in North America.
There has been a dramatic increase in the prevalence of past-year prescription drug misuse,
from 2003 - 2021 (3-5). NMPDU is indeed a risk factor for future prescription drug dependence (6),
with evidence of a relationship between increased non-medical use of opioid analgesics and increasing
rates of heroin dependence in the U.S.(4) The number of overdose deaths from prescription pain
relievers has more than quadrupled since 1999 in the U.S.(5) and new data from the Public Health
Agency of Canada indicate a 4-10 times increase in emergency room visits due to opioid poisoning in
Canada over the past 10 years. More people will die from opioid overdoses in Canada this year than
the number of people who died from HIV at the height of its 1995 epidemic (2). The age group with
the fastest growing rate of hospitalisations due to opioid poisoning this decade has been 1524 year olds (2). And despite the lower prevalence of opioid use relative to alcohol use in youth,
more youth have died from opioid use than alcohol use in the past decade in Canada (3).
With the recent emergence of highly potent illicit narcotics, such as Fentanyl, on the illicit
market in Canada, it is extremely important that prevention efforts are directed towards reducing
youth drug experimentation generally, as one single dose of Fentanyl can have fatal consequences.
Now, more than ever, there is a pressing need for effective substance abuse prevention in Canada.
Yet, very few programs have been developed to effectively address illicit drug use among youth and
even fewer have been evaluated with respect to efficacy in preventing NMPDU(3). Moreover, studies
estimate that less than 15% of North American youth are exposed to evidence-based prevention (50).
Prescription drug misuse is very common among youth in Canada, where 15-25 year olds
report the highest and fastest growing rates of prescription drug misuse of any age group (2-3).
According to the 2011 Canadian Alcohol and Drug Use Monitoring Survey (CADUMS), 23% of
Canadians aged 15 and older reported NMPDU in the last 12 months; youth aged 15 to 24 reported
past year use at a rate of 18% (3). NMPDU can involve borrowing from or providing medications to
a friend or relative (i.e., diversion), deliberately hoarding and then using higher-than-recommended
doses, and using medications together with alcohol or other drugs. The OSDUHS study (7) also asks
students about use of prescription opioid pain relievers (e.g., Percocet) without a prescription. Onein-ten (10%) students in grades 7–12 reported using a prescription opioid non-medically in the past
year. The majority (59%) of past year prescription drug misusers reported obtaining the drug from
someone at home. About 2% of students in grades 7–12 reported using prescription stimulants (e.g.,
Ritalin) without a prescription (7).
There are several reasons why we should be concerned about prescription medication use

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
There are several reasons why we should be concerned about prescription medication use

among youth. First, prescription drug use frequently occurs in the context of the simultaneous use of
other drugs (i.e., alcohol and poly-substance use; 15) putting young people at risk for experiencing
adverse drug interactions. Second, youth appear to underestimate the risks associated with prescription
drug use (16), viewing prescription drugs as less dangerous and more socially and legally acceptable
than illicit drugs. This suggests that many youth are unaware of the risk of developing medicationrelated substance dependence or side effects (17). However, one population-based study showed that
the mean age of onset for medication-related SUDs was in the early 20s (18). This suggests there may
be a very short window between the onset of prescription medication use in late adolescence and the
transition into prescription medication dependence in young adults. Consistent with this possibility,
youth who misused prescription drugs in the past year have been shown to be at increased risk for
dependence on prescription medications relative to older age groups (19). Furthermore, misuse of
prescription opioids is linked to risk for future opioid dependence (4-6) and risk for overdose (5). It
is essential that we begin to address the high rate of this very risky activity that has emerged among
youth in our country.
A need for new strategies to reduce and prevent substance misuse in young Canadians
There is a pressing need for effective substance prevention for young people, particularly for
those most at risk of developing substance use problems (18). While substance abuse prevention
programs abound in high schools across the country, few of these have been systematically evaluated
(19-20). Most school-based prevention programs are universal and use some combination of alcohol
and drug awareness, testimonials, flyers, brochures, peer education, and alcohol/drug free activities;
these have been shown to have only weak positive or even negative, iatrogenic effects (20-21). Only a
select few programs have been shown to be consistently effective in reducing alcohol and drug use in
young people, and all of these programs involve face-to-face delivery of interventions that are designed
to build coping skills and other resilience factors in youth and their families (19-21).
We recently published a systematic review of interventions to reduce opioid misuse
sepcifically. Our systematic review of three key international reports (e.g., U.S. Surgeon General’s
2016 Report on Addiction, and the 2018 UNODC Report on International Standards for Drug
Prevention) indicated that the only programs that resulted in reduced use of prescription opioids for
young people were the PROSPER framework and the personality-targeted PreVenture Program.
These effective programs go beyond mass media campaigns or classroom-based drug education. They
either require multiple years of multi-component family and school-based interventions (PROSPER)
or brief psychological workshops delivered by trained and certified professionals (PreVenture). Our
systematic review of more recently published studies also concluded that the recent scientific literature
has focused almost exclusively on pharmacological treatments of opioid use disorder for young
people, with few studies evaluating interventions for early or experimental stages of opioid use (19).
The importance of delivering targeted prevention: While universal prevention programs
might target generic factors implicated in normal drinking and drug experimentation, it is important
to recognised that they are not designed to address factors linked to risk for the development of
problematic durg use, particularly prescription drug misuse (22-25). For example, few programs have
been designed to meet the needs of young people with internalising and externalizing traits, despite
the strong relations of these factors to substance use disorders, and prescription drug misuse (26-35).
The scientific literature indicates indisputable benefits of delivering brief preventive cognitivebehavioural interventions targeting personality and mental health risk factors in schools. Such
programs have been shown to effectively reduce and prevention alcohol and illicit drug use and mental
health symptoms (by a notable 30-80%) among secondary students in multiple published randomised

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Such
programs have been shown to effectively reduce and prevention alcohol and illicit drug use and mental
health symptoms (by a notable 30-80%) among secondary students in multiple published randomised

trials (24, 37-41, 48-49). Trials with college students have also shown efficacy of the program in
reducing alcohol misuse and mental health disorder symptoms (40) and trials with communityrecruited adults living with anxiety disorders (42), and drug dependence (43) (24) have also proven the
efficacy of the personality-targeted approach, including NMUPDs. A recent summary of the findings
from 8 randomised trials of personality-targeted interventions for SUDs suggests moderate effects
sizes (average d=.37-.47) across all substance use outcomes, intervention formats and populations
targeted (44). A ninth randomised trial conducted in Canada further demonstrated long-term
efficacy of this program in reducing substance use disorders over a five-year follow-up period (51)
Despite this evidence in favour of a limited number of drug and alcohol prevention programs,
very few communities are systematically delivering these evidence-based drug prevention programs in
North America (50). Communities are having difficulty making evidence-based decisions on how to
direct their limited resources towards maximum impact. They are also having difficulty accessing the
resources they need to sustain evidence-based prevention, as less than 1% of the total costs of
substance misuse to Canadian society are attributed to the delivery of prevention programs (52).
As a clinical psychologist, researcher and expert on drug and alcohol prevention, I offer the
following recommendations to help increase the pace and quality of delivery of drug prevention in
Canada to better protect our youth in the context of an escalating drug crisis.
1. Health Canada must maintain a review process to assist communities in identifying evidence-based
drug and alcohol prevention programs. This resource will help communities to direct resources
to programs that have the highest probability of producing desired outcomes. Programs with
minimal level of evidence should be rated on the strength of the evidence according to a
transparent set of criteria (e.g., one randomised-controlled trial, one replication). They should also
be scored on a metric that reflects readiness for implementation in the Canadian context. This
resource should be modeled after the U.S. SAMHSA registry of evidence-based prevention
program and practices, or other similar State Registries (e.g., NY State’s OASAS).
2. Federal funding for drug prevention should be made available to communities demonstrating
intention and readiness to implement evidence-based prevention. These funds should be used to
support training, access to program materials, and additional implementation resources for
communities that are under-resourced. It is important to recognise that the few programs that
have been identified as evidence-based are resource-intensive and will involve a significant time
commitment from specialised educational and health professionals.
3. Additional resources should be dedicated to supporting communities in adapting and evaluating
evidence-based programs in new contexts, when knowledge gaps are identified in relation to the
existing evidence base.
4. In light of the growing health threat to young people brought about by the opioid overdose crisis
in North America, Health Canada should incentivise Provinces and Territories in setting statutory
orders and minimum standards for drug prevention.
5. Coordinated implementation resources and evaluation tools should be made available to
communities through the Canadian Research network on Interventions for Substance Misuse
(CRISM). This research network is well-established across the country, but has focused on downstream solutions to the opioid epidemic, such as, replacement therapies for substance use disorder.
Specialised surveillance tools, training and implementation resources are needed, and highly
specialised research infrastructure will help to sustain large-scale prevention efforts.
6. Health Canada should stop investing in drug prevention strategies for which there is limited
scientific evidence, such as poorly designed mass media campaigns.

text:
Supporting Effective, Safe, and Equitable
Medical Use of Opioids for Children in Pain
Recommendations to inform the Standing Committee on Health’s study:
Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
1.
We recommend that the Government of Canada prioritize quality, equitable pain care for
 children as key to addressing the opioid crisis in Canada. As part of this commitment, w
e recommend that the Government – in collaboration with the provinces and territories – suppo
rt implementation of the Pediatric Pain Management standard (CAN/HSO 13200:2023) a
s a required part of hospital accreditation and funding. The standard, released in April 2023,
 has received widespread attention nationally and internationally, but is only considered current for 5
years, giving less than 4 years to ensure it is effectively implemented nationally.
2.
We recommend that the Government of Canada recognize the inextricably linked epidemics of
 untreated pain, substance use, and mental health by prioritizing children’s pain acros
s relevant government programs and grant opportunities, such as the Substance Use a
nd Addictions Program (SUAP). Increased support to these programs is also warranted .
3.
We recommend that the Government of Canada, in alignment with the Pediatric Drug Action Plan
 (2020), recognize that improving children’s access to safe and effective medications an
d implementing ‘child-friendly pharmacare’ includes opioid-based pain medications wh
en indicated. Further, in alignment with Recommendation 7 in the 18th Report from the Stand
ing Committee on Health (“Fostering Healthy Childhoods: A Foundation for Resilient Generation
s”), we recommend that children, youth, and their families be directly engaged as partners i
n the development and implementation of pediatric-specific solutions to pharmacare, including drug and
medical opioid access for pediatric pain management.
Overview
Children are a population disproportionately impacted by pain. The undertreatment of pain is a
 major contributor to the opioid crisis, and pain relief is a primary reason for opioid prescribing
, long term opioid use, nonprescription opioid use, and opioid use disorder amongst youth. Although Canada is a world leader in children’s pain research, children still experience preventable, untreated pain in Canada. One in five children experience chronic pain and two out of three children in Canada experience painful medical procedures without any pain management. Opioids prescribed for acute, surgical, and chronic pain in youth, and poorly managed pain often start a cascade of long-term opioid use and opioid user disorder that persists into adulthood. This makes prevention of opioid use and effective pain management during childhood a leading priority to avoid a lifetime of harm. .

managing pediatric pain can be challenging,
evidence-based solutions are available and
taking steps to deliver care that mitigates this

with mental health or substance use later in life.
Who We Are
Solutions for Kids in Pain (SKIP) is a national
 knowledge mobilization network whose missio
n is to improve children’s pain management
by mobilizing evidence-based solutions thro
ugh coordination and collaboration. Base
d at Dalhousie University, SKIP is worki
ng to address the gap in knowledge mobilizat

nts and caregivers, health professionals, and
hundreds of partners from around the world to improve ch
children’s pain management.
The Canadian Pain Task Force’s final report,
An Action Plan for Pain in Canada (2021)
 recognized that providing timely, equitable,
person-centered pain care is a priority action to transform how pain is understood and treated, and
 to address the opioid crisis in our country. We know that chronic pain costs the Canadian healt
h system an estimated $40 billion annually. We also know that ensuring quality pain care is critical
to address the intersecting public health crises related to chronic pain, addiction, and mental health – espe
especially amongst Canada’s children and youth.
As Canada continues to grapple with these intersecting crises, the Government of Canada must
 address children’s pain as a key part of making children’s health a priority and improving the healt
h outcomes of young people. Critically, patterns of opioid prescribing, opioid use, opioid-relat
ed harms, and risk for opioid use disorder differ for youth as compared with adults. Recognizing
the findings and commitments presented in the 18th Report from the Standing Committee on Health (“Fostering Healthy Childhoods: A Foundation for Resilient Generations”), we emphasize that the burden of children’s pain perpetuates and reveals ongoing inequities in access to healthcare among children. “Living with pain means that a lot of my struggle is invisible and can make it hard
to understand by others. That lack of recognition only pushed me further to believe
that my comfort and wellbeing was not prioritized, instead it was being invalidated.
I was incredibly reluctant to state I had pain in fear of being labelled as ‘drug
seeking’, I equally hesitated to describe the benefits I felt from the opioid
medications to avoid being labeled with substance use disorder. The conversation
would shift from creating a care plan to treat my pain in the best way possible, to a
plan that carried the least stigma or the least risks. I no longer felt like pain control
was amongst the goals of my care team but instead a plan to cater to the stigma of
opioids”.

text:
I no longer felt like pain control
was amongst the goals of my care team but instead a plan to cater to the stigma of
opioids”.
- Youth living with chronic pain

Opioids should not be the first or the only option for pain management for youth; however, they
can be an important tool to manage pediatric pain. It is well-accepted that opioids are safe and
effective at managing certain kinds of pain. However, many young patients who need or use
opioids for moderate to severe pain – especially those in underserved or equity-seeking
populations – face stigma or barriers to care from their health professionals, peers, and family
members. Following up on the recommendations offered in a brief submitted to HESA’s Children’s
Health Study by SKIP (BR12019095 - 24 March, 2023), we offer the Government of Canada the
three above stated priority recommendations to ensure that children are receiving access to
quality pain care across Canada.
Context
SKIP recently completed the “Youth in Pain: Solutions for Effective Opioid Use” project, an 18month Health Canada-funded initiative focused on effective, safe, and equitable opioid use for
youth in pain. The project objectives were to transform evidence into action, share knowledge,
improve practice, and raise awareness about the appropriate medical use of opioids for pain in
youth for families and health professionals. Working with over 85 patient and partners, the project
delivered over 75 new resources and reached over 205,000 Canadians.
The deliverables and partnerships from the Youth in Pain project have been designed to support
the Pediatric Pain Management standard (CAN/HSO 13200:2023) (“the standard”), co-developed
by SKIP and the Health Standards Organization. This standard is the first of its kind globally,
establishing a foundation for the delivery of quality pain management for children from birth to 8
years old in hospitals. It outlines 34 specific criteria with accompanying guidelines detailing how
organizational leaders and healthcare teams can deliver equitable, evidence-based, and personcentered pain care for children. This includes specific criteria focused on safe, effective, and
equitable prescribing and use of opioids for pain. The standard actions the Canadian Pain Task
Force 2021 recommendations to develop national pain management standards to ensure that all
people in Canada have consistent access to pain care and support across jurisdictions. As of
March 31, 2024, the standard has been downloaded >1600 times in 66 countries (1052
downloads from Canada, including all provinces and two territories). The standard received
designation as a National Standard of Canada by the Standards Council of Canada (SCC).
These two efforts from SKIP – the ‘Youth in Pain’ project and the Pediatric Pain Management
standard – have taken action to improve equitable, evidence-informed, and person-centered pain
care for children, but more can and should be done. The recommendations we offer in this
briefing help to create a bridge between HESA’s priority study areas of ‘Children’s Health’ and the
‘Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis’ in Canada, ensuring that children receive the most
effective, safest, and evidence-based access to opioids and other strategies for pain
management.
Conclusion
SKIP urges the Government of Canada to consider implementing the three recommendations
above to ensure that all people in Canada – especially children – have consistent access to pain
care and support across jurisdictions. Much work has and should continue to be done to
disentangle and tackle the complex drivers and factors contributing to the ongoing crises of
mental health, chronic pain, and the opioid epidemic. We know poorly treated pain in children
plays a key role in non-medical substance use and addictions later in life. As such, our
recommendations offer three key steps in addressing pain as the major societal problem that it is,
especially for our youngest and most vulnerable Canadians.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Policy Proposal: Addressing Drug Addiction through Comprehensive Legal and Supportive
Measures
Author: T. Lewis Federal Policy Analyst
(Submitting as a Concerned Private Citizen with Indigenous family members)
Date: August 9, 2024

Policy Proposal: Addressing Drug Addiction through Comprehensive Legal and Supportive
Measures
Author: T. Lewis Policy Analyst
Executive Summary
The increasing prevalence of illicit drug use and its associated societal impacts represent a
pressing humanitarian crisis in Ontario. Public intoxication with illicit drugs has severe implications
for individual health, community safety, and societal well-being. This policy proposal advocates for
making public intoxication with illicit drugs illegal and introduces a compassionate, comprehensive
diversion program that mandates treatment over punishment. The goal is to transform the current
punitive approach into a rehabilitative one, emphasizing the restoration of human potential through
state-of-the-art treatment facilities and robust support systems.
Problem Statement
Ontario's municipalities are overwhelmed by the twin crises of homelessness and drug addiction,
exacerbated by inadequate and unpredictable funding from provincial and federal governments.
The loss of human potential due to illicit drug use, evidenced by over 2,500 annual overdose deaths
in Ontario alone, demands an urgent and multifaceted response. Current ad-hoc funding and
fragmented efforts are insufficient to address the deepening crisis, necessitating a structured and
compassionate approach to both law enforcement and rehabilitation.
Objectives
1. Make Public Intoxication with Illicit Drugs Illegal
- Introduce legislation that prohibits public intoxication with illicit drugs to enhance public
safety and community well-being.
2. Implement a Compassionate Diversion Program
- Develop a court diversion program that mandates attendance at state-of-the-art
treatment facilities instead of traditional punitive measures.
3. Secure Predictable and Expanded Funding
- Advocate for sustained, predictable funding from provincial and federal governments to
support long-term solutions for homelessness, addiction, and mental health crises.
Proposal Components
1. Legislation to Criminalize Public Intoxication with Illicit Drugs
- Draft and pass legislation that makes public intoxication with illicit drugs illegal.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Legislation to Criminalize Public Intoxication with Illicit Drugs
- Draft and pass legislation that makes public intoxication with illicit drugs illegal.

- Ensure law enforcement agencies are equipped with the necessary training to handle
cases compassionately and refer individuals to diversion programs.
Introducing legislation that prohibits public intoxication with illicit drugs is not
merely a legal maneuver but a powerful societal statement. It asserts that open drug
use, regardless of addiction status, will not be tolerated in public spaces This
legislation would make it illegal to be visibly intoxicated by illicit substances in
public areas, similar to existing laws that prohibit public intoxication by alcohol. By
establishing clear legal boundaries, the legislation would serve as a deterrent
against public drug use and help maintain order and safety in public spaces.
The rationale behind this legislation is twofold: it aims to protect the general public
from the disruptive and potentially dangerous behaviours often associated with
drug intoxication, and it sends a strong message that drug addiction, while requiring
compassionate treatment, cannot be allowed to compromise public safety. This
stance is not about shaming individuals or forcing them to hide their addictions but about
fostering a community environment that prioritizes safety and well-being. Public
intoxication with illicit drugs often leads to behaviours that are disruptive and potentially
dangerous, undermining the fabric of a strong, safe society. By criminalizing such conduct,
we set clear boundaries that protect public spaces and encourage individuals struggling
with addiction to seek help in more private, controlled environments. This measure aligns
with broader public health and safety goals, ensuring that our communities remain vibrant
and secure for all residents.
2. Diversion Program for Compassionate Sentencing:
- State-of-the-Art Treatment Facilities: Establish and fund modern, community-centred
detoxification and rehabilitation centres across Ontario. These facilities should offer
comprehensive services, including detoxification, life skills training, mental health support,
and vocational rehabilitation. Research indicates that addiction treatment can be effective,
particularly when tailored to individual needs and integrated with mental health services
(National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2023).
- Compassionate Sentencing: Develop judicial guidelines that mandate individuals
convicted of public intoxication with illicit drugs to attend treatment programs instead of
incarceration. Emphasize the goal of rehabilitation over punishment. Effective addiction
treatment involves changing deeply rooted behaviours, and relapse should be seen as part
of the recovery process rather than a failure (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2023).
Implementing a diversion program for compassionate sentencing is crucial for several
reasons. First, it addresses the root causes of drug addiction by providing comprehensive
treatment rather than punishment, recognizing that addiction is a chronic, relapsing
disorder that alters brain function and behaviour (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2023).

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
First, it addresses the root causes of drug addiction by providing comprehensive
treatment rather than punishment, recognizing that addiction is a chronic, relapsing
disorder that alters brain function and behaviour (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2023).

Research has shown that effective addiction treatment significantly improves health
outcomes and reduces recidivism, helping individuals regain control over their lives
(National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2023). Second, compassionate sentencing reduces the
burden on the criminal justice system, freeing up resources to address more severe crimes
and allowing for a more efficient use of taxpayer money. Lastly, a diversion program aligns
with the principles of public health by treating addiction as a medical condition rather than
a moral failing, promoting recovery, and reintegrating individuals into society as productive
members. This approach not only enhances individual well-being but also strengthens
community safety and cohesion.
- Holistic Treatment Approach: Ensure that treatment facilities provide individualized care
plans addressing addiction, mental health, and socio-economic factors. Incorporate
evidence-based practices and involve healthcare experts, social workers, and community
leaders in the rehabilitation process. Addiction alters brain functions related to reward,
stress, and self-control, making a holistic approach crucial (National Institute on Drug
Abuse, 2023).
- Post-Treatment Support: Implement robust follow-up programs to support individuals'
post-treatment, including housing assistance, employment services, and continuous
mental health care.
3. Funding and Coordination
- Predictable and Sustained Funding: Advocate for expanded, consistent funding from
both provincial and federal governments. This funding should be earmarked for
comprehensive addiction treatment, mental health services, and supportive housing.
- Single Point Person: Appoint a dedicated provincial coordinator with the authority,
resources, and mandate to oversee the crisis response. This role should ensure seamless
coordination across government departments and with municipalities (CBC News, 2023).
- Task Force Development: Form a task force comprising municipal representatives,
healthcare experts, business leaders, and other stakeholders to develop and implement a
detailed, actionable plan tailored to Ontario’s needs.
A three-pronged approach to funding and coordination is essential for the success of this
initiative. First, securing predictable and sustained funding from both provincial and federal
governments is critical to support long-term solutions for homelessness, addiction, and
mental health crises. This stability in funding allows for comprehensive planning and
implementation of effective programs without the disruption of ad-hoc, piecemeal
allocations. Second, appointing a single point person with the authority, resources, and
mandate to oversee the crisis response ensures seamless coordination across government
departments and with municipalities. This centralized leadership can effectively align
various stakeholders' efforts, maximizing the impact of available resources (CBC News,
2023). Lastly, forming a task force comprising municipal representatives, healthcare

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Lastly, forming a task force comprising municipal representatives, healthcare

experts, business leaders, and other stakeholders fosters collaboration and ensures that
the action plan is well-rounded and tailored to Ontario's specific needs. This inclusive
approach leverages diverse expertise and perspectives, enhancing the program's overall
effectiveness and sustainability.
4. Supporting Municipalities
- Crisis Centres: Establish 24/7 crisis centres to alleviate pressure on hospital emergency
rooms and provide immediate support to individuals in need (CBC News, 2023).
- Encampment Transition Resources: Provide tools and resources to transition individuals
from homeless encampments to appropriate support systems, including housing and
addiction treatment services.
The urgency in supporting municipalities cannot be overstated. Municipalities are on the
front lines of the drug addiction crisis, facing unprecedented challenges in managing
homelessness, public safety, and health emergencies. The lack of sufficient and
predictable funding from higher levels of government has left municipalities struggling to
provide necessary services, leading to increased strain on local resources and emergency
services. As Ontario mayors have highlighted, the crisis has escalated beyond the capacity
of municipalities to address independently, resulting in more individuals dying from
overdoses and communities feeling less safe (CBC News, 2023). Immediate and concerted
support is essential to prevent further deterioration of public health and safety. By providing
municipalities with the tools, resources, and consistent funding they need, we can ensure
that they are equipped to offer appropriate supports, such as housing, addiction treatment,
and mental health services. This not only mitigates the immediate crisis but also enables
long-term planning and sustainable solutions, fostering healthier and safer communities for
all residents.
5. Evaluation and Accountability
- Regular Monitoring and Reporting: Implement a robust monitoring and evaluation
framework to assess the effectiveness of the diversion program and treatment facilities.
Regularly publish reports to maintain transparency and accountability.
- Community Feedback Mechanism: Establish channels for community feedback to
continuously improve the program and address emerging challenges.
Evaluation and accountability are critical components of the proposed policy framework to
ensure its success and sustainability. Implementing a robust monitoring and evaluation
framework allows for continuous assessment of the program's effectiveness and provides
data-driven insights to inform necessary adjustments. Specific metrics for success
should include reductions in public intoxication incidents, decreases in overdose
deaths, and improvements in treatment completion rates. Methods for data
collection should involve regular reporting from treatment facilities, law

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Methods for data
collection should involve regular reporting from treatment facilities, law

enforcement agencies, and community feedback mechanisms. A schedule for
regular reporting, such as quarterly and annual reviews, ensures that progress is
tracked consistently. Additionally, accountability mechanisms such as independent
audits and community feedback channels help to identify and address any
shortcomings or inefficiencies. Regularly publishing reports maintains transparency,
builds public trust, and ensures that stakeholders are informed about progress and
outcomes. Additionally, accountability mechanisms, such as independent audits and
community feedback channels, help to identify and address any shortcomings or
inefficiencies. By fostering an environment of transparency and accountability, the program
can continuously improve, adapt to emerging challenges, and ensure that resources are
used efficiently and effectively. This approach not only enhances the program's credibility
but also ensures that it remains aligned with its goals of promoting public health, safety,
and well-being.
Conclusion
The proposed policy framework aims to address the complex issue of illicit drug use and public
intoxication through a compassionate and comprehensive approach. By criminalizing public
intoxication with illicit drugs and mandating treatment over punishment, Ontario can transform its
response to drug addiction, reclaim human potential, and enhance community safety. Securing
predictable and expanded funding from provincial and federal governments is crucial to sustain
these efforts and achieve long-term success.
References
1. National Institute on Drug Abuse. (2023). Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction.
[NIDA](https://nida.nih.gov/publications/drugs-brains-behavior-science-addiction/treatmentrecovery).
2. CBC News. (2023). Ontario mayors demand urgent action, more funding to address
homelessness crisis. [CBC](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/mayors-homelessnessopioid-crisis-1.6846730).
3. National Center for Biotechnology Information. (2017). Public Health and Public Order: The
Impact of Alcohol and Other Drug Use on the Urban Environment.
[NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5486507/).
