Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health - “Opioid Epidemic and
Toxic Drug Crisis”
A Rural Canada Perspective
Prepared by Holly Mathias, MA
PhD Candidate, School of Public Health, University of Alberta
June 24, 2024

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health - “Opioid Epidemic and
Toxic Drug Crisis”
A Rural Canada Perspective
Prepared by Holly Mathias, MA
PhD Candidate, School of Public Health, University of Alberta
June 24, 2024

Introduction
I am a doctoral candidate in the School of Public Health at the University of Alberta (Edmonton, AB). My
research examines the experiences of family members who provide care/support for people who use drugs
in rural Canada. Through my work, I collaborate with families, community organizations, frontline
workers and people with lived and living experience of drug use in rural communities across the Prairie
provinces. Before beginning doctoral studies, I lived in Nova Scotia, where I conducted nationally funded
community-based research on access to substance use disorder treatment programs in Atlantic Canada.
The aim of this brief is two-fold: 1) to synthesize the scientific evidence on drug poisonings within a rural
Canadian context; and 2) to present evidence from people with lived/living experience of substance use,
families, frontline workers and community members, as heard during a 2024 national webinar and
workshop on drug poisonings in rural and remote Canada.
Background
Since 2016, over 42,000 Canadians have died from apparent opioid toxicity deaths (Special Advisory
Committee on the Epidemic of Opioid Overdoses, 2024). Between January and September 2023, it was
estimated that an average of 22 Canadians died per day (Special Advisory Committee on the Epidemic of
Opioid Overdoses, 2024). In addition to mortality, unintentional drug poisonings also contribute to
substantial morbidity, including risks of HIV and hepatitis C, infections, and acquired brain injury
(Artenie et al., 2023; Xavier et al., 2023). Approximately 41,045 Canadians were hospitalized for opioidrelated poisonings and 17,551 Canadians for stimulant-related poisonings between January 2016 and
September 2023 (Special Advisory Committee on the Epidemic of Opioid Overdoses, 2024). The
COVID-19 pandemic deepened the urgency of addressing drug poisonings as the drug supply became
more toxic, and public health measures created challenges to accessing health and social services (Jenkins
et al., 2021). Some areas of Canada have declared a state of emergency in response (Government of
British Columbia, 2016; Paradis, 2023; Yukon, 2022).
The federal Canadian Drugs and Substances Strategy has identified several pillars to address substance
use, including investment in prevention, harm reduction and treatment programs for unregulated drug use
(Government of Canada, 2024). However, there can be challenges to accessing services for many people
who use drugs, particularly when living rurally or remotely (Bardwell & Lappalainen, 2021). Historically,
substance use has been portrayed as a ‘city’ problem, and most resources and investments have been
targeted to inner-city communities in Canada (Canadian Drug Policy Coalition, 2023; Proudfoot, 2024).
However, the unregulated toxic drug supply impacts communities across Canada, including those in rural
settings (Gatehouse et al., 2023; McElroy, 2023; Proudfoot, 2024). Addressing drug poisoning in rural
Canada is a public health priority (Bardwell & Lappalainen, 2021; Kornelsen et al., 2021).
Part A - The Rural Canadian Context: Evidence Synthesis
As of 2021, 6.6 million people live in rural Canada - the fastest-growing rural population among G7
countries (Statistics Canada, 2022). Due to limited monitoring and data availability, the exact number of
Canadians using unregulated drugs and/or who have experienced a drug poisoning event while living
rurally is unknown. It is important to note that there is no universal definition of ‘rural’ in Canada, adding
to the complexity of generating an exact number of Canadians impacted (Asad et al., 2020). Nonetheless,
there is some evidence that points to the gravity of drug poisoning in rural Canada.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Nonetheless,
there is some evidence that points to the gravity of drug poisoning in rural Canada.

A) Drug Poisoning Statistics
There may be a greater risk of drug poisoning in rural communities compared to urban parts of Canada.
The Canadian Institute for Health Information (2018) suggests that the opioid poisoning hospitalization
rate in small communities is more than double that in large cities in Canada. Recent research from British
Columbia also indicates higher odds of fatal drug poisoning events in rural communities compared
to urban areas of the province (Hu et al., 2022). On average, the odds of fatal drug poisoning were 30%

higher in rural communities (and in some cases up to 50% higher) compared to urban communities (Hu et
al., 2022). This is supported by 2023 data from the British Columbia Coroner Service, which shows the
highest rates of unregulated drug deaths per 100,000 people occurred in the Northern health authority (BC
Coroners Service, 2024). High rates of death may linked to the unregulated drug supply and limited
access to harm reduction services in rural communities (Hu et al., 2022). There is also a high number of
unwitnessed drug poisoning events in private residences in rural British Columbia (Fernando et al.,
2022), and these events are 12 times more likely to be fatal than those in public spaces (Hu et al., 2022).
In Ontario, the highest rate of drug mortalities is in Northern Ontario - a highly rural and remote area
(Morin et al., 2021; Russell et al., 2019). At the time of this brief, the other provinces and territories do
not publicly report disaggregated data at a level where it is possible to understand patterns in rural areas.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
At the time of this brief, the other provinces and territories do
not publicly report disaggregated data at a level where it is possible to understand patterns in rural areas.

B) Determinants of Substance Use and Drug Poisonings
Economy. In addition to universal determinants of substance use, such as socioeconomic status and
housing, there are determinants specific to rural settings (Galea & Vlahov, 2002; Johnston, 2020; Peters et
al., 2020). Evidence suggests that people working in agriculture, extractive fossil fuel industries, and
trades may be more likely to use substances – all industries common in rural areas (Hopkins et al., 2022;
Young et al., 2023). In Canada, 75% of drug poisoning deaths have occurred among men, and 30-50% of
those deaths have occurred among men working in the trades (Special Advisory Committee on the
Epidemic of Opioid Overdoses, 2024).
Geography. The isolated geography of rural communities can also influence substance use. Canadian
research suggests that many rural communities have limited health and social services availability. As a
result, people who use drugs may have to travel outside of their community to obtain required services
and support. Travel distances and costs, in addition to lack of transportation, poor road infrastructure and
dangerous travel conditions, may act as a barrier to receiving supportive services (Fernando et al., 2022;
Jackson et al., 2022; Mathias et al., 2024a; Russell et al., 2019). Rural areas are generally the most
impacted by natural disasters, such as forest fires, drought and flooding (Friedman et al., 2021). Many
communities have aging or limited infrastructure, such as seasonally available roads, that may not be
resilient to disasters and may contribute to access challenges (Pijl et al., 2022).

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Many
communities have aging or limited infrastructure, such as seasonally available roads, that may not be
resilient to disasters and may contribute to access challenges (Pijl et al., 2022).

Colonization. Indigenous peoples, many of whom live rurally and remotely, are disproportionately
impacted by drug poisonings due to a legacy of colonial violence, racism, discrimination and
intergenerational trauma (First Nations Health Authority, 2024; Lavalley et al., 2018). New data from
Alberta suggests that although First Nations people represent only 3.5% of the provincial population, they
accounted for 20% of all unintentional opioid poisoning deaths in Alberta between 2016-2022
(Government of Alberta, 2024). Notably, the life expectancy of First Nations people in Alberta has
decreased by seven years for both men and women, and this is partially linked to drug poisoning (Paradis,
2023). 2023 data from the First Nations Health Authority (2024) in British Columbia indicates that First
Nations people “died at 6.1 times the rate of other British Columbia residents.” There is a gendered
element as well, with First Nations women dying at nearly 12 times the rate of other women in British
Columbia (First Nations Health Authority, 2024).

C) Access to Services and Supports
There is a growing body of research on access to substance use services, such as harm reduction programs
and treatment programs, in rural Canada (Bardwell et al., 2023; Jackson et al., 2022; Mathias et al.,
2024a; McCutcheon & Morrison, 2014). Most evidence points to substantial barriers to accessing services
and supports in rural communities. Some barriers are associated with the services themselves, such as
limited availability, limited hours of operation, wait times, affordability, and a lack of trained and
available staff (Russell et al., 2019; Jackson et al., 2022; Pijl et al., 2022). Other barriers are linked to the
environment, including stigma, perceived lack of privacy, and risk of criminalization (Jackson et al.,
2022; Pijl et al., 2022; Russell et al., 2019). To navigate these barriers, many people travel outside their

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
To navigate these barriers, many people travel outside their

communities to access services (Jackson et al., 2022; Mathias et al., 2024a). Although virtual health
services may fill some gaps, some communities need more technical infrastructure to support this
method of delivery (Pijl et al., 2022).
Despite many barriers, there are also facilitators of access in rural Canada. Some programs offer
integrated services (e.g. social and health supports), access to transportation and childcare, and housing
support, which can address barriers to access (Pijl et al., 2022). Innovations in service delivery, such as
telehealth and mobile services, and improvements to community infrastructure, such as transportation,
may also address known barriers (Mema et al., 2019; Rioux et al., 2024). Many rural communities also
have strong support networks, comprising family, friends, people with lived and living experience, and
community members (Palombi et al., 2022). Often, families and community-based organizations will fill
the gap in rural communities with limited access to supports and services through things like providing
transportation, outreach services, emotional support and support with service navigation (AIDS
Committee of Newfoundland and Labrador, 2023; Manitoba Harm Reduction Network, 2023; Mathias et
al., 2024a; Turning Point, 2023).

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Often, families and community-based organizations will fill
the gap in rural communities with limited access to supports and services through things like providing
transportation, outreach services, emotional support and support with service navigation (AIDS
Committee of Newfoundland and Labrador, 2023; Manitoba Harm Reduction Network, 2023; Mathias et
al., 2024a; Turning Point, 2023).

Part B - Listening to Canadians: Findings from A National Workshop
In February 2024, I co-organized a national webinar and workshop on addressing drug poisonings in rural
Canada with people with lived experience of substance use, families, community organization staff, and
other researchers from Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan (CRISM Canada, 2024; Mathias et al.,
2024b). Nearly 100 Canadians gathered online to listen to an expert panel and contribute their stories and
ideas on how to address rural drug poisonings. Key ideas from these discussions are summarized below.
A) Realities of Drug Poisoning
Attendees emphasized that people from all walks of life have been impacted by drug poisonings in rural
communities, regardless of gender identity, racial identity, socioeconomic status or age. Although many
people may assume that drug poisonings are a ‘city issue’, they stressed that the drug supply is also toxic
in small communities and must be addressed. They shared that stigma and the criminalization of
substance use have made it very challenging to address drug poisonings in rural areas adequately.
B) Underlying Factors of Substance Use and Drug Poisonings
Attendees perceived experiences of trauma, shame and family history of substance use as being a
primary contributor to substance use. For many Indigenous people, experiences of colonialism, racism,
discrimination and intergenerational trauma have caused ongoing harms. Poverty, unemployment,
increased cost of living and housing insecurity were also thought to be driving substance use in some
communities. Feelings of isolation and not belonging were also pointed out. Many people explained that
limited access to health and social services, including harm reduction, treatment and housing supports,
were worsening substance use and made it difficult to prevent and respond to drug poisoning events.
C) Strengths of Rural Communities
Despite some challenging circumstances, such as limited resources and inadequate community
infrastructure, rural communities have unique strengths that may help address drug poisonings. Attendees
emphasized that there is a strong sense of community in rural places, and people are eager to help others.
Some communities have tight-knit groups of people who use drugs and have created information
networks to communicate changes in the drug supply to prevent drug poisoning. The smaller size of many
rural communities may also help facilitate strong connections between health and social service staff and
people accessing these services. Rural communities are often resourceful and creative, reflected in
service delivery. Attendees shared examples of innovative service delivery in their communities,
including mail-out services, mobile buses/vans, outreach programs, telehealth and co-location with
existing services, such as pharmacies.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Attendees shared examples of innovative service delivery in their communities,
including mail-out services, mobile buses/vans, outreach programs, telehealth and co-location with
existing services, such as pharmacies.

D) Priorities for Addressing Drug Poisoning in Rural Canada
Attendees shared their top 4 priorities for addressing substance use and drug poisonings:
1. Invest in preventative approaches to address determinants of substance use, including programs
that address poverty and housing insecurity.
2. Enhance community belonging through education and outreach events to build community
capacity and understanding of substance use, which may reduce stigma and contribute to strong
social networks. Stigma reduction and strengthened networks may prevent substance use and
remove barriers to accessing supportive services.
3. Expand the availability and diversity of community-based low-barrier health and social
services. There was strong interest in harm reduction programs (e.g., supervised consumption
sites, safe supply programs) and housing supports.
4. Increased human and financial resources to support rural health and well-being. Suggested
starting points for increased investment included recruiting and retaining trained health
professionals, paid employment opportunities for people with lived/living experience of
substance use, and long-term consistent funding for community-based organizations.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Suggested
starting points for increased investment included recruiting and retaining trained health
professionals, paid employment opportunities for people with lived/living experience of
substance use, and long-term consistent funding for community-based organizations.

Part C - Recommendations
Drawing on the scientific body of evidence and perspectives of rural Canadians, the following actions
must be taken:
1. All levels of government, including federal, provincial/territorial, municipal, and Indigenous
governance, must work closely with leading experts to generate a national public health
response. People with lived experience of drug use should be centred and meaningfully engaged
in all discussions and decisions, and they must represent Canada's diverse makeup, including
rural and remote communities and Indigenous peoples.
2. National public health monitoring must be expanded in partnership with provinces/territories to
account for drug poisoning events in rural, remote, and Northern communities. Collected data
should be shared promptly and transparently with impacted communities.
3. Increased resources should be invested across relevant portfolios at all levels of government to
support the prevention of substance use and drug poisoning, including increased investment
in housing support, mental health support, poverty reduction and support for Indigenous
communities.
4. Evidence-informed health and social services and supports must be rapidly scaled up in
rural, remote, and Northern communities. Services should be developed and led by
communities, be low-barrier, and recognize the broad range of needs of people who use drugs,
including prevention, harm reduction, and voluntary treatment programs. Regular and ongoing
evaluation of services and supports must occur.
5. The main driver of drug poisoning deaths is the toxic unregulated drug supply. Therefore, a
regulated supply of pharmaceutical alternatives to currently unregulated substances must be
provided.
6. Many families (including families of choice), friends and community members provide unpaid
support for people who use drugs to help bridge the gaps when formal services are not available.
They must be recognized as family caregivers in Canada and provided access to caregiving
benefits, credits, and caregiving and grief support. The Canadian Recovery Caregiving Benefit
was offered to caregivers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Family caregivers of people who use
drugs should receive similar support amidst this public health emergency and should also be
included in future national caregiving strategies.
7. Canadian drug policy must be reformed to support wide-scale decriminalization of psychoactive
substances. Decriminalization may help address concerns linked to fear of arrest and
criminalization, which prevent many people who use drugs from accessing supportive services.

text:
From: Sharon Koivu
Sent: Sunday, July 21, 2024 9:09 PM
To: ~Health/Santé
Subject: The London experience

OISIS Study Report: London
House Standing Committee on Health:
Mr. Chair, Members of the Committee
The London Experience.
I feel it is important to expand on details of the London experience as I believe that some
claims that have been made are not an accurate reflection of the situation.
In 2012 I recognized that there were numerous patients suffering from right-side Tricuspid
Valve Infective Endocarditis. An infectious disease specialist I worked with, Dr. Kaveri
Gupta, identified an increase in HIV among injection drug users despite London having a
robust needle exchange program run through the Regional HIV/AIDS Connection.
The number of people suffering continued to rise. In June of 2016, a public health
emergency was declared by the Middlesex London Health Unit due to high rates of HIV,
Hepatitis C, Infective Endocarditis (IE) and iGAS (Infectious group A strep).
Infectious Disease Specialists, including the Chief of Infectious Diseases at London Health
Sciences Centre, Dr. Michael Silverman and scientific researchers, including myself, were
able to prove that the rates of Tricuspid Valve Infective Endocarditis were a result of
injecting long-acting hydromorphone, also known as HydroMorph Contin. We
demonstrated that the high rate of HIV was related to sharing injection drug use
paraphernalia, specifically cookers and filters, when people were injecting long-acting
hydromorphone.
We met with numerous community agencies to develop a collaborative community
response to address this crisis. One initiative came from London InterCommunity Health
Centre (LIHC). They started a street level outreach team to reach high-risk, street level sex
workers. They began prescribing short-acting hydromorphone, also known as Dilaudid,
primarily for sex-workers who were injecting long-acting hydromorphone. The goal was to
decrease the rates of HIV transmission as well as infective endocarditis.
Of note, research in London demonstrated that stable patients with right sided infective
endocarditis had a longer life expectancy without surgery. In my experience the Cardiac
Surgeons in London are excellent and compassionate. Advising against surgery can be to
provide the best possible outcome and not an indication that patients are being
stigmatized and left to die, as was implied.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Advising against surgery can be to
provide the best possible outcome and not an indication that patients are being
stigmatized and left to die, as was implied.

The short-acting hydromorphone, Dilaudid, prescribing program started at LIHC was
created to address this infection crisis. It provided patients with the same regulated,
prescription drug, hydromorphone, that most were already using, just in a different form. It
was not created as a response to an unregulated drug supply. Illicit fentanyl was not a
problem in London in 2016. I was very aware of what drugs were being used in London at
that time.
The Ontario Integrated Supervised Injection Services Feasibility Study, Study Report:
London Ontario was published in February 2017. Authors include Thomas Kerr Director,
Urban Health Research Initiative, British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS and
Geoff Bardwell Research Coordinator, Ontario Integrated Supervised Injection Services
Feasibility Study. The report studied local drug use. 79% of injection drug users reported
using hydromorphone. It did not differentiate short and long acting. Fentanyl is not
mentioned in this report.
The 2018 Middlesex-London Community Drug and Alcohol Strategy reported substances
used at the Temporary Overdose Prevention site in London between February 12 and
August 31, 2018. 58% of clients used Hydromorphone/Dilaudid while only 11% used
Fentanyl. It did not mention illicit fentanyl and as such is more likely to indicate
prescription Fentanyl patches. The Drug and Alcohol Strategy did not mention a “Safe
Supply” prescribing of opioids. It was not a drug strategy.
To my knowledge the short-acting hydromorphone prescribing program, later call “Safe
Supply”, was not expanded to be used as an overdose prevention program until after the
Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine Conference in Vancouver in October 2018 in
collaboration with other physicians involved in “Safe Supply” initiatives.
The experience at London InterCommunity Health Centre (LIHC) involving their shortacting hydromorphone, Dilaudid, prescribing program was published in the CMAJ as
‘Clinical outcomes and health care costs among people entering a safer opioid supply
program in Ontario.”
Please note the data, as described in the article, was collected between January 2016 and
March 2019. The background information of the actual situation in London is very relevant.
Most, if not all, of the data was collected when the goal was to address the injection drug
use related infectious, public health emergency of HIV and IE.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Most, if not all, of the data was collected when the goal was to address the injection drug
use related infectious, public health emergency of HIV and IE.

In their publication they state under data source the SOS (Safer Opioid Supply) program
was initially offered to London InterCommunity Health Centre (LIHC) clients who were
experiencing “multiple, serious medical complications owing to their drug use and who
were believed to be at high risk of imminent death as a result of unmanaged health
conditions (such as recurrent infective endocarditis or untreated HIV).”

Please see also Appendix etable1. There is a detailed description of the program and no
mention of unregulated drug use or fentanyl use as a criterion to be in the program.

As per Table 1: In Baseline characteristics, fentanyl use was not mentioned. In fact, there is
no indication that any of the patients were using fentanyl when they entered the program.
Additionally, there are much higher rates of HIV and Hep C. and skin and soft tissue
infections in the “SOS” group than the “matched” group supporting that people with
infections were the target population and that the control group is not accurately matched.

The analysis of this program found benefits. However, people were not using Fentanyl
when they entered the program. This is not evidence that a Dilaudid prescribing program
would benefit people who are using the unregulated drug supply. This is not evidence of
the effectiveness of a Safe Opioid Supply program as is currently delivered.

Additionally, they did not identify alternate sources of the benefits which could be a result
of numerous things:
1) engagement in a caring, empathetic treatment program,
2) receiving wrap-around services including primary care and HIV care
3) being connected to a housing-first initiative through SLWAR (Street Level Workers at
Risk) program
4) possible stability from receiving a prescription for the short-acting version of the same
drug they were using, hydromorphone
5) income from diversion

This study does not address the unintended consequences and side effects of the
program.

As shown, at the time the “Safe Supply program started there was not a problem with illicit
Fentanyl in London. There is now!

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
There is now!

On Monday July 15 London police Chief Thai Truong stated:
"Diverted safe supply is being resold into our community. It's being trafficked into other
communities, and it is being used as currency in exchange for fentanyl, fuelling the drug
trade. That is a big concern for us."

At the news conference, police shared that in the first six months of this year, they've
seized more than 11,100 eight-milligram tablets of Dilaudids prescribed to people with
opioid addictions as part of a safe opioid supply program, among other drugs.

Truong said drug trafficking is happening at both organized and street levels, and because
there is a high supply of Dilaudids in London, their value is much lower. The street value for

one tablet is between $2 to $5 in London, but in other cities, the cost can range from $15 to
$30, he added.
"Other jurisdictions where supply is not as abundant, that's where the price of the
Dilaudids are increasing," he said. "If you think about individuals who may not have an
abundance of money to support their substance [use] disorder, they now have it in those
pills."
Since the “Safe Supply” Program started in 2016 and expanded, the harms experienced in
London Middlesex have escalated substantially, beyond the rates experienced in the rest
of the province.
Since the program was initiated the rates of HIV and TVIE have improved as part of a
community collaboration. However, the rates of all invasive infections among opioid users
have substantially increased. Overdose deaths have increased dramatically compared to
the rest of the province.
The data in the Public Health Ontario Interactive Opioid Tool illustrates the alarming trend:
Rates of death from opioid related mortality/ 100,000 population:
Before “Safe Supply”
2014: Ontario: 4.9, London Middlesex: 2.8 (43% lower than the Ontario average)
2015: Ontario: 5.3 London Middlesex: 5.3 (equal)
After “Safe “Supply”
2018: Ontario: 10.4, London Middlesex: 13.0 (25% higher than Ontario)
2019: Ontario: 10.7, London Middlesex: 12.1 (13% higher than Ontario)
2020: Ontario: 16.6, London Middlesex: 20.3 (22% higher than Ontario)
2021: Ontario: 19.1, London Middlesex: 25.4 (33% higher than Ontario)
2022: Ontario: 16.7, London Middlesex: 23.2 (40% higher than Ontario)
Youth and young adults in London Middlesex have been badly affected.

After the introduction of “Safe Supply” the increase in London in Emergency Department
visits has been striking and costly.
Additionally, the percentage of people found to be positive for Fentanyl at death has been
very similar in London Middlesex and the Province of Ontario. However, in London
Middlesex, the percentage of people positive for Hydromorphone, the main drug
prescribed in the “Safe Supply” Program has been 200% higher than the provincial
average.
While correlation is not proof of causation, the public health data consistently
demonstrates that there has been harm to the London community, particularly to youth
since the implementation of the Dilaudid prescribing / “Safe Supply” program was
initiated. This is consistent with supporting scientific evidence that an intervention
introduced in London in 2016 is contributing to harm. I am not aware of any other
intervention that can explain the increases in harms.
In conclusion, the experience in London does not support the claim that prescribing
Dilaudid to people who are using illicit fentanyl at the time of admission to a program
would benefit. There is substantial medical and public health data and police reporting to
demonstrate increased harm to individuals and the community.

RE: Brief – Committee Study on “Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada”

We are writing as a group of community and academic researchers, including young people with lived
experience of the harms of the opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis in Canada. We are members of
the Youth Health Team at the BC Centre on Substance Use and University of British Columbia. We
have led 15+ years of community-based research with youth who use drugs, and are pleased to
contribute expertise and research evidence to the Standing Committee on Health’s study of the
“Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada.” Our submission highlights the substance use
and associated treatment and care experiences and perspectives of young people who use drugs
(YPWUD; ages 14 to 29), primarily in the context of street-based homelessness and unstable housing
in British Columbia.

We contribute key findings from a report titled, Youth Voices on Treatment in the Shadow of the Overdose
Crisis: Key Recommendations and Findings for Care Providers which provides recommendations for youth
care providers. This is accompanied by a list of youth Harm Reduction Calls to Action which summarize
how harm reduction should be made more responsive to young people’s needs, priorities, and desires.

We hope that our submission provides youth-specific insights that, together with recommendations
from the other evidence briefs (e.g., Moms Stop the Harm), can support population and contexttailored policy reforms to meaningfully address the drug toxicity crisis affecting young people in
Canada.

Sincerely,

Research Brief: Youth Voices on the Toxic Drug Crisis and Substance Use Treatment

Background

Our research to date has focused broadly on youth substance use and health using longitudinal
qualitative, ethnographic, and community-based participatory methods. The reports presented in this
brief are informed by numerous peer-reviewed publications by our team and developed with the aim
of learning from YPWUD experiencing street-based homelessness and unstable housing about their
needs and priorities in the context of the opioid epidemic and toxic drug supply crisis. We sought to
provide guidance to service providers and decision-makers regarding how to care for and build
mutually-beneficial relationships with youth in our and other Canadian settings. These research studies
were conducted in partnership with the Youth Health Advisory Council (YHAC), a group of about
ten young people with lived and living experience of substance use and mental health concerns in the
context of homelessness and unstable housing. In close collaboration with the YHAC, we have
developed a shared vision for what care and harm reduction should look like through a multitude of
projects. Depicted below is our vision for a youth-dedicated overdose prevention site (OPS):

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Depicted below is our vision for a youth-dedicated overdose prevention site (OPS):

We present two reports for the Standing Committee on Health’s study of the “Opioid Epidemic and
Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada”:
1. A report based on interviews with youth and youth-focused care providers, aimed at providing
guidance to those who care for young people (Project 1);
2. A list of calls to action regarding youth harm reduction developed by youth and young drug
user activists and allies (Project 2).

This research brief details the recommendations from these projects, which provide critical insights
on supporting structurally-marginalized youth in the midst of the toxic drug crisis. These reports were
developed in partnership with youth with lived and living experience, including a majority of
Indigenous and 2S/LGBTQ+ youth. We stress the importance of emphasizing voices that are
regularly excluded in conversations about the toxic drug crisis.

PROJECT 1: Youth Voices on Treatment in the Shadow of the Overdose Crisis

The first appended publication is a report which provides guidance and recommendations for those
supporting young people experiencing street involvement and can help care providers foster more
constructive relationships built on mutual trust and respect.

This report draws on a series of qualitative research studies conducted with over [CONTACT] involvement on the unceded, ancestral and occupied territories of the Lheidli
T’enneh, Syilx Okanagan, Musqueam, Squamish, and Tsleil-Waututh Peoples. These places are also
known as Prince George, Kelowna, and Vancouver. The research activities that inform this report
include qualitative interviews, focus groups, and a summit event held in Vancouver which involved
discussion-based activities focused on critically evaluating local responses to the overdose crisis. The
members of our team’s YHAC and the youth who participated in these research activities comprise a
diverse group of individuals between the ages of 14 and 28. This includes youth experiencing
significant precarity and frequent institutionalization via child protection, criminal legal, and housing
systems, many of whom also have lived experience of broader forms of structural oppression shaped
by race, class, gender, sexuality, dis/ability, and other aspects of social location. The majority of these
youth have engaged in intensive polysubstance use and have experienced concurrent mental health
concerns. Interviews with youth-focused care providers have also informed this report. These
providers include family physicians, nurse practitioners, nurses, drug and alcohol counselors, and
social workers.

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
These
providers include family physicians, nurse practitioners, nurses, drug and alcohol counselors, and
social workers.

Main findings and recommendations

1. Centre relationship-building, self-determination, and safety in treatment and care

Many youth expressed ambivalence, suspicion, or aversion toward overly medicalized models of
care that felt like they were too focused on monitoring and pharmacotherapies, and less focused
on relationship- and trust-building. Several youth viewed overly medicalized models of care as part
of a continuum of institutional harms they had experienced across their lives and, in the case of
Indigenous youth, across generations. Hospitals in particular were viewed as unsafe places, but
youth told us that other institutional settings and practices (e.g., certification under BC’s Mental
Health Act) could signal danger.

Pharmacotherapies were framed by many youth as “quick fixes” that could not address the deeper
social and structural issues they were contending with (e.g., colonialism, the housing crisis). When
youth felt as though pharmacotherapies such as buprenorphine-naloxone were being “pushed on
them” by providers in the absence of meaningful changes in their life circumstances (e.g., stable
housing, employment), they frequently concluded that those helping them did not understand
their treatment and recovery needs and goals. Several youth described avoiding treatment settings
where they thought pharmacotherapies would be the primary focus of care.

Young people must be empowered with control over their treatment trajectories—including
decision-making around pharmacotherapies and information gathering and sharing. They must be
respectfully engaged as partners in their treatment and care, rather than approached from a
position of authority. The focus should be on building relationships and fostering trust with
individual youth rather than on monitoring and pharmacotherapies.

2. Present pharmacotherapies as one piece of a whole

Pharmacotherapies should always be presented as one piece of a whole that includes housing,
employment, income, social, and cultural supports.

3. Avoid approaches that prioritize monitoring and surveillance, which can signal danger to youth
and lead them to disengage with care

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Avoid approaches that prioritize monitoring and surveillance, which can signal danger to youth
and lead them to disengage with care

Youth were generally acutely aware of how their client files, patient charts, and other means of
information sharing could impact their current and future interactions with services, including the
child welfare, education, youth and adult criminal justice, and acute and community healthcare
systems. Monitoring and surveillance could signal danger, particularly for youth who had
experienced repeated institutionalizations across their lives and across generations. Again, several
youth described avoiding treatment and care settings where they perceived a high level of
monitoring and surveillance.

4. Seek permission before sharing information about youth with other providers

While many youth said that existing youth-dedicated services were essential supports in their lives,
they also expressed concerns about information-sharing in these settings. They worried about
“who knew what,” and the consequences of that information being passed around, which they
noted could include apprehension by child protective services. It was devastating when files,
charts, and information-sharing seemed to reinforce a view that youth were “not making progress”
or even “failing.” Some youth described trying to manage what did and did not end up in their
files. Others, including a number of Indigenous youth, described avoiding care services altogether
in order to keep themselves safe.

5. Focus on the present, not the past and do not reduce youth to their “files”

Many youth emphasized that interactions with the providers who access their files and charts go
better when providers first affirm where a young person is at in the present moment, rather than
focusing on what has happened in the past or what is written down.

6. Do not reduce youth to their “files”

Youth were distinctly aware of how client files, patient charts, and other means of information
sharing could impact their current and future interactions with services. “I am not my file” was a
sentiment that we heard expressed on multiple occasions.

7. Involve youth as partners in developing plans and timelines for opioid agonist therapy (OAT) and
psychotropic medications

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Involve youth as partners in developing plans and timelines for opioid agonist therapy (OAT) and
psychotropic medications

Youth valued individualized, multi-dimensional approaches to treatment that allowed them to
work toward futures not defined by substance use and mental health crises. Clinical practice
guidelines recommend the longer-term use of OAT, and in particular buprenorphine-naloxone, as
a first-line treatment for opioid use disorder among youth. However, most youth did not envision
being on OAT over the longer-term. Instead, they often viewed OAT as a short-term tool that
could mediate withdrawal symptoms and jump-start their “full” recovery—which would ultimately
be achieved without ongoing pharmacological intervention.

Many youth did not envision being on psychotropic medications over the longer-term. They
desired a clear pathway to tapering off of OAT and psychotropic medications. When they were
not offered this pathway, many opted to “do it on their own” and disengaged from care. With
regard to self-tapering off OAT, the result was often relapse and sometimes overdose.

From the outset, OAT and psychotropic medications should be discussed with youth
in terms of shorter timelines, with the possibility of tapering doses. Youth who had the most
success with adherence to OAT were actively involved in decision-making around what kind of
medication would work best for them, and for how long.

8. Provide youth who want treatment with access to the full range of OAT

OAT is often prescribed alongside a range of psychotropic medications, including antidepressants
and second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone, quetiapine). Youth must have access to
the full range of OAT, including methadone, slow-release oral morphine, and buprenorphinenaloxone.

9. Recognize that many youth prefer treatment modalities that give them more control and subject
them to less surveillance

Because of the sense of danger associated with highly medicalized and institutionalized settings,
many
youth
expressed
a
preference
for
treatment
modalities
that
they
could control and which do not require professional oversight. Many youth spoke positively about
using cannabis, psychedelics, and cigarettes as tools for harm reduction and treatment that they
could manage independently.

10. Acknowledge the use of cannabis as a treatment and harm reduction strategy

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Acknowledge the use of cannabis as a treatment and harm reduction strategy

The prevalence of cannabis use among youth experiencing street involvement in BC has been
estimated to be as high as 98 per cent. Youth frequently spoke about using cannabis not only for
its pleasurable effects, but also as a means of relieving longstanding mental and physical health
issues—notably, depression, anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and chronic pain.

They also used it to manage the harms of street-based homelessness, and to help them reduce
their use of or eliminate more problematic forms of substance use, including the intensive use of
alcohol, crystal methamphetamine, and heroin/fentanyl. Participants described using cannabis to
carefully “taper” their use of these other more harmful substances. They explained that cannabis
helped reduce the severity of their withdrawal symptoms and prevented relapse by satisfying
cravings.
Many youth strongly believed that regular cannabis use was preferable to the longer-term use of
pharmacotherapies, including OAT and psychotropic medications. They frequently described
using cannabis to taper off of OAT, or indicated that they planned
to use cannabis to get off OAT after undergoing treatment. Many argued that cannabis should be
integrated into substance use treatment for youth.

Care providers must attend to the ways in which youth experiencing street involvement are using
cannabis to navigate their everyday lives and needs. They should engage in conversations with
youth about their cannabis use, discussing potential benefits and risks of cannabis in the context
of their physical and mental health and substance use issues.

PROJECT 2: Harm Reduction Calls to Action from Young People who use Drugs

The second appended report lists 10 calls to action related to youth harm reduction. Supported by
university researchers, our team’s YHAC collaborated with young drug user activists and allies from
Lisbon, Portugal, and Pittsburgh, United States, to generate these calls to action.

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Supported by
university researchers, our team’s YHAC collaborated with young drug user activists and allies from
Lisbon, Portugal, and Pittsburgh, United States, to generate these calls to action.

The motivation for developing these calls to action centres on our wish to challenge the notion that
internationally-celebrated places like Lisbon and Vancouver are meeting the harm reduction needs of
YPWUD. In particular, the needs of YPWUD in the context of unstable housing, homelessness, and
ongoing poverty—a context which we summarize here as “street involvement” for the sake of
brevity—are not being adequately met. In both Vancouver and Lisbon, we have observed that some
of the benefits of harm reduction have been lost as the movement has become increasingly
medicalized and professionalized. When harm reduction is spearheaded by clinicians, researchers, and
other “professionals,” without people with lived and living experience, it can pathologize drug use and
people who use drugs.

Policy and practice calls to action

The contributors of this report make several calls to action to support the harm reduction needs of
YPWUD in the context of street involvement in and beyond our settings:

1. We oppose approaches to preventing drug-related harms among young people, including very
young people, that are premised on abstinence. We want accurate information about the risks and
benefits of different drugs and how to practice different kinds of harm reduction in our schools
and communities.

2. Young people’s engagement with harm reduction programs and sites should be kept confidential
to encourage relationship- and trust-building and sustained connection with care. Those providing
harm reduction to youth should always collaborate closely with them to determine what (if
anything) regarding their drug use and harm reduction practices can be shared with family

members, caregivers, staff, providers, and workers from the various systems of care and
supervision that YPWUD often navigate.

3. We demand investment in low-barrier, youth-dedicated, and youth-led harm reduction programs
and spaces, including safer consumption, drug checking, shelter, and housing sites. Ideally, youthoriented safer consumption sites should have a non-clinical, relaxed feel to them, and include a
welcoming drop-in space alongside private spaces for safer consumption. These should be places
where YPWUD can access harm reduction supplies and information as well as food and other
basic necessities. They should be staffed by a mix of peers and providers with experience providing
non-judgemental care, support, and camaraderie to YPWUD. These spaces are needed in
geographically-diverse locations, including remote and rural communities

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
These spaces are needed in
geographically-diverse locations, including remote and rural communities

4. Youth-oriented safer consumption, drug checking, shelter, and housing programs and spaces must
account for the needs of youth who use stimulants and polysubstance-using youth. They must
also account for the needs of BIPOC youth, gender diverse and queer youth, and self-identified
young women. There should be dedicated programing and hours for young women (at least
partially staffed by young women), gender diverse and queer youth (at least partially staffed by
gender diverse and queer young people), and BIPOC youth (at least partially staffed by BIPOC
young people). Mobile outreach vans and safer consumption rooms are critical to making harm
reduction and other forms of support more accessible to YPWUD in the context of street
involvement, and in particular those who are not residing in city centers.

5. Stop pathologizing YPWUD and trying to “save” or “fix” us. Recognize that we have the human
right to make decisions for ourselves and keep ourselves safe. We demand an end to compulsory
or involuntary abstinence-based treatment programs. Instead, we want to be listened to regarding
what drugs do for us, socially, physically, mentally, and emotionally, in our daily lives. Youthdedicated drop-in centers and service hubs should center relationship- and trust-building and harm
reduction, with treatments such as OAT easily available to those who indicate they want these.

6. The services and systems that YPWUD navigate must be re-designed to foster youth’s selfdetermination in relation to their drug use, harm reduction, care, and families. YPWUD should be
represented, engaged with, and empowered as citizens capable of making their own decisions.
YPWUD who are in government care (i.e., living in foster care, group homes, and independent
living arrangements) must be able to access harm reduction services without fear of discipline and
repercussions, including being placed in psychiatric wards, youth detention centers, and certain
kinds of housing environments by social workers and teams as a “last resort” attempt to “fix”
their substance use.

7. We add our voices to those demanding the decriminalization of drug use and an end to the war
on drugs. We demand that YPWUD be at the table in a meaningful way (and not just as token
participants in the process) as plans for decriminalization and safe supply are rolled out in BC and
elsewhere.

org: Barborini, Christian / Celis, Sofia / Chabot, Cathy / Eekhoudt, Cameron / Fast, Danya / Goodyear, Trevor / Manson, Daniel / McKenzie, Sophie
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
We demand that YPWUD be at the table in a meaningful way (and not just as token
participants in the process) as plans for decriminalization and safe supply are rolled out in BC and
elsewhere.

8. We add our voices to those demanding a safe supply of drugs via peer-led compassion clubs that
sell pharmaceutical grade cannabis, heroin, cocaine, and meth to those over 18 years of age.

9. Youth voices should be better integrated into both bottom up, grassroots and top down, statesponsored harm reduction movements and initiatives. Harm reduction organizing and

programming must be informed by an intersectional lens. It is critical to recognize and respond to
how the risks and harms experienced by YPWUD are shaped by intersections of class, race,
gender, sexuality, and dis/ability. It is also important to recognize the intersections between drug
user activism, anti-poverty activism, housing activism, and sexual health activism.

10. YPWUD in the context of greater privilege, as well as allies, should focus energy on fostering and
extending the activism of YPWUD in the context of street involvement, creating vertical
connections to power as well as horizontal connections across communities of people who use
drugs. The goal is to grow a diverse and strong collective of YPWUD locally, nationally, and
internationally.
Summary
The overarching takeaways from our work are two-fold:
First, we underscore the need for more robust investments in youth-dedicated and youth-led
mental health and substance use services integrated with housing, income, social, and
cultural supports. Second, we call for policy makers and service providers to listen to and
respect youth, uphold their autonomy and self-determination, and understand the diverse
nature of youth’s experiences while prioritizing relationship building and developing a
reciprocity with YPWUD.
More About Us

The BC Centre on Substance Use Youth Health Research Program is a qualitative, ethnographic, and
community-based research program led by Dr. Danya Fast. It focuses on how young people’s
substance use, care, and healing trajectories are influenced by social structural contexts.

text:
Written Submission for the Standing Committee on Health
Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
On behalf of
The Canada Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Research Network
May 24, 2024

Context:

Towns and cities across Canada are experiencing high rates of drug overdose and death.
Experts, policy makers and community service agencies have expressed their views on what
needs to be done and have been working on doing it.

There are polarizing views on how to solve this devastating societal issue in Canada. Any and all
of the solutions are complex. Some propose better support for youth experiencing difficulties to
help prevent their need to explore substances as a coping strategy. Others feel the solution is in
making sure that people have a safe supply of drugs so that we can keep them alive long enough
to convince them to try treatment supports, while others propose that we focus primarily on the
recovery for those struggling with substance use. Likely, we need to be doing a combination of
all of these things and more.

Many of the solutions that we frequently hear about are based on the assumption that people
using substances are fully functional when they are not using substances.

org: Canada Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Research Network
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Many of the solutions that we frequently hear about are based on the assumption that people
using substances are fully functional when they are not using substances.

This is important because programs and policy to address substance use in Canada are often
built on this premise. We know that there are people with disabilities, and specifically those with
Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), who are often unrecognized, undiagnosed and
unsupported. When this happens, we know that people with FASD are much more likely
(estimate 30+%) to become unhoused, struggle with substance use, engage in criminal activity,
become parents, interact with child welfare services, and have difficulty staying employed. Ninety
percent of individuals living with FASD will experience a mental illness. Research conducted in
2012 shows that FASD affects a staggering 4.4% of the Canadian population. This is a
conservative number due to gaps in diagnostic capacity, and the fact that this statistic is based on
research conducted over 10 years ago (due to gaps in FASD research capacity in Canada).
According to that same research, at least 57 000 individuals with FASD struggle with substance
use and dependance in Canada (again, this number could only have increased over the past
decade). These intersections are too many and too significant to ignore. Policy makers should be
considering the prevalence and impact of FASD in Canada, and the relationship between FASD
and the opioid crisis.

People with FASD can be very articulate, although often experience challenges with
understanding and absorbing information, especially under stressful situations. They often feel
that people are their friends, and can become easily exploited. This common scenario is
particularly problematic in situations involving substance use. CanFASD very often hear from
families that their loved one has lived a lifestyle involving substance use for so long that they do
not know what is normal, often returning to the streets.

org: Canada Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Research Network
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
CanFASD very often hear from
families that their loved one has lived a lifestyle involving substance use for so long that they do
not know what is normal, often returning to the streets.

Perhaps we need to design our programs on the premise that all people with substance use
issues are not fully understanding of their choices, the level(s) of support they may need, or know
how to access and/or navigate these systems. Much research has been done to look at who the
people are that are on the streets and using substances, but very few ask questions about
prenatal alcohol exposure, which might give clues to their condition of FASD. Individuals with
FASD are almost always the first ones asked to leave substance use treatment programs
because they are unable to follow the rules, understand the process of treatment, or accept the
purpose of them being there at all.

The stories are similar they are prevalent in the FASD community. An individual may have been
raised by the child welfare system, they have multiple home placements, don’t do well in school –
are suspended or quit early, fall in with “friends” that are committing crimes, get introduced to
alcohol and drugs, are sexually exploited, go to jail and return to their “friends” with new skills to

commit more crimes. Individuals living with FASD are at a higher risk of continuing in this cycle
for many years - in and out of the systems of corrections, social services, child welfare, and
mental health services. They become distrustful of professionals and protection agencies,
preferring the non-judgmental approach of the street. During this time, they may have children,
many of them prenatally exposed to alcohol and substances. This can be a motivating time to
enter support services, but without the right treatment and supports, they will likely not be able to
sustain the power to keep trying to access help.

text:
This can be a motivating time to
enter support services, but without the right treatment and supports, they will likely not be able to
sustain the power to keep trying to access help.

We need to consider the possibility that most people, if not all, who find themselves in vulnerable
situations experiencing substance use issues may have FASD. Even if they do not – the
strategies and supports propelled by evidence based FASD research will not be harmful, and
individuals without FASD who are struggling with substance use are very likely to find them
helpful. We need better identification tools to identify FASD in Canada, FASD training for
professionals who interact with the FASD community, whether it be through the education system
or justice system, access to assessment and diagnostic capacity across the country, better
prevention awareness and better evidenced based research. We need to find out how to best
support the FASD population, which is increasingly at risk of struggling with substance use and
dependence. It is a large number of people and they are not doing well.

What is missing in our approach to the opioid crisis is a more thorough understanding who the
people are that are using opioids and other substances. Thinking FASD first and adapting our
access, supports, treatment and strategies accordingly for this over represented population is an
important consideration in this devastating societal issue.

CanFASD and our network of medical experts, researchers and Canadians with lived experiences
are supportive of enhancing the capacity for FASD research and coordination of support across
Canada. We are supportive of a national framework for FASD to accomplish this. We believe
such a proactive policy to coordinate and enhance efforts to address FASD will undoubtedly lead
to better outcomes for Canadians struggling with opioid and toxic drug use, given the
interconnection between FASD and substance use.

Recommendation: That the committee consider the staggering interconnection between Fetal
Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) and substance use in Canada. As such, we recommend that,
in addition to recommendations brought forward by our peers, the committee also consider
enhancing FASD research and the coordination of FASD support resources across Canada. This
would have a positive impact on improving the outcomes of Canadians struggling with opioid use,
and their families.
The Canada Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Research Network (CanFASD) is a
collaborative, interdisciplinary research network, with collaborators, researchers and
partners across the nation. It is Canada’s first comprehensive national Fetal Alcohol
Spectrum Disorder (FASD) research network. It started as an alliance of seven jurisdictions
and operated for seven years as the Canada Northwest FASD Research Network.
CanFASD’s unique partnership brings together many scientific viewpoints to address
complexities of FASD, with a focus of ensuring that research knowledge is translated to
community and policy action. Our mission is to produce and maintain national, collaborative
research designed for sharing with all Canadians, leading to prevention strategies and
improved support services for people affected by Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder.

text:
Moms Stop The Harm Brief to the House of
Commons Standing Committee on Health
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health Witness
Statement
Presented by MSTH co-founder Petra Schulz, of Edmonton, AB, on April 29, 2024.
All personal stories are shared with the permission of the families of the deceased.
Our Organization
Moms Stop the Harm(MSTH) is a network of Canadianfamilies impacted by
substance-use-related harms and deaths. We advocate for the change of failed drug policies,
provide peer support to grieving families, and assist those with loved ones who use or have
used substances.
Moms Stop the Harm challenges laws and policies that cause harm, including those laws that
continue to drive the unregulated drug poisoning emergency in Canada. We call for an end to
the failed war on drugs through evidence-based prevention, treatment and policy change. We
support an approach that reduces the harms associated with drugs, and that is both
compassionate and non-discriminatory for people who use/d drugs (PWUD). We empower
families to use their voices without shame, to share their stories and to advocate for positive
change.
Our vision is that PWUD are not criminalized and that their rights are respected. We believe
that PWUD are deserving of safe and equitable access to health and wellness. We support all
pathways to wellness and believe that access to health and social services should not be
predicated on a requirement to abstain from drugs.
MSTH engages inadvocacy,public education, andfamilysupport.

text:
MSTH engages inadvocacy,public education, andfamilysupport.

Our advocacy is focused on:
● The decriminalization of people who use drugs. We support theDecriminalization done
Rightplatform, developed jointly with twenty othercivil society organizations.
● The provision of regulated alternatives to toxic unregulated substances for individuals
who are at risk of dying from drug poisoning. Our position is outlined in apolicy brief
developed jointly with the Canadian Civil Society Working Group for Advancing Safe
Supply.
● Rapid access to a range of evidence based and voluntary treatment options, for all
individuals seeking substance use treatment.
● Prevention that addresses social determinants of health, racial inequalities and the
harms caused by colonization
Our education and awareness activities focus on:
● We offer in-person and on-line workshops, webinars and conferences.
● Presentations at national and international conferences, to all levels of government,
schools, post-secondary institutions and community groups.
● Public awareness campaigns and events, such asInternationalOverdose Awareness
Day.
Our support programs include:
Holding Hope Groups, which are free peer-facilitatedsupport groups, for families and individuals
whose loved ones use or have used substances.
Healing Hearts Groups,which are free peer-led bereavement support groups specific to those
grieving the loss of a loved one due to overdose or substance-use related causes.
Hope for Canadian families: providing a spectrum of harm reduction and
recovery supports that save lives.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you. I am a co-founder of Moms Stop The
Harm, representing thousands of families across Canada. Most mourn a loved one due
to the toxic drug crisis, many support loved ones with lived or living experience. Our
website includes 600 images of our loved ones who have died.
Being here today is both meaningful and difficult, as tomorrow is the 10th anniversary of
the day when our son Danny died. Danny was a brother, friend, musician, and a
talented chef.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Danny was a brother, friend, musician, and a
talented chef.

Danny is a poster child for failed drug policy. He was on methadone for a while, then
abstinent, but never stable. In 2014, fentanyl appeared on the market and he was one
of the early victims. There were no warnings, he did not have access to harm reduction,
which could have saved him.
Today almost everyone knows someone who has lost a loved one. Those who die
include people who use every day, occasionally or just once, like Olivia, a thirteen year
old girl from central Alberta who died after using with a friend. We do not know what
substance the teenagers intended to use, or how much, but unregulated fentanyl killed
them both.
The increasing deaths from the toxic drug supply is driven by prohibitionist policy
decisions that have failed to keep our loved ones safe. This includes the failure to
robustly implement harm reduction measures across the country.
In Canada almost all deaths are from unregulated drugs, over 85% nationally and in
Alberta it is a staggering 98%. Yet we see political leaders create a moral panic around
the 2% while ignoring the other 98.
We are told that this is an “addictions crisis”, and that “more beds, more
abstinence-based treatment” will be the answer. Yet, the example often cited, the
Alberta Model, has failed to save lives. 2023 will be the worst year on record for deaths
in my home province.
According to national data the rate of substance use has not gone up in 10 years, yet
deaths have skyrocketed. How come? This is not a problem of “addiction” but of a toxic
unregulated supply.
Access to consumption services, drug checking, and to regulated alternatives,
and decriminalization of people who use drugs is what is needed. Sadly, such
measures currently in place are insufficient for the magnitude of the crisis and do
not reach all communities.
This is a Truth and Reconciliation issue.
The TRC report calls on the government to reduce gaps in health outcomes between
Indigenous and non-indigenous people, yet Indigenous people are disproportionately
affected by drug poisoning. In AB they are 7 times more likely to die and 5 times more
likely in BC.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In AB they are 7 times more likely to die and 5 times more
likely in BC.

Sarah Auger lost her son Lakotah in 2022. He was a doting father, a loving son, and
proud to be Cree. He used alcohol and other substances, but his use of unregulated
substances, including the Fentanyl that later took his life, escalated only after he was
incarcerated. While we know that the harm of alcohol surpasses all other substances,
one drink will not kill you.
Lakotah’s story and the story of Mike,also illustrate the danger of forcing abstinence on
people despite the well documented risks. Mike, the son of MSTH board chair Traci
Letts, was playful, thoughtful and a passionate cook. Both Lakotah and Mike died
shortly after incarceration.
Similarly Angela Welz lost her young daughter Zoe, who she describes as athletic,
funny and headstrong, shortly after two failed attempts at getting help through
involuntary detention via the Alberta PCHAD Act (Protection of Children Abusing Drugs
Act).
What is so upsetting is the fact that the deaths of our loved ones have become
politicized with misinformation and outright lies.
This is a public health issue and needs to be treated as such. I urge you to stop
the angry, harmful, misinformed and polarizing debates. Politics and ideology
must be taken out of healthcare.
Work together and focus on what the evidence tells us:
● Harm reduction, including the provision of regulated alternatives saves
lives.
● Evidence-based, voluntary and accountable treatment saves lives.
● Prevention and addressing the social determinants of health, saves lives.
This is not a harm reduction versus recovery debate. Our loved ones need and
deserve both.
Danny is on my mind every day and I know he wanted help. The day before he died he
asked me to make an appointment with his doctor and psychologist. He did not live long
enough to attend those appointments. More treatment would not have saved him, but
harm reduction and access to regulated substances would have.
Where there is life, there is hope. It is your responsibility to ensure that our loved
ones live and that we have reason to hope that the needless deaths will end.
