study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Ottawa Inner City Health is an organization that provides health care to people who are
homeless or vulnerably housed1. We offer a wide variety of shelter based and supportive
housing-based social-determinants of health services for individuals, the vast majority of
whom use drugs. Since 2001, we have been leading responses to changes in Ottawa’s
unregulated, non-prescribed drugs market including the recent acceleration of changes to
what we now call the toxic drug supply.
It is important to understand that situation on the ground across Canada is evolving rapidly
and our collective response is lagging. While the strategies of a decade ago continue to
mitigate some of the harms, that mitigation has become less effective due to changes in
the content and potency of this drug supply, the social safety net, brain and drug
clearance physiology from aging & repeated use and in the behaviour of some of those
most impacted. This is compounded by lack of meaningful investment in services to
support chronic pain, substance use and mental health including complex trauma
treatment.
The Opioid Crisis, Phase 1: The Overprescription Crisis
Only 20 years ago, there were approximately 100 people in Ottawa on methadone and one
of our first roles was to advocate for improved access to methadone. This was the first
wave of the opioid crisis, where opioid deaths were primarily driven by prescribed and
diverted OxyContin.
The based available peer-reviewed medical and experiential evidence then suggested
these harm reduction approaches; : scale up oral opioid agonist treatment (initially,
methadone was the only treatment available in Ontario), establish take home naloxone
programs, implement Housing First programs to help people find and maintain
independent housing and establish supervised consumption services for the unhoused
and other marginalized people so they could use their drugs under the supervision of staff
trained to intervene in the event of an opioid overdose and to connect people to health
and social services they needed (like OAT, Housing First, and primary care).
If everything remained the same, we would have mitigated a significant portion of the
harms associated with this public health crisis. We would still have an opioid problem, but
it would not have today’s scale nor intensity.
When we failed to properly regulate appropriate access to prescribed opioids in Canada,
we exposed a substantial segment of the Canadian population to opioids, creating
dependency and in some cases, an opioid use disorder as well.
Opioid Dependence and Opioid Use Disorder
To clarify, opioid dependence means that a person’s body requires a specific dose of an
opioid to prevent withdrawal symptomsi. For most, these withdrawal symptoms are so
severe they report that “it feels like they are dying”. Opioid dependence develops early
within a course of treatment but is safely tolerated with low dose and short duration [3

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Opioid dependence develops early
within a course of treatment but is safely tolerated with low dose and short duration [3

weeks] opioid use. Conversely, the longer the opioid exposure and the higher the dose, the
more difficult and unsafe the withdrawalii
Opioid use disorder [OUD] refers to changes in behaviour caused by the substance use coopting the pleasure and reward system of the brain, typically in people who are
predisposed by chronic stress induced by adverse childhood events and other unresolved
traumas, or systemic oppression experienced throughout the lifespan.iii
Opioids bring relief to the traumatized brain and withdrawal pain which drives some to
desperation.
Most people who use opioids chronically will experience some degree of physiologic
tolerance and dependence but most who use opioids do not have an opioid use disorder
as determined by DSM criteria.iv
In Canada, our default drug policy responses are prohibition and criminalization which
drive and/or perpetuate trauma, stigma, and marginalization/oppression7. We have been
implementing prohibition-oriented drug policies for over a hundred years despite clear
evidence of harm and zero evidence of benefit. Despite billions of dollars spent, lives lost
and communities devasted by these policies, non-regulated, non-prescribed drugs are
more; varied, potent & toxic, cheaper, and more available than ever before. Sometimes
prohibition is made more palatable when dressed down as “deprescribing”, “delisting” or
“abstinence only and/or forced treatment” but it is prohibition nonetheless and
demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of the problem and the true nature of
harm reduction, treatment and recovery.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Sometimes
prohibition is made more palatable when dressed down as “deprescribing”, “delisting” or
“abstinence only and/or forced treatment” but it is prohibition nonetheless and
demonstrates a fundamental misunderstanding of the problem and the true nature of
harm reduction, treatment and recovery.

Substance Use and Treatment
People naturally move back and forth along a continuum of substance use depending
upon their life circumstances. [see diagram]. As a person’s use trends toward the
righthand side of the continuum, the more problematic the substance use for the person
and their community, with a greater need for help and resources to reduce harm. People
who experience the most stigma, marginalization and trauma typically fit at the most
extreme right of the continuum. It is impossible to separate the substance use from the
trauma and marginalization at this point and pointless to treat any substance use
disorder(s) if we do not address the underlying social structures that the substance(s) use
is/are helping the person cope with. Note that the strategies below the continuum shift
based on severity of the presentation and at the extreme right the treatment focus is more
on the social determinants of health. The realistic expectation should be that nothing
about the substance(s) use is going to change if we don’t start making “good things”
happen to people who are chronically deprived by structural oppression and repeated
trauma exposure.
A popular understanding of substance use treatment is that the goal is to get people to
stop using drugs. Most substance use treatment is about helping people move from the
right to the left on this continuum as far as they’re able, and as resources allow. This
approach is like that used for other chronic relapsing conditions [e.g. hypertension]. We
don’t tell people with diabetes they must have their blood sugar under control before

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
We
don’t tell people with diabetes they must have their blood sugar under control before

coming in for treatment and we don’t tell them they must commit to a sugar-free life as
the only acceptable measure of success.
The recovery journey can take years or decades and it is generally recognized by the
recovery care specialists that people will relapse go back to old behaviours, include
resuming opioid use. Even short periods of abstinence from opioids significantly reduces
physiologic tolerance to opioids in the brain, particularly tolerance to respiratory
depressionv, lower tolerance means a lower amount of the substance is needed for the
same effect—including a lower dose for an opioid overdose. This is why harm reduction
teachings and practices are essential throughout the recovery journey and the distinction
between treatment and harm reduction is a false dichotomy—any evidence-based
treatment strategy must embed the philosophy and tools of harm reduction at its core.
For those who have an opioid use disorder, the standard of treatment is oral opioid agonist
treatment (methadone, buprenorphine/naloxone) with a second line treatment being
injectable opioid agonist treatment (high dose hydromorphone or diacetylmorphine),
ideally integrated with mental health for complex trauma and social supports to address
other variables influencing ongoing use and barriers to recovery. Second line treatment
and integrated trauma care is virtually nonexistent in Canada.
There is a tragic irony that many people who want substance use treatment languish on
waiting lists while there are calls for forced treatments that are not only ineffective for
sustained recovery and a waste of taxpayer dollars. Additionally, they place patients at risk
for opioid overdose induced mortality when they leave the controlled environment and
reuse due to loss of tolerance to respiratory depression effects of opioids.
The Opioid Crisis, Phase 2: The De-prescribing Crisis
The second wave of opioid crisis was the de-prescribing phase. In Ontario, this was the
phase where regulators delisted oxycontin and then high dose opioid formulations from
the Provincial drug benefit formulary and prescribers began to rapidly taper people from
high dose opioids. The impact of rapid de-prescribing instead of proper tapering drove
desperate people to the streets to source their opioids. What they found there was far
worse than oxycontin—it was illicit fentanyl, which was already making gains in the
unregulated, non-prescribed drug market in Ontario. De-prescribing oxycontin and high
dose opioids effectively created the demand for an unregulated, non-prescribed fentanyl
market and the crisis worsened.
Stopping novel exposure to long term [>3 weeks] and high dose opioidsvi was the right
policy decision but advocates amongst people who use drugs and patients with chronic
pain rightly argued that they ought to have been managed differently, given their particular
risk profile and poor immediate prospects for opioid abstinence.
We will never know the outcomes if we had maintained people on their doses and
implemented patient-responsive tapers from high dose opioids. We might have prevented
unregulated, non-prescribed fentanyl from gaining its foothold had we provided regulated,
prescribed market competition for those who were most harmed by Phase 1 of the opioid

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
We might have prevented
unregulated, non-prescribed fentanyl from gaining its foothold had we provided regulated,
prescribed market competition for those who were most harmed by Phase 1 of the opioid

crisis. In a very short time unregulated, non-prescribed fentanyl evolved from sporadic
incursions to widespread contamination, and finally to its dominance in today’s toxic drug
market.
The Opioid Crisis, Phase 3: The Toxic Drug Crisis
In Ottawa, all this was happening just as the initial strategy (investment in OAT, take home
naloxone and supervised consumption services) was rolling out. These strategies were not
adequately scaled, and we struggled to meet the demand of people exiting the medical
system rapidly from deprescribing and by the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic
challenges that fentanyl was bringing to the harm reduction/treatment landscape.vii
In addition to different levels of potency, opioids have different rates of onset and duration.

The shift from the first wave (oxycontin) to the second wave (fentanyl) of the opioid crisis
resulted in an increase in opioid related deaths as “street doses” were far more potent.
We also saw an increase in injecting as people required more frequent dosing maintain
opioid levels and avoid withdrawal.viii
The impact on health and social care services and drug use behaviour was immediate.
Supervised consumption sites were overwhelmed by demand with the requisite increased
frequency of injecting and the concerns people had that each dose was potential lethal.
The short duration of action [euphoria, tranquility] along with much reduced tolerance to
Fentanyl’s respiratory depression effect meant that people had less capacity to wait to get
into service and began to inject in public spaces just outside consumption sites—staying
as close as possible so that staff at the sites could respond to any overdoses they might
experience. Staff had to respond to more overdoses inside, and outside the sites and
encountered atypical overdoses and had to administer multiple naloxone doses to
overcome Fentanyl respiratory depression.ix Moral distress amongst staff began to grow
because we simply could not accommodate the sudden and dramatic increase in demand
caused by the shift.
Addictions Medicine was also impacted as dosing guidelines for methadone initiation were
far below street doses resulting in people not feeling any immediate relief from the longacting opioid (at therapeutic levels, methadone duration is 24 hours—which is why it is
used as a treatment). In a review done at a consumption site in Ottawa, 30% of

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In a review done at a consumption site in Ottawa, 30% of

consumption site clients reported being on methadone, but all of them were on initiation
doses, or slightly higher, none at what would be considered a therapeutic dose relatively to
their street usage.
On the individual level, frequent dosing meant that the daily cycle of substance use sped
up dramatically: once they used, they quickly needed get money for there next dose, find
their next dose, go to the consumption site, wait to use the site and then repeating that
process. The shortened usage cycle meant that even a motivated OAT client could not
commit to the schedule necessary to get to a therapeutic dose of methadone or connect
with their case manager or counsellor.
Something else was beginning to shift as well—clients started smoking stimulants (crack
cocaine, crystal methamphetamine) in association with injecting their fentanylx.
More recently, people who had previously injected fentanyl, began to smoke fentanyl,
possibly due to poor venous access from years of high frequency injecting and possibly
due to the mistaken belief that smoking fentanyl was less risky than injecting fentanyl
from an overdose perspective. Since 2020, approximately half of opioid toxicity deaths
had evidence of inhalation.xi
Only a handful of supervised consumption sites in Canada offer supervised smoking and
supervised smoking is strictly prohibited in under funder contracts in Ontario.
During the first wave of the opioid crisis the street level illicit drug trade was primarily
conducted within the community of people who use drugs in Ottawa. Diverted oxycontin
was sold by one person who uses drugs to another as a means of making money to
maintain their own use. Community norms were well established and violence was
limited. When fentanyl analogues, research chemicals and benzodiazepine-like drugs
began to infiltrate the unregulated, non-prescribed drug supply, illicit drug use became
risky and volatile as did the drug trade itself.
Powdered fentanyl is the perfect illicit market drug. It is easy to acquire, with low risk of
detection from border services or police, and profit and demand are high. This brought
outside parties into the local drug scene which led to more violence and an escalation in
intensity of violence. We have instituted “Stop the Bleed” training for our consumption site
staff due to the increasing number of stabbings happening in the area.
Impact of the Pandemic
In March 2020, Canada declared a public health emergency for COVID-19. Overnight,
people who use drugs experienced a severe reduction in access to sites and services and
safer spaces such as public libraries.
Consumption sites reduced capacity and hours of service in anticipation of staffing
shortages, OAT services developed virtual care capacity and reduced unnecessary
restrictions on take home doses, and the general support systems of day programs

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Consumption sites reduced capacity and hours of service in anticipation of staffing
shortages, OAT services developed virtual care capacity and reduced unnecessary
restrictions on take home doses, and the general support systems of day programs

shuttered overnight while organizations struggled to figure out ways to reopen with limited
information on the spread of COVID-19 and insufficient access to personal protective
equipment. Essential services that remained open shifted from relational to transactional
in the attempt to reduce exposure risk and to see as many people as possible.
Connections between clients and health care agencies began to disintegrate.
Shelters operators utilized different strategies to respond to COVID-19 amidst a housing
crisis. In Ottawa, COVID isolation centres and physical distancing centres were established
to provide unhoused people with the same capacity to keep themselves healthy as
housed Ottawans. Many decided they were better off taking their chances on the streets
and we saw an increase in encampments across Ottawa, along with an increase in open
substance use.
People who use drugs experienced a spike in material deprivation as key sources of
income (panhandling, shoplifting, sex work) disappeared. Loss of access to public utilities
led to an increase in public toileting further dehumanizing and demoralizing the unhoused.
Lack of access to public spaces that promoted community combined with the shift in the
drug trade and pharmacokinetics/dynamics of street fentanyl let to a rapid change in
community norms amongst unhoused people who use drugs in Ottawa. The positive
aspects of street culture were lost to the urgent need of the shortened substance using
cycle, contributing to an increase in violence and the general sense that society no longer
cared about them. As the only source of comfort left to people, fentanyl replaced the
relationships that brought balance to the community and social disorder began to grow.
Post Pandemic
While most Canadians have returned to a normal life, post pandemic, people who use
drugs are, in many ways, still living under COVID conditions. Most security services
implemented during COVID19 remain in place, health and social service agencies still
experience high rates of turnover in front line staff and few new investments in mental and
substance use health have been implemented.
A significant number of leaders amongst people who use drugs have been lost over the
past 5 years and complex grieving with multiple losses has continued. Repeat non-fatal
opioid toxicity events has increased the rate of hypoxemic brain injury amongst people
who use drugs, making harm reduction, substance use treatment and housing, much
more challenging.
Recommendations
Drug Policy Reform
We support wide scale decriminalization and intelligently regulated access to psychoactive
substances in Canada. We recognize the harms of prohibition and the harms of wide
scale commercialization and urge the government to adopt a regulatory framework that is
evidence-based and minimizes harms to Canadians.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
We recognize the harms of prohibition and the harms of wide
scale commercialization and urge the government to adopt a regulatory framework that is
evidence-based and minimizes harms to Canadians.

Involvement of People Who Use Drugs
Investment in community development, engagement and meaningful involvement of
people who use drugs at the service implementation level, systems planning, and policy
levels is critical. Building and restoring leadership amongst people who use drugs is
critical for any sustainable strategies to succeed in responding to the safety, engagement
and recovery needs of the most vulnerable and to address the safety needs identified by
other stakeholders.
People who use drugs have significant intersectionality that create specific vulnerabilities
and opportunities. Governments must consult with community leadership and provide
targeted funding for First Nations, Inuit, Metis and Urban Indigenous communities, African,
Caribbean and Black and 2SLLBGTQIA+ communities.
Access to prescribed alternatives
We must provide prescribed, intelligently regulated alternatives to the toxic unregulated,
non-prescribed drug supply. This would include a range of treatments to match the needs
of those who are accessing the unregulated drug supply with the overall goal of engaging,
decreasing morbidity and mortality, stabilizing and integrating into the community. Here
we see the need for both low barrier, traditional OAT treatment and the urgent need to
scale up injectable opioid agonist treatment in Canada.
Harm Reduction Housing
In Ontario, most drug toxicity deaths occur in private dwellings and most occur in
neighbourhoods of highest material deprivation. Given the barriers to recovery
experienced by those most impacted by the toxic unregulated, non-prescribed drug
supply, public and supportive housing programs must be harm reduction based. On site
opioid toxicity preventions strategies need to be core programming for housing programs
for people who use drugs. Given the increased prevalence of acquired brain injury and
complex untreated trauma, housing options must include 24/7 wraparound health care to
manage high risk behaviours and support recovery and integration.
Mental Health Care and Trauma Treatment
Trauma is a key driver of substance use and substance use disorder and is contributing to
the social disorder experienced in communities across Canada. We can begin addressing
trauma in the most vulnerable by focusing on their safety needs and engaging them to be
actively involved in restoring their connections and in integrating within the local
communities where they live. Targeted programs to treat complex trauma are required.
Supervised Consumption
Supervised consumptions sites have not been adequately scaled in Canada, with many
Provinces opting out of funding these emergency health care interventions. Policy and
regulatory frameworks have not kept pace with changes to the toxic drug supply. The
evidence of need for smoking sites is incontrovertible but few sites in Canada are able to

The
evidence of need for smoking sites is incontrovertible but few sites in Canada are able to

offer these services. Alternative forms of witnessed consumption must be expanded and
governments need to invest in novel technology to support wider access.
Drug Checking
We will never eliminate the unregulated, non-prescribed market. Providing people with the
tools and information to make informed decisions about their use of illicit drugs is a
critical, life saving service. There are many promising technologies in the field and
governments need to invest in developing these technologies and increasing access to

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, regarding the
Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
Prepared by: the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network
March 2024
Background
In response to the ongoing opioid toxicity crisis, the provision of prescribed, pharmaceutical
opioids (e.g., daily dispensed immediate-release hydromorphone) as an alternative to the
unregulated opioid supply—a practice known as safer opioid supply or prescribed safer supply—
was introduced as a harm reduction measure. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, the number
of safer opioid supply programs have rapidly expanded across Canada due to the provision of
short-term, pilot funding by Health Canada and the publication of emergency Risk Mitigation
Guidance in some provinces.
As safer opioid supply programs have expanded across the country, there has been an ongoing
dialogue about the evidence regarding their safety and effectiveness. Given that some people will
crush and inject their immediate-release hydromorphone, one concern that has been raised in
recent years is whether there is a risk of injection-related infections among people accessing
hydromorphone tablets through safer opioid supply programs. Evidence from peer-reviewed
publications and grey literature program evaluations has grown over recent years, which has
largely indicated that these programs result in improved clinical outcomes.1 In parallel, our group
has continued to monitor trends in injection-related infections across Ontario (provincially and
regionally).2 In this submission, we summarize the current state of evidence and knowledge
regarding risks and prevalence of injection-related infections among people with opioid use
disorder within the context of safer opioid supply programs.
I.
Hydromorphone Use and Risk of Infectious Complications
Current evidence indicates a formulation dependent association between hydromorphone use
and infectious complications,3-5 with an association between hydromorphone use and infections
being concentrated among recipients of controlled-release hydromorphone. A 2020 populationbased cohort study conducted in Ontario, Canada found a 3-fold greater odds of hospital
admission for infective endocarditis among people who inject drugs who were prescribed
controlled-release hydromorphone compared with those prescribed other opioids (adjusted odds
ratio 3.3, 95% CI 2.1–5.6, p < 0.001).4 In contrast, no significant association was observed
between infective endocarditis and immediate-release hydromorphone exposure relative to other
opioids (adjusted odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 0.9–3.6, p = 0.072).4 These findings are important within
the context of discussions around safer opioid supply programs, as these programs across
Ontario prescribe immediate-release, and not controlled-release hydromorphone.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
3.3, 95% CI 2.1–5.6, p < 0.001).4 In contrast, no significant association was observed between infective endocarditis and immediate-release hydromorphone exposure relative to other opioids (adjusted odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 0.9–3.6, p = 0.072).4 These findings are important within the context of discussions around safer opioid supply programs, as these programs across Ontario prescribe immediate-release, and not controlled-release hydromorphone.

II.
Prevalence of injection-related infections among people entering safer opioid
supply programs
Studies published in Ontario demonstrate that clients of safer opioid supply programs generally
have high measures of comorbidity at the time of program initiation, including high prevalence of
injection-related infections (i.e., infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, spinal
infections, and skin and soft-tissue infections), HIV and Hepatitis C.6-8 A population-based study
conducted by the ODPRN in Ontario found that clients entering the London InterCommunity
Health Centre safer opioid supply program (N=82), were significantly more likely to have a
previous hospital visit for a skin and soft-tissue infection (18.3% vs. <6.1%) in the year preceding
program enrollment compared to a matched unexposed group of people living in London with
opioid use disorder who were not prescribed safer supply.6 This is reinforced by two studies
examining safer opioid supply more broadly across the province, which have similarly
demonstrated that these programs are concentrated among people with high rates of infectious
complications and HIV at baseline.7,8 Furthermore, the evaluation of the London program,
published in CMAJ, found no monthly increase in the rate of hospital admission for infectious
complications (-1.6 infections per 100; 95% CI: -4.0, 0.8, p=0.2) following safer supply program
entry, and a significant 49% decrease in the annual rate of infectious complications (relative
rate 0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.96; p=0.04) among safer opioid supply recipients.6 Taken together,
this published evidence shows that many clients entering safer opioid supply programs have a
history of injection-related infections, putting them at higher risk of future infections; however
instead of seeing these rates continue to increase, in the year following entry into the program,
published safer supply program evaluations suggest that people’s risk of infections declines.
III.
Prevalence of injection-related infections among people with opioid use disorder
To more broadly understand the prevalence of injection-related infections among people with
opioid use disorder, a population-based study conducted in Ontario examined trends in serious
infections among this population between 2013 and 20199—a period before the expansion of
safer supply prescribing across Canada. This study reported that over a seven-year period, the
rate of serious infections among people with opioid use disorder grew significantly (7.7 to 20.6
per million; p<0.001), with the growth beginning in 2015, when fentanyl entered the unregulated
drug supply.9 Importantly, these increases were observed in all regions of the province,
suggesting that they are likely related to the short duration of fentanyl’s effects increasing people’s
need for frequent substance use when accessing the unregulated drug supply, thus increasing
their risks of infectious complications. Since this time, publicly available data from the Ontario
Drug Policy Research Network’s surveillance dashboard provides updated trends extended to the
end of 2022 (Figures 1 and 2).2
As described in the publication summarized above, there was an initial rise in annual rates of
incident hospitalizations for infective endocarditis and serious infections among people with an
opioid use disorder from 2015 to 2019; however rates began to decline in 2020 and 2021—a
period of time when safer opioid supply was rapidly expanding across Ontario.2 Overall, these
findings indicate that the largest growth in the rate of injection-related infections among people
with opioid use disorder was observed prior to COVID-19 related expansion of safer opioid supply

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
an opioid use disorder from 2015 to 2019; however rates began to decline in 2020 and 2021—a period of time when safer opioid supply was rapidly expanding across Ontario.2 Overall, these findings indicate that the largest growth in the rate of injection-related infections among people with opioid use disorder was observed prior to COVID-19 related expansion of safer opioid supply

programs across Ontario, with rates declining in parallel with this expansion. While these data are
population-level, they are consistent with what would be expected based on the findings of the
program evaluation in London described above and suggest that there is no population-level
indication of worsening injection-related infections as safer opioid supply programs have
expanded across the province.
Figure 1. Yearly rate (per 100,000 population) of incident hospitalizations for infective
endocarditis among people with opioid use disorder in Ontario from 2014 to 2022.
Note: An incident hospitalization was defined as having no prior hospitalization in the one year
before the encounter for each type of infection.

Figure 2. Yearly rate (per 100,000 population) of incident hospitalizations for other serious
infections among people with opioid use disorder in Ontario from 2014 to 2022
Note: A serious infection was defined as one of the following: non-vertebral bone infections,
spinal infections, and skin and soft tissue infections. An incident hospitalization was defined as
having no prior hospitalization in the one year before the encounter for each type of infection.
Conclusions
We request the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health to consider the following
during their study of the opioid epidemic and toxic drug crisis in Canada:
1. Clients entering safer opioid supply programs often have complex medical conditions
including a higher prevalence of injection-related infections at time of program entry,
underscoring the importance of services offered within safer opioid supply programs
which help facilitate access to primary care and medical treatment.

2. Across Ontario, the rate of hospitalizations for serious injection-related infections has
declined in recent years – specifically during the period in which safer opioid supply
programs were rapidly expanded across the province.
3. Available evidence from multiple sources in Ontario, demonstrate that immediate-release
hydromorphone does not increase risk of injection-related infections, and that infections
do not rise among people entering safer opioid supply programs, but rather decline in the
year following program entry.
We thank the Committee for considering our brief.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Overview:
The Standing Committee on Health adopted a motion to undertake a study on the Opioid
Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada and the response by federal, provincial, and
territorial governments.

A challenge Canadians face that must be addressed are the lack of access to non-opioid
(non-pharmaceutical) related options to treat and manage pain. The Canadian Pain Task
Force’s (CPTF) final report, An Action Plan for Pain in Canada, found that the lack of access to
non-opioid options to treat pain is one of the factors contributing to the opioid crisis.i

The Indigenous Chiropractic Caucus recommends the government take the following steps
to ensure that non-opioid related options are available to Canadians seeking care:
•
Recommendation: For the government to initiate a comparative review of the
Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program, to identify areas to improve
Indigenous peoples’ access to care, including reinstating coverage for chiropractic
care.
•
Recommendation: Federal leadership on addressing the burden of MSK
conditions by funding pilot projects that demonstrate innovative approaches to
treat or manage pain in Indigenous communities.
Contact

Dr. Jennifer Ward, DC, M.Sc

Dr. David Peeace, DC
 [CONTACT]

[CONTACT]
 ICC, co-chair

ICC, co-chair

Introduction

On the 27th of November 2023, leaders from the Canadian Chiropractic Association (CCA)
and the Indigenous Chiropractic Caucus (ICC) officially signed the Terms of Reference
Agreement in a formal ceremony in Ottawa. The ICC represents Indigenous Doctors of
Chiropractic across Canada, as well as advocates on issues that impact the musculoskeletal
health of Indigenous peoples in Canada.

Chiropractors are one of Canada’s largest primary contact healthcare professions and
experts in the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions,
such as back pain, headaches, arm or neck strain and diseases of the muscles and joints, as
well as the management of pain caused by these conditions.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Chiropractors are one of Canada’s largest primary contact healthcare professions and
experts in the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions,
such as back pain, headaches, arm or neck strain and diseases of the muscles and joints, as
well as the management of pain caused by these conditions.

Each year, more than 11 million Canadians suffer from musculoskeletal conditions and by
2031 this number is projected to grow to an alarming 15 million.ii Musculoskeletal
conditions are having a devastating impact on the health, quality of life, and workforce
participation of Canadians, as well as on Canada’s economy. According to Health Canada,
the total direct (healthcare) and indirect (lost production) cost of chronic pain in 2019 was
$38.2 - $40.3 billion. Over the next decade the total cost is expected to increase by 36.2 per
cent and reach $55 billion.iii

Doctors of Chiropractic are well-positioned to aid in tackling the opioid epidemic and toxic
drug crisis, while also improving the access to musculoskeletal healthcare for Canadians
and helping in the management and treatment for chronic pain.

Training, Expertise and Experience

Doctors of Chiropractic complete eight years of post-secondary education and complete
extensive training and clinical education as part of their studies. They are regulated in all
Canadian provinces and because of their extensive training are designated to use the title
doctor, like physicians, optometrists, and dentists. As experts in non-pharmacological pain
management, chiropractors can lead and facilitate an inter-professional, evidence-based,
and patient-centred approach to pain care.

Recommendation: For the government to initiate a
comparative review of the Non-Insured Health Benefits
(NIHB) program, to identify areas to improve Indigenous
peoples’ access to care, including reinstating coverage for
chiropractic care.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Recommendation: For the government to initiate a
comparative review of the Non-Insured Health Benefits
(NIHB) program, to identify areas to improve Indigenous
peoples’ access to care, including reinstating coverage for
chiropractic care.

Contrary to national and international recommended guidelines, opioids have emerged as
one of the primary means for managing non-cancerous chronic pain in primary care
settings and are often used as a first line of treatment for lower back pain and neck pain.iv
In 2023, a total of 3,970 apparent opioid toxicity deaths occurred between January-June,
which is an average of 22 deaths per day.v It is clear that better approaches are needed to
manage chronic pain in Canada. The World Health Organization (WHO) in December 2023,
released the non-surgical guidelines in the treatment of chronic low back pain in adults and
recommended conservative strategies including spinal manipulative therapy, massage,
acupuncture and exercise therapy to name a few.vi With respect to opioid analgesics, the
guideline specifically said they should NOT be used as part of routine care. Improving
access to manual therapies, like chiropractic care, may help reduce the heavy reliance and
overuse of opioids, and provide practitioners with evidence informed options in their care
plans.

Due to the long-standing experiences with colonization, the burdens surrounding muscle
and joint conditions are uniquely experienced and prevalent in Indigenous populations.
According to the 2018 First Nations Regional Health Survey (RHS), chronic health conditions
such as arthritis and chronic back pain remain some of the most commonly reported
conditions among First Nations adults, and remain the most prevalent chronic conditions
overall.vii In fact, among First Nations adults reporting a chronic health condition, arthritis
(18.3 per cent) and chronic back pain (12.4 per cent) were two of the most commonly
reported conditions.viii

The lack of coverage for chiropractic services under the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB)
program represents the most significant barrier to care. The ICC encourages the federal
government to implement Recommendation Nine in the Report of the Standing Committee
on Indigenous and Northern Affairs, published December 2022, that the government
should undertake a comparative review of the NIHB program to understand deficiencies
and ensure that it provides medical benefits that meet the health needs of Indigenous
peoples. One area to review is the accessibility and coverage of allied healthcare providers
and their services. Ensuring access to allied healthcare professionals, like chiropractors,
would allow Indigenous peoples’ access to non-pharmaceutical care options to treat MSK
conditions or manage pain.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Ensuring access to allied healthcare professionals, like chiropractors,
would allow Indigenous peoples’ access to non-pharmaceutical care options to treat MSK
conditions or manage pain.

Canadians living in rural and remote communities are challenged in accessing
musculoskeletal care. This is partially due to the fact that twenty per cent of Canadians live
in rural communities but are served by only eight per cent of the physicians.ix The federal
government can provide leadership in addressing the shortage of healthcare professionals
in rural communities, and provide tangible alternatives to care to marginalized and at risk
communities by expediting the expansion and implementation of two programs under
consideration:
•
A one-time income tax deduction for healthcare professionals, including allied
healthcare practitioners such as chiropractors, establishing clinics in rural and
underserved communities;
•
Expansion of the Canada Student Loan Forgiveness Program to include allied
healthcare professionals, including chiropractors.

These two initiatives would have an immediate positive impact on access to evidencebased, non-pharmaceutical care in rural communities. Due to the impact of colonization,
First Nations people in Canada are disproportionately affected by chronic conditions and
overdose deaths, as well as face significant barriers to accessing care. This highlights the
urgent need to support Indigenous peoples in addressing chronic pain through nonpharmacological options. For musculoskeletal conditions, like back pain, the key is to
prioritize non-invasive, conservative options without prescribing opioids or other drugs for
chronic pain.

Recommendation: Federal leadership on addressing the
burden of MSK conditions by funding pilot projects that
demonstrate innovative approaches to pain in Indigenous
communities.

The federal should fund pilot projects that demonstrate innovative alternative approaches
to pain management. The Cross Lake First Nation project is an example of a
government funded initiative that has shown successful results for the community.
Funded in part by the Government of Canada and Health Canada’s Substance Use and
Addictions Program (SUAP), World Spine Care Canada and the Indigenous leadership of
Pimicikamak Okimawin (Cross Lake First Nation) launched a research project and
health service in Cross Lake, Manitoba, Canada.

This project facilitates access to high-quality, low-cost, non-pharmaceutical, and noninvasive care for low back and neck pain as the first step in a comprehensive spine

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
This project facilitates access to high-quality, low-cost, non-pharmaceutical, and noninvasive care for low back and neck pain as the first step in a comprehensive spine

care model. The clinician triages patients and streamlines referrals to the most
effective and appropriate care when warranted. This project outlines a successful
example of federal leadership and funding for projects that move away from
pharmaceuticals as a first line of treatment for patients experiencing lower back pain
and neck pain, especially for Indigenous populations. Preliminary results demonstrated
a significant reduction in muscle and joint pain, improvements in function and a decrease
in costly referrals outside the community. Similar results have been demonstrated in
chiropractic integration into hospital settings,x healthcare teamsxi and serving military and
veterans.xii Effective triage away from expensive and unnecessary services has been
reported to be cost-effective and sustainable.

The Cross Lake Spinal Care Clinic aims to demonstrate the benefits of an interprofessional
approach to muscle and joint pain management in an Indigenous community. Additional
funding and pilot projects should be considered to ensure care and allow for innovative
services to be provided to Indigenous communities.

Conclusion

The Indigenous Chiropractic Caucus urges the Government of Canada to immediately
consider implementing these recommendations to facilitate access to evidence-based and
guideline-supported manual therapies like chiropractic care for pain. The federal
government can play an important role in ensuring that Canadians have access to nonopioid manual therapies by funding pilot projects that demonstrate innovative multidisciplinary care and ensure that allied healthcare professionals, such as Doctors of
Chiropractic, are better integrated into the healthcare system and Indigenous
communities.

The federal
government can play an important role in ensuring that Canadians have access to nonopioid manual therapies by funding pilot projects that demonstrate innovative multidisciplinary care and ensure that allied healthcare professionals, such as Doctors of
Chiropractic, are better integrated into the healthcare system and Indigenous
communities.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
In the current context of the overdose crisis, the ASPQ recommends:
-
Raising awareness of the overdose crisis and reducing social and health inequities
-
Revising the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (S.C. 1996, c. 19)
-
Increasing funding for initiatives along the addiction continuum (prevention and health promotion, harm
reduction, treatment)
BACKGROUND
While Canada recorded 40,642 opioid-related deaths between January 2016 and June 2023, and an average of
22 deaths per day between January and June 2023,1 Quebec has not been spared from the overdose crisis. The
508 deaths between October 2022 and September 2023, averaging 42 per month between July and September 2023,2
could increase dramatically and unpredictably if the illicit drug supply market changes.
According to the 2019 Canadian Alcohol and Drugs Survey,3 nearly one in five (19.3%) Quebeckers have used one or
more illegal drugs in their lifetime, and 4.2% report harms associated with it. In 2014-2015, it was already estimated
that 11% of young people aged 15 to 29 in Quebec had used drugs (other than cannabis), a higher proportion than in
other age groups.4
Overview of the overdose crisis in Quebec
The drug overdose crisis is reducing life expectancy in Canada5 and is only getting worse.6 According to the Institut de
la statistique du Québec, excess mortality is accelerating among people under 50, and may be particularly atributable
to opioid overdoses.7 In 2019, 1.7% of Quebeckers reported having experienced a drug overdose in their lifetime.8 Yet
overdose deaths are both unnecessary and preventable.
Substance use disorders
Although the use of psychoactive substances may be recreational, it poses risks of dependence and intoxication.
According to 2022 Statistics Canada data,9 6.8% of Canadians aged 15 and over will have experienced a cannabis use
disorder, and 3.6% will have experienced another drug use disorder in their lifetime (excluding alcohol and cannabis).
In fact, 13.4% of 20–24-year-olds in Canada reported experiencing drug-related harm in 2019, putting this age group
at the top of the list.10 However, 63% of people diagnosed with an alcohol- or drug-related disorder do not use mental
health or addiction medical services.11
DATA-RELATED ISSUES
An underestimated crisis in Quebec
The overdose crisis in Quebec remains underestimated. Although the number of deaths in Quebec has remained
relatively stable,12 indicators in Montreal13 show an increase in the crisis – in particular, an increase in overdoses in
supervised consumption services, naloxone distribution and Urgences-Santé intoxication interventions.
In Quebec, the total costsi associated with the use of psychoactive substances was $8.22 billion in 2020,ii
all substances combined, excluding costs associated with hospitalization, day surgery, emergency room visits and
ambulance services.14 The lack of data makes it difficult to obtain a complete picture of the financial resources
allocated.
i Healthcare, lost productivity, criminal justice and other costs, details on the CSUCH website
ii Including alcohol, tobacco and cannabis

text:

Contaminated drug overdose crisis
An analysis of coroner’s reports in Quebec15 found that polyintoxication was involved in 65% of deaths, with the
majority of overdose deaths not atributed to a single lethal substance. Self-medicationiii and supply problems during
COVID may also have contributed to an increase in polyconsumption.16
Yet, while the reality of the population demonstrates the importance of deploying efforts beyond opioids alone, the
most recent data on stimulant deaths in Quebec ends in 2020.17 This hampers the analysis of indicators needed to get
a complete picture of the overdose crisis and to deploy substantial resources beyond opioids alone.
Social and health inequities
Social determinants weigh heavily in the overdose crisis: an analysis of 340 coroner’s reports in Quebec found an
overrepresentation of socio-economic, physical and mental health issues.18 Similar observations were made across
Canada, combining contextual and individual factors such as a history of mental illness, stigma, chronic pain and lack
of health care.19
The INSPQ20 reports that deaths related to psychoactive substances are associated with accidents (overdoses, injuries,
traumas), acute or chronic physical illnesses and concomitant disorders.iv The prevalence of mental health disorders
among people with a substance use disorder in Quebec was three times higher in 2016-2017 (31%) than among those
who had never received this diagnosis since 2001 (11%).21 People living with a substance use disorder are 9.4 times
more likely to commit suicide.22
While overdose alerts atest to the role of extreme temperatures for people who use psychoactive substances,23 the
climate crisis could contribute to exacerbating the social and health inequities associated with the overdose crisis.
Homeless people, who are at higher risk of being affected by climate change,24 are overrepresented in overdose
deaths while they are underrepresented among those with a naloxone kit.25
The ASPQ recommends increasing awareness about the overdose crisis and reducing social and health inequities, in
particular by:
-
Clarifying the social determinants of health and social and health inequities specific to psychoactive
substance use and the overdose crisis, taking into account provincial, regional and local specificities
-
Calling for data to be updated in all Canadian provinces and territories to provide a realistic picture of the
crisis, so that appropriate measures can be taken for all psychoactive substances, including stimulants
-
Reducing the stigma associated with the use of psychoactive substance use, including by ensuring that health
and social service resources are free from structural stigma
LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR PSYCHOACTIVE SUBSTANCES
Drug status stigma
According to Health Canada, the stigma around drug use leads to physical and mental health harm and exacerbates
health inequities.26 Structural stigma in health and social services policies is no exception. The ASPQ believes that the
fear of legal reprisals associated with criminalization and the stigma associated with drug use can inhibit help-seeking
and lead to isolated use, increasing the risk of overdose.
Based on available data in 2020, the Scientific Working Group on the Costs and Harms of Substance Use in Canada
estimated criminal justice costs related to substance use at $1.99 billion in Quebec and $9.97 billion in Canada.27
According to the Report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (2023): “[the war on drugs] was
tantamount to a war on people, since its impact was oŌen greatest on those who were poor, and frequently
overlapped with discrimination in drug control efforts directed at vulnerable and marginalized groups.”28
iii To alleviate physical or mental health issues, including pain management.
iv Cooccurrence of mental health disorder(s) and substance use disorder(s).

text:
Rights (2023): “[the war on drugs] was tantamount to a war on people, since its impact was oŌen greatest on those who were poor, and frequently overlapped with discrimination in drug control efforts directed at vulnerable and marginalized groups.”28 iii To alleviate physical or mental health issues, including pain management. iv Cooccurrence of mental health disorder(s) and substance use disorder(s).

Safe supply
The supply of low-cost, unregulated opioids on the illicit market has contributed to an increased risk of unintentional
overdoses.29 Measures such as drug analysis and safe supplyv could be key in a context where the majority of
overdoses remain unintentional. A study of 5,882 people living with addiction in British Columbia between March
2020 and August 2021 showed a 91% reduction in the risk of death from all causes in one cohort, and an 89%
reduction in the risk of overdose when prescriptions were given for four or more days.30
The ASPQ recommends that the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (S.C. 1996, c. 19) be revised, in particular to:
-
Decriminalize the simple possession and personal use of psychoactive substances in Canada
-
Expand access and allowable controlled substances for safe supply
AN ACTION CONTINUUM
Public health measures
The Public Health Agency of Canada’s31 modelling of observed and projected opioid-related deaths in Canada suggests
that public health interventions play a critical role in the evolution of the crisis and may help reduce deaths despite
the stabilization or increase in fentanyl levels.
A study of a supervised consumption service in Calgary showed cost savings of about $1,600 per overdose by avoiding
emergency department visits and prehospital emergency services.32
The importance of enhancing prevention
More than half of overdose deaths were discovered by family and friends, with many seeking help from a friend rather
than emergency services.33 However, the signs and symptoms of an overdose are oŌen missed or ignored, reducing
the interventions needed to reverse the overdose. In an ASPQ survey of 1,008 Quebec adults conducted by Léger, 23%
rated their knowledge of overdose intervention as “good” or “very good,” and 16% rated their knowledge of naloxone
administration as “good” or “very good.”34 In addition to raising awareness of the risks of contaminated drugs, public
education could strengthen our collective ability to prevent deaths.
The ASPQ recommends increased funding for initiatives along the addiction continuum (prevention and health
promotion, harm reduction, treatment), particularly to:
-
Increase training for the general public to intervene in the event of an overdose
-
Strengthen efforts to destigmatize people who use drugs
-
Recognize the essential nature of interventions and settings that enable safe consumption, such as
supervised consumption services (SCS) and drug analysis, and call for their use in a perspective of universal
access to treatment
CONCLUSION
In addition to increasing direct intervention with people at risk of overdose in response to growing needs, the ASPQ
believes that the overdose crisis requires a massive increase in prevention efforts.
v According to Health Canada, providing prescribed medications to people at high risk of overdose is a safer alternative
to the toxic illegal drugs supply.

text:
BRIEFING NOTE
A Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Opioid Crisis in Canada - Intersection of MMIWG2S+ and the Opioid Crisis in
Montreal
Iskweu Project - Native Women’s Shelter of Montreal
Janis Qavavauq-Bibeau and Laura Aguiar
February 2024
Summary:
The Iskweu Project began in 2017 as a response to the ongoing crisis of missing and murdered
Indigenous women, girls, trans, and 2-Spirit (MMIWG2S+) people throughout Quebec. The
Iskweu Project wishes to respond to an immediate need for assistance expressed by families
and loved ones in the case where an Indigenous woman, girl, trans, or 2-Spirit person goes
missing.
Our aim is to reduce and ultimately eradicate the number of missing and murdered Indigenous
women, girls, trans, and Two-Spirit people in Quebec; to offer support and ensure adequate
response from institutions when someone goes missing or is murdered. We seek to reduce
barriers in accessing support and receiving an adequate response from institutions that have
historically discriminated against Indigenous peoples. A large part of our work is also supporting
Indigenous women, girls, trans, and 2-Spirit people who are facing violence in order to prevent
future disappearances or murders. Annually, we work with approximately 75 MMIWG2S+ family
members and survivors throughout Quebec.
Increasingly, we have observed the impact that the opioid crisis is having on Indigenous women
facing violence and the broader MMIWG2S+ crisis. Due to the lack of availability of culturally
specific healing services for survivors of violence and the MMIWG2S+ crisis, many Indigenous
women, girls, trans, and 2-Spirit people turn to drugs as a way to cope with their trauma
resulting from colonization. We have also observed how substance usage can become a further
tactic for violence and abuse through forced dependency, a form of violence in which an abusive
pimp or partner will force an Indigenous woman or gender-diverse person to use drugs against
their will. The perpetrator of this type of violence may then force a survivor to experience
symptoms of withdrawal in order to demonstrate to the survivor what will happen should they
leave. In highly controlled situations of sex trafficking, we have seen traffickers forcibly inject
Indigenous women and gender-diverse people with opioids as a way to subdue a survivor when
they may be transported between venues of trafficking or when they are forced to provide
sexual services.
The final, and perhaps most concerning way in which the opioid crisis intersects with the
MMIWG2S+ crisis is the way in which we have observed opioids used to commit femicide
against Indigenous woman, girls, trans, and 2-Spirit people. We have seen numerous situations
where an Indigenous woman was facing high-lethality levels of violence only to later be found

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
We have seen numerous situations
where an Indigenous woman was facing high-lethality levels of violence only to later be found

dead, with her death ruled as an overdose. What is worse is that in some of these cases, no
coroner’s investigation is performed simply because at the surface level, this woman died as a
result of an overdose. This presents as problematic, because it fails to look at why this woman
overdosed and what the conditions of her life were leading up to the overdose. It is
indescribably unjust to hear from an Indigenous woman that her boyfriend or partner is trying to
kill her, only for her to be found dead days, weeks, or months later and for this to be ruled as an
overdose without acknowledging that overdose for what it truly is; a murder by overdose. We
have observed this through women being intentionally given drugs laced with fentanyl and
intentionally failing to administer Naloxone or to call 911 to seek medical intervention when it
could have saved a person’s life.
Recommendations:
Increase the availability of low-barrier services that are both anti-violence and harm
reduction for Indigenous women, girls, and gender-diverse people
Many services in place that are harm-reduction oriented lack an analysis and approach relating
to violence against Indigenous women, girls, and gender-diverse people or are not culturally
safe and adapted for Indigenous peoples. Additionally, many services dedicated to anti-violence
towards Indigenous women, girls, and gender-diverse people are not adapted to working
towards women and gender-diverse people who are in active substance use, whether this
substance usage is forced, coerced, or by choice. We also acknowledge the limited options so
many Indigenous women and girls are presented with, particularly those facing homelessness.
We call on the federal government to ensure that permanent, core funding is made available to
organizations providing frontline, anti-violence services to Indigenous women, girls, and
gender-diverse people. We also call on existing harm reduction organizations and anti-violence
organizations to listen to the wisdom of survivors of MMIWG2S+ and to adapt their practices to
serve Indigenous survivors who are facing violence through forced or coerced substance usage.
Increase the availability of trauma-informed healing services for survivors of MMIWG2S+
and their families
Intergenerational trauma among Indigenous communities in Canada is incredibly widespread
and deep-seated, yet there is a lack of healing services in order to address this trauma. Opioids
and other substances that may be laced with fentanyl are sadly more accessible than healing
services and serve as a way to assist survivors of MMIWG2S+ to cope with their trauma. We
call on the federal government to increase the availability of healing services specifically for
survivors of the MMIWG2S+ crisis and to ensure that permanent, core funding is provided to
these organizations so as to ensure they are able to focus on their work without worrying about
funding.
End the criminalization of survivors of MMIWG2S+ and their families for using
substances as a way to cope with their trauma and survive

text:
End the criminalization of survivors of MMIWG2S+ and their families for using
substances as a way to cope with their trauma and survive

Given the lack of available healing and trauma supports for Indigenous women who are
survivors of the MMIW2S+ crisis and the number of survivors who use substances as a way to
cope with and survive their trauma, the criminalization of Indigenous women and gender-diverse
people who use substances to cope must end. At the present time, the criminalization of
survivors who use substances is nothing more than criminalizing Indigenous survivors for their
trauma. We call for improved screening practices to identify Indigenous women and
gender-diverse people who may be facing violence by way of forced or coerced substance use
or through forced dealing and selling of drugs to ensure that they do not face criminal charges
for being survivors of violence. Instead, we recommend that these women be connected to
supportive healing services.
Ensure that coroner and police investigations are thoroughly conducted each team an
Indigenous woman or gender diverse person dies of an overdose to identify the
conditions that lead to this overdose
In situations where an Indigenous woman, girl, 2-Spirit, or gender diverse person dies of an
overdose, the circumstances leading up to the overdose must be thoroughly explored. This is
particularly true if an Indigenous woman or gender-diverse person was in a situation of violence
prior to her death. We call on police departments, coroner’s offices, and other investigative
bodies across the country to develop and implement best practices in investigating murder
cases in the context of overdoses, particularly among Indigenous women, girls, and
gender-diverse people without further criminalizing survivors.
At the request of families (both chosen, adoptive, and biologic), re-open the cases of
Indigenous women, girls, and gender-diverse people who were in situations of violence
and whose death were classified as an overdose
Family members and friends of MMIWG2S+ often hold very intimate knowledge about the
circumstances leading to their death, particularly surrounding patterns of violence they may
have been facing prior to their death. Oftentimes, family members and friends are the last to
have seen or had contact with MMIWG2S+. It is imperative that families are listened to, and that
notions of family are expansive and include chosen family, particularly “street family” for those
who are unhoused. If family members or friends express that they feel their loved one may have
been murdered by way of overdose, police at all levels have a responsibility to listen to this and
follow through with an investigation. Without a thorough investigation, it is not possible to rule
whether or not the overdose was accidental, or whether it was a murder.
