study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Joint Submission by CAAN Communities, Alliances & Networks and the Canadian AIDS Society (CAS)
to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health regarding its study on the ‘Opioid Epidemic
and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada’
January 2024

Recommendations
1. Consider all future actions within the context of the Truth and Reconciliation Calls to Action
and Calls to Justice.
2. Work on easing stigma around HIV and the activities that lead to it.
3. Decriminalize and regulate the drug supply.
Context
The strength and resilience of Indigenous Peoples in Canada is rooted within a rich diversity of cultures,
traditions, and values that have long been nurtured by Indigenous health systems and healing practices.
Despite this, Indigenous people across generations have been and continue to be deeply affected by the
ongoing legacy of settler colonialism, institutionalized racism, and systemic discrimination in Canada. The
final reports from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) and the Missing and Murdered
Indigenous Women and Girls (MMIWG) Inquiry demonstrated how manifestations of cultural oppression,
structural violence, and abuse have resulted in long-lasting health impacts, intergenerational trauma, and
economic and social marginalization for Indigenous peoples in this country. These systems of oppression
have affected a range of social determinants of health, including income, education, employment, social
status, working and living conditions, health practices, and child development.
When these social determinants of health are affected, this is linked to higher rates of problematic
substance use; physical abuse and violence; living in poverty; and housing insecurity and homelessness.i
As stated in the TRC Report, “the residential school system was an attack on the health of generations of
Aboriginal peoples, an attack first made visible by the physical scars of sickness and abuse, but also one
that continues to punish Aboriginal peoples with a legacy of marginalized lives, problematic substance
use, mental health, poor housing, and suicide.”ii Compounding these determinants of health, Indigenous
peoples continue to be subject to disproportionate levels of criminalization and incarceration that further
fuel a cycle of disadvantage and human rights violations.
This results in increased rates of HIV/AIDS, TB, and other STBBI among Indigenous peoples. In Canada,
Indigenous peoples made up 18% of all new HIV infections in 2020, while comprising only 5% of the
population.iii Indigenous women in particular have been increasingly affected; although they make up
roughly 2.5% of Canada’s population, they represent approximately 6.6% of new HIV infections with
known ethnicity, and are often diagnosed in the later stages, severely affecting their quality of life.iv For
TB, Indigenous peoples make up 91.85 percent of cases,v highlighting the need for a strong national TB
Elimination Strategy that centers Indigenous health.
To effectively prevent new cases and treat existing cases of HIV/AIDS, TB, and other STBBI, we need to
educate and empower those most at-risk. The TRC’s Call to Action 19 urges “the federal government, in
consultation with Aboriginal peoples, to establish measurable goals to identify and close the gaps in
health outcomes between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal communities.”vi The fact that Indigenous
peoples are overrepresented in these numbers shows that lack of action on HIV/AIDS, TB, and other STBBI
is, effectively, an anti-Indigenous policy position.
Among Indigenous people living with HIV in Canada, transmissions are attributable to injection drug use
at a much higher rate than for non-Indigenous populations.vii Against the backdrop of the toxic drug
poisoning crisis in Canada fueled by an unregulated drug supply, Indigenous peoples have also suffered a
disproportionate proportion of fatal overdoses. Despite representing only 3.2% of British Columbia’s
population, First Nations people represented 15% of victims of overdose deaths in the province between

org: Canadian AIDS Society / Communities, Alliances and Networks
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Despite representing only 3.2% of British Columbia’s
population, First Nations people represented 15% of victims of overdose deaths in the province between

2021 and 2022, dying at over five times the rate of other British Columbia residents.viii Indigenous women
have suffered even more disproportionately, as statistics from the first half of 2022 indicated that First
Nations women in British Columbia were 8.8 times more likely to fatally overdose compared to other
women. While incremental steps have been taken to scale up health and harm reduction services, the
current measures used to prevent HIV/AIDS and other STBBI transmission and drug poisoning, such as
needle and syringe distribution programs, supervised consumption services, drug checking, opioid
agonist therapy, naloxone kits, and safe supply programs that provide drugs that traditionally have been
available only through the unregulated drug market, are typically not Indigenous-led nor created to be
culturally appropriate, making them inaccessible for many Indigenous peoples who use drugs. Access to
harm reduction services is an essential part of the right to health and an effective tool for reducing virus
transmission incidental to drug use.ix
Recommendation 1: Consider all future actions within the context of the Truth and Reconciliation Calls
to Action and Calls to Justice
The final report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, released
in 2019, includes 231 Calls to Justice which highlight 18 areas of public policy needing reform, including
education, justice and health. Specifically, Call to Justice 3.1 requires governments at all levels to ensure
the equitable protection of the rights to health and wellness of Indigenous peoples, and Calls to Justice
3.2, 3.4, 7.1, and 7.2 all require state actors to properly fund and resource accessible and culturally
appropriate health and wellness services for Indigenous communities, including trauma and substance
use treatment programs.x Additionally, Call to Action 19 of the TRC Report requires the government to
close gaps in health outcomes between Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities.xi
The Calls to Justice and the Calls to Action provide a key framework for the next steps for policy across
issue areas. Healthcare, mental health, and substance use services and supports specifically will require
these recommendations to be implemented in order to ensure that Indigenous peoples are properly
included in any new policy or programming surrounding easing stigma, providing resources and supports,
decriminalization and regulation, etc. Without the lens of the Calls to Action and the Calls to Justice, any
movement in policies or legislation in this area will leave Indigenous communities behind, further
widening the gap in health care service and accessibility between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples
in Canada.
The federal government has acknowledged that Indigenous-led services are more effective when
developed, implemented, and led by Indigenous peoples. This approach has been missing from previous
outreach efforts to communities experiencing problematic substance use; culturally appropriate
resources that acknowledge the history and context of Indigenous peoples in Canada and their
relationship with addictive substances, as well as the critical role that community plays in easing stigma
and establishing long-term healthy and supportive environments, must be critical components of any
policy addressing the opioid epidemic moving forward.
Recommendation 2: Ease the stigma around HIV and the activities that lead to it
In order to appropriately address HIV/AIDS transmission and treatment, specifically in relation to drug
use, significant efforts must be undertaken by the federal government – in partnership with Indigenous
organizations who are established in their communities – to reduce the stigma around both HIV and the
activities that may lead to it. Stigma can prevent people who use drugs from accessing prevention and
harm reduction messaging and services and this can lead to activities that include sharing drug use
equipment, hurried drug consumption, and using drugs in unsafe environments.
The stigma around HIV/AIDS is rooted in a variety of misconceptions: homophobia; fear of people who

org: Canadian AIDS Society / Communities, Alliances and Networks
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
The stigma around HIV/AIDS is rooted in a variety of misconceptions: homophobia; fear of people who

use drugs; transphobia, stereotypes of Indigenous peoples and drug use; and fear of people who are
unhoused, among many others. The identities of Indigenous peoples diagnosed with HIV/AIDS differ
dramatically from non-Indigenous peoples. Among the 1,520 new HIV infections in Canada in 2020, 43.8%
were among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men who do not inject drugs; 2.8% were
among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men who also injected drugs; 19.8% were among
heterosexual people who injected drugs; and 33.6% were among heterosexual people who do not inject
drugs. Overall, 16.1% of all people diagnosed with HIV in Canada are people who inject drugs.xii A 2014
Government of Canada report found that
In AIDS cases in Indigenous men, HIV infection was attributed to male-to-male sexual contact for
32.6% of cases (compared with 74.4% for males of other ethnicities) and to injection drug use for
39.2% of cases (compared with 6.5% for males of other ethnicities). For AIDS cases in Indigenous
women, HIV infection was attributed to injection drug use for 68.9% (compared with 20.4% for
females of other ethnicities) and to heterosexual contact for 29.2% (compared with 67.0% for
females of other ethnicities).xiii
These numbers indicate that traditional methods of stigma reduction targeting the LGBTQ+ community
will not be effective within Indigenous communities. This is due in part to the disparity in source of
infection, but also due to a lack of community-centered and culturally appropriate information and
programming. Without including on-the-ground programming from Indigenous-led organizations that
examine the source of infection; the settler-colonial structures that impact the physical and mental
wellbeing of Indigenous peoples; and the cultural and community-based aspect of Indigenous healing,
stigma reduction programs and policies will be ineffective.
Reducing stigma and implementing harm reduction, in addition to being culturally appropriate and
Indigenous-led, must be coupled with access to safe living spaces. This includes housing/shelters; mental
health care; access to food; access to land and Indigenous languages, access to community; and access to
education, among others. Without access to wrap-around supports that will help people who use drugs
regardless of their continued use of drugs, it is extremely difficult to shut down the trauma response that
leads many people to use drugs. A holistic approach is necessary to ensure the reintegration into an
individual’s community and the creation of a feeling of safety and security that will allow people who use
drugs to address the root causes of drug use. In order to meet people where they are, these resources
must be made accessible to people who use drugs; arbitrary barriers to resources due to drug
consumption only leads to increased drug use, overdose, and death.
Recommendation 3: Decriminalize and Regulate the Drug Supply
As UNAIDS has acknowledged, the criminalization of drug possession for personal use (i.e. “simple drug
possession”) is not a productive public health approach.xiv Criminalization and abstinence-based models
of drug regulation place people who use drugs at greater risk of acquiring HIV and other blood-borne
infections. Criminalization pushes people who use drugs into isolation and limits their ability to access
essential health care and harm reduction services while fostering unsafe practices and (e.g. sharing drug
use equipment, hurried drug consumption, using drugs alone and/or in unsafe environments to avoid
detection and arrest) and preventing their ability to take safety precautions.xv
Canada’s long-standing policy of criminalizing drugs has also resulted in an unregulated drug supply that
continues to become more potent and unpredictable year-over-year. According to a 2023 study, police
drug seizures increase rather than prevent overdose deaths, as it forces people who use drugs to use an
alternate supply which may be unknown or unsafe and have varying effects on the body. In addition, this
effect indicates that the scheduling of substances is routinely followed by the emergence of new
substances often posing greater harms from consumption.

org: Canadian AIDS Society / Communities, Alliances and Networks
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In addition, this
effect indicates that the scheduling of substances is routinely followed by the emergence of new
substances often posing greater harms from consumption.

Criminalizing drug use directly fuels discrimination and stigma (both internal and external) for people who
use drugs, which adversely affects mental and physical wellbeing and leads to exacerbated health
inequities for these communities.xvi The repercussions also extend beyond health-based impacts – the
legal aspect can have long-term impacts on an individual’s ability to access employment and housing
opportunities, and childcare and child custody. This legal framework is rooted in Canada’s history of
colonialism, and has disproportionately affected Indigenous peoples in Canada:
•
A 2020 report found that Black and Indigenous people are dramatically overrepresented in drug
charges recommended by the Vancouver Police Department. While making up 1% of the city’s
population, Black people have accounted for 6.4% of drug trafficking and possession charges in
Vancouver since 2014; Indigenous people have accounted for almost 18% of drug trafficking and
possession charges but are just 2.2% of the city’s population.xvii
•
A 2020 study found that Black and Indigenous people continue to be overrepresented in cannabis
possession arrests across Canada.xviii
•
A 2022 report analyzed non-cannabis simple drug possession arrest data from police services in
Canada. Data from 2015 to 2021 indicates that Indigenous peoples were nearly six times more
likely in Regina, five times more likely in Saskatoon, and nearly eight times more likely in
Vancouver to be arrested for drug possession than their representation in the population would
predict.xix
Continuing down the current path of criminalization goes against the recommendations of the Calls to
Action and the Calls to Justice, puts Indigenous peoples at greater risk of being victimized by a settlercolonial system, and increases the risk of people participating in unsafe practices that increase the risk of
HIV/AIDS and other STBBI transmission.
In order to move forward with decriminalizing drugs in a safe and effective way, regulation of the drug
supply needs to occur at both the federal and community level. Using current federal relationships with
safe supply companies and organizations as a framework for safe consumption, Indigenous community
organizations should be brought into these partnerships to ensure that Indigenous peoples both on- and
off-reserve are able to access the drugs that they need to prevent overdoses and deaths from toxic and
unsafe drug supplies. Other interventions to assist people who use drugs should also be made accessible,
including drug education, treatment, rehabilitation, and social reintegration services, with a specific focus
on the needs of Indigenous peoples and to traditional healing practices. Decriminalizing and regulating
the drug supply is not about stopping people from using drugs; it is about stopping people from dying
from drugs.
Conclusion
Addressing the gaps in healthcare for Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in Canada is a
reconciliatory policy action that will have significant positive long-term effects on alleviating the financial
and physical strain on our healthcare system and support the physical and emotional well-being of all
people who use drugs across Canada.
Indigenous peoples are key members of Canada’s communities, and any steps taken to address the opioid
epidemic and toxic drug crisis must emphasize programs and supports that are Indigenous-led,
Indigenous-centered, and culturally appropriate. Additionally, HIV/AIDS and other STBBI prevention,
treatment, and stigma reduction must be included, as the intersection between STBBI, problematic
substance use, and other social determinants of health must be considered in drafting and implementing
policy. These issues disproportionately impact Indigenous peoples in Canada, and thus in order to have
truly reconciliatory policies and programs, they must be highlighted.

text:
The Eastside Illicit Drinkers Group for Education (EIDGE)
Vancouver Area Network of Users
380 E. Hastings St, [CONTACT]
Vancouver, Canada
February 9th 2024
CC: the Honourable Standing Committee on Health
To whom it may concern,
The Eastside Illicit Drinkers Group for Education (EIDGE) requests that the following brief be
considered as information pertinent to your committee's ongoing study of the Opioid Epidemic
and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada.
EIDGE has a core membership of between 40 to 60 peers who are current or former illicit
alcohol users living in and around the Downtown Eastside. EIDGE defines illicit drinking as the
consumption of non-beverage alcohols (including mouthwash, hand sanitizer, and rubbing
alcohol) and the use of beverage alcohol in ways that are criminalized, most often due to coerced
use of public space due to homelessness, discrimination by service providers, or residence in a
Single Room Occupancy (SRO) hotel. EIDGE members are usually long-term, heavy drinkers
who meet established criteria for Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and who are likely to experience
high-risk withdrawal symptoms, including seizures and Delirium Tremens. Illicit drinkers across
the community experience incredibly high rates of alcohol and drug-related harm including but
not limited to drug poisoning death, accidental injury, and interactions with law enforcement, and
hepatic injury. Over 80% of EIDGE members are Indigenous, and experience high rates of
alcohol-associated harm intersecting with socioeconomic marginality and intergenerational
experience of colonial violence. The majority of our members are currently Managed Alcohol
Program (MAP) clients, live on extremely low incomes, and have not benefited from
abstinence-oriented models of care.
EIDGEs primary submission to the Committees deliberations is a written submission to the
British Columbia Ministry of Public Safety and the Solicitor General (PSSG) dated August of
2023. The attached brief was presented to PSSG during public consultations on the development
of the Restricting Public Consumption of lllegal Substances Act. During the consultation period,
EIDGE informed PSSG that, based on EIDGE members' combined decades of experience
navigating the criminalization of public substance use as a structurally marginalized group, that
the provisions of Bill 34 promote high-risk, isolated use of a volatile drug supply and subsequent
overdose risk for people who are coerced into accessing the unregulated drug market. In short,
Bill 34 is an overt criminalization of unhoused and precariously housed drug users, and will
380 E. Hastings St, [CONTACT]
Vancouver, Canada
place them at risk of further harm. Bill 34 is undeniably an attempt to legislatively weaken
the provisions of limited decriminalization of personal possession in B.C., a policy that has
significantly reduced interactions with the criminal justice system for people who use drugs
without evidence of significant increases in public drug use. Unfortunately, widespread
misinformation related to decriminalization in BC, its effects, and the necessity of punitive
legislation like Bill 34 has contributed to a rising tide of anti-harm reduction sentiment
throughout Canada that is not based in facts, evidence, or public health best practices.
We feel that it is crucial that the Committee understand the factual nature of the
arguments made against Bill 34 and the extent of the material harm that is likely to arise
from the legislation. EIDGE requests that the Committee consider the ways in which
comparable legislation, if passed in BC or in other Canadian jurisdictions, will compromise
the federal government's stated intent to reduce the harms of the drug poisoning crisis.
EIDGE would also like to strongly assert our support for safer alternatives to the increasingly
toxic unregulated drug supply, including prescribed safe supply, compassion clubs, and the
lifesaving work of the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF). We are all using some form of
controlled substances, which is where our concern lies. Illicit drinkers in Vancouver, specifically
those living in the DTES, are extremely vulnerable to drug poisoning death. Since 2021, EIDGE
has lost 10 dedicated members, several of whom died from drug poisoning. There are several
reasons for this high-rate of overdose amongst illicit drinkers. Polysubstance use involving
alcohol, a risk factor for overdose, is common amongst our members. Many of members are also
opioid-naive drinkers who are primarily stimulant users. These members are frequently exposed
to substances cross contaminated with fentanyl, benzodiazepines, and tranquilizers including
xylazine. In this context, fatal drug poisoning is common. Lastly, illicit drinkers who are
intoxicated are more likely to use an unfamiliar substance or buy from a different source,
heightening overdose risk. Any and all measures to increase access to regulated alternatives to
the toxic drug supply are endorsed by EIDGE.
We are confident that the growing evidence-base surrounding prescribed safer supply, the
positive results of DULFs pilot study, the recommendations of the BC Coroners Service, and the
recent report of BC Provincial Health Officer Bonnie Henry make clear the need for a federal
role in advancing all forms of safer supply for those who need it.
Specifically relating to safer alternatives to the adulterated drug supply, we urge the Committee
to consider the tools at its disposal to:
380 E. Hastings St, [CONTACT]
Vancouver, Canada
1) Reinstating eligibility for safer supply programming under Health Canada's
Substance Use and Addictions Program (SUAP) 2). EIDGE believes it is unacceptable to
fund safe supply for some, in the form of alcohol and other drugs, and not for others
when it has the potential to reduce harm.
2) Advising against the issuing of criminal charges against the organizers of DULF, Eris
Nyx and Jeremy Kalicum, whose compassion club meaningfully reduced risk of overdose
and other-drug related harm for participants
3) Expedite efforts at the federal level to secure access to pharmaceutical alternatives to
the unregulated drug supply for use in community settings, including but not limited to
regulated domestic production.
4) Encourage, approve, and financially support programs seeking exemption from the
Controlled Drugs and Substances Act via s. 56 to design and implement non-medical
safer supply programs and compassion clubs across Canada.
We thank you for taking the time to review our recommendations to the committee. We hope
that, in this present context of disinformation and ideological disagreement, your members will
consider EIDGEs submission as a collection of recommendations informed by scientific
evidence and motivated by unspeakable loss within our community.
Sincerely,

Background and rationale
The provincial government of British Columbia is considering the creation of enabling
legislation to prohibit the public consumption of unregulated substances at the discretion of local
municipalities. The Eastside Illicit Drinkers Group for Education (EIDGE) is a group of people
who use alcohol in ways that are criminalized, most frequently as a result of our coerced use of
public space. EIDGE members are commonly long-term heavy drinkers, over 80% of whom are
Indigenous, who experience high rates of alcohol-associated harm intersecting with
socioeconomic marginality and intergenerational experience of colonial violence.123456 Although
alcohol is a legally regulated substance, EIDGE members are criminalized by public use
legislation pertaining to alcohol as a result of socioeconomic status, housing precarity, and
racialization. Accordingly, the criminalization of illicit drinkers who use alcohol in public spaces
has been a priority issue for policy advocacy since the creation of EIDGE in 2011. Illicit drinkers
residing in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside conceptualize access to public space as a health
promoting form of harm reduction, and policies that deprive people who use any substance of

access to public space in this community as harm-inducing. While EIDGE supports large scale
interventions to improve public health that address the conditions of substance use, we urge the
PSSG to consider that population-level efforts to regulate substance use in a punitive manner will
have regressive impacts of extremely structurally marginalized people who use drugs.7 EIDGE
and the authors of this brief subsequently oppose any new prohibitions on the public use of
unregulated substances as a result of our lived, professional, and academic understandings of the
negative health consequences of said policies. This summary brief will proceed to explain:
1) EIDGE's understanding of how and why public substance use occurs in the Downtown
Eastside
2) How prohibitions on public use create new health harms for acutely structurally
marginalized persons, grounded in but not limited to the experiences of illicit drinkers
3) Benefits to public health and safety of people who drugs provided by safe public spaces
4) Harm reduction informed policy recommendations pertaining to public use drawn from
EIDGE's 2021 Vancouver Alcohol Strategy and Public Space MAP Pilot
Understanding the Upstream Determinants of Public Use
The criminalization of poor, structurally marginalized illicit drinkers is a direct result of the
material and social conditions that drive people who use substances outdoors. EIDGE members
have reported that their public use of substances occurs as a result of the following factors:
Homelessness
• Illicit drinkers are likely to experience or have experienced repeat, long-term episodes of
homelessness. Insufficient shelter allowances in British Columbia, a lack of investment in
accessible supportive housing from multiple levels of government, and the accelerating
loss of Vancouver's affordable Single Room Occupancy SRO housing stock, as well as
broader rises in market rent without adequate legislative protections, intersect with the
complex physical and mental health needs of drinkers and people who use other drugs to
create this risk. In the absence of safe, dignified private residences in which to use drugs,
low-income persons who use substances are forced to do so elsewhere, often outdoors.
Shelter capacity, rules and regulations
7 Pennay, A., & Room, R. (2012). Prohibiting public drinking in urban public spaces: A review of the evidence.
Drugs: education, prevention and policy, 19(2), 91-101.

text:
Drugs: education, prevention and policy, 19(2), 91-101.

• Demand for shelter beds currently exceeds the number of available spaces in Vancouver.8
Further, a select number of temporary and emergency shelters in the DTES enforce rules
and regulations that drive drinkers and people who use other drugs to seek shelter in
public spaces both during the day and overnight.9 For example, restrictive,
abstinence-only shelters without on-site harm reduction services do not permit people
who use alcohol or other drugs to use while inside. Crowding, theft, understaffing,
inadequate staff training, risk of violence, early morning shelter closings, and the lack of
safe indoor drop-in spaces open immediately after closings also encourage public
substance use in the absence of alternative places.
Single Room Occupancy (SRO) habitability
• SRO housing comprises the majority of the housing stock that is available at or near the
shelter rate in the City of Vancouver (approx. 7000 units)10. SROs are former short stay
hotels built approximately 100 years ago to accommodate transient resource workers.
• Buildings typically contain 10 foot by 10 foot rooms, with shared bathroom and kitchen
amenities on each floor. Privately owned SROs, which make up approximately 40% of
the available stock, have been systematically neglected by property use and public health
authorities in Vancouver, resulting in poor habitability across much of the stock.11 Living
conditions in the 60% of SRO units administered by non-profit organizations are
comparatively poor. Insufficient heating or air conditioning, broken plumbing, neglected
maintenance, infestations, mold, and unsafe premises are common to both types of SRO
housing12. Amongst these conditions, residents try to spend as little time inside as
possible, including people who use regulated and unregulated drugs in the DTES.
Drug poisoning risk, guest policies, and the SRO housing environment
• The physical layout of the SRO, neglectful management practices, and the absence of
adequate supports heighten risk of drug poisoning for SRO tenants.13 14 15 The absence of
common areas, small personal living spaces, and the existence of guest bans in some

19 As a result, the most recent available data from the BC Coroners Service indicates that
44.5% of illicit drug poisoning deaths occurred in residences including SROs and
supportive housing facilities.20 The SRO "risk environment"21 facilitates public use of
substances as a harm reduction measure, as drug poisoning, drug-related harms, or other
medical emergencies (namely seizures, falls, and delirium tremens, for drinkers)
experienced in public are more likely to be promptly responded to. Public use of
substances with a high potential for adulteration (i.e fentanyl or street "down") is often a
direct response to these conditions. EIDGE lost a beloved longtime member in the weeks
leading up to this submission - he was found in his SRO room. We create documents such
as these recommendations to ensure that his experience, and that of our other lost family,
continues to inform policy in their absence. These deaths are preventable.
Protection from social isolation
• Without alternative spaces to gather and socialize, EIDGE members report that their
public substance use is often a way to avoid social isolation, mental health decline, and
address feelings of loneliness and depression. Gathering outdoors in consistent places is a
way to be located by friends or family, and to locate others who have not been seen for
some period of time. Not finding a peer in their regular place could and has warranted a
room check or other check on their wellbeing. The creation of punitive measures to
discourage people who use drugs to use public space would disrupt these informal safety
networks.
Climate change and heat injury
• Climate change poses an escalating harm to people residing in the DTES, many of whom
live in overcrowded conditions, including shelters and poorly ventilated SRO units (as
above). During the 2021 heat dome, 10% of the 619 people who died in BC lived in
social housing, SROs, or supportive housing.22 Low-income residents of the DTES often
have multiple chronic health conditions and thus are vulnerable to heat-related injury.

• The majority of SRO tenants are over 50 years of age and, a recent research project led
by the SRO-C, found that 40% of respondents attributed high temperatures as a reason to
spend time and sleep elsewhere, including in parks.23 Further, the DTES neighborhood
disproportionately lacks access to covered green public space, contributing to a heat
island effect in the area and an increased the risk of heat injury when in public space24.
Drinkers and PWUD will continue to be pushed into public space as the climate heats
further, with predictions suggesting that there will be twice as many days above 25'C in
the 2050s as there are today.25
Anticipated harms of public use enforcement
EIDGE members have reported several negative health impacts of criminalized substance use in
public spaces. These harms are directly related to the enforcement of legislated prohibitions on
substance use in specific places, and not the physiological effects of alcohol. While these
mechanisms of harm are directly related to alcohol use, EIDGE feels that many are applicable to
people who use other substances. The following modes of enforcement exacerbate
alcohol-associated harms for EIDGE members:
Ticketing
• Section 73 of BC's Liquor Control and Licensing Act prohibits the consumption of
alcohol in a public place, except for those designated by a municipality (for example,
Vancouver's Alcohol in Parks Pilot) and section 74 enables officers to arrest and charge
people for being drunk in a public place. These offenses result in tickets and fines.
Drinkers who are reliant on public space face recurring instances of ticketing and a
significant financial and practical burden, particularly for persons living on extremely
low-incomes. If the individual facing a charge under section 73(1) of the Act does not
show up to their hearing, they are automatically assumed to be guilty and the judge is free
to set a penalty in their absence. Following a guilty ruling, the arresting officer can also
inform the court of a prior record which can be used to "support a higher penalty",
suggesting that drinkers may face substantial and recurring financial burden. If this
occurs, illicit drinkers and people who use other drugs are at risk of facing serious legal
penalties for a relatively minor offense. New public use legislation relying on any form of
ticketing or fines would tacitly expand this positive feedback loop of criminalization to
illicit substance users by creating intolerable financial burden that results in further
criminalization and advanced sanctions.

Confiscation, seizure, and "pour-outs"
• In B.C., Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch Inspectors and law enforcement
officials enforcing the Liquor Control and Licensing Act are empowered to seize or
"pour-out" alcohol consumed in a public place or while intoxicated in a public place.
Illicit drinkers' whose substance use is forced into public space, highly visible,
stigmatized, and subject to police discretion are vulnerable to confiscation and resulting
harm. For drinkers living with severe alcohol dependency and on extremely low incomes,
confiscation encourages high-risk survival drinking (acquiring and consuming higher
strength alcohol very quickly) or non-beverage alcohol use (including mouthwash,
rubbing alcohol, and hand sanitizer) to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Alcohol "pour-outs"
place physiologically dependent drinkers at greater risk of acute withdrawal, and
therefore at greater risk of high-risk behaviors to prevent withdrawal. EIDGE's
experience demonstrates that similar effects are likely to occur during the seizure of other
drugs, resulting in compounded drug poisoning risk for the impacted person. Drawing on
EIDGEs first-hand experience with the harms of confiscation, we predict that any form of
drug seizure permitted by new public use legislation would drive the affected person to
replace said substances, likely from a new and unreliable source, or engage in illicit
activity to replace the confiscated substances.
Additional lnteraction with law enforcement
• EIDGE supports minimizing opportunities for interaction between illicit drinkers and
people who use other drugs with law enforcement, as such interactions place illicit
drinkers at risk of harm. EIDGE considers the 1998 death of Frank Paul, an Indigenous
man who used alcohol in Vancouver, after being released from custody by the Vancouver
Police Department, to be emblematic of this point.26 Anecdotally, EIDGE members also
report that police holding cells for people who are intoxicated in public are dangerous and
health compromising spaces that are made so by the criminalization of public substance
use. In addition to the recommendation of a civilian-run sobering center for Vancouver
included in the 2011 Davies Commission Inquiry27 into Frank Paul's death, EIDGE
believes that interactions between people who use substances in public should be kept to
an absolute minimum, and be strictly limited to the provision of non-punitive referral to
civilian-run health and social services providers when they occur.
26 https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/frank-paul-s-death-no-accident-crown-agrees-1.975662
27 Davies Commission Inquiry into the Death of Frank Paul (BC), & Davies, W. H. (2011). Alone and Cold:

Documented benefits to public health and safety of people who drugs provided by safe
public spaces
Though there are few academic studies explicitly looking at the role of generic public space in
reducing drug-related harms, research on safe injection sites highlights the importance of formal
and informal networks of support and supervision which come with being amongst others. In
Vancouver, studies suggest that SIS are associated with reduced harms, including overdose
mortality (88 fewer overdose deaths per 100,000 person-years), 67% fewer ambulance calls for
overdoses, and a decrease in HIV infections.28 Public consumption supervised by peers,
volunteers, and community support workers is likely to have a similar effect. A review of
evidence highlights that such sites are successful when coupled with community support for the
SIS, employment of peer-workers, and relaxed regulations within SIS. Further, these sites have
benefits beyond harm reduction, including the reduction of internalized stigma, increased peer
knowledge of how to support others in emergency situations outside of the SIS, increased social
connection, and sharing of information about other support services.29
Policy recommendations from EIDGE:
I) Cease development of new provincial policy prohibiting or enabling the prohibition of the
public use of unregulated substances, as such policies are extremely likely to harm the
health and wellbeing of people who use drugs and do not address the structural
determinants of public use.
2) Ensure that people who use regulated and unregulated substances are provided with
sufficient access to safe, peer-governed alternative spaces to gather
• Illicit drinkers have already taken measures to create safer public spaces for people who
use drugs in addition to the entire community in a non-punitive way. In March 2021, a
Managed Alcohol Program, the 'Drinkers Lounge' Parklet was opened to run in
conjunction with an existing project led by PHS. The outdoor public space, negotiated
under a 'stewardship' contract with the City of Vancouver and furnished with picnic
tables and barbeque, provides participants with a safe and consistent supply of beverage
alcohol and food, as well as contact with housing and social support providers. Initial
findings highlight the importance of this designated public space for combatting
stigmatization. User "V", noted that the patio makes members "feel good" and take pride

(Accessed: 31 July 2023).

Another user suggested that the space may help to reduce the risk of alcohol related
accident injuries, saying ,"the parklet looks legit for members, and it appears to be safer
for drinkers that may fall". These responses indicate the importance of public space for
the welfare and dignity of those who consume or use criminalized substances, and for the
implementation of harm reduction measures such as MAPs.
• Ongoing discussions amongst the EIDGE research committee have also revealed the
importance of the designated space and of non-punitive peer-regulation in the parklet,
suggesting that these components make them feel safe and encourage others to use the
space and join the managed alcohol program. Sanctioned public spaces could include the
following features:
1. Harm-reduction programs for drinkers and/or PWUD, led by peers
2. An area distinct and distanced from children's amenities (such as
designated 'playgrounds' in parks). Consultation with members suggested
that this would provide safety and dignity to them as well as others.
3. Non punitive peer-regulation
4. Other amenities to encourage use - for example, the provision of a misting
shower at the parklet has been a highlight for the space, sanitation
infrastructure, food donations and celebration events
• EIDGE members also highlight the overblown and misguided perception of danger
attached to PWUD or alcohol occupying public space, which masks a reality where
individuals are strongly connected to a wider community and generally respectful to each
other and the wider population. Anecdotally, one member spoke of the code "kids on the
block" used often on Hastings Street to indicate that children were passing by. Upon
hearing this, people who use drugs know to stop and hide what they are doing. Generally
speaking, people who use alcohol and other substances in public spaces in and around the
DTES desire to do so in ways that are discrete, away from children or families, and
non-disruptive to the wider community. When these things are not attainable in specific
instances, policy and planning practices in the wider neighborhood are likely to have
played a significant role. For example, illicit drinkers in Strathcona's MacLean Park are
now forced to gather near a children's play area against their wishes after a number of
benches across the park were removed because they were used by drinkers.

RE: Brief – Committee Study on “Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada”
As university researchers with expertise in substance use and drug policy, we are pleased to
contribute evidence to the Standing Committee on Health’s study of the “Opioid Epidemic and
Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada.” Our submission draws attention to inequities in opioid use and
overdose among Two-Spirit, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and other queer
(2S/LGBTQ+) youth and offers direction for responsive policy and practice action.
This submission leverages findings and recommendations from our team’s past and ongoing
research on opioid and other substance use among 2S/LGBTQ+ youth. Specifically, we share
insights from a commentary publication about overdose among 2S/LGBTQ+ people, and from
two published articles related to our qualitative studies with 2S/LGBTQ+ youth (ages 15 to 30)
who use drugs, one of which focuses on overdose and harm reduction, and the other on opioid
use. These studies and our broader programs of research have emphasized the need to: improve
access to harm reduction and other non-judgmental, inclusive, and low-barrier substancerelated health services; and address the root drivers of the drug poisoning crisis by
decriminalizing substance use and providing a safer drug supply, using various models.

Danya Fast, PhD, Assistant Professor, Department of Medicine, University of British
Columbia & Research Scientist, BC Centre on Substance Use ([CONTACT])

Research Brief: 2S/LGBTQ+ People, Opioid Use & Overdose
Background
For the last several years, we have led various research projects focusing on substance use
among 2S/LGBTQ+ youth and young people more generally. These projects have aimed to
meaningfully engage youth, encourage dialogue about substance use, and support critical
analysis and the development of appropriate policy and practice responses to prevent and reduce
substance use harms. Three such projects form the basis of this brief for the Standing Committee
on Health’s study of the “Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada”:
1. A commentary publication focusing on overdose among 2S/LGBTQ+ people (Project 1);
2. A qualitative interview study with 50 gay, bisexual, queer, and transgender young men
who use substances, focusing on overdose and harm reduction (Project 2); and
3. A qualitative interview and photography study with 4 2S/LGBTQ+ youth who use
opioids, focusing on the social context of their opioid use (Project 3).
In this submission, we highlight insights from these studies and provide evidence-based
recommendations for responding to the drug poisoning crisis. We note that the lived experiences
of 2S/LGBTQ+ people and youth (including 2S/LGBTQ+ youth) are underrepresented in
research and policy discussions about opioid use and overdose. We are committed to ensuring
that their voices and lived experiences are foregrounded in efforts to improve drug policies and
programming, and we have included some of their quotations and photographs in this brief.
PROJECT 1: A Call to Action on 2S/LGBTQ+ People and Overdose
The first publication appended to this brief is a commentary highlighting two areas that require
scientific and public health investments to more fully measure, report, and address overdose
among 2S/LGBTQ+ people. We led this work because 2S/LGBTQ+ are at inequitably high
risk for opioid and other substance use harms, due to interrelated individual (e.g., mental
illness), social (e.g., bullying, family rejection), and structural (e.g., homophobia/transphobia)
factors. Yet, there are key gaps in the evidence base surrounding overdose in this population.
Pertinent policy and practice recommendations
• Demand that all nation-wide community health surveys and other large-scale health
surveys funded by national funding agencies (e.g., Canadian Institutes of Health Research,
Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, Health Canada, Public Health Agency
of Canada, Statistics Canada) adopt standard and inclusive metrics of sexual and gender
identity to more fully characterize how opioid use and overdose are affecting 2S/LGBTQ+
people across Canada. These measures are needed to capture data that can better contribute
to our understandings of, and responses to, overdose among 2S/LGBTQ+ people.
• Invest in entry-to-practice curriculum and continuing professional development
opportunities that can equip healthcare providers with the skills and competencies needed
to navigate conversations about gender, sexual identity, and substance use. Enhanced
education is needed to address anti-2S/LGBTQ+ and substance use stigma in healthcare.

Enhanced
education is needed to address anti-2S/LGBTQ+ and substance use stigma in healthcare.

PROJECT 2: A Study of Overdose and Harm Reduction in Young Queer Men
The second appended publication reports on a 2018 study of young gay, bisexual, queer, and
transgender men’s substance use and overdose-related harm reduction patterns amid the drug
poisoning crisis. The impetus for doing this study was that young queer men experience
elevated rates of opioid and non-opioid substance use, and are at higher risk for overdose,
though little research had explored strategies for mitigating overdose risk in this population.
This study was set in Vancouver, BC, and involved qualitative interviews with 50 cisgender
and transgender young men (ages 15-30) of diverse sexual identities, including gay, bisexual,
and queer men. We analyzed the interview data using a grounded theory approach, focusing on
these young men’s processes and contexts of responding to the drug poisoning crisis.
Summary of key findings
• Gay, bisexual, queer, and transgender young men in this study described being very aware
of and deeply affected by the contaminated drug supply, including through both personal
experiences and community experiences of overdose, and of grief and loss.
• Study participants described feeling as though the existing suite of harm reduction
services, such as supervised consumption sites, was not meant “for them.” They felt this
way because they were young (harm reduction is often geared towards adults), because
they feared facing homophobia and transphobia in these service settings, and because some
of these young men only used substances occasionally or in distinct contexts, like with sex
or when partying.
• The young men described using individual and peer-based harm reduction strategies to
mitigate overdose risk, including testing their substances for fentanyl, not using alone, and
only procuring substances from “trustworthy” suppliers, such as peers and sexual partners.
• Despite all they were doing as individuals to mitigate overdose risk, the young men
stressed that opportunities for safer substance use were restricted by social and structural
barriers, including drug criminalization, the lack of a safer drug supply, and a limited
availability of non-judgmental and inclusive substance use-related health services.
Pertinent policy and practice recommendations
• Invest in low-barrier, inclusive harm reduction programming that is specific for (or at
least friendly to) youth and 2S/LGBTQ+ people, including drug-checking services and
supervised consumption and overdose prevention sites.
• Decriminalize substance use and implement (and scale up) accessible safer supply
programs. These upstream measures are needed to address barriers to accessing harm
reduction (e.g., concerns that one will be stopped by police when doing so) and the root
cause of the overdose crisis – the unregulated, contaminated, and therefore
unpredictable and lethal drug supply.

PROJECT 3: A Study of Opioid Use Among 2S/LGBTQ+ Youth
The third appended publication reports on a 2019 study of opioid use among 2S/LGBTQ+
youth. The motivation behind this study was to develop better understandings of how
2S/LGBTQ+ youth experience opioid use, including how they started using opioids and how
their substance use connects to the social context of their lives and the transition to adulthood.
This study was set in Vancouver, BC, and involved qualitative interviews and participantdriven photography with four 2S/LGBTQ+ youth (ages 15-30) of diverse sexual and gender
identities. We analyzed the interview and photovoice data using a case study approach,
allowing us to explore in-depth the issue and context of opioid use among these youth.
Summary of key findings
• The 2S/LGBTQ+ youth we interviewed shared sentiments of internalized shame and
homophobia/transphobia in adolescence, alongside associated experiences of “feeling
trapped” and “wanting to feel free,” from which using opioids and other substances could
provide relief. These realities, combined with other social issues (like growing up in
poverty and with family violence), could partly explain disparities in opioid use within
2S/LGBTQ+ populations.
• Youth shared that their use of opioids was closely connected to their mental health,
indicating that they purposefully used opioids to cope with anxiety and social stress and to
maintain wellbeing.
• Often, youths’ experiences of distress were made worse by drug-related harms stemming
from the social context of their opioid use. Here, youth described facing significant
vulnerability stemming from poverty, the criminalization of substance use, stigma,
violence, and drug policy inaction.
Pertinent policy and practice recommendations
• Advance integrated approaches to substance use and mental health care, recognizing the
often-interconnected nature of these issues, to holistically support + 2S/LGBTQ youth who
use opioids.
• Invest in equity-oriented improvements to the “social safety net,” such as through
enhancing access to universal basic income and safe and affordable housing, to address the
social and structural issues driving opioid use and substance use-related harms among
2S/LGBTQ+ youth.
• Decriminalize substance use and invest in (and scale up) accessible safer supply programs,
to better promote and protect the health of 2S/LGBTQ+ youth who currently use opioids.

text:
Submission to the House of Commons Standing
Committee on Health, regarding the “Opioid Epidemic and Toxic
Drug Crisis”: a nurse’s perspective
January 21, 2024
Sarah Lovegrove RN, BA, MA, BScN
Professor, Vancouver Island University
Nanaimo, British Columbia

Introduction
I am a Registered Nurse (RN) in British Columbia and a Professor for the Bachelor of
Science in Nursing Program at Vancouver Island University. I have practiced as an RN in
Ontario and in Emergency Departments in both Duncan and Nanaimo on Vancouver Island,
BC. As a part of my current role, I teach nursing students in surgical and mental health acute
care settings. I have been an advocate for people who use drugs in my community since 2018
and have served as the Chair of the Nanaimo Community Action Team on the Toxic Drug
Crisis (CAT). I am also a proud member of the Harm Reduction Nurses Association.
My community of Nanaimo has been absolutely devastated by the unregulated drug
crisis. Since the provincial declaration of the overdose crisis as a public health emergency in
2016, there have been over 417 deaths in our community (as of October 31, 2023, BC
Coroners Service). According to Dr. Shannon Waters, Interim Central Island Medical Health
Officer, 85 people died in Nanaimo in 2022 and that rate has been increasing exponentially
with over 99 people dying from an unregulated supply of drugs in just the first 10 months of
2023. People in our community aged 25-44 years are injured and dying at the highest rate
with the majority of deaths occurring among males. Further exacerbating our local situation,
as the number of people experiencing homelessness increases in our community, so too does
the rate of people dying outdoors from an unregulated supply of drugs. The rates of illicit
drug toxicity deaths in Nanaimo are more than double the rate of the rest of Vancouver Island
with an average of approximately 10 deaths occurring each month in 2023 (Dr. Waters,
December 2023). As stated by BC’s Chief Coroner Lisa Lapointe (2023), “unregulated drug
toxicity is the leading cause of death in British Columbia for persons aged 10 to 59,
accounting for more deaths than homicides, suicides, accidents and natural disease
combined.”
The city of Nanaimo is located on the traditional unceded territory of the
Snuneymuxw First Nation. It is necessary to recognize and address the fact that in our
community and across BC, Indigenous and First Nations people are disproportionately
impacted by the unregulated drug supply. According to First Nations Health Authority
(2023), First Nations people represented 21.6% of all toxic drug poisoning events in
September 2023. In the first nine months of 2023, women represented 40% of all First
Nations toxic drug poisoning events. Since 2016, the year in which the public health
emergency was declared, there have been 1,960 First Nations people in British Columbia lost
to toxic drug poisoning.
According to the BC Coroners Service Death Review Panel on November 1, 2023,
“the primary driver of the drug crisis is the inherently toxic and unpredictable nature of the
unregulated drug supply”. As per reports from my clients and colleagues, at this time there is
no reliable access to unadulterated heroin or other opioids within the illicit market. What is
available to purchase, however, is referred to as “down” which is an unpredictable,
ever-changing combination of fentanyl or carfentanil, potent benzodiazepines and/or
xylazine, as well as a number of other bulking agents and adulterants. In this submission, I

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In this submission, I

will outline what I have witnessed in my own nursing practice and advocacy work in terms of
the numerous negative impacts of criminalization of illicit substances on people who use
drugs, as well as the increasingly complex nature of injuries and deaths related to an
unregulated supply of drugs. In addition to the catastrophic impacts of irreversible injury and
death on people who use drugs, the ripple effects of this crisis on community members and
frontline care providers, like myself, are important to consider within the context of a
concurrent healthcare crisis and provider shortage.
Impacts of Criminalization
The criminalization of certain substances is inherently harmful to people and
communities. Criminalization perpetuates stigma and increases the risk of harm by forcing
people to consume an unregulated supply of drugs in isolation. The use of unregulated,
unpredictable substances in isolation increases the risk of injury and death as there is no one
present to respond and offer the necessary support. Furthermore, when people who use drugs
exist in a constant state of fear of fines, arrest, or incarceration they are pushed further into
the margins of our communities and away from the people and services that could support
them, making it more difficult for healthcare providers to offer consistent care. People who
use drugs often leave the emergency department or hospital before receiving care because of
the illicit nature of the substances they consume and the fear of consequences for using drugs,
including the seizure of their substances and interactions with law enforcement. I have had
countless clients have their substances confiscated by police or security while in hospital,
leading them to resort to elopement and/or illegal survival tactics (sex work, theft, etc.) to
procure more from the illicit supply, exponentially increasing their risk of harm, injury, and
death.
Impacts of an Unregulated Supply of Drugs
Throughout my time on Vancouver Island since 2017, I have witnessed a dangerous
evolution of an unregulated drug supply that has become progressively more unpredictable,
involving more complex adulterants including (but not limited to) Fentanyl, benzodiazepines,
and Xylazine. The unregulated supply has created a deadly landscape for people who use
drugs and a distressing scenario for responders. The initial wave of the toxic drug crisis saw
an unregulated supply adulterated primarily with Fentanyl, a potent opioid that is often used
within a medical context for the treatment of surgical or traumatic pain. At that point, people
who use drugs were smoking or injecting their substance of choice, only to be met by an
unpredictable potency of opioids that caused immediate respiratory depression (cessation of
breathing). Naloxone (or Narcan) is the medical reversal agent that was brought into the
community to save people from this type of drug poisoning. However, due to the
criminalization of these substances, people who use drugs consume in isolation with no one
present to administer Naloxone when necessary.
In addition to the risk of death associated with a potent, unregulated supply, there is
also the secondary risk of irreversible acquired anoxic brain injury (injury due to decreased

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In addition to the risk of death associated with a potent, unregulated supply, there is
also the secondary risk of irreversible acquired anoxic brain injury (injury due to decreased

oxygen being delivered to the brain) after the experience of a non-fatal overdose. Anoxic
brain injuries are often permanent and have a range of effects from emotional, learning and
behavioural changes to the requirement of full-time care or hospitalization. Additionally,
“approximately 50% of people experiencing homelessness have had a brain injury with
varying symptoms and outcomes” (Brain Injury Canada, 2020).
Due to the pharmacodynamic-pharmacokinetic nature of opioid tolerance and the
shorter half-life of Fentanyl, people who use this drug require more frequent use, as well as
higher and higher dosages to meet the same need. “The increase in demand for more potent
opioids was resourcefully filled by suppliers with more affordable, accessible, and potent
alternatives, such as illicitly-produced fentanyl and potent fentanyl-related analogues (e.g.,
carfentanil)” (Russell et. al., 2023).
Further complicating an already deadly crisis was the addition of benzodiazepines to
the unregulated supply of drugs. The combination of opioids and potent benzodiazepines
such as Etizolam (a benzodiazepine-analogue which is not approved for medical use in
Canada) made for even more complicated and distressing resuscitation efforts. People are
now routinely being found unconscious and not breathing leading responders to administer
Naloxone; and while breathing may resume after administration, people are remaining
unconscious or are difficult to rouse for long periods (Ontario Harm Reduction Network,
2020). As evidenced by drug testing and post-mortem toxicology data, “there has been a stark
increase in synthetic benzodiazepine-laced opioids (i.e., ‘benzodope’).” This combination of
opioids and benzodiazepines carries distinct and amplified risks for people who use drugs
including fatal and non-fatal overdoses, increased dependence and withdrawal symptoms, and
places them in extremely vulnerable positions” (Russell et. al., 2023).
Benzodiazepines are a central nervous system depressant that lead to increased
sedation and are not reversible with Naloxone. The reversal agent or antagonist for
benzodiazepines (Flumazenil) is not a medication that can be safely administered in the
community in the same way that Naloxone is as the risks with administration include
seizures, cardiac dysrhythmias and mortality. As sedative-hypnotics, benzodiazepines slow
down brain activity and result in varying levels of drowsiness, impaired coordination,
decreased heart rate and blood pressure, as well as diminished memory including confusion,
memory loss, and occasionally hallucinations (Canadian Centre on Substance Use and
Addiction, 2021). When the sedative effects of benzodiazepines are combined with those of
opioids, the risk for adverse health problems such as respiratory depression, coma, overdose,
and mortality is markedly higher (Russell et. al., 2023).
Furthermore, qualitative evidence suggests that people who use drugs are vulnerable
to experiencing anterograde amnesia or ‘blackouts’ where they lose track of time and do not
remember their actions; and in combination with the immediate sedative effects when
smoking or injecting, places people in uniquely vulnerable positions where they can be easily
victimized (being robbed, taken advantage of, etc.) (Russell et. al., 2023). In addition to these
side effects, I am witnessing far more complex hospital visits and admissions related to injury

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
In addition to these
side effects, I am witnessing far more complex hospital visits and admissions related to injury

resulting from increased sedation including burns, compartment syndrome due to prolonged
trapped positioning of limbs, osteomyelitis and other difficult to treat infections, diabetic
ketoacidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and surgical amputations.
More recently, a complicating addition to the unregulated supply of drugs is Xylazine,
a veterinary non-opioid sedative or tranquilizer, referred to as “tranq”. Similar to
benzodiazepines, Xylazine causes central nervous system depression with effects such as
sedation, muscle relaxation, analgesia and anaesthesia. Side effects of Xylazine include
tiredness or faintness, respiratory depression, bradycardia (low heart rate), hypotension (low
blood pressure), hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) and miosis (constricted pupils). Although
Xylazine can potentially be used for its own effects, it is most frequently found in
combination with other drugs, likely used as an adulterant or as a bulking agent, as well as to
enhance or mimic the effects of other illicit drugs. It has been reported to me that the addition
of Xylazine to the unregulated supply prolongs the effects of Fentanyl and other opioids.
In addition to the complex sedative effects that come with the addition of Xylazine to
the unregulated supply, there is an increased incidence and experiences of distinct soft-tissue
wounds that become chronic as they are difficult to heal and leave people at high risk of
infection. These wounds are often associated with vasoconstrictive effects of Xylazine.
According to McFadden et. al. (2023), these wounds have a unique appearance and
progression: starting as dark purple blisters with irregular borders and intact skin, these
blisters often coalesce and harden into dry, adherent eschar, sometimes opening into deep
ulcers. Ulceration depth may reach full-thickness, with exposed tendon and bone. Some
people who use drugs and hospital-based wound specialists have noted similarities between
these wounds and chemical burns (McFadden et. al, 2023). People who are unhoused or
otherwise living rough are at very high risk of infection with the onset of wounds related to
Xylazine; and without effective, consistent wound care and antibiotic treatment they are more
likely to require surgical interventions such as debridement or amputation.
Effects on Care Providers
As a Registered Nurse and human being existing within a community being impacted
so significantly by this crisis, I also feel inclined to include information about the harms of
the unregulated drug supply on frontline care providers including peer responders, outreach
workers, students, nurses, doctors, care aids, paramedics, firefighters, social workers and
anyone else who cares for people who use drugs in our communities. Amidst a concurrent
healthcare and housing crisis, care providers working within the context of an unregulated
drug crisis report significant levels of moral injury and distress related to not being able to
provide the care that people need and deserve.
People who care for others in our communities are witnessing increased incidence of
death and suffering, are involved in more traumatic response and resuscitation efforts, are
witness to stigmatizing treatment of people who use drugs in our hospitals, and are limited in
their capacity in terms of resources and supports to offer people who use drugs, including

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
People who care for others in our communities are witnessing increased incidence of
death and suffering, are involved in more traumatic response and resuscitation efforts, are
witness to stigmatizing treatment of people who use drugs in our hospitals, and are limited in
their capacity in terms of resources and supports to offer people who use drugs, including

detox beds and recovery options. I was diagnosed with severe Post Traumatic Stress Disorder
(PTSD) in late 2018 after working in the Nanaimo Emergency Department throughout the
time of “DisconTent City” (Nanaimo’s largest and most infamous homeless encampment) and
amidst the initial “peak” of overdose deaths, forcing me to remove myself from the nursing
profession entirely and once believing I would never have the capacity to return to practice.
At a time when our healthcare system is struggling to retain enough physicians and
nurses to care for our ever-growing and ageing population, the unregulated drug crisis is
worsening our capacity to do the jobs we are trained to do causing significant distress that
negatively impacts our mental health; thus leading individuals like myself to find alternative
professions or roles away from acute care settings.
Finally, it is imperative that we recognize that each statistic and diagnosis I discussed
in the above submission represents a human being who had a once beating heart and people
who loved them - family and friends whose lives are now forever changed because of this
ongoing and worsening national crisis. Our communities will never be the same.
Recommendations
To reduce the harms associated with the unregulated drug supply, I urge the Standing
Committee on Health to consider the following recommendations as an urgent Call to Action:
1. The key intervention needed to address the toxic drug crisis is the responsible legal
regulation of all currently illicit drugs. It has been recommended by numerous
experts, including the BC Coroners Service Death Review Panel (2023), that
“providing people at risk of dying with access to quality controlled, regulated
alternatives is required to significantly impact the number of people dying.”
2. Immediate nationwide access to both medicalized and non-medicalized safe supply
with exemptions that allow for the provision of safer supply through compassion
clubs. Scale up existing prescribed safe supply programs and provide a selection of
substances adequate to displace the need to use unregulated drugs.
3. Adopt a nationwide public health response to this crisis, including the
decriminalization of all substances and the removal of criminal penalties to reduce
drug-related stigma and minimize interaction with law enforcement.
4. Increase federal support and investment in harm reduction, including drug checking
services and the implementation of overdose prevention and safe consumption sites
(OPS/SCS) nationwide; as well as voluntary, evidenced-based, culturally appropriate,
non-profit drug treatment options.
5. Immediate safe, accessible housing for all; including harm reduction-based supportive
housing for a range of needs and relationships with substances.
Thank you very much for your time and consideration of my submission as this
committee thoroughly examines this heartbreaking national crisis.

org: Centre on Drug Policy Evaluation / HIV Legal Network
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, regarding
its study on the ‘Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis’
January 2024
I. Introduction

The HIV Legal Network promotes the human rights of people living with HIV or AIDS and other
populations disproportionately affected by HIV, punitive laws and policies, and criminalization, in
Canada and internationally. For three decades, we have advocated for drug policy grounded in
evidence, human rights, and public health. The Centre on Drug Policy Evaluation works
collaboratively with governments, affected communities, and civil society to improve community
health and safety by conducting research and outreach on effective and evidence-based policy
responses to substance use. We are grateful for the opportunity to make this joint submission
detailing key legal determinants of health that have spurred the toxic drug crisis.

II. Criminalization and Canada’s Drug Poisoning Crisis

Canada’s approach to drugs, focused primarily on prohibition rather than prevention, harm
reduction, and support for people who use drugs, has done catastrophic harm, fuelling deadly
stigma, racism, epidemics of preventable illness and death, and widespread, egregious
violations of human rights. Criminalizing drugs pushes people to use their drugs in isolation,
compromises their ability to take vital safety precautions, and deters people from essential
health care and harm reduction services.i Research has shown frequent contact police have
with people who use drugs contributes to their “health risk environment through pathways, such
as syringe and naloxone confiscation, and physical and verbal harassment” which can lead to
syringe sharing, rushed injection, and isolation while using drugs.ii Furthermore, studies have
shown how police encounters act as barriers to accessing health services, including opioid
agonist therapy, HIV treatment, and needle and syringe programs.iii Black, racialized, and
immigrant communities have also described how excessive police surveillance and
criminalization impacts their ability to access public services such as health care and supervised
consumption services.iv These harms are exacerbated by a crisis of homelessness and
responses that include the involuntary displacement by police or other law enforcement of
people experiencing homelessness. As a 2023 U.S. study concluded, over a 10-year period,
decampments are “estimated to worsen overdose and hospitalizations, decrease initiations of
medications for opioid-use disorder, and contribute to deaths among people experiencing
homelessness who inject drugs.”v

org: Centre on Drug Policy Evaluation / HIV Legal Network
study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
As a 2023 U.S. study concluded, over a 10-year period,
decampments are “estimated to worsen overdose and hospitalizations, decrease initiations of
medications for opioid-use disorder, and contribute to deaths among people experiencing
homelessness who inject drugs.”v

Canada’s long-standing policy of criminalizing drugs has also resulted in an unregulated drug
supply that continues to become more potent and unpredictable year-over-year. The emergence
of high-potency opioids can be understood by the “Iron Law of Prohibition,” which dictates that
as law enforcement becomes more intense, the potency of prohibited substances increases.vi
According to a 2023 study, police drug seizures increase rather than prevent overdose deaths,
by forcing people to obtain an alternate supply with no knowledge of its potency or their ensuing
tolerance.vii In addition, the observed displacement/replacement effectviii indicates that the
scheduling of substances is routinely followed by the emergence of new substances often
posing greater harms from consumption. Drug prohibition has thus contributed to a tainted drug

supply that has resulted in 40,642 opioid toxicity deaths between January 2016 and June
2023.ix

The repercussions of drug prohibition extend beyond immediate impacts on health. Between
2019 to 2021, police in Canada made almost 200,000 arrests for drug offences; close to half of
those were for simple drug possession.x Not only does drug prohibition fuel stigma and
discrimination against people who use drugs, but criminal records impede access to
employment, housing opportunities, and shelter, affect child custody, and restrict travel.
Canada’s drug control framework is also rooted in, and reinforces, racism and colonialism, and
has contributed to the racial profiling and disproportionate arrest, prosecution, and incarceration
of Black and Indigenous people in Canada for drug offences:
•
A 2019 study of cases between 2007-2013 found that Black youth accused of cannabis
possession in Ontario were more likely to be charged and less likely to be cautioned
than white youth and youth from other racial backgrounds.xi

•
A 2020 report found that Black and Indigenous people are dramatically overrepresented
in drug charges recommended by the Vancouver Police Department. While making up
1% of the city’s population, Black people have accounted for 6.4% of drug trafficking and
possession charges in Vancouver since 2014; Indigenous people have accounted for
almost 18% of drug trafficking and possession charges but are just 2.2% of the city’s
population.xii
