text:
A different response to crime is needed, say experts,
advocates”, CBC News, (10 August 2022), online: <https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/bc-policeshootings-and-violent-crime-1.6546283>.
16 Katie Nicholson & Jacques Marcoux, “Most Canadians killed in police encounters since 2000 had mental health
or substance abuse issues”, CBC News, (4 April 2018), online: www.cbc.ca/news/investigates/most-canadianskilled-in-police-encounters-since-2000-had-mental-health-or-substance-abuse-issues-1.4602916>.

In addition to fatalities, police responses to wellness checks have brought about other physical
and psychological harms.17 Due to the criminalization of drugs, the police have necessarily had a
long history of negative interactions with drug users. Intersectional issues of race, class, sexual
orientation, and gender identity carry their own weight of negative interactions with the police,
creating further barriers for drug users whose identities fall into one of these categories. People
who use drugs and those who care for them are thus understandably afraid of calling for wellness
checks, despite the drug poisoning crisis.

Emergency  response  teams  for  drug  use  must  be  fully  decoupled  from  the  police,  thereby
avoiding the introduction of violence, weapons, or criminal charges into a tense situation. British
Columbia is currently in the process of developing Peer Assisted Care Teams as an alternative to
using the police for drug crisis calls.18 It is the BCCLA’s hope that the provincial government
continues with this project, and we would strongly encourage any national response to the Drug
Poisoning  Crisis  to  consider  the  importance  of  developing  police‐free  response  teams  for
emergency situations.

Involuntary Treatment Violates Civil Liberties and Increases Risk of Death

The  BCCLA  is  deeply  concerned  about  the  use  of  involuntary  treatment  of  drug  users  as  a
response to the Drug Poisoning Crisis. Involuntary treatment can infringe on the Charter rights of
detainees, including Section 7 rights to life, liberty and security of person, Section 12 rights against
cruel  and  unusual  punishment  or  treatment,  and  Section  15  rights  to  freedom  from
discrimination.

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Involuntary treatment can infringe on the Charter rights of
detainees, including Section 7 rights to life, liberty and security of person, Section 12 rights against
cruel  and  unusual  punishment  or  treatment,  and  Section  15  rights  to  freedom  from
discrimination.

Involuntary treatment, by its nature, involves the denial of liberty. The other Charter concerns can
be  seen  in  both  the  nature  and  the  results  of  this  treatment.  People  who  have  experienced
involuntary treatment report treatment methods can be ineffective or abusive, reinforce systemic
racism,  and  contribute  to  retraumatization  through  failure  to  use  trauma‐informed  best
practices.19 Likewise, academic research on involuntary treatment shows a high risk for human
rights abuses and a history of significant harm for detainees.20 Academic research also indicates

informed substance use policy”, (2021) 112 Can J of Public Health 456-459, online:
<https://doi.org/10.17269/s4[CONTACT]9-3>.

that involuntary treatment correlates with an increased risk of future overdose, including a higher
risk of death.21

In Health Canada’s 2021 report, the Task Force found that coercive drug treatment programs had
mixed results, including low rates of abstinence after people were released.22 The Task Force also
noted  that  involuntary  treatment essentially  reintroduces  or  reinforces  the  same problems  as
criminalization, such as punitive consequences and social stigma.23 This, too, is echoed in the
academic literature on the ineffectiveness of involuntary treatment.24

Involuntary treatment is thus inconsistent with any principled approach to addressing the Drug
Poisoning Crisis, particularly when it is linked to an increase in overdoses and deaths. Even if it
is motivated by the best of intentions, the civil liberties violations and provably harmful effects
of involuntary drug treatment cannot be justified.

Summary

study_or_consultation_title: Opioid Epidemic and Toxic Drug Crisis in Canada
text:
Summary

The BCCLA requests the Health Committee to consider the following factors during its study of
the drug poisoning crisis:
1. Criminalization of drug use continues to exacerbate the crisis, due to dangers of arrest,
stigmatization, and social support barriers.
2. Police presence during wellness checks frequently results in violence that deters people
from calling for assistance in a drug‐related crisis.
3. Involuntary treatment is a significant violation of civil liberties and increases the risk of
death.

The BCCLA also acknowledges that the drug poisoning crisis will require a holistic approach,
applying  evidence‐based  research  and  incorporating  recommendations  from  people  who  use
drugs.

We thank the Committee for considering our submissions.

text:
Submission
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Breast Cancer Screening Guidelines Study
Expert Recommendations for Breast Cancer Screening in Canada
Paula Gordon, OC, OBC, MD, FRCPC, FSBI
Clinical Professor of Radiology, University of British Columbia
Anna N Wilkinson, MSc, MD, CCFP, Associate Professor, University of Ottawa
Shushiela Appavoo, MD, FRCPC
Associate Clinical Professor Department of Radiology and Diagnostic Imaging, University of Alberta
Martin J. Yaffe PhD, C.M., FRSC
Professor, Department of Medical Biophysics, University of Toronto Senior Scientist,
Physical Sciences Platform, Sunnybrook Research Institute
Co-Director, Imaging Research Program Ontario Institute for Cancer Research
Jean M Seely, MDCM, FRCPC, FSBI, FCAR,
Full Professor of Radiology, University of Ottawa
Jennie Dale, MBA, Cofounder and Executive Director, Dense Breasts Canada
June 10, 2024

Overview
The draft breast cancer screening guidelines released by the Canadian Task Force on Preventive
Health Care (Task Force) on May 30, 2024, fail to adequately prioritize early detection of breast
cancer and the health of Canadians. This brief discusses the scientific flaws in the guidelines, as well
as issues with the guideline creation process.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
This brief discusses the scientific flaws in the guidelines, as well
as issues with the guideline creation process.

Why is early detection important?
In 2024, it is estimated that 30,500 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer and 5,500
will die from it. [1] Early detection helps to decrease the likelihood of death from this disease. Multiple
studies show strong, consistent mortality benefits on the order of 53%. [2] Living in a province that
includes screening for women in their 40s is associated with a 1.9% increase in 10-year net survival
and 3.3% in 45-49, [3] and a lower stage of breast cancer at diagnosis in women in their 40s and 50s.
[4] In addition to decreasing deaths, early-stage diagnosis means less need for harsh treatments, such
as mastectomy and chemotherapy, and less disfiguring lymphedema. [5] There is also less need for
costly drugs used for treating advanced cancer. Early detection means better quality of life for
women with breast cancer.
What are the 2024 draft breast cancer screening recommendations from the Task Force?
The 2024 draft guidelines [6] recommend against screening women aged 40-49, but allow for personal
choice. The guidelines recommend screening women 50-74 years every 2-3 years. They recommend
against supplemental screening for women with dense breasts and against screening women aged 75
and above.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
They recommend
against supplemental screening for women with dense breasts and against screening women aged 75
and above.

What are the recommendations from breast cancer screening experts?
The Canadian Association of Radiologists, [7] the Canadian Society of Breast Imaging, as well as expert
North American academic societies [8] recommend:
1. Screening annually, starting at age 40 [9] as 13.5% of breast cancers are [10} diagnosed in
women aged 40-49, and 25% of years of life lost [11] to breast cancer are to women diagnosed
in their 40s. Screening these women would reduce deaths by 3 to 4 per thousand, which
equates to 400 to 600 avoidable deaths each year in Canada. [12] There would be even more
lives saved by screening women over age 74, and by offering supplemental screening to
women with dense breasts.
2. Women with dense breast tissue should have annual mammograms [13] and be offered
additional MRI or ultrasound screening [14]. Dense tissue increases the risk of developing
cancer, as well as the risk that cancer can be hidden on a mammogram. Women with the
densest tissue are 13[15]-18[16] times more likely to be diagnosed with an interval cancer
(cancer diagnosed in the interval between planned mammograms) than women with fatty
breasts. Supplemental screening with ultrasound [17] or MRI [18] has been shown to decrease
interval cancers. A reduced interval cancer rate is considered a surrogate measure of mortality
reduction. [19]

Why are there differences in the recommendations from breast cancer screening experts and the
Task Force?

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
Why are there differences in the recommendations from breast cancer screening experts and the
Task Force?

1. Subject matter experts do not vote: While Task Force members are experts in their own fields,
they are not specialists in breast cancer. The current panel includes nurse practitioners and family
doctors, as well as a gastroenterologist, nephrologist, and emergency room doctor. The lack of
fulsome expert clinical involvement resulted in errors in the choice of and interpretation of evidence.
Subject matter experts and patients were excluded from voting on the recommendations.
2. Outdated data: Contrary to recommendations from clinical and scientific experts, the 2024
guidelines are anchored in Randomized Control Trials (RCTs) performed in the 1960s to 1990s. This is
in part due to a rigid attitude of Task Force leadership that the only high-quality evidence comes from
a RCT. The RCTs do not reflect the reality of diagnostic and treatment advances and current practice.
The inclusion of 40–60-year-old data overlooks the many advances in screening technology and
breast cancer treatment. In addition, only trials which included “screened” and “unscreened” arms
were allowed to be included, limiting the ability to use modern data (race, ethnicity, density). [20]
3. Downgrading of Observational Studies: The Task Force downgraded recent observational studies
involving millions of women comparing screening to no screening with updated diagnosis and
treatment. In 2024, the Ottawa Evidence Review Team assessed the mortality reduction benefit from
the old RCTs at 15%, and benefit from observational data at 53%. [21] Even though the observational
trials were generally performed in the 1990’s and later, and results showed consistent substantial
benefit, their data was automatically downgraded using GRADE to below RCT data. A comparison of
old RCTs versus more recent observational studies is given in the Forest plots (Figure 1). Downgraded
studies include the Pan Canadian study involving 2.8 million women screened over 20 years, which
demonstrated a 44% reduction in breast cancer mortality in women in their 40s. [22] Similar studies in
Sweden show 50 to 60% mortality reduction for women aged 40-74 years detected via screening
compared to those diagnosed symptomatically. [23]
Figure 1.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
Downgraded
studies include the Pan Canadian study involving 2.8 million women screened over 20 years, which
demonstrated a 44% reduction in breast cancer mortality in women in their 40s. [22] Similar studies in
Sweden show 50 to 60% mortality reduction for women aged 40-74 years detected via screening
compared to those diagnosed symptomatically. [23]
Figure 1.

4. Systematic Discrimination: The RCTs were performed in Europe and North America, mainly with
white subjects. The CNBSS was based on 98% white participants. [24] The peak incidence for Black,
Asian, and Hispanic women is in the mid-forties. (Figure) [25] Recent Canadian analysis shows that
White women are the only group whose peak incidence is beyond age 50. [26] The Task Force
acknowledged data showing higher mortality in Black women in the 40s but did not lower the
screening age. Data on Black mortality, in part led to the US Task Force lowering the screening age.
[27] Preliminary data from Statistics Canada suggests similar findings to the US. See Figure below.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
See Figure below.

5. Increasing incidence: Recently published data shows the rate of breast cancer in women under the
age of 50 in Canada has increased significantly in the past 34 years. [28] Increasing incidence in
younger women is seen across the globe. [29] The US Task Force cited this as another reason for
lowering the screening age to 40. [30]
6. Harms vs Benefits: The Task Force concluded that the balance between benefit and harm was less
favourable for younger women, than for older women. Given that the benefits include 53% fewer
breast cancer deaths, [31] and better quality of life, one might wonder what the “harms” are. The first
“harm” is described as the anxiety that women may experience if recalled for additional imaging.
Mammography is not perfect; some examinations will prompt a recall to increase the confidence that
no cancer is present. The Task Force no longer refers to callbacks as “false positives,” but
overemphasizes the harm of transient anxiety. After the additional tests, 95% of recalled women are
told that they do not have cancer. [32] The Task Force uses a false equivalency: in the benefits to
harms weighting, they equate transient anxiety to avoidable death. The Task Force does not include
the benefit of earlier stage diagnosis in their 1000 person tool, which is used to facilitate shareddecision making.
The Task Force also disproportionately focuses on “overdiagnosis” (the diagnosis of a cancer which
would never have caused problems for an individual). Overdiagnosis is only a harm if overtreatment
occurs. We currently do not know which, if any, cancers do not require treatment, so all are treated.
Whereas overdiagnosis was estimated to be 48% in the 2018 guideline, [33] it is now estimated to be
11% when including the discredited CNBSS and 6% when the CNBSS is excluded. [34]
7. Shared decision making: The Task Force couches its recommendations in “shared-decision
making”, between patient and primary care providers. When family physicians receive inaccurate
information about harms and benefits, with a recommendation NOT to screen, it undermines
decision-making.
8. The Task Force does not monitor the outcomes of its recommendations: After the Task Force
changed its recommendation in 2011 to not routinely screen women in their 40s, women aged 40-59
in provinces without access to screening until age 50 were more likely to be diagnosed with more
advanced cancers and had poorer survival. [35] There was a 10% increase in stage IV breast cancer in
women in their 40s and 50s between 2011 and 2020. [36]
9. A failure to act on the risks of dense breasts The Task Force acknowledged that women with
dense breasts were twice as likely to develop breast cancer as women with non-dense breasts, but
ignored the reduced sensitivity of mammography in women with dense breasts. The Task Force
arbitrarily extrapolated data from “average risk women” instead of reviewing the many trials that
look at breast density. [37]

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
The Task Force
arbitrarily extrapolated data from “average risk women” instead of reviewing the many trials that
look at breast density. [37]

The Task Force ignored high quality RCTs that showed that screening with ultrasound or MRI in
addition to mammography reduced the interval cancers (those cancers found by symptoms after a
normal mammogram) by 80% and by 50%.[38] Interval cancers are larger and more often spread, and
lead to poorer outcomes, so reducing interval cancers is a goal of screening. Reduction of interval
cancers has been shown to be an acceptable surrogate for reduction of breast cancer mortality,
which takes 10 years or more to demonstrate.[39]
What are the guidelines internationally?
On April 30, 2024, the US Preventive Services Task Force lowered the screening age from 50 to 40.
Seven other countries start screening at age 40: Iceland, Sweden, USA, Brazil, Japan, Korea, and
Turkey. Austria, Cyprus, Hungary, Israel, Columbia, and Portugal start at 45, but women in Austria
and Hungary may opt to start at 40.
Supplemental screening for women with dense breasts is recommended in 11 European countries.[40]
In Europe, women aged 50-70 with the highest density are recommended to have MRI every 2 to 3
years. This chart shows that although the incidence of breast cancer in Canada is lower than Norway,
Austria, Sweden and the USA, our mortality is higher. [41]
Canadian Cancer Society: In May 2024, the Canadian Cancer Society changed their recommendation
to recommend breast cancer screening begin at age 40.

Why do the Task Force guidelines matter?
Even though 10 out of 12 Canadian jurisdictions have already lowered the screening age to the 40s or
have committed to do so, Task Force recommendations influence provincial clinical practice
guidelines and physician’s and women’s access to screening. The variability in provincial screening

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
The variability in provincial screening

policies has led to inequity. This has resulted in differences in stage at diagnosis [42] for women, based
on where they live, which may affect their survival.
Currently, the following provinces offer self-referral at 40: BC, PEI, YT, NS, NL, NB
Starting soon: ON (Fall) SK (Jan 2025)
Under review: QC, MB
Self-referral at 45 or after first screen 40-44: AB, NWT
What are the financial costs of poor screening practices?
The guidelines also lead to higher long-term costs. Researchers have shown the exponential costs of
treating cancers with increasing stages.[43] (Table 1). Stage IV breast cancer is up to 11x more costly to
treat than stage I breast cancer. Mean cost is $39,263 for stage I and $370,398 for stage IV. [44] A
recent Canadian study found that screening women annually with mammography from age 40-74 not
only pays for itself, it could save 350M dollars annually in Canada.[45]
Recommendations: Breast Cancer Screening Practices
1. Risk assessment beginning at age 25-30 and revisited every few years.
2. Screening average-risk women 40-49 annually by self-referral.
3. Screening women 50 and older every 1 to 2 years for as long as they are in good general
health, with a life expectancy of 10 years.
4. Supplemental screening if an individual has category C or D density.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Dale, Jennie / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
Supplemental screening if an individual has category C or D density.

Recommendations: Task Force Reform [46]
1. Restructure the Task Force with a robust governance and accountability structure.
2. Monitor outcomes and any deteriorating outcomes should be quickly addressed.
3. Involve ethicists in both the restructuring of the Task Force as well as the choice of topics.
4. Involve patients at every level. Provide adequate training and support for patients.
5. Require full disclosure of the credentials of panel members in all documentation, including the
final published guidelines.
6. Modernize methodology using updated concepts, such as EBM+.

The Canadian Society of Breast Imaging Statement in
Response to the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health
Care (Draft) guidelines for Breast Cancer Screening
The Canadian Society of Breast Imaging (CSBI) does not support The Canadian Task
Force on Preventive Health Care (CTFPHC) draft guidelines for breast cancer
screening in average and moderately increased risk women* released on May 30, 2024.
The CTFPHC released their draft guidelines around the age of systematic screening in
women at average and moderately increased risk. Much to the dismay of the vast
majority of breast screening experts, provincial and national organizations such as the
CSBI and patient advisors, the CTFPHC recommends against screening for average
risk eligible women in their 40s.
This recommendation conflicts with the recommendations from international
organizations such as the US Preventive Services Task Force, the European
Commission on Cancer Screening, American College of Radiology, and Society of
Breast Imaging and national organizations including Canadian Cancer Society,
Canadian Association of Radiologists and Canadian Society of Breast Imaging.
1. Annual screening from ages 40-49 has been shown to save the most lives.
1. An additional 3/1000 lives are saved by including this age group in
annual screening https://www.mdpi.com/1718-7729/30/11/686
2. Incidence of breast cancer in women under 50 has been increasing
since the 1980s
https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08465371241246422
3. Breast cancer in non-white women peaks in their 40s and screening
which starts at age 50 ignores the earlier age of disease in racialized
women, delaying diagnosis https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29516087/
2. Earlier detection and diagnosis saves lives

Earlier detection and diagnosis saves lives

1. Screening programs which include women ages 40-49 have a
significantly higher survival rate at the 10-year mark, and reduced
mortality, compared to those that only include women in their 50s and
above. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.23.00348
2. In regions that do not include women aged 40-49 in their screening
program, these women have a significantly higher occurrence of stage
2, 3 and 4 disease (metastatic disease).
https://www.mdpi.com/1718-7729/29/8/444
3. Earlier detection and diagnosis saves the healthcare system money
1. Costs for breast cancer treatments have dramatically increased in the
past 10 years and rise exponentially with
stage.https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10527628/
2. Preliminary data shows screening women annually for breast cancer
starting at age 40 would save the Canadian Health Care system
~$459.6M per year ,translating to $1880 per woman screened.
https://cslide.ctimeetingtech.com/breast24hybrid/attendee/confcal_1/pr
esentation (Presentation 174P ESMO Breast Cancer Annual
Congress, Berlin, Germany May 15-17, 2024 publication in progress)
4. The Task Force equates the impact of a life saved as being quantitatively equal
to the perceived harm of an abnormal screening recall or a potentially
overdiagnosed cancer. The impact of the harm of a delayed diagnosis of breast
cancer is much greater than that of an abnormal recall or a potentially
overdiagnosed cancer. Collaborative modeling to compare different breast
cancer screening strategies demonstrate 80.7 Quality-Adjusted Life-Years
(QALYs) with biennial screening in ages 50-74 versus 97.5 in the age group
40-74 which increased to 104.2 and to 125.0 QALY’s when screened annually.
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2818285
CSBI continues to strongly encourage all eligible women* aged 40-49 to undergo
screening mammography every year, aged 50 to 74 to undergo screening
mammography every one to two years and women over the age of 74 to have screening
mammography at one to two-year intervals if they are in good health with life
expectancy of ~7 or more years.

https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2818285 CSBI continues to strongly encourage all eligible women* aged 40-49 to undergo screening mammography every year, aged 50 to 74 to undergo screening mammography every one to two years and women over the age of 74 to have screening mammography at one to two-year intervals if they are in good health with life expectancy of ~7 or more years.

The CTFPHC recognizes that women with dense breasts are at moderately increased
risk. Dense breast tissue is an independent risk factor for the development of breast
cancer and decreases the likelihood of breast cancer being detected on screening
mammography. CSBI recommends that supplemental screening with breast MRI or
breast ultrasound may be considered for patients with dense breast tissue (ACR C & D
density categories).
CSBI is committed to supporting evidence-based breast cancer screening in eligible
people aged 40 and above and will continue to update its recommendations as the
knowledge evolves.
*Cisgendered women, eligible transwomen, transgender men and nonbinary or other
individuals assigned female at birth (who did not have bilateral mastectomy)

SUBMISSION TO THE HOUSE OF COMMONS STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH AND TO THE
HONOURABLE MINISTER HEALTH August 5, 2024
REGARDING CANADIAN TASK FORCE ON PREVENTIVE HEALTH CARE DRAFT BREAST SCREENING
GUIDELINES Submission BY: Renée Pellerin on July 18, [CONTACT]. Jean Seely, and my colleagues and I read the submission by Renée Pellerin, and we could
not let her comments identified below stand unopposed.
That has generally not been the case, as our breast screening programs have relied on the simple
message that mammograms save lives. It is so much more complicated than that, and the rhetoric
that dominated the committee hearings in June is not helpful.
Breast screening programs have a history of almost 30 years in Canada and are based on extensive
research showing the benefits of screening mammography. They are also founded on the ability of a
woman to self-refer for a screening mammogram and leave the decision to women to decide if
screening is for them or not. The participation rates in Canada in screening mammography are around
54%, and do not reach the target of 70% for maximal effectiveness of screening for Canada (1). These
participation rates are based on a woman’s choice to be screened or not. Women are informed of the
risks and benefits of screening and make the choice based on this information.
Once the industry was born, it didn’t much matter that other studies came along, testing hundreds of
thousands of women, without ever proving that screening saved more than a few lives from breast
cancer. Nor has it mattered that early detection hasn’t reduced the number of women who die from
all causes, the true measure of a screening intervention. Belief in early detection is engrained.
This perspective is not evidence based and belies the marked benefits noted by adopting screening
mammography programs in almost every developed country in the world. Breast cancer mortality
reductions have been noted in all countries with breast screening programs, and in Canada the
reduction of breast cancer mortality exceeds 47% since screening mammography was introduced in
1989 (2,3). A combination of benefits of earlier detection with screening and treatment advances have
contributed to this remarkable impact, with a stage shift to earlier detection from screening. The lead
investigators of the early studies were driven to reduce the terrible mortality from breast cancer in the
1980s where the mortality rates were steady for years. Unfortunately, in countries that have no
screening programs, such as India, the breast cancer mortality rates are among the highest in the world
in 2024 (4). The “few lives” above refers to the lives saved per thousand women screened over a period
of time, which has been shown with modeling to equate to thousands of lives each year in Canada. If
one considers the value of screening only women 40-49, that is 400-600 lives, and of course when the
50-74-year-old women are screened, it’s hundreds more.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
If
one considers the value of screening only women 40-49, that is 400-600 lives, and of course when the
50-74-year-old women are screened, it’s hundreds more.

The Task Force’s modelling analysis found that among those 1000 women, 368 will endure additional
testing, 55 will have biopsies. 19 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer. One or two will die in
spite of being screened. Among 1000 who are not screened, 17 will be diagnosed with breast cancer,
two will die.
The modeling done by the Task Force has not been published and the assumptions to derive these
estimates are unknown. Without knowing these values, it is impossible to derive accurate conclusions
from their modeling. In fact, they contradict the modelling studies from the USA, and our own Canadian
modelling studies with Oncosim which show that including women in screening every year in their 40s
will avert 3 deaths per 1000 women screened (5). The USPSTF has shown that adding screening for
women in their 40s every 2 years will avert an additional 1.5 per 1000 lives (6). Ms. Pellerin is quoting
the CTF as a law unto itself, which is not based on peer-reviewed evidence.
Yet in most cases, DCIS does not progress to invasive cancer, and one of the important harms of
screening is the resulting overtreatment of a DCIS finding.
While overdiagnosis is recognized as possible harm of screening mammography, it occurs in 1-10% of all
cancers diagnosed. It occurs much less frequently in women in their 40s, who are more likely to benefit
from early detection of breast cancer than older women diagnosed with breast cancer who more often
may die of other causes than breast cancer (7,8). Ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS) is found in about 20%
of screened women, however, the comment that in most it does not progress to invasive cancer is
incorrect. The literature has shown that about between 14 and 53% of DCIS will progress to invasive
cancer, depending on the grade of DCIS and other risk factors, and to cause death from breast cancer if
left untreated (9-12). The treatment of DCIS is evolving and depends very much on the type of DCIS. It is
never left untreated if higher than low grade, and although the research for the treatment of DCIS is
under investigation, the standard of care is to treat DCIS. In fact, the UK AGE randomized trial found a 25% reduction in invasive breast cancer after screening women in the 40s was done, indicating that there
was a benefit of detection of earlier stage 0 DCIS from the screening (13). In Canada, we studied the
incidence of breast cancer (BC) for women living in a province with a screening program for women in
the 40s and found that the incidence of invasive BC in women in their 50s was in fact lower in those
provinces indicating the indirect benefit of the earlier detection of DCIS (14). Ms. Pellerin is making
comments about DCIS that are not reflective of the science and which are based on unvalidated opinion,
not medical knowledge.
Ms. Pellerin has addressed only breast cancer deaths (mortality) and has done so inaccurately. She has
completely ignored the other benefits afforded to women by early detection of breast cancer, namely
reduction in the harshness of treatment: When detected earlier, many women can avoid mastectomy,
and have a less disfiguring lumpectomy instead. When breast cancer is detected earlier, women can
have a sentinel node biopsy rather than an axillary dissection, and avoid the lifelong complication of
lymphedema, swelling of the hand and arm that occurs in 1/3 of those women. And importantly, when
cancer is found early many women can avoid chemotherapy. Women consider these significant benefits,
not considered by Ms. Pellerin.
There has been a concerted campaign to discredit the Canadian Task Force for well over a year, forged
by an alliance between a small group of breast imagers and a patient advocacy group that has

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
There has been a concerted campaign to discredit the Canadian Task Force for well over a year, forged
by an alliance between a small group of breast imagers and a patient advocacy group that has

publicized anecdotes from women who say their doctors refused to refer them to screening. The
trouble with these anecdotes, is that we cannot know the exact nature of the conversation. Did
doctors outright deny a referral, or did patients have a proper discussion with their physicians about
the pros and cons of screening, and later regretted their choice? But even if we accept the anecdotes
at face value, it is wrong to blame the Task Force. The 2018 recommendations clearly stated that for
women in their forties, screening should be a choice based on personal preference and good
information.
Unfortunately, these are more than anecdotes, and the summary of the survey results have been
published (15). They are reflective of many disenfranchised patients who have lived experience of being
denied screening by their healthcare providers. Many radiologists and oncologists have attested to the
veracity of the stories of their patients, all telling a similar story. Ms. Pellerin is incorrect to not blame
the Task Force recommendations, which are followed very closely by Family Physicians who rely on the
Task Force for their medical recommendations. There is no research to back up Ms. Pellerin’s claims,
and she has not provided this evidence.
The evidence reviews conducted by teams at the University of Ottawa and the University of Alberta
adhere to international standards for guideline development. The process involves public engagement
and feedback, and stakeholder consultation. In drafting the breast screening guidelines, the Task
Force included three oncologists and a senior radiologist to be part of the core working group. The
Task Force should be respected for its work, not maligned.
The expert testimony provided at HESA belies these comments and indicated the interference by the
Task Force on the evidence review team. Their testimony contradicts this statement. Furthermore, the
Canadian Task Force Guidelines are contested by multiple specialties in most of their major guidelines
(16). It is not merely a group of breast cancer specialists, who are challenging the guidelines. There are
fundamental questions raised about the methodology itself, which has led to multiple Canadian
guidelines lagging behind other countries and even many provincial guidelines. Questioning the
processes and guidelines produced by the Task Force is, itself, a matter of scientific rigour.
It is also troubling that the lobby has repeatedly attempted to misinform the public, saying that the
Task Force was relying only on randomized screening trials, when in fact, the evidence review
included observational studies and modelling. They also said the randomized trials were sixty years
old. Yes, the first one took place in the 1960s, but others were done in the 1980s or later. The lobby
does not mention 3 that the Age trial in the UK, a modern randomized study designed specifically to
answer whether screening women in their 40s rendered benefit, initiated in 1991 and completed in
1997, found no mortality benefit. Patients were followed for 17 years.
There is no lobby to misinform the public, rather the inverse is true. The Task Force has said that it used
all the randomized controlled trials (RCTs) however they used the GRADE approach, causing the
mortality benefit of the order of 50% measured in the observational trials to be downplayed (17). They
prioritized the 15-20% mortality reduction in the RCTs. The Task Force misinformed the public and
physicians in several ways: inflating and misrepresenting the harms associated with screening,

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
The Task Force misinformed the public and
physicians in several ways: inflating and misrepresenting the harms associated with screening,

minimizing the evidence coming from more modern observational trials and overweighting evidence
from 40-60-year-old trials that used screening and treatment methods that are now obsolete, setting
artificial thresholds for clinical significance and delivering its recommendations before having completed
its computer modelling work. Limitations of the evidence review due to Task Force interference are
summarized in an archived manuscript and its appendices written by the Ottawa Evidence Review Team
and its invited scientific clinical and patient expert advisors.
Ms. Pellerin’s repeated use of the term “lobby” is misleading. The group opposing the Canadian Task
Force guideline is a group of volunteers. There is no financial support or incentive and no registered
lobby group. The involved individuals use their own spare time and are motivated to advocate by
concern for their patients, for the health of Canadians and for the integrity of medical research.
Another important factor in the debate that came, up in your June meetings was the use of relative
versus absolute numbers. Sheila Appavoo suggested the Task Force’s use of absolute numbers was a
manipulation of information. I would argue the opposite. For instance, what if, in a clinical trial, 100
people were given a drug for a headache, and 100 were given a placebo, with the results that after
one hour, 10 people given the drug no longer had pain, while only while 5 in the placebo group no
longer had pain. Using the relative number, you would compare the 10 people to 5 and say twice as
many people obtained relief on the drug. Using the absolute numbers, you would say 10 out of 100
obtained relief on the drug compared to 5 out of 100 on placebo.
Both statements are correct. Based on her example, it would also be correct to say that if 10 million
Canadians suffer from headaches this drug would be better than a placebo for 5% of them or that
500,000 Canadians would benefit. Ms. Pellerin misquoted Dr. Appavoo, who suggested that both
absolute and relative numbers be used (18). Further, to use a drug trial as an example is a misuse of the
intent to use relative numbers, as most people want to know that if they have breast cancer, what are
the chances of dying of their breast cancer and what are their chances of requiring more aggressive
therapy, such as chemotherapy or a mastectomy. There is no intent to hide the absolute numbers, but
to use the relative numbers to make the risks and benefits more relatable to patients, who require this
information to decide on whether to screen or not. Use of relative numbers and totals per country are
well accepted for knowledge tools and is, in fact, used by the US Centres for Disease Control to express
benefits of seatbelt use (19). While it is true that most women will not develop breast cancer, they are
choosing to be screened to mitigate the impact on the chance that they may be diagnosed with breast
cancer. To the women whose lives may be saved, this is critical information. To refuse to explain in both
relative and absolute terms is to deliberately hide information.
Practice guidelines developed by independent bodies are critical checks and balances against
guidelines produced by specialist groups, which inherently have conflicts of interest. Radiologist Paula
Gordon would have every woman screened annually from age 40 until as long as she has the
likelihood of living ten more years. This is a point of view from a professional whose entire career has
been in breast imaging. She should be asked about the cumulative radiation exposure from annual
screenings.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
She should be asked about the cumulative radiation exposure from annual
screenings.

There is ample evidence that the risk of cumulated radiation from annual screening from age 40-80
years is extremely low, and the risk of causing fatal breast cancer is between 2 and 25 per 100,000
women screened (20-22). Dr. Paula Gordon is an expert radiologist and is aware of the risks and benefits
of screening mammography. Her recommendations are based on the literature, and experience of
diagnostic breast cancer in patient with either screen detection or symptomatic detection, at more
advanced stages. Her i10 index is 27, which is exceptional for a clinician who has never received research
support (23).
Physicist Martin Yaffe was a founding member and (according to the Volpara 2023 annual report) still
holds shares in a company that provides breast imaging software, and which promotes software
specific to identifying dense breasts.
Dr. Martin Yaffe is a research medical physicist and a university professor, who has been working in the
field of breast cancer for over 40 years. He has published over 320 peer-reviewed papers, most directed
toward research on breast cancer. His i10 index is 305 and he was inducted as Fellow of the Royal
Society of Canada on the basis of his research (24). He has advised international and Canadian bodies on
breast cancer screening including The International Agency for Research Against cancer (IARC), The
International Atomic Energy Agency and The Canadian Partnership Against Cancer. He did the original
work to develop digital mammography, and then contrast-enhanced mammography and worked with
epidemiologists on much of the original research related to breast density. He is currently helping lead a
large NCI-funded clinical trial to evaluate digital breast tomosynthesis. He is on salary and receives no
additional funding personally for his work. The grants he successfully applies for pay for staff and
supplies only. He was one of the founders of Volpara, at one time was a shareholder, but is no longer
and was not in a position to benefit financially at the time he made his statement to HESA. He does
collaborate in research with a commercial company under an agreement managed by his hospital
institution but receives no personal income or other considerations from this.
They, along with radiologists Jean Seely and Sheila Appavoo want to persuade you that they are the
“experts”. They may be specialists, but that does not make them experts in public health policy,
epidemiology, or creating evidence-based guidelines. Their conflicts of interest should be noted.
Ms. Pellerin is not aware of the body of research that Dr. Jean Seely has published on the science of
screening and has an H index of 32, that exceeds most academic researchers and attests to the number
of citations of her work in the literature. Dr. Seely has an i10 index of 63 and her work on screening has
been cited over 4826 times in the literature, 2894 since 2019 (25). Dr. Seely is considered an expert in
the field of screening mammography and is an invited expert reviewer for journals of epidemiology,
preventive health care and public health care policy Dr. Seely has been an expert in the creation of
several guidelines, including the Ontario Provincial Evidence Based review for Breast MRI and the
Canadian Association of Radiologists. None of this academic work is remunerated and uses volunteer
time in addition to clinical work which is based on shared income within a group practice. There is no
compensation for the advocacy work or benefit from earlier detection of breast cancer in women in

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
There is no
compensation for the advocacy work or benefit from earlier detection of breast cancer in women in

their 40s. To call Dr. Seely a specialist but not an expert is an ad feminam attack and is misinformed or
misguided.
Dr. Shiela Appavoo receives no research support. We have worked together on volunteer work on the
Breast Imaging Referral Guidelines for the Canadian Association of Radiologists, which compiled the
evidence to inform the published guidelines (26). We volunteer on the Standing Committee for the
Mammography Accreditation Program of the Canadian Association of Radiologists (27). She is a general
radiologist working within a group practice. Mammographic screening is one of the lowest paid activities
in her repertoire.
Nor has it mattered that early detection hasn’t reduced the number of women who die from all
causes, the true measure of a screening intervention.
Some have suggested (or insisted) that the definitive proof that breast cancer screening is effective is
demonstration of a reduction in deaths from all causes (all-cause mortality or ACM). This sounds
reasonable at first – it is desirable that breast cancer deaths are reduced without an increase in other
types of mortality (for example, deaths due to cardiotoxicity from treatment of screen-detected breast
cancer). But when one thinks carefully about this, expecting to observe a reduction in ACM is highly
unrealistic, even when breast cancer deaths have been reduced substantially, unless an extremely large
randomized trial is conducted, specifically designed to measure effects on ACM.
Here is the logic:
1. We all die eventually, so over a 100-year time window all-cause mortality (ACM) is virtually
100% for everybody.
2. Therefore, for ACM to have any meaning, it must be defined over an appropriate time window
of observation.
3. The purpose of breast screening is specifically to facilitate reducing deaths and morbidity from
breast cancer through earlier detection and treatment. Breast screening is not designed to
reduce deaths from any other cause (although the interaction of women with the health care
system through screening could have secondary beneficial effects on other diseases). But
reasonably we should only expect screening to reduce breast cancer deaths.
4. Because we all die from something, reducing mortality from one cause (breast cancer) results in
eventual death being more likely to take place due to another cause (because more people are
alive and at risk for death from car accidents other types of cancer or stroke).
5. Less than 3% of women die from breast cancer – excellent news!
6. Under ideal circumstances (high quality screening, full participation of women) mammography
screening might reduce deaths due to breast cancer by 40-50%, for simplicity, let’s say half. So,
over a full lifetime, 1.5% of women would die of breast cancer and breast cancer deaths in the
other 1.5% would be prevented.
7. So even with ideal results from screening and nobody dying of other causes (totally unrealistic!)
we might at most expect a 1.5% reduction in ACM over a full lifetime.

org: Appavoo, Shushiela / Gordon, Paula / Seely, Jean M. / Wilkinson, Anna N. / Yaffe, Martin J.
text:
So even with ideal results from screening and nobody dying of other causes (totally unrealistic!)
we might at most expect a 1.5% reduction in ACM over a full lifetime.

8. To observe a reduction in ACM due to breast cancer screening means that over a prescribed
time window, it would be necessary to measure this 1.5% change accurately.
9. Given other causes of mortality and fluctuations in these (e.g., COVID), this would require an
extremely large (many millions of women) well-monitored randomized trial, far larger than the
trials performed to measure the reduction in breast cancer deaths from screening (28).
10. There is another problem though. To capture the full measured benefit from breast cancer
screening an observation window (beginning of screening to end of follow-up) of at least 20
years would be required over which the cumulative breast cancer deaths would be compared
between screened and unscreened women. But (see Points #1 and 4), the longer we observe
the population, the more people will die from other causes. This has nothing to do with
screening, but this natural increase in “other-cause mortality” with age will cause ACM to
increase. Therefore, observing the population long enough to measure the full impact of breast
screening will likely increase ACM.
11. In other words – too short an observation window, we don’t see the full breast cancer death
reduction; too long and other-cause mortality drives ACM up. Dr Yaffe’s paper shows how one
would choose the population size and observation period to look at the effect on ACM (28).
12. There is an exception and that occurs when the population considered includes only women
diagnosed with breast cancer. Because the observation period for these women begins, not
when screening begins but when the cancer is diagnosed, it can be shorter and other cause
mortality has less opportunity to increase. For this group the effect of screening in reducing
both breast cancer mortality and all-cause mortality has been observed (29).
13. Another possible exception is for younger women (in their 40s), where breast cancer represents
the major cause of premature death there are very few competing other causes. Nevertheless,
a very large, controlled study would be required to see this effect as the observation period
would have to extend for over 20 years and rising other-cause mortality unrelated to screening
would start to become a factor (30).
Ms. Pellerin’s focus on financial conflict of interest is reminiscent of accusations that anyone provaccination must be on the payroll of Big Pharma. It is a personal attack based on an assumption of
motivation (31). In any field, most topic experts will have some degree of financial conflict, but to
conflate professional interest with corporate interest is illogical and systematically excludes the deepest
subject knowledge.

Dear Health Minister Mark Holland,
I am writing to thank you for requesting a review of the Canadian Task Force recommendations on breast screening
that includes the voices of breast cancer experts along with the public. Thank you for your efforts to protect
women’s health and save lives. I, like so many other women, am sharing my story in the hope that the Canadian
Task Force will see the grave danger in their decision and revise the current breast screening guidelines. This month
marks one year from my first 2 chemotherapy treatments. I had 8 treatments over 4 months. Perhaps if I had been
screened at 40 this treatment could have been avoided and my story would be a little different.
My name is Julie McIntyre. I am a mother, a wife, a daughter, a sister, an aunt, a cousin, a friend, a teacher. Last
February my world was turned upside down when I was diagnosed with Invasive Lobular Carcinoma. I was 49 and
thought I was in good health. I ate well, exercised regularly, was rarely sick, and to my knowledge had no direct
family history. How could this be happening?
In January 2023 I found a lump in my breast. I periodically examine my breasts, having learned the importance of
self exams from friends who have been diagnosed with breast cancer over the past 10 years, all in their 40s. Some
are survivors but others have tragically lost the battle, leaving behind loved ones and a life that was cut brutally and
unfairly short. I cannot imagine if I followed the Task Force Guidelines which advises against self-examination
because I would not have noticed the new lump and taken the steps to have it investigated.
After finding the lump I went to see my doctor and I will be forever grateful that he sent me for both a mammogram
and an ultrasound. Throughout this process I have learned that I have category D dense breasts. Category D
places me at a higher risk for breast cancer. Unfortunately, I had never heard about breast density and its
subsequent increased risk because I had never had a mammogram until I found my lump at 49 years old. As
you know the Canadian Task Force guidelines do not recommend mammograms before the age of 50 unless you
have a family history or carry the BRCA mutations, and so I did not qualify. A mammogram is the only way to
determine breast density and therefore many women in their 40s are completely unaware of their breast
density and the increased risk it can carry. Like me, they are left to find it on their own, at which point it has
progressed to a size that is large enough to be noticed, and likely more advanced than it would have been if
detected earlier through regular screening. This is criminal. If the guidelines were changed to screening at 40,
women would have mammograms earlier, learn about their density and be monitored more frequently with
appropriate screening modalities. Additional screening methods are needed along with mammograms for
women who have dense breast tissue to accurately detect cancer because both cancer and dense breast
tissue appear white on a mammogram which makes it difficult to identify cancerous growths.
After a waiting period of 2 weeks my worst nightmare came true, the biopsy was positive for cancer, Invasive
Lobular Carcinoma. The Canadian Task Force argues that screening at 40 causes unnecessary stress and anxiety
that comes with call backs and waiting for results. There is no comparison to the stress and anxiety that
accompanies a cancer diagnosis, a year of cancer treatment, surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, side effects from
treatments and from medication to prevent recurrence, living with the fear of recurrence and metastasis, having to
tell your children that their mom has cancer, having to tell your partner, your parents, family and friends that you
have cancer….the list goes on. A few weeks of worry while waiting for results is nothing compared to a lifetime of
stress and an illness that is life altering, affecting your physical, mental and emotional health and quality of life.

stress and an illness that is life altering, affecting your physical, mental and emotional health and quality of life.

Once the diagnosis was made, ultrasound and MRI imaging estimated my tumor to be 2 cm, however, after surgery,
pathology reported a much larger tumor of 6 cm AND a second smaller tumor. I was in complete shock at this
news, sadly I am not alone, this happens to many women. In addition to having dense breast tissue, I have Invasive
Lobular Carcinoma. Although this is the 2nd most common type of breast cancer it is a type that can be more
difficult to detect because of the way the cancer grows in lines. The larger sized tumor meant that my treatment
plan would now require chemotherapy. I was angry and upset thinking about how much further advanced my
cancer would have been if I hadn’t self-examined and been aware of my “normal” lumps, if I hadn’t gone
immediately to my doctor, and if I hadn’t been sent for both a mammogram and ultrasound, but also at that fact
that if I had been screened at 40 and been aware of my breast density my cancer would have been caught
earlier and I would have been spared some of the treatments, harsh side effects and have a better prognosis.
Lowering the age of screening to 40 is essential to detecting cancer earlier. Evidence shows that an early
diagnosis leads to a better prognosis and can reduce the need for aggressive treatment. We also know that
treatments for advanced stages of cancer are significantly more costly. I am only one of thousands of Canadian
women who has a more advanced stage of cancer because of these outdated and flawed recommendations.
It is very apparent that the Task Force Guidelines DO NOT have the interests of women at heart. They continue to
cite the “evidence”, but I’m confused as to which evidence they are referring because in the year that I have had
cancer the evidence seems to unequivocally point towards the need for earlier screening. Women are being
diagnosed at an earlier age and at more advanced stages. Breast cancer is the leading cause of death for women
aged 40 – 55 and breast cancer risk increases significantly after age 40. The current guidelines are dangerous and
responsible for lost lives and incredible pain and suffering. How can you possibly argue against screening at 40?
Please ensure that the necessary changes are made to breast screening so that we can catch cancer earlier,
make a difference in the health and quality of lives of women, and save lives. It is time to listen to the science, the
experts and advocacy groups, countless women and family members who have been affected by this horrible
disease and all Canadian women. It is time to do right by the women of Canada. I am asking you to ensure that the
following actions are taken:
 Reduce the breast screening age to 40.
 Provide supplemental screening in addition to mammography for women with dense breasts.
 Raise awareness and education about breast cancer and breast health and ensure that breast
screening programs are easily accessible.
 Extend breast screening beyond age 74
Sincerely, and in hope for a better future for all women,
Julie McIntyre

DRAFT BREAST SCREENING GUIDELINES
SUBMITTED BY:
Renée Pellerin
Journalist and author
July 18, 2024

I am a health journalist who began to follow the breast cancer screening debate in the 1990s, while I was
a producer at the CBC’s investigative consumer program, Marketplace. In 2018, after four years of indepth research into the history and politics of screening, I wrote the book Conspiracy of Hope, the Truth
about Breast Cancer Screening, published by Goose Lane Editions. I concluded at the time that early
detection resulted in harms as well as benefits, and therefore women should be given objective and
complete information, before choosing whether or not to participate in screening. That has generally not
been the case, as our breast screening programs have relied on the simple message that mammograms
save lives. It is so much more complicated than that, and the rhetoric that dominated the committee
hearings in June is not helpful.
Breast screening has always been a highly debated topic, said to be the most contentious in medicine,
and angry reaction to the draft recommendations from the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health is
not surprising. The controversy goes back to 1973 when the US National Cancer Institute and the
American Cancer Society jointly instituted the Breast Cancer Detection Demonstration Project, a fiveyear program to offer free mammograms to about 250,000 women across America. The problem was,
there had been just one screening trial, which had provided weak evidence that early detection made a
difference in older women, and no evidence at all there was benefit for women under 50. The project
had critics who lamented the lack of good science behind it, but enthusiasm for anything with a hint of
promise prevailed. The demonstration project was the beginning of an industry that involved radiologists
who up to then had been involved only in diagnosing cancer, not in screening asymptomatic, healthy
citizens, and by manufacturers who profited from selling imaging equipment. Breast cancer charities,
including the American Cancer Society, also benefited from a compelling, hopeful, message that would
surely increase donations. Once the industry was born, it didn’t much matter that other studies came
along, testing hundreds of thousands of women, without ever proving that screening saved more than a
few lives from breast cancer. Nor has it mattered that early detection hasn’t reduced the number of
women who die from all causes, the true measure of a screening intervention. Belief in early detection is
engrained.
For a woman who fears breast cancer, what happens at the population level may not matter. She may
not want to risk not being screened, in case she happens to be one of the one or two out of 1000
women aged 40-49 screened over ten years who will benefit. But should she not understand what her
actual risk of dying is? And the risk of harm? The Task Force’s modelling analysis found that among those
1000 women, 368 will endure additional testing, 55 will have biopsies. 19 women will be diagnosed with
breast cancer. One or two will die in spite of being screened. Among 1000 who are not screened, 17 will
be diagnosed with breast cancer, two will die. Among the women screened, two will be diagnosed with
cancer that would never have caused a problem in their lifetimes. This is what’s known as overdiagnosis.
It’s a significant problem as it results in unnecessary surgery, the risk of harm from radiation treatment,
and the risk of long-term disability resulting from damage to the arms in lymph node removal.
I don’t believe any of the witnesses you heard from in June talked about ductal carcinoma in situ, DCIS.
DCIS is a cancer confined within a milk duct, as opposed to invasive cancer which spreads beyond the
duct into surrounding tissue. DCIS usually cannot be felt. When a mammogram sees it however, women
are typically treated with surgery and possibly radiation, and sometimes it can be scattered in such a way

When a mammogram sees it however, women
are typically treated with surgery and possibly radiation, and sometimes it can be scattered in such a way
within the breast that lumpectomy would be disfiguring and mastectomy, plus reconstruction, is a

preferred option. DCIS accounts for one in five screen-detected breast cancers. Yet in most cases, DCIS
does not progress to invasive cancer, and one of the important harms of screening is the resulting
overtreatment of a DCIS finding. There are now several international studies testing a wait and watch
approach to DCIS. Women should know this. And committee members, please be aware that there are
large advocacy groups that have great concern about this harm.
There has been a concerted campaign to discredit the Canadian Task Force for well over a year, forged by
an alliance between a small group of breast imagers and a patient advocacy group that has publicized
anecdotes from women who say their doctors refused to refer them to screening. The trouble with
these anecdotes, is that we cannot know the exact nature of the conversation. Did doctors outright deny
a referral, or did patients have a proper discussion with their physicians about the pros and cons of
screening, and later regretted their choice? But even if we accept the anecdotes at face value, it is wrong
to blame the Task Force. The 2018 recommendations clearly stated that for women in their forties,
screening should be a choice based on personal preference and good information. The current draft
recommendations reinforce that idea and make it clearer that doctors should not deny women who wish
to be screened, if their choice is informed. But the Task Force stopped short of recommending systematic
screening for this age group because the evidence of benefit is very low quality, and benefit may not
outweigh the harms.
It is troubling to see the Task Force so attacked for its reasonable interpretation of the data. It is a
venerable institution that has been a world leader in helping family physicians practice evidence-based
medicine since 1976. In fact, it pre-dated the formation of the US Preventive Services Task Force which
was modelled on the Canadian experience. The Task Force is an arms-length independent body that is
meant to be free of political interference. Its members are unpaid for their public service and operate
under strict conflict of interest rules. The evidence reviews conducted by teams at the University of
Ottawa and the University of Alberta adhere to international standards for guideline development. The
process involves public engagement and feedback, and stakeholder consultation. In drafting the breast
screening guidelines, the Task Force included three oncologists and a senior radiologist to be part of the
core working group. The Task Force should be respected for its work, not maligned.
Practice guidelines developed by independent bodies are critical checks and balances against guidelines
produced by specialist groups, which inherently have conflicts of interest. Radiologist Paula Gordon
would have every woman screened annually from age 40 until as long as she has the likelihood of living
ten more years. This is a point of view from a professional whose entire career has been in breast
imaging. She should be asked about the cumulative radiation exposure from annual screenings. Physicist
Martin Yaffe was a founding member and (according to the Volpara 2023 annual report) still holds shares
in a company that provides breast imaging software, and which promotes software specific to identifying
dense breasts. They, along with radiologists Jean Seely and Sheila Appavoo want to persuade you that
they are the “experts”. They may be specialists, but that does not make them experts in public health
policy, epidemiology, or creating evidence-based guidelines. Their conflicts of interest should be noted.
It is also troubling that the lobby has repeatedly attempted to misinform the public, saying that the Task
Force was relying only on randomized screening trials, when in fact, the evidence review included
observational studies and modelling. They also said the randomized trials were sixty years old. Yes, the
first one took place in the 1960s, but others were done in the 1980s or later. The lobby does not mention

The lobby does not mention

that the Age trial in the UK, a modern randomized study designed specifically to answer whether
screening women in their 40s rendered benefit, initiated in 1991 and completed in 1997, found no
mortality benefit. Patients were followed for 17 years.
Another important factor in the debate that came up in your June meetings was the use of relative
versus absolute numbers. Sheila Appavoo suggested the Task Force’s use of absolute numbers was a
manipulation of information. I would argue the opposite. For instance, what if, in a clinical trial, 100
people were given a drug for a headache, and 100 were given a placebo, with the results that after one
hour, 10 people given the drug no longer had pain, while only while 5 in the placebo group no longer had
pain. Using the relative number, you would compare the 10 people to 5 and say twice as many people
obtained relief on the drug. Using the absolute numbers, you would say 10 out of 100 obtained relief on
the drug compared to 5 out of 100 on placebo. The absolute numbers are more useful in making a
decision whether or not to take the drug because now you can see that it makes a difference in only 5
out of a hundred people. However, if you are the drug manufacturer, it would suit your marketing
purposes to use the relative number which looks so much more impressive.
This is why the Task Force insists on absolute numbers, i.e comparing 19 diagnosed out of 1000 to 17
diagnosed out of 1000, as described above.
The screening lobby often cites a figure from a Canadian observational study to argue that screening
saves lives. The Pan-Canadian Study of Mammography Screening and Mortality from Breast Cancer,
published in 2014, in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, compared breast cancer mortality in
provinces that screened women in their forties, to mortality in provinces that did not. It reported that
screening reduced mortality by an average of 40 percent. Screening advocates cite this figure repeatedly.
But what an individual in the 40-49 age group might want to know is another number from the same
study: 1247 would have to be screened over ten years to prevent one death. Or this number: the 10year mortality rate was 1.02 per 1000 women who participated in screening, which represents the 40
percent reduction in mortality compared to 1.7 per 1000 women who were not screened.
As the Task Force points out, the evidence of benefit for screening at any age is low or very low quality.
There are many questions that cannot be answered, and like the US Preventive Services Task Force, the
Canadian group describes a desperate need for more data. There needs to be more research into the
balance of benefits and harms in diverse races and ethnicities, particularly among Black and Indigenous
populations. Newer studies using modern screening technique and treatments are needed to determine
impact on mortality, stage at diagnosis and overdiagnosis. It’s often said that early detection makes the
cancer easier to treat, with less invasive therapy, but there needs to be more supporting data. More
research is needed to determine appropriate screening strategies for dense breasts. Perhaps the lack of
good data is an area the committee could explore. And perhaps a call for more research would be
helpful.
In 1973, breast cancer screening seemed to make sense. But back then, cancer was regarded as a single
disease. Today we know there are hundreds of different cancers, including many types of breast cancer.
The outcome of a diagnosis does not simply depend on the size of a tumour. It depends more on the
cancer type, the genetics of the specific tumour, other health issues a patient might have, and advances

It depends more on the
cancer type, the genetics of the specific tumour, other health issues a patient might have, and advances

in treatment. Given the knowledge we’ve gained over the last five decades about how cancer actually
works, shouldn’t we consider where better to place resources than on an outdated intervention that is
only marginally effective at best?
