Providing counselling, advocacy, and support for abused women.
Brief to the Standing Committee on Health
Submitted by: Jennifer Dunn, Executive Director, London Abused Women’s Centre (Canada)
April 15, 2024
Chair and Members, Standing Committee on Health:
The London Abused Women’s Centre (LAWC) is a feminist organization that supports and advocates for
personal, social, and systemic change directed at ending male violence against women and girls. LAWC is a
non-residential agency that provides women and girls over the age of 12 who have been subjected to abuse,
assault, sexual exploitation, trafficking, and non-state torture with immediate access to long-term, traumainformed counselling, advocacy, and support.
In 2023, LAWC had over 11,000 service interactions. Of those 11,000, over 4,000 individual counselling,
group and urgent support service interactions. This includes approximately 400 women and girls who
reported being trafficked or were at risk of being trafficked. This also includes 112 women who reported
being subjected to non-state torture. During this same time, LAWC also answered over 7,000 calls for
support.
It is impossible to study women’s health without looking through the lens of male violence against women
and inequality. Despite strides toward ending male violence, women continue to navigate through societal
structures that perpetuate their vulnerability. This brief explains the dimensions of women's health based on
the work we do at the London Abused Women’s Centre which we are hoping will “Shine the Light”1 on the
urgent need for comprehensive support and systemic change.
Violence and abuse often manifest in physical injuries and chronic health conditions, ranging from bruises
and fractures to sexually transmitted infections and reproductive health issues. Abuse, especially in intimate
partner relationships, can lead to severe physical trauma, including traumatic brain injuries, chronic pain
syndromes, and even fatality. Patriarchal structures exacerbate these health disparities by perpetuating norms
that prioritize men's control over women's bodies, resulting in limited access to healthcare and reproductive
rights, for example.
Women subjected to violence and abuse frequently suffer with mental health issues such as depression,
anxiety, and post-traumatic stress.2 The psychological toll of enduring abuse can lead to self-harming
behaviors, suicidal ideation, and diminished self-worth, perpetuating a cycle of trauma and despair for them.
Women experiencing violence and abuse face social isolation, stigmatization, and economic dependence,
1 Shine the Light on Woman Abuse Campaign, https://www.lawc.on.ca/shine-the-light-on-woman-abuse-campaign
2 Status of Women Canada, 2018 - https://cfc-swc.gc.ca/violence/strategy-strategie/breaking-briser-en.html

Women experiencing violence and abuse face social isolation, stigmatization, and economic dependence,
1 Shine the Light on Woman Abuse Campaign, https://www.lawc.on.ca/shine-the-light-on-woman-abuse-campaign
2 Status of Women Canada, 2018 - https://cfc-swc.gc.ca/violence/strategy-strategie/breaking-briser-en.html

further exacerbating their vulnerability. The economic consequences of abuse, including job loss, financial
control by abusers, and limited access to resources, hinder women's autonomy, and ability to escape abusive
situations.
Young women and girls aged 15 to 24 are five times more likely than women aged 25 years and older to have
been physically or sexually assaulted. 3 Young women and girls between the ages of 12 to 21 are at the highest
risk of being sexually exploited, groomed, and lured into the sex trade, often by traffickers who are their
intimate partners.
Women from marginalized communities, including LGBTQ+ individuals, women of colour, indigenous
women, and those with disabilities, face compounded forms of violence and discrimination, resulting in
exacerbated health disparities. Intersectional approaches are crucial for understanding the unique challenges
faced by diverse groups of women and developing proper interventions that address their intersecting
experiences.
The status of women's health in the face of violence is a stark reminder of the inequalities and injustices
embedded within our society. For meaningful change, challenge societal norms that perpetuate male violence
against women, and prioritize the well-being of women. By advocating for comprehensive support services,
investing in trauma-informed care, and amplifying the voices of survivors, we can work toward a future
where all women live healthy, fulfilling lives free from violence and oppression.
The London Abused Women’s Centre believes the work must start with the goal of shifting the social culture
that normalizes men’s violence against women and girls for future generations.
To that, we propose the following recommendations to the committee for the purpose of the study on Women’s
Health:
1. The Government of Canada commit to the development of legislation to end men’s violence against
women and girls in all its forms including amendments to the criminal code to recognize intimate
partner violence and abuse as separate and distinct from random acts of violence.
2. The Government of Canada work in collaboration with each province to develop a national
mandatory men’s violence against women school curriculum for all levels of education from
kindergarten to high school.
3. The Government of Canada commit to provide an appropriate level of core funding to violence
against women organizations providing front-line service to women and girls.
We know for certain that with changes in legislation, education, and funding, men’s violence against women
can be reduced which will improve the health of women and girls in our country.
Jennifer Dunn
Executive Director

Maria Beatriz Ospina, PhD, Associate Professor, Department of Public Health Sciences,
Queen’s University
April 2024

Black people are a growing population in Canada. Between 2016 and 2021, the Black
population in Canada grew from 3.5% to 4.3% of the total Canadian population (Statistics
Canada, 2023). As of 2021, Black people comprised 16.1% of the racialized population in
Canada, with approximately 1.5 million people identifying as Black.
Black women experience poorer economic and social outcomes than the general Canadian
population. More than any other immigrant women, Black African immigrant women are likely
to be overqualified for their jobs (Houle, 2020). Despite higher education levels among secondgeneration Black women compared to the general Canadian population, they still report earnings
that are 10% lower. Additionally, Black women are more likely to live below the poverty line
(Public Health Agency of Canada, 2020). According to a recent analysis of Canadian census
data, the economic outcomes of Black women have deteriorated over time (Banerjee et al.,
2024). Black women experience discrimination and racism in all sectors of society including
employment and education with severe consequences for health outcomes.
Black women experience poor health outcomes. Black women are at a higher risk of
developing cardiovascular diseases than Black men and are more likely to receive substandard
treatment and management for heart disease compared to White women (Chiu et al., 2015). A
recent Statistics Canada report highlighted that Black females are at increased risk for a range of
serious health issues, including HIV/AIDS, stomach and corpus uteri cancers, lymphomas,
multiple myeloma, diabetes mellitus, and endocrine disorders (Tjepkema et al., 2023). A notable
mortality difference in the report is that Black women experience a 21 times greater risk of
HIV/AIDS compared to White people. Black women are more likely to develop aggressive
forms of cancer at an earlier age and to die as a result (Bowden, 2023). Moreover, Black women
are disproportionately affected by gender-based violence (Duhaney, 2022) and face poorer
perinatal health outcomes (Maxwell et al., 2024). For instance, the preterm birth rate among
Black women in Canada is significantly higher at 8.9% compared to 5.9% among White women
(McKinnon et al., 2016). An Ontario-based retrospective cohort study found Black women (and
their children) were at an increased risk of gestational diabetes mellitus, preeclampsia, placental
abruption, preterm birth, spontaneous preterm birth, all caesarean sections, emergency caesarean
section, low birth weight, small-for-gestational-age, neonates, neonatal intensive care unit
admission, and hyperbilirubinemia requiring treatment (Miao et al., 2022). Fibroids are three
times more common in Black women and oral hormonal therapy for fibroids may not be
effective for fibroids in Black women (Jaques et al., 2024). A recent analysis of the Canadian
Community Health Survey by members of our team has also found that Black women have
higher odds of not receiving a pap smear (2.62; CI 1.82, 3.78) compared to the White origin
group, increasing their risk of late diagnosis of cervical cancer (Salami et al., Submitted February
2024). Despite limited data, anecdotal evidence suggests a higher maternal mortality among
Black women (Maxwell et al., 2024).
The health of Black women in Canada is specifically impacted by anti-Black racism. The
experiences of Black women are shaped by systemic racism dating back to decades of
reproductive oppression and dehumanization within the healthcare system. For instance, Sims
(known as the father of gynecology) perfected his techniques and many instruments used today
in women’s health (such as the speculum) by experimenting on Black women without their
consent or pain medication. He described the agony of one Black woman he experimented on
without consent and pain medication: "Lucy's agony was extreme. She was much prostrated, and
I thought that she was going to die…. from the effects of this unfortunate experiment”

I thought that she was going to die…. from the effects of this unfortunate experiment”

(Domonoske, 2018). These unethical and unjust practices have consequences for Black women’s
trust in the healthcare system and shapes their willingness to access and use health services. Our
interviews with 30 Black women about their experiences accessing healthcare services further
revealed instances of racism and discrimination (Olukotun et al., Submitted April 2024). Many
reported feelings of distrust or mistrust and noted that their health concerns were often dismissed
by healthcare providers. Participants stated that increasing the number of Black health service
providers and enhancing social support could improve their access to healthcare. Furthermore,
our findings indicate that addressing intersecting factors such as race, gender, income, culture,
and language is crucial for improving healthcare access and utilization for Black women. Global
studies also indicate that maternal-child health outcomes improve when Black people receive
care from Black healthcare professionals (Greenwood et al., 2020).
Despite the aforementioned evidence, there is paucity of data on Black people’s health in
Canada. For example, some evidence in Canada points to the possibility of higher rates of
maternal mortality among Black women (Miao et al., 2022). Data from the United States and the
United Kingdom revealed three-fold higher maternal mortality in Black women compared to
their White counterparts (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2024; MBRRACE-UK,
2024). Despite the lack of race-based data in Canada, our team believes similar disparities exist
in Canada. The lack of quantitative data and limited qualitative data on perinatal mortality and
morbidity in Canada have prevented targeted interventions to address this major issue that has an
impact on Black women, Black children, and the broader Canadian society. Also, research on
Black populations is often deeply problematic with limited sustained involvement and also
without attending to ethical issues related to community engagement with Black communities,
such as the EGAP (Engagement, Governance, Access and Protection) framework (Black Health
Equity Working Group, 2021). All these point to the need for more research with rather than on
Black communities in Canada.
Addressing the health disparities facing Black women in Canada is an urgent and essential
priority for population health in Canada. The United Nations’ Working Group of Experts on
People of African Descent report concluded that “Canada’s history of enslavement, racial
segregation and marginalization has had a deleterious impact on people of African descent,
which must be addressed in partnership with communities” (United Nations, 2017). In line with
this, our recommendations aim to enhance the health of Black people in Canada, and particularly
of Black women, by proposing the following targeted actions by the Government of Canada:
• Develop a national Black health strategy: Collaborate with Black communities to form
a comprehensive national Black health strategy for improving Black women’s health;
• Increase funding for research on Black women’s health in Canada through the
creation of a specific stream in the National Women's Health Research Initiative;
• Race-concordant care: Increase the representation of Black healthcare providers at all
levels (including leadership) to enhance race-concordant care and increase trust and
better outcomes within the Black community.
• Data collection: Invest in systems and strategies that support the collection of race- and
ethnicity-disaggregated data in the health and social sectors in partnership with
communities to better understand and address health disparities following the EGAP
framework;

Black healthcare providers at all levels (including leadership) to enhance race-concordant care and increase trust and better outcomes within the Black community. • Data collection: Invest in systems and strategies that support the collection of race- and ethnicity-disaggregated data in the health and social sectors in partnership with communities to better understand and address health disparities following the EGAP framework;

• Mandate research accountability: Require that health researchers, through the
Canadian Institutes for Health Research, include consideration for race and racism in
their grant proposals;
• Address intersectionality: Address the multifaceted aspects of Black women’s
experiences, including through education and legislative advocacy
These actions are crucial for improving the health outcomes of Black women. By addressing
systemic anti-Black racism, fostering collaboration with Black communities, increasing the
presence of Black professionals in healthcare leadership, and enhancing the economic status of
Black women, the Government of Canada can significantly improve the health of Black women
and, by extension, the overall health of women across Canada.

Brief to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Prepared by: Dr. Ryan Van Lieshout, MD, PhD, FRCPC ([CONTACT])
Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioural Neurosciences,
McMaster University
Hamilton, ON
The Perinatal Mental Health of Women, Pregnant Persons, Mothers and Birthing Parents
in Canada: Perinatal mental health problems affect up to 1 in 5 mothers and birthing parents,1
rates that increased to 1 in 3 during the COVID-19 pandemic.2 Every case of postpartum
depression (PPD) alone is associated with costs of up to $125,000 over the lifespan3 or $2.5B for
each single year of births in Canada. The offspring of mothers with PPD are up to five times
more likely to develop a clinically significant behavioural problem, and up to four times more
likely to develop depression in their lives.4,5 Even though effective treatments can help both
mothers and their children, as few as 1 in 10 pregnant and postpartum persons are able to access
evidence-based care in Canada.6
Barriers to Care: There are many barriers to the receipt of timely perinatal mental health care in
this country. One of the most significant is the current absence of structured and coordinated care
pathways7 that identify sufferers and match the right person to the right treatment at the right
time. Since most individuals with perinatal mental health problems will respond to
psychotherapy and/or medications, another significant challenge is the limited knowledge
possessed by front-line physicians about the relative safety of these medications during
pregnancy and lactation. Finally, the profound lack of access to evidence-based psychotherapies,
driven primarily by a lack of scalable interventions and a shortage of healthcare providers trained
to provide them, prevents us from meeting our goal of becoming the best country in the world to
raise a child.
Canadian Innovation: However, there are many reasons for hope. A group of Canadian
clinician-scientists are working with the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments to
prepare national practice guidelines for perinatal mental disorders which can be used to help
better inform frontline providers, and to guide the creation and application of Canadian-specific
care pathways. These structured care pathways – integrated systems that involve the detection of
mental health problems, direct patients to the right resources at the right time, and provide
treatment and follow-up,7 need to be tailored to the Canadian context and implemented.
Once these pathways are created, they will enable us to use evidence-based psychotherapies
developed and tested in Canada to optimize treatment. However, there exists a substantial
shortage of trained mental healthcare professionals required to deliver these interventions. To
address this, our group has developed and tested several effective scalable psychotherapeutic
interventions that can be delivered by public health nurses or even individuals who have
recovered from perinatal mental health problems (i.e., peers), and that can serve both as initial
and more intensive steps in care models. For example, our 1-day cognitive behavioural therapy
(CBT)-based workshop for postpartum depression can effectively treat up to 30 individuals at a

For example, our 1-day cognitive behavioural therapy
(CBT)-based workshop for postpartum depression can effectively treat up to 30 individuals at a

time and be delivered online or in-person by healthcare professionals or recovered peers.8-11 Our
9-week group CBT intervention has also proven effective,12-16 and its delivery has already been
successfully task shifted to recovered peers12,13 and public health nurses14-16 with limited to no
previous psychiatric training. We have already scaled these in Canada, Europe, and the US.
Effects of Treatment on Parents and Families: We know that when mothers get these
treatments, they not only help them, but their offspring as well. Our group has also shown that
treating mothers not only benefits them, but their entire family. Up to 70% of the costs associated
with perinatal mental disorders are due to their downstream effects on daughters and sons.3
Recent research by our group and others around the world has showed that treating those with
PPD leads to clinically meaningful improvements in mother-infant interactions, infant
neurodevelopment and emotion regulatory capacity, and even the mental health of older children
in the home.17-19 This is in keeping with research from around the world that suggests for every
dollar invested in early childhood interventions, society reaps a $7 return on investment.20
The Future of Perinatal Mental Health Care in Canada: Perinatal mental health problems in
Canada can be prevented detected and treated, and we already have the know-how to support
mothers and disrupt the intergenerational transmission of mental disorders in families. The
Federal Government can help by working together with experts to implement Canadian-specific
care pathways, scale the perinatal mental health workforce to meet current needs, and work
together with the provinces to implement these systems. Such developments will enable our
Canadian-made discoveries to improve the health and lives of all Canadians.
Recommendations: I humbly submit three recommendations that may be within the federal
mandate for health that could help to mitigate existing challenges to giving all individuals access
to appropriate, evidence-based perinatal mental health care when and where they need it:
1. Canadian-Specific Care Pathways: The tailoring and implementation of structured
models of care can help to determine human resource needs, guide care coordination, and
enable the delivery of effective, timely treatment for those with perinatal mental
disorders.
2. Training Frontline Providers: For these models of care to make the biggest impact,
family physicians, obstetricians, and midwives require training to optimize detection and
treatment.
3. Addressing the Psychotherapy Provider Shortage: While the training of frontline
providers can help to enhance detection and treatment with medications, for these models
of care to succeed, we need to increase the number of individuals who have the
knowledge and skills required to provide perinatal-specific psychotherapies. If we can
scale up the mental health workforce (by task shifting or sharing psychotherapy delivery
and/or training more providers) to provide psychotherapy and support coordination
within regions, we would have an effective system that could prevent the adverse effects
of mental health problems across two generations.

Victim-Centered Knowledge
The victim-centered relational knowledge shared is specific to the population of women who
as children and or as adults survived torture committed by non-State actors. Our Grassroots
Science began in 1993, in Nova Scotia. Laws, policies, and practices have nationally imposed
discriminatory silencing on women’s mental health and their ability to openly address the
impacts of non-State torture victimization in a manner that supports their human dignity, hope in
their healability, and in being healed.

Definition of Non-State Torture (NST)
It is torture committed by non-State actors in public or in private, in relationships,
perpetrated within families, in human trafficking, in prostitution, in pornographic exploitation,
by violent groups and gangs, dismissed as socio-cultural, traditional, or religious acts or norms,
and can be committed during migration, displacement, in humanitarian and civil unrest. It
involves intentional infliction of, for example, mental or physical severe pain and suffering with
electric shocking, water torture, forced drugging, group raping, beatings, whippings, cut, burnt,
impregnations and abortions.1

As a young woman in her late 20s, Sara was just beginning to try to heal. In the hospital for

A 2016 United Nations report, 3stated that when a specific group is statistically invisible,

Non-State Torture Victimization-Traumatization Informed Care
To heal, women who survived non-State torture victimizations generally need to integrate
their victimization memories. Our Model is Non-State Torture Victimization-Traumatization
Informed Care.5 It differs from “trauma informed” care which generally does not integrate
victimizations. There are three steps to our Model which:
1. NAMES the CARE as non-State torture victimization-traumatization informed.
2. NAMES HER VICTIMIZATION:
a. Tells her she suffered A CRIME, putting responsibility on the torturer-traffickers.
b. Can help eliminate Self-blaming, as women commonly thought the victimization
was their fault and they were to blame.
c. Her victimization needs to be listened to and processed if she decides to tell.
d. Integrating torture ordeals is a global standard in healing and promotes resilience.
3. NAMES HER CONSEQUENTIAL TRAUMATIZATION RESPONSES
a. Guiding question: How do we expect a woman or girl to act who survived a nonState torture perpetrating system?
b. Traumatization consequences need working through for healing.
c. We replace PTSD (disorder) by understanding her survival responses are normal
and call these PTSR (the “R” for responses) as women did not want to be labelled
as disordered.

exclusion, discrimination, and stigmatization experiences block their truth-telling. These cause
ongoing emotional pain, adding to the torture pain already suffered, and compounding the pain
re-experienced during the hard work of healing.

2024 Map of Breast Cancer Screening Age Guidelines Across Canada
Breast cancer screening is not equitable across Canada, with varying age guidelines and
referral policies (see Figure 1). In provinces where the screening age is high, women are not
able to access the same level of early-stage diagnosis compared to someone living in a
province with a lower screening age. Also, some provinces and territories allow a
mammogram request through self-referral but for those without a self-referral policy,
potentially coupled with a high screening age and no access to a primary care provider, this
presents a major disadvantage in access to health care.
In addition to this, sufficient resources will need to be provided to ensure that each province
and territory is equipped to support the increased volume of screening requests that will
occur due to the lower screening age including qualified personnel, adequate equipment
and technology, patient support services and infrastructure. There will need to be adequate

There will need to be adequate

support for provincial and territory health care systems as well, with a likely new influx of
breast cancer patients who will be diagnosed through the improved screening process. This
includes increased support for primary care providers who are the main contact for patients,
and overall oncology support - particularly in hospitals - such as timely access to
chemotherapy, radiation, ultrasound clinics, blood tests, mental health support programs,
and more. Improved screening is vital for improving the health of Canadians and these
changes will need to be properly supported to ensure effective access to care is maintained
and improved.
Importance of Breast Cancer Screening
Decreasing Risk
Early detection through regular screening mammograms can save lives, detecting breast
cancer before it has the chance to spread. When breast cancer is detected early and has not
spread, the 5-year relative survival rate is 99%.8 The later that a breast cancer diagnosis is
discovered and the ensuing care and treatment delayed, the lower the odds of survival.
Research at the Ontario Institute for Cancer Research showed that if you started screening
women annually at the age of 40 until age 74 then the reduction in breast cancer deaths
could be as much as 50%.9 Recall the statistics that there has not been an improvement in
breast cancer death rates over the past 20 years.
There are also populations who are more at risk for a breast cancer diagnosis at a younger
age, including Black and Hispanic women. Triple-negative breast cancer is one of the more
aggressive forms of breast cancer and Black and Hispanic women represent 10-20% of this
diagnosis.10 Women with dense breasts are also more at risk of delayed diagnosis as they
have a greater chance of initial diagnosis being missed due to the fibrous tissue in their
breasts,11 are generally younger and therefore not eligible where screening restrictions
begin at age 50 and if they lack access to MRI diagnostic imaging.

as it minimizes the risk of complex treatment and complications which also reduces the
burden on health care systems. This can result in a reduction in therapy intensity, both for

Submission to the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health
Reducing Stillbirths in Canada
Submitted by the Canadian Collaborative for Stillbirth Prevention (CC4SP)
For questions related to this brief, please contact [CONTACT]
The CC4SP is a collaborative of individuals and organizations working together to raise awareness of
stillbirth in Canada and urge the federal government to develop and implement a nati nal action plan to
reduce stillbirths in our country. At the CC4SP, we envision Canada as a nation where no parent must
endure the grief of a preventable stillbirth. To learn more, you may visit our website at www.cc4sp.ca

To learn more, you may visit our website at www.cc4sp.ca

Reducing Stillbirths in Canada
In 2018, the House of Commons Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social
Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities (HUMA) heard powerful witn ss
testimonies from parents who have been affected by pregnancy and infant loss on what the government
could do to support families after the loss of a child and ensure parents no longer suffer undue financial
or emotional hardships after such a loss1. Unfortunately, the committee report did not address what the
government could do to prevent some of those losses, namely stillbirths, from ever happening.
That same year, the Australian Senate established the Select Committee on Stillbirth Research and
Education to report on the future of stillbirth research and education in Australia. In it
committee concluded:
report, the
“Stillbirth is one of the most devastating and profound events that any parent is ever likely to
experience. It is 30 times more common than Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) but stillbirth
receives far less public or government attention than other infant and childhood deaths. Stillbirth
is a hidden tragedy. The culture of silence around stillbirth means that parents and families who
experience it are less likely to be prepared to deal with the personal, social and financial
consequences. This failure to regard stillbirth as a public health issue also has significant
consequences for the level of funding available for research and education, and for public
awareness of the social and economic costs to the community as a whole.”2
Stillbirth is a public health issue that is neglected, invisible and absent in current Canadian public
policies. Every year in Canada, more than 3,000 babies die in the womb at or after 20 weeks of
pregnancy3. Research presented to the Australian committee estimated that for each stillbirth, there are
another 99 births that narrowly avoided ending in death. In 2016, The Lancet journal published its series
on ending preventable stillbirths, issuing a call to action for high-income countries as evidence shows
that their stillbirth rate can be reduced further4. For example, the Netherlands has reduced its late
stillbirth rate (stillbirths at or after 28 weeks of pregnancy) by an average of 6.8% a year between 2000
and 2015, while Canada averaged at 0.8%5. In fact, Canada’s late stillbirth rate has not significantly
improved in more than 25 years.

We, at the Canadian Collaborative for Stillbirth Prevention (CC4SP), are asking the federal government
to take action to reduce stillbirths in our country by 30% by 2030 by following the lead of countries such
as the UK and Australia. Both countries have taken action by implementing national action plans in order
to reduce and prevent stillbirths. For example, the UK’s first action plan, Saving Babies’ Lives Care
Bundle, contributed to a 20% decrease of stillbirths in those maternity units where it was deployed
between 2015 and 20196. Its success prompted the government to implement versions 2 and 3 of the
plan with the ambitious aim to reduce stillbirths by 50% by 20257. As for Australia, it published its first
National Stillbirth Action and Implementation Plan in 2020, aiming to reduce late stillbirths by 20% or
more by 20258.
Both action plans revolve around implementation of care and education “bundles,” (i. . practical
information that encourages parents and health-care professionals to discuss the risks of stillbirth and
how antenatal care can be individualized to reduce those risks). For example, Australia’s Safer Baby
Bundle, which was developed by the Stillbirth Centre of Research Excellence, and based on the UK’s
Saving Babies’ Lives Bundle, includes:
•
supporting pregnant patients to stop smoking;
•
regular monitoring for signs that the fetus is not growing as expected, which is known as fetal
growth restriction;
•
explaining the importance of acting quickly if fetal movement changes or decreases;
•
advising pregnant patients to go to sleep on their side after 28 weeks;
•
and encouraging patients to talk to their doctors about when to deliver because in some cases
that may be before their due date.9
In meetings with the CC4SP, Australian officials have already offered to share materials and collaborate
with Canadian government officials in the development of our own action plan. In fact, a Canadian
action plan could easily be adapted from the Australian action plan and its 5 key action areas:
1. Ensuring high-quality stillbirth prevention and care
Under this key area, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) would develop national
guidelines and best practices in stillbirth prevention that could be easily included in a revised

adapted version of the Australian Safer Baby Bundle. The September 2023 clinical guideline of
the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) on Antenatal Fetal Health
Surveillance is a significant step forward in that regards as it now states that all pregnant
individuals should regularly monitor their baby’s movements in the third trimester regardless of
the method used, whereas previous guidelines restricted fetal movement monitoring to
pregnancies at risk of complications.10
Culturally and linguistically appropriate models for stillbirth prevention and care would be
developed for high-risk groups such as First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, rural and
remote communities, immigrants and refugees and Black individuals.
2. Raising awareness and strengthening education
Unfortunately, many people are unaware that stillbirths still occur in Canada each year. PHAC
needs to promote community awareness and understanding of stillbirths, ensuring consistent
messaging to encourage conversations about stillbirth and educating parents and the public
about the risks. That is why the petition e-2467 presented to the House of Commons in February
2021 called for a national awareness campaign to inform pregnant individuals of the risk of
stillbirth and the importance of fetal movements during the third trimester11.
A stillbirth education program for health care professionals is a critical component of the
implementation plan for a bundle of care. Canada could start by adapting the stillbirth e-
learning modules developed by the Stillbirth Centre of Research Excellence. Health care
professional education needs to include information on culturally safe care consistent with
national guidelines.
3. Improving holistic bereavement care and community support following a stillbirth
Witnesses told the HUMA committee studying how to support families after the loss of a child,
that:
“It is crucial that there is a system that reaches out quickly to bereaved families. While
some communities have strong peer support available, many do not. The coverage
across Canada is not equal. [Witnesses] felt that the government needed to do more to
ensure these networks were both supported and complemented by professionals. In
addition, witnesses underscored that services and support networks need to be
10 SOGC (2023). Guideline No. 441: Antenatal Fetal Health Surveillance. Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology of
Canada; 45(9):665-667. https://www.jogc.com/article/S1701-2163(23)00394-8/abstract
11 https://www.ourcommons.ca/petitions/en/Petition/Details?Petition=e-2467

Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology of
Canada; 45(9):665-667. https://www.jogc.com/article/S1701-2163(23)00394-8/abstract
11 https://www.ourcommons.ca/petitions/en/Petition/Details?Petition=e-2467

accessible. Accessibility in this context requires systematic outreach and follow-up to
bereaved parents and families.”12
PHAC would develop national guidelines for bereavement care and best practices for care
during subsequent pregnancies. The federal government could also provide stable funding for
organizations providing bereavement support to families across Canada.
4. Improving stillbirth reporting and data collection
High-quality perinatal mortality audits combined with initiatives to improve medical practice
have been found to reduce stillbirths and neonatal deaths. Poor-quality data for stillbirths,
however, remains a major problem across all high-income countries, including Canada13. For
example, while summary statistics are published by Statistics Canada annually, more in-depth
analyses, such as the cause of fetal death, are conducted by PHAC through the Canadian
Perinatal Surveillance System. But these statistics exclude data from Quebec since the province
does not contribute to the Canadian Institute for Health Information’s Discharge Abstract
Database.
Implementation of national review programs for perinatal mortality using rapid reporting
systems is increasing in countries such as New Zealand, England, Ireland, and Scotland. In
Canada, national audit tools would support high-quality investigation and classification of all
perinatal deaths in a timely way to enable local, jurisdictional, and national reporting. Secondary
goals include supporting clinician education and informing future research.
5. Prioritizing stillbirth research
Women’s health remains under-researched and underfunded. Much is still unknown about
stillbirth and conflicting messages continue to be perpetuated by those whom parents should be
able to trust the most – their own healthcare provider. It is clear that the Government of Canada
must invest in research to develop safer stillbirth prevention protocols and to ensure that
providers understand the best clinical practices for stillbirth prevention and bereavement care.
In Australia, a government-funded collaborative research group called the Stillbirth Centre for
Research Excellence is raising the standard of perinatal care around the world. Through its
research, it is uncovering new knowledge on stillbirth. The Centre also advises care providers on
how to translate these research findings into practice. In the U.K, Tommy’s has provided this
leadership. Canada has yet to establish an organizational leader in stillbirth research.
It is crucial that Canada embraces responsible innovation as a means of facilitating a greater
understanding of individual healthcare needs and encouraging patient participation. Digital
12 HUMA Committee (2019). Pages 36-37.
13 Flenady, Vicki and al. (2016). Page 692 (Key Messages).

Page 692 (Key Messages).

health tools can help parents to recognize fetal movement patterns, identify changes that could
indicate fetal distress, and make more informed health decisions. This data, and how it relates
to maternal health experiences and outcomes, would provide critical insight for researchers and
care providers.
Canada must act now to protect families. Each week, at least 59 stillbirths occur in Canada. With simple
and easily implemented actions, the Government of Canada could reduce stillbirths by 30%, thereby
saving 1,000 babies per year. That’s a thousand families who will not suffer through the devastating
loss of their child. Reducing stillbirths also protects mothers by reducing maternal morbidity. Indeed,
women who have stillbirths are at substantially higher risk for severe maternal morbidity (such as major
organ dysfunction or failure and hysterectomy) than those who have live birth, regardless of the cause
of stillbirth.14
Therefore, we submit the following recommendations to the Standing Committee on Health:
1. That the Government of Canada, through PHAC, develop a national action plan to reduce
stillbirths by 30% by 2030, which would include the 5 action areas of the Australian action plan.
2. That the Government of Canada, through PHAC, put in place a national awareness campaign to
inform pregnant individuals of the risks of stillbirth and how to reduce those risks.

BACKGROUND
In its report Alcool au féminin (Alcohol use among women), ASPQ presented a picture of alcohol use among
women in Quebec, based on scientific literature, information obtained from organizations and the public,
surveys, and an analysis of the alcohol industry’s marketing strategies. This brief summarizes the report’s
main findings and recommendations to encourage initiatives to reduce alcohol’s impact on women’s health.
MAIN FINDINGS
Alcohol use among women has changed over the past few years. In 2020-2021, 79% of women in Quebec
aged 15 and over drank alcohol at least once in the previous year, compared to 84% of men [1]. In 2019, this
percentage was lower in the rest of Canada, with corresponding rates of 75% for women and 78% for men [2].
Even though women drink less than the average for alcohol consumption, women accounted for the sharpest
increase in heavy drinking,1 with corresponding rates rising from 10% to 21% in Quebec between 2000 and
2021 [1] and estimated at 15% in 2018 in the rest of Canada [3].
However, based on consumption of an equal amount of alcohol, women’s health may be more vulnerable to
the effects and impacts of alcohol use [4]. Women who drink alcohol are exposed to greater risks to their
physical health, such as breast cancer and liver disease [4]. Few women seem to be aware of the levels of risk
involved, and this underscores the urgent need for education and awareness-raising campaigns. Women’s
mental and psychological health plays a crucial role in their relationship with alcohol, since more women are
diagnosed with an anxiety or depressive disorder [5].
How and where alcohol is used presents major challenges because 8 out of 10 women claim that they do not
feel safe at bars in Quebec [6]. As a result, some women drink much faster because they are afraid that a drug
could be slipped into their glass [7].
Women who drink are judged more as there are different social expectations for women. Mothers, pregnant
women, and women with an alcohol use disorder are particularly affected by the stigma associated with
drinking, and 7 out of 10 people believe that women are judged more harshly than men if they get drunk [7].
This stigma may result in greater risk of harm and interfere with access to services.
Alcohol marketing also contributes to influencing gender roles [8], and specifically targets women with
promotional offers, feminized products and the use of sexist language. This raises ethical concerns, in light of
alcohol’s harmful effects on women.
1 Surveys currently define heavy drinking as having consumed four or more drinks per occasion at least once a
month in the past year.

RECOMMENDATIONS FROM THE REPORT
Strengthen measures to prevent and raise awareness about alcohol use
The findings in the report stress the importance of destigmatizing alcohol use among women in order to
improve women’s health. Initiatives to strengthen such measures must reflect the diversity of women in terms
of age, social background and life circumstances.
– Launch an awareness-raising campaign about alcohol-related risks for women: Increase access
to information on risks, including information on mental and physical health, in order to facilitate
informed decision-making.
– Launch a campaign aimed at destigmatizing alcohol use among women, such as by addressing
the influence of targeted marketing, social inequalities in health and gender-based differential
treatment.
– Raise awareness about the portrayal of women who drink in popular culture: sharing experiences and
representing a diverse range of lived experiences will serve to counter alcohol-related gender
stereotypes.
ASPQ recognizes the value of a hybrid approach that not only highlights gender-based social inequalities
in health, but also adopts universal prevention principles.
Improve women’s safety at locations where alcohol is served
Until community measures are strengthened, women can take steps to reduce risks to their personal safety.
– Encourage establishments to adopt practices that improve women’s safety: training staff at places
where alcohol is served (e.g., restaurants, bars, clubs, organized events) can improve women’s
safety. The design of the premises (e.g., lighting in key spaces, surveillance cameras) helps create
safer environments. These establishments could facilitate access to safe transportation services.
– Review the role of the Régie des alcools, des courses et des jeux (RACJ): The RACJ could require
ongoing training and safety measures that focus on women at places where alcohol is served.
Tailor addiction and prevention services and resources to women
A gender-sensitive approach to treatment and rehabilitation gives due consideration to the importance of family
relationships, the prevalence and history of trauma and violence, common patterns of co-occurring disorders
and specific recognition of caregiving responsibilities [9–11].
– Support development of dedicated resources for women facing challenges related to alcohol use
in order to address their needs more effectively.
– Strengthen intersectoral partnerships: Strengthen collaborations involving organizations along the
addiction continuum and the health and social services networks, in order to improve continuity
of services.
Improve accessibility to addiction and prevention services and resources
Community resources should be adapted to community needs and based on local realities. The visibility and
awareness of these community resources are essential to guaranteeing improved accessibility.

The visibility and
awareness of these community resources are essential to guaranteeing improved accessibility.

– Ensure the visibility of available resources in order to increase awareness of their existence and
enable women to better navigate services based on their needs.
– Increase funding for addiction organizations to improve accessibility for women, including those
outside the public system.
Involve women in services for women and encourage empowerment
The report’s findings stress the need to involve stakeholders in developing addiction services. This will help
create useful and appropriate addiction services and resources.
– Promote mechanisms that facilitate the active participation of women, such as by implementing
formal and inclusive mechanisms that encourage women to actively participate in developing
prevention, harm reduction and treatment resources.
– Support women’s empowerment in terms of their ability to make informed choices: Strengthen the
agency and critical mindset of women vis-à-vis alcohol use and encourage self-determination in terms
of managing this psychoactive substance.
Review alcohol marketing rules
Evidence shows that alcohol advertising has an impact on drinking habits [13]. ASPQ supports banning
marketing that encourages consumption of psychoactive substances, including alcohol. However, if permitted
in Quebec, ASPQ proposes the following recommendations in order to reduce health-related impacts and
encourage more equitable and responsible advertising practices.
– Limit strategies that encourage alcohol use among groups that experience more alcohol-related
harms, including women (e.g., targeted promotions, free distribution, regulating sponsorships,
advertising restrictions).
– Conduct a review of the Regulation respecting promotion, advertising and educational programs
relating to alcoholic beverages: The rules for alcohol marketing should cover health-related matters,
as is the case for other legal psychoactive substances, such as cannabis and tobacco.
– Ban sexist alcohol commercials in Quebec: the use of sexist language reinforces gender
inequalities (e.g., sexualization of women or gender stereotypes).
Continue gender-based research and development efforts concerning alcohol
In order to ensure that intervention strategies are effective, it is important to understand the role that alcohol
plays in women’s lives, as well as the individual, sociocultural and political factors involved.
– Conduct longitudinal studies concerning alcohol use among women to track changes in social
contexts and habits associated with alcohol use over time, by offering an in-depth perspective of
related trends.
– Include gender-based analyses (GBA+) when implementing alcohol-related initiatives: Incorporating
intersectional issues, such as sex and gender, facilitates the ability to accurately analyze healthrelated social inequalities when implementing projects, programs and policies.

CCS believes transitioning to primary HPV testing, with the option to self-collect, as the
primary method of cervical cancer screening will increase screening uptake and improve the
process and accuracy of screening results among people in Canada and reduce the burden
of cervical cancer on our population in the long term. As provinces and territories prepare
for this change, the swabs used for HPV tests have an indication that they must be done by
a healthcare provider. Health Canada has an opportunity to update this indication, validate
for laboratories what is needed for self-sampling or self-collection, and remove this barrier
in providing at-home tests. CCS calls upon Health Canada to make this update promptly.
Improve HPV vaccination rates
About 75% of sexually active people contract an HPV infection at least once in their
lifetime.8 Usually, HPV infections will clear on their own; though sometimes the infection
persists. A high-risk HPV infection can lead to changes in the cells of the cervix, which can
develop into cervical cancer if they are not found early. Getting vaccinated against HPV is
the best way to eliminate the risk of HPV infection, as well as reduce the likelihood of
several cancers. CCS recommends children and adults between the ages of 9 and 45 are
vaccinated against HPV to help reduce the risk of HPV-related cancers. As well, we believe
HPV vaccines should be used alongside, and not instead of, cervical cancer screening for
people with a cervix, to maximize protection. The federal government should:
Provide the support needed to achieve the National Immunization Strategy goal of
90% full vaccination coverage among those 17 years of age by the year 2025.
Provide provincial and territorial governments support for HPV immunization catchup programs to help provide vaccines to eligible people who experienced because of
COVID-19.
Alcohol policy
Alcohol is the most commonly used psychoactive substance in Canada and is linked to over
3,300 cancer cases in Canada each year.9 Drinking any type or amount of alcohol increases
the risk of developing at least 9 different types of cancer amounts — including breast,
colorectal, esophageal, laryngeal, liver, mouth, pharyngeal, stomach and pancreatic cancers.
Despite this, over 40% of people in Canada are not aware that alcohol consumption
increases cancer risk.10

reduce its consumption.12 Alcohol labelling, along with continued education, will ensure
more people in Canada can make informed decisions for their health.
CCS calls on the federal government to develop and implement effective, equitable and
culturally appropriate policies and initiatives to reduce women’s risk of developing alcoholrelated cancers. CCS recommends:
Implementing mandatory labels, including health and safety messaging, on all
alcoholic products sold in Canada;
Increasing clear, consistent and comprehensive health messaging about the risk of
cancer related to alcohol consumption through multiple channels;
Placing restrictions on alcohol sponsorships targeting youth and young adults;
Replacing the GST on alcoholic beverages with an increase in excise tax rates
calculated per litre of ethanol, with equivalent rates across different beverage
classes, and continue to index this tax annually to the cost of living;
Implementing a federal tax and minimum price per standard drink at all outlets
where alcohol is sold;
Requiring alcohol companies to report information about the products sold, sales
volumes and marketing activities and expenditures to the federal government.
Breast cancer screening
In Canada, an estimated 1 in 8 women is expected to be diagnosed with cancer during their
lifetime. Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death for people in Canada aged
30 to 49.13
Before the pandemic in Canada, breast cancer screening programs were not meeting the
national goal for participation rate of 70%. Data from the United States has shown that
while breast cancer incidence peaks for white women after the age of 50, it peaks before
the age of 50 for Black, Asian and Hispanic women.14 Current clinical practice guidelines
initiating breast cancer screening at age 50 may result in missed opportunities for early
detection among women in these communities. Timely access to breast cancer screening is
critical to find breast cancer early when treatment is more likely to be successful.
CCS supports expanding access to breast cancer screening for women aged 40-49 at
average risk of developing breast cancer. Further, according to a CCS-funded Leger survey
in October 2023, most people in Canada (87%) support expanding access to breast cancer
screening to include women ages 40-49. CCS recommends to:
Continue to invest in research to improve access to, and follow-up after, breast
screening;

as outlined in the pan-Canadian cancer data strategy15 (including race-based data)
and align it with the work underway on the pan-Canadian Health Data Charter.16
Tobacco control policy
Among women in Canada, tobacco use is the leading modifiable risk factor for cancer cases
and deaths. Tobacco use is also the leading preventable cause of disease and death overall
among women. Total direct healthcare costs in Canada attributable to smoking are $5.4
billion per year.17
Smoking increases the risk for not only lung cancer, but also at least 15 other types of
cancer including colorectal, cervical, ovarian, oral, stomach, bladder and pancreatic.
Smoking increases the likelihood that women who have breast cancer will die as a result. 18
While progress has been made at reducing smoking prevalence, an enormous amount of
work remains to achieve the target of under 5% tobacco use by 2035. There are still 1.6
million women and girls in Canada who smoke, representing 10% of the population aged
12+,19 and even more including other tobacco products.
Youth vaping has increased considerably. Among girls in grades 10-12 in Canada, vaping in
the 2021-22 school year was 26%, up from 7% in the 2014-15.20
A comprehensive strategy of taxation/legislation/enhanced programming is needed to
reduce tobacco use among women and girls, and to reduce youth vaping. CCS recommends
that, federally:
Tobacco taxes be increased by $6.00 per carton,
Bill C-59 measures for a cost recovery fee be adopted, and subsequent regulations
recover the cost of all initiatives in Canada’s Tobacco Strategy from the tobacco and
vaping product industries;
Tobacco legislation be strengthened by banning all remaining tobacco promotion;
banning flavours in all tobacco products; adopting measures for both tobacco and ecigarettes including increasing minimum age from 18 to 21 and banning Internet
sales;
Measures be adopted to reduce youth vaping, including banning flavours (except
tobacco flavour) in e-cigarettes;
Cessation, mass communication, youth prevention and other programs be enhanced;
Nicotine pouches be sold on a prescription-only basis, or that their sale be
temporarily suspended until a necessary federal/provincial/territorial regulatory
framework is in place.

Supports for caregivers
Caregivers provide vital support to people with serious conditions including cancer. They
provide unpaid practical, physical and emotional support to loved ones. It is anticipated 1 in
2 people in Canada will be a caregiver at some point in their lifetime.21 In 2018, women
accounted for 54% of all caregivers, however 64% of those provided 20 hours or more of
care per week.22
Caregivers provide 5.7 billion hours each year providing care.23 Estimates suggest more
than 25% of caregivers in Canada make employment adjustments including quitting their
job, retiring early and changing work roles and schedules to accommodate caregiving.
Additionally, employed caregivers typically have higher stress levels and poorer physical
health compared to the general population which is associated with higher rates of
depression, anger, distress, fatigue and anxiety. Lost economic productivity due to care
responsibilities is estimated to cost us $1.3 billion annually.24
The Government of Canada has made an effort to recognize the tremendous role that
caregivers play in day-to-day. The Canada Caregiver Credit was introduced as a nonrefundable tax credit in 2017 to provide financial relief to caregivers who support a lowincome spouse or common-law partner or low-income dependent with a physical or mental
impairment. About 70% of caregivers reported they had received social or financial support
for their caregiving activities, but less than 8% indicated they had received a federal tax
credit, and 68% of caregivers with unmet caregiving needs indicated they still lacked
financial support.25 According to Statistics Canada, while families and couples in lowerincome deciles were more likely to claim the Canada Caregiver Credit, the uptake of this
credit amongst families and couples in the lowest-income decile is lower because it is a nonrefundable tax credit, so families and couples have little incentive to claim this credit since
they have no or little income tax to pay.26
CCS calls on the federal government to improve supports for current and future caregivers
by:
Implementing or enhancing accessible, refundable federal tax credits for caregivers
to help compensate expenses incurred to purchase services, equipment and supplies
that assist their loved ones to live independently at home;
Improving flexibility criteria for the existing EI caregiver benefits by allowing
caregivers to receive benefits for partial weeks;
Allowing caregivers to continue receiving the compassionate care benefit for the
entire 2-week bereavement period following the death of their loved one;
Developing national standards that both governments and employers can use to
measure and evaluate the overall success of programs, services and supports to
meet the needs of working caregivers;
Improving national research on caregiving and systematic, standardized data
collection by developing data systems.

House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Study on Women’s Health

Breast cancer screening guideline and screening concepts from the
Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care

Submitted February 14, 2024, by:
Dr. Guylène Thériault, Co- Chair, MD, CCFP
Dr. Ahmed Abou-Setta, Co- Chair, MD, PhD
Dr. Scott Klarenbach, Vice-Chair, MD, MSc, FRCPC

Introduction
In 2024, the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care (Task Force) will release
recommendations on screening for breast cancer to update our 2018 guideline (1). This is a
priority for the Task Force and is important to Canadians, primary care providers, and other
stakeholders. Since last summer, the Task Force has been working to provide updated
recommendations based on a detailed, comprehensive review of available evidence using
international best practices.

This submission aims to provide information on the guideline update and general screening
concepts.

org: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
text:
This submission aims to provide information on the guideline update and general screening
concepts.

This guideline update is for women* at average and moderately above average risk of breast
cancer and not for those with genetic risks or signs and symptoms of breast cancer (e.g. breast
lump) (3).
• To include the best available, current evidence, we have expanded our review to include
different types of studies (randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and are
conducting modelling). Research plans are publicly available (3).
• Given the volume and complexity of the workload, the evidence review and modeling
teams have requested more time to complete their tasks (1). We are also working with
the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) and Statistics Canada to identify data on
breast cancer by ethnicity.
What are the current (2018) Task Force recommendations on breast cancer screening?
•
The evidence showed a close balance between potential benefits and harms. Evidence
also demonstrated that when informed of benefits and harms, some or many women
would choose not to be screened, indicating variable patient preferences (5). The 2018
guideline recommended that patients and clinicians openly discuss the benefits and
harms so that patients can decide based on their preferences and values (5); also known
as shared decision-making (6).
• For women ages 40 to 49, the guideline recommended against routine screening. If a
woman was interested in getting screened (5), it recommended shared decision-making.
It was confirmed that if someone chooses to be screened, they should have access to
mammography (7).
• For women ages 50 to 74, the guideline recommended screening every 2–3 years and
shared decision-making about whether screening aligns with their preferences and
values (5,7).
External input
• The Task Force invited over 120 individuals from 87 organizations and 22 individual
experts to provide critical input on key documents (research plan, systematic review,
draft guideline) for the breast cancer screening guideline.
o 24 reviewers from 17 organizations, and 2 individuals gave input on the research
plan; responses to all comments will be published.
• In August 2023, the Task Force hosted an online portal through which people provided
145 documents from 19 individuals and 9 organizations, that the Evidence Synthesis
teams reviewed for potential inclusion (8).
• Further, we will invite the public to provide feedback on the recommendations before
they are finalized.
When did the Task Force decide to update their breast cancer screening guideline?

org: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
text:
When did the Task Force decide to update their breast cancer screening guideline?

•
In February 2023, the Task Force voted unanimously to update the guideline as it had
been several years since the 2018 publication. This was expedited following publication
of the United States Preventive Services Task Force draft recommendations in May
2023.
Screening concepts
What is screening?
•
Screening invites otherwise healthy and asymptomatic persons to undergo testing. This
is very different from individuals with signs, symptoms, or concerns presenting to their
health care provider. Because of this, there must be clear evidence of benefit, and that
the benefit outweighs the harms.
•
All screening tests have harms, which range from minor (discomfort of blood test) to
serious (diagnosing and treating a cancer that would have never become symptomatic).
Screening tests vs. diagnostic tests
• Screening tests are used to find early disease, before any signs or symptoms are
present. Screening that works can detect disease early, when it may be more treatable.
• Diagnostic tests are used when there are signs or symptoms, like a breast lump to
determine if disease (e.g., breast cancer) is present, or to confirm a positive screening
test.
Screening can identify an elevated risk (e.g., of a fragility fracture), a pre-disease (e.g.,
precancerous cervical lesions), or a disease itself (e.g., breast cancer). In this last example, the
goal of screening is to find disease early to prevent harm or death but there are other possible
outcomes.

Unfortunately, not all screening is beneficial. While the Task Force’s goal is to identify screening
and prevention practices that improve Canadians’ health, many practices do not lead to
benefits, and all screening has some harms. This is why it is critical to identify high quality
evidence on whether screening works. Inviting healthy people to undergo screening tests that
don’t improve health would not be responsible or ethical.

Example: Thyroid cancer screening
Routine screening for thyroid cancer is shown to find more cancers. However, evidence shows
that despite finding more cancer, it doesn’t benefit patients – there is no change in thyroid
cancer deaths (9). Subjecting otherwise healthy people to screening, with some requiring
biopsy or surgery, without improving health is not acceptable. Because of this, screening for
thyroid cancer is not practiced.

org: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
text:
Because of this, screening for
thyroid cancer is not practiced.

The Task Force’s guidelines are evidence-based. What does evidence-based medicine mean?
Evidence based medicine involves integrating clinical experience with the best available
evidence identified using systematic methods (10).

To determine what is the best available evidence for a clinical guideline, a formal and
transparent system for evaluating evidence should be used. The Task Force uses the Grading of
Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system, which is
internationally recognized, developed and constantly refined by experts in evidence-based
medicine, and used by guideline panels around the world (11).

Additional Information
Guideline Trustworthiness
Many organizations around the world produce clinical practice guidelines. It is important that
health care providers and patients choose trustworthy guidelines. Several groups have
evaluated the breast screening guideline (and other Task Force guidelines) using standard tools
and consistently rate them as among the highest quality in the world.
o American College of Physicians in 2019 (12)
o A group of researchers in 2022 (13)
o ECRI Guidelines Trust (14)

The ECRI Guidelines Trust, a global non-profit organization appraises all Task Force guidelines
on how they adhere to the National Academy of Medicine Standards for Trustworthy
Guidelines (14). This includes evaluating the guideline group’s expertise, rigour of evidence
review, foundation of the recommendations, independence/disclosure of funding, conflict of
interest policies, and external review processes.
o 2018 breast cancer guideline rated 58/60
o Across all guidelines (since 2017), average 59/60
o Last 4 guidelines since 2020 scored 60/60

org: Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care
text:
This includes evaluating the guideline group’s expertise, rigour of evidence
review, foundation of the recommendations, independence/disclosure of funding, conflict of
interest policies, and external review processes.
o 2018 breast cancer guideline rated 58/60
o Across all guidelines (since 2017), average 59/60
o Last 4 guidelines since 2020 scored 60/60

PHAC also evaluated the Task Force in 2022 and found that its methods were sound and
followed internationally recognized best practices (15). It made three recommendations to
improve guideline creation:
1. Explore ways to improve timeliness of guideline development;
2. Explore potential changes to address funding issues and adapt the funding model;
3. Clarify PHAC's role versus that of the ERSCs with respect to scoping and conducting
systematic reviews.
Conclusion
Evaluating evidence to develop clear, science-based recommendations for breast cancer
screening in Canada is important and complex. The Task Force is working hard to evaluate the
best available evidence to provide guidance for women and health care professionals who care
for them. We hope that the scientific community will continue to research the best screening
methods and treatments for breast and other cancers that affect women and Canadians.

*Cisgendered women, adults assigned female at birth, transgender men and nonbinary people

Impact of Menopause Symptoms

The impact of menopause symptoms when not adequately managed is staggering. In a survey
from the Menopause Foundation of Canada (MFC) in 2022 in Canada, one in two women felt
unprepared for menopause and 4 in 10 women felt alone during this 7me. 3 The effect of
symptoms on work productivity is being recognized worldwide, including in Canada, with a
reported $3.5 billion per year proposed loss to the economy from lost productivity, missed days
of work and lost income. 4 Up to 10% of women will quit their jobs because of severe symptoms
that impact their ability to function. With midlife women at the prime of their work life, these
numbers are very concerning. Furthermore, untreated moderate to severe vasomotor
symptoms has been linked to negative outcomes later in life including cardiovascular disease. 5

Inadequate Care for Menopause in Canada

With more than 10 million women in Canada currently at the age of perimenopause or post
menopause the 7me is now to ensure there is adequate support for midlife women.
Unfortunately, the level of menopause care available in Canada is inadequate and many women
are not ge^ng the help they need. 3 Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) is the most effective
therapy to manage bothersome menopause symptoms. Guidelines recommend that MHT is safe
to consider in women who are less than 60 years of age or less than 10 years since their last
menstrual period (and without contraindications). 6 However, the use of Health Canada
approved MHT products in Canada is very low, reported less than 10% of eligible women. 7
Imagine if 90% of hypertensive patients were not offered safe and accessible antihypertensives.
In a recent multinational survey of 8 countries, Canada had the lowest proportion of women
using MHT of all the countries in the study. 8

In a recent multinational survey of 8 countries, Canada had the lowest proportion of women
using MHT of all the countries in the study. 8

The reasons for inadequate menopause care are multifold. Unfortunately, there is still a stigma
towards menopause and ageing women. There is also fear with the use of MHT from both
women as well health care providers. This fear stems from the publicity surrounding the release
of the initial results of the Women’s Health Initiative study in 2002 showing an increased risk of
cardiovascular disease and breast cancer with estrogen and progestin. 9 More than 20 years
later, even with increasing evidence demonstrating the safety of MHT in the right population,
there has been lifle change in overall thinking.10 This bias has impacted access to menopause
care in Canada and around the world. The trivialization of symptoms for a condition that
primarily affects females may reflect gender discrimination in our healthcare system.

Issues with menopause care in Canada include:
Lack of access to menopause care: There are only a few specialized menopause clinics
across Canada. Many women do not have access to a family physician and those that do,
there is oFen inadequate 7me to address all the symptoms and concerns in a 10 - 15
minute appointment.

Inadequate knowledge and skills of health care providers (HCP) with menopause:
Primary care physicians and other HCP have lifle comfort and experience in dealing with
menopause this may stem from lack of education at the undergraduate and
postgraduate/residency level.

Primary care physicians and other HCP have lifle comfort and experience in dealing with

postgraduate/residency level.

Lack of understanding about menopause: Canadian women have expressed they felt
unprepared for menopause. There may not be an awareness on the changes with
menopause or how to access evidence-based resources. In addition, there may be
resistance from their HCP who may not be willing to start that conversation. In the
survey by MFC, only 4 out of 10 women sought medical advice and 72% of these women
did not find the advice helpful or somewhat helpful.3 In addition, misinformation and
disinformation on menopause is a major issue, women can become vulnerable to using
unregulated menopausal products.
Lack of funding for menopause care: Currently, there is inadequate renumeration for
health care providers. Menopause care takes 7me as multiple systems are affected.
Cardiovascular disease is the major killer of women aFer menopause. Many women
carry known genetic diseases for cancers that are not identified and could be possibly
treated. A menopausal comprehensive assessment would allow healthcare providers to
address symptomatology and risks that would improve mid-life women’s health and
quality of life. Another issue is the cost barriers to proven menopausal therapies which
highlights inequity in the system. Many provincial health plans do not provide coverage
for the individual therapies that women may need to successfully treat their symptoms.

We recommend the following:
1. Improve and coordinate education opportunities nationally for menopause and aging
in females at all levels including undergraduate, graduate, post-graduate and
continuing professional development for all health disciplines. This includes funding
for certified fellowship programs for all health disciplines.
2. Increase funding for research on hormones and aging in women.
3. Establish center of excellence for menopause care across Canada.

4. Promote public educaLon with trustworthy informaLon for women.
5. Promotion of a menopause health assessment to evaluate cardiovascular and genetic
risks as well as treat symptomatology of the menopause.
6. Establish a billing code for menopause care.
7. Encourage provinces to fund medications for menopause.

Canadian Menopause Society sincerely appreciates the opportunity to submit this brief and
recommendations to the HESA Committee. We are happy to elaborate on any of these
recommendations and collaborate on future initiatives to further women’s health.

Background
In Canada, it is estimated that more than 650,000 people have dementia. That number
is anticipated to grow to more than 1.7 million by 2025. These people live with
Alzheimer’s dementia, vascular dementia, young onset dementia, or one of over 50
different diseases or conditions that can cause dementia.
Alzheimer disease and dementia are women's issues
In high-income countries, for roughly every 1 male that is diagnosed with dementia, 2
females will be diagnosed. In 2020, an estimated 61.8% of persons living with dementia
in Canada were female. By 2050, our study projects that over 1 million women will be
living with dementia in Canada.
Women are also doubly affected, as they provide the majority of care to people living
with dementia in Canada. Statistics Canada found that in 2022, women who were
unpaid caregivers for care-dependent adults spent an average of 10 hours a week
providing care, compared with 6 hours for men.
Also, the nature of dementia requires, on average, more hours of caregiving: the
Canadian Institute for Health Information has found that “caregivers of seniors with
dementia provide an average of 26 hours of care each week. This is substantially higher
than the 17 hours provided by caregivers of those without dementia.”
By 2050, if current Canadian trends continue, women will provide more than
800,000,000 hours of caregiving for people with dementia every year.
Sex and gender differences in dementia
Both sex and gender can shape a person’s dementia experiences. There are sex and
gender differences in the number of people affected by dementia; in risk factors for
developing dementia; in how symptoms are expressed; and in care needs and
caregiving.
Here are some examples of how sex and gender can impact dementia experiences:
• Dementia in women tends to progress faster.
• Early symptoms can present differently in women and men – for instance, women
may present with more depression, and men with more apathy.
• Research subjects have typically been men, so it is unclear whether current
dementia treatments are as effective for women.

More facts and figures
Dementia is a term that describes a set of symptoms caused by what is most often a
progressive loss of brain function and structure over time.
Symptoms of dementia can include (but are not limited to) memory loss, language
difficulties, impaired judgment, changes in mood or behaviour, decreased ability to
perform daily activities, disorientation, and problems with abstract thinking. Some forms
of dementia can affect other areas of functioning, including vision and movement.
The Many Faces of Dementia in Canada – Landmark Study Report #2 has many
more data related to sex and gender differences in Chapter 4.
Visit alzheimer.ca/manyfaces to view the full report.
Following this cover letter, you will find:
(1) the Alzheimer Society of Canada’s recommendations from the report
addressing sex and gender in dementia, and
(2) an infographic that summarizes the key findings from the Landmark Study on
this topic.
Overall Recommendations
The National Dementia Strategy is in the final year of a 5-year funding commitment. We
are looking to the federal government to renew and increase its investments beyond
2024. Both Landmark reports have clear recommendations that can help the
government create an effective plan. By fully funding and implementing the strategy we
will be able to prepare for, mitigate and address the large, diverse wave of Canadians
with dementia that is coming in the next few decades.
Alzheimer Society of Canada can be a key solution provider because we are trusted by
Canadians and have the presence and infrastructure at the national, provincial and local
levels across Canada. We are positioned to increase our work to support the
populations most at risk and could both increase and accelerate our progress with more
funding.
Sincerely,

SOME KEY RECOMMENDATIONS AROUND SEX,
GENDER AND DEMENTIA
• Alzheimer Societies should continue to recognize that the experience of living with dementia
and caregiving may affect women, men and nonbinary people differently.
• Health care systems should expand dementia supports with sex and gender differences in mind.
• Federal governments should address structural inequities in policies and programs to better address sex
and gender differences in caregiving and in risk factors for dementia.
• Provincial and territorial governments should actively promote brain health with sex- and gender-specific
campaigns through their public health services.

and 2SLGBTQI+ individuals who live with dementia or support individuals living with dementia.
