Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Women’s Health Study
December 15, 2023
Submitted by:
Janet Ko, President and Co-Founder
The Menopause Foundation of Canada

Perimenopause is the time leading up to menopause and can last anywhere from six to eight years.
During perimenopause estrogen and progesterone levels fluctuate – sometimes dramatically – leading to
many symptoms that can have a negative impact on health and quality of life. Most women are in
perimenopause between the ages of 40 and 50.
Women are postmenopausal for the rest of their lives. Women experience symptoms for years,
sometimes decades, and yet, they are not supported by the health system, their employers, or society as
a whole.
Menopause: a women’s health issue
There are over 30 symptoms associated with perimenopause and menopause, including but not limited
to lack of energy, depression, flushing and night sweats, muscle and joint ache, insomnia, bladder control
issues, heart palpitations and headaches. There are too many to be included in a brief. Canadian women
typically have a low awareness of the symptoms associated with menopause/perimenopauseiv. Every day
millions of women in Canada are suffering through menopause without understanding what is
happening to their bodies and where to turn for help.
Beyond the symptoms, once a woman has reached menopause she is at greater risk for osteoporosis,
heart disease and genitourinary issues. Leading up to and throughout this period, it is essential that
middle-aged women have access to primary care providers who can support them in understanding and
managing their health risks. These are some of the ways in which women’s health is impacted post
menopause, primarily due to the lack of estrogen. Women have estrogen receptors throughout their
bodies.
•
Osteoporosis - Women begin losing bone density at an annual rate of two percent beginning one
to three years before menopause and lasting five to 10 years in post-menopause. This results in
an average loss of bone mass density of 10% in the spine and hip.
•
Heart Health - After menopause, a woman’s risk of heart disease increases steadily due to a lack
of estrogen. 1 in 3 women will develop heart disease.
●
Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause - The genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)
affects up to 80% of menopausal women and is caused by low estrogen levels in the tissues of
the urinary tract and the female genital tract. Symptoms include vaginal dryness, painful sex,
burning, urinary tract infections and general irritation of the genital area. In contrast to hot
flashes and night sweats that usually improve over time, GSM generally gets worse without
effective therapy.

In contrast to hot
flashes and night sweats that usually improve over time, GSM generally gets worse without
effective therapy.

Menopause care begins with information. Incorporating menopause into women's health strategies is
essential. This inclusion ensures that women have access to evidence-based health information as they
age. It helps them better understand the changes occurring in their bodies and empowers them to
choose the most suitable options to support their health outcomes. Four in 10 women surveyed have
sought medical advice, but 72% find it to be not helpful or only somewhat helpfulv.

Treatments do exist to support women with their troubling symptoms. However, women are struggling
to access treatment, and are not being provided evidence-informed information about their treatments
and options. The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada and the North American
Menopause Society recommend menopausal hormone therapy as the first-line treatment for vasomotor
symptoms for both menopausal and perimenopausal patientsvi .

To achieve optimal health for women we need to change the conversation on ageing which means we
need to break the silence and stigma of menopause.

To achieve optimal health for women we need to change the conversation on ageing which means we
need to break the silence and stigma of menopause.

In collaboration with Christi Belcourt, artist and Tanya Kappo, lawyer, hosts of “Notokwew Ponkiyokewin
- Indigenous Centred Menopause”, we are submitting their indigenous experience.
“The Indigenous experience of the transition into menopause and menopause is multilayered and where access to care and supports might already be considered wanting for
the general population on this subject, Indigenous people face even more challenges to
access care and support. The historic and ongoing impacts of colonization in Canada have
much to do with this as within our communities we faced major disruptions to the
transference of traditional knowledges around menopause and traditional Indigenous
healthcare methods due to the forced assimilationist policies, violence and genocide
perpetrated by Canada on Indigenous community systems of governance, language,
midwifery, traditional medicines, outlawing of ceremonies, and attempts to destroy
matriarchal leadership through imposed patriarchy. Further we know that there is little
to no research that has been done specifically on Indigenous experiences with
menopause. Through our own personal experiences, we are seeing unique challenges
that Indigenous people face when going through this stage in their lives. What figures
prominently is the lack of medical support for the physical challenges; the lack of
psychological support for the emotional challenges; and the lack of mental health
support for the challenges to our ongoing well-being. Having to navigate a health system
that is plagued by systemic racism compounds and prevents access to health care for
Indigenous people over and above what would be considered challenges for the general
population in support for menopause. The transition to menopause and menopause is
one of the important stages of life for Indigenous people that has significant spiritual
meaning and impacts. It’s been painful to realize that much of this has been taken from
us or lost because of colonization. This, coupled with the challenges to accessing health
care and support have mobilized us to start important conversations about the
menopause transition and our own ways to restore the knowledges around this stage of
life that empowers people in our communities.”
Christi and Tanya
Menopause: a workplace and economy issue
A recent report released by the Menopause Foundation of Canada entitled Menopause and Work in
Canada confirms that women over the age of 40 make up one quarter of our labour force and are a key
driver of Canada’s economy. The fastest growing segment of working women in Canada are those aged
45 to 55 – the time when most women reach menopause. The country could experience a 27% growth in
the number of working women 45-55 by 2040vii.

The country could experience a 27% growth in
the number of working women 45-55 by 2040vii.

Women are the backbone of critical sectors, providing much needed wisdom, experience and a deep
level of competence. They are mentors to younger employees and important leaders in their
organizations. Women continue to make up the bulk of historically female-dominated sectors, such as
health care/social assistance (81%) and education (69%). They are well-represented in areas like
government services (65%), business (64%), and finance (50%); other sectors increasingly rely on women
too, including agriculture (30%), construction (29%), manufacturing (29%) and mining (19%)viii.
The federal government is the largest single employer in Canada. It prides itself in achieving nearly
gender parity in the upper echelons. Out of the over 300,000 active civil servants, 55 percent are
women, and the average age of employees is 44 years. Of the executives, the average age is 50 years
old, with 49 percent of these leadership roles in the hands held of womenix. There’s an interesting
disparity. While the country is doing better at male-female equity, Canada’s response to a major
influence in the lives of these women is severely lacking.

Women in the prime of their career – in private and public sectors – are reducing their hours or not
taking a promotion because they could not access appropriate care and treatment for their menopause
symptoms and health outcomes. 10% of women will stop workingx. This comes at a significant cost, not
only to the Canadian economy but to the social fabric of our country.

This comes at a significant cost, not
only to the Canadian economy but to the social fabric of our country.

Unmanaged symptoms of menopause cost the economy an astounding $3.5 billion every year. An
estimated $237m in lost productivity and 540,000 lost days of work attributed to symptom management
of menopause. At the height of their earning potential, women are opting to reduce their hours and/or
pay or are leaving the workforce altogether, resulting in a $3.3B in loss incomexi.
There is a powerful opportunity for employers in Canada to unleash the full potential of this sizeable
workforce demographic with better supports.
Addressing menopause: crucial steps ahead
There is a great deal that can be done to improve the health and well-being of women as they live
through menopause. Women do not want to be sidelined at a time when they have so much to
contribute.
Recommendation 1: Increase menopause health education opportunities for healthcare providers and
professionals.
Recommendation 2: The women’s health strategy must provide specific attention to mature women’s
health and well-being as they journey to and through menopause.
Recommendation 3: Create menopause-inclusive workplaces, starting with the civil service of Canada.
Recommendation 4: Dedicate and increase research amounts to be granted specifically for women’s
health, including in menopause.
Recommendation 5: Stabilize and build resiliency in Canada’s menopause hormone therapy supply.

Conclusion
The menopause knowledge gap is real. It contributes to millions of women needlessly suffering through
symptoms that have negative impacts on their health, their quality of life and their contribution to the
Canadian economy. With a strong national voice, we can support all women in this stage of their lives. By
closing this knowledge gap, by opening the doors to more menopause care services and promoting
menopause-inclusive workplaces, we can empower women to continue being leaders in their
community and in their place of work. Our recommendations aim to pave the way to a healthier, more
equitable future for women during and after menopause. Together, we can break the silence and stigma
surrounding menopause, and ensure this wide-sweeping demographic receives the support and care it
deserves.

text:
Submission to the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health
The Urgent Need for Universal Coverage of
Prescription Contraception
Submitted by the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
Please address any correspondence related to this brief to Heather Olszewski at
[CONTACT]

Purpose

This brief describes the urgent need for universal coverage of prescription contraception in Canada. With
approximately 40% of pregnancies in Canada being unplanned1, there is a significant and measurable
cost burden to the health care systems that is quite preventable.

Introduction

As a national professional organization of experts in women’s health, The Society of Obstetricians and
Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) believes that access to contraception is essential for gender equity.
Contraception allows women to have a reproductive life plan and to time their pregnancies. This in turn
means that they are more likely to complete their educational goals, participate more fully in the
workforce, enjoy more economic stability which benefits other children in the home, and have healthy
pregnancies and carry to term when they do choose to have children. Financial barriers can limit the
choice of contraception, leaving individuals to choose the cheapest method - not necessarily the most
effective - or to use no method of contraception at all.

What does this cost the health care system?

Most unintended pregnancies do not result in abortion; approximately 57% will result in a birth1. The
direct cost of unintended pregnancies in Canada is $320 million per year2. This analysis does not take
into consideration any downstream costs to the individual and society. The SOGC, with the support of
several national medical organizations, strongly recommends universal contraception coverage for all
Canadians.

Current state of contraception coverage in Canada

Sterilization, such as vasectomies and tubal ligations, is covered by provincial health insurance plans.
However, these procedures are only appropriate for people and couples who are done growing their
families.

org: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
text:
However, these procedures are only appropriate for people and couples who are done growing their
families.

Canada is the only country worldwide with universal healthcare that lacks coverage for prescription
drugs. The Government of Canada has committed to the implementation of a national pharmacare
program. A federal policy for the universal coverage of prescription contraception in Canada is an
important, immediate, and symbolic first step in the implementation this program and an affirmation of
the Government's ongoing commitment to the protection of reproductive rights and the advancement of
gender equality.

British Columbia became the first Canadian province to make prescription birth control free to women as
of April 1, 2023. Since then, about 188,000 people have accessed free contraceptive methods3.
Manitoba’s recently elected provincial government indicated their intent to make all prescription birth
control free in their Throne Speech on November 21, 2023. And currently in Ontario, the NDP presented
a private members’ bill for coverage of prescription contraception on November 29, 2023. It is clear that
the provinces understand the need for this coverage.

However, this policy would be best at a federal level. A person’s ability to access effective contraception
and plan their family should never depend on their postal code. This policy is too important to be left to
the changing priorities of provincial and territorial governments. Given the current government’s
commitment to a national Pharmacare program, this would be an important and meaningful first step
towards that goal.

org: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
text:
Given the current government’s
commitment to a national Pharmacare program, this would be an important and meaningful first step
towards that goal.

Unintended pregnancies in Canada, by the numbers
•
Women spend approximately 35 years of their lives being fertile. For a woman who plans to have
two children, she will spend, on average, 5 years trying to conceive, being pregnant, and
postpartum. This means that Canadian women spend 30 years of their lives, on average, trying
not to get pregnant4.
•
Approximately 40% of pregnancies in Canada are unintended, resulting in 160,000 unintended
pregnancies every year1.
•
While some of these pregnancies will result in abortion, most result in a birth.
•
Every year in Canada, one-third of births (90,000) are unintended1.
•
Most taxpayer-funded healthcare plans in Canada do not cover contraception, apart from
sterilization.
•
The estimated direct health care costs of unintended pregnancies in Canada is $320 million
annually2.
•
Cost modelling was done in British Columbia to estimate the costs of this program showed cost
neutrality partway through Year 2 of funding5.
•
Estimates have been done in both the US and the UK for Return on Investment (ROI). The US
modelling showed a $7 USD ROI6, and the UK modelling estimated a £9 ROI7.
•
The most effective forms of contraception (long-acting reversible contraceptives, or LARCs) are
also the most expensive. Intra-uterine devices or subdermal implants have high up-front costs
(typically $300-$500).

Recommendations

The SOGC strongly recommends a universal policy for coverage of prescription contraception for all
women in Canada. This funding should cover all forms of prescription contraception, for all women in
Canada. These would include:
•
Hormonal contraceptive pill, patch or ring
•
Depo medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA – “the shot”)
•
Subdermal implants
•
Intrauterine contraceptives (copper or levonorgestrel-releasing)

Summary and Supporters

In every province and territory in Canada right now, the healthcare system is under tremendous
pressure. Unintended pregnancies place incredible strains on women, their families, and add to stresses
on the healthcare system. While most of these can be prevented with a reliable method of

contraception, it should be noted that contraception offers much more than preventing pregnancies - it
allows women to make a reproductive life plan.

org: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
text:
contraception, it should be noted that contraception offers much more than preventing pregnancies - it
allows women to make a reproductive life plan.

When women plan their pregnancies, they are more likely to finish their education, have financial
resources to care for their children, and participate more in the workforce. Far from simple cost savings,
this policy also makes society stronger.

The SOGC has been working alongside several other groups to petition the federal government to
consider this important policy. These supporters are:
•
The Contraception and Abortion Research Team at the University of British Columbia
•
Project EmpowHER, a grassroots organization founded by Dr. Rupinder Toor of Calgary
•
Action Canada for Sexual Health & Rights

I. Executive Summary
Introduction
Women's health is integral to individual health and to the overall well-being of our society. We
hear many stories in the media of women who are interested to empower their own healing and
personal growth but they require a model, guidance and support. We may personally know
women who are struggling. Women can experience many situations that create traumatic
memories and limiting beliefs (mental imagery), resulting in health issues. Research now shows
mental imagery is connected to emotions and that by resolving intrusive mental imagery,
symptoms can be relieved and even resolved.

Research now shows
mental imagery is connected to emotions and that by resolving intrusive mental imagery,
symptoms can be relieved and even resolved.

For context, think of a splinter. You don’t leave a splinter in the body. You remove it to prevent
illness and allow healing. Likewise, removing intrusive mental imagery (such as traumatic
memories) can prevent illness and allow healing. Research into the role of mental imagery in
emotional distress calls for new treatment models to resolve intrusive mental imagery. (Brewin et
al., 2010)

Key Findings
A key element of women’s health issues is based on patterns that are embedded in past
experiences and cultural norms. Beliefs, memories and fantasies are stored as frozen mental
imagery which triggers stress responses that lead to acute and chronic health issues.
Logosynthesis offers a comprehensive model with a repeatable, measurable technique to heal
mental imagery and relieve emotional distress.
Recommendations
Logosynthesis offers an integrated approach to identify and neutralize distressing mental
imagery to relieve distressing thoughts, emotions and physical sensations. It is recommended that
this model is piloted to:
1. introduce into professional self-care ini5a5ves to reduce stress / burnout and empower
women in their own health.
2. Integrate into research projects to measure the impact of specific illnesses.

There is a common theme with these conditions in that many involve long-standing patterns,
psycho-somatic symptoms and roots to Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) and/or traumatic
experiences.
Challenges in Current Approaches
A key challenge for many chronic health issues is to offer immediate and lasting relief of
symptoms, without introducing new issues.
III. Understanding Mental Imagery and Emotional Distress
Role of Mental Imagery in Health
Understanding of and research into the role of mental imagery in overall health and wellbeing is
relatively new. Recent studies across a wide variety of health issues highlight a connection
between intrusive mental imagery and distressing thoughts, emotions and physical sensations
(think of re-experiencing traumatic events). These studies call for a comprehensive treatment
model to resolve distressing mental imagery. A paper titled “Intrusive Images in Psychological
Disorders: Characteristics, Neural Mechanisms, and Treatment Implications” (Brewin et al.,
2010) offers an overview of the topic.
Gender-Specific Considerations
Mental imagery is a human condition and affects the health and wellbeing of men, women and
children. Women face unique challenges related to mental imagery influenced by cultural norms,
societal expectations and personal experiences. Sexual assault, domestic violence and traditional
and changing gender roles create both painful memories and belief systems that result in
stressful, reactive patterns. This StatsCan report is one report that offers context:
https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/85-002-x/2019001/article/00017-eng.htm

IV. Case for Logosynthesis in Women's Health
Logosynthesis: An Overview
Logosynthesis is a healing and development model that is being used internationally by
psychotherapists, counsellors, life and executive coaches, educators and others to support healing
and empowerment. Logosynthesis is also used for self-coaching to address personal issues
related to stress, anxiety and goals.

Logosynthesis International Association (LIA) is a non-profit association founded in 2014 and
based in Zurich, Switzerland. It protects the quality of training and further development of the
model. Research is recognized as a priority for LIA members although most members at this
point work in private practice and are not affiliated with research institutions.

Research is recognized as a priority for LIA members although most members at this
point work in private practice and are not affiliated with research institutions.

Logosynthesis offers an integrative model with one repeatable, measurable technique to identify
and resolve mental imagery triggering women’s health issues, including:
-
Stress and burnout
-
Autoimmune disorders and psychosoma5c illness
-

-

-

Empirical Evidence
The first peer-reviewed published research is: “Efficacy of Logosynthesis in Reducing PTSD
Symptoms and Distress among Adults with Adverse Childhood Experiences” (Beltran-Salanguit,
2022); Additional published research is: "A New Approach to Healing Traumatic Memories:
Using Logosynthesis to Resolve Subjective Units of Stress Related to Intimate Partner Violence"
‘(Jones, 2023) and The Effectiveness of Logosynthesis: New Methods in Integrative
Psychotherapy. (von Blumenthal et al., 2022).

These studies support case reports available in books, articles and videos that speak to
‘immediate and lasting relief of distress related to the presenting issue’. Although the model is
not yet widely researched, it offers a very specific intervention that can offer measurable and
repeatable results.
Testimonials and Success Stories
Dr. Willem Lammers has written books about theory and case studies. Dr. Laurie Weiss has
written self-coaching books. I wrote two books (Caswell, 2017) (Caswell, 2020) about my
personal experience and an overview of the model in everyday terms. I offer ‘Why
Logosynthesis Works’ as a podcast / YouTube series, speaking with over 30 professionals to
support healing and development using Logosynthesis.

VI. Recommendation to pilot to offer relief and measure results

Recommendation to pilot to offer relief and measure results

There is an opportunity to incorporate this integrative model into research on a wide variety of
women’s health topics. Here are three recommendations:
Recommendation #1: Pilot to address health issues identified by Canadian
Federation of Nurses Union.
The Canadian Federation of Nurses Union has submitted a parliamentary brief calling for the
government to address issues impacting the health of its members. Post-traumatic stress disorder
(PTSD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), depressive disorder, suicidal thoughts and clinical
burnout. Logosynthesis can be piloted with this group for professional self-care to address these
issues and measure deltas pre- and post-intervention. The model can be introduced through
workshops, app-based courses, guided videos and 1-1 coaching.
Recommendation #2: Pilot Research Studies on Specific Health Issues
The research into healing traumatic memories related to Intimate Partner Violence creates a
starting point for further research. Given that many health issues fall under provincial
jurisdiction, there is an opportunity for an initial pilot project from a women’s health perspective
to work with female military members and veterans, on the topic of assault and burnout.
Recommendation #3: Educate employees of Health Canada through self-care
programs.
Logosynthesis is an empowering model that can be used as a self-coaching model to resolve
everyday issues in work and life. Educating staff of Health Canada allow a better understanding
of how mental imagery impacts health and how to resolve distressing mental imagery.
VII. Potential Challenges
Shifting Paradigms
Many current psychotherapeutic and coaching models teach individuals to learn to cope with
distressing mental imagery. The paradigm shift comes with:
1. The knowledge that mental imagery and distressing thoughts, emo5ons and physical
sensa5ons are fused.
2. The knowledge that there is an integra5ve model that energe5cally uses the power of
words and inten5on (non-invasive) to iden5fy and resolve distressing mental imagery
for immediate and las5ng relief.

The knowledge that there is an integra5ve model that energe5cally uses the power of
words and inten5on (non-invasive) to iden5fy and resolve distressing mental imagery
for immediate and las5ng relief.

Resource Allocation
Many academics and clinicians, understandably, are interested and focused in further researching
their area of work. Allocating financial and human resources may require a strategic decision in
addition to identifying interested teams.
VIII. Conclusion
Summary of Key Points
There are a wide variety of issues related to women’s health. Research into the connection
between mental imagery and emotions is calling for new treatments that focus on resolving
intrusive, distressing mental imagery. Logosynthesis is a certified psychotherapeutic and
coaching model that offers a precise, repeatable technique (intervention) to identify and
neutralize distressing mental imagery and offer immediate and lasting relief.
Call to Action
Canada has an opportunity to introduce an innovative approach to women’s health.
Logosynthesis can identify and resolve distressing mental imagery for healing and
empowerment.

Dear Committee members,

RESOLVE welcomes the opportunity to submit to the Standing Committee on Health’s study of Women’s
Health. We thank you for this valuable opportunity and we applaud the committee's effort to conduct a
study to advance our understanding of women's health.

RESOLVE1 is a tri-prairie, community-based research network that engages in research and education
aimed at reducing the incidence and impact of family/gender-based violence. Our three centres are
located at the Universities of Manitoba, Calgary, and Saskatchewan. RESOLVE is also a member of the
Alliance of Canadian Research Centres on Gender-Based Violence2, a consortium of five research
centres formed in 1992 by the federal government in direct response to the 1989 Montreal Massacre.
We write this brief based on decades of engaging in collaborative research with community
organizations across the country, as well as survivors.

org: Research and Education for Solutions to Violence and Abuse
text:
We write this brief based on decades of engaging in collaborative research with community
organizations across the country, as well as survivors.

Gender-based violence (GBV), including intimate partner violence (IPV) remains a pervasive issue in
Canada. IPV includes many forms of violence and abuse, including (but not limited to) physical abuse,
emotional/psychological abuse, sexual violence, criminal harassment (also referred to as stalking),
financial/economic abuse, reproductive coercion, coercive control, and domestic homicide (WaGE,
2021)3. Research shows that women in Canada are at higher risk than men of experiencing certain types
of violence, including sexual assault and IPV. In 2022, the rate of police-reported IPV was more than
three times higher among women and girls than among men and boys (Statistic Canada, 2023)4. This is
especially true in the Prairie Provinces, where rates of IPV tend to be the highest in the country
(Statistics Canada, 2021)5. In contrast, men make up the majority of perpetrators of these types of
violence (Savage, 2019)6. Canadian research demonstrates that women disproportionately experience
the most severe forms of IPV (Burczycka, 2016)7, such as being choked, assaulted, sexually assaulted, or
threatened with a weapon. Additionally, women are more likely to experience more frequent instances
of violence and more often report injury and negative physical and emotional consequences as a result
of the violence (Burczycka, 2016). Between, 2010-2019 there were 718 cases of domestic homicide in
Canada, and 80% of these involved female victims. It is also important to note that certain groups of
women, including Indigenous women experience greater rates of IPV, more severe violence, and more
serious injuries (Statistics Canada, 2021)8. Therefore, it is imperative that IPV (and its solutions) be
considered from a gendered and intersectional lens.

Over the last seven years, our country has witnessed an escalation of IPV across Canada. In fact, it is now
considered to be an epidemic, warranting immediate and urgent attention (Globe and Mail, September
15, 2023)9. The costs of IPV are enormous, including the costs to women's health and wellbeing. IPV
often results in injury, emotional harm, and, for too many Canadian women, death (CDHPI, 2022)10. We
highlight particular health impacts of IPV in our submission and present the range of serious
consequences that IPV has on women's health. We hope this committee considers IPV (and its
consequences) in its response to improving women's health and wellbeing.

There are many short and long-term impacts that IPV has on women's physical health, including chronic
pain/broken bones, irritable bowel syndrome/Crohn’s disease, Chronic Fatigue/Fibromyalgia, Hepatitis
C, and HIV (Tutty et al., 2019)11. However, for this brief we focus on mental health/substance use,
traumatic brain injury, and domestic homicide. We underscore the urgency of addressing IPV as a
national emergency and public health crisis, and advocate for a national, comprehensive strategy to
mitigate its devastating consequences.

Impact of IPV on Women's Mental Health
Women abused by their partners are often diagnosed with significant mental health issues including
depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Tutty et al., 2019). Substance use and
suicidal ideation (including suicide completion) are also dire consequences of IPV. In fact, IPV survivors
are four times as likely to attempt suicide. Indeed, the long-term consequences on women's mental
health can persist for years, affecting survivors' quality of life, and their loved ones.

org: Research and Education for Solutions to Violence and Abuse
text:
Indeed, the long-term consequences on women's mental
health can persist for years, affecting survivors' quality of life, and their loved ones.

IPV and Women's Substance Use
IPV survivors are six times as likely to experience substance use disorders (RESOLVE, 2023)12.
Perpetrators also use tactics of mental health and substance use coercion to engage in coercive and
controlling behaviours toward their partner’s mental health or substance use, including coercing or
forcing a partner to use substances, undermining a partner’s sanity or sobriety and recovery efforts, and
discrediting a partner with potential sources of protection or support, and jeopardizing custody
(RESOLVE, 2023). Importantly, there are several sex and gender-related differences in substance use
which result in women using substances differently, responding to substances differently, and facing
unique barriers to treatment (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2020). These differences are the result
of biological, environmental, and sociocultural factors that converge to make women more vulnerable
to the effects of substance use and the development of addiction (RESOLVE, 2023). Women are also
more likely to encounter barriers to seeking and completing treatment than men. Shame, harmful
stigma, and stereotypes play a large part in deterring women from seeking treatment, as women face
greater stigmatization for substance use, especially for mothers, who are often labelled as having moral
failings if they use substances or experience addiction. Financial constraints, as well as the lack of
childcare are also formidable barriers for women accessing treatment use (RESOLVE, 2023).

IPV and Traumatic Brain Injury
An emerging area of concern for survivors of IPV is traumatic brain injury (TBI). TBI is commonly
experienced by IPV survivors because of the high frequency of head, neck, and facial injuries;
strangulation; and the chronic/recurrent nature of the violence. Almost 75% of survivors sustain TBIs,
with many experiencing multiple TBIs (Haag et al., 2022)13. TBI is a leading cause of disability worldwide
and is more prevalent than breast cancer, spinal cord injury, HIV/AIDS, and multiple sclerosis combinedi.
Widely recognized among those who experience falls, motor vehicle accidents, and sport-related
injuries, TBI remains invisible among IPV survivors, due to a lack of awareness and training on IPVrelated TBI among those working with survivors. Resultingly, TBI is undiagnosed and untreated among
IPV survivors. Untreated, TBI can lead to serious consequences, including an increase in deleterious/
worsening symptoms, developing mental health and substance use disorders, impairing survivors' ability
to hold jobs, care for their children, and complete tasks of daily living. TBI can even lead to premature
death (Brain Injury Canada, 2022)14. Recognizing and treating TBIs in IPV survivors is critical for providing
appropriate medical care and support.

Domestic Homicide
The most extreme and tragic outcome of IPV on women's health is domestic homicide. As noted
above, women make up most victims (up to 80%). Indigenous women are at even greater risk. While
they only accounted for about 5% of all women in Canada, they accounted for 21% of all women killed
by an intimate partner between 2014 and 2019 (83 victims). In 2020, 53 women, 11 of whom were
Indigenous, were killed by their partner in Canada (Government of Canada, 2022)15. Of course, domestic
homicide has a profound impact on loved ones left behind, many of whom who suffer severe
psychological effects for years (Winfield, 2021)16.

In conclusion, IPV remains a serious and pervasive public health issue in Canada that has profound
implications for women's health. Our submission highlights three areas of concern such as mental
health/substance use, traumatic brain injury, and domestic homicide. Meaningful change is needed in
Canada, including a national comprehensive response to addressing IPV in Canada. This involves a
collaboration among government, academics/researchers, community organizations, and survivors.

partners to address gendered violence. AVA is offering community internships to help build evidence to
support optimal approaches to address gendered violence. AVA was also recognized and funded by the

Again, we thank the committee for carrying out this important study and for soliciting feedback on
issues pertaining to women's health. However, we would like to acknowledge our disappointment that
of the 12 members, only two are female. It is disconcerting that a committee whose focus is on women's
health (including drafting policy recommendations) has such poor representation of women. We
strongly encourage the committee to reconsider its membership and include more women for this
committee and other committees in the future. Gender parity must be a priority for this government,
especially in the selection of committee membership. As noted earlier, IPV is a gendered phenomenon,
with women experiencing the most severe forms of violence and physical and mental health impacts.
Any solutions aimed at ending gender-based violence (including IPV) must incorporate a genderanalysis.

This brief uses the term “woman” to mean adult human female and “man” to mean adult human
male, while gender non-conforming male (“GNC males”) refers to males who identify as
transwomen or non-binary, and “gender” is the societal expectations based on an individual’s sex.
Introduction
It was traditionally believed women’s health mostly mimicked men’s health. Along with the view
that using women as research subjects is problematic because of fluctuation from menstrual cycles,
resulted in a limited number of females as research subjects. This has caused a major disparity
between men’s and women’s medical research. Heart attacks, for instance, present differently in
women than men. While there has been knowledge about male heart health since the early 1900s, it
wasn’t evident until the late 2000s that heart attacks present differently in women. To this day, just 1
in 3 research subjects are women (Heart and Stroke Foundation 2018, p.4). Recent research has
shown that treatments that work for men can detrimentally impact women. In other fields
experiments have sometimes been carried out without considering sex in scientific research. Scientists have
often used only one sex (generally male) for experiments and applied the findings to both sexes, without
solid grounds. These kinds of inadvertent extrapolations might cause unintentionally harmful results to the
neglected sex and economic loss (Lee, p. 167).
A 2009 survey analyzed sex bias in journal articles published in 10 major biological discipline
research fields. Over 50% of articles in general biology and immunology fields did not specify the
sex in the study. In articles that defined the sex, male bias was observed in 8 of the 10 fields (Lee,
p.168).
One change in women’s health is language. For over 1,000 years, the terms ‘woman’ and ‘mother’
have been used. Over the last six years, those terms have been removed from the lexicon in favour of
terms like ‘bleeder,’ ‘birthing body,’ ‘non-man,’ and many other terms with the goal of kindness and
inclusivity. In 2021 the federal government changed its definition of ‘woman’ to ‘anyone who
identifies as a woman whether they are cisgender or transgender,’ which renders ‘woman’ an
ambiguous term that ignores the fact that women are a sex class. These changes are
in response to Queer Theory-derived concerns, [wherein] many organizations and individuals are changing
the language they use to describe women so as to prioritize gendered understandings and avoid sexed
terminology [...] intended to avoid distress, are described as inclusive, and are encouraged by diversity,
equity, and inclusion initiatives. [...] However, there appears to have been little consideration of the ethics
of these changes, including the principles of avoiding harm and health maximization, or how they may
impact on women's and children's rights (Bartick, p. 2).
Impact on women’s health
The results from a lack of research on women and de-sexing language include:
1.
Early detection and preventative women’s healthcare;
2.
Lack of known effective treatments for women;
3.
Dehumanization of women;
4.
Decline in women’s health campaigns; and,

Decline in women’s health campaigns; and,

5.
Exclusion of the most vulnerable women.
88% of primary care physicians and 68% of cardiologists did not feel prepared enough to assess heart
disease in women (Heart and Stroke Foundation 2018, p. 6), let alone knowledgeable enough to
speak to female patients about heart disease. The diagnosis tool used for men, such as the treadmill
test for cardiac output, is much less sensitive for women, showing further research and major
campaigns involving women’s health are needed. Few women are referred to cardiac rehabilitation
programs compared to men, and half as likely to attend and complete the program because of missing
psychological and social support (Heart and Stroke Foundation 2018, p. 10). However, it was found
that there was a marked improvement in those numbers when there were women-only programs. This
is just one of many women’s health conditions that requires more attention.
New changes in de-sexing language when referring to women are a result of efforts to being kind and
inclusive. The average woman finds the new language dehumanizing and offensive because the
language refers to women by organs or reproductive functions, completely disregarding the principle
of respectful language. For example, The Lancet medical journal’s September 24, 2021 cover
featured the title, “Historically, the anatomy and physiology of bodies with vaginas have been
neglected.” The same rule hasn’t applied to men’s health. ‘Man’ is not replaced by the term ‘people
with prostates,’ nor should such changes be made.
Another consequence of de-sexing language is the exclusion of the most vulnerable women, whose
rights must be protected. Women with disabilities, for instance, require their rights to be preserved –
and that includes access to healthcare, which isn’t possible if individuals are unable to understand
healthcare campaigns. The entire point of using the words ‘woman’ or ‘mother’ is to make it clear to
people who don't understand terminology like “cervix-haver,” or “menstruator,” if the information is
intended for her. Gendered language is required in order to be able to focus on the needs of women
based on their sex. It allows quick diagnosis in order to eliminate or explore a wide range of
conditions based on physiology - endometriosis, for instance. It is also a quick way to disseminate
effective health campaigns targeting women, such as promoting pap smears for cervical cancer
screening.
De-sexing language has promoted the false idea that GNC men can be women and literally change
their sex. This has caused confusion and led to the demand for medical services that are not required.
For example, there are some GNC males who believe they have menstrual periods - something that is
impossible given there is no lining for a uterus to shed. Another example is an assertion that GNC
males should be able to access gynecological services when gynecologists specialize in and treat
issues related to female physiology. As medical science is aware, the medical issues or symptoms a
male or female has do not change, even after sex reassignment surgeries and cross-sex hormone
therapy. There have also been reported medical problems from this exact issue wherein an individual
is deprived of essential services related to the individual’s sex. For example, in the UK, one GNC
female insisted on being male at a hospital. The staff did not question the patient as the patient was
classified as male in the National Health Service’s system since the patient had legally changed their

The staff did not question the patient as the patient was
classified as male in the National Health Service’s system since the patient had legally changed their

sex to male. The patient was pregnant and lost the baby because the medical staff didn’t treat the
patient as a female (Geanous). As another example, there is now medical research that uses terms like
“non-pregnant people” and “pregnant people” in researching COVID-19 in relation to pregnant
women versus “non-pregnant women.” Both the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
and the Australian Department of Health have used this term. This research was widely published,
including in the New England Journal of Medicine (Bartick, p. 4).
Another issue with de-sexing women’s language is that it is not inclusive of all women, further
straining the lack of knowledge women have about their own health. In Canada, just 11% of women
can name one or more female-specific risk factors for heart disease (Heart and Stroke Foundation
2023, p. 8). In a 2023 poll, “47% of American women say they don't understand the difference
between a Pap test and an HPV test,” while “48% say the guidance about recommended pap test
frequency is confusing” (Carr). These statistics are not isolated to a particular country and are similar
in numerous other countries. Phrases like “cervix owner” is not helpful in communicating
information to women, especially women who are vulnerable or who don’t speak French or English.
Women with communication, cognitive, sensory, or mental health disabilities or challenges are also
disadvantaged by this language. These disorders include aphasia, Alzheimer's, learning disabilities,
and schizophrenia (SLP, p. 10). Marginalized and minority women, such as these, cannot be denied
their rights to effective medical treatment due to inappropriate inclusivity protocols.
De-sexing language has resulted in the inaccuracy of facts, resulting in confusion in that populations
have been included in campaigns and statements that do not concern them, such as “parents”
replacing “mother.” This removes the ability to concentrate on female-specific health issues, like
breastfeeding, resulting in invisibility. It ignores that women have unique health issues and
vulnerabilities and require protection. “The intent of “additive language” is to encapsulate pregnant
and birthing females or female parents as a group but to do so in a way that avoids offense to those
who do not wish to be named as women or mothers” (Bartick, p. 4). However, these terms change
meaning from sexed terms that are inclusive of all female persons to gendered terms that may be
confusing or inappropriately inclusive.
What does the phrase “women and birthing people” actually mean? This construction could be interpreted
in a literal way as meaning that “women” are not people. Another interpretation occurs if “women” is
meant or read in a gendered sense so including males with the gender identity of “woman” who cannot be
pregnant or give birth. [...] The change in meaning of “women” from a sexed term to a gender identity can
also mean that those women who do not have a belief in gender identity as a concept do not see themselves
reflected in the gendered use of “women.” Consequently, they may feel objectified by terms [...] Although
sprinkling some “additive language” is often presented as a simple solution, it has its own risks, particularly
when there is a need to be specific (Bartick, p. 4).
Using statistics to include everyone in conditions impacting only or mainly women, like, ‘1 in 20
people suffer from endometriosis’ compared to ‘1 in 20 women suffer from endometriosis’
cognitively deemphasizes the impact on women as a population (Bartick, p. 4) and makes it more
difficult to effectively advocate for women (Bartick, p. 5). What we see is “‘women’ disappear into
‘people’” (Bartick, p. 5).

What we see is “‘women’ disappear into
‘people’” (Bartick, p. 5).

Recommendations
The government revert back to using the definition of ‘woman’ to ‘human adult female’ in policy,
legislation, and any communication with the general population. in order to ensure communication is
clear. Sexed language must be used in publications, policies, legislation, and communications with
the general population. The government and its agencies may choose to use desexed language when
communication is not specific to women.
About Women’s Rights Matter
Women’s Rights Matter is a Canadian non-profit organization. We are a non-partisan
volunteer-driven grassroots organization that focuses on educating, advocating, and empowering
women regarding their rights in Canada.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
Submission to the Standing Committee on Health Consultations on Women’s Health
Heart & Stroke
November 30, 2023

Background
Canada’s healthcare system is faced with a continued lack of awareness and understanding
around women’s heart and brain health. Two-thirds of participants in clinical trials on heart
disease and stroke have historically been men, and when women are included, sex and genderbased analysis and reporting (SGBAR) is not always conducted or included in reported results.
Half of women who experience heart attacks have symptoms go unrecognized, and they are
less likely than men to receive the treatments and medications they need or receive them in a
timely manner. Women represent more than 50% of our population; it is time this massive gap is
adequately addressed. Women are key contributors to societies and our economy; yet endure
hardships that can lead to chronic disease risk and even to cardiac arrest, partly due to their
important supportive role to society that they play. Efforts to improve and safeguard women’s
health will contribute to a more resilient economy and society.
At Heart & Stroke (H&S), we strive to live in a world where all women receive the care they
need when it comes to heart and brain health. This means that women receive health
information, diagnoses and care that considers their distinct risk factors related to gender and
sex, risk factors that impact women differently, as well as intersecting and overlapping factors
that add to their risk such as race, ethnicity, Indigeneity, socioeconomic status, sexual
orientation, geography, body size, ability and others. To bring our vision to life, we must
continue to build upon the recent inroads that we’ve made in women’s health.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
To bring our vision to life, we must
continue to build upon the recent inroads that we’ve made in women’s health.

Call to Action: Continuing Women’s Heart & Brain Research
In 2016, H&S received $5M/5 years from the Government of Canada to undertake foundational
work to address women’s historic disparities in access to care. That investment was directed
toward the H&S Advancing Women’s Heart & Brain Health Research Initiative and resulted in
26 studies, more than 100 publications and more than 10 policies, tools and guidelines that now
inform research and clinical practice. Outcomes of this initiative led researchers, clinicians and
policy makers to report being more willing to employ SGBAR and improve policies and practices
to include women. At H&S, we made SGBAR a requirement of our research and programing,
along with influencing our stakeholder engagement practices. The initiative also identified
significant gaps in Canadian research and practice that we aim to address via our Women’s
Heart & Brain Initiative 2.0 (WI2.0)
WI2.0 is a 10-year roadmap aimed at tackling the core, systemic issues that underlie the
problem of inequity in care. Health equity and Indigenous wellbeing will be addressed through
analyzing systemic barriers faced by racialized and other equity-deserving groups and be
reflective of Indigenous voices, principles and knowledge. This will be pursued through key
partnerships with research and postsecondary institutions, as well as corporate, community and
Indigenous health organizations.
In the WI2.0, the term “women’s health” reflects an evolving concept that broadly includes the
multidimensional concepts of sex and gender. This initiative goes beyond sex and gender binary
and welcomes the experiences and needs of all people who identify as a woman, girl, inter-sex
and/or underrepresented gender identities.
WI2.0 will include three key pillars that were developed with expert consultation. Those pillars
are: 1) public awareness/education; 2) the healthcare journey; and 3) research, which consists
of two components: Personnel Awards (aimed at building the next generation of diverse
scientists focused on women’s health) and Research Networks of Excellence (RNE). This
submission will solely focus on RNE as it is the one component requiring government support.
Greater details of the initiative are available upon request.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
Greater details of the initiative are available upon request.

The Research Networks of Excellence
Women face distinct risk factors for heart disease and stroke, and at different points in their
lives, including during pregnancy and menopause. Additionally, as they age, women acquire
cardiovascular risk factors at a faster rate than men. Moreover, certain types of heart conditions
are more common in women, and women can be impacted differently by heart disease and
stroke.
RNE will be established in a multi-disciplinary, multi-institutional and a multi-provincial manner
and will be pivotal to the advancement of women’s heart and brain health in Canada. These will
drive innovation, build research capacity, and accelerate knowledge translation in women’s
heart and brain health. Each RNE will focus on a specific challenge to women’s heart and brain
health. Two RNEs have been announced with funding primarily from H&S and a contribution
from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research. The first RNE will focus on risk factors that
are women-specific, and the second will focus on diagnosis and treatment of certain types of
heart and brain conditions and understanding how they impact women. The third RNE will be
focused on women’s rehabilitation and recovery. H&S requires government funding in order for
this third RNE to be established.
Our plan begins with an open call requiring multi-institutional teams of researchers to register
and provide a summary of their research proposal. Eligible submissions will be peer-reviewed
by an international selection panel overseen by H&S’s Scientific Review Committee.
Recommendation #1:
A Government of Canada investment of $5 million over five years beginning in 2024 that will
fund a Research Network of Excellence and accelerate innovation and knowledge translation in
women’s rehabilitation and recovery from heart disease and stroke.
Call to Action: Saving Lives Through Public Awareness and Training

A key pillar of the work at H&S is public awareness and education. We know that Canadians
can – and want – to help save the lives of their family, friends or even a stranger. Unfortunately,
when it comes to cardiac arrest, male victims are more likely to receive help in public spaces
than women, leading women to be in a more vulnerable position fighting for their lives.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
Unfortunately,
when it comes to cardiac arrest, male victims are more likely to receive help in public spaces
than women, leading women to be in a more vulnerable position fighting for their lives.

In Canada, at least 35,000 people per year (1 every 15 minutes) experience cardiac arrest
outside of a hospital setting and fewer than 10% survive. Several Canadian studies have
confirmed that women are less likely to be resuscitated by lay responders than men in public
spaces. These outcomes are partially due to bystander reluctance to perform CPR on women,
and women experience a lower proportion of shockable initial rhythms than men. Some
survivors of cardiac arrest experience lasting physical and/or neurological damage, as well as
debilitating personal and family trauma. Due to societal and/or family expectations of women,
the impact of cardiac arrest can be wide-ranging when a woman who usually has more
caregiver responsibilities experiences a cardiac arrest.
Cardiac arrest happens when the heart suddenly and unexpectedly stops beating and is no
longer able to pump oxygen-carrying blood to the brain and other vital organs. It can happen to
anyone, anywhere, at any age, often without warning. For every minute that passes without
cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) or defibrillation (using an automated external defibrillator

or AED), the probability of survival declines by about 10%. Brain injury can begin within five
minutes. That's why it is critical for lay responders to act quickly – doing CPR and using an AED
can the double chance of survival.
Furthermore, public awareness and education initiatives that spotlight, for example, the
difference between a cardiac arrest and a heart attack can help to protect the health of
Canadians and can help to save lives. We can enable Canadians to recognize the signs of
cardiac arrest in men and women, empower them to call 9-1-1, perform hands-only CPR and
use an AED. It is also important to open conversations about helping women. We believe these
steps will improve women’s survival rates.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
We believe these
steps will improve women’s survival rates.

Creating Everyday Heroes
Mass public engagement campaigns have been proven to work. A 2009-2013 mass media
campaign in Australia that focused on cardiac arrest led to increased survival rates (a 6.4%
reduction in mortality rates). A similar multi-faceted media strategy and high-profile CPR and
AED-focused educational events could be duplicated in Canada with similar impressive results.
Moreover, H&S already has experience in program delivery. Each year, hundreds of thousands
of Canadians, including those in healthcare, learn life-saving skills through H&S’s extensive
network. We’ve taught CPR to two million Canadians through awareness events such as “Call
Push Restart” and “CPR Makes You Undead”– a campaign which trained more than 8,000
people, obtained nearly 1 million YouTube views and generated more than 92 million media
impressions. We also have a record of leveraging media effectively in building public awareness
and education: in B.C., we implemented campaigns in the last two decades using TV, print and
digital ads, and interactive websites. Similarly, our FAST campaign in Ontario and Quebec has
been proven to substantially increase the number of Canadians who can recognize the signs of
stroke, which resulted in swifter action in seeking medical attention.
H&S is a trusted partner for the health sector and the public. We are a founding member and
the only Canadian council representative on the International Liaison Committee on
Resuscitation (ILCOR), an organization that reviews resuscitation research and science and
summarizes the evidence-based findings into treatment recommendations. These
recommendations are then released internationally, and each member council localizes and
applies them to their jurisdiction. Through our role in ILCOR, we adapt these treatment
recommendations for CPR, emergency cardiovascular care and first-aid into guidelines for all of
Canada.
Our guidelines form the basis of all H&S resuscitation training programs, which are recognized
as the gold standard in Canada. Our guidelines also form the basis of all other resuscitation
training programs offered by training organizations across Canada.
We are also a founding partner and primary funder of the Canadian Resuscitation Outcomes
Consortium (CanROC), a national network of resuscitation researchers and
EMS/paramedic/firefighting partners. CanROC’s focus is developing a nationwide registry of
out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, which is important to our healthcare system as we seek to
understand how we respond to cardiac arrests.

org: Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
text:
CanROC’s focus is developing a nationwide registry of
out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, which is important to our healthcare system as we seek to
understand how we respond to cardiac arrests.

Canadians are willing to be trained and educated to help save lives. A March 2022 poll
conducted by Sentis Research found that 95% of Canadians support government funding for
public awareness and education campaigns on recognizing and responding to cardiac arrest.
Given the pressures on our healthcare system and the need to improve response times, now is
the time to invest in public awareness and training. We can empower Canadians to recognize
the signs of cardiac arrest and act to achieve better results for women, from bystander support
to survival rates. These funds would support public awareness and education campaigns for the
general population, as well as campaigns for identified populations (such as women, youth and
some racialized groups who are at higher-risk for cardiac arrest) in need of specific intervention.
We believe that such a campaign with the support of the Government of Canada could save
more than 2,000 lives a year.
Recommendation #2:
A Government of Canada investment of $15 million over two years for the implementation of a
national, bilingual public awareness CPR and AED campaign to improve outcomes and
increase survival rates of cardiac arrest.
Summary
Women in our lives frequently encourage us to look after ourselves and put others’ needs ahead
of their own. It is time that we correct historical imbalances and invest into research and health
promotion that prioritizes them. RNE and CPR/AED awareness and training will allow the
women in our lives to be in our lives longer and continue to make our society stronger. Early
intervention into heart and brain conditions will also allow them to live on their own longer,
hereby supporting one directive of the Health Minister’s mandate.

Overall, these recommendations will better enable provinces and territories to bring more
equitable access to quality health care services and mitigate health inequalities and help to
create a healthcare system that is truly built for everyone.
###
Heart & Stroke has been leading the fight to beat heart disease and stroke for 70 years. We
generate the next medical breakthroughs so Canadians don’t miss out on precious moments.
Together, we are working to prevent disease, save lives and promote recovery through
research, health promotion and public policy.

1 Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights works to promote health, well-being, and rights related to sexuality and reproduction. We provide direct
support, referrals, and information to the public and work with decision-makers to advance progressive policies on access to abortion, stigma-free
healthcare, gender equality, 2SLGBTQ+ rights, and inclusive sex-ed.
Our vision is for all people everywhere to have full control over, and to decide freely upon, all matters related to their sexuality, reproduction, and
gender, including their reproductive and sexual health.
For more information, contact Insiya Mankani, Public Affairs Office ([CONTACT]) or Kelly Bowden, Director of Policy and Advocacy

org: Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights
text:
For more information, contact Insiya Mankani, Public Affairs Office ([CONTACT]) or Kelly Bowden, Director of Policy and Advocacy
([CONTACT])

Introduction
Health as defined by the World Health Organization is not only the absence of disease or infirmity, but the
complete physical, mental, and social well-being of each person. The WHO states that “the enjoyment of
the highest attainable standard of health is one of the fundamental rights of every human being without
distinction of race, religion, political belief, economic or social condition”. In short – a woman’s right to
health is equal to all others, and her health is defined by her whole of being, not strictly the management
of diseases.
Despite this, significant gaps remain for women across our country to fulfill their right to health.
Specifically addressing the unmet needs of women’s sexual and reproductive health is both crucial for
addressing the individual needs of women and to addressing wider social goals such as gender equality.
Ensuring universal access to sexual and reproductive health information, education, services, and
supplies will improve public health outcomes, reduce financial and structural pressures on the health care
system, and contribute to narrowing the gap in health disparities among different populations –
specifically addressing the needs of the most marginalized women in the country.
Canada's International Obligations to Address Sexual and Reproductive Health
Access to sexual and reproductive health services is a basic human right codified in several international
treaties to which Canada is a signatory. According to the most recent visit to Canada of the UN Special
Rapporteur on the Right to Health “Canada has a strong public health system that is firmly rooted in the
principles of equity and fairness and the notion that access to health care should be based on need and
not on the ability to pay. While the public health system includes many elements compatible with the right
to health, a human rights-based approach is still needed for the State comprehensively to comply with its
obligations to protect, respect and fulfil the right to health.” In relation to women’s health specifically, the
federal government has received several recommendations from UN instruments over the years to act,
including the recommendations to:
-
(a) Ensure access to legal abortion services in all provinces and territories; (b) Make affordable
contraceptives accessible and available to all women and girls, in particular those living in poverty
and/or in remote areas. (Committee on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against
Women, 2016)2

org: Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights
text:
recommendations from UN instruments over the years to act, including the recommendations to: - (a) Ensure access to legal abortion services in all provinces and territories; (b) Make affordable contraceptives accessible and available to all women and girls, in particular those living in poverty and/or in remote areas. (Committee on the Elimination of all Forms of Discrimination against Women, 2016)2

-
Strengthen sexual and reproductive health programmes and services provided to all adolescents,
paying particular attention to preventing unwanted pregnancies (Committee on the Rights of the
Child, 2022)3
Right now, women who face the most obstacles to sexual health care services are those who face
intersecting systemic barriers caused by race, socioeconomic status, disability, age, gender identity,
status, or geographic location. In practice these barriers may look like services being located further away
from communities, high costs and logistics associated with having to travel to access services, high
procedure costs for those who are uninsured, language barriers and lack of access to paid sick leave,
childcare, or other supports to attend or navigate appointments or making informed decisions about one’s
care. To truly address and inform Canada’s ability to fulfil the right to health for women, policy making
should address not only putting in place free and accessible services that seek to navigate diverse needs,
but also address the underlying social determinants of health. This brief will speak to three of the areas of
sexual health with continued and persistent access gaps for women in Canada and suggest
recommendations for addressing and filling those needs.
2 https://uhri.ohchr.org/en/document/b578d001-7b53-461e-af5f-c884cfea8cec
3 https://uhri.ohchr.org/en/document/e997abbe-ftidf-45ea-ae23-4f3148ff41db

org: Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights
text:
This brief will speak to three of the areas of
sexual health with continued and persistent access gaps for women in Canada and suggest
recommendations for addressing and filling those needs.
2 https://uhri.ohchr.org/en/document/b578d001-7b53-461e-af5f-c884cfea8cec
3 https://uhri.ohchr.org/en/document/e997abbe-ftidf-45ea-ae23-4f3148ff41db

Abortion
Abortion is a common outcome of pregnancy. Of all the people who can get pregnant, one in three will
have an abortion in their lifetime. Even though the need for abortion is common, and that it is a safe and
routine medical procedure, and that it is an insured medical service in Canada, access to abortion
services is still not guaranteed for all people in this country. Despite the notable advances in access due
to the introduction and up take of medication abortion in Canada, challenges in accessing surgical
services remain. Depending on your geography, services may only be available until 12 weeks, and so
care beyond the first trimester means travelling outside of one’s community. Procedures offered later in
the pregnancy are often scheduled over several days which means needing to take more time off work,
arranging care for children and other dependents, and bringing on more logistical and financial hurdles.
Currently, given longer wait times for accessing healthcare, there is an increased risk of people
exceeding the gestational limits of the abortion facilities not only in their province but in rare cases the
country. When services are rendered unavailable in Canada there are people, effectively, denied care –
specifically those who are undocumented, people without I.D., or those in situations of intimate partner
violence where freedom of movement is compromised.
Undocumented people are not eligible to become insured within the public health system and most
migrant workers must wait three months to have active insurance. Often, Temporary Foreign Workers are
bound by coercive employment contracts tied to their migration status and lack the freedom, privacy, and
access to information necessary to seek abortion care. In 2022, Action Canada's Access Line (a national
telephone, text service and fund for those facing financial barriers to accessing sexual and reproductive
care) received an average of 400 calls per month from across Canada, the vast majority of which were
related to abortion care. Of those calls that went on to receive our financial and logistical assistance in
acing abortion services, over 45% were uninsured, undocumented, or with precarious migration status.
Recommendation: Make Health Canada’s Sexual and Reproductive Health Fund permanent
The Sexual and Reproductive Health fund, announced in Budget 2021 and renewed in 2023, has made a
significant impact. It supports abortion care, centers Two-Spirit and Indigenous experiences, and
promotes sexual health for Autistic youth. For example, Action Canada’s Access Line phone and text
service supported over 3,000 callers from 2021 – 2022, 70% of whom faced major barriers to accessing
abortion services. Many callers who access our emergency financial assistance are from smaller, rural,
and remote areas. They are disproportionately people of low socio-economic status, youth, racialized,
facing intimate partner violence, coping with substance use disorders, living with disabilities, homeless, or
in precarious immigration status. Making the Sexual and Reproductive Health fund permanent is crucial to
avoid leaving marginalized groups without essential services while the long-term policy work of
addressing underlying causes of the social determinants of health are addressed.
Recommendation: Guarantee the provision of healthcare to undocumented people and migrant
workers through a no-exclusions regularization program granting full and permanent immigration
status
The Government of Canada has taken many meaningful steps to enhance access to abortion in Canada.
We urge you to take this opportunity to continue this important human rights work and ensure that sexual
and reproductive health services, including abortion, are available and accessible for all people.
Guaranteeing full and permanent immigration status for all moves us closer to a world where everyone’s
rights are realized and upheld.
Contraception
Canada is the only country worldwide with universal healthcare that lacks coverage for prescription drugs.
Right now, many people are falling through the cracks of patchwork provincial drug programs, forced to
choose between paying rent and paying for their contraception. Contraception is essential for family
planning and ensuring women are in control of the timing and spacing of children they decide to have, as

org: Action Canada for Sexual Health and Rights
text:
Contraception is essential for family
planning and ensuring women are in control of the timing and spacing of children they decide to have, as

well as providing support to manage conditions such as endometriosis and the prevention of certain
cancers. The best form of contraception will differ from person to person depending on a variety of factors
such as side effects, ease of access, privacy concerns and effectiveness. Cost is regularly cited as the
primary barrier to accessing the contraception of choice for people across Canada. Those without private
drug coverage will often not be able to afford contraception or can be forced to compromise when making
decisions, using methods they can afford instead of the most effective one or the one that works best for
them.

Recommendation: Invest in universal contraception
Equitable access to contraception is a human right and it is also a key to realizing public health goals,
reducing health care costs, reducing health disparities, and achieving gender equality. Ensuring
contraception for everyone would mean that women are more in control of whether, when and with whom
to have children – resulting in more planned pregnancies that equate to higher rates of education
completion for women, higher rates of overall participation in the workforce and more civic participation.
Increasing overall contraception uptake would mean a reduction in unintended pregnancies as well as
abortions. It would ensure pregnancies are intentionally timed and spaced, resulting in an increase of
overall maternal health outcomes. Fundamentally, it would save the healthcare system resources by
reducing the output costs associated with birthing and abortions despite an initial ongoing investment to
implement a contraception program. Evidence from previous programs implemented in Europe and
across the United States have demonstrated an overall positive return on investment, with the investment
in a universal program becoming cost neutral within 2 years of the onset of a program. Additional
research has shown a $9 dollar savings for every $1 invested in contraceptive programming.
Furthermore, recent Abacus polling showed that 83% of Canadians approve of a federal policy for free
prescription birth control across Canada and 7 in 10 Canadians believe creating policies to secure access
to birth control in Canada is an urgent issue4.

to birth control in Canada is an urgent issue4.

Sexual Health Information
The stigma that already surrounds sexual and reproductive healthcare undermines efforts to address
access issues and has great public health impacts. Increased stigma or confusion caused by mis or
disinformation can delay or prevent people from seeking care, can isolate people from personal and
community support networks, and can discourage organizations, institutions, elected officials, and
community leaders from taking necessary steps to ensure better access to sexual and reproductive
health and rights. The lack of access to accurate and unbiased information on sexual and reproductive
health is evidenced in the rising number of sexually transmitted blood-borne illnesses (STBBI) across the
country. Rates of STBBIs in Canada hit an unprecedented high in 2019 and have continued to rise5.
STBBI rates are one benchmark pointing to the lack of access to comprehensive sexual health
information.
Recommendation: Ensure robust evidence in support of SRHR and create an ongoing system
within Health Canada to monitor and counter misinformation on sexual health.
Canada must counter SRHR mis- and dis-information through infodemic management including the
systematic publication and promotion of accessible SRHR information and resources on Health Canada’s
website. The information and resources must be evidence based, rooted in human rights, inform people
of their rights to access SRH services, and regularly updated to respond to emerging trends in mis-and
dis-information. It is worth noting that dis-information and misinformation on SRHR cannot be effectively
addressed without disaggregated data and evidence. Budget 2021 allocated $7.6 million over 5 years for

the period of 2026-2031 for the next iteration of the survey

Submission to the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health Study on
Women’s Health
Endometriosis in Canada
Submitted by Kate Wahl, Katie Luciani, and Liane Belland
Questions concerning the content of this brief should be directed to:
[CONTACT]
[CONTACT]
[CONTACT]

Purpose
This submission describes the challenges facing women, transgender, non-binary, and twospirit people living with endometriosis in Canada. It also highlights opportunities for the federal
government to support the more than 1 million Canadians who have this disease by leading
coordinated action to ensure timely diagnosis and management.
Endometriosis affects 1 in 10 Canadian women
Endometriosis impacts at least one in ten women and unmeasured numbers of transgender,
non-binary, and two-spirit individuals. It is a complex and debilitating chronic disease that occurs
when tissue that is like the lining of the uterus implants outside of the uterus to form lesions,
cysts, and deep nodules. These growths are inflammatory and can be invasive, resulting in
severe distortion of pelvic anatomy and infiltration of the abdominal cavity. Although
endometriosis is commonly thought of as a gynecological disease, growths are often found on
non-gynecological structures such as bowel, ureters, bladder, diaphragm, and even lymph
nodes and the lungs.1 Left unmanaged, invasive endometriosis can result in life-threatening
complications including bowel obstruction and organ death.

There is no definitive cause or a known cure for endometriosis. Symptoms of endometriosis
often begin in adolescence and include, but are not limited to, severe menstrual pain, chronic
pelvic pain, and infertility as well as whole-body symptoms like fatigue. People with
endometriosis also experience high rates of anxiety, depression, and suicidality.2 Endometriosis
is managed with medication, specialized surgery, and multidisciplinary services depending on
the individual's goals and severity of disease.

org: Canadian Society for the Advancement of Gynecologic Excellence / EndoAct Canada / The Endometriosis Network Canada
text:
People with
endometriosis also experience high rates of anxiety, depression, and suicidality.2 Endometriosis
is managed with medication, specialized surgery, and multidisciplinary services depending on
the individual's goals and severity of disease.

It takes an average of at least 5 years for an individual to receive a formal diagnosis of
endometriosis in Canada.3 In that time, persistent and chronic symptoms associated with
endometriosis limit participation in daily life – adolescents with symptoms are 10 times as likely
to miss school than their healthy peers, and adults lose 11 hours of work per week.4 People with
endometriosis also face disruptions to developmental milestones like getting professional
training or starting a family, and undergo potentially unnecessary investigations and treatment
for other conditions.5 This diagnostic delay is in part attributed to low awareness of the disease
– many health care providers and members of the public think that the severe pain experienced
by women and people with endometriosis is normal.6
