The CTFPHC guideline emphasized that usual perinatal care should involve the
prenatal or postpartum care provider discussing past and current mental health
symptoms with patients, citing the Canadian national guidelines for family-centred
maternity and newborn care32. Interestingly, these guidelines actually encourage the
use of instrument-based screening for perinatal depression. The EPDS is a screening
tool, not a diagnostic tool, and can be used to facilitate a nuanced conversation
between patient and provider. The lack of mandated instrument-based screening tools
to facilitate usual care leaves screening approach to the discretion of the service
provider, who may not have the training necessary to recognize symptoms of
depression exhibited by patients. Indeed, evidence shows that healthcare providers
consistently report a lack of training in perinatal mental health and the need for further
professional development in this area33,34.

Unfortunately, the CTFPHC’s endorsement of “informal” perinatal depression screening,
when conducted by healthcare providers who lack confidence and resources, will
realistically place the burden on patients to bring their symptoms to the attention of
healthcare professionals. It is the most privileged of patients who have the greatest
capacity to advocate for their own care, and White patients who are more likely to have

their concerns taken seriously, thus perpetuating health inequalities and further
marginalizing Canada’s most vulnerable. Research has demonstrated particularly that
when perinatal depression screening is left to the discretion of the healthcare provider,
racialized patients are less likely to get screened35. The CTFPHC does acknowledge
that there could be a negative impact of their recommendation against instrument-based
screening on marginalized groups “Some marginalized individuals report barriers to
disclosing depressive symptoms or concerns with their health care provider (e.g., being
unsure how to bring up the topic of depression, concerns about stigma, aversion to
antidepressant medications or psychotherapy), in which case a recommendation
against screening may result in some individuals with depression not being identified.” It
is perhaps most egregious of all that this doesn’t seem to have been given much weight
in the development of the recommendation.

Overall, the CTFPHC’s analysis prioritizes concerns about speculative harms over
documented benefits, the perspectives of patients, and the opinions of experts.

We are gravely concerned about the potential impact of this CTFPHC guideline, given
that family physicians rely on CTFPHC guidelines to inform their practice. We have
already heard from colleagues anecdotally that they “don’t have to worry about
screening anymore”. This undermines decades of work by experts in BC and across
Canada to promote screening using the EPDS, and places the burden of advocating for
their mental health on Canadian women at an incredibly vulnerable time in their lives.

Recommendations

We are calling for an urgent re-evaluation of the CTFPHC guideline on perinatal
depression screening.

This re-evaluation should be conducted by an expert panel representative of diverse
stakeholders (clinicians, patients, researchers, decision makers) that is at arms-length
from any of the current authors of the guideline, and ideally external to the Public Health
Agency of Canada.

We recommend that the re-evaluation adopt the most cutting-edge approach to
guideline development: EBM+28.

While the guideline is under re-evaluation, it should be clearly labelled as such.

The BC Reproductive Mental Health Program

The BC Reproductive Mental Health program is a national leader in perinatal mental
health care, providing direct patient care for >5,000 patients per year, indirect patient
care for countless patients through a rapid consultation service to primary care
providers in support of their patients, as well as setting the standard of care for BC
through clinical practice guidelines, resources, and interdisciplinary education.

The Role of Physiotherapy Expertise in Women’s Health
A Submission to the Federal Standing Committee on Health for the Women’s Health Study
(October 5, 2023)

The Role of Physiotherapy Expertise in Supporting Women’s Health & Well-Being:
Ensuring that women receive access to physiotherapy care in Canada is essential as it provides
numerous health benefits including improved health outcomes, reduced healthcare costs, increased
equality, empowerment, and self-autonomy.

Physiotherapy professionals are highly skilled at addressing specific women’s health issues such as
pelvic floor dysfunction, pregnancy-related musculoskeletal conditions, postpartum recovery, menstrual
pain management, pre-and post-surgical rehabilitation, management of chronic pain conditions,
osteoporosis management, breast health, and lymphedema.

Recommendation 1: Ensure that women in Canada have equitable, publicly funded access to pelvic health
physiotherapy.

Recommendation 1: Ensure that women in Canada have equitable, publicly funded access to pelvic health
physiotherapy.

Physiotherapists play a crucial role in supporting women with a variety of needs, but access to pelvic
health physiotherapy is limited despite being established as a first-line treatment for a variety of issues1.
Pelvic health physiotherapy is well-established in many countries globally but continues to be an area of
growth for the Canadian healthcare system.
France, for example, has prioritized this care with a publicly funded pelvic floor rehabilitation program that
provides post-natal patients with 10, and up to 20 pelvic health physiotherapy sessions. This unique
program allows women to re-educate their pelvic floor following pregnancy and to resolve common issues
such as urinary or fecal incontinence, pelvic organ prolapse, and pelvic pain conditions2 3.
Providing equitable access to pelvic health physiotherapy remains challenging in Canada however as
practitioners with expertise in this area are limited and unavailable in rural and remote areas. This results
in Canadians needing to travel longer distances to access this important pelvic health care4.
To improve access to pelvic health physiotherapy care, we recommend that the federal government:
•
Allocate funding for additional research and educational initiatives to promote the benefits of
pelvic health physiotherapy. This could include explorative studies on the effectiveness of pelvic
health physiotherapy services.
•
Invest in telehealth programs or virtual care services to improve access to pelvic health
physiotherapy in rural, remote, or underserved areas.
•
Expand the eligibility of the existing Canada Student Loan forgiveness measure to include
additional health professionals – like physiotherapists, who work in designated rural and remote
communities5.
Recommendation 2: Integrate physiotherapists into primary care teams to support Canadians with chronic pelvic
pain care.
Patients diagnosed with pelvic pain conditions such as endometriosis, adenomyosis, irritable bowel
syndrome, and vaginismus are typically managed by their primary care physician through medication and
specialist referral. Patients who experience pelvic pain without a medical diagnosis, often have pelvic
floor dysfunction6, which affects the biomechanics of the rest of the body and the regulation of its
neurological system, making it challenging to treat this complex population within the current healthcare
model.

Patients who experience pelvic pain without a medical diagnosis, often have pelvic
floor dysfunction6, which affects the biomechanics of the rest of the body and the regulation of its
neurological system, making it challenging to treat this complex population within the current healthcare
model.

There is significant evidence that shows that physiotherapy care for pelvic pain is effective7. Therefore, it
would be beneficial to immediately integrate physiotherapists into primary care teams as they can assist
women right away while alleviating the strain on our health care system. This model would also decrease
the demands on primary care physicians, reduce the need for specialist referrals, and ensure that those
with chronic pelvic pain can access timely physiotherapy care.
Recommendation 3: Increase access to perinatal and postnatal physiotherapy care for Canadians
Physiotherapists with pelvic health training have the competency8 to perform internal examinations and
can therefore help during pregnancy by providing exercises and techniques that help strengthen pelvic
floor muscles that sustain substantial changes during pregnancy9. This can help reduce the risk of pelvic
floor dysfunction and assists with improved labour and delivery10.
In addition, women who have undergone a cesarean section are often given weight-carrying restrictions.
Access to physiotherapy care following a cesarean section will equip women with movement guidance
and strategies to support their function and maternal demands11 12.
As such, we recommend that the federal government take these actions to support access to perinatal
and postnatal physiotherapy care for Canadians by:
•
Increasing funding for perinatal and postnatal physiotherapy services. The federal government
can allocate additional funding to support the availability and accessibility of perinatal and
postnatal services nationwide. This could be funding for clinics, training programs, and research
initiatives.
Recommendation 4: Increase access to physiotherapy to support improved outcomes for gynecological cancer
treatments.

Gynecological cancers account for over 11% of all cancer diagnoses in Canada, with over 12,000 new
individuals diagnosed each year13 14. As survival rates have increased for gynecological cancers, there
has been a correlated increase in urinary incontinence, sexual dysfunction, and fecal incontinence15 16.
These dysfunctions are known to lead to feelings of distress in women who have survived cancer, to
reduce participation in activities of daily living and social activities, and to consequently lower overall
quality of life17 18.

These dysfunctions are known to lead to feelings of distress in women who have survived cancer, to
reduce participation in activities of daily living and social activities, and to consequently lower overall
quality of life17 18.

With a pelvic health physiotherapy intervention, using various treatments such as pelvic floor muscle
exercises and bladder training, recent evidence indicates that urinary continence and pelvic floor muscle
strength was preserved or significantly improved19 20. Further, pelvic floor muscle relaxation exercises and
dilation therapy has been found to benefit gynecological cancer survivors experiencing pain during sexual
intercourse21 22

Unfortunately, access to pelvic health physiotherapy services in the public health care system remains
limited and uneven across communities.

We recommend that the federal government:
•
Consider mechanisms to support improved access to the full spectrum of gynecological cancer
care by including physiotherapy care for gynecological cancer treatments.

Recommendation 5: Promote physiotherapy expertise for breast cancer and osteoporosis care.
Physiotherapy care in women’s health extends beyond pelvic health - it also supports women with postsurgical breast cancer care and osteoporosis.

Over 26,000 women are diagnosed with breast cancer each year23. Patients undergoing cancer treatment
suffer from many additional health complications including chemotherapy-related peripheral neuropathy
(loss of or decreased sensation in the extremities), lymphedema (tissue swelling resulting from fluid
accumulation) after breast cancer surgery, fatigue, and cachexia (disease-related muscle loss). Exercise
has been demonstrated to improve treatment-related side effects and decrease cancer recurrence24 25 26.

Osteoporosis is more common in women than in men. The 2010 Clinical Practice Guidelines recommend
weight-bearing aerobic exercise, resistance and core training, and balance training for individuals with
osteoporosis to help improve quality of life, physical function, pain reduction, muscular strength, and
balance 27.

The 2010 Clinical Practice Guidelines recommend
weight-bearing aerobic exercise, resistance and core training, and balance training for individuals with
osteoporosis to help improve quality of life, physical function, pain reduction, muscular strength, and
balance 27.

As movement experts, physiotherapists are well-positioned to support caring for women with either of
these conditions and should be the natural choice to provide exercise guidance that improves patient
outcomes and reduces pressure on the current system.
Conclusion
For women’s health, physiotherapy professionals provide specialized care in pelvic health, pre- and postnatal care, chronic pain, and musculoskeletal issues specific to women. As such, we strongly recommend
that the federal government engage physiotherapy professionals when designing federal programs that
impact and or support women’s pelvic health, pregnancy and postpartum care, and postoperative care, as
our expertise can contribute to improved healthcare outcomes, greater access to specialized care, and
better overall well-being for women across Canada.
Who We Are - The Canadian Physiotherapy Association Women’s Health Division
The Women’s Health Division (WHD) is a not-for-profit Canadian Physiotherapy Association (CPA)
division managed, operated, and advanced by volunteers passionate about women’s health and pelvic
health. We are national in scope and facilitate the communication, education, and service delivery for
physiotherapy practitioners on topics specific to women’s health and pelvic health.

The Canadian Physiotherapy Association (CPA) represents physiotherapy professionals, including
registered physiotherapists, physiotherapist assistants, physiotherapy technologists, and students across
Canada. Physiotherapy professionals provide essential rehabilitative care and treatment, enabling
Canadians to live well and actively participate in all facets of their lives.

Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions

Introduction
The Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions (CFNU) is the largest nurses’ organization in Canada,
representing 250,000 frontline unionized nurses and nursing students across the country. Our members
work in every sector of health care – from home care and long-term care to community and acute care –
and practice as licensed/registered practical nurses, registered nurses, registered psychiatric nurses and
nurse practitioners.
Nurses are the largest regulated profession in health care with a total of 466,014 regulated nurses
eligible to practice in Canada in 2022, as identified by the Canadian Institute for Health Information, and
an estimated 90% of them are women.1 There are many workplace issues in health care that have
significant health consequences for nurses, regardless of the individual nurse’s sex or gender. However,
since a vastly disproportionate number of nurses are women, it is important to recognize these health
issues as directly impacting women’s health in Canada.
Amid a health human resources crisis, with record nurse vacancies in health workplaces across the
country, it is even more imperative that the issues contained in this brief are addressed with robust
support from the federal government.
Mental health
Before the pandemic, one in three nurses screened positive for major depressive disorder, one in four
screened positive for generalized anxiety disorder and clinical burnout, one in three reported having
suicidal thoughts, and over 20% screened positive for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and panic
disorder. These findings come out of a landmark study commissioned by the CFNU with leading
researchers in the field from the University of Regina, who intentionally paralleled the methods and
designs of an earlier study they conducted on the mental health of public safety personnel (PSP). The
nurses’ study revealed that nurses screened positive for mental disorder symptoms at equal or higher
rates to PSP.2
Two pan-Canadian surveys of nurses carried out in 2021 and in 2023 reveal that these symptoms
worsened over the course of the pandemic. In 2021 two in three nurses said their mental health was
worse when compared to one year earlier, and in 2023 nearly half of nurses said their mental health was
worse when compared to a year earlier. In the 2021 survey, 94% of nurses said they had been
experiencing symptoms of burnout, with 45% experiencing severe burnout.3 In the 2023 survey, 73% of
nurses reported having symptoms of anxiety and depression within the last two weeks.4
Similarly, a study on nurses in British Columbia found increased prevalence of reports of anxiety and
depression resulting from the pandemic, particularly among nurses working in long-term care settings.5
Evidence also suggests that critical care nurses within Canada experienced psychological distress in the

While nurses and other health care workers commonly experience post-traumatic stress injuries, the
federal government focused on providing resources specifically to PSP through its Action Plan on PostTraumatic Stress Injuries. Given the success achieved through the federal government-funded pilot on
internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy for PSP (known as PSPNET), and the reality that other
workers in Canada – predominantly in female-dominated sectors – also experience alarming rates of
mental disorder symptoms and post-traumatic stress injuries, there exists an opportunity to tailor this
program toward these sectors.

Given the success achieved through the federal government-funded pilot on
internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy for PSP (known as PSPNET), and the reality that other
workers in Canada – predominantly in female-dominated sectors – also experience alarming rates of
mental disorder symptoms and post-traumatic stress injuries, there exists an opportunity to tailor this
program toward these sectors.

The Public Health Agency of Canada has expressed interest in partnering with the CFNU and the research
team behind PSPNET to tailor the PSPNET program to meet the needs of nurses and pilot the program.
The CFNU is pushing for federal funding to tailor the program and pilot it nationally, making it open to
any nurse or nursing student in the country.
While interventions such as these are critical, we cannot lose sight of the underlying cause of high rates
of mental disorder symptoms among nurses. The conditions of work are primarily responsible for nurses
experiencing such alarming rates of mental disorder symptoms, and only until chronic staffing shortages
are addressed will we be able to adequately tackle this issue. Nation-wide surveys consistently show a
large majority of nurses report their workplaces or units are regularly overcapacity, and many give safety
at their workplace a failing grade and report being subjected to routine violence and harassment.
Recommendation: That the federal government invest in internet-delivered cognitive behavioural
therapy for nurses (a female-dominated profession) just as it has done for public safety personnel (maledominated professions), through supporting the tailoring and piloting of PSPNET for nurses.
Excess hours of work
Nurses have long been reporting working between 16- and 24-hour shiŌs, which is significantly longer
than the typical 12-hour shiŌ. In 2022, the average number of weekly overtime hours performed by
nurses and allied health professionals stood at 8.2, which represents an increase of almost two full hours
since 2000 and is the highest amount on record.7
In a female-dominated profession, while women in Canada continue to do most of the unpaid household
work, the additional workload for nurses compounds feelings of overwhelm and burnout from taking on
too many responsibilities. It also prevents nurses from being present for their loved ones, at times
missing important milestones in the lives of their children and others. Nurses are commonly concerned
about their work-life balance, and a growing number are leaving or turning down unionized jobs with
pensions to work for private nursing agencies that gives them the flexibility to choose and refuse shiŌs
as well as a significantly higher wage.
Occupational fatigue arises, as well, with nurses working too long consistently, coupled with inadequate
periods of rest and recovery. Over time, occupational fatigue can lead to fatigue-based impairment,

7 htps://www.statcan.gc.ca/o1/en/plus/4165-nurses-working-harder-more-hours-amid-increased-labour-shortage

leading to adverse consequences for the well-being of the nurse and workplace safety outcomes that
endanger patients. As occupational fatigue increases, cooperation and trust among colleagues
decreases, and toxic workplace culture such as bullying and aggression increases.
The known occupational health and safety risks posed by fatigue has led to formal regulations around
work hours across most safety-critical industries. In civil aviation, transport (truck drivers, bus operators
and railway employees) and the nuclear industry, federal restrictions on work hours set limits on the
total number of consecutive work hours, the number of successive night shiŌs and the minimum periods
for recovery. However, no such regulations are in place for nurses, and the safeguards within collective
agreements are broken every day.
The CFNU is working with a leading researcher in the field to conduct a research report on this issue,
with the report set to be released in the fall of 2023.
Recommendation: That the federal government work closely with the provinces and territories to ensure
legislation and regulations are enacted around safe hours of continuous work and safe hours of work per
week in nursing in Canada.
Violence
Violence against nurses and other health workers has been a national emergency for many years – long
predating the pandemic. A 2019 report from the Standing Commitee on Health sounded the alarm,
issuing nine recommendations to the federal government. With nine in 10 nurses experiencing some
form of abuse in the last year, action cannot wait.

Nurses experience routine violence in the workplace, with female nurses oŌen experiencing sexual
harassment and assault from patients. These nurses face patients and their family members who spit,
kick, punch, grab, grope and at times inflect extreme violence toward them. Similarly to the underlying
cause of mental disorder symptoms among nurses, the key underlying factor leading to systemic levels
of violence against nurses is insufficient staffing of workplaces, which leads to higher frustration among
patients and their family members and increases the risk of violence directed at nurses and other health
care workers.

Similarly to the underlying
cause of mental disorder symptoms among nurses, the key underlying factor leading to systemic levels
of violence against nurses is insufficient staffing of workplaces, which leads to higher frustration among
patients and their family members and increases the risk of violence directed at nurses and other health
care workers.

We applaud protections introduced for health care workers in Bill C-3 but are concerned by the lack of
enforcement. The government must work to beter inform prosecutors and public safety personnel of
updates to the Criminal Code that strengthen protections for health care workers and ensure these
changes are enforced.
Nurses are looking to the federal government to show bold leadership through a health workforce
violence reduction plan that would include key recommendations from the above-referenced 2019
report, such as a national awareness campaign, a pan-Canadian framework on preventing such violence
enshrined in federal legislation, and targeted funding to upgrade infrastructure and training for
violence-prevention programs (i.e., devices linked to security, personal alarms, security de-escalation
training, flagging of patients with a history of violence, etc.).

Recommendation: That the federal government establish a health workplace violence reduction plan,
that includes a national awareness campaign, a pan-Canadian framework for the prevention of violence
in health care settings enshrined in federal legislation, appropriate training of prosecutors and public

safety personnel in relevant legislation, and targeted funding to the provinces and territories to upgrade
violence-prevention infrastructure and training.

safety personnel in relevant legislation, and targeted funding to the provinces and territories to upgrade
violence-prevention infrastructure and training.

Diseases and overnight shiŌs
Research has been able to demonstrate a relationship between prolonged rotating night shiŌs and the
development of breast cancer among nurses. The risk of breast cancer among nurses was shown to
increase during early adulthood and aŌer five or more years with six or more consecutive night shiŌs.8
In addition to breast cancer, night shiŌ work has been associated with several other diseases and health
problems, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, metabolic disorders, digestive problems,
depression and sleep disorder. Such workers might also have an increased risk for reproductive health
challenges, such as irregular menstrual cycles, miscarriage and preterm birth.9
As nurses are predominantly women, several of these health risks are heightened in this working
population as compared to other professions, and this cannot go unnoticed. These nurses require
additional tailored supports to ensure these health risks are mitigated through healthy lifestyle habits
and health risk indicators are consistently monitored.
Recommendation: That the federal government work with the Canadian Institutes of Health Research to
beter understand ways to mitigate associated health risks, and that the federal government ensure
proper monitoring and tracking of nurses’ health through overnight shiŌ work.
Conclusion
As the largest regulated profession in Canadian health care, made up predominantly of women, the
health of Canada’s working nurses is an important aspect of women’s health. Despite numerous health
challenges facing Canada’s nurses, nursing remains a rewarding profession with a unique opportunity to
change the lives of patients and residents for the beter.
Looking ahead, it is important for the federal government to work closely with provinces, territories and
employers to address nurses’ working conditions, which would ultimately improve their mental health,
lower their susceptibility to violence in the workplace and achieve a greater work-life balance with less
overtime, leaving more time for themselves and with loved ones. Let us work together to ensure femaledominated professions are provided with the same level of support as male-dominated ones, at all levels
of government.

Dear Chair Casey and Distinguished Members of the Standing Committee on Health:
On behalf of Beautycounter and Environmental Defence, we are raising the gendered impacts
of exposures to harmful product ingredients in personal care products as a disproportionate
impact that should be addressed as part of your study of impacts to women’s health, and
request that you provide officials with recommendations that support the Health Minister’s
mandate to introduce mandatory labelling of harmful ingredients in consumer products.
Ingredient transparency and disclosure not only provides individuals with the right-to-know
what is in the products they use, it also drives product reformulation to safer chemicals. This is
a large sector in Canada, with revenue in the Canadian personal care products market
expected to generate $11 billion CAD in 2023 and is projected to grow significantly. Harmful
substances must be phased out of these products, and ingredient transparency will help to
drive transformation in this sector.
As a mission-driven clean beauty brand, Beautycounter has built a movement for improved
transparency and accountability across the personal care products industry. Since our launch
in 2013, Beautycounter has led advocacy efforts across North America to update regulations
that have not kept pace with a growing body of science that demonstrates that harmful
chemicals do not belong in personal care products. Beautycounter’s mission is to get safer
products into the hands of everyone and we believe that advocating for more health-protective
regulations is a key part of delivering on this mission. With various third-party certifications and
awards for our unique approach to safety, we have prohibited 2,800 harmful or questionable
ingredients from our formulations. Additionally, we diligently screen each ingredient used in our
formulas against 23 health and environmental checkpoints, using the best available science to
help us determine what is safe.
Consumers are increasingly aware of potentially harmful ingredients used in personal care
products, including makeup, soap, lotion, hair products and fragrance. The government’s own
research found overwhelming public demand for labelling transparency and disclosure. Nine
out of ten people are concerned about the potential environmental and health impacts of the
products they buy and use; and seven out of ten say that ingredient information influences
their purchasing decisions. Including information on the chronic health effects of products on
product labels is important to most Canadians (79%), with the large majority saying it should
be mandatory to do so (75%).
Laws must keep pace with the growing scientific evidence underscoring the adverse effects of
harmful chemicals used in personal care products on our health and the environment.
Beautycounter has advocated for reforms to the Canadian Environmental Protection Act
(CEPA) since the company’s expansion into Canada in 2016 and has partnered with
Environmental Defence which has a long history of advocating for stronger laws and
regulations around toxics and harmful chemicals. In addition to continuing to strengthen CEPA,

In addition to continuing to strengthen CEPA,

Beautycounter proposes the following to reduce exposures to harmful chemicals in personal
care products:
1. Ensure mandatory product labeling of potentially harmful substances in
cosmetics.
The Government’s 2021 election platform promised that by Spring 2022, they would move
forward with mandatory labeling of potentially harmful chemicals in consumer products,
including personal care products. The government recently announced a Notice of Intent to
label so-called “CEPA-toxic” substances, but this is inadequate because these specific
chemicals have long been substituted by similarly hazardous substances (e.g., flame
retardants and bisphenols). In addition, the government has
announced amendments to the Hazardous Product Act, to apply hazard labels and ingredient
disclosure to products, but this proposal excludes cosmetics.
To be effective, labelling requirements must be applied to substances that have been identified
as potentially harmful. This approach has been implemented for several years in Europe and
several states in the U.S., including California. We need to harmonize the Cosmetic Ingredient
Hotlist with substances banned in the European Union, along with requiring complete
disclosure for products.
2. Close the fragrance loophole.
Companies are not required to disclose ingredients used for a particular scent, yet ingredients
listed simply as “parfum” or “fragrance” may contain dozens of chemicals of concern, and
companies are not required to disclose them to consumers. Ingredients in synthetic fragrances
have been linked to cancer, endocrine disruption, skin and lung irritation. There is a proposed
regulation to label fragrance allergens, but this proposal will fail to disclose these other
potential health harms. In our 2016 report, we identified several fragrance health hazards, and
we continue to seek disclosure for the public on these substances. People who are attempting
to avoid hazards such as carcinogens and endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in fragrance
are currently unable to access this information, and unless this regulation is expanded to
require labelling for hazards outside of allergens, this information will remain hidden.
Exposure to synthetic fragrance through the daily use of personal care products is pervasive.
We urge the federal government to close the “fragrance loophole” to deter companies from
using synthetic ingredients that may harm consumers, and urge it to include carcinogens,
EDCs and irritants in fragrance hazard labelling requirements, regardless of package size.
3. Tighten the rules for companies claiming “confidential business information”
when they refuse to disclose information about substances that are potentially
toxic.
Currently, businesses can claim that specific ingredients and information, such as scientific
studies on chemicals, constitute confidential business information (CBI) and thereby prevent
public access to information on the chemicals used in consumer products. This places
business interests over the health of people in Canada and their right to know the health and
environmental risks of what they are exposed to. Information pertaining to the health or
environmental risks of a chemical should be made public and never granted confidentiality.
While Bill S-5 -- the bill proposing reforms to CEPA -- proposes a higher degree of
accountability on CBI claims, CEPA should reverse the onus of proof regarding CBI so that the
requesting party must demonstrate the essential business need for chemicals names, data, or
other information provided to the government on chemicals to remain confidential for
confidentiality to be granted. Chemical names should only be kept confidential in exceptional
situations.
Clean beauty is not just a trend; it’s the new way of doing business. In fact, Beautycounter has
rapidly grown from a small start-up in 2013 to a company that enjoyed one of the largest

In fact, Beautycounter has
rapidly grown from a small start-up in 2013 to a company that enjoyed one of the largest

private investments in the history of the beauty industry, valuing Beautycounter at USD $1
billion. Beautycounter is here to prove that improved safety, transparency and accountability do
not hinder the industry’s ability to deliver on consumer expectations and fuel the economy. We
urge lawmakers to support stronger health-protective laws that ensure the safety of personal
care products sold across Canada.
If there is an opportunity for Beautycounter and Environmental Defence to appear in front of
the Committee to discuss these issues further, we would welcome the opportunity.
Thank you for your attention to this crucial issue.

Brief to the 44th Canadian Parliament,
1st Session Committee on Women's
Health
Authored by Manvir Sandhu

Dear Members of the Committee,

As we gather to discuss and enact legislation pertaining to the
health and well-being of Canada's women, our commitment to
inclusivity, equal opportunity, and the inherent dignity of every
individual. This brief aims to provide concise yet
comprehensive insights into the prevailing women's health
issues in Canada and recommends specific amendments for
our consideration.

1. Breast Cancer

Breast cancer remains the most commonly diagnosed cancer
among Canadian women, accounting for 25% of all new
cases. There is an apparent necessity to ramp up efforts
toward early detection and timely treatment.

Recommendation: Increase funding for the Canadian Breast
Cancer Screening Initiative and mandate coverage for regular
mammograms for all women over the age of 40 by private and
public health insurers.

2. Maternal Mortality

While Canada enjoys one of the lowest maternal mortality
rates globally, some communities, particularly Indigenous
women, experience disproportionately higher rates. This
disparity signals the need for a targeted approach.

Recommendation: Allocate additional funding to the Canada
Prenatal Nutrition Program, particularly in underserved
regions. Strengthen cultural competence training for
healthcare providers to address health disparities better.

3. Mental Health

Canadian women report higher rates of mood and anxiety
disorders than their male counterparts. Unfortunately, mental
health issues remain underfunded and often misunderstood.

Recommendation: Create a national strategy to increase
funding and resources for women-specific mental health
services, including trauma-informed care and support for
victims of domestic violence.

4. Sexual and Reproductive Health

Access to contraceptives and reproductive health services
varies across provinces, often resulting in inequitable service
delivery. All women, regardless of location, should have equal
access to these essential services.

Recommendation: Standardize access to sexual and
reproductive health services across all provinces, ensuring
equitable availability of contraceptives, abortion services, and
fertility treatments.

5. Aging and Elder Care

Women comprise the majority of Canada's elderly population,
and the feminization of aging presents unique health
challenges.

Recommendation: Increase funding for gender-specific elder
care research and support services, and ensure that long-term
care facilities meet the unique needs of aging women.

Conclusion and Recommendations Summary

Conclusion and Recommendations Summary

Health equity remains our guiding principle as we move
forward. We must strive to understand the nuanced needs of
women, recognizing their heterogeneity and diverse lived
experiences. Our recommendations are as follows:

1. Increase funding and coverage for breast cancer screening.
2. Allocate more funding to prenatal programs and improve
cultural competence in healthcare.
3. Develop a national strategy for women's mental health.
4. Standardize sexual and reproductive health services across
provinces.
5. Increase funding for women-specific elder care research
and services.

These recommendations insist that we look to progress; we
build a Canada that safeguards every woman's health and
recognizes their indispensable role in our collective future. We
should strive to create a nation where every woman can reach
her full health potential and where no woman is left behind.

I appreciate your commitment to these critical issues.

are also at the heart of the company’s concerns. The company has implemented sustainable business
practices to reduce its impact on the environment and is actively involved in its community, for
example with Le Chaînon in Montreal.
Canadian context: Unmet health needs of women
Although Canada is a developed country, health needs of women remain unmet, particularly among
marginalized and vulnerable populations2. Yet little effort is being made to better understand how
disease incidence, symptoms and treatment responses vary by gender3, and there are numerous
impacts. For example, women are diagnosed almost two years later than men for the same diseases4.

One of the most important women’s health issues in Canada is related to reproductive health, and this
goes far beyond fertility issues. From the onset of menstruation through menopause, easy access to
affordable, quality sexual and reproductive health care is essential to maintaining women’s health.
Mental health is also an important issue, and the recent pandemic has clearly demonstrated this,
especially for women9. Women are more likely than men to suffer from depression, anxiety and posttraumatic stress3. Social factors such as discrimination, violence and economic inequality can
contribute to these mental health problems. Targeted interventions such as psychological support
programs and promotion of gender equality can help reduce this burden.
Finally, chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease and cancer are important health
issues for women. Women are more likely than men to develop some of these diseases, and risk
factors such as smoking, physical inactivity and diet can have a disproportionate impact on their
health3. Programs to prevent and manage these diseases are therefore essential to improving the
health of women in Canada.
Women’s health in Canada is a complex and multifaceted issue. It is imperative that Canada make a

Unplanned pregnancies
While it may seem that unplanned pregnancy is no longer a
problem in Canada, in reality it remains a significant public
and reproductive health issue in Canada and around the world.
It is important to understand the difference between
unintentional and unwanted. Unintentional does not mean that
the baby was not wanted at all, but that the timing of
conception was not necessarily the best, for a multitude of reasons. In Canada, nearly 50% of
pregnancies are unplanned.
Unplanned pregnancies represent a significant direct and indirect cost to individuals and society.
Women who have an unplanned pregnancy are at increased risk of problems for themselves and their
child. A 2015 study estimated that the annual direct cost associated with unintended pregnancies in
Canada was more than $320 million1010. Unintended pregnancies also entail personal financial costs,
which may be even more difficult to bear at a time when many women have lost their jobs or faced
new financial pressures during the pandemic.
Unintended pregnancies do not only occur when contraception is not used. They can also result from
misusing or not using the contraceptive method. Efforts should be made to better inform women
about the range of contraceptive methods available so they can make the best choice for their
own situation.
Infertility: for optimal access
Conversations about fertility can be difficult for many people. This is often due to persistent stigma,
limited resources and countless barriers. However, Canadians should not suffer alone since one in six
Canadians experience infertility6. There are countless barriers to overcome in the fertility journey,
such as financial burdens, access outside of urban centres, as well as cultural, social and legal
factors11.
Access to fertility services varies considerably by province, income, and public or private insurance
coverage. The Minister of Health’s mandate letter refers directly to improving access to fertility
services for all Canadians: “With the support of the Minister of Women and Gender Equality and
Youth, work to ensure that all Canadians have access to the sexual and reproductive health services
they need, no matter where they live, by reinforcing compliance under the Canada Health Act,
developing a sexual and reproductive health rights information portal, supporting the establishment of
mechanisms to help families cover the costs of in vitro fertilization and supporting youth-led
grassroots organizations that respond to the unique sexual and reproductive health needs of young
people12.” Fertility issues are affecting a growing number of Canadians – it is essential that
access to these services be improved and financially supported.

this condition is not widely recognized or understood.
Patients do not feel adequately informed on this issue,
and most health professionals have received minimal

menopausal symptoms is neglected by the health care
system, workplaces and society.
Beyond menopause itself, the hormonal changes associated with menopause have an impact on other
health-related variables. For example, sex hormone levels after menopause are associated with an
increased risk of cardiovascular disease later in life. In postmenopausal women, high testosterone
levels are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease, and heart
failure13.13
As a global leader in women’s health, Organon is particularly well positioned to fill this knowledge
gap and highlight the unique impact menopause can have on various aspects of a woman’s life. For

because information, support and access to care are not readily available.

Conclusion: National Women’s Health Strategy
In conclusion, women continue to face systemic barriers in accessing health care and resources, such
as high costs, gender inequalities, gender stereotypes and gaps in women’s
health research. In addition, the COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the
vulnerability of women and the disproportionate impact of the disease on their
mental health, economic security and access to health care.
A national women’s health strategy could address these challenges and
ensure that women have access to safe, effective and responsive health
care throughout their lives. By focusing on prevention, early detection and
comprehensive women’s health care, such a strategy would help improve the
health and well-being of all Canadian women, regardless of age, ethnicity,
socio-economic status or sexual orientation. At Organon, we firmly believe that healthy women are the
backbone of thriving communities, societies and economies for generations to come. It is therefore
imperative that the Canadian government invest in a national women’s health strategy as soon
as possible to address the pressing needs of women in our country.

THE PROBLEM
Canada is falling short of global breastfeeding targets
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that “children initiate breastfeeding within
the first hour of birth and be exclusively breastfed for the first 6 months of life. From the age of 6
months, children should begin eating safe and adequate complementary foods while continuing
to breastfeed for up to 2 years and beyond”. Very few countries meet these recommendations,
and Canada is no exception. Recent data from The Public Health Agency of Canada indicate that
91% of parents initiate breastfeeding, but by 6 months just 35% of Canadian babies are
exclusively breastfed – falling far short of the 2025 WHO global target of 50%. Unfortunately,
breastfeeding rates are even lower among First-Nations and Inuit populations in Canada.
Accordingly, the Truth and Reconciliation Calls to Action 19 and 55.iv demand efforts to close the
maternal-child health gap between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal communities.
Breastfeeding supports women’s health, yet we lack a fundamental
understanding of human milk and lactation physiology
Breastfeeding saves lives and prevents illness - not only among children who are breastfed, but
also among women who lactate. Babies who are not breastfed have an increased risk of mortality
and infectious disease during infancy, and higher rates of asthma, obesity and diabetes later in
life. Women who do not lactate after pregnancy have an increase in all-cause mortality and
higher risks of ovarian and breast cancers, mood and anxiety disorders, diabetes, obesity,
hypertension, and cardiovascular disease.
Yet, remarkably, we still don’t fully understand the composition of breast milk, the physiology of
lactation, or the biological basis for its many health effects. In fact, more scientific papers have
been published on headaches than breastfeeding, and more federal research dollars from
Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research
Council of Canada have been invested to study canola (~42 million CAD) than breast milk (~$6.5
million CAD)
Protecting the choice to breastfeed promotes health equity, but is not prioritized
by the Canadian government
Breastfeeding is the normal way to feed an infant. Women experience health risks when the
choice to breastfeed is not protected by law, society and healthcare. For years the Canadian
strategy to improve breastfeeding rates has been to target individual families with education and
marketing. These efforts succeeded in improving breastfeeding intentions but leave Canadian
women disappointed in their inability to access their infant feeding choices. The ‘choice’ to
breastfeed or formula feed is often viewed as a simple decision the mother makes – but in reality,
women describe many structural barriers to breastfeeding that make that choice unattainable.

The ‘choice’ to
breastfeed or formula feed is often viewed as a simple decision the mother makes – but in reality,
women describe many structural barriers to breastfeeding that make that choice unattainable.

For example:
• Many hospitals do not have Baby Friendly Initiative designation, a WHO / UNICEF set of
guidelines to ensure breastfeeding support and care.
• Many medical staff have inadequate and often biased breastfeeding knowledge.
• Community primary care is currently unable to meet families’ breastfeeding care needs.
• International Board Certified Lactation Consultants (IBCLCs), health professionals with
specialized training and clinical skills, are unavailable in many hospitals, and absent in primary
care clinics.
• Public insurance does not cover breastfeeding education and IBCLC services. Private
insurance has variable and inconsistent coverage for breast pumps and IBCLCs.
By not investing in systems that make breastfeeding a feasible and actionable choice, the
government is failing to protect the health of women who choose to breastfeed. This
perpetuates health inequities because women with privilege (white, higher education and
socioeconomic status with adequate social supports) are more likely to actualize breastfeeding.

This
perpetuates health inequities because women with privilege (white, higher education and
socioeconomic status with adequate social supports) are more likely to actualize breastfeeding.

CALLS TO ACTION
The World Alliance on Breastfeeding Action emphasizes that breastfeeding is a shared
responsibility. To truly protect a woman's choice to breastfeed, structural changes must be made
at all societal levels, beginning with data collection and research, implementing access to
equitable quality care in our hospitals and communities and applying continuous feedback and
quality improvement from Canadian families who feed human milk. We propose four calls to
action.
1. Increase funding for collection and accurate reporting of infant feeding data
There is a lack of Canadian data on lactation, breastfeeding and other infant feeding practices
and barriers. Without accurate data and reporting, our government is unable to make informed
and accurate decisions about where to invest time, resources and money.
The most comprehensive national data collection tool, the Maternity Experiences Survey, has
been inactive since 2006 (over 15 years). A recent national report on breastfeeding was published
by the Public Health Agency of Canada, but it uses data that are already five years old (from
2017/18) and does not report on breastfeeding beyond 6 months. High-level statistics from the
Canadian Community Health Survey are reported every year, but they are not detailed enough
(i.e. do not measure total length of breastfeeding or ask about barriers among vulnerable
subgroups such as Indigenous peoples). In addition, no data are collected on breast milk
pumping, an increasingly common practice with differential impacts on maternal and child health
outcomes compared to breastfeeding directly at the breast.
Specific Recommendations
•
We call for mandatory data collection and reporting on lactation, breastfeeding, and other
infant feeding practices in hospitals and in the community, as well as infant feeding
experiences, motivations and barriers for all Canadian families.
Specifically, we ask for:
• In hospital and community, a national standard for electronic medical records for reporting
on breastfeeding intention, initiation and duration.
• More detailed and standardized collection and reporting of national data on lactation,
breastfeeding, and other infant feeding practices from national surveys (e.g. the biennial
Canadian Community Health Survey).
• A comprehensive maternity-specific survey to be collected and reported on at regular
intervals.

2. Secure and standardize insured, equitable and evidence–based breastfeeding
care and devices (such as breast pumps) that protect breastfeeding choice
Currently, there is substantial variability in breastfeeding and lactation standards, policies and
insured services across Canadian hospitals, organizations and provincial healthcare legislation.
For example:
• While some hospitals have the Baby Friendly Initiative (BFI) designation, many more do not.
Common barriers to BFI designation include gaps in staff knowledge and skills, high workloads
and lack of continuity of breastfeeding support.
• Because provincial healthcare does not offer consistent lactation care, third-party insurers
have played a key role in providing access to lactation consultants, lactation supplies (e.g.
pumps, shields, storage containers), or human milk substitutes when mother’s own milk is
not available. However, this coverage is often limited and inconsistent.
• The Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) program of Indigenous Services Canada provides
coverage for electric breast pumps, but only after the infant is born and a specific form is
filled by a health provider, creating barriers. For infants who have feeding concerns, NIHB
does not provide coverage for breastfeeding assessment and management by an IBCLC, even
for vulnerable infants with growth faltering, prematurity, low birth weight, or other feeding
concerns. Instead, NIHB covers the cost of formula, putting Indigenous mothers and children
at an even greater health disadvantage.
Specific Recommendations
•
We call for national guidelines that recommend every Canadian province and territory
equitably provide the highest standard of evidence-based breastfeeding and lactation
care.
•
We call for accessible, equitable and increased insured coverage for all Canadian families
who want to breastfeed, or who want access to human milk feeding.
Specifically, we ask that:
•
In every Canadian hospital, BFI designation is required, including standardizing
breastfeeding and lactation education among health workers, complying with the
International Code on Human milk Substitutes, and providing expert care to vulnerable
families at risk.
•
In every Canadian community, provincial and federal governments provide insured
coverage for IBCLCs, including adding IBCLC allied health in primary care offices.
•
Every third-party insurer is mandated to include lactation consultation, and coverage for
breast pumps and breastfeeding supplies in their plans with clarity and consistency.

Unfortunately, due to longstanding gender bias against women, the function of the mammary

poor, leaving those who want more knowledge to seek it out independently, often from sources
that are incomplete or out of date. To have effective, equitable, and inclusive care for women
and lactating parents at this very common and important phase of life, we need high national
standards and expectations for education in this field.

healthcare practices.

all geographic locations.

We believe the Canadian government has several
opportunities to protect and promote breastfeeding
and lactation choice and equity in Canada to
improve women’s health. Systemic barriers and lack
of public investment make breastfeeding and

Introduction
BGC Canada, Canadian Child Care Federation, Canadian Mental Health Association,
and YWCA recently released a policy brief about burnout impacting ECEs and Child
and Youth Workers. Ninety-six percent (96%) of ECEs in Canada are women1 and Child
and Youth Workers are also disproportionately women. In addition, access to child
care plays a large role in women’s overall well-being. As they are disproportionately
primary caregivers, a fully funded child care system is essential to improving women’s
economic and health outcomes.
This submission puts forward recommendations for how government can best support
the mental health of women working with children and youth to reduce burnout, foster
good mental health, and strengthen the national child care system. The full report can
be found here.
Background
It goes without saying that the pandemic has left, and will continue to leave, a lasting
mark on our lives. Extensive research makes clear the significant impact the pandemic
has had on the global economy, our mental health, our healthcare system, and
countless other facets of society.

Thirty-seven percent (37%) of Canadians report a deterioration in their mental health
since the onset of the pandemic.2 In addition, the impact on frontline staff working with
children and youth is disproportionately high, and yet only one third of employees have
access to programs to prevent burnout.3 Additionally, only one third of employees say
they would feel comfortable talking to their supervisor about mental health issues and
believe this would not impact their career.4
One in three Canadians are worried about their finances and 16% worry about having
enough food5. The social determinants of health like employment, food security,
adequate housing, and income supports all contribute to our mental health and wellbeing6. The pandemic has put pressure on these supports, causing an increase in
mental health challenges. This is particularly felt by those working with children and
youth who often earn low wages and are in precarious work.
We do not yet know the long-term impacts of the pandemic on our mental health, but
we do know that frontline workers have experienced higher levels of stress, anxiety and
depression.7 Women, 2SLGBTQ+ individuals, racialized individuals, (im)migrants and
parents have experienced compounding impacts on their mental health, with reported
higher levels of stress, anxiety and depression than the general population. This
includes those working with children and youth, from teachers to youth workers, and
Early Childhood Educators to parents. Extended periods of isolation, social
disconnection, school and childcare closures, limited contact with family, friends and
community, together have shone a light on caregiver labour in our society.
During the pandemic, women have taken on the majority of responsibilities when it
comes to care work and domestic labour. A recent study found that although four in
ten Canadians reported an increase in hours spent on domestic work during the

Ninety-six percent (96%) of ECEs in Canada are women12 and Child and Youth Workers
are also disproportionately women. They have faced additional burdens during the
pandemic, including providing essential services, homeschooling or child care, as well
as the extra burden of unpaid caregiving.13 Many women have left their jobs in order to
meet these domestic demands. “Unless the care economy is better supported, a
generation of women may exit the labour force entirely, reducing household spending

Early Childhood Educators (ECEs) and Child and Youth Workers are vital to the
success of the economy. However, their work is grossly undervalued and overlooked, as
evidenced by stagnant wages and chronic underinvestment in what is an essential
part of our social safety net. Due to historic underinvestment at all levels of
government, these roles have become increasingly precarious, offering workers little
security, even while the need for their services has grown radically.16
The undervaluing of child care work has meant a steady decrease in the number of
people entering the child care sector. In addition, approximately 50% of ECEs leave the
field within the first 5 years17. Many people want to come into the field, but a lack of
funding means employers pay low hourly wages and are unable to offer sufficient
hours.
In addition to the overarching challenges within the sector, the COVID-19 pandemic
has introduced some new and emerging challenges for Early Childhood Educators and
Child and Youth Workers.
Staffing Shortages
Child care programs across the country are facing staffing shortages. For example, an
organization in BC received 2 resumes for open ECE positions from September to
December, 2021, and both individuals canceled their interviews. That organization has
50 toddlers on a waitlist, but they don’t have the staff to support these families.
Another organization indicated that they sometimes need parents to pick up their
children early because they don’t have the staff to remain open. This causes a ripple
effect in the economy as workers (mainly women) with children may need to leave their
jobs or reduce their hours if they do not have access to care.
This staffing shortage adds additional stress for existing staff who have to manage a
higher workload. Many frontline staff report feeling guilty for taking days off because
of the impact it would have on their coworkers, who are already overworked and
stretched, and risking burnout.
16 A Feminist Economic Recovery Plan for Canada, YWCA Canada and Institute for Gender and the
Economy, 2020 https://www.feministrecovery.ca/the-plan
17 https://childcarecanada.org/documents/child-care-news/16/06/one-five-early-childhood-educatorsplan-leave-profession

“You only take days off when you need it like for a doctor's appointment. You’re not
taking vacation days or ‘me days’ because it’s going to negatively impact your
coworkers.” - Frontline worker

High Turnover

High Turnover

As previously stated, approximately 50% of ECEs leave the field within the first 5
years.18 This high turnover rate further contributes to staffing shortages as well as to a
lack of consistency for children and their families.

The largest issue in the ECE and Child and Youth sector is low wages. ECEs require a
post-secondary education and specialized skills, but the salary does not reflect that.
Many people in the field have trouble supporting themselves, or their families, on their
salary and therefore look for other opportunities even if their passion is early
childhood education or child and youth work.
Mental Health
Given all of the challenges outlined, it is no wonder that ECEs and Child and Youth
Workers are struggling with their mental health. Many workers stress the need for
additional mental health supports – citing concerns about growing waitlists, and
trouble finding the time for their own therapy with so many other responsibilities.
Recommendations
We need to see systemic-level change across all levels of government to address the
immediate and pressing workforce issues that are experienced by Early Childhood
Educators and Child and Youth Workers and better support women in these essential
jobs. Supporting the child and youth sector will also have compounding effects on
allowing people, particularly women, to get back into the workforce which in turn
supports the social determinants of health. Our recommendations include:
• Strengthen the ELCC system, including developing workforce strategies that
prioritize increasing wages, access to benefits, and paid time off.
•
As an element of workforce strategies, establish programs to incentivize careers
as ECEs and Child and Youth Workers including significant tuition subsidies and
18 https://childcarecanada.org/documents/child-care-news/16/06/one-five-early-childhood-educatorsplan-leave-profession

Our recommendations include:
• Strengthen the ELCC system, including developing workforce strategies that
prioritize increasing wages, access to benefits, and paid time off.
•
As an element of workforce strategies, establish programs to incentivize careers
as ECEs and Child and Youth Workers including significant tuition subsidies and
18 https://childcarecanada.org/documents/child-care-news/16/06/one-five-early-childhood-educatorsplan-leave-profession

wage replacements. These programs need to be high-quality, affordable,
expedited, and offer paid experiential learning opportunities.
•
Increase access to flexible funding to support the mental health of the child
care workforce and as an element of workforce strategies.
•
Invest in greater mental health supports for children and youth and caregivers,
including parents, grandparents, and guardians.
•
Increase funding for community-based mental health services and supports
delivered to front-line child and youth workers, including health promotion and
mental illness prevention and early intervention programs.
Conclusion
The pandemic has been challenging for all frontline workers including ECEs and Child
and Youth Workers. The sector is vital to the growth and development of our economy,
allowing people, particularly women, trans, and non-binary people to get back into the
workforce which in turn supports the social determinants of health. ECEs and Child
and Youth Workers are essential, and by implementing the above recommendations
we can ensure they are better supported and contribute to better outcomes for women
across Canada.

Policy Brief
www.ccsa.ca • www.ccdus.ca
October 2022
Policy Brief
Standing Committee on Health: Women’s Health
Brief
Who we Are
The Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) is the only national organization with a
legislated mandate to reduce the harm of alcohol and other drugs on people in Canada. Created by
an act of Parliament almost 35 years ago, CCSA provides national leadership by harnessing the
power of research and providing evidence-informed guidance to decision makers, curating
knowledge and bringing together diverse perspectives to galvanize individual and collective efforts.
Calls to Action
1. CCSA brief the Standing Committee on Health on taking an evidence-based approach to
providing substance use health care within the continuum of care of women’s health.
2. The Standing Committee on Health includes substance use health and addiction as part of the
continuum of care of women’s health by improving research, public education, awareness and
prevention.
3. The Standing Committee prioritize the data collection and research to include all women to
improve all women’s health across the gender and sex spectrums.
Background
CCSA welcomes the opportunity to provide a brief to the Standing Committee on Health’s focus on
women’s health. Sex and gender are essential in understanding the role substance use plays in
human health, risks of diseases and conditions, personalized clinical and consumer advice, and
effective health promotion.
It is important for practitioners and policy makers to consistently reflect on sex- and gender-based
evidence to tailor their approaches to substance use and addiction health, promotion, prevention,
treatment and policy issues. Therefore, the impacts of substance use on health are important
considerations within the women’s health sphere.
As sex and gender can be broken into several components, this brief provides input from our
research that examines the impact on the female sex-related factors (e.g., genes, hormones and
enzymes, physiology and anatomy, neurobiology) and the cisgender females’ existence (e.g., identity,
roles, relations and institutions) . In Canada, alcohol and cannabis are the most common
psychoactive substances used by the general population and by those who are pregnant. As such,
we have provided evidence on these two substances to show why it is important to include
substance use and addiction health within women’s health.

org: Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction
text:
As such,
we have provided evidence on these two substances to show why it is important to include
substance use and addiction health within women’s health.

Lastly, CCSA acknowledges substance use is an important consideration for all women and that
women’s health includes all women, not just those who are cisgender. However, there is a lack of
data available to do so extensively.1 To improve health for all women in this country, there must be
improved availability and access to data that is inclusive.
Canada’s Low-Risk Alcohol Drinking Guidelines
Women are particularly susceptible to alcohol-related harms because of both sex (biological) and
gender (social) factors. Biological factors enhance the effect of alcohol, causing more harm and
faster intoxication with lesser amounts in females. Social factors, including alcohol marketing tactics,
gender roles, attitudes and expectations increase girls’ and women’s vulnerability to many harms
from alcohol use. CCSA’s recent update of Canada’s Low-Risk Alcohol Drinking Guidelines (LRDGs)
includes evidence-based sex- and gender-specific advice. It addresses reproductive health, which is
also compromised by alcohol use.
Canada’s first LRDGs were originally published by CCSA in November 2011 (Butt et al., 2011). On
Aug. 29, CCSA released an update of the LRDGs for public consultation. An important part of this
revision is addressing factors and influences related to alcohol consumption for women.
Psychological differences between men and women do not significantly impact lifetime alcohol
related death risks. However, women are at greater risk than men of health harms from alcohol
consumption above low levels (two standard drinks a week). This is because biological factors
increase the impacts of alcohol on the female body, including faster intoxication, increased disease
risk (including breast cancer) and long-term harms. Biological factors impact the processing of
alcohol and are affected by sex-related factors, including enzymes, genes, body weight and size.
Women’s health includes reproductive health, which is another component impacted by alcohol
consumption. While there is mixed evidence on the impact of alcohol on pregnancy and delivery,
alcohol is a teratogen. This means that alcohol can cause malformation of the fetus. Drinking alcohol
while expecting can cause brain injury, birth defects, cognitive problems, learning disabilities,
behavioural problems and other health problems with lifelong effects. Both short-term exposure of high
consumption levels (more than six standard drinks a week) and low levels of exposure have resulted in
these effects. This is why, during preconception and pregnancy, it is safest not to drink at all.
Breastfeeding can also be negatively affected by alcohol because it can lead to decreased milk
production, early discontinuation of breastfeeding and changes in infant sleep patterns. Because
alcohol can enter breastmilk, a breastfeeding infant can be exposed to alcohol but will not be able to
metabolize it. For this reason, it is best not to drink alcohol while breastfeeding.
Sex, Gender and Alcohol
CCSA commissioned a report entitled Sex, Gender and Alcohol: What Matters for Women in Low-Risk
Drinking Guidelines? (Greaves et al., 2022). The report was written for practitioners, policy makers
and scientists who work in the substance use field and who design alcohol-related policies or
research. The authors review the evidence on how sex- and gender-related factors can determine the
effects and impacts of alcohol use, with a focus on women and women’s health. The report also
1 For example, in our Sex, Gender and Alcohol report, no systematic reviews were found specifically related to alcohol and gender identity.
However, several studies indicate potential gender influences on drinking for young people identifying as transgender, such as the links
between alcohol use and risky sexual behaviour, and identity formation as college students (Emslie et al., 2017; Hotton et al., 2013;
Tupler et al., 2017;).

explores the evidence on sex, gender and reproductive health, and how this informs understanding
of alcohol use and fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding.
The key findings of this report include:
•
Sex and gender both affect the use, impact and health effects of alcohol.
•
Sex-related factors enhance the impact of alcohol on female bodies, causing more
harm from lesser amounts of alcohol.
•
Gender-related factors contribute to the negative impacts of alcohol consumption,
especially for women [for example, perpetrators of sexual assault often target
someone who has been drinking alcohol or is intoxicated].
•
Sex, gender and factors such as trauma and poverty interact and make dependence
on alcohol and recovery more difficult for women.
•
Females need to know that their bodies can be more damaged by drinking
compared to males.
•
Practitioners need to recognize that both biological and social factors affecting
alcohol use create differential impacts on, and require tailored responses for
women, men and gender diverse people (Greaves et al., 2022, p. 1).
Cannabis Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding
A growing body of evidence suggests that cannabis use can negatively impact people’s lives,
including mental and physical health and pre- and postnatal development among children. In CCSA’s
Clearing the Smoke on Cannabis: Cannabis Use During Pregnancy and Breastfeeding report, we
explored the effects of prenatal cannabis exposure on offspring, including birth outcomes,
neurodevelopment processes, behaviour and mental health of children (Renard & Konefal, 2022).
This is an important part of women’s health and those who can get pregnant as the science is
emerging and requires facilitation to ensure pregnant or breastfeeding parents are informed.
The key findings of this report include:
•
Elements of cannabis can pass through the placenta and affect the fetus’s
development. Frequent cannabis use during pregnancy is associated with low birth
weight and is part of a cluster of risk factors related to other adverse birth
outcomes.
•
There are also affects on behaviour in children and young adults, including attention
deficits, emotional disturbances, increased hyperactivity and impulsivity, sleep
disorders, and increased likelihood of substance use...
•
Elements of cannabis can pass into breastmilk during lactation, which the infant
absorbs and metabolizes.
•
The effects of cannabidiol (CBD) use during pregnancy or breastfeeding are
unknown. Both clinical and preclinical studies are urgently needed to evaluate the
safety of CBD use during pregnancy.
•
Younger age, polysubstance use, lower socioeconomic status and history of mental
illness were factors associated with cannabis use during pregnancy. Concomitant

org: Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction
text:
Concomitant

use of tobacco, alcohol or both were risk factors for cannabis use among pregnant
women.
•
Information on the effects of cannabis use during pregnancy is essential to help
healthcare providers advise patients about the effect of cannabis use and improve
the health and well-being of patients and their children.
•
Pregnant or breastfeeding parents should have informed discussions with
healthcare providers about the potential adverse effects of cannabis use during
pregnancy to help them better understand the potential risks and help them make
informed and healthy choices (Renard & Konefal, 2022, p. 1).

Women’s Health Study
September 9, 2022
Submitted by:
Benjamin Davis
Senior Vice-President, Mission
The Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Society of Canada

Introduction

The Multiple Sclerosis (MS) Society of Canada is pleased to provide
this submission to the Standing Committee on Health’s study on
women’s health.

Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the
world. An estimated 90,000 Canadians live with the autoimmune
disease and, on average, 12 Canadians are diagnosed every day.

Women are three times more likely to be diagnosed with MS than
men. Most people are diagnosed with MS between the ages of 20 and
49 – the age at which many women are starting their careers and
perhaps building a family – and the unpredictable effects of the
disease will last for the rest of their lives.

MS is classified as an autoimmune disease of the central nervous
system. The immune system attacks myelin, the protective covering of
the nerves in the brain, which disrupts communication between the
central nervous system and the rest of the body. The disease course of
MS is unpredictable, often occurring in a pattern of relapses and
remissions, also known as an episodic disability. There is currently no cure for MS, though multiple
disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) exist to help manage symptoms.

The immense socioeconomic impact of MS for women

The cost of paying for medication, services, equipment, and treatment is a significant economic burden
for people with MS and their families. The unfortunate truth is that women with disabilities are more
likely to live in poverty compared to the general population. We also know that MS affects women at a
much higher rate than men – 75 per cent of Canadians living with MS are women. Women already face
challenges with income security, averaging lower incomes than their male counterparts, which in turn
makes them more susceptible to poverty.

Women already face
challenges with income security, averaging lower incomes than their male counterparts, which in turn
makes them more susceptible to poverty.

The DisAbled Women’s Network (DAWN) Canada report states that up to 33 per cent of people who live
in poverty are women with disabilities.1 DAWN’s More Than A Footnote campaign also reports that
women with disabilities are the largest and poorest minority group worldwide. These women face the
highest rates of physical, systemic, financial, psychological, and family violence.2

Income levels have a direct impact on the health and well-being of women living with MS. A team of
researchers, including Dr. Helen Tremlett from the University of British Columbia, published research in
2019 that showed that socioeconomically disadvantaged people living with MS tend to have greater
disability.

In this multinational study of [socio-economic status] and long-term outcomes in MS, we

have demonstrated an association of lower [socio-economic status] at onset of MS with
an increased hazard of reaching key disability milestones and the onset of secondary
progression.3

Further research findings presented at the 2021 Americas Committee for Treatment and Research in
Multiple Sclerosis (ACTRIMS) suggest that socioeconomic status also impacts the speed at which the
nervous system is damaged, leading to greater disability.
Michelle Hewitt, a longtime volunteer with the MS Society, has experienced firsthand the struggle of
having a stable income. She had to leave her job as a school principal after her MS diagnosis in 2008.
“People with disabilities, especially those with invisible and episodic disabilities like those that come
with a diagnosis of MS, lived in poverty before the pandemic and their lives have only worsened during
the pandemic,” Michelle said. “[Eradicating disability poverty] can only happen with major systemic
change, such as the Canada Disability Benefit. I hope that all levels of government can recognize that
they need to come together and act quickly for people with MS, and all disabled people.”
Income security is a top priority for the MS Society and we are extremely supportive of the Canada
Disability Benefit. This benefit would be a major game changer for people – especially women – living
with MS and the MS community is highly engaged with us on this issue.
The negative impact of COVID-19 on women living with MS

The uncertainty of the pandemic resembles what it’s like to live with MS. Every day, people with MS wake
up to adversity and do everything in their power to persevere. There is no cure, and the disease-modifying
therapies (DMTs) available to mitigate the impact of MS symptoms often weaken or alter an individual’s
immune system, leading to an impossible choice – forgo treatments or risk worse outcomes from a COVID19 infection. A recent study found that people living with MS experienced increased feelings of isolation
and had a negative outlook on their mental health and physical wellbeing as the pandemic went on.4 The
increased social isolation from public health restrictions puts them at greater risk for mental health issues
such as depression, which is already much higher for people living with MS than the general population,
as well as longer-term health impacts.
