People with MS in long-term care facilities experienced a lack of connection with the outside world due

Breakthrough MS research offers hope

One of the biggest breakthroughs in MS research came earlier this year, when researchers at Harvard
University published a landmark study showing an association between Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)
infection and MS. Researchers have long believed that MS is caused by a combination of genetics,
lifestyle, and environmental factors. EBV, a virus that causes infectious mononucleosis, has long been
suspected of being a risk factor for MS.

The Harvard study showed that the risk of MS increased 32-fold after infection with EBV. The
researchers also found that serum levels of neurofilament light chain, a biomarker of MS
neuropathology and neurodegeneration, was increased only after EBV infection, suggesting EBV
infection preceded the development of MS. Furthermore, researchers at Stanford University looking at
this association have found a potential mechanism for how EBV infection may trigger MS.

This finding is one of the biggest breakthroughs in MS research and potentially holds the key to
preventing MS for future generations of Canadians. This research could greatly impact the future of
Canadian women living with MS. However, we know that women’s health research is underfunded, with
women’s health grants composing fewer than 10 per cent of Canadian Institutes for Health Research
(CIHR) grants.5 Given that MS is often called “Canada’s disease” because of the prevalence of MS among
our population, the MS Society recommends the government invest critical funds in research focused on
MS prevention and therapeutics strategies targeting EBV.

Julia Nimilowich, a woman who lives with MS, has stated that she is encouraged by the research as she
often worries that her children could one day be diagnosed with the disease.
As a parent living with MS, the possibility of my kids developing MS weighs heavily in the
back of my mind. It’s a question that my husband and I had for my doctors when we
decided to try and start a family. Could our children develop MS? Is it hereditary? The
truth is they can’t say with 100% certainty if our kids would develop MS. It’s a risk we
had to take… The recent findings of the connection between MS and the Epstein-Barr
Virus give me hope in preventing my children from developing MS.

Conclusion

Canada has one of the highest rates of MS in the world and women are disproportionately impacted by
MS – 75 per cent of people living with MS are women. These women are more likely to live in poverty
and have been more negatively impacted by the pandemic than the general population.

Many women living with MS don’t have a stable source of income, which is why our MS community,
including the MS Society of Canada, is highly supportive of the immediate implementation of the Canada
Disability Benefit. We would like to see this benefit implemented, making direct payments to individuals
who live with a disability and specifically including episodic disabilities as defined in the Accessible
Canada Act.

With new research on the horizon about the cause of MS, the time is now for the Government of
Canada to invest in MS research so we can work to prevent future generations of Canadians, especially
Canadian women, from experiencing this episodic yet progressive disease.

Declaration of the Parliament of Canada
(Assisted Human Reproduction Act, 2004. 2012)
In an unusual move, Parliament prefaced this Act with a declaration of 7 principles:
The health and well-being of children born through the application of assisted human
reproductive technologies must be given priority in all decisions respecting their use;
The benefits of assisted human reproductive technologies and related research for individuals,
for families and for society in general can be most effectively secured by taking appropriate
measures for the protection and promotion of human health, safety, dignity and rights in the
use of these technologies and in related research;
While all persons are affected by these technologies, women more than men are directly and
significantly affected by their application and the health and well-being of women must be
protected in the application of these technologies;
The principle of free and informed consent must be promoted and applied as a fundamental
condition of the use of human reproductive technologies;
Trade in the reproductive capabilities of women and men and the exploitation of children,
women and men for commercial ends raise health and ethical concerns that justify their
prohibition;
Human individuality and diversity, and the integrity of the human genome, must be preserved
and protected.
Overview
The AHR Act (AHRA) is long overdue for a full and comprehensive Parliamentary review.
Building a family is not easy for the 1 in 6 Canadians who suffer with infertility. Assisted
conception can be confusing, costly and both physically and emotionally distressing. In most
provinces it is easier to get complete comparative information on a used car than an IVF clinic.
The privatization of fertility services has meant that corporations now control essential human
health and safety data for these services. Fertility treatments are just another unregulated
business transaction between a company and a customer. The unregulated and variable costs
of these services raise equity and access issues for the infertile. There is no way to assess if the
“add-ons” that are promoted to patients contribute to the success or safety of treatments.
Faced with infertility and in order to give informed consent, Canadians are searching for
independent information to help them decide what treatment is the right choice. They want a
simple tool that calculates success rates in exactly the same way for each clinic so that they may
select the best providers for the clinical services needed.

They want a
simple tool that calculates success rates in exactly the same way for each clinic so that they may
select the best providers for the clinical services needed.

Aside from self-promoting pregnancy data, corporations have little interest in the long-term
follow-up of the effects of treatments on the health and well-being of children born from these
treatments or the persons who must undergo multiple interventions. For example, a mainstay
of IVF treatment, frozen embryo transfer (FET) has been shown in Nordic government studies
to increase the risk of both childhood cancer and macrosomia ( Sargisian N, Lannering B, et al.
(2022) Cancer in children born after frozen-thawed embryo transfer: A cohort study. PLoS Med
19(9): e1004078. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1004078) . Another study concluded
that FET, unlike a fresh embryo transfer increases the risk of a hypertensive crisis for a pregnant
woman (https://www.news-medical.net/news/20220706/Pregnancies-following-frozenembryo-transfer-have-higher-risk-o f-hypertensive-disorders.aspx).
A comprehensive review by Dr. Leader of the policies of the provincial regulatory bodies has
shown that there is a wide variation in the ways in which the provinces regulate assisted human
reproduction. Patients, donors, surrogates and gametes move freely across this country. It’s
time to use existing laws and professional bodies to establish standard rules applicable across
Canada. Canadians in need of this medical treatment deserve no less.
We know that with some effort and co-operation, that this can be done. Some provinces are
already acting to address this problem. For example, Quebec has introduced an extensive
framework, including detailed clinical practice parameters, facility standards and an active
program of oversight of insemination and IVF therapies. Working together, Alberta,
Saskatchewan and Manitoba have recently developed a specific accreditation model based on
International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards for non-hospital surgical facilities
that provide assisted reproductive therapies. Ontario and British Columbia inspect IVF facilities
as private surgical facilities. Ontario does not inspect the IVF laboratories. Nova Scotia and New
Brunswick have IVF clinics but offer no specific programs for oversight. Prince Edward Island,
Newfoundland and the territories do not have IVF clinics. None of the provinces use
performance indicators to assess IVF clinics or their laboratories.
We recommend that Canada follow the approach now taken by Australia, another federal state,
and support an audited and publicly available comprehensive data system on maternal and
perinatal outcomes applicable to all IVF clinics in each province.
Commercialization and Surrogacy
The Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies recommended against the
commercialization of reproductive technologies and related practices, including surrogacy.
Parliament followed that recommendation. Commercial reproductive procedures and practices,
including surrogacy, are prohibited under the Criminal Code. For whatever reason, this law has
not been used. On-line shopping by Canadians for donor eggs and sperm from paid donors
continues. The regulations currently in force provide a layer of protection for women and
reassurance for intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement, but some practices are
prohibited by section 6 generally and section6(1) of the Act. If normalizing the practice of

If normalizing the practice of

surrogacy is the aim of regulations, then greater clarity and transparency are essential. We
believe that the Criminal Law is not the proper tool to address the problem of the
commercialization of reproductive services and practices such as surrogacy.
Action going forward
Looking to the future, how we can improve the quality of reproductive health care for women
in Canada? Part of this process has already been accomplished. The federal and provincial
governments have worked together in the past to bring their family and estate laws up to the
date to meet the changing nature of families. In so doing, they have clarified the legal status of
children born from women who have used these reproductive technologies. The two levels of
government must now extend their collaborative efforts to address the other pressing issues
described in this submission.
Reproduction and Research
As a result of medical-scientific and genetic research, at which Canadians excel, we have seen
remarkable, exciting game-changing advances in reproductive biology and the treatment of
infertility and inheritable conditions. The updating of the Act to ensure that this research is
both favoured and funded must be a priority. Canadians have the human right to benefit from
the advancement of science and its application (article 27, Universal Declaration of Human
Rights, 1948). The criminal bans on specific research should be reassessed to ensure that they
do not negatively affect human genetic and reproductive research. Some options already exist.
Alternatives to amending the Act have been recommended by legal scholars. For example,
under the Food and Drug Act there are nuanced regulatory schemes backed by criminal law
powers capable of protecting public health and safety without overly restricting health
innovation (Bubela T, Kleiderman, Master Z et al. (2019) Canada’s Assisted Human
Reproduction Act: Pragmatic Reforms in Support of Research.Front.Med. 6:157). As well, “there
are many examples of the evolution of criminal law as societal values and views of what
comprises reprehensible conduct shift over time.” (Bubela T, et al. 2019).
In Summary
Canada’s Assisted Human Reproduction Act is long overdue for a full and comprehensive
Parliamentary review with a specific mandate to recommend legislative action to bring the Act
up to date and make it fit for the purpose of improving the health and well-being of Canadians.
The Supreme Court of Canada’s decision made it clear that the provinces have jurisdiction in
the provision of reproductive medicine and related therapies and practices involving AHR
technologies such a s IVF. However, there remains a key co-ordinating and funding role for the
federal government to provide the leadership that is required to address the most pressing
clinical issues and to establish “a proportionate, responsive and considerate regulatory regime
for research using human reproductive materials in ways that are currently prohibited” (Bubela
T, et al. 2019).

Purpose
This submission details the unique role that birthworkers play in promoting
positive health outcomes for pregnant and birthing people, children, families,
and communities. It also provides an overview of the current landscape of
abortion access in Canada’s North and outlines the role of birthworkers—
specifically, abortion doulas—in providing abortion support.

While this study is titled “Women’s Health,” we would like to acknowledge that
many aspects of health and the health system that impact cis-gender women
also affect people of all genders, including transgender men and non-binary
people. Therefore, while not to detract from the gender-specific impacts of
various policy decisions, the Northern Birthwork Collective chooses to employ
terms that are inclusive of all persons who may experience pregnancy, birth, or
birth-related concerns (i.e., “pregnant person”).
Introduction
What is Birthwork?
Birthworkers, more commonly known as midwives or Doulas, work with
individuals to provide full-circle support throughout the reproductive journey.
Birth workers are unlike nurses, obstetricians, or midwives as they do not offer
medical or obstetrical care. Birthworkers practice holistically by providing
physical, emotional, mental, spiritual, and informational support for the
pregnant person and their family.

There have always been people in the community who assisted with
reproductive care. Specifically, Indigenous birthing people have traditionally
delivered their babies at home surrounded by local birth attendants (birth
keepers, grandmothers, aunties, and knowledge keepers) and family.
Knowledge was transmitted intergenerationally and included logistics of
birthing, as well as traditional medicines. Birthworkers extend the role of
traditional birth attendants by connecting birthing people to social support,
maintaining boundaries within the medical birthing experience, and
supporting Indigenous birthing people to create a positive experience for
themselves.

Birthworkers extend the role of
traditional birth attendants by connecting birthing people to social support,
maintaining boundaries within the medical birthing experience, and
supporting Indigenous birthing people to create a positive experience for
themselves.

Birthworkers also advocate for the needs of the pregnant person and their
family to ensure their voices are heard, and birth preferences are respected.
Birthworkers are companions throughout the entire reproductive journey and
provide continuous support during pregnancy, birth, infant or pregnancy loss
and the postpartum transition. Birthworkers practice the foundational
principles of respect, advocacy, and compassion to support pregnant people
and their families to have empowering experiences, as they define.

The Importance of Birthwork
Canada’s Birth Evacuation Policy1
Since 1892, birthing persons who live on reserve or in remote communities have
been forced to give birth in urban medical centres. While Canada stated that
this policy aimed to reduce infant mortality among Indigenous birthing
persons, it has undermined longstanding Indigenous birthing practices and
traditions.

Birth evacuation leaves the birthing person at risk of birthing-related
complications, including an increased risk of preterm labour, fetal
neurodevelopment, and decreased rates of breast/chestfeeding, affecting
relationships and family bonding.

Hospitals in the NWT have experienced shutdowns of their obstetrics units due
to insufficient staffing. As a result, many birthing people experiencing urgent
delivery challenges are transported via air ambulance to nearby urban
centres, such as Edmonton, to give birth. In some cases, evacuations are also
required for abortion care. This is an unnecessary and unjust health inequity.
Access to Birthworkers in the North
Birthwork is not currently a regulated profession, nor is it well-known in the
North. The lack of access to birthworkers leaves birthing persons with few
options for giving birth in their home communities, which perpetuates birth
evacuations and their associated harms. NBC has a strategic priority to
increase awareness around birthwork and its benefits, increase the number of
birthworkers across the NWT, and provide cost-supported care to Northern
pregnant and birthing people.

Doulas and Abortion Care
Abortion Access in the NWT
Rural and remote communities face inequitable access to abortion services. In
the NTW, many pregnant people must travel outside their home communities—
if not outside of the territory—for abortion services.

The NWT’s Health and Social Services Authority operates the Northern Options
for Women program, a self-referral program designed to provide access to
Mifegymiso, a combination product of two drugs (Mifepristone and
Misoprostol) that are taken in sequence for the medical termination of a
pregnancy. The Department covers the cost of travel to Yellowknife or Inuvik, as
well as the costs of the prescription for those without government or employersponsored health benefits.2 In 2019, Health Canada’s removed the requirement
for an ultrasound before receiving Mifegymiso. Unfortunately, the Department
has not yet created a policy to ensure those residing outside of Yellowknife or
Inuvik can receive Mifegymiso without an ultrasound.

For those looking for abortion services after the nine-week gestation period,

Abortion Doulas
Abortion Doulas are trained to provide physical, mental, and emotional support
before, during, and after one receives an abortion. Abortion doulas are not
currently integrated into the formal health system; instead, they often provide
services through grassroots, not-for-profit organizations. Most Canadian
abortion doula services tend to receive funding via donations. Some
organizations that offer abortion doula services may receive grants or other
funding, but this is likely due to the provision of different sexual and

and to ensuring that every student we serve has the opportunity to succeed and

Catholic teachers take a broad view of our responsibility to make this province, and

their family.
1.04
Simply put, teachers have a front row seat to the impact that socio-economic factors
and the social determinants of health play within a student’s educational journey –
and this has steeled our resolve to make this province, and world, fairer and more
just for all.

to make impossible choices between purchasing much-needed medications and buying food for their family. 1.04 Simply put, teachers have a front row seat to the impact that socio-economic factors and the social determinants of health play within a student’s educational journey – and this has steeled our resolve to make this province, and world, fairer and more just for all.

1.05
It is with this context in mind that Catholic teachers offer the strength of our voice to
supporting the principles and purpose behind Bill C-64.
1.06 Background
The reality is, in Ontario, well over a million people have no prescription medication
coverage of any kind (Conference Board of Canada 2022). Looking nationally, in 2019
Statistics Canada estimated that as many as 7.5 million Canadians had no access to
drug coverage (Yang and Gupta 2024).
1.07 However, this tells only part of the story – in addition to the millions of uninsured
Canadians, there are many more who are under-insured. A recent poll by Leger found
that almost one-quarter of Canadians (22 per cent) have reported splitting pills,
skipping doses of medication, or deciding not to fill or renew a prescription due to
cost. In addition, 10 per cent of Canadians who identify as having one or more chronic
conditions have ended up in the emergency room due to worsening health because
they were unable to afford prescription medications (Leger 2024).
1.08 The simple fact is, despite repeated promises from successive Canadian federal
governments to lower drug costs over the past four decades, Canadians today pay
more per capita for prescription medications than residents of any other country,
except for the United States and Switzerland (Lindsay and Birak 2023).
1.09 Canada also holds the dubious distinction of being the only country in the world that
has a universal health care system, but does not also provide universal coverage for
prescription drugs (Zimonjic 2024). According to the Parliamentary Budget Office

According to the Parliamentary Budget Office

(PBO), in 2021-22 Canadians spent more than $5.1 billion out-of-pocket for
prescription medications (Barkova and Busby 2023).
1.10 Against this backdrop, Bill C-64 has the potential to be transformative to the lives of
millions of Canadians. Beyond the obvious health-related benefits, this legislation has
the potential to generate significant economic benefits, as research has clearly
demonstrated that public service investments in areas such as health and education
produce substantial savings in other areas over the long term. For instance, a 2023
study published in the JAMA Health Forum concluded that, over a three-year period,
providing prescriptions free of charge to Canadians saved the public health care
system an average of $1,488 per patient, per year – by helping to prevent costs such
as unexpected trips to the hospital (Persaud et al. 2023).
1.11 For these and other reasons, Catholic teachers support the passage of Bill C-64. At the
same time, there are several notes of caution – as well as recommendations – that the
Association believes the committee must consider as the legislation enters its final
phase of debate.
2.
CHALLENGES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
2.01 While the Association supports the principle and purpose of Bill C-64, there are several
areas that HESA must keep in mind, and address as the bill moves through the
legislative process.

CHALLENGES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
2.01 While the Association supports the principle and purpose of Bill C-64, there are several
areas that HESA must keep in mind, and address as the bill moves through the
legislative process.

2.02 Federalism and Provincial/Territorial Negotiations
Given the nature of Canadian federalism, and the fact that health care falls under
provincial and territorial jurisdiction, the federal government will be required to
engage in a series of bilateral negotiations to operationalize this legislation.
2.03 A recent history lesson in Ontario serves to highlight the potential difficulty with this
proposition. Optimism arose in 2021 after the federal government announced the
Canada-Wide Early Learning & Child Care (CWELCC) plan, a national framework to
work toward a goal of $10-a-day child care by 2026.
2.04 One by one, provinces reached agreement with the federal government and saw child
care fees reduced almost immediately. The Ford government proved the outlier, and
for months Ontario held the dubious distinction of being the only province in Canada
that had refused to sign-on to the federal child care plan.
2.05 When a deal with Ontario was finally reached in March 2022, news began to emerge
regarding the nature of the Ontario government’s holdout. An investigative exposé by
the Toronto Star revealed that the Ford government had quietly made concessions to
for-profit daycares, stripping a series of checks and balances from Ontario’s funding
rules, dropping a restriction on “undue profits,” and refusing to implement a wage grid
that would have standardized and increased pay for early childhood educators
(Mendleson and Kennedy 2022).
2.06 Today, the program’s very existence has come under threat due to the Ford
Conservative government’s refusal to reach sustainable funding agreements with
providers (CBC News 2024). Across Ontario, child care centres are contemplating

Across Ontario, child care centres are contemplating

closure as the provincial government refuses to provide the funds necessary to
maintain operations (Yazdani 2023; Khan 2023).
2.07 This anecdote serves as a cautionary tale about the fraught nature of federalprovincial/territorial negotiations, especially under the current Ontario regime led by
Doug Ford. Beyond negotiations with the provinces and territories, the federal
government will also need to consider its approach to negotiations with pharmacists,
which may create unique challenges.
2.08 The Association urges the federal government to prioritize the signing of
bilateral agreements with provinces and territories concurrently with the
progression of Bill C-64 through the legislative stages. The Association also
requests that any funding that flows through the provinces and territories be
accompanied by stated requirements and obligations for these monies to be
spent as intended.
2.09 Clarity, Robust Funding, and Future-proofing Legislation
At the time of writing, a number of important questions remain regarding the specifics
of Bill C-64. To this end, the bill proposes to provide universal single-payer, first-dollar
coverage for two categories of medicines: contraceptives and certain diabetes
treatments. While this is a positive step, the legislation as proposed excludes many of
the most common and most expensive medications within these categories, such as
semaglutide. As such, the Association recommends that the federal government
commit to significantly expanding the scope of medications covered by Bill C64.

As such, the Association recommends that the federal government
commit to significantly expanding the scope of medications covered by Bill C64.

2.10 To maximize program effectiveness, the federal government should also
dramatically increase its planned investment. In March 2023, the federal
government announced an investment of up to $1.5 billion over three years as part of
its pharmacare plan. However, according to Diabetes Canada, in 2022 the out-ofpocket medication cost for Canadians with Type 1 diabetes was up to $18,306 per
person; and for those with Type 2 diabetes, out-of-pocket costs could exceed $10,000
per person. With almost 12 million Canadians living with diabetes, the cost of
medications far exceeds the government’s planned investment. More broadly, the PBO
estimates that in 2021-22, total prescription drug spending in Canada, excluding
hospital medications, amounted to $36.6 billion – a 28 per cent increase compared to
2015-2016 (Barkova and Busby 2023) – with roughly 15 per cent not covered by any
public or private insurance sources.
2.11 A third factor to consider is the program’s longevity and sustainability. It is an open
question as to whether a change in government would see the continuation of a
national pharmacare program, should it not be fully implemented by the time of the
next federal election. As such, the Association calls on the government to work
swiftly, not only to pass this legislation – with our recommendations – but
also to finalize agreements with provinces and territories.
2.12 Respecting Supplementary Coverage
A national pharmacare plan is both noble and necessary, and will benefit millions of
Canadians – especially the approximately 20 per cent of Canadians who do not have
access to prescription drug insurance (Yang and Gupta 2024). At the same time, in
developing this plan, the government must take care to avoid inadvertently
disadvantaging any Canadians who currently have access to prescription medication
coverage. While the inclusion of “first-dollar coverage” in the legislation is welcome,

While the inclusion of “first-dollar coverage” in the legislation is welcome,

the federal government must ensure to acknowledge and respect those
Canadians with supplementary coverage.
3.
AN IMPORTANT STEP FORWARD
3.01 Accessible and affordable health care is a cornerstone of Canada. To this end, Bill C-64
represents a significant enhancement to Canada’s health care system, and will have a
profound impact both at an individual and societal level, in the short and long terms.
OECTA urges the government to consider the recommendations presented in this
submission, and to quickly move Bill C-64 through the legislative process and to full
implementation.

The Canadian Association of University Teachers

Need for a universal single-payer
pharmacare program
Expenditures on prescription drugs keep increasing
every year. In 2023, spending on prescribed drugs was
estimated to be just over $41 billion. Forty-three per
cent of this spending was by public sector/governments
($17.7 billion), 37 per cent from private
insurers/employers ($15.2 billion), and 20 per cent was
out-of-pocket costs for people ($8.3 billion).
Alongside other organizations, including the Canadian
Health Coalition, of which CAUT is a member, and the
Canadian Labour Congress, CAUT supports a singlepayer, universal pharmacare program. Bill C-64 is a
first step towards this program. With many Canadians
struggling to access prescription drugs and managing
higher costs-of-living, the need for a national
pharmacare program is obvious and immediate.
Of all the beneficiaries covered under the private
insurers’ share of prescription drug expenditure, 30 per
cent are public sector employees at the federal,
provincial, territorial, and municipal levels.1
Private and public drug plans have out-of-pocket cost
barriers for many people through premiums,
copayments, deductibles, and annual and lifetime limits.
A universal public pharmacare programs will improve
the health of Canadians, offer significant savings for
individuals, businesses, and public institutions, and
support a healthy and resilient workforce required for a
robust economy.
One in five Canadians, or 7.5 million people in Canada,
have no prescription drug insurance and pay out-ofpocket for prescription medications.2
The significant savings from a pharmacare program
will mean that workers and employers can invest more
towards better wages, enhanced retirement savings,
and improved services.
One in ten people in Canada were not able to afford
one or more of their prescription drugs, with 38 per
cent of these people having private insurance coverage
and 21 per cent having public insurance coverage that
did not sufficiently cover the cost of the medication.3
Recommendations
A new national poll released in February 2024 found
that more than one in four adults in Canada have had
to make difficult choices to afford prescription drugs,
such as cutting back on groceries, delaying rent,
mortgage or utility bills, and incurring debt.4 The poll
also found nearly one-quarter of Canadians (22 per
cent) have reported splitting pills, skipping doses, or
deciding not to fill or renew a prescription due to cost.
1. Quickly pass Bill C-64 to ensure timely access
for millions of Canadians to contraception
and diabetes drug and device coverage.
2. Sign bilateral agreements with the provinces
and territories concurrently with the
progression of Bill C-64 through the different
legislative stages.
In 2021, 16 per cent of adults aged 25 to 34 and four per
cent of seniors 65 years and older did not adhere to
taking their drugs as prescribed because they could not
afford it.5 As a result, one in ten Canadians (10 per
cent) with chronic conditions have ended up in the
emergency room due to worsening health because they
were unable to afford prescription drugs.6
3. Expand Bill C-64 to a national, universal,
single-payer pharmacare program with firstdollar coverage for a comprehensive list of
prescription drugs.
4. Ensure due diligence in member selection for
the Committee of Experts and ensure that
there are no conflicts of interest that would
influence the operations or financing of a
pharmacare program.

Ensure due diligence in member selection for
the Committee of Experts and ensure that
there are no conflicts of interest that would
influence the operations or financing of a
pharmacare program.

Conclusion
Employment-tied private
prescription drug insurance
Canada is the only developed economy in the world
with a universal health care system without a universal
prescription drug program. A recent CIHI report
highlight that “prescription drug prices in Canada are
the third highest among the Organisation for Economic
Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries and
are expected to rise. Due to these rising drug prices,
many Canadians encounter significant obstacles in
accessing necessary medications.”7
Labour force inequities for workers are mirrored in
employment-tied private insurance drug plans. Higher
waged employees have better private prescription drug
coverage compared to low waged employees. People
working part-time jobs, or any precarious jobs, get little
to no benefits plan for prescription drugs.
This is particularly relevant for approximately onethird of our members who are contract academic staff
(CAS). CAS access to health insurance benefits varies.
Even when CAS and their families may have benefits,
they may lose access to them over the summer, in
between contracts. With growing precarity in the
academic workforce, consistent access to health care
benefits that offer prescription drug coverage will
become a larger issue.
Bill C-64 offers a first step forward towards ensuring
that all Canadians have access to the prescription drugs
they need, and that our country benefits from the
efficiencies of a single-payer, national pharmacare
program.

Statement of Principles
Lilly believes that all Canadians should have access to medicines they need. Canada
currently operates as a dual-market system, meaning that Canadians are either
publicly or privately insured for their medicines. Relatively speaking, a very small
number of Canadians do not currently have drug insurance.

Lilly supports a pharmacare model that provides coverage for those Canadians that are
currently uninsured while maintaining Canada’s existing dual-market system. Lilly
supports efforts to provide uninsured individuals with access to drug insurance, while
incorporating the following principles:
• Lilly supports healthcare reforms that provide access to those who currently lack
it, while preserving or improving access for those who have it today;
• All patients should have access to innovative therapies as part of their overall
health benefit;
• Patients should be active participants in their healthcare;
•
A competitive private market is an effective means of delivering efficient and highquality care for patients; and
•
Access to prescription drugs is crucial to meeting the needs of various vulnerable
patient populations covered by public insurance programs.

Based on its text, Bill C-64 is not aligned with these principles. The legislation contains
provisions that could unnecessarily replace the coverage for privately insured individuals,
disrupt access to innovative medicines, and potentially exacerbate supply disruptions for
medicines.

Lilly maintains that the most appropriate and effective method of extending coverage to
individuals who are un- or under-insured is by way of a ‘fill-the-gaps’ model that
addresses need in a directed and targeted manner.

Recommendation
Lilly recommends that section 6(1) and 6(2) of Bill C-64, An act respecting pharmacare,
be amended to remove the requirement that pharmacare measures be contingent on a
single-payer, first-dollar implementation. Instead, the Bill should support a ‘fill-thegaps’ model that provides access for the uninsured and the continued operation of
Canada’s dual public-private market system.

Instead, the Bill should support a ‘fill-thegaps’ model that provides access for the uninsured and the continued operation of
Canada’s dual public-private market system.

By applying a fill-the-gaps approach to pharmacare that supplements rather than
eliminates private insurance for specified medicines, the federal government will ensure
that all Canadians have access to the drugs and related products they need, while
respecting the existing Canadian market with a targeted application.

Lilly firmly believes that no Canadian should go without access to medicines they need
because they are unable to pay. However, we are concerned that the single-payer, firstdollar implementation proposed in Bill C-64 is likely to impact Canada’s
competitiveness in the life sciences sector and its ability to attract new and innovative
medicines in comparison to its global peers, which will have consequences for
Canadian patients and Canada’s life sciences industry in the long term.

Policy Implications and Unintended Consequences
Section 6(1) of Bill C-64 is particularly problematic from Lilly’s perspective. While the
remainder of the legislation deals with future-looking work to establish national
pharmacare, this section provides the Minister of Health with the ability to make
payments to provinces and territories to increase universal, single-payer, first-dollar
coverage for the specified list of medicines upon the conclusion of negotiations with
provinces, whether or not a pharmacare framework is established.

This single-payer, first-dollar nature of the legislation as set out in section 6(1) and
reinforced in section 6(2) could compel public coverage of diabetes and birth control
medicines cited in the backgrounders, whether or not a patient has existing private
insurance. Given that over 97 per cent of Canadians already have some form of private or
public drug coverage
1, this is an unnecessary overreach.

Given that over 97 per cent of Canadians already have some form of private or
public drug coverage
1, this is an unnecessary overreach.

From an industry perspective, expropriation of the private market by the government
would raise significant concerns about the predictability of launching innovative new
medicines in the Canadian market and the relative competitiveness of our market to peer
jurisdictions. In further disrupting the Canadian market, the impact to patients,
healthcare professionals and systems perspectives cannot be understated – presently,
only 1 in 5 new innovative therapies launched globally are launched in Canada
2. We
believe the unpredictability of the future private market potential in Canada may impact
the timing or likelihood of medicines being brought to Canada or, at a minimum, the
confidence of manufacturers in pursuing public access for future innovative therapies,
should their entire private market be at risk of expropriation by the government.

Pharmaceutical and biologic supply chains are immensely complex. Healthcare reforms
that can have a seismic shift on how and which medicines and biologics are used need to
account for the impact on supply chains and ensure that sufficient redundancy is created
to endure supply chain disruptions and shortages in order to minimize impact on patient

care and healthcare systems. Further, manufacturers need to be properly engaged and
consulted to ensure stability of supply. Bill C-64 creates tremendous potential for future
supply challenges and disruption in access to essential medicines. This cannot be
understated, in particular, when dealing with reference biologics and biosimilars like

Further, there are no details within the legislative text nor by way of accompanying

Bill C-64 ought to codify the process and criteria for prescription medicines to be

Submission on Bill C64 An Act respecting pharmacare
BIOTECanada offers comments on the proposed legislation with a focus on ensuring the needs of
patients, particularly those with current barriers of access to safe, effective medicines and
ensure they have the benefit of timely treatments. The landscape of public policy issues
currently facing the entire Canadian healthcare system is complex and generating extensive
public concern regarding the ability of the system to meet patient needs.
As providers of today’s game changing, and in many cases now lifesaving medicines and
therapies, the biotechnology sector in Canada regards the needs of patient care paramount in all
the sector's representations made to governments at all levels. This is particularly relevant as the
world of medicine is changing rapidly, with the system seized with delivering the new, complex
therapies forthcoming from throughout the sector, including gene and cell therapies,
combination biologics and many others. Canada needs to address the long-standing issue of
delays in listing new medicines for physicians and their patients to actually access and seek to
match the performance of our global peers.
BIOTECanada is concerned Bill C-64, An Act Respecting Pharmacare is a piecemeal and
uncoordinated approach to addressing gaps in healthcare coverage which risks disrupting the
current balance of public and private programs for drugs. This disruption will have significant
implications for Canadian patients at a critical time when remarkable new drugs and drug
technologies are emerging from the biotech sector, including those being developed by
Canadian biotech companies.
There currently exists a series of processes and analysis applied to medicines entering the
Canadian spectrum of care, each of which addresses the value and cost of those medicines.
Adding another potentially limiting formulary process to address gaps which could in fact be
addressed by the existing processes already in place, may jeopardize the intent of the
government to fill the existing deficits of care. It is important for the system of care, already
complicated and lengthy, not endure any further constraints on its ability to adopt and benefit
from new solutions to improve care for Canadian patients.
The goal for regulators, payers, innovators and federal and provincial governments alike, should
be a streamlined system of regulatory and health technology assessment aimed at delivering
access to the best of new, life changing therapies, to meet the dynamic of scientific innovation in

The goal for regulators, payers, innovators and federal and provincial governments alike, should
be a streamlined system of regulatory and health technology assessment aimed at delivering
access to the best of new, life changing therapies, to meet the dynamic of scientific innovation in

a safe, timely and effective manner. In this context, initiatives such as pharmacare must ensure
Canada remains at the forefront of a regulatory system designed to meet patient needs, while
adapting to the scientific discoveries imminent throughout the sector.
RECOMMENDATIONS:
Recommendation 1: The Government of Canada should build on Canada’s extensive existing
coverage instead of replacing it with limited public formularies.

Ensuring Canadian patients have timely, efficient and fair access to the medicines they need is
imperative for all Canadians. The current framework of the pharmacare legislation suggests
creating yet another stream of decision making that will undoubtedly add further confusion,
potentially stress the system of care with administrative requirements outside of existing
processes, and ultimately have limited effect for those in need of care. Rather than creating a
separate new system, federal investment and intervention should in fact build on the existing
systems already in place, with the ambition of streamlining and simplifying methods of access to
care.
Recommendation 2: The federal government needs to work to improve and accelerate access to
new medicines and strengthen Canada’s life sciences environment to attract clinical trials and
promote research and development. With hundreds of world leading technologies and products
being developed in Canada, the future of health care outcomes brings much promise. The
ecosystem supporting that work is comprised of academic, research hospitals, small and
emerging companies and global commercial companies each contributing with research,
expertise or investment. The global competition for this work has grown to unprecedented
levels. Canada needs to ensure it does not create any potential negative impacts on the
ecosystem.
ABOUT BIOTECanada:
BIOTECanada is the national industry association with 240 members representing the broader
Canadian biotech ecosystem including start up and emerging companies, research organizations,
established commercial companies, academic and research organizations and investors, all
dedicated to developing modern science-based solutions to improve human health, food
security, and our environment.
BIOTECanada continues to work to represent the opportunities for Canada to modernize its
healthcare system using the best of new technologies and solutions emanating from throughout
the Canadian ecosystem and global network of researchers, entrepreneurs and manufacturers
building the solutions patients need today and in the future.

Re: Written Submission in Response to Bill C-64, An Act Respecting Pharmacare
Dear Members of the Standing Committee on Health:
The American Chamber of Commerce in Canada (AmCham Canada) is a private, nonprofit, membership organization that promotes the two-way flow of trade, goods,
services and investment between Canada and the United States. On behalf of the
members of AmCham Canada, we welcome the opportunity to provide our perspective
on Bill C-64, An Act Respecting Pharmacare. We commend the Government of
Canada’s aspiration to improve public health and reduce healthcare system strain
through providing more equitable access to prescription drug coverage.
However, we believe the proposed single-payer system as set out under Bill C-64
presents significant challenges that could disrupt existing care systems and increase
uncertainty for Canadians. Our primary concern with the Bill, as currently drafted, is its
potential negative impact on the accessibility and availability of new innovative
medicines in Canada. We remain concerned that there has been no assessment on
supply chain implications and the risks this could create from a patient, health case
system and industrial impact must not be understated.
Canadians deserve timely access to the medicines they need under any coverage
scheme. Public plan patients experience significantly longer wait times for new
medicines compared to those with private insurance. Currently, Canadians must wait
over two years to access new medicines through current public drug plans, which is a
year longer than in many other developed countries.

Currently, Canadians must wait
over two years to access new medicines through current public drug plans, which is a
year longer than in many other developed countries.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) has estimated the cost of a full single-payer
pharmacare plan to be $33.2 billion in its first fiscal year, increasing to $38.9 billion
within three years. We are concerned that the approach contemplated in C-64 does not
adequately account for the important role of employer-sponsored benefit plans, which
offer timelier access to a much broader range of medications.
Bill C-64 proposes covering select diabetes medications and contraceptives. However,
the proposed list may not be evidence-based and would fall substantially short of the
current coverage levels provided by private plans. Potentially transitioning Canadians
away from well-functioning private insurance to a much more narrow public plan for
these medications would escalate public costs without improving (and perhaps
reducing) overall access to medicines.
Analysis by the Conference Board of Canada indicates that 97.2% of Canadians
already have some form of prescription drug coverage. The uninsured gap of 2.8%, as
well as jurisdictional plan design issues, would be better addressed through targeted
policy measures, comparable to the approach being pursued under the Government’s
Canadian Dental Care Plan, rather than overhauling the entire system.
A targeted approach would extend drug coverage to the minority of Canadians without
it, ensuring practical and financially sustainable improvement in the overall health of
Canadians while ensuring continuous benefits for the 27 million Canadians currently
covered by employer-provided insurance.
We believe a pharmacare system should focus on bridging current coverage gaps
rather than duplicating existing coverage or replacing it with less effective options.
Implementing a single-payer system as proposed would likely reduce existing coverage,
delay access to innovative therapies, and place additional strain on the Canadian
healthcare system.
Further, addressing the 10% of Canadians who are eligible to a public or private drug
plan but not enrolled should be a focus of Government’s efforts.

Rather than rushing to adopt a flawed model and risk disrupting access to medicines for
the majority of Canadians, we strongly recommend a more thoughtful reconsideration of
the single-payer universal system proposed in Bill C-64. A targeted approach that
preserves and expands timely access to prescription drugs across Canada should be
the focus of the Committee’s deliberations and amendments to the legislation. For
instance, the Committee could inquire with the Government what gaps in coverage
could be address if the $1.9B was used across therapeutics areas.
We ask the Committee members and the government to prioritize addressing specific
gaps in coverage while maintaining efficient collaboration with provinces and territories.
