Recommendation 9: That a registry be created to track drug penetration rates in Canada and
compare them with similar countries.
The Government is supportive of the intent of the recommendation to track and compare drug
penetration rates. Decisions based on data and science are critical to the Government of
Canada. We would like to highlight several initiatives that are already helping to address these
needs.
To enhance the sustainability and future readiness of Canada’s drug system, the Government,
as noted previously, has created the CDA-AMC. The CDA-AMC, with its focus on public value
within Canada’s drug and health technology systems, has programs in place to improve the
collection and use of data and analytics to inform and support decision-makers across the
country, especially those who work in the pharmaceutical sector.
Additionally, the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) and the PMPRB work
collaboratively to develop and maintain the National Prescription Drug Utilization Information
System (NPDUIS), which provides critical information and intelligence on price, utilization and
cost trends for patented and non-patented medicines. This allows for more comprehensive and
accurate information on medicine use and sources of cost pressures. The NPDUIS holds most
prescription drug claims data for publicly funded drug programs in Canada, and also captures
drugs paid through private drug plans or paid for “out-of-pocket” in certain provinces. This data
is linkable to other data sets at CIHI, supporting analysis related to use, effectiveness and safety
of pharmaceuticals. This is particularly true for drugs for rare diseases where pan-Canadian data
is often required due to smaller patient populations in individual jurisdictions. To respect the
need for a fair, independent, and impartial price monitoring process, PMPRB performs NPDUIS
work independently of the price monitoring activities of the PMPRB.
CIHI is advancing a 5-year Pharmaceuticals Data and Information Roadmap to modernize the
data holding that it shares with the PMPRB’s NPDUIS group, build a comprehensive data
foundation to address stakeholders’ needs and priorities, expand data access, and enhance
analytics. This work will support health system planning and decision-making across federal,
provincial and territorial governments, as well as other organizations with decision-making
needs in the drug space, including the CDA-AMC. The Government also relies on CIHI to deliver
comparable and actionable information to accelerate improvements in health care, health
system performance and population health across the continuum of care.
Another source of quality information is the PMPRB’s Meds Entry Watch report, which explores
the market entry of new medicines in Canada and other countries. Building on a retrospective
analysis of trends since 2017, this report focuses on medicines that received first-time market
approval through the US Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency,
and/or Health Canada, and analyzes their uptake, pricing, sales, and availability. This
publication informs decision makers, researchers, and patients of the evolving market dynamics
of emerging therapies in Canadian and international pharmaceutical markets.
For a global perspective on the pharmaceutical landscape, the Government uses or refers to, as
necessary, the services of global experts in advanced international analytics in the life sciences
industry to obtain comparative data across various aspects of
healthcare. As an example, we
monitor the research projects of the Centre for Innovation in Regulatory Science, which is a
neutral, scientific and independently run global forum for policy leaders from government
regulators, health technology assessment agencies, the pharmaceutical industry, and other
stakeholders in healthcare, such as patient organizations and academia. The Government’s
commitment to evidence-based work requires that our sources of information be both
domestic and international to guide government policy and funding decisions.
In holding to our commitment on prioritizing science and evidence in decision-making, the
Government has worked diligently to ensure that the right measures are in place to support
evidence-based decision making. We will therefore continue to leverage the
PMPRB, the CDA-AMC and other existing resources to monitor key pharmaceutical
efforts of CIHI,

Recommendation 10: That the Government of Canada maintain a public registry of publicly
funded innovations, alone or in partnership with the industry, and ensure that what it funds
is available in the Canadian marketplace.
The Government is supportive of the intent of the recommendation to improve access to health
innovations in Canada, and to ensure that information regarding such investments is available
to the public.
The Government recognizes the importance of encouraging, supporting and growing innovation
across the life sciences sector and continues to invest in health innovations and ensures that
these investments are well documented for public interest. In 2021, the Government launched
the Biomanufacturing and Life Sciences Strategy (BLSS), with the objective of attracting
investments and supporting the re-build of a competitive, innovative and sustainable
biomanufacturing and life sciences sector, better positioning Canada to confront future health
emergencies. These efforts have translated into investments of more than $2.2 billion across 38
projects to grow the domestic life sciences ecosystem. All projects which receive funding are
published, such as on departmental webpages. To further enhance accountability and
transparency, the contracts and funds awarded are also subject to proactive market disclosure
available online on the Open Government website.
As part of the BLSS, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research is also advancing the Clinical
Trials Fund to strengthen clinical trials infrastructure in Canada and support the training of new
clinical researchers. More recently, building on investments from March 2023 to establish five
Research Hubs through the integrated Canada Biomedical Research Fund and Biosciences
Research Infrastructure Fund, the Government announced on May 6, 2024 an investment of
$574 million in 19 projects at 14 research institutions across Canada that the Research Hubs will
oversee. The Hubs combine the strengths of academia, industry and the public and not-forprofit sectors to jointly improve pandemic readiness and the overall health and well-being of
the Canadian population. Thanks to these efforts under the BLSS, Canada has attracted major
investments from leading global companies.
The Government endeavors towards funding agreements or arrangements that support the
outputs of funded activities being made available in Canada, including by leveraging existing
investments to build new strategic partnerships. However, it is important to note that federal
funding does not ensure that resulting innovations will be made available in Canada. Some
innovations, such as those involving health products and manufacturing facilities, may be
subject to regulatory requirements to ensure their safety, efficacy and quality, including those
under the
and its Regulations. If evidence is insufficient, Health Canada will
not grant a marketing authorization for the innovation.
Food and Drugs Act
Other considerations outside of the
federal purview may impact whether an innovation is available in Canada, such as the decisions
of private rights holders.
In addition, provincial and territorial governments are responsible for
the delivery of health care for their residents, including determining which health products are
reimbursed and under what conditions for their eligible populations.
The Government also acknowledges the importance of communicating how public funds are
supporting innovation, and has various policies and requirements to facilitate making this
information accessible to the public. As a foundation, the
Directive on Open Government
provides a framework for building and maintaining transparency and accountability to meet
expectations for increased access to federal information. Additionally,

Keeping

The Government has taken decisive
steps, through several important federal initiatives, to encourage innovation and invest in
strengthening our domestic life sciences ecosystem while ensuring this information is accessible
to
Conclusion
The Government is committed to collaborating with the PMPRB as well as with partners and
stakeholders to ensure that Canadians have access to the safe and high-quality care they need
and deserve, including as it relates to prescription medicines. It will continue to prioritize
actions that will improve health equity, accessibility, affordability, and outcomes, and that have
the potential of long-term savings to the health care system.
Once again, I would like to thank you, Mr. Casey, and all members of the Standing Committee
on Health for this Report and its recommendations. I would also like to thank the PMPRB again
for their continued dedication to protecting and informing the Canadian population as it relates
to excessive pricing for patented medicines.

Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)
Submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Study: Government's Advanced Purchase Agreement for Vaccines with Medicago
December 06, 2023
Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is one of the world’s leading independent emergency
humanitarian medical organizations. For decades, we have witnessed people being denied treatment for neglected or
deadly diseases because the medicines they need have been priced out of reach by private pharmaceutical companies or
never made available in places where they live — even when those medicines were discovered using public funding,
including money provided by the Government of Canada. This system cannot continue.

In recent years, MSF has consistently called upon the Government of Canada to ensure that public funds are used to
benefit public health over private profits. Canadians support taking action to improve access to the medicines and
vaccines that our government is paying to develop. In October 2020, we wrote to then-Minister of Health, Patty Hajdu,
and provided her with a copy of an MSF petition calling on the Canadian government to make the hundreds of millions of
dollars of public funding it invests in medical research and development (R&D) each year conditional on recipients of
those funds ensuring that the lifesaving medicines, vaccines, or other health technologies developed with it are affordable
and globally accessible to patients who need them. This petition was signed by 91,206 people.

To ensure that public funding, which supports research and development (R&D) through to biomanufacturing, prioritizes
public health, MSF has repeatedly underscored the need to ensure that public funding comes with reasonable conditions
attached that ensure affordable access to the products that result from such funding. In 2018, the Standing Committee on
Health made recommendations along similar lines in its report “Towards Open Science: Promoting Innovation in
Pharmaceutical Research and Development and Access to Affordable Medicines both in Canada and Abroad”, which
contained recommendations relevant to the current topic of government funding for Medicago’s COVID vaccine research
and development, such as:

“That the Canadian Institutes of Health Research attach a Global Access Licensing requirement to recipients of its
research funding that wish to commercialize their research findings”.

study_or_consultation_title: Government's Advanced Purchase Agreement for Vaccines with Medicago
text:
“That the Canadian Institutes of Health Research attach a Global Access Licensing requirement to recipients of its
research funding that wish to commercialize their research findings”.

Similarly, responding to the serious global inequities in access to COVID-19 vaccines in its report “Overcoming the Barriers
to Global Vaccine Equity and Ending the Pandemic”, the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International
Development recommended:

“That the Government of Canada ensure that its agreements to provide research and development funding include
clauses that allow intellectual property resulting from that funding – including vaccines, therapeutics, and diagnostics –
to be easily licensed to manufacturers serving low- and middle-income countries.”

Both of these recommendations relate to the management of medical technologies and the underlying intellectual
property rights that were developed with Canadian public funds, and are clear that Canada should be doing more to
include common-sense access and affordability requirements into its funding agreements to develop them. Thus far, the
Government of Canada’s response to these basic, sensible measures to ensure public funding prioritizes public health has
been discouraging. Indeed, the Government of Canada has actively undermined this idea in fora like the negotiation of the
WHO Pandemic Instrument; in particular, Canada’s support for a legal baseline of licensing and technology transfer of
crucial medical tools that would not exist without considerable public funding occurring solely on “voluntary and mutually
agreed terms” with pharmaceutical companies neglects what happens when, as has frequently been the case historically,
no such terms are reached. This is not to suggest agreements on “voluntary and mutually agreed terms” are never

appropriate; however, the COVID-19 pandemic has underscored that there must be a backstop for when agreements on
such terms do not occur, or else the result is a fatal imbalance in access where billions of people may be deprived of
access to lifesaving medicines and vaccines that they need because pharmaceutical companies fail to launch these
products in low- and middle-income countries, or only make them available at unaffordable high prices. Funding
agreements provide the place for such backstops to be inserted.

study_or_consultation_title: Government's Advanced Purchase Agreement for Vaccines with Medicago
text:
Funding
agreements provide the place for such backstops to be inserted.

This brings us to the present Medicago case, where Canada invested a considerable amount of money – at least 300
million dollars – in a homegrown company that produced a vaccine that received Health Canada approval, but today has
no vaccines, no domestic manufacturing capacity, and no intellectual property to show for its investments. Tying strings to
its investments could have ensured that even despite some factors outside of Canada’s control, Canada could have
received at least some return on its investment, such as making the science available through open science platforms,
sharing the intellectual property rights with generic manufacturers, or some other means.

It is entirely possible to attach a wide range of such strings to government funding. If it is helpful to the Committee’s work
on this issue, we would be pleased to provide the Committee with examples of approaches that have already been used in
other countries to place access and pricing conditions within funding agreements, licenses, and collaborative research and
development activities between government researchers and non-government entities for the research and development
of medicines, vaccines, and other health technologies. We would also welcome the opportunity to appear before the
Committee during its study of this issue.

Nathalie Vaillant:
If I Had Known
Submitted to:
Standing Committee on Health (SCH)
Subject:
Monitoring of Medical Devices
(Breast Implants)
30 April 2023

PREAMBULE
Quebec’s motto is “Je me
souviens” . . . well, mine is:
IF I HAD KNOWN

INTRODUCTION
This memorandum is being submitted without a presentation and will describe all the
struggles I have had that could have been avoided . . . IF I HAD KNOWN, IF I HAD BEEN
CLEARLY INFORMED.

If you’re in good health, why be afraid of the word cancer?
In your family, you have one sister who had breast cancer very young; you’re not immune.
You perform your breast self-exam and find a small lump. You tell yourself, “Nah, not me,
that can’t be!” When you see your treating physician and ask for every test imaginable to
rule out any likelihood of bad news and she tells you, “Just because your sister had cancer
doesn’t mean you’ll get it.”

So again, I am asking the question: Why be afraid of the word cancer?
When you read my history, you will notice that all the surgeries I’ve undergone are in red,
to highlight the importance of monitoring medical devices.

MEDICAL HISTORY
2008
September: Lump in left breast
October: Mammogram and X-rays
November: Ultrasound
December: Ultrasound biopsy
December: Malignant tumour of the left breast
2009
January: Surgery
April to May: Radiation therapy
2010
June: Genetic testing and results: BRCA2+
At that time, my sister was in the midst of her second relapse of breast cancer, and when I
got my results, I had an 80% chance of relapsing with breast cancer and a 50% chance of
developing uterine cancer. The medication I was taking at the time contributed significantly
to the latter possibility. So it was “easy” for me to make the decision to have surgery, as I
did not want to have to hear this kind of news again.

23 December: Triple operation: Total hysterectomy + bilateral breast reconstruction +
expanders

23 December: Triple operation: Total hysterectomy + bilateral breast reconstruction +
expanders

2011
I had tissue expanders for six months. The doctor would inject saline solution into the
expanders, allowing my skin to stretch. I would see my chiropractor regularly to correct
my posture, as the implants were hurting me . . . IF I HAD KNOWN.

June: Surgery to place silicone implants, 350 c.c. each
From that moment, IF I HAD KNOWN
July: Infection of left breast – 10 days of antibiotics
August: Urgent hospitalization for necrosis of left breast, until 9 September.
September: IV antibiotics via central (PICC) line for six weeks, twice a day. Each treatment
would last several hours.
September: Surgery on left latissimus dorsi and left breast reconstruction surgery (was
given a small implant for healing)

2012
May: Surgery on left breast (reinsertion of 350 c.c. implant)
December: Surgery on both breasts: adjustment of left breast (larger) and right breast
(scar was too tight)

2013
May: Lipo injections to left and right breasts, scar correction
2014
February: Lipo injection in right breast and changes to left breast (smaller)
In the five years that followed, from 2015 to 2019, I had routine tests, including chest Xrays, bone density testing, bone scans, blood work, etc.

It is important to mention here that I was suffering from a number of symptoms* (see list
at the end), and these resembled the symptoms of menopause. According to the doctors, it
was normal to live with this, but . . . in 2019 I was INCREDIBLY FORTUNATE to see
the new story on breast implants, and it was a revelation. At last, there was a name for my
nameless issues. At last, I could see light at the end of the tunnel and I had some hope of
living a “more normal” life that would look like my old life. At last, I was understood.

At last, I was understood.

2019
Then began the testing process ahead of my implant removal with the same surgeon I had
been seeing since the start in 2010. I saw him and explained that I no longer wanted
implants and wanted to have them removed. At that time, he agreed, and my mental relief
began as I underwent a number of tests.
September: Breast ultrasound (left implant had ruptured), so my surgery was given priority.
December: Pre-operative examinations for the surgery scheduled for January 2020.

I had to see the surgeon to discuss the operation and explain my expectations, but I got a
slap in the face: he would not be performing the implant removal scheduled for three weeks
later. His explanation was very simple, stating that following a plastic surgeons’
conference, the group had decided to refuse all implant removal surgeries. I was devastated.
How would I achieve my goal of having the implants removed? Undeterred, I took
possession of my medical file and decided to make calls to find a surgeon willing to
perform this type of operation.

I had to wait two years, until 2021, to have my implants removed.
2021
October: Bilateral total capsulectomy with en bloc excision of breast implants.
SYMPTOMS
Here is an overview of the symptoms related to breast implants.

Fatigue
-
Cognitive dysfunction (brain fog, difficulty concentrating, fumbling for words,
memory loss)

Muscle pain, pain and weakness, joint pain

Hair loss

-

-
Low libido
-
Shortness of breath
-
Night sweats
-
Skin eruptions
-
Insomnia
-
Numbness and tingling of the arms and legs
-
Burning pain around the chest wall and breasts
-
Cold and discoloured hands and feet

SUBMISSION ON A REGISTRY FOR MEDICAL DEVICES (BREAST IMPLANTS)
The following submission details my personal story with Breast Implants and the reasons why
we need a registry.
In 2009, I had surgery to place Allergan textured implants (under MSP), after a double
mastectomy. The only advice given at the time was my implants had a warranty of 10 years.
Since the surgery, I have increasingly been unwell, with most symptoms seeming to relate to
Breast Implant Illness (BII) as well as capsular contracture and pain. In my long search for
medical answers for being so ill, I was ridiculed by the medical system due to a lack of
knowledge.
Late in 2021 while continuing to search for answers, I found a Breast Implant Illness site that
mentioned implant recalls. Mine were noted as being recalled in 2019 due to incidences of
BIA-ALCL cancer. I immediately contacted my original plastic surgeon and was initially brushed
off. Later this surgeon indicated he must have missed me on the recall, despite still being at the
same address and phone number. He stated he even involved the Interior Health Authority for
assistance in his search for recalled patients. He made light of BII and removal and said many
of his patients chose to leave them in, perhaps due to this minimization.
I also contacted Health Canada for confirmation of the recall. Several letters and several months
later (necessitating involving my MP), I finally received recall confirmation.
Not being notified of the recall has had longer-range implications for me. To facilitate the
removal of my recalled implants, I contacted several plastic surgeons specializing in explant,
including the two who are presenting - Dr. S. Nicolaidis and Dr. P. Lennox. Every plastic surgeon
contacted could not perform explant surgery as their waitlists were too long for MSP patients
(Health Act prevents private removal) despite the implants being recalled.The BC Health
Ministry was contacted and was unable to assist. In desperation, I booked explant surgery with
a surgeon in the USA as a private pay, but by that time I was diagnosed with lung cancer (on the
same side that I was having problems similar to symptoms of BIA-ALCL). I blame the implants -
that have now been in my body for 14 years - as a contributor to my now terminal lung cancer.
A registry won't help me, but please institute one so others don't suffer as I have. Plastic
surgeons have a vested interest in their business, so I feel some are reluctant and unreliable to
deal with a recall. Health Canada was also totally useless in assisting me.
Thank you for considering this submission.
Diane Gane

Dear Members of Parliament,

I am writing to you to share my personal experience with having textured Mentor breast implants for 14
years in hopes this may urge you to consider establishing a Breast Implant Registry in Canada. I hope
that my story will serve as a testimony to the need for a comprehensive database to track breast
implant-related complications and adverse events.

Within 6 months of implantation, I developed questionable lumps that required monitoring every 6
months via mammograms and ultrasounds. As time went on, I started experiencing digestive issues,
ongoing rashes, vision issues, headaches, neck and shoulder pain, intense brain fog, chest pains, and
difficulty breathing. These symptoms also caused multiple bouts of depression.

Despite visiting multiple doctors and specialists and being told that everything was fine and perhaps all
was stress related, I finally felt that my underlying issues were finally validated after receiving a letter
from my implanting surgeon outlining the symptoms of Breast Implant Illness (BII) associated with my
breast implants. My immediate reaction was to make an appointment with him to discuss the letter and
have the implants removed. Unfortunately, my visit was unwelcome, and I was dismissed as the letter
was only sent out of obligation and not because of his belief in BII. He told me that I would look
disfigured by removing them and that he honestly did not believe they were causing my issues.
Foolishly, I followed his advice and left the implants in.

As time passed, my symptoms worsened to the point that I had undergone multiple heart and
pulmonary tests. I was looked at like I had three heads as I did not fit the typical heart disease patient.
But some preliminary testing indicated I could have issues. Thankfully, an angiogram proved I was okay,
but I still continued to have breathing issues and chest pains. I then suggested to my Internist that
perhaps my implants could be causing my issues, but he quickly dismissed this idea and said my
breathing issues had nothing to do with my breast implants.

I further researched to learn more about BII and came across two very informative and helpful Facebook

Reading these pages was like reading a biography, and I learned that many others experienced exactly
the same things I did. I immediately hit the ground running and researched the list of surgeons who
believe in BII and felt it was important to go with a surgeon who also no longer implants. With that, I
consulted with Dr. Stephen Nicolaidis and immediately decided to have my implants removed despite
the 7-hour drive from Northern Ontario to Montreal to reach him.

Dr. Nicolaidis was so informative regarding every aspect and yet so comforting that I knew I would be in
good hands with him. He and his team have been instrumental in my healing process. He performed a
En Bloc and Total Capsulectomy breast implant removal one week ago today, May 2nd, 2023. I still have
a lot of healing ahead of me, but immediately my breathing has been restored, which I honestly was
skeptical that any of my symptoms would improve, but here we are, one week out. I am now waiting for
my pathology results and I hope they return with no issues.

For all I have endured, as many others have, I wholeheartedly believe a Breast Implant Registry should
be established. This registry would allow for a better understanding of the long-term health effects of
breast implants and provide the information necessary to make informed decisions about
implantation. This would also provide valuable data for researchers.

If I had known then what I know now (and experienced), I would not have gotten my implants, and I
believe that many others would share this sentiment. My experience has shown me that there is a need
for more comprehensive tracking of breast implant-related complications and adverse events. I implore
you to consider establishing a Breast Implant Registry to protect the health and well-being of Canadians
who choose to undergo breast implant surgery.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Good morning to all members of the HESA Committee,
After observing the meetings of the past weeks, I felt compelled to write to all of you. Thank you for

My name is Dawn Criss, and I am a BIA ALCL survivor, a BII patient and a member of the advocacy team
alongside Ms. McGregor, Ms. Elliott and Ms. Pratt. I was the first BIA ALCL patient diagnosed in Alberta
in 2018 and I am also a patient of Dr. Tervaert.
It seems widely agreed upon, that an implant registry is long overdue. However, had we incorporated a
registry when implants were first introduced to the market 60 years ago, we would have had enough
data to contact patients with recalls of defective products, recalls for BIA ALCL and other cancers and
also to pull data for our own Canadian studies. To start from scratch now, it will take many years to
gather what’s required to accomplish any of these tasks. Perhaps we could find a way for patients AND
plastic surgeons to add previous surgical/pathological data and adverse reaction events into the new
registry, allowing us to grow the database much quicker? This registry should be an "opt out" database
similar to an excel spreadsheet, where all information can eventually be sorted and filtered to pull data
for any study required. Personal and private patient information should be hidden so that access can
ONLY be made by the implanting/explanting surgeon in case they need to be contacted. To answer a
question that was asked of our advocates on May 11th, I feel that we would have an over 90% inclusion
rate with an "opt out" registry vs an "opt in" Patients understand how beneficial a registry is, very few
will choose not to be included.
Why has Health Canada not done a deep dive into the safety studies completed in other countries, like
Dr Tervaert mentioned in his testimony on March 11th? It seems that in other parts of the world, breast
implants have also had much controversy as to safety concerns. Maybe it would be prudent to “pause”
all augmentation surgeries until Health Canada’s team can provide an updated risk assessment? It is
beyond deplorable that after 60 years we cannot properly inform women of the real time dangers of
these products.
In previous years, breast implants were approved by Health Canada with “post market approval”. This is
a term used to apply to products that require a human host to trial the product. Manufacturers are
given approval to sell their product with the “guarantee” that they will provide the long-term data, both
the good and the bad from the information gathered from the patients who unknowingly are being used
as test subjects. Unbeknownst to me, I was not told that my implants were not fully approved. I was
never followed or studied or asked any questions until I ended up with cancer. And now, after 5 years,

fact, the Cross Cancer Clinic decided after two years that I didn’t need to follow up anymore and sent
me on my merry way with the words, “We will probably not catch your cancer again until it presents as
stage 3 or 4, so really no point in doing PET scans unless you have symptoms”. Lucky me!
When I was diagnosed in 2018, we had information on approximately 300 cases of BIA ALCL worldwide.

textured implants and some even contracted BIA ALCL after already beating breast cancer. WHAT ARE

My submission on my breast implants
From a dream to a hard reality!
“Why didn’t God give me breasts? I don’t feel like a woman or desirable with my small breasts. I
swear that one day I will end up getting a pair!” These were the thoughts that ran through my
mind every day, every time I looked in the mirror when I woke up.
Consultation was the first step
After several years of mental torture, thinking about it , and once I was sure I was done having
babies, at the age of 31, I decided to see a surgeon to eventually get breast augmentation surgery.
My partner was completely against it, but I wasn’t doing this for him. I was doing this for myself,
to feel better and to gain self-confidence. So, early in 2008, I met with Dr. Marc Dufresne, a plastic
surgeon, at his clinic in Chicoutimi. After a quick review of my medical records, he asked me why
I wanted to have breast augmentation surgery and then conducted a physical examination of my
chest. He also asked me what my expectations were of the aesthetic outcome. I told him that I
wanted something natural and not too big because I played a lot of sports and engaged in physical
activities and I didn’t want them to become uncomfortable. I told him that I just wanted to have
a chest proportional to my body type and, at the same time, fill the void and sagging caused by
breastfeeding. Dr. Dufresne presented me with two types of implants. The first was round,
smooth and filled with saline solution. The second had a slight profile in the shape of a water
droplet, was made entirely of gel (silicone) and its shell was textured like sand paper. I mentioned
my concerns about silicone implants given the problems that occurred in previous years,1 but he
told me that the problems with silicone implants had been resolved and that Health Canada
authorized their use again in 2006. He assured me that this type of implant is safe and has
significant benefits by providing a more natural result because of its shape, remaining in place due
to the textured surface and by not exposing me to the risk of the outer shell failing and having
saline water leak into my body. Once reassured and delighted by these properties, I opted for the
cohesive silicone gel model. Dr. Dufresne explained that because of these “benefits,” these
implants cost twice as much as the ones that are round, smooth and filled with saline water. I was
a bit surprised, but he convinced me that they were really worth it and that I wouldn’t regret it.
Then I asked him about their lifespan, and what I need to watch to make sure everything is normal.
He told me that everything is relative. Some people will have the same implants for 5, 10 or 15
years, some would even have them for the rest of their life. He told me to come back if there was
a mass, fever, redness, hardness or swelling. In short, consult if I notice a change in my breasts,
although the possibility is infrequent and rarely severe based on experience. Based on the
surgeon’s reassuring words and recommendations, I opted for the model he suggested: 310cc
Inamed 410FM Biocel by Allergan with a moderate profile. We scheduled a date for the surgery
and discussed payment terms.
D Day
On May 13, 2008, at the age of 31, I had my breast augmentation surgery at the Chicoutimi
hospital. The implants were placed under the pectoral muscle. I was given the card for my
implants. They were part of batch no. 1466967 and had serial numbers 12878993 (left) and

The suffering started
Being in good health and having followed the post-operative recommendations, I recovered and
healed quickly. But after a few months, a few health problems emerged. The first was some
unexplained skin rashes. There were large, red and puffy patches all over my trunk and swelling
on my face. The doctor I saw did not find a reason for this. Time and antihistamines eventually
caused the patches to disappear. Over a 10-year period, I had a wide range of health problems,
including inflammation and general swelling of my body, various allergies, food intolerances,
numbness of the limbs, memory and concentration problems, joint pain, irritability, sleep
disorders, night sweats, muscle weakness, shortness of breath, chronic fatigue, significant hair
loss, vision disorders, dizziness, nausea, total loss of sex drive, suspected onset of Sjogren
syndrome, sensitivity to sounds, light and odours, and digestive disorders. It was a slow process,
but the symptoms appeared, one after the other. It got to the point that I was embarrassed to see
doctors who came up with prognoses like ADHD, early osteoarthritis, depression and vitamin D
deficiency. They implied that the problem was in my head, and for the last three years before
having them removed, I thought I was going crazy. I was so tired and weak that I was having a
hard time doing my work in the morning. I had to go to bed as soon as I got home. As someone
who always had energy to spare and had a healthy lifestyle, I didn’t understand what my body
was trying to tell me with all these ailments.
The shock
One evening in November 2018, when I was watching the episode Danger sous la peau2 on
Enquête, I finally figured out what was going on with my body. I was literally struck by the fact
that my breast implants were most likely responsible for the onset of all my ailments. Never in a
million years would I have imagined that my implants were making me so sick and disabled, since
my breasts did not appear to be a problem. All of this was happening surreptitiously through my
immune, endocrine, digestive and cognitive systems. On top of that, I was shocked to learn that
I had actually paid to have devices put inside me that could cause me serious cancer and that
NOBODY had informed me up until then. I felt completely cheated by the people and authorities
who were responsible for my health and safety in connection with these medical devices. It was
clear to me that I now had to remove this poison from my body as soon as possible. But despite
the satisfaction of finally having answers as to what was going on in my body and the hope of
being able to get healthy again, I felt devastated because I knew I would have to grieve the loss of
my breasts. Not only that, but I now had to get a significant amount of money that I didn’t just
have lying around.
The release
On March 26, 2019, Dr. Stephen Nicolaïdis removed my implants by total capsulectomy (also
referred to as en bloc surgery). I was nervous and anxious about the aesthetic outcome, but I was
happy that these toxic implants were removed. My implants were given to me when I woke up
and the capsules were sent to the lab for analysis. I hoped I’d get my health back and I prayed that
it wasn’t too late and that the capsules were negative for any trace of cancer. Good news for me,
the results were negative. Given all the successive health problems, I had already paid a very high
price for my health. Within a week of removing my implants, several of my symptoms faded and
some even disappeared almost instantly. To date, three years later, I can confirm that almost all
of my ailments have disappeared, and I am in good health.

I am grateful that I did not develop cancer such as anaplastic large cell lymphoma that can be

from the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean CIUSS that informed me of a low risk of cancer that could be

removed, after the Enquête episode publicly revealed what manufacturers, surgeons and

ensure their profits were not diminished.

Considering all the shortcomings in the safety studies that had to be conducted by the
manufacturers, the lack of oversight of plastic surgeons, the rate of increase in cancer cases
related to breast implants and the increasing number of women complaining about ailments
related to their breast implants, maintaining a registry of all breast implants placed, regardless of
type, should be mandatory. The sale of any type of breast implants should be suspended and
prohibited until a registry is set up. Everyone is or was entitled to be informed of the dangers
associated with these devices that are put in their bodies. Lives could have been saved, mine could
have been improved.

Dear Mr. Thériault,
I am writing to express my strong support for the establishment of a centralized national
breast implant registry, administered by the government, under the OVERSIGHT OF
MEDICAL DEVICES (BREAST IMPLANTS) commitee.
Breast implants are class IV medical devices representing the products with the
highest risk potential. (1) Oversight should be conducted accordingly.
- These products create a risk of a lymphoma that is specific to breast implants,
BIA-ALCL. (2) Patients should be notified quickly and formally, not be made to
stumble on the information in a support group.
- Other issues seem to be related to breast implants and are constantly being
added. (3) If it turns out that BII (Breast Implant Illness) or another condition
finally becomes medically recognized, carriers will need to be notified promptly
also to make an option of discussions with their treating physician.
- In particular, the registry would act as a surveillance tool for pathologies related
to breast implant use. It would be used to advise patients of the symptoms to
watch for and to follow up with their physician, if necessary.
- Health Canada has no way of determining how many patients in Canada have
received these types of implants.
- Automotive manufacturers notify their customers of potential problems even if
they are rare (4), yet nothing is done about devices implanted in patients’ bodies
that potentially pose a serious health risk.
- I have never been contacted, either by my surgeon or by public health, to
inform me that my textured cohesive gel implants had serious potential health
risks and were ultimately being removed from the market.
MY STORY:
In March 2005, at the age of 42 following 3 pregnancies and breastfeeding, hoping to
restore a few things, I received textured cohesive gel implants with the brand Inamed

were inherent in any operation. I was told there was nothing to worry about and that

internist) to try to find solutions to alleviate the symptoms. At NO time did I suspect a

I tried unsuccessfully several medications, including methotrexate, to reduce the pain. In
spite of everything, I continued to work in a very demanding sales management job. I
continued to take care of my three children. But I was a shadow of a person. I had no

that I could no longer work.

problems. I was only 40 years old.

replace the product concerned. In this case, we are talking about the health of

information was obtained from a Facebook group, and it is even more

the surgeons who implanted the breast implants. Is the status quo
recommended?!? I was left with a time bomb in my body and I was simply told
that, if the implants rupture, I would be put on a waiting list so that these toxic
bags that are poisoning my body can be removed at the government’s expense.

Brief Concerning the Oversight of Medical Devices

Introduction
I would like to thank the members of the Committee for the invitation to submit this brief so I
can provide my views regarding the oversight of breast implants.
Evolution of breast implants
Between January 1992 and October 20, 2006, Health Canada imposed a moratorium on
silicone implants to protect the health of all Canadian women and to ensure that these
products are safe. These implants were withdrawn from the Canadian market due to safety
concerns and the fact that they cause serious health problems for women, including cancer,
connective tissue diseases and autoimmune diseases.
Thirty years later, we are still having the same debates, the same health challenges and the
same doubts vis-à-vis the safety of these products.
Anaplastic large cell lymphoma cases are trending higher, as are incidences of other breast
implant-related diseases.
The time for oversight has passed—it is now time for action.
Stronger oversight measures, in the form of a medical devices registry, should have been put
in place at the appropriate time, when the moratorium on silicone breast implants was
imposed in 1992. This would have made it possible to track all breast implants and maximize
oversight for Canadian women.
The moratorium and the Special Access Program
Lack of a “breast implant registry” resulted in ineffective oversight, prevention and safety
considerations.
Even though Health Canada did not approve these prostheses during the moratorium, it did
provide Canadian surgeons with special access programs, disregarding its own guidelines in
the prohibition regulations, without obtaining the consent of the individuals concerned or even
considering the consequences. These cosmetic surgeries provided to women with breast
cancer were neither essential nor urgent and were not even performed to remove or treat the
cancer, let alone ensure the survival of these patients.
There was no oversight, and safety was compromised for this group of women. The
prohibition regulations should have applied to everyone, without exception. Women with

Women with

breast cancer were never given the protection available to healthy women who were covered
by the moratorium.
Inadequate oversight
The Special Access Program during the ban amounted to irresponsible conduct, since there
was no known study to establish whether women with breast cancer would be safe with these
silicone prostheses. Moreover, these unlicensed implants could not have been deemed safe
because they had not been subjected to a thorough assessment or to the same level of review
required to be licensed. Safety considerations and oversight were completely lacking for
women with breast cancer. They were left completely unprotected.
Health and safety, a mission of commitment
The health and safety of all Canadian women should be a top priority. The provision of a
Special Access Program, despite the known risks of these implants, failed to reflect the
mission and vision of a commitment to improving lives. Given Health Canada’s responsibility
for health-related matters, it had a duty to prevent and reduce health risks as much as
possible. Furthermore, the agreement to deliver these special access programs was
unacceptable and far from insignificant given the troubling facts that emerged during the
moratorium concerning a criminal investigation involving one of the breast implant
manufacturers. It did not make any sense to disregard the prohibition regulations and offer
these special access programs; doing so defied any logic.
Report submitted to the 39th Parliament, January 17, 2007
On January 17, 2007, during the 1st Session of the 39th Parliament, the government presented
its response to the Third Report of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
concerning “Silicone Gel-Filled Implants: Areas of Concern” (see reference 2).
In this report, the federal Minister of Health stated that “my Department has considered each
recommendation carefully and prepared a response to the concerns and advice contained in
the Committee’s report.”
Moreover, the detailed responses to the Committee’s recommendations indicate that “Health
Canada granted licences with conditions” to manufacturers of silicone gel-filled breast
implants.
Given the conditions to be met for approval of the licences, how many of these requirements
were fulfilled? It is important to note that manufacturers avoided having to comply with these
requirements, and the breast implants remain on the market (see reference 3). How should
one react in light of all these policy statements that should have been enforced?
Health Canada was unable to fulfill its obligations. Oversight was inadequate.
Data collection
Scientific data released by Europe PubMed Central in October 2021 (see reference 1) present
alarming findings about the risks of developing breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell
lymphoma (BIA-ALCL). This increases to 1/355 for women with silicone implants following
breast reconstruction.

This increases to 1/355 for women with silicone implants following
breast reconstruction.

Research on the number of women who received breast implants yields contradictory and
inconsistent data. The registry would provide us with reliable and consistent data across
Canada.
When one particular healthcare facility was asked how many women received textured
silicone implants between January 1992 and October 2006, the response was “approximately
179”; this information came with a note indicating that [TRANSLATION] “this number may include
a margin of error due to human intervention in various information systems.”
These are Class IV medical devices, which are products with the highest potential risk. It is
inconceivable that accurately determining the number of women who received breast
implants appears to be impossible. A registry would have prevented these types of errors or
omissions.
An access to information request was also made to obtain the number and types of complaints
reported for my type of implant (e.g., rupture of implant, cancer and disease) during the
moratorium between 1992 and 2006, which also included a request for information on
complaints received after the implant was licensed in October 2006. None of the information
appears to present data concerning the breast implants I obtained through the Special Access
Program.
At the very least, one case – mine – should have been documented, because I had textured
silicone implants and was also diagnosed with cancer in 2018. No one appears to have
recorded my case. How many others unknown cases are out there?
Despite the fact that I had a total double mastectomy, including the removal of nipples, to
treat breast cancer in 2003 and also received chemotherapy, took medication for 5½ years
and had regular follow-up, I was once again diagnosed with cancer in 2018. This was
surprising because I no longer had any mammary glands, only breast implants.
Observations and considerations
A breast cancer registry is the only way to ensure adequate safety; this has become
indispensable for the reasons mentioned above.
This option has been proposed in the past, but nothing came of it. Such a registry is now
urgently needed to prevent others from suffering the negative consequences of breast
implants.
Considering the lack of reliable data concerning the number of women who have had health
problems associated with all types of breast implants;
Considering the rising cases of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma
(BIA-ALCL), as well as the rising number of deaths in the past three years and all the cases
of breast implant illness (BII);
Considering the lack of reporting and underreporting of all implant-related issues that should
have been reported by manufacturers (see reference 3);

all types of breast implants; Considering the rising cases of breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), as well as the rising number of deaths in the past three years and all the cases of breast implant illness (BII); Considering the lack of reporting and underreporting of all implant-related issues that should have been reported by manufacturers (see reference 3);

Considering the lack of oversight of breast implants for years and during the moratorium;
And recognizing that women who had breast cancer prior to the licensing of silicone breast
implants were not protected by the moratorium in place between 1992 and October 20, 2006,
I hereby submit and propose the following recommendations.
Recommendation 1: That the government establish a central registry for all breast implants
to provide Canadian women to maximize safety and minimize health risks. This registry is the
only option for ensuring permanent, ongoing oversight.
Recommendation 2: That the government enforce the prohibition of the sale of all breast
implants on the Canadian market until a registry is implemented to shed light on the health
problems reported and to address the issue of breast implant safety.
Recommendation 3: That the government set up a special compensation and reparations
program for women with breast cancer who received silicone implants during the moratorium.
Exemptions from the regulations by the Special Access Program violated the ethical values
in the charter of rights and freedoms.
1. Women with breast cancer did not enjoy the same rights to equality or security as did
all other Canadian women during the moratorium. This Special Access Program
deprived us of this protection (the moratorium) imposed by regulation between
January 8, 1992, and October 20, 2006.
2. We are currently excluded from the class action against the breast implant
manufacturers. Once again, we are forced to deal with the additional challenge of
exclusion, since this class action only covers implants used as of 2006, in other words,
those licensed and approved by Health Canada. Since our implants were not
authorized for sale in Canada, we are once again suffering from the damages caused
by all of Health Canada’s failings vis-à-vis the silicone implants that were made
available during the moratorium.
Recommendation 4: That the government launch an investigation into all special access
programs related to silicone breast implants that were made available in Canada during the
moratorium.
Health Canada imposed requirements on health professionals who applied to these special
access programs. These health professionals were required to comply with the regulations
and report incidents within 72 hours after they came to their attention. Reports were required
for issues related to failure of the device or a deterioration in its effectiveness, any inadequacy
in its labelling or in its directions for use; or that led to the death or serious deterioration in the
state of health of a patient. Registration of implants that were imported or sold for the
purposes of a Special Access Program was also required.
One is left to wonder whether all those concerned complied with the conditions of the Special
Access Program.

One is left to wonder whether all those concerned complied with the conditions of the Special
Access Program.

In order for Health Canada to fulfill its mandate, including its mission to protect, the
department must sanction breaches of conditions and refer any person who violated the
regulations for activities related to breast implants to the appropriate authorities for
investigation and prosecution.
Conclusion
Minimize breast implant-related health risks in order to maximize safety for all Canadian
women. The registry is the only option.

HESA Submission – Oversight of Medical Devices (Breast Implants)
The Breast Implant Safety Alliance (BISA) is an organization of patient advocates and knowledge
experts that work with patients and leaders in Canada, the US and all over the world. We are
pleased to have the opportunity to be a voice for patients and consumers and share our
valuable insight from our lived-experience and professional training with members of the
Standing Committee on Health. With limited time and resources, this brief was prepared by
Terri McGregor, a BIA-ALCL survivor Expert BIA-ALCL Patient Advocate and part of the BISA core
leadership team as a result of collaborative efforts with members of BISA including Canadian
Representative Julie Elliott and Canadian Patient Advocate Nancy Pratt, founder of the BIFI
Society of Canada and co-founder of the Canadian Breast Implant Failure and Illness support
group.

Breast implants are not life saving devices and thus there should be a very low tolerance for any
risk to health, especially risks that impose huge costs on the healthcare system. There is no
informed consent without data. Healthcare delivery and costs cannot be optimized without
data. We appreciate that the House of Common Standing Committee on Health is taking steps
to examine the feasibility of creating a nationwide registry to advance our common goal of
patient safety.
Harm & Risk
The risk of BIA-ALCL in breast cancer reconstruction patients with exposure to Allergan Biocell
implants may be as high as 1 in 100.i Prospective data in cosmetic augmentation patients
presented at the American Association of Plastic Surgeon’s meeting in May 2023 and pending
publication shows similarly high risks.ii An adverse event with a risk of 1 in 100 is properly
described as common and not rare.iii Women that received implants after prophylactic
mastectomies for hereditary risks of breast cancer may have increased risk for BIA-ALCL as well
as increased risk for more aggressive disease.iv v Many cases of BIA-ALCL have occurred in
patients after prophylactic mastectomies.vi Textured breast implants are linked to an increased
risk of breast cancer recurrence.vii

An Effective Registry is Feasible
The challenges of developing an effective registry can be overcome. In 2024, the German Breast
Implant Registry is “expected to be the first mandatory registry for public and private hospitals.
Thus a national 100% coverage rate for private and public clinics is to be achieved. Patients,
clinics and health insurance companies are obligated to report to the database.”viii According to
Madris Kinard of Device Events and member of the Breast Implant Safety Alliance, “Canada can
learn from the mistakes made with respect to registries in the U.S. and set this up correctly
from the outset. There is the potential to do this right and do it well.”ix

Recommendations
*The following recommendations were the collaborative efforts of the Breast Implant Safety
Alliance (BISA) including Canadians Terri McGregor and Julie Elliott, and Canadian Patient
Advocate Nancy Pratt of founder of the BIFI Society of Canada and co-founder of the Canadian
Breast Implant Failure and Illness support group.
1. Require that breast implant patients be notified of the need for breast MRIs.

2. Extend mandatory adverse event reporting regulations to include private clinics.

3. Require participation of patient advocates in developing a registry as well as in its
administration.

4. Require manufacturers to ensure patients are given and execute the informed consent
checklist with oversight by Health Canada. Manufacturers should be prohibited from
selling implants to doctors that fail to provide informed consent. If manufacturers fail to
monitor such doctors and impose such consequences, their license to sell implants
should be revoked.

5. Utilize UDI (Unique Device Identifiers) which function like a digital fingerprint,
containing information on model and production characteristics such as lot, batch, serial
number which provides a quick and definitive way to identify a medical device which
could also be useful in the event of a recall.x

6. Pause or limit the sale of breast implants until there is a full investigation of: (a)
regulatory failures and manufacturer violations, including failure to report adverse
events and the failure to meet implant approval conditions; (b) the impact of BIA-ALCL
and other implant-associated adverse events on the healthcare system, including
patient access to necessary medical evaluation, testing, and treatment and the costs of
such care on the public healthcare system; (c) the shortcomings of the current
mandatory reporting system; and (d) misleading marketing of breast implants.

Additional Questions & Considerations
Conflicts of interest problems are so pervasive in the breast implant industry that oversight is
even more important than in other areas of medicine.xi

As of October, 2011, Health Canada was aware of 69 Allergan ALCL case reports worldwide,
which included 3 Canadians. Approximately half of those reports were in Allergan-sponsored
clinical studies, including 3 Deaths attributed to metastatic ALCL. Reminder, HC’s approval was

conditional, not absolute.xii

Why did Health Canada permit Allergan clinical studies to be terminated after BIA-ALCL was
emerging, despite a carefully crafted clinical study that was only measuring breast & lung
cancers?xiii

Why did the Breast Implant Follow Up Study (BIFS), the post approval study of
Allergan (formerly Inamed Corporation) that was meant to capture data in the tens of
thousands over a 10 year period, fail to provide the quantitative and qualitative data? xiv

The 2011 response from industry and professional societies to BIA-ALCL reflects an
organizational conflict of interest.xv That response set the foundation of denial, minimizing, and
patriarchal gaslighting which continues to harm today’s patients by delaying their access to
diagnosis, treatment and reporting.xvi xvii

Why were manufactures so slow to respond to adverse event reporting? Why did HC permit the
manufacturers to delay follow up reporting, allowing an additional delay of 19 months before
sending a letter? xviii

What consequences were levied in the 2019 data dump? xix

Oversight of Medical Devices (Breast Implants)
GS1 Canada is grateful for the opportunity to provide its recommendations on the
oversight of breast implants.
GS1 Canada is a neutral, not-for profit organization that creates and maintains
global supply chain standards in collaboration with GS1 Member Organizations in
116 countries (we are often best known for the global barcode standard). Through
a federated model, collectively, we help millions of companies around the world use
common identifiers on their products, locations, and services, to enable traceability
and recalls, inventory management, and visibility within the supply chain.
The GS1 global supply chain standards already play a significant role in the
oversight of breast implants, globally. Due to regulatory requirements from other
jurisdictions such the US and EU, the majority of breast implants that come to, or
are made-in, Canada, already have GS1 identifiers (ie: a global barcode) on its
product. This acts as a unique device identifier (UDI) for the product that is
recognized globally. Therefore, Canada is already starting with a strong foundation
for proper oversight of breast implants including for traceability capabilities, recalls
and a data-rich registry critical for research and analytics. We are pleased to be
currently engaged with the Medical Devices Directorate within Health Canada to
support in the development of an optimal UDI policy for Canada.
Healthcare’s Unrealized Potential – Key Recommendations
In Canada, other sectors such as grocery, foodservice, and pharmacy, have fully
embraced GS1 global supply chain standards and embedded them in their business
practices. For this reason, it is easier to track and trace a bottle of water than it is
a medical device, such as a breast implant, in our country. This must change.
It is critical that Canada leverage this global infrastructure that is in place with the
following recommendations:
1) Establish a government-led directive requiring the use of a global
barcode. A GS1 DataMatrix barcode is ideal for breast implants considering
it can contain critical elements needed for traceability including the Global
Trade Item Number (GTIN), lot, batch, expiry, and potentially serialization (a
unique identifier for each breast implant). This requirement would allow the
specific product information to be tracked and traced throughout the supply
chain with the identifiers embedded in the patient record – this is critical to
enable lot-based recalls.

This requirement would allow the
specific product information to be tracked and traced throughout the supply
chain with the identifiers embedded in the patient record – this is critical to
enable lot-based recalls.

2) Ensure a national breast implant registry that is not siloed. One of the
key benefits of a breast implant registry is the opportunity to obtain rich
quality product data that is foundational to meeting the objectives of a breast
implant registry. We caution against an implant registry enabled by

proprietary identifiers that are not interoperable with other category
registries (hip, knee, between healthcare organizations, and/or countries).
Proprietary product identifiers will create significant limitations and data
quality challenges.

The GS1 Canada healthcare community is requesting that the Government of
Canada invest in what the community has already created and continues to
build through neutral and non-competitive collaboration: Canada’s National
Product Registry, ECCnet. More than twenty years since its founding that was
initially funded by the Federal Government, ECCnet is now the largest
product registry in Canada and the backbone to the supply chains of grocery,
foodservice, cannabis, and retail pharmacy sectors. It is ready to do the
same for healthcare with an already existing foundation in place. ECCnet has
over 90% of all pharmaceutical, food and cannabis products sold/used in
Canada. GS1 Canada is now working with the healthcare community to bring
in medical devices, with the community recently agreeing on a minimum data
quality level plan.

GS1 Canada is now working with the healthcare community to bring
in medical devices, with the community recently agreeing on a minimum data
quality level plan.

With over 8,000 users, 800,000 products, and over 270,000 annual updates
to existing data, GS1 Canada’s National Product Registry users benefit from
data excellence, trusted Canadian sector expertise, increased product
visibility, standardized content in both official languages, and a single point
of access to all product content which in-turn, allows them to operate
efficiently and most importantly, provide consumer protection through safety
measures such as recalls. GS1 Canada’s National Product Registry is proven,
based on global standards, with data integrity as its core foundational
principle.
The GS1 Canada community is asking that the Government of Canada bring
in breast implant product data that they can trust, to the national breast
implant registry, through ECCnet. While perpetually updated and cleansed
product data from ECCnet, would only be one element of a national implant
registry, it would be a critical one to support relevant Canadian patients and
the people that care for them, including practitioners and researchers.
3) Leverage GS1 Canada’s Community Management Process to enable
the adoption of the standards and registry that would meet the needs
of the full supply chain including the patient. As a neutral body that
supports communities as whole, GS1 Canada’s Community Management
Process allows for a safe space for everyone to come together to align on the
standards specifics (such as attribute identifiers right in the barcode as well
as in the registry, location identifiers, etc.) It is the process that has aligned
multiple sectors in Canada including grocery, foodservice, pharmacy, and
cannabis.

Value of GS1 Global Standards Implementation
If the above were in place, the following would be enabled:
•
The ability to track breast implants manufactured anywhere in the world,
right down to the patient in Canada
•
Confidence that the data is accurate, updated, and perpetually cleansed and
in both official languages
•
The ability to issue quick and efficient recalls, including lot-based recalls
•
Production of high-quality data for research, analytics, and procurement
•
Interoperability with any relevant stakeholders, including the thousands of
healthcare facilities that would be involved in breast implant surgeries and
care.
•
Be in alignment with the Canadian and global direction for UDI policy
The healthcare community in Canada has been working diligently for decades to
align to global standards with significant results over the last several years. It is
critical that a proprietary framework for breast implants in Canada does not move
in the wrong direction, setting Canada back and the extreme value that comes with
GS1 supply chain standards and supporting tools and registries.

HESA Submission – Oversight of medical devices (breast implants)
The Canadian Cancer Society (CCS) is the only national charity supporting Canadians with
all cancers in communities across the country. As the voice for Canadians who care about
cancer, we are pleased to share with members of the Standing Committee on Health
background information on breast cancer in Canada and how breast implants play a role in
the recovery of people living with breast cancer. It is estimated that about 1 in 8 Canadian
women will develop breast cancer during their lifetime and 1 in 34 will die from it.1

Overview of breast cancer in Canada
It is estimated that in 2022:
28,600 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer. This represents 25%
of all new cancer cases in women in 2022.
5,500 Canadian women will die from breast cancer. This represents 14% of all
cancer deaths in women in 2022.
On average, 78 Canadian women will be diagnosed with breast cancer every day.
On average, 15 Canadian women will die from breast cancer every day.
270 Canadian men will be diagnosed with breast cancer and 55 will die from breast
cancer.1

Role of breast reconstruction and prostheses
If needed as part of treatment plan, surgery for breast cancer may include breastconserving surgery (lumpectomy) or mastectomy (removes all of the breast). After surgery
to remove breast cancer, a person living with breast cancer may find it difficult to cope with
the loss of their breast and the change to their appearance. Breast reconstruction and
breast prostheses are options that are intended to help individuals feel better about
themselves and their bodies. But many women choose not to reconstruct or wear a
prosthesis – they choose to “stay flat.” Only the individual undergoing surgery can decide
what is best for them.

But many women choose not to reconstruct or wear a
prosthesis – they choose to “stay flat.” Only the individual undergoing surgery can decide
what is best for them.

Safety
Some women may have concerns about how silicone breast implants could affect their
health. Recent monitoring of silicone breast implants in Canada found that they were safe
and did not increase health problems.
In very rare situations, women with breast implants (silicone and saline) can develop a rare
type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma called breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell
lymphoma (BIA-ALCL). It starts in the scar tissue that forms around the implant. Recent
research suggests that the risk is higher in women who have textured implants rather than
those with smooth surfaces. In 2019, Health Canada suspended its medical license for one
brand of textured breast implants. Health agencies around the world are still collecting more
information about how many women are diagnosed with BIA-ALCL.2
In 2019, France became the first country to end the manufacturing, sale and use of all
macro-textured breast implants and polyurethane-coated breast implants. The decision was
made as a precautionary measure in order to reduce the risk of BIA-ALCL, which although
rare, is serious.3
In September 2022, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a safety
communication about reports of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and various lymphomas

2 Types of breast reconstruction | Canadian Cancer Society
3 L’Agence nationale de sécurité du médicament et des produits de santé | Dispositifs de surveillance des implants

located in scar tissue around breast implants, which is different from BIA-ALCL. They
indicated that the risk of SCC and other lymphomas are rare, but healthcare providers and
people who have or are considering breast implants should be aware that cases have been
reported to the FDA and in the literature.4

Recommendations
Assess the continued safety of selling textured implants in Canada.
Ensure healthcare providers including surgeons are equipped with guidance and
information on breast implants so that people looking to undergo the surgery can
make informed decisions.
Ensure healthcare providers including surgeons provide continued care and support
for patients who already have breast implants.

Health Canada regulates breast implants as class IV medical devices, the category
representing the highest risk. Breast implants are associated with a wide range of
adverse effects, including a type of cancer of the immune system known as “breast
implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma.” For decades, the federal
government has been called upon to make regulatory changes to enhance the safety of
breast implants, yet important gaps remain in the oversight of these devices. Breast
implant recipients continue to be insufficiently protected from adverse outcomes. The
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health undertook a study to follow up on
the improvements put in place as part of Health Canada’s 2018 action plan on medical
devices, as well as to assess the feasibility of the creation of a central breast implant
registry. The committee heard strong support from plastic surgeons, researchers and
patient advocates for the creation of a national breast implant registry. Such a registry
would improve the traceability of implants, facilitate recalls and advance research
related to breast implants. Other concerns identified during the study include
shortcomings in the process for reporting adverse effects to Health Canada, deficiencies
in the safety information Health Canada presents to consumers, as well as a lack of
research on breast implants. Gender inequity within the health care system was cited as
one of the reasons why women’s experiences with breast implants have been historically
overlooked.
The federal government should take immediate action to protect the health and safety
of those who have received or are considering getting breast implants. In this report, the
committee puts forward 10 recommendations on how the Government of Canada can
strengthen the oversight of breast implants. Notably, the committee recommends that
the federal government establish a national breast implant registry as soon as possible,
require private practices to report adverse events, invest in research on breast implants,
and make improvements to Health Canada’s website to better inform consumers about
the risks of these medical devices.

Recommendation 1
That, as soon as possible, the Government of Canada establish a national
breast implant registry that would allow:
•
breast-implant recipients to receive information and be contacted in
the event of a recall;
•
reliable and comprehensive data on the risks and benefits of breast
implants to be collected; and
•
the long-term safety of these devices to be proactively tracked.

Recommendation 2
That the Government of Canada quickly establish a committee made up of
officials from Health Canada, experts and patient representatives, and work
with provinces and territories to achieve this goal.

Recommendation 3
That the Government of Canada ensure that the national breast implant
registry is implemented via a mandatory, uniform informed-consent form that
has a clear checklist, that is signed by the surgeon and patient, and that offers
the patient the possibility of opting out of the registry.

Recommendation 4
That the Government of Canada ensure that the national breast implant
registry has stable and long-term funding, that the registry uses a cost-recovery
model, and that the costs are funded by breast implant manufacturers.

Recommendation 5
That the Government of Canada ensure that the national breast implant
registry includes patient-reported outcome measures and tracks other devices
implanted at the same time as the breast implants, such as mesh or clips.

Recommendation 6
That Health Canada continue to work with the Canadian Institute for Health
Information and provinces and territories to develop and implement data
standards.

Recommendation 7
That the Government of Canada facilitate the process of reporting adverse
events to Health Canada and extend the obligation to private practices.

Recommendation 8
That the Government of Canada publish, on its website, clear and
comprehensive information on the risks associated with the different types of
breast implants, as well as photographs showing the adverse effects of breast
implants.

Recommendation 9
That Health Canada recognize breast implant illness.

Recommendation 10
That the Government of Canada fund research on breast implants, including,
but not limited to, long-term health effects.

Calls for better oversight of breast implants in Canada stretch back decades. Since 2004,
multiple bills have been introduced in Parliament to establish a national breast implant
registry, but none have progressed beyond first reading.1 In 2006, the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health (the committee) published a report on silicone gel-filled
breast implants.2 The report identified several areas of concern regarding the oversight of
these implants in Canada and made recommendations to the Government of Canada on
safety assessments, special access, informed consent and post-approval surveillance.
Certain changes were later made to the oversight of medical devices. In 2014, the
Protecting Canadians from Unsafe Drugs Act (Vanessa’s Law) was enacted to improve
the safety of drugs and medical devices. Among the measures implemented by
Vanessa’s Law is the requirement for hospitals to report incidents involving medical
devices.3 In 2018, Health Canada published an action plan on medical devices, with the
aim of improving safety, effectiveness and quality.4 As part of this plan, the department
established a Scientific Advisory Committee on Health Products for Women (SAC-HPW)5
and extended mandatory incident reporting to medical device manufacturers.6

Despite these initiatives, many of the issues identified in the committee’s 2006 report
persist. Canada still does not have a national breast implant registry. The safety of breast
implants, informed consent prior to implantation and the post-market surveillance
of implants remain areas of concern. In light of this situation, the committee, on
9 February 2022, adopted a motion to study the oversight of breast implants. The
motion read, in part:
That, pursuant to Standing Order 108(2), the committee undertake a
study to follow up on the improvements that have been put in place to
tighten Health Canada’s rules and improve oversight of medical devices
(breast implants) in 2018 and assess the feasibility of establishing a
central breast implant traceability registry that would make it mandatory
for practitioners who implant, remove, or replace breast implants to
enter certain data into the registry.7
The committee held four meetings on this study between 25 April 2023 and 11 May 2023
and heard from 11 witnesses. Witnesses included government officials representing
Health Canada, the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) and the Canada Health
Infoway, as well as plastic surgeons, professional associations, researchers and patient
advocacy groups. In addition, the committee received 42 written briefs.8
This report discusses certain key themes that emerged from the testimony: the need for
a national breast implant registry; the optimal design for such a registry; concerns over
pre- and post-market vigilance of breast implants; inadequate consumer information
and informed consent; the need for further research on breast implants; and issues of
gender equity and body image. The report also offers the federal government
recommendations on how to strengthen the oversight of breast implants.

section_title: THE NEED FOR A NATIONAL BREAST IMPLANT REGISTRY
text:
The committee heard strong support from witnesses for the creation of a national breast
implant registry.9 Witnesses generally expressed dismay that no such registry exists in
Canada, despite repeated calls to action spanning more than 30 years.10 Canada was said
to be the only G7 country without a breast implant registry.11 A number of witnesses
indicated that a registry is necessary to improve traceability, facilitate recalls and
advance research related to breast implants.
According to the testimony, breast implant recipients comprise an estimated 3% to 4%
of women in Western countries.12 Around 70% of those with implants had the surgery
for cosmetic reasons.13 The remainder have implants for medical reasons, such as
reconstruction after mastectomy or gender-affirming surgery. The committee heard
how the lack of a registry leaves breast implant recipients insufficiently protected from
potential adverse outcomes associated with these devices.
Health Canada categorizes breast implants as Class IV medical devices, representing the
highest risk to health.14 According to the department, breast implants are associated
with a variety of risks and adverse events that range from minor to life-threatening,
such as:
• post-operative complications (e.g., swelling, bleeding, mild to serious
infection, and changes in nipple and/or breast sensation);
