As a Canadian, I will always remember the harm our government caused during
the COVID pandemic. It will forever be a dark cloud in our history. The playgrounds
that were shutdown, fences put up. The masking that was forced on our children,
despite data showing that the rate of transmission in children was low. How the entire
country had to lockdown, to protect the vulnerable when we should’ve protected the
vulnerable and allowed the rest of the country to continue living their lives. This was a
virus that had a very high survival rate early on, and it got even higher as the Omicron
variant emerged. As of June 12th, Ontario’s total deaths are 90.5 deaths per 100,000.
That works out to 0.000905% (Ontario Public Health website). To think the risk of dying
from this virus was so incredibly low, yet these lockdowns caused such harm in so
many aspects of life – it’s truly devastating.
Yes, sadly people passed away from this virus. The majority of the deaths in
Canada were in the elderly or people that had multiple co-morbidities. This was not a
virus that was showing to take out healthy people. Yet even with data to support this,
we locked down our entire Country multiple times. We locked down our schools before
we locked down our airports – how does that make sense if we knew the virus was
coming from overseas?
For our children, they were forced to stay home, away from their friends, away
from their extended families. We put children in harm, as many children in Canada find
refuge and safety in their school community. Many depend on the lunch program, and
other services, all which they weren’t able to run. Mental Health issues are at an alltime high in both children, and adults and I hold our government accountable for that.
Children should not have been locked in their houses when they were not adding stress
to our hospitals and not experiencing serious illness from the virus. The majority of
children’s COVID cases, recovered at home. My children didn’t know what their
teacher’s smile looked like, didn’t know what some of their friends looked like because
they were forced to hide behind a mask for a large portion of the year. Despite COVID
mask restrictions being recently lifted in most public settings, children are still walking
around, feeling they need to wear a mask for protection. This has been a devastating
time in their childhood, and instilled fears and anxieties that may never go away.
Not only did these lockdowns cause harm to our children, they created mass fear
in Canadians. The message from the government made it seem that if you left your
house, you were going to get COVID and be severely ill and end up in the hospital.
People were afraid to go to an ER and so many chose not to, and I’m sure some of
those decisions resulted in people dying at home due to non-COVID related challenges
(ex. Cardiac arrests). Lifesaving surgeries were put on hold. People died waiting for
surgery, people avoided going for their regular screenings resulting in more advanced
staged cancers being diagnosed. We are now in a HUGE backlog of surgeries and will
never get caught up. People will die as a result of this poor handling of the pandemic.

(so no long term data) to be bad people. As other countries drop the vaccine
passports, including proof of negative tests, masking, we in Canada are keeping 20% of
our population in a prison, not allowing them to leave.
In conclusion, I hope we can reflect on how we mishandled this pandemic, and
learn from it. I hope going forward, our government will act with integrity, while
putting their politic platforms aside. As a parent, I can’t imagine telling my
grandchildren in 30 years, that I was part of a government who did this to Canadians –
who lied, who didn’t act in the best interest of the Country, and who tried to divide
Canada and discriminate against people based on a personal health choice. I honestly
don’t know how our government sleeps at night knowing that families are suffering as a
result of their power hungry mandates. For the future of Canada, I truly hope that our
MPs, no matter their political affiliation, will start standing up for what’s right and that is
freedom for all Canadians. It’s time for Canada to start healing, and we can’t do that
until this discrimination ends.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Dr. Kelly O’Brien, PhD, PT
Associate Professor, Department of Physical Therapy, University of Toronto
Co-Director, Rehabilitation Science Research Network for COVID, Temerty Faculty of Medicine,
University of Toronto
Canada Research Chair in Episodic Disability and Rehabilitation
Co-Director, Disability and Rehabilitation, Long COVID Physio
Brief Submission
June 13, 2022

SUMMARY POINTS & RECOMMENDATIONS
•
Long COVID presents with multi-dimensional clusters of symptoms that can fluctuate, sometimes
unpredictably, whereby symptoms adversely affect general well-being and ability to perform dayto-day activities, exercise, or work.
•
We propose that Long COVID should be conceptualised as an episodic health condition,
characterised by health-related challenges (or disability) that may be multi-dimensional, episodic,
and unpredictable in nature.
•
Dimensions of disability experienced by people living with Long COVID may include physical,
cognitive, mental and emotional health challenges, difficulties with daily activities, challenges to
social inclusion, and uncertainty, with uncertainty and worrying about the future a key dimension
of disability.
•
The role for rehabilitation is critical for people living with Long COVID, offering a goal-oriented,
person-centred approach to prevent, mitigate, and address episodic disability.
•
There is a need to establish valid and reliable measures of episodic disability, assessing
effectiveness of rehabilitation approaches and interventions, and building on existing international
collaborations and community-engaged partnerships to advance practice, research, and policy.

Introduction

A growing number of individuals are living with persistent and prolonged signs and symptoms following
infection consistent with COVID-19, referred to as Long COVID or Post-COVID Condition. Defined by the
World Health Organization, “Post COVID-19 condition or Long COVID occurs in individuals with a history
of probable or confirmed SARSCoV-2 infection, usually 3 months from the onset of COVID-19 with
symptoms that last for at least 2 months and cannot be explained by an alternative diagnosis. Common
symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath, cognitive dysfunction but also others and generally have
an impact on everyday functioning. Symptoms may be new onset following initial recovery from an
acute COVID-19 episode or persist from the initial illness. Symptoms may also fluctuate or relapse over
time.”

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Symptoms may also fluctuate or relapse over
time.”

An estimated 144 million individuals are living with Long COVID globally. A systematic review involving
50 studies, concluded the pooled global prevalence of Long COVID globally was 43% among hospitalized
(53%) and non-hospitalized patients (34%) (Chen et al, 2022). Systematic review evidence examining
symptoms among individuals after COVID-19 reported that 38-72% were living with >1 symptom for at
least 2 months, from COVID-19 onset and up to 54% were living with persistent symptoms for 6 or more
months (Nasserie, 2021; Domingo, 2021; Michelen, 2021; Whitaker 2021; Groff, 2021).

As of June 2022, an estimated 2 million people in the United Kingdom (3.1% of the population) selfidentified experiencing symptoms continuing greater than 4 weeks after COVID-19, and among those
with Long COVID, 30% had COVID prior to when alpha became the main variant, 12% in the alpha
variant period, 21% in Delta period, and 31% in the Omicron period, suggesting Long COVID can develop
regardless of variant (Office of National Statistics in the UK, June 2022).

The long-term trajectory of Long COVID remains unknown. Therefore conceptualising disability in Long
COVID is essential for better understanding the lived experiences and health-related challenges of
people living with and affected by Long COVID, to inform effective rehabilitation approaches and
interventions to enhance clinical practice, policy, and research.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Therefore conceptualising disability in Long
COVID is essential for better understanding the lived experiences and health-related challenges of
people living with and affected by Long COVID, to inform effective rehabilitation approaches and
interventions to enhance clinical practice, policy, and research.

Long COVID and Episodic Disability
Long COVID is characterized by ‘clusters of symptoms’ that can overlap and ‘fluctuate and change over
time’, described as ‘prolonged’, ‘relapsing and remitting’, which may be termed episodic (Brown &
O’Brien, 2020). Episodes may fluctuate with Long COVID within the day, between weeks, or over a
longer continuum. The multi-dimensional, episodic and sometimes unpredictable health consequences
of Long COVID resembles episodic disability, a concept derived from the context of HIV, where health
challenges can fluctuate daily or over longer periods of time (O’Brien et al, 2008, 2009).
Fatigue continues to be the most common reported symptom with Long COVID, among 55% of those
self-reported living with Long COVID in the UK followed by shortness of breath (32%), cough (23%) and
muscle aches (23%). (Office of National Statistics in the UK, June 2022). A community-led online survey
across 56 countries highlighted an average of 56 symptoms spanning nine organ systems including
fatigue, post exertional malaise (PEM), and cognitive dysfunction, with 86% of respondents experiencing
relapses in symptoms triggered by exercise, physical or mental activity, or stress (Davis et al, 2021).

The multi-dimensional nature of disability experienced by people living with Long COVID, can adversely
impact daily function, return to employment, family life, relationships, and ability to care for others. For
instance, among those living with Long COVID, 71% reported adverse affects to day-to-day activities,
with 20% reporting significant limitations to daily activities (Davis et al, 2021). Long COVID further
disproportionally affects people aged 35-59 years (prime career building years), females, people living in
deprived areas, those working with social care, teaching, education or health care, and those with other
activity limiting conditions or disability (Office of National Statistics in the UK, June 2022).

These health challenges can affect return to employment, relationships, access to services, stigma, and
mental health, further contributing to disability after acute COVID-19. Among respondents in a
community-led survey led by the Patient-Led Research Collaborative, 45% were working reduced hours,
and 22% were not working at all due to their illness. (Davis et al, 2021).

Episodic Disability Framework in Long COVID

Utilising an existing framework of disability developed from others living with episodic illness can
provide a foundation for understanding disability experienced among people living with Long COVID.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Utilising an existing framework of disability developed from others living with episodic illness can
provide a foundation for understanding disability experienced among people living with Long COVID.

The Episodic Disability Framework was derived from the perspectives of people living with HIV in
Canada to characterise the multi-dimensional and sometimes fluctuating nature of health-challenges
(O’Brien et al, 2008, 2009). The Episodic Disability Framework provides a novel way to conceptualise
disability experienced by people living with Long COVID. For instance, someone living with Long COVID
may experience dimensions of disability spanning physical health challenges (fatigue, post-exertional
symptom exacerbation, or shortness of breath), cognitive health challenges (difficulty thinking or
concentrating; “brain fog”), resulting in mental-emotional health challenges (anxiety, or depression),
difficulties carrying out day-to-day activities (showering, meal preparation, or walking), and impacting
challenges to social inclusion (meaningful life roles or employment). These disability dimensions may be
influenced by contextual factors, exacerbated by stigma including a lack of belief of health challenges,
or alleviated by practical and emotional support (eg: peer support) and rehabilitation services.
Furthermore, disability dimensions can be triggered by factors such as physical activity or exercise,
prolonged cognitive activities, or other health conditions.

A team of researchers, clinicians, and community members are collaborating on a CIHR-funded Long
COVID and Episodic Disability Study, to characterize the multi-dimensional and episodic nature of
disability experienced by adults living with Long COVID. Given the importance of terminology to provide
clarity of understanding and communication among community and health providers, we recommend
the use of the term ‘episodic disability’ to characterise the multidimensional, episodic and unpredictable
health-related challenges associated with Long COVID.
Uncertainty and Long COVID

Uncertainty and worry about the future is a key feature of disability experienced among people living
with long COVID. Uncertainty was found to be a key dimension of disability and predictor of mentalemotional health and social inclusion for adults living with HIV (O’Brien 2019). In Long COVID, the impact
of living with the uncertainty of when an episode of disability might arise, the severity and duration of
that episode, and the long-term implications on health, including the financial, practical, and emotional
consequences are unknown.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
In Long COVID, the impact
of living with the uncertainty of when an episode of disability might arise, the severity and duration of
that episode, and the long-term implications on health, including the financial, practical, and emotional
consequences are unknown.

Uncertainty experienced among people living with long COVID includes not knowing when an episode of
disability might arise, the severity and duration of that episode and the long-term implications on health
and life decisions. The long term outcomes and trajectory of Long COVID recovery remain unknown,
and new uncertainty exists about what might occur in the event of a re-infection of COVID-19 among
people living with Long COVID. Diagnostic uncertainty exists whereby Long COVID can be difficult to
ascertain, particularly for those without a COVID-19 PCR, antigen or antibody test, and can add
complexity to those faced with challenges accessing employment or income benefits after leaving the
workforce during illness, further contributing to disability and reduced quality of life after acute COVID19. Financial uncertainty may exist for those unsure if, when, or how to return to workforce, as well as
uncertainty among employers and human resource professionals as to how to accommodate and
facilitate return to work. Finally, uncertainty also exists among health and rehabilitation professionals as
to how to safely and effectively treat people living with Long COVID.
Role of Rehabilitation in Long COVID

With the ‘severely disabling’ potential of Long COVID, the role for rehabilitation is critical to help
prevent, address, mitigate disability and enhance health outcomes. Rehabilitation (including
physiotherapy and occupational therapy) involves any services or providers who address or prevent
disability focused on the physical, mental-emotional, cognitive and social domains of health and
disability, and hence is well-positioned to address episodic and multidimensional disability among
people living with Long COVID. Rehabilitation should be disability focused, goal-oriented, personcentred, focused on function, tailored to an individual’s goals, abilities, and interests.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Rehabilitation should be disability focused, goal-oriented, personcentred, focused on function, tailored to an individual’s goals, abilities, and interests.

Rehabilitation is not limited to exercise and physical activity. World Physiotherapy has been
instrumental in developing safe and effective rehabilitation approaches in Long COVID. Caution with
exercise has been recommended in physiotherapy guidelines as exercise is not a safe rehabilitation
intervention to treat fatigue among people experiencing post-exertional symptom exacerbation. It is
important to consider the length and burden of assessments and whether they have the potential to
trigger an episode of post exertional malaise. This is because physical exertion is a common trigger for
symptom exacerbation among people with Long COVID. See the World Physiotherapy Briefing Paper on
safe rehabilitation approaches for people living with Long COVID.

There is a critical need to assess the impact of rehabilitation interventions to reduce episodic disability
and enhance health outcomes for people living with Long COVID. Development of a robust research
agenda involving disability and rehabilitation will be important for moving forward including a
coordinated response, evidence to support; appropriate safe and timely and effective rehabilitation
strategies, interventions and models of care are needed.

Measurement of Episodic Disability in Long COVID

To provide optimal care in the context of Long COVID, we need comprehensive, feasible tools to
understand the profile and episodic nature of disability over time. Standardized patient reported
outcome measures designed to capture the nature and extent of disability and its fluctuation over time
are critical to guide the provision of care, determine the effectiveness of interventions, and inform
workplace policies (such as phased return to work) and access to services (such as rehabilitation) for
people living with Long COVID.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Standardized patient reported
outcome measures designed to capture the nature and extent of disability and its fluctuation over time
are critical to guide the provision of care, determine the effectiveness of interventions, and inform
workplace policies (such as phased return to work) and access to services (such as rehabilitation) for
people living with Long COVID.

The HIV Disability Questionnaire (HDQ) is a patient-reported outcome measure which describes a range
of health challenges a person might experience and the extent of fluctuation to better address the
disability needs of people with chronic illness. Based on the Episodic Disability Framework, this tool is
the first known measure of episodic disability, addressing gaps in previously existing health status
measures to capture uncertainty and elements of social inclusion (relationships, employment). The HDQ
possesses reliability and validity for use with people living with HIV in Canada, Ireland, United Kingdom,
and United States (O’Brien 2015, O’Brien 2019, Brown, 2019).
The newly formed Episodic Disability Questionnaire (EDQ) is the first known measure of episodic
disability, addressing gaps in previously existing health status measures to capture uncertainty and
elements of social inclusion (relationships, employment). There is an opportunity to build from existing
validated instruments in episodic disability with other chronic episodic conditions, to identify key
features of disability specific to persons living with Long COVID, to help indicate areas in which to direct
supports, interventions, and resources. Members of the international Long COVID community (COVID
Long Haulers Support Group Canada, Long COVID Support UK, Patient-Led Research Collaborative, Long
COVID Ireland, and Long COVID Physio) who are knowledge users and collaborators on the CIHR-funded
Long COVID and Episodic Disability study are working to establish the Episodic Disability Questionnaire.

Foundational data on the presence, severity and episodic nature of disability and contextual factors that
may influence disability are critical for guiding treatment approaches. Universal measurement of
disability over time may facilitate clinical management, specifically tracking episodic disability trends to
better tailor rehabilitation resources and approaches among people living with chronic episodic
conditions. Long-term measurement of disability will contribute to existing databases to document
longitudinal profiles of disability and situate disability as a key construct in health services research. This
will allow tracking of disability trends to evaluate implementation of interventions and policies for
enhancing labour force participation and income support that acknowledge the fluctuating and
unpredictable nature of chronic illness.

Community engaged rehabilitation response to Long COVID rehabilitation.

Finally, taking a community-engaged response to Long COVID rehabilitation will help to foster timely,
relevant and meaningful interventions and approaches to rehabilitation, and the application of research

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Finally, taking a community-engaged response to Long COVID rehabilitation will help to foster timely,
relevant and meaningful interventions and approaches to rehabilitation, and the application of research

evidence about appropriate service planning and delivery. Disability and rehabilitation-focused
responses should include people living with and affected by the pandemic.
International partnerships and collaborations fostered in other health conditions provide a strong
foundation from which to establish a coordinated, relevant and meaningful approach for advancing
rehabilitation for people living with Long COVID. Access to timely, safe, effective, and accessible
rehabilitation is a critical area in need of development and highlights the opportunities and importance
of partnering with other chronic conditions to foster a ‘strength in numbers approach’ with other
chronic and episodic illnesses to advance policy and programming related to Long COVID rehabilitation
such as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis (ME) and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS).
In Summary

The role for safe and effective rehabilitation is critical in the context of Long COVID. It is essential to
better understand episodic disability experienced by people living with Long COVID, establish tools to
measure the presence, severity, and episodic nature of disability, in order to target timely and
appropriate rehabilitation interventions and mitigate disability to enhance health outcomes for people
living with Long COVID. While evidence continues to emerge, rehabilitation professionals are well
positioned to address episodic disability in Long COVID. Opportunities exist to build on successful
disability and rehabilitation models from other chronic and episodic illnesses, in the context of Long
COVID.
For more information: Long COVID Physio is an international patient-led association of physiotherapists
living with Long-COVID and allies which provides a wealth of resources and videos on Long COVID,
research evidence, and safe approaches to rehabilitation.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Thank you for making the time to accept this Brief.
I am speaking on behalf of my twin brother, Stephen MacDougall. He died on May 25,
2021, 4 weeks after receiving his first dose of Astra Zeneca vaccine, at the age of 45.
Before I delve into details, I thought I would speak a little about who Stephen was.
Stephen was beloved by so many people. To know Stephen was to experience love,
and a joy for life.
Stephen could best be described as a bright light. He drew people in, everywhere he
went, and made people feel better for knowing him. He was magnetic.
When he died, people from every part of his tremendous life reached out to extend their
condolences and share their stories. Friends, teachers from every school (including
substitute teachers from elementary school), co-workers, classmates, teammates, and
family shared not only their love, but specific– sometimes ridiculous and funny– details.
.
A common thread emerged: Stephen made people feel better, he was compassionate,
he was joyful, he extended a hand to all. He could bridge divides. He always assumed
the best of intentions of others and had a way of making us all see each other through a
different lens. A better, more compassionate lens. It was as if he was a flashlight,
shining light everywhere he went.
He was a devoted son, a caring brother. He was a cherished husband. His most
beloved title was that of “Daddy”. He leaves behind a grieving family including his 2
beloved children, Rielle and Kieran.
I am here today to attempt to shed a little light on not only Stephen’s life, but also his
death. He received his vaccine on Friday, April 23, 2021. He started to experience
symptoms soon after his vaccine. His symptoms continued to worsen. By the following
Friday, he went to the ER at Peterborough Regional Health Center, was seen, and
released. Saturday morning, he collapsed in the shower. His wife Kim, drove him to the
ER, where she was met at the doors. Stephen was wheeled into the ER. He was
admitted to the hospital. By Sunday he was transferred to the ICU. By Monday he was
placed on a ventilator. He spent 3 agonizing weeks in the ICU, with family by his side.
On May 25, at 8:00 pm, he died in the loving arms of his wife Kim and his adored
children, Rielle and Kieran. Family and friends gathered for an impromptu vigil outside
his hospital window, with others “zooming in” from around the continent.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Family and friends gathered for an impromptu vigil outside
his hospital window, with others “zooming in” from around the continent.

In sickness and in death, Stephen continued to draw people in. The people in charge of
all of Stephen’s care, again, both in sickness and in death, have been compassionate
and good people.
But the system that these good, hard working people are working within, has flaws.
Flaws that– I believe– we as a country can work to illuminate. I have faith that the good
people of Canada, and those of you that we have elected to represent us, can work to
find a better path forward for the next Stephen. Because, unfortunately, there will
always be a “next Stephen.”
Stephen believed in vaccination. He believed in science. And because of these beliefs,
we must shine the light on the faulty system (Stephen was the Shop foreman for
Mercedez and was an expert at diagnosing problems—and then he came at the
problem with a solution).
But we must have the courage to look at the faults and then work toward a solution.
Stephen’s autopsy was completed in December of 2021. His official cause of death is:
Myopericarditis following covid 19 vaccination.
And with that I ask of you:
1) Stephen's case is appropriately and amply captured in both federal and provincial
data as a death following Covid-19 vaccination, both in the interest of public health and
pursuing science. And we, the family, need to be able to verify his inclusion. His death
must carry a constant reminder that as the Health Committee your decisions have
consequences, even unintended. Please acknowledge his life and death. He was
important.
2) Transparency with the Vaccine “Injury” Support Program. As it stands, we have
worked through endless entities, including Ontario Public Health, Peterborough Public
Health, the Coroner's office and PRHC, as his case “fell through” several cracks. Had it
not been for his enormous support system, his case would likely have never been
recorded. Along the way, we have encountered obstacle after obstacle. VISP is now the
latest obstacle. The burden of proof lies on the family. The next cycle of emails and
follow up phone calls to be certain his case is not forgotten.
3) Full report of the vaccine "injured" made open to the public.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
The next cycle of emails and
follow up phone calls to be certain his case is not forgotten.
3) Full report of the vaccine "injured" made open to the public.

Want List:
1) That the hateful discourse from all sides: red, blue, orange and green, cease. We are
a people. Our fight should be united against a virus.
2) As a country, our elected officials assumed the risk of the vaccine (as opposed to the
manufacturers) so we must step up and step into supporting those now left fatherless.
3) Options to receive vaccine exemptions without prejudice, and a system to facilitate
that decision.
4) Removal of Vaccine mandates for employment and engagement in society.
With that, I would like to finish up with some expressions of gratitude.
1) To the great people of Canada who continue to recognize Universal Health care
as a basic human right, and not privilege.
2) To you all, who have all answered the vocation to represent us, your constituents,
and the great people of Canada. God knows, your job is difficult and comes with
little fanfare. As members of the standing committee dealing with health matters, I
cannot begin to imagine how difficult your job has been. A special acknowledgement
to Dr.Stephen Ellis, who made time to hear Stephen’s story and to help keep
his case moving forward.
3) Gratitude to the ICU team at Peterborough Regional Health Center, especially
Dr. Mark Maraschiello and Dr. Greg Bishop, who definitely pulled out all the
stops to do everything they possibly could for Stephen. Registered nurses,
respiratory therapists and physicians on his team provided excellent care
throughout his extended stay.
4) To Dr. Paul Dungey, the Regional Chief Coroner for Eastern Ontario, who
worked tirelessly to provide us with weekly updates as to the process and
progress of Stephen’s post mortem care.
5) To Dr. Thomas Piggott, Medical Officer of Health and CEO of Peterborough
Public Health, who took the time to look into Stephen’s case and made time to
talk with us personally.

In closing, in shining the light toward our faults, may we end up in a better spot than
we started. Our hope is that the next “Stephen” finds the system easier to navigate
than was our experience.
Thank you.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Throughout the pandemic I feel that we, as a country, completely lost sight of our humanity. I work at
multiple healthcare facilities throughout my community, both acute surgical, medical and long term
care. The stress and horror at witnessing patients having to come to the hospital alone for very sensitive
issues that very much warranted family support, or having to witness patients pass away alone while
their family members stood outside and watched through a window was traumatic to say the least. We
never should have initiated policies that prevented visitors from supporting their loved ones, nor should
we have the power to do so.
Being an unvaccinated Canadian I faced job loss, was prevented from taking part in society, was/am
discriminated against by the very leader of my country, and to be honest feel stress and a sense that I
am doing something wrong when I enter the rec center to take my young daughters swimming or to a
movie even to this day.
My husband and I continue to be banned from travelling by plane due to senseless travel bans and
restrictions that continue unnecessarily for unvaccinated Canadians. These rules have prevented us from
seeing my husbands’ family on the other side of Canada for over 2 years.
Reflecting on the past two years I am horrified by the trauma induced on Canadians, and for what? In
the end the majority of us have contracted Covid. We have been mocked, ridiculed, shamed, lost our
jobs. We have been segregated from society. Masked our children. Isolated them from their friends.
Created more and more economic unsteadiness and mental health and addictions crises.
When we discovered that the virus wasn’t as deadly to the general public as originally thought I
wholeheartedly feel that politicians should have done a pivot, and instead moved to protecting the most
vulnerable in our society, and allowed the rest of the population to lead regular lives. This was modelled
in Sweden, which turned out to work quite well for them.
I certainly hope that should we as Canadians ever face a situation like this again in my lifetime that we
face it with humanity, compassion, and follow the “science”. Not the science that is censored, warped
and created for political gain and fear mongering.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
To: The Standing Committee on Health,

I am writing this brief in the hopes that adding my voice to the millions of others who have been
negatively affected by the Covid mandates and restrictions, can lead to a change in this country. I hope
our voices will be heard and taken seriously.

Speaking simply as a wife, mother, daughter, granddaughter and Canadian citizen, I am
appalled at the continued draconian measures in response to Covid 19. Early on in the pandemic, when
there was much uncertainty in regards to the severity, spread and possible death-toll, the various
mandates, restrictions and bylaws made sense – we were all a little unsure how things would play out.
But it didn't take long to see that things did not pan out as seriously as predicted, but instead of relaxing
the mandates, the government of Canada (and provincial governments) seemed bent on continuing to
restrict Canadians from living as free citizens, and even increasing the restrictions in place.

Forced masking, closing of businesses and places of worship, punitive threats on any type of
social gathering and, eventually, forced vaccination (by using coercive threats, measures, and
punishments) have all impeded our rights to live as free citizens of Canada. We were told we were no
longer allowed to make choices for ourselves, that we must do as told or be punished with fines, lack of
service (in health care settings, for example), imprisonment (to see Canadian pastors put in prison – I
never thought I'd live to see the day!), loss of jobs, inability to travel, etc. How dare this “free” country
of Canada limit its citizens of these very basic, God-given rights!

text:
How dare this “free” country
of Canada limit its citizens of these very basic, God-given rights!

Here we are, nearly 27 months into this pandemic, and I've lost track of the ways my family and
I have been negatively affected by the various Covid mandates that have been or are still in place. My
children have lost more than 2 years of “normal” life, they have missed birthday parties, playdates with
friends, family gatherings, the ability to participate in sports. They have missed seeing faces, unable to
get to know and trust those who should have been considered trust-worthy individuals in their lives –
doctors, police officers, teachers, etc. How can I explain to my 3-year old that she can trust this person
whose face she cannot even see?! I was unable to see my both my grandmother and grandfather in the
last year of their lives because of covid restrictions, and many family members were unable to attend
their funerals due to ridiculous gathering restrictions – how cruel to be unable to say goodbye to loved
ones either in person before death, or through mourning at a funeral after death! And, no, neither of
them died of Covid OR “with” Covid, but their fast decline was likely exacerbated by their inability to
see or interact with 99% of their loved ones in their final months of life. My husband lost an
opportunity to speak and teach outside of Canada because he in unable to travel due to the unjustified
government-enforced travel mandates. The inside of our Canadian Passport says, “The Minister of
Foreign Affairs of Canada requests, in the name of Her Majesty the Queen, all those whom it may
concern to allow the bearer to pass freely without let of hindrance and to afford the bearer such
assistance and protection as may be necessary.” And yet, within our very own country, the government
is not allowing it's citizens to “pass freely without let of hindrance.” What hypocrisy!

the name of Her Majesty the Queen, all those whom it may concern to allow the bearer to pass freely without let of hindrance and to afford the bearer such assistance and protection as may be necessary.” And yet, within our very own country, the government is not allowing it's citizens to “pass freely without let of hindrance.” What hypocrisy!

The above are just a few examples of the ways in which the measures the Government of
Canada have taken have negatively affected myself and my family. We are but one family, consider the
millions of other Canadians who have also been unjustly treated – who continue to be unjustly treated,
having our freedoms ripped from our very hands. Canadians deserve REAL evidence for these
continued tyrannical measures that are in place. And given the utter lack of evidence to justify them,
Canadians deserve the right to live freely and peaceably – to have their freedoms re-instated to travel,
move about, do as they see fit in regards to their own personal health.

I strongly urge this committee to immediately and fully suggest and support that the
Government of Canada remove all Covid [CONTACT] – once again granting to Canadians
their Charter-defined, God-given right to live as free citizens.

Thank you for your time and consideration,
Mavis Snyder

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
May 30 2022
To the Committee Members,
My name is Courtney Hobbs and I am a Canadian Citizen, teacher and mother. I have had the
privilege of travelling to many regions of the world. I have seen Canada from coast to coast. I
have lived in another country. I hold 3 degrees and have 2 children. I am a contributing member
of society. And the Covid-19 pandemic nearly killed me.
I have been battling mental health issues for most of my life. But in 2015 I started my path to
becoming the healthiest version of myself. In January 2020 when I gave birth to my second child
I was the best version of myself I’ve ever been. I was thriving. Fast forward to July 2021 and I
was writing goodbye letters to my beautiful daughters and planning how I would take my own
life.
It actually wasn’t the lockdowns. I was blessed to have family and friends that were willing to

text:
Personal Experience of Maureen Thompson
When the pandemic started I was having my third miscarriage after several years of infertility. I
thought I was nearing the end of my personal nightmare, but I had no idea it was just beginning.
I contracted Covid-19 in March of 2020. It was not pleasant but I recovered with an outpatient
visit to my doctor. I got pregnant again in August of 2020. This pregnancy was successful, and
we have a wonderful, healthy vibrant son. While pregnant I experienced several lockdowns
where I could not see anyone outside of my husband including my biggest support, my mother. I
was isolated and lonely, missing my favorite events like Christmas and having a baby shower.
What should have been the happiest time of my life was one where I was deeply sad, often
despondent and felt a general sense of hopelessness. There were many days where I could not
control my crying, and it would last for hours because of the cruel and inhumane way I was
forced to exist. As my due date neared and my husband worked nights, no one could stay with
me due to the Covid rules. I was incredibly anxious I would go into labor alone which was
against my wishes. My mom took my birth class with me online. When I went to the hospital to
deliver she was told to go home as the rules had changed that morning. I was incredibly anxious
and heartbroken which resulted in my labor stalling. It took me 44 hours to deliver after the
support I needed was carelessly stripped.
The vaccine rollout occurred while I was pregnant. I was not eligible. With no long-term
research or data, suddenly I was being pushed to get it while breastfeeding. After my infertility
and miscarriage experience, I decided I was not comfortable getting an mRNA injection which is
a new technology and was only in Phase 2 clinical trials at the time. I have three medical
concerns that also contraindicate this as a good option, not to mention natural immunity. I do
believe I could have a severe adverse reaction, or die, as a result of being injected. As someone
who is health conscious I weighed the risks and benefits and engaged in informed consent
assuming this would be respected as it always had in the past. I had no idea that what I
experienced while pregnant was just the beginning.
In the summer of 2021, Justin Trudeau called a snap election and weaponized the ‘vaccination’
status (with the very definition of vaccine changed to suit this injection, which is more of a
therapeutic) of millions of Canadians for votes. In his now infamous speech he said that the
‘vaccine’ free take up ‘space’ and asks if they should be ‘tolerated’. His actions and speeches
have revolved around dehumanizing, scapegoating and blaming those who chose not to take this
‘vaccine’ for all the problems occurring in Canada, because every issue can be fixed by being
vaccinated twice. And then taking a booster. Trudeau has went as far to say that because of
personal medical decisions, a group in Canada is misogynistic, racist, and a fringe minority with
unacceptable views.
In the fall of 2021 the vaccine passports were put into place. My husband and I took September
to get in some fun things while we could. We took our son to the museum and swimming. Then,
as a new mom on maternity leave, I was shut out of society. I was treated like a diseased parasite
who was putting others at risk despite having natural immunity and being healthy. Needless to
say, over the fall and winter I got a taste of what being dehumanized feels like. I was allowed to
go to friends’ houses, but wasn’t allowed to go indoors to use the bathroom or breastfeed my

Statement for Standing Committee on Health Meeting on Monday, June 13, 2022
The effects of Long COVID – where symptoms of the COVID-19 virus persist beyond four weeks from initial
infection – are disrupting our health, our labour force and our economy. An estimated 10 to 30 per cent
of COVID-19 survivors are currently experiencing a range of Long COVID symptoms, which means that
more than one million Canadians could be affected. This is roughly equivalent to the population of
Ottawa.
Viral Neuro Exploration (VINEx), a non-profit corporation, was established in April 2020 by the private
medical device company Rocket Science Health. Its initial goal was to compile scientific evidence to
determine if SARS-CoV-2, a respiratory virus, could directly or indirectly impact the central nervous
system. Impacts across the human system had been observed in previous viral pandemics, and therefore
there was a precedent to believe the same would be true for this pandemic.
VINEx recruited a Science Advisory Council of leading experts in virology, immunology, neuroscience and
neurology, and conducted an extensive literature review of the phenomenon of viruses impacting the
brain. The work to gather scientific evidence from around the world—as well as mainstream media
coverage—continues with the publication of a by-weekly newsletter called The Grapevine.
As Long COVID became a reality, VINEx recognized the need to include the voices of people with lived
experience to understand the full scale of the impacts and patient priorities. Despite the growing evidence
base, people with lived experience struggled to be heard as individuals; social media gave them platforms
to organize and create a movement to attract medical, media and government attention. Survivor Corps
in the US has nearly 200,000 members; COVID Long Haulers Support Group Canada has nearly 17,000
members, and internationally the Long COVID Alliance has been coordinating advocacy groups.
VINEx joined with the COVID Long-Haulers Support Group Canada and Neurological Health Charities
Canada (NHCC) to leverage science, clinical research, and lived experiences.
In the spring of 2021, and again this spring, VINEx and its partners prepared a survey of Canadians with
Long COVID. These surveys were distributed through the COVID Long-Haulers Support Group Canada and
NHCC memberships.
Both surveys included responses from more than 1,000 COVID long-haulers from across Canada. At the
time of publication in June 2021, the first survey was the largest publicly available survey of people living
with Long COVID in Canada.
The first survey (report) demonstrated the broader impacts of Long COVID on quality of life, with
responses suggesting economic, health and societal costs with consequences on the health sector and

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
The first survey (report) demonstrated the broader impacts of Long COVID on quality of life, with
responses suggesting economic, health and societal costs with consequences on the health sector and

labour force. The second survey (report) highlighted the negative brain health impacts of Long COVID.
Indeed, over 80% of respondents said the virus has negatively or very negatively impacted their brain
health.
Though Long COVID affects the entire body, many of the most persistent symptoms are linked to brain
health. These symptoms include headaches, ‘brain fog,’ chronic fatigue, impaired memory or
concentration, anxiety, depression and insomnia.
Key findings from the two surveys include:
•
In both surveys, over 87% of respondents identified as women. This is consistent with studies
which demonstrate that women are disproportionately affected by Long COVID, by as much as
a 4 to 1 ratio.
•
Before having COVID-19, nearly 63% of respondents did not have a long-term health condition.
•
More than 85% of participants were not admitted to hospital during their initial infection.
•
Only a quarter of respondents were initially believed and received appropriate care when they
described their Long COVID symptoms to a healthcare professional.
•
In both surveys, about 70% of respondents had to take leave from work as a result of living with
Long COVID, sometimes for over a year, with some having to leave the workforce. More than
half had to reduce working hours, with 74% reducing their working hours by 50% or more.
•
For those experiencing neurological or psychiatric symptoms, more than 80% say it has
negatively or very negatively impacted their daily life.
•
Close to 75% of long-haulers surveyed have sought medical care for their neurological or
psychiatric symptoms.

While much of the focus on Long COVID has been limited to the health impacts, the surveys revealed that
its consequences affect all aspects of society and the economy, and are contributing to the larger
pandemic mental health crisis.
Long COVID is having an impact on the economy and the labour force. The question that remains is the
magnitude. The Centre for Addiction and Mental Health estimates poor mental health costs the Canadian
economy more than $50 billion annually, of which more than $6 billion is due to lost productivity. And
according to the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association’s latest data, Canadian insurers paid out
$420 million in psychology claims in 2020, a staggering 24 per cent increase from 2019.
But the numbers do not tell the whole story; we need to hear from people who are trying to live their dayto-day life with Long COVID, some in constituencies represented by members of this Committee. And we
need to address the different impacts of Long COVID and take a long view to monitoring these impacts,
which may continue for months and years, and find solutions that do not leave a large subset of the
population behind as the pandemic becomes endemic and the issue is no longer in the public view.
As civil society advocates, VINEx, the COVID Long-Haulers Support Group Canada and NHCC are working
to keep this issue to the forefront. VINEx approached the Chief Scientist of Quebec to secure $2 million in

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
VINEx approached the Chief Scientist of Quebec to secure $2 million in

provincial funding to expand the work of Dr. Emilia Falcone, to include examining brain health impacts of
Long COVID by partnering with Dr. Lesley Fellows at the Montreal Neurological Institute. It lauded the
Liberal Party’s election platform commitment to invest $100 million into Long COVID research, with $20
million confirmed in the last Budget. But more needs to be done to help Canadians living with Long COVID,
and given the different dimensions of Long COVID, research cannot depend solely on the usual timelines
and quantum of CIHR funding.
1. We need to continue the work to develop a concise definition of Long COVID and develop a
single test for diagnosing Long COVID. This will allow us to better understand the size and
impact of the problem;
2. We need to bring attention to the stories of people with lived experience and counter the
stigma being faced by those who are not believed because the illness is not well-defined and
not always properly diagnosed. Beyond the mental health stress, this has an impact on the
ability to access unemployment benefits and disability insurance;
3. We need to establish more multidisciplinary care clinics to be able to treat the different
dimensions of Long COVID;
4. We need to increase funding for multidisciplinary research and longitudinal studies, in order
to advance our understanding of what causes Long COVID, how to treat it, and the potential
long-term impacts, which may include contributing to the development of neurodegenerative
diseases in the future. This is not just up to governments. Businesses and the private sector
have a role to play and a stake in funding such research; and
5. Finally, from a workplace perspective, employers need to provide more flexibility and a
gradual return to work for those ready to come back.

One last thought: we can look to the US for some lessons learned as we chart an accelerated path forward.

One last thought: we can look to the US for some lessons learned as we chart an accelerated path forward.

From The Missing Part of America’s Pandemic Response - The Atlantic:
The slow pace of the NIH’s grant-funding mechanism is another factor undermining innovative
research. The dreaded syndrome known as Long COVID was first reported in May 2020. Estimates
of how many Americans it afflicts range from 7.7 million to more than 20 million; according to the
CDC, 20 percent of adults under age 65 who are infected by the coronavirus experience symptoms
potentially attributable to Long COVID. To bring life back to normal, the U.S. at least needs to
know how frequently the syndrome occurs, who is at highest risk, how much vaccines protect
people from it, and how to prevent and treat it. Yet only nine of about 240 currently
registered Long COVID studies are funded by the NIH. In December 2020, Congress allocated more
than $1 billion to the NIH for the study of Long COVID; the NIH subsequently approved $470
million in September 2021 to create a research consortium, with a plan to have more than 200
recruitment sites up and running in early 2022. But two years after Long COVID was first
recognized, this study has enrolled less than 15 percent of the necessary participants.
Respectfully submitted by Inez Jabalpurwala
Global Director – Viral Neuro Exploration (VINEx)

Thank you for receiving feedback from Canadians regarding the “Emergency Situation Facing

authorities and media.
In the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic I think it is fair to say that the majority of the
public, the government nor the health officials knew how long it would last, how deadly it was
or was not going to be or what exactly to do. Taking that into consideration I am able to feel
that in the beginning everyone was doing the best they could. I have two big concerns with the
months that followed in 2020. First the numbers of reported cases and deaths. We now know
that these numbers weren’t accurate or truthfully portrayed by the government or media.
Secondly, the lockdowns, vaccinations and mandates. During 2020, watching these things
happen around me, it seemed that more harm was happening than was warranted given the
actual threat of the virus. It felt to me that there was an overreaction happening that was
causing more fear, division and isolation. Once the vaccination was made available, the
coercion to receive it was strong with harsh words from the prime minister, other government
officials, health officials and the media. At one point there was an article saying that

heard over and over the words, “do the right thing” which for me does not show having faith in
the public to make healthy choices for themselves or their families. The strong push toward
getting vaccinated did not feel like a choice for me and if my husband wanted to continue
working he had to take the vaccination. That’s not really choice; that’s almost blackmail. Do

vaccine passports saved lives. I never received an answer. All we heard was that vaccine
passports save lives. HOW? I think the passports were used to control, coerce, divide and
segregate people. I still don’t know how using them saved lives.
The things that didn’t make sense to me was the misleading information that seemed to be
coming from the government, health authorities and the media. We were told people were
dying from the virus when in fact they were dying from other things, but may have had the virus
which did not kill them. The numbers made no sense if you actually looked all of the
information in the health portals available. It made absolutely no sense that I was allowed to
drive over 530 kms to another community in my own province but I was told that I wasn’t
allowed to drive 385 km to a community outside of my province without risk of being pulled
over by the RCMP, facing fines and negative responses from people. It made no sense to me

precisely and in sterile conditions such as a hospital. These mandates have had dire effects on

Vaccine mandates- it is absolutely astonishing and un-Canadian to fire hardworking, dedicated
Canadians from their jobs and careers because of a personal medical choice. It is an
embarrassment to democracy. We now have greater nurse shortages, in addition to shortages
in transport workers and a wide array of other careers due to the mandates and in the end, it is
Canadians that suffer due to the poor service and care that can be provided, as well as the
economic failure that will ensue when you thrust thousands upon thousands of Canadians into
financial instability. It is horrific that the government ever okay-ed this. My mother is still

had to watch perfectly healthy colleagues be fired due to their personal choices. And now, my
mother is being called in all the time to cover for colleagues who sick, even though they’re

ineffective and unlawful measures.

The Standing Committee on Health

Below is a letter written by my daughter, who wishes to remain anonymous.
To Whom It May Concern,
I believe the mandatory COVID-19 vaccination policy is unnecessary and unethical, and it
is still impacting my life today.
I was hesitant to get the COVID-19 vaccine until there had been more testing done,
especially because I have a neurological disorder and I knew that the vaccine might affect that.
So, when I started my first year at the University of Western Ontario this September, I was able
to get an approved vaccine exemption based on creed.
I am a theatre major, and the whole reason I wanted to go to Western is because of their
excellent theatre opportunities. I got a main role in the first play I auditioned for, but the offer
was retracted when they found out I was not vaccinated. I got my first vaccine the next day. It
was too late to re-join the play, but I knew I would keep missing out on things without it. I did
not get the vaccine for safety reasons or because I thought it was the best choice for me, but
because I had to get it if I wanted a normal school experience. That felt like the wrong reason to
get a medical injection.
The day after I got first dose of the Pfizer vaccine, I got an itchy rash on my neck. A week
later, I got a rash on my chest. The rashes got more frequent, and then on November 22nd (my
18th birthday), my chest and stomach were covered in hives. I called the doctor that night, and
they immediately put me on high doses of Reactine and told me not to get the second dose of the
vaccine until it cleared up. She gave me an eight-week exemption (which has since expired), but

text:
She gave me an eight-week exemption (which has since expired), but

it has been six months, and it has not cleared up. She told me she could not extend the exemption
unless I had an immediate anaphylactic reaction from the vaccine.
After two months, the Reactine stopped working and I was put on an even stronger
antihistamine prescription, which I have been taking since then.
My first year at university came and went, and I could not participate in any theatre
productions. Course selection for second year begins soon, and I still don’t know if I can keep
attending Western at all with their new vaccination policies, let alone continue with my theatre
major.
I started saving money for university at seven years old. I have always loved learning, and I
didn’t exactly know what university was yet, but I knew it would be a place where I could study
the subjects that I was passionate about. I spent my entire elementary and high school experience
working as hard as I possibly could so that I would have the marks to get into a good university
and the experience to get scholarships. I spent more time on school than most kids I knew, I
joined every club I could, I volunteered, I started my own community service projects, and I
even got onto my school board as a student trustee. I graduated high school with a 98% average,
and I received a full scholarship to Western.
Now, with Western’s vaccination policies, I might not even be allowed to continue
attending university there. If I cannot attend Western in the fall, I will not just lose the education
I have been waiting for since I was seven years old, but I will lose tens of thousands of dollars of
funding.
This education is my whole life, and I have been on the brink of losing all of it for the last
six months. And all over one vaccination that I did not even want and now I cannot even get, that
has unreliable efficacy, for an illness that many of my already-vaccinated friends and family got

In January 2022 my father’s health began to deteriorate. I live in a different province and had been
waiting for the snow to let up so that my family could drive out there and be with him; however,
unfortunately this year the snow continued later than usual. As I am pregnant and have a 2-year old, I

and he died without his daughter or grandson there to hold his hand. The flight to be with him is less
than an hour and would have allowed me to be there with him, but I am not allowed to board a plane in
my own country because I am not vaccinated for Covid. I specifically chose to not get vaccinated as I was
already having fertility issues and didn’t want to tamper with the protocol that I was on (my specialists
supported my decision). I am not comfortable taking any medications during pregnancy and I don’t
believe that’s unreasonable.

able to physically get to him while he was sick and dying. I am extremely traumatized by this situation
and it has taken a huge toll on both my physical and mental health during pregnancy. I am begging you to
consider the impact of these travel mandates on innocent citizens so that others do not have to endure
what my family went through.
Kind regards,

Resident of Edmonton
Mother of one (soon to be two)

situation as a whole and we would have been able to focus more resources to the vulnerable
population. Instead, the government was dictating harsh rules to to people and their businesses
without any consideration and based those decisions on modelling (which was never accurate)and
under the guise of public safety and public ignorance. Fast forward to the end of year one, I have an
aunt who passed away from cancer who didn’t have a funeral and whom I could not visit before she
passed due to capacity limitations. Another aunt in the hospital with cancer who also can’t have visitor,
and 2 weddings postponed.There were/are elderly people living in seniors homes literally losing the will
to live out of loneliness, children losing out on education and being forced to wear masks and only one
option being provided as the “way out”. People who decided to wait to get the coveted vaccine –
regardless of their reason, even if it was to ensure the supply was there for people with compromised
immune systems or the elderly etc. were made to feel like second class citizens. That rhetoric
progressed to turn them into selfish villains in a heartbeat with the aggressive divisive language used by
our very own prime minister. At this point in the pandemic – facts were considered “misinformation” or
“disinformation” and the public was considered too dim witted or simple to be able to distinguish the
truth so the government decided to do that for us meanwhile they are still using that faulty “modelling”
to make decisions without regard for over a year of actual live data. Then came the vaccine mandates
which completely divided our beautiful nation that has been pumped full of fear for well over a year.
The vaccine passport was only to create division – and it worked. Anyone who mentioned that the
vaccine doesn’t stop transmission which by all accounts meant the passport system was about
segregation and not about health was ostracized and ridiculed - and in my case – put on an unpaid leave
of absence right before Christmas from a job that I worked at for over 10 years and had been working
from home since March 2020. The handling of this pandemic has caused nothing but division, distrust
and animosity between citizens, the healthcare system, families and friends all due to public officials
who seem to have forgotten their role as public servants. It will take a long time to repair what has been
broken in our country over the past 2 years and at this point it doesn’t even look like the leaders of this
country are interested in even attempting it as even now – in May of 2022 – they are fuelling this fire of
division and hateful rhetoric and unscientific policies and acting like children in the House of Commons.
At this point in time I find it absolutely appalling that what was once a great country known for its
kindness and beautiful landscape is now applauding the fact that it is the only country who won’t let it’s
own citizens leave the country or even fly within it if they haven’t injected themselves with a
pharmaceutical product. In my life I have never thought of moving out of Canada and now find myself in
a position where the only way I could, would be to escape. Let that sink in.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
To whom it may concern,
My name is Melanie and up until December 27th, 2021, I had been a long term employee of over 11
years at a Long Term Care Home north of Toronto, ON. November 10th, 2021 was my final day of
employment, as myself and several other of my co-workers were informed we no longer met the
requirements of employment due to personal medical choices made. I am writing this letter to reveal
the devastation and hardship myself and my co-workers have had to endure since the termination of
our employment.
First and foremost, I would like to open up and tell you about how this termination has impacted my life
personally. Since December 27th, 2021 I have had the challenging job of advancing on with life as
though I had interest in continuing to live it. I have lost my career as a nurse, my business providing
advanced footcare to the seniors, and also have lost my ability to financially support myself, my family
and make my mortgage payments. My sense of purpose in life is now questioned daily. I took great
pride in being a nurse and helping our seniors. I had devoted my life and a great deal of my time into
caring for our resident’s as this is what made me happy and fulfilled my heart. I now work a minimum
wage job and am falling further and further behind financially. I am 31 years old and having to restart
and reevaluate my entire life.
Terminating myself, and the others is one thing, but leaving our resident’s in a position where they now
have less staff to care for their needs is unjust. It is not a secret that the staffing levels in Long Term Care
are at a critical level, our residents deserve more dedicated staff, not less. This is truly disgraceful!
I would like to briefly talk about another devastating reality one of our fellow coworkers endured. I am
sharing this story with her permission, as this is an unfortunate correlation due to her termination.
Approximately a month ago, one of our fellow terminated healthcare workers attempted to take her
own life. She mentioned to me she was having a hard time finding any kind of relevant employment
relating to her specific skillset and she was feeling depressed and overwhelmed. Bills were adding up,
mortgage payments overdue, a family to provide for and she felt in that moment there were “ no other
options”. She spent 4 days in hospital following the attempted suicide. She is still having difficulty
finding work and not eligible to apply for unemployment insurance for additional financial assistance.
Thankfully, we have been there to support one another through this difficult time. However, we are all
experiencing levels of mental health we never could have imagined and the depth of being terminated
from our careers.
The lack of support from the management has to be the most desolating and lasting memory for all of
us. There was no goodbye, no mention of a thank you for the collectively combined 50+ years of service
provided . It was a very cold and emotionless departure due to the absence of our management team.
There was no proper goodbye to residents who depended on our reliability. These residents are
often like a part of our family.
We were not provided a reasonable alternative to termination in order to keep our careers, such as,
daily testing, which would have provided and ensured continued safety to our fellow coworkers and
vulnerable residents. We would have all be willing to test daily and pay for testing out of pocket.
However, because we were not comfortable receiving the Covid19 Vaccination, we were only given one
option: Termination.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
I live 300kms away from my elderly parents but thankfully that is a distance that I can quite easily drive.
Over the course of the last two years, I've made that trip almost every six weeks to check in on them and
make sure that they were okay since their support system is rather small. Last December I had plans in
place to drive down to see them the week before Christmas. We were all really looking forward to it.
We've never missed a Christmas together before and this was to be no exception. But then the
unthinkable happened. I live in BC and as you might have heard, we had massive flooding that cut off
every highway between the Lower Mainland, where my parents live, and the rest of the province. We
were devastated. Particularly my mom. The obvious solution was to just get on a plane and fly down
instead but since I am not vaccinated, I was not permitted to do that. It made no difference that I had
recently recovered from covid and had paperwork from a lab proving that I had antibodies. No vaccine,
no flying. So, I promised my mom that I would come for a visit just as soon as the highways were open
and safe and that we would just celebrate Christmas late.
It was not to be. At the end of January, she fell ill and was hospitalized. For 18 days I tried to get into the
hospital to see her but I was not allowed due to my vaccination status. Trying to get information over
the phone was nearly impossible as the hospital was so short staffed that there were times that nobody
on the ward was available to pick up the phone. It was extremely stressful and very traumatic to know
that my mom was dying and there was nothing I could do to get to her and I didn’t always knowing what
was happening with her. Six hours before she died, I was finally allowed in but by that time she was
unconscious. It was bittersweet. We never got our last Christmas together, something that will hurt me
forever and knowing that she spent her last 18 days alone in the hospital, possibly wondering why I
didn’t visit her, will haunt me forever.
It is no secret that the last two years have been exceptionally difficult in many ways, but nothing I’ve
experienced compares to the awful way in which I lost my mom. It never should have happened the way
that it did. I should have been allowed to spend her last Christmas with her. I should have been allowed
to spend every day of her last 18 days with her. Worse, it was all for nothing as we now know that none
of these mandates did anything to stop the spread of covid. Every day I try to forgive the people who
had a hand in this tragedy. Maybe someday I’ll be able to. But I’ll never forget.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
To Whom It May Concern:
I am a Canadian citizen affected by the COVID-19 pandemic measures. As a student, I
was nearly forced out of university this past year for not declaring my vaccination status to the
institution I attend (even though my courses were online). As an Indigenous person who
returned to university to become a teacher, my life was turned upside down when the
government took away those dreams. I thought I wouldn’t have the chance to become a
teacher on my remote reserve. I thought I wouldn’t be able to help my community, including
many of my relatives, make better lives for themselves and the future generations of my
community. The disappointment in myself and the fear of being a disappointment to my family
and community weighed heavy on me and continues to, as the measures don’t seem like they
will end. Not only have I had issues in the education area, but also in the workforce.
I was offered employment with a federally regulated corporation for the summer that I
had to decline because I refused to share my private medical information to earn a living in this
country. This position was fully remote, so I was shocked when, after my province “lifted” the
mandates, the federal government was still enforcing the mandates through specific industries.
I wonder if I will even be able to teach in my community because my reserve is situated within
Canada. I am just absolutely appalled and without words that the federal government is using
corporations to deny civil liberties to Canadians while at the same time using media outlets to
misinform the public that the mandates have ended. They clearly have not, and the
governments do not have us fooled.
I know the mandates have not ended because when my 88-year-old grandmother was
dying in the hospital from a heart attack, I could not book a plane ticket to see her one last time
before she died. To comfort her in a hospital, an uncomfortable place for a person who doesn’t
speak any English, where she could only have one visitor at a time. A place where she died
alone and afraid. A place she begged my uncle to take her out of so she could take her last
breath around the people who loved her. A woman who raised nine children on reserve and
many grandchildren. This has personally affected me and makes me question the government
and public health sector. Canada and public health have done many troubling things to
Indigenous peoples in its short history, and in my view, the government-imposed vaccine
passports and mandates can be added to this list. The only difference is it’s not only happening
to Indigenous peoples this time. These are crimes against humanity.
Canada’s Indian Policy aims to assimilate Indigenous peoples, but Canada makes it
impossible for many of us even to want to take part in Canadian society. Unvaccinated and
Indigenous? I feel like you may as well cease to exist in Canada if you identify as either of those
terms and primarily if you identify as both. Many of my relatives are unvaccinated and have
given up on life because of these nonsensical mandates. Suicide rates have increased since the
pandemic began, and my relatives are more and more sharing their suicidal thoughts with me.
They ask themselves, what’s the use in bettering themselves and getting a job in or closer to
the city? For what purpose? So the government can control us even more, including the
medical procedures and treatments the government claims we have a “choice” to participate
in? I have struggled with determining the purpose of life if the feds control everything I do. As
an Indian, as defined in the Indian Act, I already carry a card with a unique number that divides
me from most people. I do not want another card or QR code that further separates me from
my fellow Canadians.

text:
I do not want another card or QR code that further separates me from
my fellow Canadians.

Giving up our bodily autonomy and our self-determination in the name of public health
doesn’t make sense, especially since the science emerging has proven the vaccines to not only
be ineffective but they are not safe. Unfortunately, as a person who must see specialists
regularly due to a life-threatening disease, I am constantly questioning my doctors because the
system is so disconnected. Doctors are seemingly trained to make it somebody else’s problem.
There is zero accountability in the public health system. I questioned my doctors before the
pandemic, and I doubt them even more now that they don’t seem to be on the same page as
the medical science that is coming out. I know several people who have been disabled due to
vaccine side effects that doctors avoid like the plague because they don’t want to be
accountable for that. They also don’t qualify for disability or unemployment insurance. I know
people whose children have dropped dead unexpectedly with no answers and a death
certificate that reads “unascertained.” These people have either lost their livelihoods or their
family members because the government is having a temper tantrum. After all, only about 20%
of Canadian citizens refuse to be vaccinated. I don’t know how else to say this, but this is
incredibly disturbing and suspicious.
To me, unvaccinated is the new Indian. And if these mandates don’t end immediately,
we are all in for a ride in this country. Division was never the answer in the past, and it is not
the answer now. The last 200 years should be used as an example of what Canada should not
do to its people, and instead, we are on a trajectory of repeating history. Please end the
mandates immediately.

Thank you for your time,
