Brief to The Standing Committee on Health
Re: Covid-19 Response
I believe that the Parliamentary Health Committee failed Canadians on many counts in their
handling of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Considering only “health” implications and not all factors affecting well being in Canadians.
Allowing the entire Pandemic response to be based on reducing hospitalizations.
Not focusing on health promotion as a means to minimize risk and reduce the impact of
Covid-19.
Not focusing on early treatment as a means to reduce hospitalization and death.
Not focusing efforts on the most vulnerable when it was clear almost immediately who was the
most vulnerable.
Allowing the censorship of informed, expert views other than those expressed by the official
narrative.
Allowing the censorship of valid, published, peer-reviewed studies other than those that
supported the official narrative.
Ignoring the data on lockdowns. They don’t work.
Allowing a vaccine rollout while not requiring proof nor ensuring the effective evaluation of the
safety and efficacy of Covid vaccines.
Allowing the vaccines to be mandated for federal and federally regulated organizations.
Incentivizing the provinces to incentivize, coerce and mandate vaccination wherever possible.
Allowing the use of inaccurate tests including PCR tests which deliver excessive false
positives.
Not actively countering misinformation like the fact that the flu had been eliminated during
Covid.
Allowing the promotion of continued mask use even after evidence was produced confirming
its ineffectiveness.
Allowing the ban of unvaccinated people from flying, taking the train or a ship in Canada.
Allowing the ban of unvaccinated people from traveling outside of Canada.
Allowing the continued requirement of masks on airplanes in Canada.
Allowing the coercion of children to be vaccinated.
Allowing the promotion of the policy that children should be sacrificed for the elderly rather
than requiring the effective care and protection of the elderly in institutions (where the majority
of deaths occurred).
Ignoring the lack of vaccine efficacy while still allowing coercion and mandates.
Ignoring the fact that most policies adopted to “control the spread” did more harm than good.
On a personal note, my husband is a 30 year career pilot who hasn’t worked since October
2021 due to the federal vaccine mandates. Just prior to his termination, he was flying Covid
positive patients on medivacs and never contracted Covid. Isn’t this a common theme? Just
like all the health care workers, police officers, etc. that survived Covid or didn’t even contract
it who got suspended or fired for not taking the injection. We had family members living with us
who had the original strain and neither my husband or I got it. We eventually probably got
Omicron. We have antibodies and tcell immunity, but by the federal mandate, he still can’t
work. He’s also ineligible for EI because of his vaccination status. He has been a taxpaying,
contributing Canadian and our government believes it’s fair and just to treat a person like this
because of a virus with a survival rate equivalent to a severe flu. We have four children (all
supporting themselves, thankfully). One is a nurse who’s employment was also affected by the
mandates. Two others lost part-time jobs due to the mandates. My son was unable to return to
his seasonal job with a contractor for the city because of the mandates. I’m aware that these
are provincial and city, not federal but federal policy incentivized and coerced provinces and
cities to adopt these policies. They’ve all had Covid (as have my parents who are in their
seventies) and did not use a single hospital resource. We believe that our health comes from

our daily lifestyle habits and we are proof that this is so. Imagine if actual health promotion got

It’s not too late to address all of this. And please for the future, let’s learn from what we now
know and broaden our perspectives, dive deeply into the data, watch for manipulations and
not simply accept recommendations from those with the most to gain from our acceptance of
them. Let’s evaluate those objectively with a well-rounded team of experts. For example, let’s

can’t even donate unused doses to an impoverished country? And have you seen the vaccine
manufacturers profits?
Thank you for your time and attention.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Members of the Standing Committee on Health,
I, like many other Canadians, deeply regret trusting the so-called leaders of this country to guide
us through the emergence of a novel coronavirus outbreak. I watched with disbelief and horror
as politicians, relying on public health representatives, repeatedly implemented the worst
possible measures to counter the effects of viral contagion. Every step of the way, I naively
assumed these politicians would seize the opportunities provided to them to step away from
the folly. Every time I was aghast as they doubled down, insisting that the only way to fight this
virus was through more measures, more policing, stiffer fines, more authoritarianism.
When the initial wave subsided, I assumed the governments would seek a politically palatable
way to navigate away from the initial panic-induced lunacy that wrought so much destruction
and produced so little value. Instead, they created more measures, often with alarming levels of
inconsistency and absurdity, which served no purpose other than to divide, isolate and control
the population. Businesses ruined, jobs lost, families divided, suicides, depression, and despair.
Institutions such as the mainstream media were easily corrupted with taxpayers’ money in order
to control the masses. Unions and professional orders were cowed into accepting and even
encouraging the decrees issued undemocratically by virtue of the various states of emergency
that were abused by all levels of government as they consolidated power and silenced
opposition.
When the vaccines arrived, I again falsely assumed the governments would use this opportunity
to conduct a vaccination program, achieve some arbitrary percentage of coverage that would
allow them to then walk back the abusive measures that were still wreaking so much havoc on
Canadian society. Instead, much deeper division was sown and instrumentalized to coerce,
threaten and sanction citizens who dared to demonstrate their ability to think critically for
themselves and disobey the increasingly menacing tyrants.
As a veteran, I am disgusted by the callousness with which so many hard-won freedoms were
illegally sacrificed and thrown by the wayside by our public servants. The lack of courage,
integrity, duty, and honor that has been displayed by so many institutions, including the
Canadian Armed Forces, has been disheartening.
However, as we decide to move forward as a society, one thing is clear to me: we must fortify
the guardrails that prevent society from being led astray by charlatans in positions of power and
influence. We must do this if we are to heal our nation and reestablish the massive loss of trust.
I believe that men and women of character and resolve will stand up and step forward to begin
to accomplish these tasks and lead us out of the abyss.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
To whom it may concern,

Pandemic plans out the window.
Closure of businesses.
People dying alone.
Divided families.
Divided friendships.
Divisive and hateful language from our supposed leader.
Coercion to get a medical experiment.

Masking CHILDREN.
Closing schools and taking away what could be a child’s only safe space.

Travel restrictions forcing families to be apart during some of the most precious
moments in life.
Kids unable to play sports unless they took the experimental shot.
Parents unable to watch their kids play sports unless they took the experimental shot.
People could pack Walmart and Costco but couldn’t go out for a mean with family
unless they took the experimental shot.
And now thousands can sit in arenas and watch professional sports but can’t board a

Some of the many harmful outcomes.

None of the above were because of a virus. They were because of the RESPONSE to a

That’s not science. That’s vindictive, hateful, and punitive.

Signed a concerned, once proud, Canadian Citizen

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Dear Standing Committee on Health,
05.29.2022
I am writing to you as part of an initiative to raise awareness of just how disparaging the federal
COVID-19 mandates are to Canadians. I’m going to share how the mandates have impacted me
in hopes that my story may help you change your position on the matter.
I’m an American who moved to Canada and married a Canadian at the end of 2019. My family was
sad about the move because we are very close, yet they supported me nonetheless. Of course, my
husband could have immigrated to the states, but circumstantially, Canada worked best for us. The
person who was most concerned about the move was my dad. He was worried that something
would cause the US/Canada border to close and he wouldn’t be able to get to me. I assured him
that would never happen. My parents and sister lived a short six-hour drive away in Portland and I
thought I would be able to visit them whenever I want — I was wrong.
A few months after our wedding, the pandemic reached Canada and the land borders were shut down
to all “non-essential” travel. Among many things, family reunification was classified as non-essential and
it broke my heart. The move to Canada was already difficult enough, but the border closures made it
exponentially harder. I couldn’t see my family for most of 2020 because visiting the states
now required a flight I couldn’t afford and two weeks of quarantine upon my return to Canada. I only
managed to pull off a trip once that year.
In 2021 things worsened with the introduction of vaccine mandates. Once those were established, I
could no longer board a plane, train, or boat. Looking back, I wish I had flown home more when I had
the chance. Both I and my entire family chose to remain unvaccinated, but at a great emotional cost.
The following November, the US reopened the land borders to vaccinated travellers and US citizens.
Fortunately, I am a US citizen so we have a legal means of escaping this country, unlike many others.
In December of 2021, we travelled to my childhood home in Sacramento, California. Our trip was full
of hugs and tears. We were able to reunite with family members we hadn’t seen since our wedding. It’s
unusual for me to go that long without visiting California. As sweet as our time together was, returning
to Canada was a nightmare. We spent countless hours tracking down and booking PCR tests offered
by places such as Walgreens. We ended up taking one test that never delivered the results and driving
40 minutes for another scheduled test whose employees never showed up. Apparently, the company
decided to give everyone a holiday and they didn’t even bother to notify us. We ended up finding a
third place that charged a couple of hundred dollars per test for same-day results.
Upon our arrival at the Canadian border (with our expensive negative test results in hand), we were
warned about the consequences of breaking the Quarantine Act: up to three years in prison and up
to $750,000 in fines. They then handed us two day-one testing kits and two day-eight testing kits. As
soon as we got home, we booked our appointments and tested the following day. Our results for day
one and day eight all came back negative, but we were still required to quarantine for the full 14 days.
Additionally, we had to check into the ArriveCAN app daily and answer every call from contact tracers.
One missed call resulted in a government official showing up at our door. We were literally on house
arrest. Why are good, upstanding citizens being treated like criminals in their own country?

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Why are good, upstanding citizens being treated like criminals in their own country?

Because of our vaccination status, my husband was forced to use some of his paid vacation time
to quarantine. With the current criteria in place, we can’t afford to keep making trips to the states,
but right now it’s the only way we can see my family since they aren’t allowed into Canada at all.
We were only able to swing one more trip for my sister’s wedding. It’s only April and my husband has
already used up most of his vacation time, we’ve spent hundreds of dollars on tests, and I don’t know
when we’ll be able to see my family again. I don’t even know when we’ll start having kids because the
idea of my parents being barred from seeing their grandchildren is unbearable. While most Canadians
are getting by just fine, millions of others are suffering under these cruel and tyrannical policies.
I still don’t understand why vaccinated foreign nationals can easily vacation to my home country with
no issues, but I can hardly go because the Canadian government is bent on punishing me. They say
they are following the “science,” but it’s always been at the cost of ethics — which should have never
happened in a free and democratic society. At the very least, they should have made exemptions for
families. Now that the science clearly supports ending restrictions, we are pleading to have them
lifted. If you are an advocate for human rights, I pray that you have a change of heart and fervently
support equality for all, regardless of their medical status.

text:
Censorship on the scale that we are currently witnessing, and have witnessed over the
last two years, should never be permitted in a free country such as ours. It isn’t right to
censor open-ended discussions and debate. It isn’t right that we, as citizens of a free
country are not allowed to question anything about the narrative that’s constantly being
forced down our throats. As a country, we can’t just silence the dissidents and then
pretend there’s a consensus about the right thing to do. Especially when there are so
many doctors among them. Doctors, who spend their time literally saving lives, are not
and have not been permitted to even discuss the best way forward on how to continue
to save lives. How can they possibly practice the most effective way to do so under
such circumstances? The answer is obvious: They can’t. And this is only one way in
which we are shooting ourselves in the foot when it comes to how we are and have
been dealing with this pandemic.
Science is a process that gives us data, and based off of that data, as well as our
values as human beings, we have to make decisions and ultimately policies for our
society. The policies made by our current government show that both the data and our
values as a nation have been discarded. These policies are pushed forward as though
they are manifested from some desire to protect civilization, but we’ve come to a point
where it’s abundantly clear these policies do the complete opposite, and yet they are
still being pushed. We are far past the point of these policies making any sense at all.
With the aid of the media, they instill fear, divide the people of this country, and fuel
hatred.
Which leads to the question why did Canada ever develop a pandemic response at all?
We didn’t use it. Instead we threw out all of our “preparedness” to adapt policies that
had never been tried and didn’t have any data to prove their efficacy. Seems somewhat
irrational. This is the equivalent of practising for fire drills only to run around screaming
and lie on the floor when a real fire occurs. Absolute insanity.
We know now that policies implemented had little to no effect on the pandemic. One
only needs to look to places like Sweden, or parts of the United States such as Florida
or Texas to see Canada got it completely wrong. So has the government reassessed?
Nope. We are plummeting full steam with the same narrative. In spite of the Pfizer
documents proving that vaccines are not safe and effective for pregnant or nursing
mothers. The vaccines do not reduce viral load, transmission, or prevent disease. In fact
the Pfizer trial documents prove vaccines have little to no efficacy at all, and slips into a
negative efficacy after a week. Places like the U.K, Canada and Israel that mandated
vaccines now have higher rates of hospitalization, and it’s the vaccinated contributing to
these rates.
The vaccines come with great risk. Pfizer’s own documents showed a 3% risk of
adverse effects. Risk for something that again doesn’t prevent transmission or prevent
disease. A disease in which healthy people age 0-19 have a 99.997% recovery rate, 2049 have a 99.98% recovery rate, 50-69 have a 99.5% recovery rate, and 70+ have a
94.6% chance. This leads to the question what about those affected by the shot?

text:
This leads to the question what about those affected by the shot?

Silencing these people, seems dismissive and evil. Yet this is what our government is
choosing to do.
Early treatment has proven to be greatly advantageous and effective. Most studies have
found it to range from 70-90% effective. Yet there is no mention of those? Why aren’t we
focusing on those? Every news story, every politician only talks about the vaccine. Why
continue to spew nonsense, when we have other far more plausible solutions on the
table? It is clearly evident that any policy centering on vaccination status needs to be
scrapped. Not only do they go against our values of freedom and bodily autonomy, they
don’t help at all, and they are actively hurting Canadians. Which leads back to the
question. Why are the injured shunned and shushed? If we care about health then why
no mention of people that have been injured? Instead we persist with the fear
mongering which begs the question is it really about health? Most certainly not,
otherwise we would have been distinguishing from the beginning cases of
hospitalization and death from Covid-19 and with Covid-19. This would have provided
us with the most accurate data.
None of how this pandemic was handled was effective, efficient, or even close to
accurate. It seems to have had a political motive from the beginning and had very little

Our public health officials should not be on the boards of pharmaceutical companies this
should be a direct conflict of interest, as should anyone receiving any sort of benefit
from any pharmaceutical company monetary or otherwise being allowed to implement
policies affecting the health choice of individual citizens.
This is not the Canada that I once knew – the country I once loved. I used to be proud
to be Canadian. Now, living here feels like some kind of cruel joke, with no hope of a
future for my family – for my children. Like many other Canadians, I am seriously
considering selling everything and leaving this country, because it’s no longer safe. And
that isn’t because of COVID. It’s because of our government. It’s because of policies
that hurt far more than they help. So, where does that leave us, the people? No freedom
of thought, no freedom of choice, no freedom of bodily autonomy. We are
disenfranchised. We are wretches with no hope and no control over our own lives. We
are prisoners, bound to the dictates of this tyranny. We are Canadians. And we deserve
better.
The corruption in all forms of government has been exposed during this pandemic.
Hopefully this inquiry is about discovering and exposing the truth and not just more of

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
We all wish we had a crystal ball to know when the pandemic will be over, or if it will ever end.
Every pandemic comes with its own personality. Some diseases come and go like SARS in 2003,
while others, like H1N1, are adapting and we are adapting to it. We learn to live with them.
COVID-19 is here to stay in one form or another. This does not mean that we should just give
up. In its current form, SARS-CoV-2, including all its variants, is still a pathogen that is not only
fatal, but can also have lingering effects on those who catch it. This makes it all the more
important to continue to do everything we can to stop its progress. It will take years to measure
the real long-term impact of the disease on people who continue to have symptoms months after
contracting it, as well as on our healthcare systems.
Several scenarios are emerging as to how many waves there are and how long the pandemic will
last. But whatever the scenario, it is likely that we will never be rid of COVID-19. The virus will
wane over the years, but it will still be fatal to much of the older, immunosuppressed population,
a bit like a form of influenza, but more severe. However, we must draw on the lessons learned
from what we have experienced now to better prepare for subsequent waves and for a future
pandemic.
Continuing on from the analysis I started in my book, Prêts pour une prochaine pandémie (ready
for a coming pandemic), I see two key aspects to pandemic preparedness. Despite the myriad
pandemic preparedness plans, the ability of our institutions to respond quickly is limited. To
correct this situation, we need to work not only on coming up with medium- and long-term plans,
but also on operationalizing these plans, which must be done in real time and on an ongoing
basis, to ensure that the infrastructure is ready when a pandemic is declared. Plans are useless if
they are left on a shelf and only dusted off for the next pandemic. I therefore think it is essential
to set up an organization or working group whose sole mission is to ensure that our society is
prepared for future pandemics; implement the plan, including the necessary consolidation steps
between pandemics; and evaluate it. Currently, responsibility for implementing preparedness
plans is scattered across different departments and levels of government. Preparedness plans
cover a wide range of issues:
1. maintaining an emerging pathogen surveillance system based on the One Health concept
2. ensuring the supply of personal protective equipment and laboratory test material

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Preparedness plans
cover a wide range of issues:
1. maintaining an emerging pathogen surveillance system based on the One Health concept
2. ensuring the supply of personal protective equipment and laboratory test material

3. training healthcare providers and organizing simulations
4. setting up teams of vaccinators
5. modernizing computerized public health information sharing tools
6. physically upgrading nursing homes (ventilation, common areas)
7. organizing an ongoing campaign to counter misinformation, especially on vaccines
8. organizing physical resources to accommodate patients in a pandemic scenario
9. supporting the local (Canadian) development of vaccines, pharmacological treatments
and personal protective equipment
Implementing these plans must come with a timeline and there must be accountability. However,
in many cases, particularly when there is not a pandemic, health authorities are faced with the
immediate, day-to-day management of networks, and pandemic preparedness is not a priority.
That is why I recommend setting up an organization whose sole mandate is to ensure that the
plan’s time frames are met. It could include experts from various fields (public health, research,
public safety, health services organizations, vulnerable groups, social science) and report
regularly to the government and the public on the state of affairs. This organization would be in
place at both the federal and provincial level.
The second point that I would like to highlight here is the need for a holistic emerging pathogen
surveillance program that combines human, animal and environmental surveillance. If we follow
the principle of One Health and understand the origin of zoonoses, we will see that siloed
surveillance systems that do not cover a variety of pathogens able to cause a pandemic and that
are not internationally linked will fail to prepare us adequately for a new health crisis.
Ultimately, the best way to prepare for pandemics is to rethink our relationship with animals and
our environment by approaching it from the One Health concept. The COVID-19 pandemic has
certainly humbled us in this regard.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Study on the Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19
Pandemic
May 9, 2022

OVERVIEW

HealthCareCAN, the national voice of Canada’s hospitals, research institutes and healthcare
organizations, welcomes the opportunity to submit this brief to the Standing Committee on
Health as part of its study on the Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID19 Pandemic.

While citizens and governments across Canada are eager to put COVID-19 behind them in
favour of a post-pandemic normal, healthcare workers and organizations across the country are
still in crisis. This is in part due to the strains imposed upon them by the pandemic. However,
the challenges facing healthcare in Canada right now are symptoms of a much larger problem:
Our health system is not built to handle modern needs and has been slowly crumbling under
decades of mounting population and demographic pressure. COVID-19 simply pushed the
system beyond its breaking point.

One of the main worries we hear from our member institutions is that governments and the
health sector will fail to act on the lessons learned during the pandemic and choose instead to
lapse back into the pre-pandemic status quo once the worst of COVID-19 is past. We cannot let
this happen. As a nation, we desperately need to come together and use our experiences
during the pandemic – and the decades of research and experience before it – to build a system
that works seamlessly across the country, for everyone.

This requires cooperation among all levels of government, working with health system
stakeholders, including patients, providers, researchers, healthcare advocates, and
underrepresented and underserved groups such as Indigenous peoples, to implement policy
solutions that reimagine healthcare in Canada for the better and achieve improved health
outcomes for all.

As an association representing healthcare and health research organizations and focused on
building a better health system, HealthCareCAN advocates for several key system-level
changes, the need for which has only been further reinforced by the pandemic. The remainder
of this brief outlines these recommendations.

RECOMMENDATIONS

Build a health system that meets modern needs

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Build a health system that meets modern needs

The foundation of Canada’s current healthcare system was conceived for a different time. What
we call medicare in Canada was established nearly 70 years ago when most healthcare in
Canada was privately funded and delivered. Canada’s population then (16.5 million people) was
a little less than a half of what it is now (38.3 million people), the median age of the population

was just under 28 (today it is just over 41 years old), and the average life expectancy was
approximately 69 years (today it is approximately 82 years).

Medicare was created to provide acute care to a far smaller, far younger population that did not
contend with the complex, chronic conditions many people live with today. Governments of the
past likely could not conceive of the demands that are being placed on our health system. Why
then do we continue to think that a seven-decades-old framework that has seen few updates
could possibly serve the needs of people in Canada today?

Medicare, and the health system more broadly, must evolve to meet changing care needs.
Hospital and physician services are still vital forms of care, but they are not the only types of
care needed to live a healthy life. Mental health and substance use care, older adult care,
pharmacare, dental care, vision care and many other types of care crucial to healthy living are
not covered by medicare.

We must also adapt how we deliver care to align with the best available evidence, including
providing more patient-centred, integrated care that reflects the different ways people want to
access care, including at home and virtually. Healthcare must also be delivered in a way that is
culturally appropriate and safe, free of racism and discrimination, and inclusive of all.

It is the duty of all governments – federal, provincial, and territorial – to ensure that Canada’s
health system meets peoples’ needs. Fulfilling that duty will require policy changes, additional
funding, more efficient and effective investment of healthcare dollars, and accountability to the
people governments serve to deliver better health outcomes for all.

Recommendation 1: Governments at all levels must work together to reimagine healthcare in
Canada and build a system that meets modern needs.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Recommendation 1: Governments at all levels must work together to reimagine healthcare in
Canada and build a system that meets modern needs.

Recommendation 2: Increase federal health transfers to reflect rising healthcare costs and
enable provinces and territories to enhance healthcare services and deal with the impacts of the
pandemic, including medical procedure backlogs. Transparent targets for improved health
outcomes to create accountability to people across Canada are crucial to this process.

Bolster the health workforce

Healthcare workers, who account for nearly 10% of everyone employed in Canada and more
than 66% of all health spending – which equates to approximately 8% of Canada’s GDP – are
our health system’s greatest resource. Yet labour shortages and demanding working conditions
in the health system are among the biggest barriers to delivering timely high-quality healthcare
in Canada.

Canada’s health sector has battled workforce shortages for years, but the problem has grown
exponentially worse during the COVID-19 pandemic. The latest data from Statistics Canada

show that there were 126,000 vacancies in the healthcare and social assistance sector in the
fourth quarter of 2021. This is almost double the vacancies seen in 2019 (64,000) and
represents nearly one in seven job vacancies across the country.i
Workforce shortages undermine patient care, and take a substantial physical, mental and
emotional toll on healthcare workers at all levels and across the continuum of care. The havoc
COVID-19 is wreaking on healthcare workers is considerable and will endure long after the
pandemic over. It is crucial that governments address health workforce shortages with both
short-term and long-term action. Such concerted action is vital to ensure Canada has the health
workforce it needs to continue dealing with COVID-19, tackle medical procedure backlogs, and
provide high-quality care to those who need it.

Recommendation 3: Improve the immigration process to better leverage the skills of
immigrants and newcomers to help fill current vacancies over the short- and medium-term.

Recommendation 4: Support interprovincial/territorial coordination of education and licensing.

Recommendation 5: Support the health, wellness, safety, and resilience of the healthcare
workforce by expanding mental health and wellness research, programs, and resources specific
to healthcare workers.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Recommendation 5: Support the health, wellness, safety, and resilience of the healthcare
workforce by expanding mental health and wellness research, programs, and resources specific
to healthcare workers.

Recommendation 6: Implement a pan-Canadian health workforce planning strategy with the
goal of gathering and analyzing workforce data to gain a better understanding of the current
workforce and system needs, forecast future need, develop solutions to tackle the shortage of
healthcare workers, and address the factors hindering recruitment and retention.

Recommendation 7: Collaborate with provincial and territorial governments, regulators, and
educational institutions to train more Canadian healthcare workers – particularly from
Indigenous communities and other underrepresented groups – in the professions and fields
necessary to meet the long-term needs of the health system.
For additional details on these recommendations, see HealthCareCAN’s submission to the
Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of
Persons with Disabilities.

Strengthen health research and innovation

COVID-19 provided clear and compelling evidence of the return on investment in health
research and innovation. Canadian researchers helped lead the global fight against COVID-19,
by being the first to profile the body’s immune response to the virus and developing the lipid
nanoparticles to deliver mRNA to the body’s cells – a breakthrough based on 40 years of
research.

The pandemic not only exposed cracks in Canada’s health research ecosystem, such as limited
investment, a lack of pan-Canadian coordination, and a landscape that hinders partnerships, it
sounded the alarm that Canada must make supporting health research and innovation – which
are intertwined – a larger priority. The time has come to fully leverage health and life sciences
organizations, including research hospitals and healthcare organizations, not only for the role
they play in treating Canadians and keeping them healthy, but also as economic and innovation
engines with tremendous national and global potential.

The increasing occurrence of health emergencies due to climate change and new viruses,
Canada’s aging population, and Canada’s transition to an innovation and knowledge-based
economy signify that the health sector – and health research and innovation more specifically –
is vital to ensuring a healthy and productive nation, and a robust and globally competitive
economy.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
The increasing occurrence of health emergencies due to climate change and new viruses,
Canada’s aging population, and Canada’s transition to an innovation and knowledge-based
economy signify that the health sector – and health research and innovation more specifically –
is vital to ensuring a healthy and productive nation, and a robust and globally competitive
economy.

Recommendation 8: Make transformational investments in health research to protect
Canadians from future health crises and capitalize on economic opportunities, starting with a
minimum annual floor of two per cent of public spending on health ($3.7 billion), to be put
toward fundamental health research, strategic initiatives to tackle pressing social issues, and
knowledge translation.

Recommendation 9: Adjust health research and innovation funding structures, policies, and
levels of investment to better support strategic and integrated health research. This includes reinvesting in fundamental science through the Tri-Councils and centralizing investments in
strategic science through an agency such as the proposed Canada Advanced Research
Projects Agency (CARPA).

Recommendation 10: Establish a government branch and/or funding program(s) focused on
knowledge translation to move health research evidence into practice and commercialize
research innovations.

Recommendation 11: Fund health research priorities identified by the pandemic, including
research into primary care prevention, health care equity/inequities, and social determinants of
health.

Recommendation 12: Develop a pan-Canadian framework for clinical trials that will make
Canada a more attractive place to conduct clinical trials and become a leader internationally.
This includes establishing a body to direct the development and implementation of such a
framework.

Recommendation 13: Build or renovate hospital facilities to create much-needed lab and
incubator space that attracts and brings together researchers, universities and colleges,
industry, innovators, and non-profit organizations.

Recommendation 14: Facilitate the creation of health networks or hubs around research
hospitals that bring together academia, industry, start-ups and incubators, and business.

Recommendation 15: Evaluate federal and Tri-Council funding programs to make the criteria
less restrictive and more flexible to foster partnerships.

Recommendation 16: Improve health system interoperability to support partnership creation,
including through the creation of a pan-Canadian health data research strategy and repository.

For additional details on these recommendations, see HealthCareCAN’s submission to the
Standing Committee on Science and Research.

Modernize Health Infrastructure

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Modernize Health Infrastructure

Over the last 20 years, Canadian capital investment in health infrastructure has fluctuated, with
a noted decline in recent years despite overall healthcare spending increasing steadily over this
same time.ii Counter to the trend among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and
Development (OECD) countries of increasing capital investment since 2010, Canada invested
14% less in real terms in 2019 compared to 2010.
Healthcare organizations have felt the impact of decreased capital investments, with
accumulated deferred maintenance for hospitals alone estimated to be roughly $28 billion in
2015.iii Failing to sufficiently invest in capital affects the ability to deliver accepted or emerging
standards of care to patients, especially when such standards require expensive technology for
diagnosis and treatment.iv
The pandemic starkly revealed that Canada’s outdated health infrastructure puts the health of
Canadians at risk, including in long-term care where in many outdated facilities it is nearly
impossible to comply with infection, prevention and control protocols. Modern infrastructure is
crucial in enhancing access to services and patient outcomes.
Recommendation 17: Ensure infrastructure funding reaches the health sector by providing
healthcare organizations, such as hospitals, research institutes, health authorities, and longterm care facilities, with direct and equal access to federal infrastructure funding.
Recommendation 18: Increase capital investments in healthcare to a minimum of 0.6 percent
of gross domestic product (GDP) (approximately $12.5B) to better align with Canada’s OECD
counterparts.
Recommendation 19: Support the expansion of virtual care and digital health, including
through improvements to information technology and digital infrastructure across the health
system.
Recommendation 20: Bolster the healthcare sector’s cybersecurity capabilities through
investments, programs, and standards.

i Statistics Canada. 2021. Job vacancies, fourth quarter 2021. https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/dailyquotidien/220322/dq220322a-eng.htm.
ii Teja B. et al. 2020. Ensuring adequate capital investment in Canadian health care. CMAJ Jun 2020, 192
(25) E677-E683. https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.191126.
iii Ibid.
iv Ibid.

text:
April 27, 2022
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health’s Study
on the Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19
Pandemic
Summary:
The COVID-19 pandemic has had a dire effect on wait times for medical imaging procedures across the
country. Canadians who may have postponed diagnostic and necessary follow-up imaging early in the
pandemic are now in more urgent need of care. This has created a massive influx of patients attempting
to reschedule their appointments, not to mention the additional treatment that will be required for those
undiagnosed or with worsening conditions. If we do not take action, the increased pressure on radiology
will catch up after the pandemic, the growing baseline demand for imaging, and the existing capacity
limitations in radiology departments will combine to continue to damage the healthcare system.
Excessive and lengthening wait times for medical imaging is reducing efficiency across our healthcare
system and leading to burnout in our health workforce. Canadians are being diagnosed later into the
progression of their ailments, leading to a reduction in treatment options, increased recovery time, and
worsening patient outcomes. Investments must be made quickly to support more up-to-date modern
imaging equipment and information technologies.
Overview:
Medical imaging is our healthcare system’s gateway for diagnosing diseases, and patients from every
demographic rely on it to detect and treat these conditions. Radiologists find abnormalities, such as
tumors and heart disease; screen for breast, colon, lung, and other cancers; treat conditions using
minimally invasive procedures guided by imaging; conduct image-guided biopsies; and ensure the safe
use of radiation.
At the heigh of the pandemic, there was a 50% to 70% decrease in radiology services across the
country as a result of pandemic-related closures of healthcare services. Even prior to the pandemic,
patients were waiting on average [CONTACT] scan diagnostics and up to 89 days for MRIs. This is
20-52 days longer than the recommended wait time set by the by the Canadian Wait Times Alliance
and supported by the Canadian Association of Radiologists.
This situation is especially concerning for individuals needing breast and colorectal cancer screening,
patients undergoing cancer treatment, or those who may need imaging but have delayed seeking care
due to fears or other factors associated with the pandemic. Without immediate investment, this backlog
will most certainly mean some tests will come too late, and that some patients will never recover from
otherwise treatable conditions.

text:
Without immediate investment, this backlog
will most certainly mean some tests will come too late, and that some patients will never recover from
otherwise treatable conditions.

For example, delays for medical imaging have hindered the detection and management of many
diseases, including colorectal cancer. A preventable disease, colorectal cancer is the third most
common cancer and second leading cause of cancer-related death in men, and the third leading cause
of cancer-related death in women in Canada. The pandemic heavily impacted routine endoscopy and
colonoscopy screening – and patients who were identified as average risk were recommended less
effective methods of screening as a replacement to medical imaging.
These delays are also being experienced across the country. As found in The Value of Radiology Part
II, a report conducted by the Conference Board of Canada1, in 2019 provinces had the following number
of patients exceeding maximum recommended wait times for medical imaging:
•
In Alberta, 40% of patients for CT and 65% of patients for MRI;
•
In British Columbia, 45% of patients for both CT and MRI;
•
In Quebec, 40% of patients for CT and 64% of patients for MRI;
•
In Manitoba, 45% of patients for CT and 70% of patients for MRI;
•
In New Brunswick, 50% of patients for CT and 45% of patients for MRI;
•
In Newfoundland and Labrador, 35% of patients for CT and 70% of patients for MRI;
•
In Nova Scotia, 45% of patients for CT and 70% of patients for MRI;
•
In Ontario, 35% of patients for CT and 45% of patients for MRI;
•
In Prince Edward Island, 45% of patients for CT and 70% of patients for MRI; and
•
In Saskatchewan, 25% of patients for CT and 45% of patients for MRI.
These wait times have been exacerbated due to pandemic-related health measures and will continue to
grow due to increased demand for medical imaging. A contributing factor is Canada’s aging population.
Today, we are at a 20 year low for investment in new imaging equipment. Although the March 25
federal budget announcement of a $2B one-time top-up to the provinces and territories to help address
immediate pandemic-related healthcare system pressures, including for diagnostics, is welcome, further
investments in medical imaging are needed to ensure that Canadians have timely access to
diagnostics.
Recommendations:
Investing it radiology is key in maintaining patient health and preventing future output losses to the
Canadian economy. In order to better support Canada’s healthcare workforce, and to ensure that
patients have timely access to important diagnostic tests, the Canadian Association of Radiologists
recommends that:
1. The Government make a federal investment of $1.5B over five years in medical imaging
equipment, information technologies and health human resources to support the increased
capacity. Newer imaging equipment can help reduce examination times by providing better
diagnostic performance and less radiation exposure for patients.
2. The Government implement a strategy for increasing health human resources in medical
imaging by hiring more staff, implementing new training programs, and expanding on existing
programs.

Of urgent note, we are well past these timelines.

With the potential emergence of new variants of SARS-CoV-2 in the future,
hospitals across the country could once again be at risk of exceeding capacity.
When resources are stretched as thin as they are currently, a test to assist
clinicians in triaging the most at-risk patients is extremely valuable in
providing the best possible patient care and limiting the strain on hospital
staff. RALI-Dx™ IL-6 is a made-in-Canada medical technology readily available
to help with patient assessment. However, authorization of this technology by
Health Canada has been delayed.
Supplementary Information: Clinical Study Summary
Risk stratification of patients presenting in the Emergency Department with
COVID-19 is difficult. The RALI-Dx™ IL-6 Severity Triage Test provides insight
into the patient’s inflammatory profile by leveraging IL-6 values with the
oxygen partial pressure to flow ratio (P/F) to rapidly (<90 minutes) assess the
severity of a patient’s response to COVID-19 and whether that patient is at risk
of intubation with mechanical ventilation (IMV). The RALI-Dx™ IL-6 Severity
Triage Test is to be used in conjunction with other clinical findings which can
help guide the clinical team in the determination of patient management
strategies in the hospital.
To support the intended use, 256 symptomatic COVID-19 confirmed positive
patients were enrolled in a clinical validation study. Of the 256 patients
included in the combined cohort clinical performance analysis, 29 patients
subsequently underwent IMV. Of the 29 patients that received IMV, only 1
patient having an IL-6 concentration ≤ 35 pg/mL and the oxygen partial
pressure to flow ratio (P/F) ≥ 150 mmHg was incorrectly identified as at risk for
intubation with mechanical ventilation. The concentration of IL-6 at the initial
assessment (>35 pg/mL) illustrates the best combination of sensitivity and
specificity in predicting those patients at risk for IMV at various geographical
locations and stages of the pandemic.
There are three key strengths of this clinical validation study. Firstly, clinical
data have been collected at three sites in three different countries (Canada,
USA, and Brazil). There are no statistical differences between the country
cohorts indicating the universality of the RALI-Dx™ IL-6 Severity Triage Test to
assess patient risk of intubation with mechanical ventilation. Secondly, the
clinical validation study includes a Canadian-based site, which directly relates
to the intended market and reflects Canadian-based patient management
strategies. Thirdly, the clinical data represents a continuum of COVID-19
patients and patient management from April 2020 to May 2021, which
corresponds to the time course of the pandemic.

text:
CANADIAN LUNG ASSOCIATION’S STATEMENT FOR THE
STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH
Monday April 4, 2022

Recommendation:
That the government identify a plan for research funding to ‘invest in the study of the long-term
health impacts of COVID-19, including of long COVID on different groups, notably vulnerable
populations and children’ as noted within government mandate letters.
Background
What is long COVID?
As we recover from the acute impacts of COVID-19, a new impact has begun to gain attention.
Most people who develop COVID-19 resume a normal life about two weeks after their illness1.
However some individuals experience long-term symptoms including cognitive issues, such as
brain fog, headaches, dizziness, anxiety, and/or persistent respiratory symptoms1. These symptoms
have been grouped together and called ‘long COVID’, or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2
(PASC), however the long-term impacts on lung health and support for management and/or
treatment for those suffering largely remains unclear 2.
Most common long lasting symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, and cognitive
challenges2. These symptoms are not simply minor inconveniences. Many people experiencing
long COVID describe them as ‘crushing’; ‘overwhelming’ ‘unmanageable’ and ‘unpredictable’ 2.
Many of these patients may be experiencing symptoms that are challenging to explain. In fact a
small pilot, which has since been expanded to a larger study, based out of the UK tested a new
approach of using xenon gas to measure lung functioning3. In this pilot study, xenon gas mimicked
oxygen in the lungs and demonstrated lung abnormalities amongst those suffering with
long-lasting breathlessness from COVID. This was amongst individuals who had received normal
CT scans and x-rays 3.
Lingering symptoms of a viral infection are not completely new. In fact evidence of long term viral
respiratory symptoms were first discovered with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) where
studies demonstrated the long-term impairment of exercise capacity and health status4. However,
in Canada there were only 251 reported cases of SARS and so the number of impacted individuals
was far less. As we move beyond the COVID pandemic the numbers are far more significant 4.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
As we move beyond the COVID pandemic the numbers are far more significant 4.

Who is likely to experience long COVID
Generally there is a lack of data both in Canada and worldwide to give a clear proportion of how
many people will be impacted by long COVID. This is owed in part to varying testing capacities
and a lack of research on long COVID itself. Recent studies suggest anywhere from 10%-30% of
individuals who had COVID-19 may experience long lasting symptoms5,6. Some studies have
indicated that as many as 1 in 2 people with lab confirmed infection demonstrate at least 1
persisting symptom2.
As of April 2022, Canada has reported almost 3.5 million cases of COVID-197. Using those figures,
anywhere between 350,000 and 1,050,000 Canadians may experience symptoms of long COVID.
However this does not capture individuals who were never tested or were probable COVID cases,
and so may be higher.
A recent study of 6000 health care workers from Quebec in 2020-2021 estimated that 40% of those
with COVID who were not hospitalized and 70% of those who were hospitalized had at least one
lingering symptom7.
Likelihood of long-COVID:
Early indicators suggest that some individuals may be more likely than others to experience
long-COVID. For example, rates appear to be higher amongst women over men. Other studies
show a link between diabetes type 2 and appearance of symptoms as well as previous occurrence
of epstein barr syndrome8. It does not appear that long COVID symptoms are linked to the
severity of initial COVID symptoms8. The impact on children is unclear and additional research is
needed in this area in particular9. More research is needed to create a more clear understanding of
who may be more likely to experience longer lasting symptoms 8,9.
New and emerging evidence indicates that vaccination status may reduce the likelihood of
long-COVID symptoms10. Given Canada’s relatively strong vaccination rates this could be a
promising finding, however this research is new and as such more is required in this area to
understand more about associated risk factors.
Finally. there is an unequal experience of disease burden in Canada and worldwide. This has been
the case with COVID-19 with some communities experiencing higher prevalence rates. It goes to
reckon then that similar inequities could exist with the experience of long-COVID 11.
A limitation of many of these studies is that the human body is not a sterile environment. This
means that variables such as treatment from initial COVID (ie. ventilator and/or steroid use) may
be challenging to isolate for7. Additionally, issues like measuring increase in fatigue can be
complicated to quantify objectively 7.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Additionally, issues like measuring increase in fatigue can be
complicated to quantify objectively 7.

As we look to recover from COVID-19, we must acknowledge the lasting impact. A full recovery
requires significant dedicated funding to better understand how to diagnose, manage, and treat
the symptoms associated with long COVID.
Joyce’s Story
Joyce was 30 when she had a suspected case of COVID-19 in March 2020. Joyce, an entrepreneur,
healthcare advocate and avid traveller, was abroad when she became sick.
While Joyce was not officially diagnosed with COVID-19 at the time
due to limitations of tests, the symptoms she experienced were
linked to COVID-19. Among her symptoms were extreme fatigue,
dry cough, sore throat and chest pain. “The chest pain was as if
someone was sitting on my chest,” Joyce shares.
While most of Joyce’s symptoms faded quickly, the cough and chest
pain
persisted.
After
a
few months of gradually worsening
symptoms, Joyce sought help from her family doctor and was
referred to a respirologist. Both have treated her case as suspected
“long COVID.” Joyce has gone through a series of tests, including a
chest x-ray and pulmonary function tests to determine the cause of
the chronic cough and chest pain.
“The most difficult part of this experience for me has been dealing with the uncertainty. It’s hard not
to think the worst when you have chest pain, and since so little is known about long COVID,
it’s been a journey to understand the cause of my symptoms and the prognosis.”
Knowledge Gaps
Lung disease in Canada has long been underfunded and yet, now more than ever, an investment in
lung health is critically important12. Given the relatively novel manifestation of long COVID there
exists a wide knowledge gap in terms of prevention, management, and treatment of long COVID
symptoms.
There are a number of gaps in long COVID including, but not limited to: education and awareness
raising through patient education, public awareness, as well as health care practitioner education;
research into demographics, risk factors, and protective elements to long COVID; long lasting
physiological changes to respiratory health and other body systems, and then management,
support, and treatment options.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
There are a number of gaps in long COVID including, but not limited to: education and awareness
raising through patient education, public awareness, as well as health care practitioner education;
research into demographics, risk factors, and protective elements to long COVID; long lasting
physiological changes to respiratory health and other body systems, and then management,
support, and treatment options.

Service and support gaps
The UK is one of the countries leading a dedicated effort to investing in and supporting patients in
COVID recovery13,14. This effort includes resources, education, and support to manage and treat
symptoms of long COVID13,14.
In Canada, there is a need for coordinated national efforts to support those experiencing long
COVID. In the face of a lack of evidence and options, private alternatives are beginning to emerge
in North America, where organizations are seeing an opportunity to fill a need and demand15.
Greater research could help establish whether these alternative options and treatments have a role
in a holistic approach to addressing long COVID.
At the same time, anecdotal evidence is suggesting that the existing services and support for
people with lung disease and other chronic diseases are being overburdened with new patients
with long COVID seeking solutions.
What is happening in Canada?
In the 2021 Federal Election, the Liberal Government included within their platform, $100 million
in dedicated funding for long COVID. This intention was reinforced in the mandate letters of
Ministers of Health and Science, Innovation, and Economic Development.
It is unclear to date how those funds will be released and the types of research and/or
programming that will be included.
The Canadian Lung Association will continue to monitor as the 2022 Federal Budget is released on
April 7 for indications of the continued commitment to funding long-COVID research.
Summary
As we move from pandemic to endemic, we must continue to invest in research to understand the
longer lasting implications from COVID-19. There is a dearth of information on long-COVID to
help guide healthcare decisions, patient education, as well as management and treatment options.
Recovery from this pandemic requires addressing the potential chronic systems that will remain.
Currently long COVID is poorly defined both in terms of symptoms and patient profiles. The
landscape of COVID and long COVID is ever evolving and requires responsive and progressive
approaches to research and support. Other jurisdictions, such as the UK, offer some insight into
the types of research and services that are required to recover from COVID. New research with
respect to vaccines as a protective factor are promising and require further research.
The government acknowledged and demonstrated the need for further research on long-COVID,
particularly amongst vulnerable populations. The Canadian Lung Association strongly encourages
the government to fulfill this commitment to help Canadians better recover from the lasting
impacts of this pandemic.

text:
BioCanRx submission to the Standing Committee on Health’s study on “The emergency
situation facing Canadians in light of the COVID-19 pandemic”
Introduction
BioCanRx is Canada’s Immunotherapy Network. We focus exclusively on harnessing the
enormous expertise in clinical and scientific cancer immunology from across Canada to
bring forward the most promising novel cancer immunotherapies to patients through
clinical trials. We are the only national not-for-profit network composed of academic health
centres across the country focused on connecting required expertise and infrastructure to
bring the most promising novel cancer immunotherapies to patients through clinical trials.
BioCanRx “makes the right tools available at the right time” to translate research and
accelerate the speed at which the public will start to benefit from research investments
made over many years by federal and provincial governments, NGOs and cancer charities.
As it relates to the Health Committee’s study on “The emergency situation facing Canadians
in light of the COVID-19 pandemic”, we are increasingly concerned that the impact of
pandemic restrictions on delayed cancer diagnostics and postponed treatment for
Canadians with will lead to a reduction of treatment options, as well as the need to employ
more aggressive treatment.
Immunotherapy harnesses the immune system to preferentially seek and destroy tumor
cells, and is a revolutionary approach to treating cancer. It has the potential to replace some
more aggressive treatment options, and to provide an alternate route for treatment for
patients who have exhausted all other options. However, a funding and expertise gap has
meant that made-in-Canada discoveries in cancer research are forced to move up the value
chain in the USA or elsewhere. As a result, Canadian patients do not gain access to madein-Canada discoveries as development and ensuing clinical trials are run in other countries.
This inability to move our discoveries from the bench to the clinic and then clinical practice
came into sharp focus as a result of COVID-19 as did Canada’s inability to manufacture
COVID-19 vaccines domestically at scale.
Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on cancer diagnosis and treatment options
Cancer continues to be the leading cause of death in Canada. Of the nearly 1 in 2 Canadians
expected to receive a cancer diagnosis in their lifetime, about 1 out of 4 Canadians is
expected to die of this disease. However, the true human cost of cancer extends beyond
the loss of life to also include long-term side effects of chemotherapy and radiation, and the
far-reaching physical, emotional and financial implications for patients and their support
networks. Nine out of 10 Canadian families affected by cancer report some form of financial
challenge as income declines and household costs increase. As a result, cancer costs

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
As a result, cancer costs

Canadians in excess of $20 billion per year from a combined loss of wages, taxes, corporate
profits and direct healthcare costs.
Cancer never waits, but during the COVID-19 pandemic, its diagnosis and treatment had to.
According to a survey commissioned by the Canadian Cancer Survivor Network (CCSN),
many cancer diagnostic tests and treatments were cancelled or postponed because of
COVID-19. These delays led to increased fear and anxiety among patients and caregivers,
which continue today.
Overall, 54% of those surveyed have had their cancer care appointments cancelled,
postponed, or rescheduled because of COVID-19. The same was reported by about 75% of
prediagnosis and recently diagnosed patients. Because delays in cancer care can lead to
progression of cancer, “It was disheartening to think we might face a public health crisis
down the road when more patients might develop into late-stage cancer [because of delays
to their treatment]”, says Jackie Manthorn (CCSN, Ottawa, ON, Canada).
Because cancer screening, surgeries and interventions essential to cancer care being
postponed, the Canadian Cancer Society (CCS) is deeply concerned that we will see cancer
cases diagnosed or treated too late. And with delayed diagnosis often comes a reduction in
treatment options, or the necessity for more aggressive treatment options.
This concern is rooted in worrisome trends in cancer care delays across the country.
According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information, between April and September
2020 there was a 20% reduction in cancer surgeries compared to the same timeframe in
2019. We know that when cancer is found and treated early, the changes of successful
treatment are better. A recent Canada-UK study showed a 4-week delay in cancer treatment
increases the risk of death by 10% and additional deaths and a shift toward diagnosis of more
advanced cancers is expected. If cancer treatment capacity is recovered but not increased in
2021, approximately 21 247 excess cancer deaths and 335, 172 life years will be lost in Canada
over the next 10 years due to pandemic-related delays. Ensuring continued support of
preclinical to clinical translation of ground-breaking Canadian innovations to support clinical
trials using novel immunotherapies will continue to provide options to Canadians faced with
advanced cancers.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Ensuring continued support of
preclinical to clinical translation of ground-breaking Canadian innovations to support clinical
trials using novel immunotherapies will continue to provide options to Canadians faced with
advanced cancers.

Immunotherapy harnesses the immune system to preferentially seek and destroy tumour
cells: it is a revolutionary approach to treating cancer. This approach has revolutionized the
treatment for melanoma and several other types of cancer and many new immunotherapies
are currently under development in Canada. Access to these innovative treatments is a driver
of improved patient outcomes. Immunotherapy has already contributed in a reduction in
lung cancer mortality in the USA; this has economic and societal implications, from increased
workforce participation and productivity to reduced premature mortality and financial
toxicity to patients and their families.

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Immunotherapy has already contributed in a reduction in
lung cancer mortality in the USA; this has economic and societal implications, from increased
workforce participation and productivity to reduced premature mortality and financial
toxicity to patients and their families.

However, access to innovative oncology treatments takes longer in Canada compared to
the United States – increasing the number of clinical trials in Canada by supporting the
biomanufacturing and research translation of immunotherapies is an important pathway
for patients to access new treatment approaches in a timely manner.
The potential of immunotherapies: the example of CAR T-cell therapy
CAR T therapy is a powerful new tool for treating cancer. It is personalized (a patient’s cells
are genetically engineered), so there is considerable infrastructure and expertise required
to deliver treatment safely and successfully. There have been very few CAR T clinical trials
in Canada (2 vs 63 in the USA between 2016-2018), and 0 trials in Canada, where the CAR
T-cell was manufactured in Canada. Faced with the inability to both manufacture CAR Tcells and treat patients in Canada, BioCanRx pioneered the delivery of personalized pointof-care manufacturing of this highly effective immunotherapy for patients with refractory
leukemia and lymphoma: the first made-in-Canada CAR T-cells.
‘Cure’ is a rare term in oncology. In a 10-year follow-up of the first patients having received
CAR T-cell therapy, Carl H June, MD stated “We can now conclude that CAR T-cells can
actually cure patients with leukemia,”. Similar results are currently in evidence in the work
of the BioCanRx network and being achieved for Canadian patients that had received a grim
prognosis on recurrence of their blood cancers. Ottawa patient Owen Snider was given
three months to live. And yet, a year later, Snider is alive and his non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
is in remission as a result of the biomanufacturing and CAR T cell program put in place by
BioCanRx.
Recommendations
To meet the challenge of delayed diagnosis of and reduced treatment options for cancer in
Canada, as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government should:
1. Increase diagnostic and cancer treatment capacity, including clinical trials, to save
lives resulting from pandemic-related cancer care delays.
2. Ensure that each segment of Canada’s biomanufacturing ecosystem is supported: 1)
talent and skills training; 2) favorable conditions exist to retain IP and companies to
stay in Canada; 3) adequate and sustained funding is available to organizations with
demonstrated impact and value, like BioCanRx; and 4) provide for a mechanism that
supports integration and coordination among all actors in the life science ecosystem
to deliver value to the Canadian patient and taxpayer.
3. Commit to increasing Canada’s Global Innovation Index ranking to the top 10 by
investing in bridging the biomedical research translation gap.

text:
Canadian Ophthalmological Society Submission to the
Standing Committee on Health
Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the
COVID-19 Pandemic
February 2022

Recommendations
1. Increase specific funding for cataract surgeries and increased access to surgical operating room time.
2. Fund and provide increased access to mental health supports, specifically for physicians and allied
health workers.

3. Create a Federal Vision Health Desk within Health Canada or PHAC to support the creation of a
national vision strategy.

Key Issues

Impact of Covid-19 on surgery backlogs

Jurisdictions worldwide ramped down ophthalmic surgeries to mitigate the effects of COVID-19, creating
a global surgical backlog. Since the start of the pandemic in 2020, the overall estimated number of
patients awaiting surgery grew by 129% and 150%, respectively. The estimated mean wait time for
patients for all subspecialty surgeries in Ontario increased to 282 days in March 2021 compared with 94
days in 2019. The provincial monthly additional resources required to clear the backlog by March 2023
was estimated to be a 34% escalation from the pre-pandemic volumes (4626 additional surgeries).

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
The provincial monthly additional resources required to clear the backlog by March 2023
was estimated to be a 34% escalation from the pre-pandemic volumes (4626 additional surgeries).

Cataract surgeries, one of the most common surgeries performed in Canada, has been particularly
impacted. We know that cataract surgery is enormously important to patients: not only does this sightrestoring surgery increase their quality of life, but it also helps prevent falls and other injuries. The
Conference Board of Canada report Ophthalmology in Canada has highlighted the importance of
ophthalmological procedures and the associated costs savings to the health care system. For example,
treating vision loss is projected to save $1.6 billion in direct health care costs in 2020, a number that’s
expected to reach $4 billion by 2040. Also “by treating vision loss, approximately 82,500 negative
medical outcomes will be avoided, including injuries or other associated health care needs such as falls,
hip fractures, depression, anxiety, admission into long-term care, and use of home care or caregiver
services.”1
The provinces have all responded to these backlogs in different ways: some have expanded operating
times to evenings and weekends, and some have initiated the creation of new non-hospital surgical
centers.
We believe more needs to be done to help close the backlog, we therefore ask for an increase specific
funding for cataract and other ophthalmic surgeries and increased access to surgical operating room
time.
1 Conference Board of Canada, “Value of Ophthalmology in Canada”, October 2020, https://www.cos-sco.ca/wpcontent/uploads/2020/10/Value-of-Ophthalmology-in-Canada.pdf

Impact of Covid-19 on Ophthalmologists

Ophthalmologists are physicians and surgeons. As such, they are the members of the eye care team who
have provided around the clock care for patients throughout the pandemic. Many are on call service 24
hours a day, 7 days a week. Like their fellow healthcare colleagues, ophthalmologists have worked
through the pressures of this exceptionally difficult time. Ophthalmologists, like other health care
providers are experiencing a lot of stress and burnout, but due to the current shortages of doctors
within our sub-specialty, the impact can be much greater for some.

Governments need to work with universities to increase the number of doctors in the future but
currently they also need to provide tailored and specific mental healthcare for physicians and allied
health professionals who are dealing with an extremely unique and trying experience.

Vision Health Desk

study_or_consultation_title: Emergency Situation Facing Canadians in Light of the COVID-19 Pandemic
text:
Vision Health Desk

Eye health and vision health care are absent from federal health priorities. This, despite a 2018
commitment made by Canada at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Conference, to increase
accessibility to eye care for all Canadians.
Recent studies, including the above mentioned 2020 report by the Conference Board of Canada (CBoC),
call for greater action by the government of Canada to address the growing demand for eye and vision
healthcare, including the need for a national vision strategy. There is an intersectionality of issues
warranting the creation of a National Vision Health Desk: workplace development and planning;
effective collaborative care networks; and access to and integration of drugs and technologies.
Eye health and vision health issues can impact anyone but are most prevalent among certain groups
such as seniors, children, and populations with higher incidence of diabetes. There were 1.1 million
major ophthalmological interventions performed in Canada in 2018. Approximately 90 per cent of these
procedures were performed on Canadians aged 65 and older. Timeliness in diagnosis and treatment can
be especially important in young children while their visual systems are growing. Delays in treatment of
visually impactful ocular problems in children can have irreversible lifelong implications due to
maldevelopment of the visual pathways in the brain called amblyopia.
Overall, the economic impact of vision loss is immense. In 2019, the cost of vision loss in Canada was
estimated at $35.9 billion and is expected to grow to $56 billion in 2050.2 In 2007, the cost of vision loss
in Canada was estimated at $15.8billion and is projected to grow to $30.3billion by 2032. In 2010, eye
conditions made up 5.8 percent of the direct health care costs in Canada.
Federal leadership and national standards are therefore critical. As such, we recommend the creation of
a Federal Vision Health Desk within Health Canada or PHAC to support the creation of a national vision
strategy. We look forward to discussing this matter with you more in the coming months.

The Canadian Ophthalmological Society (COS) is the national, recognized authority on eye and vision
healthcare in Canada. As eye physicians and surgeons, they are committed to assuring the provision of
optimal medical and surgical eye care for all Canadians by promoting excellence in ophthalmology and
by providing services to support their members in practice.

The COS' membership includes over 1,100 ophthalmologists and 220 ophthalmology residents. They
work collaboratively with government, other national and international specialty societies, their
academic communities (ACUPO), provincial partners and affiliates and other eye care professionals and
patient groups to advocate for health policy in Canada in eye and vision health.

text:
Brief Prepared for:
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Topic:
National Medical Licensure; Petition e-3378
Author:
Dr. Kyle Sue, MD, MHM, BSc, GCPain, CCFP(PC)
Author Affiliations:
a) Rural/Remote General Practitioner, Clinical Assistant Professor, Discipline of Family
Medicine, Memorial University of Newfoundland
b) Pediatric Palliative Care and Developmental Pediatrics Specialist, Clinical Assistant
Professor, Department of Pediatrics, University of Alberta
