text:
With this in mind, we make the following recommendations.
7 Health product shortages in Canada: Fiscal year 2024 to 2025 in review

Recommendation 1 – Focus public efforts on strategic segments of the
pharmaceutical chain rather than aiming for complete self-sufficiency.
Canada should focus its public efforts on specific segments where local or regional
capacity can actually enhance security of supply. These segments should include essential
medicines,
products
particularly
vulnerable
to
supply
disruptions,
specialized
manufacturing capabilities, emergency production, as well as certain aspects relating to
research, development and contract manufacturing.
This approach would take into account the real limitations of the Canadian market, the globalized
structure of pharmaceutical production, and the international concentration of certain critical links,
including active pharmaceutical ingredients. It would also avoid a goal of complete self-sufficiency
that would be costly, difficult to achieve and unrealistic, while concentrating public resources
where they can produce concrete gains in resilience.
Recommendation 2 – Implement targeted economic incentives to support
industrial players essential to pharmaceutical sovereignty.
Canada should put in place economic incentives aligned with the industrial capabilities it
wishes to develop or maintain on its territory. These measures should support not only
drug manufacturers but also wholesalers and the wider biotech ecosystem.
These incentives should include appropriate tax measures, finely tuned support programs, better
support for growth financing, and mechanisms to promote industrial networks and the
development of local sectors. The development of sustainable local capacity cannot be based
solely on declarations of intent. It requires an economic environment that allows companies to
invest, grow and maintain viable operations in an industry with long development cycles, high
capital requirements and significant risks.
Recommendation 3 – Review generic drug pricing policies to better reflect
changes in manufacturing costs.
Canada, in collaboration with the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance, should review the
mechanisms for setting and adjusting generic drug prices to ensure that selling prices
reflect changes in manufacturing costs. This revision should also include transportation,
warehousing, regulatory compliance and distribution costs, as well as the possibility of
indexation when costs increase significantly.
Generic drugs play a central role in access to treatment and in the financial balance of public
plans. However, when manufacturing costs rise while selling prices remain fixed or continue to
decline, profit margins shrink and some products become less attractive to maintain in the market.
This situation particularly weakens low-volume products, older drugs and segments already
vulnerable to shortages. From a perspective of access, security of supply and local production,
pricing policies must therefore better reflect the economic reality of manufacturers.

org: Association des bannières et des chaînes de pharmacies du Québec / Association québécoise des distributeurs en pharmacie
text:
From a perspective of access, security of supply and local production,
pricing policies must therefore better reflect the economic reality of manufacturers.

Recommendation 4 – Ensure systematic government monitoring of the health of
the drug supply chain, including shortages.
Canada should establish systematic government monitoring of the pharmaceutical supply
chain to better track vulnerabilities, anticipate disruption risks, and coordinate responses
in the event of shortages. This monitoring should include a specific component on
shortages, supported by better transparency of data on stocks, production capacities,
vulnerable products, manufacturing disruptions, increases in demand, and shipping
delays.
Such a measure would make it possible to move from a largely reactive management of shortages
to a more preventive approach. It would facilitate a smoother flow of information between public
authorities, manufacturers, wholesalers, distributors and other market players. It would also allow
for the faster identification of substitute products, alternative sources of supply, or mitigation
measures. As shortages have become one of the main indicators of the fragility of the
pharmaceutical chain, a more structured and transparent strategy is needed.
Taken together, these recommendations aim to inscribe pharmaceutical sovereignty within a
framework of resilience rather than self-sufficiency. They are based on the idea that a more solid
system is not necessarily one that produces everything locally, but one that knows how to better
target its priorities, support its strategic capacities, adapt its economic tools, streamline its
regulatory processes and better anticipate the risks of supply disruptions.

Introduction
Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty begins with the generic and biosimilar medicines
industries, which supply more than 80% of the prescription medications needs of Canadian
patients.
As a starting point, pharmaceutical sovereignty will require decision makers to recognize that
cost-saving generic and biosimilar medicines are not just budget line items — they are strategic
assets that must be treated as health, economic, and national security priorities.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is about protecting the health of Canadians through a reliable,
secure, and sustainable domestic supply of medicines. It means ensuring that Canada has the
domestic capacity and policy frameworks in place to reliably supply and produce essential
medicines to meet the needs of Canadians.
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the fragility of global pharmaceutical supply chains. Border
disruptions, export restrictions, shortages of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and geopolitical
tensions revealed a simple truth: when supply chains fracture, Canadians are vulnerable.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty will require government decision makers to prioritize actions to
address the significant existing barriers to market entry for generic and biosimilar medicines.
This is needed to both ensure a robust pipeline of new generic and biosimilar medicines for
Canadians and to support domestic generic drug manufacturers who want to grow their
manufacturing and R&D capacity here in Canada.
The lack of predictability and significant risk companies are facing in Canada today is
unprecedented. It is difficult for our member companies to plan and build a business case to
make the investments needed to bring new cost-saving medicines to the Canadian market.
Inadequate regulatory resource capacity at Health Canada and red tape are important causes of
domestic supply delays and disruptions. As the federal government seeks to expedite regulatory
approval processes across sectors of the Canadian economy, a return to predictable and timely
generic and biosimilar drug submission reviews should also be prioritized to support Canadians’
access to timely drug competition and reassert Canada’s position as a world-class regulator.
Economic factors are a major root cause of domestic drug shortages. Over the past two
decades, pricing pressures and procurement policies that prioritize the lowest cost have steadily
eroded domestic production incentives and decreased the financial viability of supplying some
products to the Canadian market. At the same time, there have been significant increases in the
costs of manufacturing inputs, production, labour and transportation, and generic drug
manufacturers are unable to increase the prices of their products to account for economic
shocks and these realities.

At the same time, there have been significant increases in the
costs of manufacturing inputs, production, labour and transportation, and generic drug
manufacturers are unable to increase the prices of their products to account for economic
shocks and these realities.

The government’s intention to create a Whole-of-Government Competition Plan provides a
timely and important opportunity to remove regulatory and policy barriers that impede generic
and biosimilar competition, strengthen domestic manufacturing incentives, and improve the
resilience of Canada’s medicines supply.
There are thousands of prescription medications sold in Canada today. While it would be
impossible to make all these medicines here, there are important opportunities to strengthen
both Canada’s domestic generic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and our strategic
international pharmaceutical supply chains.
1. Ensure Predictability and On-Time Performance for Health Canada Drug Reviews

Accelerating access to medicines for Canadians is a stated priority for federal, provincial and
territorial governments. The regulatory review process for generic and biosimilar medicines is
broken and urgently needs to be fixed to support Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty. There
are exceptionally long and unpredictable delays in Health Canada drug submission reviews.
Planned launches of new generic and biosimilar medicines in 2026 and 2027 are in jeopardy.
There are currently over one hundred generic drug submissions in backlog. Some targets have
been missed by years.

Health Canada’s review processes for generic and biosimilar drug submissions provide an
enormous societal benefit. Unfortunately, they have been underfunded for many years and are
not adequately resourced to deal with the growing volume and complexity of drug submissions
despite the significant fees paid by sponsors under the department’s cost recovery regime.

Every day of delayed drug competition can result in millions of dollars in extra costs for the
healthcare system including federal and provincial drug plans, businesses who provide drug
benefit programs for their employees, and individual Canadians who pay for medicines out of
pocket. Provincial governments have also expressed concern with Health Canada about the

Such delays directly increase costs for the federal government for the four federally-funded

for the federal government through its funding of the Public Service Health Care Plan for federal

coverage for about 1.7 million Canadians.

These delays also harm the significant domestic life sciences interests and investments of
generic pharmaceutical companies that manufacture medicines in Canada for Canadians and
for export to more than 100 countries worldwide. These investments are a strategic asset for

Canada, providing well-paying Canadian jobs and positively supporting the health and economic

Investments in Health Canada’s drug review process for generic and biosimilar medicines to
address existing resource challenges are investments in our domestic health security that will
have the additional benefit of lower costs for the drug benefit programs provided by the
Canadian government, its provincial and territorial partners, and for Canadian employers that

The problem will require additional permanent staff resources to address the existing backlog
while also ensuring Health Canada is able to meet the growing workload for drug submission
reviews due to the increasing number of submissions for review and the increasing complexity
of products for review. These increased staff resources would be largely offset by industry
through the significant cost recovery fees manufacturers currently pay for drug submission

It is important to note that the needed investments are relatively small when compared to the
exponentially broad savings generated from timely access to generic and biosimilar medicines
for Canadian patients and healthcare systems. Canada will be unable to achieve
pharmaceutical sovereignty without these investments.

That the Government of Canada address significant drug submission review delays for generic
and biosimilar medicines by providing increased, long-term funding for Health Canada drug
submission review to ensure sustainable resourcing going forward, eliminate submission

2. Rebalancing Canada’s Pharmaceutical Intellectual Property Regime to Support Timely
Access to Cost-Saving Generics and Biosimilars

a) Skinny Labels

Recent court decisions have changed the pharmaceutical patent litigation landscape in Canada
in ways that were not anticipated or intended by federal law and policy. Patents covering new
uses or indications can now prevent the entry of generic and biosimilar medicines into the
Canadian market even where the sponsor does not indicate that their product should be used
for the patented indication and where they do not intend to market the product for that
indication.

Patents covering new
uses or indications can now prevent the entry of generic and biosimilar medicines into the
Canadian market even where the sponsor does not indicate that their product should be used
for the patented indication and where they do not intend to market the product for that
indication.

As a result, Canadians are being denied access to generic and biosimilar medicines for years
even where the intended use is non-infringing. This has created a significant imbalance in
Canada’s pharmaceutical intellectual property system.

An urgent correction to the patent regime is needed to ensure that Canadians can continue to
have timely access to cost-saving generic and biosimilar medicines and to ensure that domestic
generic manufacturers can be competitive in attracting new R&D and production mandates to
Canada.

b) Incentives and Damages

The current intellectual property regime for pharmaceuticals is imbalanced. Contrary to all other
areas of patent law in Canada, originator companies in Canada can obtain automatic 24-month
injunctions to block generic and biosimilars manufacturers from entering the market, without any
upfront burden of proof. This system –known as “patent linkage” – does not exist in the
European Union, the United Kingdom and many other countries as it is deemed to be anticompetitive and is an unnecessary barrier to generic and biosimilar drug competition.

The cost of litigation to an originator company is a small business expense when compared to
the large monopoly profits they are highly motivated to maintain. The current patent linkage
system in Canada does not include incentives for generic and biosimilar manufacturers to
challenge weak and frivolous patents and bring cost-saving drug competition to the market – an
important balancing feature in countries where patent linkage systems do exist.

While there is a damages provision, not a single damage award has been made by the courts to
a generic or biosimilar manufacturer since the regulations were last amended in September
2017. A simplified and expedited process for damage awards would allow generic and
biosimilars companies to recoup their legal investments when they are successful in litigating
weak and frivolous patents.. It would also allow them to make more timely investments in
domestic manufacturing operations to bring new generic and biosimilar medicines to the
Canadian market.

Any efforts to increase pharmaceutical IP and market exclusivity periods for originator

Canada’s Whole-of-Government Competition Plan, and must be firmly rejected by the

3. Whole-of-Government Competition Plan Should Address Barriers to Drug Competition
On April 28, the Spring Economic Update 2026 announced the government's intention to launch
a Whole-of-Government Competition Plan. The Plan will seek to ensure that existing and future
policies across the federal government prioritize the promotion of competition and limit to the
extent possible the potential negative impacts on competition that can stem from government
policies. The plan will also focus on removing inefficient government policies that impede
competition arising from regulation, procurement, and industrial support.
This proposed Plan provides an important opportunity to support Canada’s Pharmaceutical
Sovereignty by prioritizing and addressing federal policies and systemic issues that are creating
delays and unnecessary barriers to generic and biosimilar drug competition.
Examples of issues that should be addressed as priorities under the Whole-of-Government
Competition Plan include:
•
Recognizing that Health Canada regulatory approval delays do not just delay generic and
biosimilar drug market entry – they unfairly extend patent monopolies and increase costs for
taxpayers and the healthcare system. Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty requires
restoring Health Canada’s position as a world-class regulator that has the resource capacity
to meet performance targets and the internal expertise to review more complex medicines
submissions that now represent the majority of generic drug submissions.1

•
Putting an end originator patent evergreening strategies that are now blocking generic and
biosimilar drug competition for unpatented uses of older drugs by amending the Patent Act.

Canadian generic pharmaceutical manufacturers currently export Canadian-made prescription
medicines to more than 100 countries. They need tariff-free access to foreign markets to sustain
and grow their domestic manufacturing and R&D investments.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty does not mean isolation. Canada will always be part of global
supply chains. But sovereignty does mean having sufficient domestic capacity and trusted
partners so Canadians are not at the back of the line when risks of supply chain shocks occur.

Conclusion
Pharmaceutical sovereignty depends on a reliable, affordable base supply of essential
medicines – the vast majority of which are generics and biosimilars. We have a strong
foundation, but it cannot be taken for granted.
Competition policy, IP balance, and procurement rules should be aligned with resilience goals:
predictable market entry, fair competition, and sustainable supply. Targeted federal actions —
improved regulatory resource capacity, pro-competition IP clarity, life sciences investment tools
and supply chain security agreements – can improve resilience without compromising the
quality, safety and efficacy of the medicines approved by Health Canada.
By addressing current barriers, Canada can strengthen its pharmaceutical sovereignty by
expanding generic pharmaceutical manufacturing, strengthening supply chains, and ensuring

Study on Pharmaceutical Sovereignty

Recommendations

1. Develop and implement a pan-Canadian research ethics system
2. Improve Canada’s Drug Approval Pathway
3. Establish robust and sustainable clinical trial funding to make Canada the world’s fastest
country to launch a clinical trial
4. Improve post-approval drug access pathways

Executive Summary

Pharmaceutical sovereignty cannot be achieved through domestic manufacturing alone. For
life-saving medicines (particularly oncology therapies), Canada’s long-term security, affordability,
and access depend on anchoring investment across the full medicines lifecycle, from discovery and
clinical trials through to production and patient access.

The Canadian Cancer Society (CCS) urges the Standing Committee on Health (HESA) to recognize
that a robust, internationally competitive clinical trials ecosystem is a foundational pillar of
pharmaceutical sovereignty. Countries that succeed in hosting trials are more likely to attract
downstream investment and ensure early and reliable access to innovative medicines for patients.

In addition, pharmaceutical sovereignty cannot be achieved if medicines are approved but remain
inaccessible to patients. This includes efficient health technology assessments (HTAs),
coordinated price negotiation and timely and consistent public reimbursement across Canada.
When access to essential medicines is delayed, fragmented, or dependent on ad hoc mechanisms,
Canada remains vulnerable to external decision-making, market instability, and supply
disruptions. A sovereign pharmaceutical system must ensure approvals lead reliably to timely,
funded, and equitable patient access across the country.

By reducing regulatory fragmentation, aligning approval pathways with peer countries,
strengthening patient access pathways and stabilizing clinical trial funding, Canada can send a
clear and credible signal that it is serious about anchoring pharmaceutical innovation domestically.
For cancer medicines, where delays can cost lives and alternatives are often unavailable, these
policy levers are particularly urgent.

Why Clinical Trials Matter for Pharmaceutical Sovereignty

Why Clinical Trials Matter for Pharmaceutical Sovereignty

We echo the testimony of witnesses who repeatedly underscored how Canada is losing ground as
an attractive jurisdiction for pharmaceutical investment, citing slow approvals, regulatory
fragmentation, pricing uncertainty, and delayed time to listing— delays that can be life-or-death
for people with cancer. International examples, such as in the UK and Australia, demonstrate
clinical trials are not a peripheral activity, but a strategic investment:
•
Jurisdictions that host trials are more likely to see medicines launched earlier
and maintained on market
•
Trials anchor skilled health and research workforces
•
Trials create predictable demand signals that justify local production and supply chain
investment

Canada’s inability to attract research and clinical trials has increased reliance on global supply
chains, leaving patients vulnerable during shortages and geopolitical disruptions. As global tides
shift, it will become ever more important to not be reliant upon the United States to export
medication to Canada, especially since global supply chain disruption and most favored nation

pricing can deeply impact what Canada has access to, how much of it and at what cost. A strong
domestic clinical trials ecosystem contributes to resilience by:
•
Prioritizing Canadian participation in global development programs
•
Supporting domestic expertise to validate and adapt alternatives during shortages
•
Enabling earlier identification of supply risks for essential oncology medicines

For cancer patients, where “substitution” is often not clinically feasible, trial participation may be
the only timely access pathway during supply disruptions.

In December 2025, CCS published the Clinical Trials Action Plan. This was developed through a

This work was complemented by public opinion research conducted in partnership with the Angus

Together, these inputs provided a comprehensive, pan-Canadian view of systemic challenges and

perspectives, and comparative analysis of best practices in peer jurisdictions, ensuring that the
priorities, actions, and sub-actions it recommends are both evidence-informed and practically
implementable.

As CTAP relates to pharmaceutical sovereignty, we recommend the Government of Canada:

1. Develop and implement a pan-Canadian research ethics system
Canada’s fragmented ethics reviews and duplicative approvals slow trial start-up, making Canada
less attractive for global studies and delaying patient access to new therapies. Canada needs a
single, pan-Canadian ethics review system to eliminate redundant reviews at the institutional,
provincial and territorial levels, such as a model similar to the US National Review Board. This
review should include experts in both pediatric and adult oncology and people with lived and living
experience with cancer.

Beyond reducing administrative burden, a single, pan-Canadian ethics review system would
position Canada as a more reliable and predictable partner in global clinical development. In a
competitive global environment, jurisdictions that can activate trials quickly and efficiently are
prioritized for early-phase studies, which in turn attract downstream investment and
manufacturing decisions. Reducing duplicative research ethics board reviews and enhancing
agreement work are necessary changes to improve efficiencies in the clinical trials ecosystem.

2. Improve Canada’s Drug Approval Pathway
Many drugs considered standard of care in other countries are still experimental in Canada. We
need a strategy to align Canadian drug approval processes based on successful trial results. We
encourage the government to align Canada’s drug approval process with those of other G7
countries by allowing simultaneous submissions of the same documentation to both the US Food
and Drug Administration (FDA) and Health Canada to expedite approval so that medications
proven to work in trials can be timely and accessible to Canadian people with cancer.

We
encourage the government to align Canada’s drug approval process with those of other G7
countries by allowing simultaneous submissions of the same documentation to both the US Food
and Drug Administration (FDA) and Health Canada to expedite approval so that medications
proven to work in trials can be timely and accessible to Canadian people with cancer.

Alignment with G7 approval pathways is particularly critical for oncology, where global
development programs often move rapidly from trial completion to regulatory submission.
Compared to trials for novel cancer treatments in the US and many European countries, Canada
currently lags. That means Canadians must travel to other countries for novel or experimental
treatments and manufacturers may deprioritize the Canadian market entirely, leaving patients
without access to therapies widely available elsewhere. Ensuring regulatory alignment and
expedited pathways for life-saving medicines strengthens both access and supply security.

3. Establish robust and sustainable clinical trial funding to make Canada the world’s fastest
country to launch a clinical trial
To improve access to clinical trials in Canada, we need to transform the system. We recommend
setting a national benchmark of 75 days to have a concrete target to work toward and measure
progress. Furthermore, we recommend targeted federal investments of $120 million over 3 years
to streamline long and overlapping processes will go a long way towards creating the conditions
that will boost Canada as a destination for patient-centered innovations.

We support the investments made through establishing the Clinical Trials Fund in January 2023,
and the second round of clinical trials funding with an investment of $43.1 million for 14 new
projects again in August 2024. However, the government has not committed to renewing the
funding beyond 2025. Stable, long-term funding at federal, provincial and territorial levels
supports critical infrastructure, staffing, patient education and essential services, such as labs and
imaging. Short-term or uncertain funding undermines the ability to plan multi-year trials, retain
specialized staff, and build partnerships with industry. Stable funding is therefore not only an
operational necessity, but a strategic economic signal that supports sovereignty objectives.

Access Pathways

Pharmaceutical sovereignty is not realized when medicines exist in Canada in theory, but only
when patients can reliably access them in practice. This means timely regulatory decisions as well
as streamlined and coordinated processes that ensure approved medicines reach patients without
avoidable delay. Even when medicines receive Health Canada approval, access for patients is
often delayed by lengthy and uncertain post-approval pathways, including HTAs, pricing
negotiations and public reimbursement decision-making.

Even when medicines receive Health Canada approval, access for patients is
often delayed by lengthy and uncertain post-approval pathways, including HTAs, pricing
negotiations and public reimbursement decision-making.

For many cancer medicines, the period between regulatory authorization and public coverage can
span years, during which patients have limited or no access to these proven therapies. In addition,
infrastructure, access to biomarker testing and appropriate care pathways all require system
preparedness. Differences in coverage decisions, eligibility criteria, and timelines across provinces
and territories mean access to lifesaving cancer medications can vary significantly based on
location rather than clinical need. Such variability forces patients to navigate complex systems,
pursue private or out-of-province options, or forgo treatment altogether. A sovereign
pharmaceutical system requires coherence and coordination across jurisdictions to ensure access
to essential medicines is equitable and nationally consistent.

When timelines and outcomes are unpredictable, manufacturers may deprioritize the Canadian
market, delay supply commitments, or reconsider launching subsequent indications. In oncology,
where patient populations may be small, treatments may be very targeted or alternatives are
limited, such uncertainty can directly affect a therapy’s availability. A sovereign pharmaceutical
system must provide clear, consistent, and timely access pathways that support sustained market
presence, rather than relying on protracted negotiations and provincial decisions that weaken
supply resilience and delay patient access. These downstream delays undermine the promise of
early approvals and weaken Canada’s ability to function as a predictable and reliable market for
new innovative medicines.

Exceptional and compassionate access mechanisms play a critical role in enabling access to
treatment in urgent or extraordinary circumstances. However, when these pathways become a
routine means of access for patients with cancer, they signal fragility in the standard access
system. Reliance on discretionary or temporary programs shifts administrative burden to
clinicians and provinces, creates uncertainty for patients, and exposes gaps between approval and
funded access. From a sovereignty perspective, routine access pathways reduce the need for
exceptions and enhances the stability and reliability of medicine access in Canada.

Reliable access pathways are a critical, but often overlooked, component of supply resilience.
Medications are more likely to remain available in markets with predictable approval,
reimbursement, and funding environments. Treating clinical trials, approvals, and access pathways
as interconnected parts of a single system is essential to achieving pharmaceutical sovereignty
and reinforcing Canada’s attractiveness as a stable market.

To that end, CCS recommends the government:
1.
In partnership with provinces and territories, Indigenous governments, health charities
and people with lived experience, accelerate approval and funding decisions for
medications by streamlining HTA and price negotiation processes. CCS advocates for
process improvements within Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA), Institut national
d’excellence en santé et en services sociaux (INESSS) and the pan-Canadian
Pharmaceutical Alliance (pCPA) to identify opportunities to reduce duplication, enable
parallel regulatory and reimbursement processes and shorten avoidable delay;
2.
Address uncertainty by setting clearer timelines for pCPA negotiations to align more
closely with global norms, and ensuring predictable and timely provincial and territorial
formulary listings following a federal Letter of Intent;
3.
Strengthen routine reimbursement pathways for cancer drugs by preserving flexibility in
funding frameworks, including time-limited reimbursement models that can
accommodate extended trial periods and by incorporating real-world evidence and
patient-reported outcomes to support reassessment and continued coverage.
Conclusion

The priorities outlined in this submission—streamlining ethics reviews, aligning drug approval
pathways with peer jurisdictions, stabilizing and growing clinical trials funding, and strengthening
patient access pathways—represent practical, evidence-informed actions that the federal
government can take now to strengthen Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty. Together, they
address the regulatory inefficiencies, investment uncertainty, and workforce challenges that
witnesses before HESA repeatedly identified as barriers to domestic pharmaceutical resilience.

Canada has the scientific expertise, clinical talent, and patient engagement needed to lead in
pharmaceutical innovation. Treating clinical trials as strategic national infrastructure and
improving post-approval access pathways are essential to realizing that potential and to ensuring
that sovereignty in pharmaceutical policy delivers real benefits for patients.

Executive Summary
Canada is not capturing the post-patent opportunity to supply its own medicines. While generic and equivalent
medicines account for the majority of prescriptions dispensed in Canada, only a small proportion, estimated at
12% in 2022, are manufactured domestically. As a result, our country remains heavily reliant on multinational
pharmaceutical companies for the supply of essential medicines.
In a well-functioning system, the period following patent expiry should enable Canadian companies to compete,
supply lower-cost alternatives and expand domestic production. In practice, this transition is not occurring.
Market dynamics continue to favour large, non-Canadian firms, limiting competition and preventing domestic
manufacturers from gaining meaningful market share. This dynamic also limits price competition, resulting in
higher costs for public drug plans and Canadian patients, and limiting the savings that should be realized
following patent expiry. This structural problem not only increases the risk of supply disruptions that can affect
patient care, but also results in higher and unavoidable costs for the healthcare system at a time when
governments can least afford unnecessary spending.
This is not a question of capacity. Canadian companies exist, are growing and are already investing in domestic
manufacturing. However, current market conditions do not provide the predictability or fairness required to
support long-term investment in local production.
The result is a structural weakness: Canada continues to rely on external suppliers even when viable domestic
alternatives are available. This dependency undermines supply resilience, constrains economic opportunity, and
leaves the country more vulnerable to disruption.
Effectively addressing this challenge means supporting competitive post‑patent markets and creating
conditions that allow Canadian companies to invest in and scale domestic manufacturing.
Summary of Recommendations
1) Improve national coordination of post-patent market policies.
Convene provinces and territories to align and coordinate policies that govern the transition to lower-cost
alternatives, ensuring consistent implementation and more predictable market outcomes across jurisdictions.
2) Clarify and strengthen competitive market guidance.
Call on the Competition Bureau to provide clear guidance on market conduct that may delay or discourage
competition following patent expiry, including practices that preserve originator market share and limit
uptake of lower-cost alternatives.
3) Support domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Strengthen incentives for domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing by (a) supporting Canadian-owned
companies investing in local manufacturing capabilities, (b) fast-tracking drug submissions submitted by
Canadian-owned companies with local manufacturing facilities, (c) prioritizing Canadian-owned companies
for government supply needs, and (d) ensuring that market conditions enable Canadian-owned companies
to compete and scale production following patent expiry.
4) Provide financial support to Canadian-owned companies having local manufacturing facilities:
(a) Remove annual DIN fees on drugs marketed by Canadian-owned companies, (b) decrease by 75% fees
charged by Health Canada on NDS, sNDS, ANDS and sANDS submitted by Canadian-owned companies, and
(c) provide tax credits of 75% of salaries paid by Canadian-owned companies for employment related to
manufacturing in Canada.

competition in the Canadian biologics market. JAMP is
also investing in domestic manufacturing capacity,
including its production facility in Lévis since 2024,
while actively considering the potential to further
expand local production of essential medicines over
time as part of its long-term commitment to
strengthening Canada’s supply resilience.
2.2. Policies designed to enable competition are
not delivering
Policies exist to support competition following patent
expiry. These are intended to create predictable market
conditions and enable new entrants to compete.
In Canada, these policies are typically implemented
through reimbursement mechanisms, where
continued public coverage is contingent on
transitioning to lower-cost alternatives within defined
timelines. In theory, this should create a clear pathway
for lower-cost alternatives to gain uptake following
patent expiry.
JAMP makes this submission not simply as a market
participant, but as a Canadian manufacturer directly
affected by how Canada’s pharmaceutical system
functions in practice. With the capability to supply
medicines domestically, JAMP is well positioned to
contribute to strengthening Canada’s pharmaceutical
supply chain, but only if market conditions allow for
effective competition and growth.
However, implementation is inconsistent and often
insufficient to drive real-world market shifts. Where
policy does not translate into uptake, competition
remains limited and market share does not rebalance.
In practice, uptake is influenced by how the market
functions in real-world conditions.
In a well-functioning system, the period following
patent expiry should enable companies like JAMP to
compete, supply lower-cost alternatives and scale
domestic manufacturing. This is the point at which
Canadian firms can impactfully participate in the
market and contribute to a more resilient and selfsufficient supply chain.
2.3. Consequence: Canadian companies cannot scale
When competitoin does not materialize, Canadian
manufacturers are unable to gain significant market
share. Without predictable access to the market,
companies cannot justify the investment required to
expand domestic production. Developing and
supplying these medicines requires significant upfront
In practice, this transition is not occurring at scale.
Established multinational firms retain market
dominance well beyond patent expiry, limiting the

Established multinational firms retain market
dominance well beyond patent expiry, limiting the

investment, which depends on predictable market
access and the ability to compete for share. At the
same time, limited competition reduces downward
pressure on pricing, meaning Canada pays more than
necessary for medicines where lower-cost
alternatives exist.
This highlights the risks of relying on external
manufacturing for essential medicines. A more resilient
system would include domestic production capacity for
critical therapies, with companies like JAMP exploring
the potential to manufacture acetaminophen at its
Lévis facility.
These dynamics not only limit competition but also
reduce the financial benefits that post-patent markets
are designed to deliver.
3.4. Missed economic opportunity
When domestic companies cannot compete, Canada
loses the opportunity to anchor more of its
pharmaceutical supply chain locally, including job
creation and infrastructure investment.
3. What this means for
pharmaceutical sovereignty
4. Evidence of the problem
in practice
3.1. Continued dependence on external supply
Canada remains dependent on multinational firms for
the supply of essential medicines, even in areas where
domestic alternatives are available.
In certain areas of the pharmaceutical market, lowercost alternatives have entered but have not achieved
meaningful uptake. Biologic medicines represent one of
the fastest-growing segments of pharmaceutical
spending in Canada, accounting for more than onethird of total drug expenditures.
This dependence creates structural risk, as supply
decisions are made outside of Canada and may not
prioritize Canadian demand.
3.2. Limited incentive for domestic manufacturing
Domestic manufacturing requires long-term
investment. Where market conditions are uncertain or
do not support competition, companies have limited
incentive to invest in local production.
Case study: Biosimilars and post-patent
market dynamics
In some therapeutic categories, including
those where biosimilar alternatives have entered
the market, originator products and their
associated portfolios retain the vast majority of
market share well after patent expiry. This
demonstrates that price alone does not drive
competition and that structural market factors
determine outcomes.
This directly undermines Canada’s ability to build
domestic manufacturing capacity.
3.3. Real-world consequences: Supply vulnerability
Canada’s reliance on external supply chains has
already resulted in disruptions. In 2024-2025 alone,
Canada reported more than 2,500 drug shortages,
reflecting the instability of global supply chains. This
instability is compounded by Canada’s reliance on
external manufacturing.
For example, following the introduction of
biosimilar versions of ustekinumab in Canada, the
originator product and its associated offering
retained more than 90% of the market in the first
24 months following biosimilar entry. Despite the
availability of lower-cost alternatives, market share
did not shift as expected.
Case study: Pediatric acetaminophen shortage
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Canada
experienced shortages of pediatric
acetaminophen. Governments sourced supply
internationally. However, differences in
formulation and viscosity limited usability in
certain settings, including higher viscosity that
affected administration in neonatal care. A
significant portion of supply arrived after the peak
shortage and was later destroyed due to expiry.
This outcome reflects entrenched market dynamics that
delay or prevent the transition to competitive supply. It
limits the ability of new entrants to gain meaningful
share, reducing the competition and the opportunity to
expand domestic production. It also limits the cost
savings that should be realized through competition,
resulting in higher overall spending on medicines.

It also limits the cost
savings that should be realized through competition,
resulting in higher overall spending on medicines.

While the acetaminophen example illustrates the risks
associated with limited domestic manufacturing
capacity, the biosimilars example demonstrates how
current market dynamics prevent that capacity from
developing in the first place.
5. The path forward
Canada has the companies, capabilities and
infrastructure required to strengthen domestic
pharmaceutical supply.
Canadian manufacturers are actively investing in local
capacity. This includes companies such as JAMP,
which are investing in domestic manufacturing and
evaluating opportunities to expand local production.
To realize this potential, Canada must ensure that:
Post-patent markets function competitively
Canadian companies can gain meaningful market
share
Market conditions support long-term investment in
domestic manufacturing
Conclusion
Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty depends
on more than policy intent. It requires a market that
functions in practice. This includes the ability not
only to access medicines but to produce them
within Canada.
Today, Canada is not capturing the opportunity to
supply its own medicines following patent expiry. As a
result, the country remains dependent on multinational
firms, even where domestic alternatives exist.
Canadian-owned companies, especially those having
manufacturing facilities in Canada, should receive the
full support of the Canadian government, including
through the measures highlighted in Recommendation
3 and 4 of the Executive Summary above.
By strengthening competition and enabling domestic
investment, Canada can reduce reliance on external
suppliers, improve supply resilience and build a more
competitive pharmaceutical sector.
Canadian companies are ready to play this role. The
system must allow them to do so.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
May 5, 2026
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Study on Canada’s
Pharmaceutical Sovereignty

Executive Summary
The Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management (CAPDM), now
known as Vital - Canada’s Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Alliance, represents the
companies responsible for delivering the vast majority of medicines across Canada.
From this system-wide vantage point, pharmaceutical distributors have a unique
understanding of how medicines move from global supply to patient care, and how
policy decisions impact access.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is an important policy objective, often framed in terms
of domestic manufacturing and reducing reliance on international suppliers. While
these are important considerations, ensuring that medicines reach patients reliably
requires a broader system perspective.
Ultimately, pharmaceutical sovereignty is determined by whether medicines
reach patients reliably, safely, and on time.
Canada already has a critical national asset that supports this objective: a highly
regulated, nationally integrated pharmaceutical distribution system that ensures
physical access to medicines across the country every day. Distribution is the
system that connects supply to patients.
Distributors operate at the centre of the supply chain, connecting hundreds of
manufacturers to over 12,000 points of dispensing. From this position, they see how
policy decisions—on pricing, procurement, and manufacturing—directly affect
access to medicines for Canadians.
Canada will continue to rely on global supply chains for a significant share of its
medicines. The policy objective should therefore be to ensure that this supply can
be reliably accessed and delivered to patients.
Vital recommends that the Committee:
1. Recognize pharmaceutical distribution as critical health system
infrastructure and ensure that physical access is considered in all relevant
policy decisions.
2. Ensure that pricing and procurement policies support the sustainability of
supply and distribution, especially for rural and remote communities that are
the costliest to serve.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
Ensure that pricing and procurement policies support the sustainability of
supply and distribution, especially for rural and remote communities that are
the costliest to serve.

3. Enable a diverse and resilient supplier base by reducing barriers to entry and
avoiding restrictive procurement approaches that limit market participation.
4. Take a targeted approach to domestic manufacturing that strengthens
sovereignty while preserving access to global sources of supply.
Introduction
Vital represents Canada’s pharmaceutical distributors, who deliver the vast majority
of medicines across the country to community pharmacies, hospitals, and other
points of care.
Distributors operate within a highly regulated system and serve Canadians in every
province and territory—from major urban centres to remote communities—across a
geographically vast and complex landscape.
They ensure medicines are physically accessible to patients across Canada, when
and where they are needed. Distributors make it possible for the majority of
Canadians to have access to out-of-stock or special-order medications at their
local pharmacy or hospital on a next-day basis.
From their position within the supply chain, distributors maintain a national,
system-wide perspective that provides insight into pressures, vulnerabilities, and
opportunities across both domestic and global supply networks.
The Role of Distributors in Ensuring Access
Pharmaceutical distributors ensure physical access to medicines across Canada.
Practically, they:
•
Coordinate the movement of thousands of products across therapeutic
categories;
•
Connect hundreds of manufacturers with over 12,000 points of dispensing;
•
Maintain buffer inventory to absorb disruptions and mitigate shortages
before patients are impacted; and
•
Deliver medicines daily to communities across the country, including rural
and remote areas.
This function is essential in a country as geographically large, sparsely populated,
and diverse as Canada.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
This function is essential in a country as geographically large, sparsely populated,
and diverse as Canada.

Distributors also operate within a highly regulated system, ensuring that
medicines—including narcotics and controlled substances—are handled, stored,
and delivered in compliance with all federal and provincial requirements.
Beyond logistics, distributors provide a system-wide view of supply. Managing a
broad portfolio of medicines allows them to identify emerging pressures and
vulnerabilities across therapeutic categories, including areas where supply is
concentrated among a limited number of manufacturers.
System Pressures and Vulnerabilities
1. Distribution Sustainability
Canada’s pharmaceutical distributors are operating under sustained economic
pressure.
Distribution compensation is derived from the price of medicines, which are shaped
by public policy and reimbursement frameworks. Over the past two decades,
generic drug prices have declined by more than 70%.
At the same time, the structure of the industry has contracted. The number of
distributors has declined from 19 to 17, and distribution centres from approximately
50 to 30 over the past decade, increasing the distances medicines must travel to
reach patients.
The cost of operating has increased due to:
•
Expanding regulatory compliance and reporting requirements;
•
Labour and workforce pressures;
•
Transportation costs, including rising fuel and logistics costs across a
geographically vast country; and
•
Expanding cold chain and specialized handling requirements for
temperature-sensitive medicines.
These cold chain requirements, particularly for biologics and vaccines, require
significant investment in infrastructure, monitoring, and quality assurance, and now
represent a growing share of operating costs.
However, the cost and complexity of delivering medicines across Canada have not
decreased accordingly.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
However, the cost and complexity of delivering medicines across Canada have not
decreased accordingly.

For example, the distribution compensation associated with a bottle of atorvastatin
(for treating high cholesterol) is less than the price of a postage stamp, regardless
of whether it is delivered to a major urban centre or a remote northern community.
This creates a structural imbalance in which distribution compensation is declining
while costs are increasing, placing ongoing pressure on the sustainability of
distribution operations, particularly in rural and remote areas where service is most
resource intensive.
2. Supplier Concentration and Supply Risk
From a portfolio perspective, a growing number of medicines in Canada are
supplied by only one or two manufacturers. This concentration increases
vulnerability to supply disruption.
Recent shortages, including those affecting pediatric medications, demonstrate
that even where some domestic manufacturing exists, sudden increases in demand
or production disruptions can overwhelm available supply.
Resilience depends not only on where medicines are produced, but on the
availability of multiple suppliers and the system’s ability to respond dynamically
when disruptions occur.
3. Restrictive Procurement Approaches
Certain policy approaches can unintentionally weaken the resilience of the
pharmaceutical system by limiting the number of suppliers in the market.
Restrictive procurement approaches, including those that favour domestic sourcing
or otherwise narrow supplier eligibility, are often intended to strengthen Canadian
capacity. However, in practice, they can discourage participation in the Canadian
market, particularly among international manufacturers.
Over the past two decades, hospital procurement in Canada has become highly
concentrated. Virtually all hospitals are now represented by one of three Group
Purchasing Organizations (GPOs): HealthPro Canada, Mohawk Medbuy Corporation,
and Quebec’s Centre d'acquisitions gouvernementales (CAG). Outside of Quebec,
where procurement is centralized through CAG, most provinces are effectively
served by one or two GPOs, creating monopsony purchasing structures in the
majority of jurisdictions.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
Outside of Quebec,
where procurement is centralized through CAG, most provinces are effectively
served by one or two GPOs, creating monopsony purchasing structures in the
majority of jurisdictions.

In this environment, if a manufacturer is unsuccessful in securing a contract for
hospital-specific medicines, such as saline solutions, there are often no alternative
buyers. This can lead manufacturers to withdraw from the market or maintain
dormant product listings, reducing the number of active suppliers. The result is
increased supply concentration and a higher risk of shortages for essential hospital
medicines.
Canada relies on global supply for approximately 70% of its medicines and
represents a relatively small share of global demand. Maintaining access to a broad
and competitive supplier base is therefore essential. Policies that reduce the
number of suppliers, including a “Buy Canadian” policy, can increase the risk of
shortages by concentrating supply among fewer manufacturers.
Experience has shown that systems with limited supplier diversity are more
vulnerable to disruption when a single manufacturer encounters production
challenges or when demand surges unexpectedly. A more resilient approach is to
support supplier diversity and enable new sources of supply, both domestic and
international, to enter the market quickly when needed.
Implications for Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
Pharmaceutical sovereignty cannot be achieved through manufacturing policy
alone. Even with increased domestic production, Canada will continue to rely on
global supply chains for a significant portion of its medicines.
A resilient and sovereign system must therefore:
•
Support a diverse supplier base;
•
Enable flexibility in responding to disruptions; and
•
Ensure that medicines can be delivered efficiently and reliably across the
country.
Distribution connects supply to patients. Recognizing and strengthening this
system is essential to achieving the Committee’s objectives.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
Recognizing and strengthening this
system is essential to achieving the Committee’s objectives.

Recommendations
Vital recommends that the Committee:
1. Recognize Distribution as Critical Health System Infrastructure
Formally recognize pharmaceutical distribution as critical health system
infrastructure, comparable to other essential national systems such as energy and
transportation.
Distributors operate a continuous, nationwide network that ensures medicines are
delivered safely and reliably to patients across Canada, including in rural and
remote communities.
This role becomes even more critical during emergencies. In situations such as
wildfires, floods, and other disruptions, distributors maintain the flow of essential
medicines by adapting delivery routes, deploying alternative logistics (e.g., air
freight), and ensuring continuity of supply to affected communities.
As seen during recent natural disasters and the COVID-19 pandemic,
pharmaceutical distribution is a key component of Canada’s emergency response
capacity. The system must therefore be recognized and supported accordingly.
All policy decisions, including those related to pricing, procurement, and
manufacturing, should be evaluated based on their impact on this infrastructure
and its ability to ensure patient access.
2. Ensure Pricing and Procurement Policies Support Access
Ensure that pricing and procurement policies do not undermine the sustainability of
supply and distribution.
Policies should reflect the realities of delivering medicines across Canada, including
the rising costs of regulatory compliance, labour, transportation, and specialized
handling requirements for cold chain therapies.
They should also be designed to avoid unintended consequences that weaken
service levels or reduce the system’s ability to ensure consistent access,
particularly in rural and remote communities.

org: Canadian Association for Pharmacy Distribution Management
text:
They should also be designed to avoid unintended consequences that weaken
service levels or reduce the system’s ability to ensure consistent access,
particularly in rural and remote communities.

3. Enable a Diverse and Resilient Supplier Base
Promote supplier diversity by reducing regulatory and administrative barriers to
entry and avoiding procurement approaches that limit the number of suppliers.
Maintaining a broad supplier base is essential in a small, import-reliant market such
as Canada, where reduced participation can quickly lead to supply concentration.
Policies should enable new sources of supply, both domestic and international, to
enter the market quickly when needed, including through timely and efficient
pathways that support rapid access during shortages.
This flexibility strengthens resilience and reduces the risk of supply disruptions
affecting patients.
4. Take a Targeted Approach to Domestic Manufacturing
Focus domestic manufacturing efforts on a targeted list of critical medicines where
supply disruptions pose the greatest risk to patient health.
Existing tools, such as Health Canada’s Critical and Vulnerable Drugs List, can serve
as a useful starting point to identify priority areas for action.
Given Canada’s ongoing reliance on global supply, these efforts should
complement, rather than displace, access to international sources of supply.
A targeted and pragmatic approach will strengthen resilience while preserving the
flexibility needed to respond to changing supply conditions.
Conclusion
Canada has a strong foundation on which to build pharmaceutical sovereignty.
A highly regulated and nationally integrated distribution system already ensures
that medicines reach patients across the country every day.
Strengthening this system, alongside targeted and pragmatic manufacturing
policies, will improve resilience and ensure that Canadians can continue to access
the medicines they need.

Vital remains committed to working collaboratively with government and
stakeholders to support these objectives and would welcome the opportunity to
contribute further to the Committee’s work.

Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty

National pharmaceutical sovereignty ensures that Canadians have reliable access to highquality medicines and treatments when they need them. This means having a strong
domestic manufacturing capacity and integration into key supply chains. Medicines and the
systems that produce them sit at the intersection of public health, economic growth and
national security. When a country’s pharmaceutical industry is dependent on foreign-owned
firms and imported inputs, it may not reflect domestic priorities, leaving the country
vulnerable to market forces and supply chain disruptions.

Canada relies heavily on global supply chains for access to pharmaceuticals: almost all
active pharmaceutical ingredients used in Canada are imported, with a majority from China
and India, creating a concentration risk in critical inputs.i Canada also faces persistent and
significant drug shortages. A stable supply is necessary to keep costs down, avoid expensive
solutions to sudden shocks or emergencies and maintain access for all Canadians. The
government should seek to bolster Canada’s biopharma capacity and self-suIiciency
through targeted policy action and closer collaboration with industry.

Other countries already recognize domestic drug manufacturing as a core component of
national security. The United States’ Defence Production Act makes explicit that America
views building biopharmaceutical resilience as an important national security priority.
Similarly, the European Union’s Critical Medicines Act seeks to modernize and expand its
domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity. Canada must act to support its own
pharmaceutical and biomanufacturing sectors to ensure resiliency.

There are genera)onal consequences to handing off innova)on a5er the discovery phase for
others to commercialize. The discovery of insulin in Canada over 100 years ago led to the crea)on
of Novo Nordisk. At its peak, it reached a market capitaliza)on exceeding the GDP of its home
country, Denmark.

At its peak, it reached a market capitaliza)on exceeding the GDP of its home
country, Denmark.

Canada has struggled to translate its success in research and its highly educated workforce
into commercialized innovation and globally competitive firms. Canada accounts for just 6
of the world’s top 478 pharmaceutical and biotechnology R&D performers (1.3%).ii Our
current model relies on assumptions that no longer hold. We depend heavily on global
supply chains while seeking resilience, and we invest in early-stage research without
consistently retaining the value it creates. We attract capital and firms into Canada but do
not ensure that intellectual property, production capacity or long-term economic benefits
remain anchored here. This creates a structural pattern where Canadian innovation is
developed domestically but scaled and commercialized elsewhere.

Canada has relatively strong inventive capabilities in the life science and biopharmaceutical
sectors, but Canada’s performance has been slipping. In 2021 biotechnology and
pharmaceutical firms in the US and the rest of the world spent considerably more on R&D

than their counterparts in Canada: for every US$1,000 of GDP, US firms spent US$5.90 on
R&D, while Canadian firms spent only US$0.49.iii

Canada needs a system and regulatory frameworks which support firm scaling. In a 21stcentury economy, economic prosperity, innovation and security are now deeply intertwined
and countries that succeed are those that create and control intellectual property. The
Council of Canadian Innovators’ recent policy report, Care at Scale, demonstrates that
public systems including healthcare, actively shape markets and determine where value
occurs and firms scale.

On behalf of CCI’s membership of over 180 of Canada’s fastest-growing companies, we
present the following recommendations:
1. Build and scale Canadian pharmaceutical and biotech firms using public
procurement as a strategic lever
2. Ensure public investment translates into domestic economic value by retaining
and commercializing Canadian intellectual property
3. Improve the speed, predictability and global competitiveness of Canada’s
healthcare system by modernizing regulatory frameworks
4. Improve resilience and anchor production in Canada by strengthening domestic
manufacturing capacity
5. Ensure Canadian firms can expand domestically and prevent relocation and
early exits by unlocking capital for growth and scale

Recommendations

Build and scale Canadian pharmaceutical and biotech firms using public procurement
as a strategic lever

Build and scale Canadian pharmaceutical and biotech firms using public procurement
as a strategic lever

Canada’s healthcare system represents one of its largest areas of public spending. In 2024,
Canada spent $372 billion on healthcare; these costs were projected to rise to $399 billion
in 2025 – over 12% of Canada’s GDP. This is a substantial amount of money that can be
strategically deployed to further Canada’s healthcare and biopharmaceutical sovereignty.
Procurement decisions shape market outcomes: they determine which firms grow, which
technologies are adopted and where intellectual property and economic value ultimately
reside. The government should seek to leverage procurement to support important national
priorities, including biopharmaceutical sovereignty.

The federal government should adopt procurement criteria that is able to account for
domestic manufacturing, Canadian-controlled intellectual property and integration with
local supply chains. Through doing so, the government can anchor demand for Canadiandeveloped products. In areas like veterans’ health services and the Canadian Armed Forces,

where the federal government has direct oversight, they can implement such policies
directly. For healthcare spending under the purview of the provinces and territories, the
government should encourage a harmonized “Buy Canadian” policy.

Canada’s procurement system should also employ clear and predictable pathways from
pilot projects to scaled procurement contracts, allowing successful innovations to move
beyond early testing. Many innovators in the biopharma and healthcare space report
experiencing the “valley of death” – the gap between demonstrating a prototype and
technology and securing a contract for its widespread implementation and adoption.

Ensure public investment translates into domestic economic value by retaining and
commercializing Canadian intellectual property

Canada produces high-quality research and innovation but struggles to retain and
commercialize the resulting intellectual property. From 2001 to 2020 Canada filed 39,400
patents in the biopharmaceutical space. Based on its scientific publication output however,
Canada would have been expected to file roughly 90,900 patents, highlighting a significant
commercialization gap.iv As the share of Canadian-invented patents assigned to foreign
firms continues to rise, there needs to be a concerted whole-of-government eIort to lessen
this gap.

Based on its scientific publication output however,
Canada would have been expected to file roughly 90,900 patents, highlighting a significant
commercialization gap.iv As the share of Canadian-invented patents assigned to foreign
firms continues to rise, there needs to be a concerted whole-of-government eIort to lessen
this gap.

The federal government should align research funding with commercialization outcomes by
introducing incentives for domestic licensing and development. More emphasis must be
placed on universities and the role of technology transfer oIices to ensure the research
conducted at public universities remains and generates value in Canada. The current
patchwork of policies and lack of harmonization causes issues for firms looking to work with
industry and for academics looking to spin-oI or commercialize their research. The
consequences of this are clear: Canadian universities are less likely to commercialize
research than their US counterparts. Government should consider employing royaltymatching programs to encourage the domestic commercialization of research generated in
academic institutions.

The government should also consider creating a federal patent or “innovation” box – a tax
incentive policy tool allowing companies to apply a reduced rate to profits linked to
intellectual property assets – to encourage companies, including in the biopharmaceutical
space, to commercialize their IP in Canada.

Improve the speed, predictability and global competitiveness of Canada’s biopharma
sector by modernizing regulatory frameworks

Canadian pharmaceutical manufacturers face significant regulatory burden, especially
relative to comparable markets. Between 2002 and 2016, Canada’s median drug approval
time was 364 days, compared to 371 for the European Medicines Agency and 304 days for

the FDA; concerning given both of those markets have roughly ten times Canada’s patient
population.v The complexity and length of Health Canada’s approval process is especially
problematic given the small size of the national market; firms may decide that operating in
the market is too onerous and not worth the associated costs.

the FDA; concerning given both of those markets have roughly ten times Canada’s patient
population.v The complexity and length of Health Canada’s approval process is especially
problematic given the small size of the national market; firms may decide that operating in
the market is too onerous and not worth the associated costs.

Ongoing eIorts to reduce red tape, including using the decisions and documents produced
by trusted foreign regulatory authorities in assessing drug submissions and the proposed
modernized regulatory framework for clinical trials, are positive first steps. The government
should consider further changes to the clinical trial process to ensure Canada remains an
attractive jurisdiction for biopharma and life science research and firms. For all clinical
trials, Health Canada requires a 30-day regulatory review of a Clinical Trial Application (CTA)
in addition to Research Ethics Board (REB) approval; this is more onerous than comparable
jurisdictions like Australia. In Australia, Phase 1 and 2 clinical trials of unapproved medicines
require only a Human Research Ethics Committee approval, who conduct the primary
scientific and ethical review. The trial is then notified to Australia’s Therapeutic Goods
Administration rather than undergoing a separate scientific assessment. Canada should
consider adopting a similar notification scheme to make Canada a more attractive
jurisdiction for early-phase studies.

Improve resilience and anchor production in Canada by strengthening domestic
manufacturing capacity

Domestic biopharmaceutical manufacturing capacity cannot be created quickly in
response to a crisis; it must be maintained through sustained investment and predictable
policy signals. The government should introduce targeted investment incentives to support
the modernization and expansion of biopharmaceutical manufacturing in Canada. The
European Union’s Critical Medicines Act lays out a clear plan and associated tax incentives
and financial support to improve capacity.vi Similarly, the United States has seen an inflow
of investment from pharmaceutical companies looking to reshore in America, and capacity
building has been explicitly made a government priority.

The government should support industrial activity in the pharmaceutical space by taking
equivalent measures and providing incentives for firms to keep and expand production here
including tax credits for technology upgrade, facility expansion and product transfers.
Strengthening manufacturing capacity will improve supply resilience while supporting highvalue economic activity within Canada.

Ensure Canadian firms can expand domestically and prevent relocation and early exits
by unlocking capital for growth and scale

Access to capital remains a critical constraint for Canadian pharmaceutical and biotech
firms, particularly at the growth stage. This contributes to a pattern of relocation, where firms
move to countries with deeper capital markets to scale, meaning a significant exodus of

This contributes to a pattern of relocation, where firms
move to countries with deeper capital markets to scale, meaning a significant exodus of

value from Canada. Investment programs and government venture capital – including
through the BCD’s biotech fund – should seek to correct this by crowding in private
investment and encouraging patient capital deployment. Many existing tax policies and
regional development programs are designed primarily for small and medium-sized
enterprises, rather than firms in scaling and growth stages. If the federal government is
seeking to bolster Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty, it needs to ensure domestic
biopharma companies can grow at home and provide support that will anchor them and their
IP in Canada.

Innovative Medicines Canada Brief on “Canada’s Pharmaceutical
Sovereignty” – Submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Introduction
Innovative Medicines Canada (IMC) respectfully submits the following brief to the
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health regarding its study on “Canada’s
Pharmaceutical Sovereignty.”
This study comes at a pivotal moment for Canada’s life sciences sector, national
security, and Canadian patients. The global pharmaceutical landscape is changing
rapidly. The introduction of the most-favoured nation (MFN) drug pricing policy in
the U.S., which aims to lower American prices and shift a greater share of
innovation costs onto countries like Canada, has triggered a global chain reaction
that is intensifying competition and influencing which countries get innovative
medicines first. This move comes alongside President Trump’s recent executive
order to impose a 100 per cent tariff on imported patented medicines and active
ingredients.
For Canada, this exposes a critical vulnerability: we have long benefited from U.S.-
funded pharmaceutical innovation, while keeping our domestic drug prices low,
ultimately limiting our availability of innovative medicines. Addressing this
vulnerability starts with the fundamental premise that pharmaceutical sovereignty
cannot happen in a vacuum. Any credible strategy must balance increased domestic
capacity with the inherently global and interconnected nature of supply chains for
innovative medicines.
Canada has the foundation to get this right. Our innovative pharmaceutical industry
is an economic engine that contributes $18.4 billion in economic impact, invests
$3.2 billion in research and development, and supports over 110,000 high-value
jobs. Underpinning this economic footprint are world-class researchers and
academic institutions, and rigorous drug safety and efficacy standards that have
made Canada a G7 leader in clinical trials. But market conditions must be right for
these advantages to translate into concrete outcomes.
Quebec's experience is an instructive example. In the 1990s, the province was a
hub for drug research and development, partly because of BAP-15, a
pharmaceutical policy designed to protect the price of patented drugs. It enabled
companies like Merck-Frosst and AstraZeneca to bring their research and
development sites to Canada, where they discovered and developed life-changing
therapies for asthma, blood pressure, and HIV. But when the government abolished
BAP-15 in 2013, many companies left and took their investments with them.

MFN pricing did not create Canada's challenges; it exposed them. Net price
compression, long access timelines, limited predictability in a globally
interconnected market—these are not new issues. They have always made it harder

What has changed is the urgency. The global drug policy shifts we are seeing are

competitive—we will remain exposed to forces beyond our control.
