Executive Summary
The goal of strengthening Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty is widely shared, and
strengthening domestic supply and improving patient access is critical to realize this goal. But
successful pharmaceutical sovereignty requires a balanced, whole-system approach that
includes all aspects of the innovation and pharmaceutical supply sectors. A narrow policy lens
that favours domestic biomanufacturing in isolation must carefully consider downstream
implications specifically on Canadians; those for whom these policies are being considered.
Biomanufacturing is deeply connected with global supply chains, drawing on a complex, globally
distributed network of innovators and suppliers, each providing critical components. Any policy
that solely prioritizes domestic biomanufacturing, without an equal investment in other aspects
of the pharmaceutical supply chain and innovation, can reduce competitive pressure, slow
development, constrain supply and ultimately exacerbate the current risk of increased drug
shortages as well as increasing costs and barriers to patient access.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is often discussed in terms of manufacturing capacity and upstream
supply, but it must ultimately be measured by whether medicines reliably reach patients. True
sovereignty is realized at the point of care. While strengthening domestic production and
diversifying supply sources are important objectives, they are insufficient on their own if
medicines cannot be accessed, substituted, or sustained when the system experiences
disruption.
Community pharmacies represent the last mile of Canada’s pharmaceutical system and are
where fragility can impact health care. Every day, pharmacies manage shortages in real time,
work with prescribers to adjust therapies, protect access for vulnerable patients, and stabilize
care amid global uncertainty. For this reason, pharmacies should be recognized as critical
health care infrastructure and incorporated early into pharmaceutical policy, supply chain
planning, and system level response strategies. A whole system approach to pharmaceutical
sovereignty must therefore include not only how medicines are made, but how they are
delivered, maintained, and accessed by Canadians when it matters most.
Considerations: Why Pharmaceutical Sovereignty Requires a
Balanced, Whole-System Approach

Considerations: Why Pharmaceutical Sovereignty Requires a
Balanced, Whole-System Approach

1. Pharmaceutical supply chains are globally intertwined
Pharmaceutical manufacturing depends on access to Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs),
reagents, bioprocessing materials, and specialized equipment sourced worldwide. These inputs
are produced by a diverse and highly specialized network of global suppliers, each contributing
essential components that enable safe, consistent, and scalable drug production. Modern
biomanufacturing is therefore not a self‑contained process; it is built on a foundation of global
interdependence, where expertise, raw materials, and technologies flow across borders.
Because no single country can produce the full range of inputs required for today’s
pharmaceutical and biologics manufacturing, every nation, including Canada, relies on
international partners to maintain a stable and resilient supply chain. This interconnected
system has enabled decades of innovation, efficiency, and access to high‑quality medicines.

This interconnected
system has enabled decades of innovation, efficiency, and access to high‑quality medicines.

This global interdependency means that policy approaches must recognize the global nature of
pharmaceutical production to avoid creating bottlenecks or vulnerabilities by narrowing sourcing
or manufacturing options.
When global disruptions occur, their effects are often felt most acutely at the pharmacy counter,
where shortages or delays become visible to patients and providers. This is where upstream
fragility becomes a real barrier to care.
2. Domestic capacity is uneven and insufficient
Canada’s domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity remains uneven, and our country
does not yet have the scale, infrastructure, or specialized capabilities required to meet national
demand on its own. Essential inputs including APIs, intermediates, reagents, and specialized
equipment are sourced from a wide range of international suppliers because they are not
produced in sufficient quantity or variety within Canada.
At the same time, Canada continues to face persistent drug shortages driven by global
disruptions. A policy approach focused solely on domestic production, without parallel attention
to broader structural factors, may not fully address the root causes of shortages. When
shortages or production delays occur, or when domestic capacity cannot meet demand, the
resulting medication gaps are managed by pharmacies, which must source alternatives, adjust
therapies, and support patients through uncertainty.
Ensuring a resilient and reliable drug supply therefore requires policies that strengthen domestic
capacity while preserving open, diversified, and globally connected supply channels.
3. Access and affordability become significant barriers
An approach that focuses solely on domestic biomanufacturing risks constraining the overall
supply of medicines available in Canada by limiting access to globally sourced products and
reducing the diversity of suppliers. As demand for medicines, particularly specialized and high
cost therapies, continues to rise, a more restricted supply base may place upward pressure on
prices.
Higher production costs associated with domestic manufacturing, combined with reduced
competition, can further increase overall system costs. In response, public payers and
governments may need to manage expenditures through tighter formulary decisions, delayed
reimbursement for new therapies, or increased cost-sharing. Patients may face higher
out‑of‑pocket costs, reduced formulary options, or delays in accessing new and necessary
therapies.
Pharmacies are where these affordability and access pressures become visible, as patients
encounter stockouts, substitutions, or higher costs at the point of dispensing. As the final point
in the pharmaceutical supply chain, pharmacies play a critical role in translating supply into
actual patient access by managing disruptions, coordinating alternatives, and maintaining
continuity of care when upstream pressures arise. In this way they function as a stabilizing
component of the system, ensuring that medicines ultimately reach patients in a safe, timely,
and reliable manner.

In this way they function as a stabilizing
component of the system, ensuring that medicines ultimately reach patients in a safe, timely,
and reliable manner.

Ensuring affordability and timely access requires a policy framework that promotes competition,
sustains multiple supply sources, maintains strong global market connections, and guarantees
that pharmacies can reliably access the medicines they are expected to dispense. Recognizing
the role of pharmacy within the supply chain is essential to ensure that efforts to strengthen
pharmaceutical sovereignty result not only in available supply, but in consistent and dependable
access for patients.
Recommendations

1. Broaden Canada’s Biomanufacturing and Life Sciences Strategy
Rather than prioritizing domestic production in isolation, Canada may wish to consider a
whole‑of‑system approach that strengthens capacity across the innovation ecosystem while
preserving access to global inputs, technologies, and innovation. These elements are essential
to a resilient and competitive pharmaceutical supply chain and a thriving life sciences sector.
This means building domestic strength without disconnecting from the global networks that
supply critical materials, expertise, and market opportunities, including:

•
Research and Development (R&D) support. Targeted investments can accelerate
innovation, protect intellectual property, and attract private sector partnerships to reduce
risks in early-stage development. Strengthening R&D ultimately benefits patients by
expanding the pipeline of new life-saving therapies and ensuring Canada remains
competitive.

•
Incentives to scale production and market innovation. Financial and regulatory
incentives including streamlined clinical trial processes, modernized drug approval
pathways, and efficient health technology assessments can help bring new products to
market more quickly and ensure a broader range of therapies are available in Canada. For
pharmacies and patients, this translates into more stable supply, fewer disruptions, and
improved access to innovative treatments.
2. Modernize regulatory flexibility and strengthen the pharmacy workforce
A resilient pharmaceutical system depends on pharmacies’ ability to maintain continuity of care
during disruptions. Pharmacy professionals already spend an estimated 20% of their time
managing drug shortages by coordinating with prescribers, sourcing alternatives, compounding
therapies, and, in some jurisdictions, independently prescribing therapeutic substitutions. This
essential work is largely unfunded, strains workforce capacity, and is hindered by inconsistent
regulations that limit pharmacists’ ability to fully apply their expertise across Canada.

This
essential work is largely unfunded, strains workforce capacity, and is hindered by inconsistent
regulations that limit pharmacists’ ability to fully apply their expertise across Canada.

When supply becomes unstable, the burden shifts immediately to the pharmacy counter.
Pharmacy teams are expected to manage patient expectations, prevent gaps in therapy, and
absorb operational pressures without the staffing capacity or regulatory flexibility required to
respond effectively. These constraints create delays, increase strain on other parts of the health
system, and undermine patient confidence in access to care.

To strengthen Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty, federal policymakers should prioritize
modernizing regulations to enable a more flexible, nimble, and fully utilized pharmacy

workforce. This includes addressing workforce capacity through targeted support for staffing,
training, and retention, while ensuring pharmacists can act efficiently during disruptions.

Two key federal actions would advance this goal. First, champion consistent, pan-Canadian
authority for pharmacists to therapeutically substitute medications, ensuring patients maintain
timely access to appropriate therapies even during shortages. Second, permanently recognize
pharmacists as practitioners under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, replacing the
current patchwork of time-limited exemptions. This would reduce regulatory burden, support
more consistent implementation across provinces, and enable pharmacists to better manage
opioid and other controlled substance prescriptions in both routine and shortage scenarios.

Together, these measures would reduce delays, prevent avoidable visits to emergency
departments and clinics, and ensure continuity of care when supply is unstable. Strengthening
workforce capacity alongside modernizing regulatory frameworks will allow pharmacies to
respond effectively at the point of care; where pharmaceutical sovereignty is ultimately realized.
3. Improve supply‑chain visibility, traceability, and data infrastructure including at
the pharmacy level

A resilient pharmaceutical system requires the ability to detect and respond to emerging
shortages early, yet today, Canada lacks the visibility needed to act before disruptions reach
patients. Pharmacies are critical healthcare infrastructure within Canada’s pharmaceutical
supply chain and are often the first point in the system to see signs of stress: sudden spikes in
demand, unexpected backorders, and early indications that supply is tightening. Despite this
front-line role, pharmacy insight is rarely incorporated early in pharmaceutical policy, pricing, or
supply-chain planning. Currently real￼time intelligence is not systematically captured or
integrated into national monitoring systems, leaving policymakers without the full picture of
where pressures are building.

Currently real￼time intelligence is not systematically captured or
integrated into national monitoring systems, leaving policymakers without the full picture of
where pressures are building.

To address this gap, Canada must strengthen supply‑chain visibility, traceability, and data
infrastructure including at the pharmacy level. This means creating systems that connect
manufacturers, distributors, regulators, and pharmacies through real‑time inventory monitoring,
early‑warning mechanisms, and standardized reporting. It also requires better traceability
across the supply chain so Canada can see where medicines are, how long they remain at each
stage, and where bottlenecks occur. These insights help distinguish whether a shortage stems
from manufacturing, distribution, or demand, enabling more targeted and timely interventions.

Recognizing pharmacies as critical supply￼chain infrastructure ensures that the point of care
where shortages are first felt is included in national planning, forecasting, and response
strategies. With better visibility and traceability, Canada can identify shortages earlier,
coordinate responses more effectively, and reduce the impact on patients.
4. Deepen global partnerships through the Trade Diversification Strategy
Canada’s long‑term competitiveness depends on deepening its global economic relationships,
rather than narrowing them. For a country that relies on international sources for the majority of

its APIs, intermediates, and finished drug products, maintaining strong global partnerships is
essential to ensuring a stable and predictable supply of medicines.
Expanding partnerships with trusted allies and pursuing opportunities in new and emerging life
sciences markets strengthens supply‑chain resilience by diversifying sources of critical inputs
and reducing exposure to regional disruptions. It also enhances market access for Canadian
biopharmaceutical firms, enabling them to scale, innovate, and contribute more fully to
Canada’s economic growth.
A globally connected strategy is essential to preventing and mitigating drug shortages,
maintaining affordability, and ensuring Canadians continue to benefit from the full range of
high‑quality pharmaceutical products available worldwide. For Canadians, this means more
reliable inventory, fewer disruptions, and the ability to consistently access the medicines they
need.
Summary of Recommendations

Summary of Recommendations

Neighbourhood Pharmacies encourages the Committee to consider a balanced, whole-system
approach to pharmaceutical sovereignty that:
•
Strengthens capacity across the full innovation and life sciences ecosystem.
•
Recognizes pharmacies as critical infrastructure in the pharmaceutical supply chain and
ensures pharmacies have the staffing and regulatory tools needed to respond quickly to
supply disruptions and maintain continuity of care.
•
Builds real-time, connected systems and infrastructure that includes the pharmacy-level for
increased visibility to detect shortages earlier and coordinate faster interventions.
•
Deepens global partnerships to diversify supply, maintain access to essential inputs, and
support stable, affordable access to medicines for Canadians.
Conclusion
Canada’s pursuit of pharmaceutical sovereignty is well served by a balanced, whole‑system
approach that strengthens domestic capacity while maintaining access to global inputs,
technologies, and markets. A strategy that reinforces domestic strengths while remaining
connected to global supply chains can enhance resilience, support affordability, and help
ensure Canadians continue to have access to the medicines they rely on.
But sovereignty is only achieved when medicines reach the point of care. Pharmacies
experience the consequences of drug shortages and supply disruptions every day, and their
ability to maintain continuity of care is directly shaped by upstream decisions about
manufacturing, sourcing, and regulatory policy. As the final point of distribution and care,
community pharmacies are uniquely positioned to see how supply‑chain fragility affects
patients, caregivers, and providers and to provide early warning signals when pressures begin
to build.
Strengthening the full pharmaceutical ecosystem from research and manufacturing to
distribution and dispensing therefore requires ensuring that pharmacies have the workforce

capacity, regulatory flexibility, and real‑time visibility needed to respond effectively to shortages.
Embedding pharmacy‑level insight and capability into national planning, forecasting, and
shortage‑response strategies is essential to building a system that is reliable, sustainable, and
responsive to patient needs.
Neighbourhood Pharmacies appreciates the Committee’s attention to this issue and welcomes
the opportunity to contribute to this important study. We stand ready to support further analysis,
share operational insights from the front lines, and work with federal partners to advance a
modern, resilient pharmaceutical supply chain that delivers for Canadians.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Streamline Canada’s Drug Approval and Reimbursement System
Canada’s drug review and reimbursement system remains one of the most fragmented and
sequential in the OECD. After receiving regulatory approval from Health Canada, new therapies
must move through separate assessments by Canada’s Drug Agency and Quebec’s INESSS,
followed by negotiations through the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance and individual
provincial or territorial funding decisions. On average this process takes over two years.4 Each
stage operates independently, and each often requires companies to re‑submit the same
information in different formats. This structure creates avoidable delays and makes it difficult
to predict when a therapy will reach patients.
The effects of this fragmented structure also extend beyond public drug plans. Two‑thirds of
Canadians obtain funded access through employer‑sponsored insurance, which is typically
faster but is now increasingly shaped by the public system’s sequential evaluation, negotiation,
and funding steps.
Canada’s delays also affect our position in global supply planning. When manufacturing capacity
is limited, companies must allocate product to markets where timelines and processes are
predictable. Canada’s current structure makes that planning more challenging than in
jurisdictions where regulatory, HTA, and pricing steps are better aligned.
A more coordinated system would reduce duplication and improve predictability. Allowing
regulatory review, HTA, and pricing discussions to proceed in parallel – rather than waiting for
one step to finish before another begins – would shorten the overall pathway without changing
the standards used to evaluate safety or effectiveness.
There are already examples within Canada that show what better alignment can achieve.
Ontario’s FAST (Funding Accelerated for Specific Treatments) pilot program5 accelerates public
funding for select high‑priority cancer drugs by enabling coverage to begin after a positive
recommendation from Canada’s Drug Agency, rather than waiting for price negotiations to
conclude. FAST does not change evaluation criteria; it simply aligns decision‑makers earlier so
that reimbursement can begin sooner.
Federal drug plans are well positioned to adopt a similar approach, enabling coverage to start
more quickly while negotiations continue in parallel. Over time, these practices could be scaled
across jurisdictions to create a more consistent, coordinated national approach to timely access.

2. Position Canada as a Stronger Launch Market by Better Valuing Innovation
Canada’s ability to secure dependable access to new medicines is closely linked to how
therapies are evaluated and funded after regulatory approval. The speed and clarity of health
technology assessments, pricing discussions, and reimbursement decisions shape how
predictable the Canadian environment appears to global companies. When these steps take
longer than in comparable jurisdictions, or when investment in innovative medicines remains
relatively limited, Canada can be viewed as a more challenging market in which to introduce
new products. That perception influences where companies research new therapies, when
companies file regulatory submissions, and how they sequence global launches.
These pressures are intensifying as international pricing policies evolve. The U.S. MFN initiative
has increased scrutiny on how countries set reimbursement levels, since decisions in smaller
markets can have implications for pricing in larger ones. In this context, Canada’s comparatively
modest spending on new therapies – about 0.32% of GDP, compared to roughly 0.78% in the
United States6 – can reinforce the view that Canada is a lower‑priority launch market. This has
direct implications for pharmaceutical sovereignty: markets perceived as less predictable or
slower to adopt innovation often face later access and less secure supply.
Strengthening how Canada values innovation would help address these challenges. A more
predictable, evidence‑driven approach that reflects long‑term patient outcomes and
system‑level benefits would give companies greater confidence when planning submissions. To
remain competitive with jurisdictions modernizing their own frameworks, Canada will also need
to update elements of its pricing and assessment architecture. This includes giving Canada’s
Drug Agency a clearer mandate to evaluate the full benefits of new medicines, ensuring that
pCPA negotiations balance affordability with timely access, and refining federal pricing policies
to reflect current North American market conditions.
Canada should also consider whether certain public‑facing pricing practices create unnecessary
exposure in an MFN context. When Canada’s Drug Agency publishes “recommended price
reductions,” those figures can be interpreted by foreign authorities as proxies for net prices,
even though Canadian agreements remain confidential. Re‑examining this practice would
reduce avoidable MFN‑related risk for both payers and manufacturers while preserving
transparency where it meaningfully supports patients and the health system.
3. Modernize IP and Data Protection to Support Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
A predictable and efficient intellectual property (IP) and regulatory data protection (RDP)
framework is essential for attracting investment, supporting innovation, and ensuring that
Canada remains an attractive market for new medicine launches. Today, however, Canada’s
system does not provide the level of clarity or reliability seen in peer jurisdictions. Patent Term
Adjustment (PTA) and Certificates of Supplementary Protection (CSP) were introduced to
restore time lost during regulatory and patent office delays, but the way they are currently
structured does not give innovators a clear understanding of how much effective protection
6 EY, Spending on Innovative Medicines Research Brief Prepared for PhRMA by EY Quantitative
Economics & Statistics, June 27, 2025.

Term Adjustment (PTA) and Certificates of Supplementary Protection (CSP) were introduced to restore time lost during regulatory and patent office delays, but the way they are currently structured does not give innovators a clear understanding of how much effective protection 6 EY, Spending on Innovative Medicines Research Brief Prepared for PhRMA by EY Quantitative Economics & Statistics, June 27, 2025.

each mechanism provides. This limits Canada’s competitiveness at a time when other countries
are strengthening their frameworks to secure supply and encourage earlier launches.
To address this, Canada needs a more coherent and internationally aligned approach to term
restoration and data protection. Ensuring that PTA and CSP operate as independent, sequential
tools – each addressing a different source of delay – would provide clearer expectations for
innovators and better reflect the distinct purposes of each mechanism. Strengthening
regulatory data protection, particularly for biologics, would further align Canada with peer
jurisdictions and support long‑term investment in high‑value therapeutic areas.
4. Strengthen Access Through Trusted Trade Partnerships
Canada cannot meet all pharmaceutical needs through domestic production. Modern medicines
rely on specialized manufacturing, complex API supply chains, and global research networks.
International procurement is therefore a core feature of reliable access, not a weakness. The
WHO notes that access depends on strong procurement and supply systems, including
streamlined sourcing of quality‑assured medicines.7
Some products will remain difficult to produce at scale in Canada. Biologic medicines and
precision therapies, rare disease treatments, products requiring highly specialized
manufacturing, and newly innovative products still protected under intellectual property law
are examples of categories where establishing domestic production at scale can be challenging.
Likewise specialized treatments for rare diseases, or patients with specific sets of comorbidities,
mean that even a broad formulary of products manufactured domestically cannot
comprehensively meet the health needs of all every Canadian patient. Canada therefore
requires stable, predictable, and trusted trade relationships to secure these products.
Recent disruptions in Canada-US trade have highlighted the risks of relying heavily on a single
partner. This has accelerated efforts to diversify and deepen ties with other high‑standard
jurisdictions, including the European Union. The Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and
Trade Agreement (CETA) provides a strong basis for this shift. The EU maintains rigorous quality
and safety standards and offers a stable regulatory environment, which attributes that matter
in a period of supply‑chain fragility and geopolitical uncertainty.
In this context, reliance on distributed production networks is important. These networks
reduce exposure to single‑site failures and corridor disruptions, and they provide redundancy
across jurisdictions with strong regulatory standards. For our part, Boehringer Ingelheim
operates a multi‑site manufacturing and supply footprint across EU member states, anchored
in Germany. This structure supports continuity of supply and reflects the type of resilient
capacity Canada should look for when assessing international partners.
For this reason, we recommend that the Committee encourage the federal government to
strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU and German pharmaceutical sector, ensuring that
Canadians’ access to pharmaceutical products not manufactured domestically is anchored in
reliable and trusted partner countries, and with dependable pharmaceutical manufacturers.
7World Health Organization, WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd list (2023).

For this reason, we recommend that the Committee encourage the federal government to
strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU and German pharmaceutical sector, ensuring that
Canadians’ access to pharmaceutical products not manufactured domestically is anchored in
reliable and trusted partner countries, and with dependable pharmaceutical manufacturers.
7World Health Organization, WHO Model List of Essential Medicines – 23rd list (2023).

5. Advance Innovation and Patient Access by Supporting Clinical Trial Activity
Clinical trials are one of the most direct and meaningful ways that innovative pharmaceutical
companies provide Canadians with early access to new medicines. Participation allows patients
to receive promising therapies – including those for serious or complex conditions – before they
are commercially available. For patients with limited treatment options, this early access can be
critical.
Industry‑sponsored clinical trials benefit nearly two million Canadians each year.8 They support
early patient access, build Canadian research capacity, train clinicians and scientists, and
strengthen the competitiveness of Canada’s life sciences ecosystem. Canada’s Drug Agency
(CDA) has recognized this link between clinical trials and timely access through its Time‑Limited
Reimbursement framework, which ties accelerated review to the generation of clinical trial
evidence.
In this environment, the contribution of research‑intensive companies is important. Their
clinical trial activity brings new therapies into the system earlier, generates evidence for
regulatory and reimbursement decisions, and supports the development of Canadian research
sites. For our part, Boehringer Ingelheim Canada conducts clinical trials across our core
therapeutic areas, with 38 active studies across 222 trial sites in 2026. These trials provide early
access for participants, expose Canadian clinicians and researchers to emerging science, and
generate the evidence that ultimately supports broader access to BI therapies for all Canadians.
The relationship between clinical trial activity and patient access is well established. The World
Health Organization defines essential medicines as those that meet priority health needs and
are available in sufficient quantities within functioning health systems.9 Clinical trials,
particularly those led by research‑intensive companies, are a core mechanism for generating
the evidence that moves new therapies from development into those systems and ultimately
into broad patient use.
For these reasons, we ask that the Committee recommend that the federal government take
concrete steps to strengthen Canada’s clinical trial environment, including supporting timely
study start‑up, reducing administrative barriers, and aligning regulatory, reimbursement, and
evidence‑generation processes.
Conclusion
Canada has an opportunity to strengthen its pharmaceutical sovereignty by modernizing the
systems that determine how new medicines are reviewed, assessed, and protected. A more
coordinated and predictable approach across regulatory, reimbursement, and intellectual
property frameworks would help ensure that Canada is equipped to secure supply, respond to
emerging health needs, and remain competitive in a rapidly evolving global environment.

Written Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee
on Health (HESA) Study on Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
Submitted by:
Andrew Booth, CFO
May 5, 2026

Executive Summary
Canada has the scientific foundation to be a global leader in biotechnology, yet it continues to
capture only a fraction of the economic and strategic value generated by its own innovation.
While Canadian researchers and companies are highly successful in discovering and advancing
promising new therapies, these assets are too often sold to foreign firms prior to
commercialization. This results in the loss of intellectual property (IP), high-value jobs, assets for
national security, and long-term economic returns that could otherwise benefit Canadians.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty cannot be achieved solely through supply chain measures or by
relying on multinational firms to operate within Canada. Instead, it requires a deliberate strategy
to build globally competitive, Canadian-headquartered biopharmaceutical companies that retain
IP, scale domestically, and commercialize medicines from within Canada. Achieving this
objective will require targeted policy reforms, including modernizing the SR&ED program to
support growth-stage firms, implementing a Patent Box regime to incentivize IP retention,
investing in critical infrastructure, and defining what constitutes a “Canadian Company” that is
poised to scale up in a modern, globally integrated industry.
Our Recommendations
Contained herein are AbCellera’s recommendations on securing Canada’s
pharmaceutical sovereignty. We are recommending the following:
1. Create a definition of what is a “Canadian Company” to align with our national interest in
scaling companies domestically. Eligibility should focus on the location of headquarters,
senior leadership, IP ownership, assets, and core R&D operations;

2. Develop an Anchor Company Strategy to build and scale globally competitive technology
anchor companies here in Canada;

3. Focus government supported procurement, infrastructure investments, capital
investments and tax policies (SR&ED and Patent Box) to deliver significant benefit to
Canadian Companies. This treatment would be expected to drive domestic and
international private investment to Canadian Companies; and

4. Continued targeted programs in biotech infrastructure, including wet labs and
biomanufacturing capacity as well as streamlining clinical trials through Health Canada,
ultimately to the benefit of IP creation in Canada towards commercialization and to the
benefit of Canadian patients.

Continued targeted programs in biotech infrastructure, including wet labs and
biomanufacturing capacity as well as streamlining clinical trials through Health Canada,
ultimately to the benefit of IP creation in Canada towards commercialization and to the
benefit of Canadian patients.

Introduction and Context
Pharmaceutical sovereignty has become an increasingly prominent issue in recent years, driven
by global supply chain disruptions, geopolitical instability, and heightened competition in
strategic sectors such as biotechnology. In Canada, much of the discussion has focused on
vulnerabilities in access to medicines and the need for domestic manufacturing capacity. While
these concerns are valid, they represent only part of the broader challenge. For example,
multinational companies that want to start or continue to participate in the U.S. market face
increasing pressure to build a stronger presence in the United States, including establishing and
growing manufacturing capabilities.
At its core, pharmaceutical sovereignty is about ensuring that Canada has the ability to not only
contribute to scientific discovery, but also to develop, produce, and commercialize the resulting
medicines. It is fundamentally an economic and industrial question as much as it is a health
policy issue. Countries that lead in biotechnology have recognized this and have implemented
comprehensive strategies to support companies across the full value chain, from early research
through to commercialization.
Canada has the opportunity to adopt a similar approach; however, doing so will require a shift in
perspective. We must move from a defensive focus on mitigating risks to an offensive strategy
aimed at building globally competitive companies that are rooted in Canada and capable of
succeeding on the world stage.
Canada’s Current Position
Canada benefits from a strong foundation in life sciences and biotechnology. The country is
home to world-class academic institutions, leading research hospitals, and a highly skilled
scientific workforce. Canadian researchers and companies have contributed to the discovery of
numerous important therapies, demonstrating a consistent ability to generate high-quality
early-stage innovation.
Despite these strengths, Canada faces persistent challenges in retaining the value of this work
as it matures to be exportable commercial-stage assets. A defining feature of the Canadian
ecosystem is the tendency for promising drug candidates to be sold or licensed to foreign firms
before reaching late-stage clinical development or commercialization. While these transactions
may provide short-term returns, they result in the transfer of IP ownership, decision-making
authority, infrastructure investment for scale up, and future economic benefits to other
jurisdictions.

While these transactions
may provide short-term returns, they result in the transfer of IP ownership, decision-making
authority, infrastructure investment for scale up, and future economic benefits to other
jurisdictions.

This pattern reflects a broader structural issue. Canada has been highly effective at generating
ideas, but less successful at building companies that can carry those ideas through to global
markets. As a result, the country lacks a sufficient number of large, globally competitive
biopharmaceutical firms that can anchor domestic ecosystems and sustain long-term growth.
Despite discovering many medicines that deliver impactful health benefits to patients globally,
Canada is the only country in the G7 without a major pharmaceutical company. This puts
Canada in a large trade deficit position in the global trade balance of drugs: it also puts us in a
position of vulnerability for the health infrastructure assets required for national resilience.
The economic consequences of this dynamic are significant. For example, with a market
capitalization that exceeds the GDP of Denmark’s domestic economy, the exports and profits of
Novo Nordisk have a giant economic impact on the country. Canada has a growing
pharmaceutical trade deficit, reaching approximately $18 billion in 2024. In short, we import
high-value finished medicines while exporting the early-stage innovation that created them. The
profits associated with successful drugs, along with the associated tax revenues and
reinvestment into research and development (R&D), are realized elsewhere. In addition, the
absence of large domestic firms limits the creation of high-paying jobs in areas such as clinical
development, regulatory affairs, and executive leadership.
Defining Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
To develop effective policy, it is essential to clearly define what pharmaceutical sovereignty
entails. In this context, sovereignty should not be understood as complete self-sufficiency or
isolation from global markets. Biotechnology is inherently international, and collaboration will
remain essential.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty should be understood as the capacity of a country to participate in
the global biopharmaceutical system as a producer of high-value innovation. This includes the
ability to discover and develop new therapies, retain ownership of the underlying IP, advance
therapies through clinical development, and commercialize them in a way that captures
economic value domestically.
Achieving this requires more than infrastructure or procurement tools. It requires companies—
Canadian Companies—with the scale, expertise, and resources to operate across the full value
chain. It also requires a policy environment that supports these companies as they grow, rather
than one that inadvertently encourages them to sell or relocate.

It also requires a policy environment that supports these companies as they grow, rather
than one that inadvertently encourages them to sell or relocate.

The Definition of a Canadian Company
Today’s definitions of Canadian companies for eligibility of certain tax and granting programs are
not serving the needs of today. The two existing definitions are:
1. SMEs - Small and Medium-sized Enterprises; and
2. CCPCs - Canadian Controlled Private Corporations.
Both of these definitions in the vast majority of today's innovation economy represent
companies that are not going to move the needle in achieving Pharmaceutical Sovereignty.
Ultimately this will be achieved by large and sustainable investments from the private sector.
SMEs are by definition, “small and medium sized.”
CCPCs require domestic capital to be available to invest in the sector. While domestic capital
may be available for many industries well known to Canadian investors, life sciences, biotech,
and pharma does not exist in Canada at the scale necessary to succeed (i.e. develop a drug) .
Ironically, Canada is trying to encourage foreign investment and we see no need to penalize
companies based on shareholder composition when the desired investments, assets,
employment, activities and risks of the company are in Canada.
We propose a new definition of a Canada Company to suit the needs of today with a focus on
private enterprise that can scale up and provide the known benefits of an anchor companies to
the country.
A Canadian Company should be defined as a company where:
1. The parent legal entity at the top of the company’s global org chart is in Canada;
2. A critical mass (>50%) of the Executive Team of the company is in Canada, including a
minimum of the CEO, CFO and COO (or equivalent);
3. A threshold of the assets of the company are in Canada. For example, a requirement
that more assets of the global company are in Canada than in any other single
jurisdiction; and
4. The Intellectual Property of the company is in Canada.
To further emphasize the importance of companies in the scale up phase of their evolution, a
potential 5th criteria could be:
5. Companies must have more than 500 employees globally.

Companies must have more than 500 employees globally.

This definition would pick up where the SME definition (fewer than 500 employees) ends and
streamline eligibility for companies of true scale up potential. Today there is a strange incentive
in Canada to be smaller than 500 employees. We need to create the incentive and path for
scale up of Canadian Companies to and above 500 employees, which is where true economic,
employment, and employee training benefit to Canada kicks in.
With such a clear definition, incentives such as granting programs, procurement initiatives, and
tax policy can be tailored for eligibility exclusively to Canadian Companies.
Key Barriers to Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
A number of structural barriers currently limit Canada’s ability to achieve pharmaceutical
sovereignty through a robust scale up environment for private companies and investment. One
of the most significant is the absence of access to a low cost of capital that endures along the
journey of growth for Canadian Companies as they scale.
SR&ED is a flagship Canadian innovation tax program that appropriately incentivizes early
stage R&D investment. Canadian companies are excellent at this early-stage development and
this program contributes materially across all innovation industries. The SR&ED program has
been highly effective at lowering the cost of capital for investment for early-stage private
enterprise research. SR&ED’s benefits diminish as companies grow and lose either their SME
or CCPC status. Ironically this size of private sector company is precisely when low cost of
capital is needed the most to promote the scale up of companies in Canada to achieve anchor
company status and materially contribute both economically and in the creation of assets that
would build pharmaceutical sovereignty.
The existing legislation creates a paradox: it actively penalizes Canadian life science companies
for successfully attracting the foreign investment needed to fund domestic operations and lose
their CCPC status. When a company's Board of Directors, executive leadership, headquarters,
and the vast majority of its R&D activities remain firmly rooted in Canada, the geographic
distribution of its retail and institutional shareholders should not disqualify it from innovation
incentives, provided the activities attracting the incentives are in Canada. Modernizing this
definition to focus on domestic economic activity - rather than capitalization tables - will ensure
that SR&ED support does not diminish exactly when companies are scaling and creating the
most value for the Canadian economy. The creation of a Canadian Company definition would
allow Canada to extend similar earlier stage benefits of programs like SR&ED to qualifying
companies to aid in their scale up.

The creation of a Canadian Company definition would
allow Canada to extend similar earlier stage benefits of programs like SR&ED to qualifying
companies to aid in their scale up.

Strategic procurement should be directed towards Canadian Companies to lower their cost of
capital through the organic growth of their business with a valued and dependable customer,
such as the government. This happens in other jurisdictions (“Buy American”) and is a welcome
recent emphasis in the Canadian retail sector to “Buy Canadian.” However, there is not a crisp
definition of what a Canadian Company is. Should a robust definition exist, such as the
definition provided here, on the announcement of large procurement contracts it would be
possible to state that “only Canadian Companies are eligible.” Companies, voters, and the
government would know precisely what this means. This would be immediately useful for
procurement groups, such as Canada’s DIA (Defense Investment Agency).
Canada has a robust set of granting programs such as Industrial Research Assistance Program
(IRAP) and the Strategic Response Fund. IRAP is only available to SMEs. The Strategic
Response Fund (SRF) should be directed towards bigger investments with a bias - if not
requirement - to be a Canadian Company. This lower cost of capital funding can be critical to
companies looking to scale up.
Canada lacks a competitive tax regime for income derived from IP. When a company discovers
a new potential therapy, it files patents to protect the composition of matter (typically the
chemical structure or DNA sequence of the new therapy). Patents are always filed before
initiation of clinical trials, and typically 10 years before a drug is approved and sales are
realized. It is typical for a company to move this IP to the most favorable tax jurisdiction - which
requires the movement of clinical trials, employees, manufacturing and management for the
company to avail themselves of profits in the favourable tax regime. These are precisely the
investments that are made during the second 10 years of a patent's validity. Because the move
of IP is done long before the drug is proven to work, there is little cost in moving IP between
jurisdictions. Many peer jurisdictions have implemented Patent Box systems that offer
preferential tax rates on income generated from patented innovations. These regimes create
strong incentives for companies to retain IP and commercialize products domestically. The
result is that future tax on the profits of successful drugs is highly concentrated in low tax
countries. This is a large part of the reason that Ireland, a nation of only 6 million people,
exports over $50 billion USD of pharmaceuticals annually, while Canada, a nation of 40 million
people, exports essentially $0 in branded pharmaceuticals. A competitive Patent Box could be
made available in Canada, but only to Canadian Companies to reward those companies that
were founded and scaled here domestically.
In the absence of similarly competitive tax tools, Canadian firms face pressure to move IP and
related activities to more competitive jurisdictions. In biotech we see this happen time after time.

In biotech we see this happen time after time.

Capital constraints for large physical investment in infrastructure also play a critical role in
building up biotech assets. Biotechnology is a capital-intensive industry that requires long-term
investment. Competitive debt programs for such investments from EDC, BDC or regional
programs such as PacifiCan should prioritize low cost of capital loans - backed by physical
assets - to Canadian Companies who face challenges in accessing the scale of capital needed
to compete globally. This is particularly true in Canada where our large banks who exclusively
service the domestic market do not understand biotech assets, such as GMP manufacturing
facilities and wet lab space. Without access to low cost debt tailored to biotech investments
domestically, promising companies will leave to make those investments elsewhere where debt
markets are more productive for biotech related investments. These constraints can force
companies to conduct critical activities abroad, even when there is a strong preference to
remain domestic.
Finally, Canada’s ecosystem lacks a sufficient number of large, globally competitive firms that
can act as anchors. These companies play a vital role in recruiting and developing talent,
attracting investment, creating networks of suppliers and partners, and creating spin off
companies that will become the next anchor companies of the ecosystem. Without the starting
anchors, the ecosystem remains fragmented and less competitive. This ultimately sets up our
Canadian biotech inventions and firms to be purchased by international companies (largely in
the United States) and then sold back to us to treat Canadian patients.
Recommendations
Addressing these challenges will require a coordinated set of policy actions focused on enabling
scale and retaining value within Canada. AbCellera proposes the following:
1. Establish a definition of Canadian Company for firms over 500 employees with a
requirement of the top legal entity, management, assets, and intellectual property to be
in Canada;
2. The SR&ED program should be reformed such that the benefits currently offered to
Canadian CCPC companies be extended to Canadian Companies, without any grind
down or cap to the SR&ED benefit;
3. Procurement programs such as DIA or, eventually, DIS should have a preference or
required quota for Canadian Companies;
4. Government investment programs such as SRF should have a preference or
significant required quota for Canadian Companies;
5. Implement a Patent Box regime that applies a competitive tax rate to income derived
from patented innovations for Canadian Companies. Such a system would incentivize
companies to retain IP, investment and employment in Canada and would align Canada

Such a system would incentivize
companies to retain IP, investment and employment in Canada and would align Canada

with other jurisdictions that are actively competing for high-value biopharmaceutical
activity;
6. Make low cost debt available for targeted investments in infrastructure as required
to address critical gaps. Expanding wet lab space and biomanufacturing capacity will
be essential to supporting the growth of domestic companies. These investments should
be aligned with the needs of scaling firms and designed to ensure effective utilization;
and
7. Adopt a deliberate strategy to build and anchor globally competitive companies.
This requires sustained support through all stages of development, with a particular
focus on enabling firms to conduct clinical trials in Canada and reach commercialization.
These companies will generate export revenue, create high-value jobs, and reinvest in
future innovation, strengthening the overall ecosystem.
Economic and Health System Benefits
A strategy focused on building domestic biopharmaceutical companies will deliver significant
economic and health system benefits. From an economic perspective, it will contribute to
increased productivity, GDP growth, and tax revenues. High-paying jobs in science,
engineering, and leadership will support a more robust and diversified economy.
From a health system perspective, a stronger domestic industry will enhance supply resilience
and improve access to new therapies to Canadian patients. In addition, the economic activity
generated by successful companies will provide a sustainable source of funding for public
services, including healthcare.
Perhaps most importantly, retaining IP and commercialization capacity within Canada will
enable a virtuous cycle of innovation, in which the success of one generation of companies
supports the development of the next.
Conclusion
Canada has the talent, research capacity, and entrepreneurial base to be a global leader in
biotechnology. However, without targeted policy reforms, it will continue to fall short in capturing
the full value of its innovation.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty should be understood as an industrial and economic priority
objective: building and retaining companies that develop, own, and commercialize medicines in
Canada. By aligning policy with this objective, supporting scale, retaining IP, and enabling

commercialization, Canada can strengthen its health system, economy, and global
competitiveness.
The opportunity is clear. With the right policy framework in place, Canada can move from being
a source of early-stage innovation to a global leader in biopharmaceutical development and
commercialization.

Introduction
The Coalition solidarité santé is a Quebec-based coalition of labour organizations, community
groups, citizens’ committees and organizations representing feminists, seniors, people with
disabilities and caregivers. Our work is grounded in defending the core principles that have
shaped the health system since its inception: public ownership, free access, availability,
universality and comprehensiveness.
For many years, we have advocated for the implementation of a universal public pharmacare
plan. On several occasions, we have emphasized that any future plan must be publicly
administered, universal, accessible, equitable, viable, independent and respectful of provincial
jurisdiction.1 In our view, the issue of Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty has become a matter
of fundamental importance in the current context.
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed Canada’s dependence on foreign companies not only for
medicines but also for a broad range of medical supplies. The challenges surrounding vaccine
procurement during the crisis also underscored the importance of being able to rely on domestic
production capacity. Such capacity becomes especially critical when other countries attempt to
restrict or reduce exports of pharmaceutical products or seek to limit the use of licences that
allow third parties to manufacture patented products.
The U.S.-led trade war is creating significant uncertainty about the possibility of tariffs on
pharmaceuticals. Researchers warn that such tariffs would increase costs and weaken supply
chains.2 We are concerned that this situation will lead to more supply disruptions, to the
detriment of public health. In its 2026 annual report, the Office of the United States Trade
Representative raised concerns about Canada’s patented medicine pricing framework.3 It argues
that the exclusion of Switzerland and the United States from Canada’s reference basket—even
though those countries have some of the highest drug prices in the world—devalues innovative
medicines. Even these modest efforts to limit pharmaceutical profits are characterized as barriers

The cornerstone of pharmaceutical sovereignty: A
universal public pharmacare plan
We can attest to the shortcomings of Quebec’s prescription drug insurance plan. Quebec was a
pioneer in 1997 when it implemented a prescription drug insurance plan covering its entire
population. However, Quebec’s current hybrid public-private system has failed to ensure
reasonable and equitable access to drugs, contrary to the objectives set out in Quebec’s Act
respecting prescription drug insurance.5 Numerous surveys show that a significant proportion of
the population do not take medication due to cost, with one survey placing this figure at nearly
one quarter of respondents.6 In addition to the many growing inequities, skyrocketing drug costs
are now threatening the funding of many other essential health services. The shortcomings of
Quebec’s system are known and well documented.7
For the Coalition solidarité santé, the implementation of a universal public pharmacare plan must
be the cornerstone of any strategy aimed at strengthening pharmaceutical sovereignty. Such a
plan is, in our view, an essential prerequisite for developing institutional capacity in areas such as
the management of reimbursed medicines, price negotiation with manufacturers and the
appropriate use of medicines. We therefore call on the federal government to resume efforts to

In this regard, Canadian public policy needs to change. Beginning in the 1980s, Canada
encouraged higher prices for patented medicines in exchange for a commitment from the
industry to invest 10% of its sales in research and development (R&D). This strategy has failed.
Despite the fact that prices in Canada are among the highest in the world, industry investment is
plummeting. The ratio of R&D to sales in Canada fell from 11.7% in 1995 to 4.1% in 2024.8
Moreover, the vast majority of patented medicines do not constitute a major innovation compared
to what is already on the market. The Patented Medicine Prices Review Board (PMPRB) itself
has questioned the effectiveness of this policy. Repeated attempts to reform the system and
reduce prices have largely been undermined by pharmaceutical industry lobbying.
We are also concerned that the pharmaceutical industry exerts far too much influence over public
health policy. Several researchers, including Joel Lexchin, have criticized the close alignment
between Health Canada and industry interests.9 This proximity weakens public protections. In
addition, pharmaceutical companies may advertise directly to consumers as long as they do not
simultaneously mention both the product name and the condition it treats. In recent months,
there has been an explosion in advertisements for Wegovy, an expensive drug to treat obesity.
This concern is compounded by the lack of transparency surrounding payments from
pharmaceutical companies to doctors, a practice known to influence prescribing behaviour.10
For these reasons, we are calling for a package of measures to strengthen the government’s
independence from the pharmaceutical industry, ranging from a pricing reform for patented drugs
to a ban on drug advertising and greater independence for Health Canada.

A Crown corporation producing drugs
The creation of a Crown corporation playing a complementary role to the private sector has many
advantages in terms of the country’s pharmaceutical sovereignty, although it is not a panacea.
First, it would strengthen the balance of power of the universal public pharmacare plan to better
control costs. It could serve as a safeguard against collusion or too little competition due to a low
number of bidders in tenders. While competition exists in the generic drug market, manufacturers
can sometimes find themselves in a monopoly situation for a given drug. According to Quebec’s
Commissaire à la santé et au bien-être, this “may result in higher prices for the product
concerned, in addition to increasing the risk of supply disruptions [TRANSLATION].”12
In addition, a Crown corporation could play an important role in stepping in when private
companies stop producing essential drugs for reasons of profitability, thereby guaranteeing
supply. In the context of trade tensions and efforts by the United States to bring manufacturing
companies back to American soil, this proposal takes on even greater relevance.
Such a corporation could also be mandated to focus on the production of less profitable, but
medically necessary, drugs. Sweden has one such state-owned company, Apotek Produktion &
Laboratorier (APL).13 It plays a secondary, yet important, role in producing more complex drugs
to meet specific needs, especially those of children.14
Finally, a portion of the profits made by such a Crown corporation could be reinvested in areas of
research that are of little interest to the industry, such as antibiotics and vaccines. Over the past
fifty years, the big pharmaceutical companies have gradually abandoned vaccine research. After
each public health crisis (Zika, MERS, SARS and Ebola), private companies very quickly
abandon their research because there is no short-term profit.15 Strengthening pharmaceutical
sovereignty also means that the state must direct research into the pharmaceutical sector and
invest more resources to better protect against epidemics and pandemics. Such investments
would also contribute to job stability in the research sector.

Preparing for the next disruption
The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted governments’ lack of preparedness. There were shortages
of equipment, medical supplies and essential medicines. Several organizations have called for
the establishment of a strategic stockpile of medicines based on a list of essential medicines.16
Most proposals focus on strengthening and enhancing Canada’s National Emergency Strategic
Stockpile, which was established in 1952 during the Cold War.17 The stockpile includes medical
equipment and supplies, pharmaceuticals and social service supplies such as beds and blankets.
Stockpiles also exist in other countries, including the United States and Australia. They face the
same criticisms: poor management (expiring stocks), lack of reliable inventory data and waste of
public resources.18 To solve these problems, some propose integrating the National Emergency
Strategic Stockpile into the commercial supply chain.19 A prime vendor would be created,
whether a Crown corporation or a not-for-profit organization, to manage inventory, negotiate with
manufacturers and organize logistics and distribution. The prime vendor would therefore be
responsible for maintaining warehouse inventories at maximum capacity and selling the various
products to hospitals and health facilities to avoid waste and ensure products are used before
they expire.
Strengthening the National Emergency Strategic Stockpile and improving its management could
be part of a package of measures to strengthen Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty and
reduce disruptions in the supply of essential medicines. However, this would require close
cooperation between the federal government and the provinces. The strategic stockpile should
first be used to build up reserves of essential medicines and drugs that are particularly vulnerable
to shortages in hospitals, rather than focusing solely on private pharmacies.

Conclusion
As this brief has demonstrated, ensuring Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty will require a
range of concrete actions. For the Coalition solidarité santé, all public policies in this area must
serve public health policies. Partners must contribute to the implementation of comprehensive,
sustainable and equitable solutions, while developing a shared vision for the future of
pharmaceutical sovereignty in Canada.
List of recommendations
• We call on the federal government to continue working with the provinces and territories to
establish a universal public pharmacare plan, while providing Quebec with the right to opt
out with full compensation, provided that it implements a plan offering coverage equivalent
or superior to that of a future Canada-wide plan.
• We call for a package of measures to strengthen the government’s independence from the
pharmaceutical industry, including a more effective pricing reform for patented drugs, a
genuine ban on drug advertising, greater independence for Health Canada and the
development of stronger manufacturing capacity.
• We call for the implementation of a pharmaceutical industrial policy aimed at rebuilding
local production capacity and creating stable, high-quality jobs while remaining compatible
with rigorous control of drug costs.
• We recommend that the federal government rapidly assess the feasibility of establishing a
Crown corporation dedicated to pharmaceutical production in order to improve cost control,
secure our supply of essential drugs, fill gaps in the private sector and stimulate research
in areas essential to the public interest.
• We recommend that the federal government strengthen the National Emergency Strategic
Stockpile and improve its operation.

Key Issues

Domestic manufacturing

Canada relies heavily on imported drugs. According to one industry estimate, 56% of our generic
drugs are imported as finished products – mainly from the US – along with 90% of the active
pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) used in domestic manufacturing.1 This dependence can be
weaponized by foreign governments and exploited by for-profit companies.

The government should increase domestic manufacturing to reinforce our supply chains and
protect access to medicine – making substantial investment in public manufacturing. A public
entity could make essential medicines available at cost, while supporting innovations that are
socially necessary, not just profitable. History shows public manufacturing has enormous
potential, like Connaught Labs and the instrumental role it played in the mass
production/distribution of insulin.

A public producer would be insulated from overseas political pressure. It would not pack up and
leave, hike prices, or change course to pad its bottom line. This is critical in the wake of strongarm tactics from the Trump administration – demanding companies raise prices internationally to
offset costs in the US2 and threatening 100% tariffs on products for companies who didn’t move
production there.3

We’ve seen industry representatives tout their investments in Canada, but major companies have
abandoned Canadians before. Stellantis moved production to the US after receiving some $220
million from the federal government – alongside $15 billion in promised ‘incentives’.4 Where
agreements with private companies are necessary, the government must ensure they are
accountable to the public.

Accountability

The federal government has become increasingly deferential to large corporations at the same

influencing the health of Canadians – and we caution policymakers not to conflate oversight and
transparency with inconvenience or ‘regulatory burden’.

surveillance as well as compliance and enforcement”, stating that “eliminating barriers to trade
will reduce business costs, increase productivity and contribute to Canada's economic growth”.20

Our recommendations: Strengthen Access and System Performance
Building on this evidence, Canada can advance pragmatic, evidence-aligned actions:
1. Streamlining access pathways across regulatory review, HTA, and price negotiations
Aligning regulatory review, HTA, and pricing processes can shorten time to patient access without
compromising safety or rigor. International experience shows that parallel models support timely access while
maintaining high standards. Ensuring that patients are not adversely affected by negotiation timelines,
through appropriate mitigation mechanisms, helps balance system stewardship with patient‑centered access.
2. Advance value-based decision-making
By capturing the full system‑level value, including reduced hospital use, productivity gains and caregiver
effects, as well as downstream cost offsets supported by clinical evidence and local footprint, this approach
aligns with established health economic evidence and enables more efficient public spending.
3. Support research to enhance innovation and clinical trial activity
Jurisdictions that provide predictable access pathways and robust data protection are better positioned to
attract clinical trials, enable early patient access, and strengthen domestic scientific and clinical expertise.
Ensuring that medicines developed through Canadian research are subsequently adopted within the
Canadian health system reinforces the research-to-care continuum, sustains late-phase clinical research
activity, and maximizes opportunities for Canadian patients to benefit from early access. This alignment
supports Canada’s role not only as a centre of discovery, but also as a jurisdiction where innovation is
translated into practice.

4. Unlock AI to gain health system efficiencies to enable sustainable innovation
Innovative medicines act as enablers of health system performance by preventing disease progression,
reducing reliance on acute care, and supporting sustained workforce participation. OECD and World Health
Organization analyses consistently show that these therapies generate value beyond short‑term clinical
endpoints, including improvements in quality of life, prevention outcomes, and long‑term system efficiency.
To fully realize these benefits, jurisdictions should adopt assessment frameworks that capture the complete
value of medicines, not only overall survival outcomes, but also quality‑of‑life gains, preventive impact, and
meaningful incremental improvements over existing care.

Conclusion
Evidence from Canada and internationally demonstrates that timely access to innovative medicines contributes
to better health outcomes, improved system efficiency, and greater resilience.
By reinforcing predictability, advancing value-based frameworks, and aligning policies across jurisdictions,
Canada can build on its strong foundations to ensure that patients benefit more rapidly and consistently from
scientific progress, while strengthening the sustainability and economic performance of the health system.

Executive Summary
The Best Medicines Coalition (BMC) welcomes the opportunity to contribute to the Standing Committee
on Health’s (HESA) study on Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty. Canada’s ability to ensure reliable,
timely, and equitable access to medicines is a foundational element of both public health and economic
resilience.
From a patient perspective, pharmaceutical sovereignty must be understood not as isolation or
domestic self-sufficiency, but as strategic resilience. This means the committee must consider how to
protect access to medically necessary drugs across therapeutic areas, ensure continuity of supply,
attract innovation and early launches, and deliver equitable access for all patients in Canada. This
includes medicines for common chronic conditions, cancer and rare cancers, and therapies for rare
diseases, which can be sensitive to market uncertainty, regulatory delays, and pricing instability.
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is particularly consequential for Canadians living with cancer, rare cancers,
and rare diseases, where treatment timelines are often narrow and therapies increasingly personalized.
Delays in regulatory approval, clinical trial start-up, or reimbursement decisions can result in missed
treatment windows, poorer health outcomes, and premature death. For patients with rare diseases,
including rare cancers, where standard-of-care options may be limited or non-existent, access to
innovative medicines and trials are often the only viable therapeutic pathway. A sovereignty framework
that does not explicitly include a strategy to improve the development of and early access to innovative
therapies – including innovative oncology and rare disease therapies - risks further entrenching existing
inequities for some of Canada’s most vulnerable patients.
This submission outlines how sovereignty strategies should be designed to strengthen access for all
patients. In particular, the needs of those relying on high-volume medicines for common conditions,
those awaiting therapeutic innovations for unmet needs, and low-volume therapies for cancer and rare
diseases must be embedded in the strategy. This should be done in concert with reinforcing Canada’s
broader health system sustainability, research capacity, and biomanufacturing abilities.
The Best Medicines Coalition, which represents more than 30 patient groups across Canada, thanks
HESA for inviting us to provide testimony to its study on pharmaceutical sovereignty. We encourage
further engagement with patients and patient groups to ensure the study is inclusive and has integrity.
