2 https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/47/8/1257/156808/Hyperglycemic-Crises-in-AdultsWith-Diabetes-A

Rationale for Domestic Insulin Manufacturing
The absence of any Canadian insulin production creates multiple vulnerabilities:
•
Global Supply Chain Shocks: Recent events like the COVID-19 pandemic
revealed how quickly international medicine supply chains can break down under
crisis3. Border closures, export restrictions, or global shipping disruptions can
immediately threaten Canada’s insulin supply. With insulin requiring cold-chain
distribution and sophisticated manufacturing, countries without local production
risk being “at the back of the line” for supplies during emergencies.
•
Reliance on Foreign Producers: Insulin manufacturing is highly concentrated
in a small number of overseas companies and facilities. If any major supplier
were to downscale Canadian distribution or face output issues, Canada would
have no alternative local source to fill the gap. In Canada, between 1995 and
2006 over 30 types of insulin were withdrawn (many older formulations),
prompting Parliamentary hearings in 2003. Canada’s dependence on insulin
manufacturing done overseas leaves us vulnerable to supply disruptions or
foreign regulatory changes.
•
National Security Risks: Insulin is a strategic, life-saving commodity for
Canadians. National security experts recognize that just as energy or food
independence is crucial, so is the ability to produce essential medicines at home4.
A scenario where a foreign geopolitical conflict or export ban disrupts insulin
shipments to Canada is not remote; similar restrictions have happened with other
critical meds in global crises. Unlike many products, insulin cannot be easily
stockpiled (it expires), and no alternative therapy exists for those who need it.
Therefore, even a short-term supply halt could precipitate a national health
emergency if not mitigated by domestic production capacity or strategic reserves.
•
Healthcare Impact: A secure domestic manufacturing capability, designed
primarily for emergency and surge use, would strengthen Canada’s resilience
without displacing existing commercial supply. Its core purpose would be to
ensure continuity of access during supply disruptions, rather than to compete
with or replace internationally sourced insulin Importantly, the move could
rekindle Canada’s early insulin legacy, where insulin was provided at cost to
patients, aligning with a public health ethos.
Domestic insulin manufacturing capacity should be structured as a contingency asset,
activated only in clearly defined circumstances -such as global supply chain failures,
export controls, plant shutdowns, pandemics, or geopolitical disruptions that materially

Alignment with Federal Initiatives
Reinvesting in insulin production capacity aligns seamlessly with the Government’s key
initiatives:

project, based in Edmonton, focuses on building domestic production for critical
medicines. An additional federal investment of $50 million was recently

Recommendation

the creation of the capacity to manufacture at least one fast-acting and one long-acting

capitalizing on Canadian biotech expertise (e.g. in Alberta) to produce high-demand

vulnerability in our healthcare system by creating a reliable, Canadian-made insulin
capacity as “insurance” against global disruptions.
This proposal is timely and achievable. It directly supports the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health’s focus on pharmaceutical sovereignty, which emphasizes
that Canadians must not be “left at the back of the line” for essential medicines in a
crisis8. With strong political will, legislative alignment, and strategic funding (through

Conclusion
In summary, the case for domestic insulin manufacturing in cases of emergency is clearcut and compelling. It would immediately bolster our national health security by
guaranteeing supply of a life-critical drug (especially for the 300,000+ Canadians who
would face life-threatening risks within days of an insulin shortage). Moreover, it aligns
with Canada’s broader strategies in critical drug production and defense, turning policy
commitments into tangible action. Canada’s leadership in diabetes care and innovation,
combined with targeted investment, can restore the capacity to produce insulin
domestically when required, ensuring that Canada retains the ability to produce insulin
for Canadians in emergencies rather than relying exclusively on foreign supply in all
circumstances.
By swiftly advancing this initiative, Canada will strengthen its pharmaceutical
sovereignty, protect vulnerable citizens from supply shocks, and reaffirm its role as a
global leader in life sciences – all in a concise, credible response to the challenges
highlighted by the Standing Committee on Health’s study on pharmaceutical sovereignty.

uninterrupted access to insulin is now.

Built on U.S. Plasma: Canada’s Sovereignty Problem
A Brief on Pharmaceutical Sovereignty in Plasma-Derived Therapies
April 16, 2026

Dear Members of the HESA Committee:

This brief concerns pharmaceutical sovereignty with respect to plasma-derived medicinal
products (PDMPs), especially immunoglobulin. These medicines are essential for patients with
immune deficiencies and other serious conditions, and they depend on a very large and reliable
supply of collected plasma.

Canada remains heavily dependent on plasma collected in the United States. If Canada is to be
sovereign over this part of the pharmaceutical supply chain, there is no feasible path apart from
welcoming a larger domestic commercial plasma collection sector.

This dependence is more serious given rising demand for immunoglobulin, one of the medicines
made from plasma. Our need for this medicine has nearly doubled over the past ten years, and
is on track to nearly double again over the next ten years.

I write as an ethicist and public policy scholar who has conducted extensive comparative
research on plasma collection, donor safety, and plasma self-sufficiency across Canada, the
United States, Australia, New Zealand and Europe, including the UK.

Sincerely,

Peter M. Jaworski, Ph.D.
Professor of Ethics in Strategy, Ethics, Economics, and Public Policy,
McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University

Director, Georgetown Blood and Plasma Research Group

Member of the Network of Experts,
International Patient Organization for Primary Immunodeficiencies

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
● Canada is not sovereign over its plasma medicine supply chain. We are heavily
dependent on plasma collected in the United States.

● By July of 2025, Canada collected only 27 to 28% of the plasma needed for
immunoglobulin, leaving a shortfall equivalent to roughly 39 commercial plasma centres
in the United States, or 130 non-commercial plasma centres like the Plasmavie centres
in Quebec.

● Around the world, countries that achieve or approach plasma self-sufficiency are those
that permit domestic commercial compensated plasma collection. Countries that do not
permit such collection rely on plasma medicines sourced from commercial collection
systems elsewhere, overwhelmingly the United States.

Countries that do not
permit such collection rely on plasma medicines sourced from commercial collection
systems elsewhere, overwhelmingly the United States.

● Non-commercial collection alone is not a realistic path to Canadian plasma sovereignty.
It is about a quarter as productive, and two to four times more costly than commercial
collection.
● The sovereignty challenge is becoming more difficult as demand for immunoglobulin
grows in Canada and globally. Canadian Blood Services reported double-digit demand
growth this year and last.

● The available safety evidence does not support the claim that commercial plasma
collection is less safe than non-commercial collection.

● Ethical objections to compensated plasma collection are often raised but they do not
change the central policy fact: no country has achieved plasma sovereignty without
relying on commercial compensated collection, whether domestically or from abroad.

● Canada therefore faces a practical choice: either directly compensate Canadians for
plasma donations at home, or indirectly compensate Americans for plasma donations in
the U.S.

CANADA’S CURRENT DEPENDENCE ON THE U.S.

The United States currently supplies approximately 68% of the world’s supply of plasma for the
manufacture of plasma-derived medicinal products (PDMPs).1 The U.S. makes up
approximately 5% of the global population, yet collects more plasma than the rest of the world
combined.

At the end of 2025, the U.S. was home to 1,247 plasma collection centres, which is more than
Costco locations, and more than U.S. Tim Hortons locations. Those centres collected an
estimated 62.5 million litres of plasma in 2025. The U.S. has approximately 216,000 donations
every day.

About half of the plasma collected in the United States is used to shore up plasma collection
shortfalls in other countries, including Canada.

In 2025, Canada, outside of Quebec, was 27% self-sufficient in plasma for immunoglobulin, one
of the medicines made from plasma, while Quebec was 28.3% self-sufficient (see Figs. 1, 2, &
3).

In 2025, we collected enough source and recovered plasma to produce 3.1 million grams of
immunoglobulin, importing 8.1 million grams from the U.S. One concrete way of thinking about
our shortfall is that for every ten plasma donors that Canadian patients depend upon for their
immunoglobulin needs, only three are Canadian, while seven are Americans.

One concrete way of thinking about
our shortfall is that for every ten plasma donors that Canadian patients depend upon for their
immunoglobulin needs, only three are Canadian, while seven are Americans.

Our imports of immunoglobulin translates into a plasma collection shortfall of nearly two million
litres of plasma. This is the amount of plasma collected by about 39 commercial plasma centres
in the United States, that’s as many centres as are found in Missouri (28) and Kentucky (11)
together. So another way of concretizing our shortfall is to think that Missourians and
Kentuckians rolled up their sleeves and donated plasma just for Canadian patients in 2025.

Our dependence is made more serious by persistent growth in immunoglobulin demand not just
in Canada, but globally. We have seen our demand grow from 6.2 million grams in 2015 to 11.2
million grams in 2025, or 6.1% each year. At that rate, demand will reach 20.3 million grams by
2035 (see Fig 4).

Legislators in the U.S. have not moved to restrict plasma exports, though they have flirted with
this in the past. Legislators there have exempted plasma and plasma medicines from tariffs and
other restrictions, at least for now. We do not know what tomorrow will bring, and this
uncertainty in the security of supply of lifesaving medicines is what pharmaceutical sovereignty
should seek to eliminate.
1 For U.S. data, see 2026, “America’s plasma contribution to the world: 2025,” Blood Plasma Quarterly,
Georgetown Blood and Plasma Research Group.

THE INFEASIBILITY OF NON-COMMERCIAL PLASMA COLLECTION

To reach self-sufficiency, Canada needs 39 more commercial plasma centres beyond the 17
currently operated by Grifols. Alternatively, Canada would need more than 130 plasma
collection centres like those run by Canadian Blood Services or the Plasmavie centres operated
by Hema-Quebec.

Non-commercial centres are about a quarter as productive as commercial centres, and cost two
to four times more to collect a litre of plasma than their commercial equivalents, according to a
2018 Health Canada Expert Panel.2

This is why it is, for all practical purposes, not possible to be self-sufficient or sovereign over our
plasma supply without a domestic commercial compensated plasma collection industry.

This is why it is, for all practical purposes, not possible to be self-sufficient or sovereign over our
plasma supply without a domestic commercial compensated plasma collection industry.

Practically, we have one of two options. We can either welcome companies to give honoraria to
Canadians for donating plasma, or we give money to companies who will use it to compensate
Americans. Either way, we will, as we have for over three decades, rely on commercial
compensated plasma collection.

INTERNATIONAL EVIDENCE

The global picture reinforces this point.

Globally, only countries that allow commercial compensated plasma collections collect enough
plasma to meet the needs of their patient communities. Every country that does not have a
domestic commercial sector imports finished products from the U.S. commercial sector.

Today, there is no exception to this. The last country to collect enough plasma without a
commercial sector was New Zealand in 2014. New Zealand is now 74% self-sufficient and
trending downward (see Fig. 5).

Australia has perhaps the world’s most efficient non-commercial, non-compensated system of
plasma collection in Red Cross Lifeblood. However, Australia’s self-sufficiency has declined
from a high of 78% in 2012 to 43% in 2025 (see Fig. 6)

The United Kingdom is 23% self-sufficient (see Fig. 7, along with a technical note).
2 According to the Expert Panel: “…the cost of collecting large volumes of source plasma utilizing
volunteer donors is 2-4 times more expensive than the commercial plasma collection model and thus it
remains more economical for jurisdictions to purchase IG and PDPs from the commercial market, all of
which are made from plasma from paid donors. Finally evidence indicates that notwithstanding the
funding for blood operators to meet collection targets to achieve self-sufficiency, often source plasma
programs based on volunteer donors just simply can’t make their targets.” See p. VIII of 2018, “Protecting
access to immune globulins for Canadian patients: Final report of the expert panel on immune globulin
product supply and related impacts in Canada,” Health Canada (EN, FR)

The European Union as a whole is nearly 40% dependent on plasma collected in the United
States. France is only about a third self-sufficient, Spain is 29% self-sufficient (see Fig. 8), Italy
was 59% self-sufficient in 2024 (see Fig. 9), and Denmark was 49% self-sufficient in 2024 (see
Fig. 10).

France is only about a third self-sufficient, Spain is 29% self-sufficient (see Fig. 8), Italy
was 59% self-sufficient in 2024 (see Fig. 9), and Denmark was 49% self-sufficient in 2024 (see
Fig. 10).

Only Germany, Austria, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are self-sufficient. These are the
countries in Europe where commercial collectors operate side-by-side with non-commercial
blood operators.

The evidence from around the world is overwhelming: Countries either welcome assistance from
the commercial sector and move toward plasma sovereignty, or they rely on the commercial
sector in the United States and thereby cede plasma sovereignty.

SAFETY OF PLASMA DONATION

Recent tragedies in Winnipeg have understandably raised concerns, but they should be
understood in proper context. Plasma donation is extraordinarily safe.

In Canada, over the past ten years, there have been three deaths following a donation. Health
Canada concluded that none of these were connected to the plasma donation, and the
Manitoba medical examiner agreed after a separate investigation of the two most recent events.

Such events, while tragic, are not unprecedented, including in public non-commercial systems.
For example, over the past 10 years, the UK also had three deaths following a donation at NHS
Blood and Transplant (none of which were connected to the donations themselves), while
France’s public system had four deaths, only one of which was ruled as “possibly” connected to
the donation.

For comparison, data from Germany and the United States reveals no evidence for the claim
that the commercial sector is less safe than the non-commercial sector. The data across all
these countries and Canada shows that for both sectors, such events are exceedingly rare.
(Addendum A offers a fuller discussion of the comparative safety data).

RECOMMENDATIONS

If Canada wishes to be sovereign over the plasma supply chain, there is no feasible or practical
option apart from expanding the domestic commercial sector. The non-commercial model alone
cannot collect enough plasma to secure Canada’s supply of plasma-derived medicines.

Canada should therefore pursue four practical steps:
1. Welcome expansion of commercial plasma collection.

The partnership between Canadian Blood Services and Grifols is a good start, doubling
self-sufficiency in just three years. But it is only a start. Ontario could support more than 50
commercial collection centres, yet currently has only four. Canada should welcome additional
firms to establish and operate centres here.
2. Remove legal barriers to compensated plasma collection.

Remove legal barriers to compensated plasma collection.

The provinces should be encouraged to repeal their barriers to compensated plasma collection,
including Ontario’s and BC’s Voluntary Blood Donations Act and its equivalent in Quebec, as
Alberta did in 2020. We cannot credibly seek plasma sovereignty while legally obstructing the
model on which that sovereignty depends.
3. Encourage exports of surplus plasma and plasma-derived medicines.

Canada should welcome the export of plasma-derived medicines manufactured from Canadian
plasma when domestic needs are met, as we accept exports from the United States. A serious
commitment to sovereignty means participating in the global plasma economy, not merely
drawing from it.
4. Create conditions for additional domestic fractionation.

Canada should aim not only to collect more plasma domestically, but also to create the
conditions under which companies will seriously consider Canada as a site for fractionation
facilities. That will require a stable and credible policy environment for plasma collection,
including the removal of legal barriers to collection and a clear willingness to permit exports of
surplus plasma-derived medicines. No firm will seriously consider Canada as a site for major
investment while we continue to treat the commercial model as politically contested. Canada
cannot credibly seek pharmaceutical sovereignty while resisting at home the very commercial
model on which we already depend upon from abroad.

Addendum A: Safety of Plasma Donation

This addendum places the recent tragic events in Winnipeg in comparative context. We should

In Canada, over the past 10 years, there have been three deaths following a donation, with a
cluster of two deaths in the span of four months. According to both Health Canada and the chief
medical examiner for Manitoba, none of these deaths were connected to the plasma donation.

Such events are not unprecedented in 100% public, non-compensated systems.

Over the most recent 10-year period, the UK had three deaths temporally associated with a
donation with one in 2019 and a cluster of two in 2022, a frequency and pattern remarkably
similar to Canada’s. None of these were found to be related to the donations themselves.3

Addendum B: Ethics of Commercial Compensated Plasma Collection

As an ethicist, and because objections to compensated plasma collection are more often ethical
rather than practical or empirical, I offer the following note.

Patients

We should begin our moral inquiry with the moral point and purpose of our blood and plasma
collection systems.

The point of a collection system is not to give donors an opportunity to express their altruism,
nor to give the rest of us another occasion for solidarity or to celebrate national identity. The
moral point and purpose of blood and plasma collection is to meet the needs of patients.

Morally speaking, this is the most important metric by which to evaluate a collection system:
does it meet the needs of patients?

Wrongful Commodification

Some say that giving donors money means commodifying body parts. This objection
misunderstands what the money is for.9

This objection
misunderstands what the money is for.9

In Canada, as in Europe, the practice is not to pay for the plasma itself as one purchases
property. Rather, compensation is provided in recognition of the time, effort, inconvenience, and
expense involved in donation.

In the European Union, the recently adopted Regulation on Substances of Human Origin forbids
direct payment for plasma, but allows compensation to offset the costs, inconvenience, and
burdens associated with donation through a fixed-rate allowance. In Germany and Austria, this
kind of compensation is commonly understood as an acknowledgment of effort in service of the
common good (what they call an “aufwandsentschädigung”).

Canada’s practice is similar. Grifols offers an honorarium when donors give plasma. The plasma
is not assigned a price according to its features or characteristics, nor do donors bargain over a
price as though they were selling property.
9 For additional responses to the charge of wrongful commodification, see Section 3 of Donation Ethics,
“Ethicists and economists express concerns about banning compensation for plasma donors with regards
to ensuring the security of a safe immune globulin product supply,” Submission to the Expert Panel on
Immune Globulin product supply and related impacts in Canada, January 16, 2018.

Wrongful Exploitation

Some say the industry exploits donors. This objection is often based on the thought that donors
receive too small a share of the billions generated from plasma medicines; the companies make
billions in profit while donors get just $50 for a donation.10

This comparison mixes unit-level and aggregate-level analysis. For a fair comparison, we need
to compare either unit-to-unit or aggregate-to-aggregate.

In the aggregate, plasma donors in the United States received $4.7 billion in donor
compensation in 2025.11 Companies, meanwhile, made $3.8 to $5.2 billion in profit that same
year, depending on the profit measure used. Donors did not receive a pittance, they received
billions, as did the companies.

On a per-unit basis, the total revenue from a litre of plasma is about $190. Of this revenue, the
donor receives $70, while the company receives $15 in profit (see Fig. 12). Donor
compensation is much higher and profit is much lower than critics assume. Plasma collection is
a high-volume, low-margin business.

On an aggregate-to-aggregate or unit-to-unit comparison, the practice does not appear
exploitative, but fair.

Ethics summary

Ethics summary

The moral debate has a long history, and the above replies are not the final word on the matter.
But one part of this debate should be beyond debate: The first duty and obligation of a blood
and plasma collection system is to collect enough to meet the needs of patients. We do this
when it comes to blood and plasma for transfusion, but we are very far from doing this when it
comes to plasma for fractionation.

We make a grave moral error if we get our priorities mixed up and place abstract and symbolic
concerns over the health needs of patients who depend on plasma-derived therapies.

Executive Summary
Pharmaceutical sovereignty requires a balanced, coordinated approach that
strengthens domestic capability while maintaining diversified, globally connected
supply chains. As Canada’s national group purchasing organization serving over
2,100 hospitals and health-system providers, HealthPRO Canada has direct visibility
into the vulnerabilities that lead to critical drug shortages, supply disruptions, and
escalating costs.
A sustainable strategy must prioritize:
•
ensuring uninterrupted patient access
•
building targeted domestic manufacturing capacity for clinically critical
medicines
•
modernizing procurement to value reliability and redundancy
•
enhancing regulatory agility
•
strengthening supply-chain transparency through data sharing
•
aligning manufacturing, health, and innovation policy
•
combining strategic domestic capacity with diversified global sourcing
Canada cannot achieve pharmaceutical sovereignty through isolation or full
self-sufficiency. The most resilient model combines strategic domestic capability with
diversified, allied global supply networks supported by coordinated national policy.

Considerations
Ensuring Reliable Access for Patients
Uninterrupted access to safe, effective, and affordable medicines must remain the
central objective of any pharmaceutical sovereignty strategy. Recent shortages,
including sterile injectables, antimicrobials, and paediatric formulations have
demonstrated how heavily Canada relies on globally concentrated supply chains for
essential medicines. Hospitals and providers are increasingly forced to manage
unpredictable supply, leading to increased risk with substitutions, rationing, and
clinical workarounds that strain staff and can compromise patient care. Any policy
changes must therefore be evaluated through the lens of reliable patient access and
continuity of care, particularly during global disruptions.
Strategic Domestic Manufacturing Capacity
Canada is not currently positioned to pursue full pharmaceutical self-sufficiency.
Pharmaceutical manufacturing is capital-intensive and relies on sustained scale
across multiple product classes. Replicating end-to-end manufacturing capacity
across all drug classes would require significant investment and sufficient volume to
support it, conditions that Canada cannot currently sustain.

Replicating end-to-end manufacturing capacity
across all drug classes would require significant investment and sufficient volume to
support it, conditions that Canada cannot currently sustain.

Instead, domestic manufacturing should be strategically targeted to areas of highest
clinical and system risk such as sterile injectables, antimicrobials, emergency and
critical-care medicines, and high-volume hospital-based products. This should be
informed by Health Canada’s Critical and Vulnerable Drug List (CVDL) which focuses
on medications that present a serious risk of harm to human health and vulnerable to
shortages. Strengthening domestic capability must also include upstream
components such as Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), Key Starting
Materials (KSMs), and onshore storage of critical inputs as these building blocks
represent the earliest point in supply chain vulnerability. This targeted approach
enhances resilience where it matters most, without introducing inefficiencies or
escalating costs across the system.
Smart Procurement as a Policy Lever
Public-sector purchasing power is one of the most effective tools available to
strengthen pharmaceutical sovereignty. Traditional procurement models often
emphasize short-term cost considerations and do not fully account for the broader
impacts of supply-chain risk.

Incorporating risk-adjusted evaluation criteria such as supply reliability, redundancy,
sustainability, and domestic production can incentivize manufacturers to invest in
more resilient and diversified production. These approaches can be designed using
non-discriminatory, outcome-based criteria focused on supply continuity, resilience,
and system performance, applied transparently and consistently across all bidders to
remain compliant with trade obligations while supporting domestic capability and

These approaches can be designed using
non-discriminatory, outcome-based criteria focused on supply continuity, resilience,
and system performance, applied transparently and consistently across all bidders to
remain compliant with trade obligations while supporting domestic capability and

long-term supply security. This could be aligned with the Government of Canada’s
Buy Canadian Policy.
Regulatory Agility and Predictability
Faster, streamlined, and predictable regulatory pathways are essential to attract and
retain pharmaceutical manufacturing in Canada. Manufacturers consistently cite
regulatory uncertainty and long approval timelines as barriers to investing in domestic
production or bringing alternative suppliers to the Canadian market. Strengthening
predictability and reducing administrative burden would make Canada a more
competitive jurisdiction for both innovative and generic manufacturers.
Priority review for clinically critical and shortage-prone drugs (per CVDL), alignment
with trusted international regulators, and expedited pathways for alternative suppliers
during shortages would significantly improve responsiveness. These measures would
help ensure that new sources of supply can be approved quickly when disruptions
occur, reduce the duration and severity of shortages, and signal to industry that
Canada is committed to a modern, efficient regulatory environment. A more agile
regulatory system is a foundational component of pharmaceutical sovereignty and a
prerequisite for meaningful domestic manufacturing growth.
Data Sharing Builds Supply Chain Transparency and Early Warning
Canada lacks a coordinated national approach to real-time data sharing on drug
demand, inventory levels, and manufacturing disruptions. This creates blind spots
across the system and limits the ability of governments and health-system partners to
anticipate emerging shortages before they escalate. Today, information is fragmented
across multiple jurisdictions and supply-chain actors, making it difficult to identify
early signals of stress or coordinate mitigation strategies in a timely manner.
Improved transparency through data sharing across governments, manufacturers,
distributors, group purchasing organizations, and providers would enable earlier
intervention and reduce the need for reactive crisis management. Consistent,
standardized data sharing would support more accurate demand forecasting, better
allocation of limited supply, and clearer visibility into upstream risks. Starting with
medicines of highest clinical and system risk - such as sterile injectables,
antimicrobials, emergency and critical-care medicines, and high-volume hospitalbased products - a national early-warning and forecasting approach, supported by
real-time data and shared accountability, would strengthen preparedness and enable
a more proactive, coordinated system response.

antimicrobials, emergency and critical-care medicines, and high-volume hospitalbased products - a national early-warning and forecasting approach, supported by

a more proactive, coordinated system response.

Alignment of Manufacturing, Health, and Innovation Policy
Pharmaceutical sovereignty requires coordinated action across health policy,
manufacturing strategy, innovation, and tax policy. These domains often operate in
parallel, yet the effectiveness of any one lever depends on how well it aligns with the
others. For example, domestic manufacturing incentives are far more impactful when
paired with regulatory agility, predictable procurement signals, and a clear
understanding of clinical priorities across the health system. A coherent,
cross-government approach ensures that investments in sovereignty translate into
tangible improvements in supply security and patient access.
Targeted incentives, including capital investment support, advanced manufacturing
technologies, and workforce development, should be tied to clear public-interest
outcomes such as supply security, affordability, and long-term system resilience. At
the same time, policies must be designed to avoid unintended consequences such as
reduced competition, delayed generic entry, or increased costs for public and private
payers. Ensuring that manufacturing and innovation policies reinforce, rather than
inadvertently strain, the broader health system is essential to building a sustainable
and balanced approach to pharmaceutical sovereignty.
Collaboration Over Isolation: Balance Domestic with Global Sourcing
The most resilient and cost-effective approach combines strategic domestic capacity
with diversified global sourcing, strong partnerships with trusted allies, shared
early-warning systems, and coordinated shortage-mitigation efforts. This balanced
model allows Canada to strengthen supply security for clinically critical medicines
while continuing to benefit from the innovation, efficiency, and redundancy that global
supply networks provide.
Focusing solely on domestic production could unintentionally narrow supplier options
or increase system costs. A collaborative approach, one that reinforces domestic
strengths while maintaining broad international connections, offers a more practical
and sustainable path to long-term resilience.

A collaborative approach, one that reinforces domestic
strengths while maintaining broad international connections, offers a more practical
and sustainable path to long-term resilience.

Recommendations
1. Prioritize uninterrupted patient access as the central objective of Canada’s
pharmaceutical sovereignty strategy.
2. Develop targeted domestic manufacturing capacity focused on a defined list of
clinically critical medicines - such as sterile injectables, antimicrobials, and
emergency and critical-care drugs - along with key upstream inputs (APIs and
KSMs), using clear prioritization criteria and phased implementation.
3. Modernize public-sector procurement to incorporate more risk-adjusted
evaluation criteria, including reliability, redundancy, sustainability, and
domestic capability, while remaining fully trade-compliant.
4. Enhance regulatory agility through predictable, streamlined pathways,
including priority review for critical and shortage-prone drugs and expedited
approval of alternative suppliers during disruptions.
5. Establish a coordinated national system for real-time data sharing,
early-warning, and demand forecasting across the pharmaceutical supply
chain.
6. Align manufacturing, health, innovation, and tax policy to support supply
security, affordability, and system resilience while avoiding unintended impacts
on competition or costs.
7. Strengthen international collaboration with trusted partners to diversify supply,
share early-warning intelligence, and coordinate shortage-mitigation efforts.

Conclusion
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is best advanced through a balanced approach that
strengthens targeted domestic capability while maintaining diversified, globally
connected supply chains. HealthPRO Canada’s decades of experience across the
hospital and acute-care system shows that resilience depends on reliable access to
essential medicines, modernized procurement practices, regulatory agility, and
coordinated national action supported by timely, transparent data.
A thoughtful, collaborative strategy, one that reinforces domestic strengths, leverages
trusted international partnerships, and aligns policy, will help ensure that Canadians
continue to have stable access to the medicines they rely on. HealthPRO Canada
appreciates the Committee’s leadership on this issue and remains committed to
sharing system-level insights and working with federal partners to enhance the
security and sustainability of Canada’s pharmaceutical supply chain.

The pandemic and the rise of global geopolitical tensions have highlighted uncomfortable
truths:
• Domestic capacity must be in place before a crisis; it cannot be created quickly
enough when supply chains falter.
• Border disruptions, export restrictions, and geopolitical shocks can destabilize
international medicine supply. Canada requires a dependable domestic base as
part of a diversified resilience strategy.
• Predictable policy drives investment: companies invest in modernization and
expansion when regulatory and procurement signals are stable and competitive.
Geopolitical instability makes the case even stronger: Canada must be able to rely on its
own productive capacity for a significant share of its medicine needs.
Additionally, Canada’s price environment has become increasingly unsustainable. Generic
medicines, which represent most prescriptions, cannot be adjusted for inflation and are
often tied to decade-old pricing. This erodes the viability of domestic production,
accelerates market exits, and increases reliance on fragile global supply chains.
Canada also faces a widening access gap for new medicines. Pharmascience operates both
a generic and a branded portfolio, and through Pendopharm we bring to Canadians
therapies that some multinational companies choose not to launch domestically, including
pediatric formulations addressing unmet needs. Yet, according to recent PMPRB market
entry data, only a fraction of medicines launched in the U.S. and Europe ever reach
Canada. Emerging U.S. pricing policies, such as Most Favored Nation concepts, may further
reduce incentives to launch products in smaller markets. This creates a new type of
vulnerability: Canadians may never gain access to certain treatments unless policy
frameworks evolve to make Canada a more attractive first launch market.
Beyond economic pressures, modern defense readiness depends on secure medicine
access. The WHO documented in Ukraine that when access collapses, over 84% of deaths
stem from chronic diseases, illustrating that medicines are strategic infrastructure.
Recent analyses, including a 2026 New England Journal of Medicine report, highlight deep
fragility in globalized drug supply chains, with significant quality deficiencies in foreign
manufacturing hubs. Canada is acutely exposed: 88% of generic medicines sold
domestically are manufactured abroad, mainly in India; Canada reports one of the highest

Canada is acutely exposed: 88% of generic medicines sold
domestically are manufactured abroad, mainly in India; Canada reports one of the highest

active drug-shortage rates globally; and India remains the country with the highest FDA
non-compliance observations. These realities underscore the urgency of strengthening
resilient Canadian manufacturing.
3. Procurement & national security: Canada should be its own best customer
International peers, notably the U.S. and EU, view pharmaceutical production as a national
security imperative and have deployed procurement preferences and industrial incentives
accordingly. Canada has begun moving in this direction through the Buy Canadian policy and
Defense Industrial Strategy.

Recommendations
1. Formally recognize medicines as national security goods, unlocking procurement tools
under existing security exceptions in trade agreements.
2. Establish domestic value-added criteria in procurement (e.g., substantial transformation
in manufacturing steps and significant R&D performed in Canada).
3. Develop reliability weighted procurement criteria, rewarding manufacturers with
validated domestic capacity and strong historic continuity of supply.
4. The federal government should lead by example by prioritizing Canadianmanufactured- medicines in the drug plans it directly administers—including those
serving veterans, members of the Canadian Armed Forces, federal inmates, First Nations
communities, and federal public servants—thereby reinforcing domestic production and
advancing Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty.

4. Regulatory modernization that supports sovereignty
A. Ensuring Reliance mechanisms support, rather than weaken, Canadian capacity
Pharmascience fully supports regulatory modernization, including targeted reliance
mechanisms, tools that allow Health Canada to streamline its reviews by basing part
of its assessment on the scientific evaluations or decisions of trusted foreign
regulators, with the goal of accelerating patient access.
However, if the proposed Reliance Order is applied too broadly, it risks creating
structural advantages for foreign importers and unintentionally weakening Canadian
developers and manufacturers. A balanced framework is essential if modernization is
to reinforce Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty.

A balanced framework is essential if modernization is
to reinforce Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty.

To ensure the Reliance framework supports rather than disadvantages domestic
manufacturers, we strongly encourage Health Canada to systematically consult
Canadian producers before publishing new regulations or reliance policies. Recent
experiences, including the implementation of the Reliance Order and issues such as
nitrosamine guidance, illustrate how lack of early coordination can create unintended
disadvantages for Canadian firms. A structured, predictable consultation process,
combined with a defined priority review pathway for drugs developed or
manufactured in Canada, would ensure that reliance accelerates access without
undermining domestic competitiveness.
A priority review pathway for drugs developed or manufactured in Canada would
ensure that domestic producers, who invest in Canadian jobs, facilities, and R&D, are
not disadvantaged compared to foreign manufacturers who may leverage reliance to
accelerate market entry.

The reliance framework must also be narrow and strategic, with a carefully defined
list focused on areas where reliance truly adds value, such as pediatric formulations
or rare disease therapies. Broad application to generic medicines would carry greater
risk of unintended consequences and should be avoided.

B. Addressing structural bottlenecks: Notices of Non-Compliance, predictability, and
review capacity
A key concern relates to how Notices of Non-Compliance (NONs) are issued. NONs are
sometimes delivered very late in the review process, occasionally only hours before
the deadline, for issues that could have been clarified earlier in the assessment. This
forces companies to restart the review cycle unnecessarily, delaying approvals by
several months and reducing predictability for manufacturers. Addressing these
structural bottlenecks is essential to ensure that modernization initiatives, including
the implementation of the Reliance Order, deliver real improvements.
Improving reviewer capacity and process efficiency, establishing clearer
communication channels, and ensuring that clarifications can be requested before a
NON is issued would create a more collaborative and effective review model.
Beyond improving the timing and communication around Notices of Non-Compliance,
strengthening early scientific advice pathways would also improve predictability.
Access to structured, expert guidance from Health Canada and the National Research

Access to structured, expert guidance from Health Canada and the National Research

Council (NRC) can significantly derisk the development of Canadian made innovations,
such as novel formulations, yet this channel remains underused. Formalizing access
to early advice, with clear timelines and scope, would help companies choose Canada
as a preferred jurisdiction for first development and scaleup.
C. Unblocking the approval pipeline: patent evergreening and skinny labels
Patent evergreening delays competition and raises costs, weakening Canada’s
competitiveness and sovereignty. A related bottleneck is the inconsistent treatment
of indication carveouts (“skinny labels”) that allow generics and biosimilar
manufacturers to launch products for indications that are off patents. Recent
developments have created uncertainty by exposing manufacturers to infringement
risk even when patented indications are excluded from Health Canada-approved
product monographs. Unlike jurisdictions like the US where a clear regulatory
framework facilitates timely market entry of skinny label generic products and
predictable investment decisions, Canada lacks a clear, sovereignty aligned
framework. We recommend the establishment of a clear model and the issuance of
explicit guidance from Health Canada on indication carveouts to restore legal certainty
for skinny labels and ensure alignment with public health and pro-competition
objectives.

D. Targeted exclusivity pathways to unlock access-first launches
Canada provides data exclusivity for patented new chemical entities, but not for
certain follow-on innovations introduced by companies that do not hold the original
patent/data, even when these products bring therapies otherwise unavailable to
Canadians. The EU and U.S. offer targeted exclusivity pathways that can apply to multiindication or non-patented follow-on innovations; Canada should pilot a limited,
criteria-based exclusivity pathway to encourage access first launches where unmet
need is demonstrated
5. Fiscal measures that anchor manufacturing in Canada
Canada must match global competitors who are using predictable and attractive industrial
incentives to secure pharmaceutical manufacturing. Pharmascience proposes:
1. Refundable 10% profit-based manufacturing credit

Refundable 10% profit-based manufacturing credit

Shared 5% federal / 5% provincial, applied to profits from the sale/export of Canadianmanufactured medicines. This directly rewards domestic production and improves
competitiveness.
2. Federal C3I-style refundable investment & innovation credit
A 15% refundable credit to accelerate modernization, automation, and advanced
manufacturing technologies, focused on strategic sectors designated by the Buy Canadian
policy.
3. Modernized SR&ED aligning with Québec’s CRIC
Expand eligibility to pre-commercial activities and certain capital expenditures; provide
enhanced refundable rates; and create specific guidance for generic development.
4. Restore tax incentives for medicine donations
Reinstate preferential tax treatment for donations of Canadian-manufactured medicines
to improve access for vulnerable populations and reduce waste.
6. Mitigating shortage risks through domestic production
Canada experiences one of the highest reported rates of drug shortages among comparable
jurisdictions. Strengthening sovereignty requires reinforcing existing domestic production
capacity, particularly as geopolitical instability intensifies risks.
Given Canada’s heavy reliance on foreign suppliers, approximately 88% of medicines sold in
Canada are manufactured abroad, the most impactful strategy is to:
•
Strengthen and expand brick-and--mortar production sites already operating- in Canada.
•
Encourage incremental capacity upgrades for complex generics and high-value
medicines.
•
Enhance policy predictability for Canadian manufacturers through procurement and
regulatory alignment, ensuring sustained domestic output.
•
Recognize that geopolitical instability makes reliance on foreign manufacturing
increasingly fragile, reinforcing the need for a stronger Canadian base.
This approach strengthens supply assurance and reduces the risk that Canadians face delayed or
unavailable treatments during global disruptions.
7. What success looks like

Within 12–24 months, Canada can achieve:
•
Faster and more predictable approvals for Canadian-developed and manufactured
medicines.
•
Procurement practices that reward domestic value-add and reliability.
•
Increased modernization investments in Canadian plants.
•
Stronger resilience to global disruptions, including those driven by geopolitical tensions.
Conclusion
Canada has an opportunity, and an obligation, to strengthen its pharmaceutical sovereignty. By
modernizing regulation responsibly, aligning procurement with national security objectives, and
deploying targeted fiscal tools, Canada can reinforce its domestic pharmaceutical base and ensure
reliable access to medicines for Canadians.
Pharmascience stands ready to support Parliament, Health Canada, Finance Canada, and
provincial partners in implementing this vision.

Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Canada Inc. appreciates the opportunity to provide input to the House
of Commons Standing Committee on Health as part of its study on Pharmaceutical Sovereignty.
Introduction
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is a shared objective: ensuring that Canadians have reliable, timely,
and affordable access to essential medicines, including during periods of global disruption.
From the perspective of a global generic pharmaceutical manufacturer with a strong Canadian
footprint, Dr. Reddy’s believes this objective is best achieved through a balanced and pragmatic
approach that strengthens domestic capacity while fully leveraging trusted global manufacturing
and regulatory partnerships, supported by an efficient and predictable regulatory environment.
Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories offers the following recommendations on securing Canada’s Drug
Sovereignty.
1. Place access to generics at the centre of pharmaceutical sovereignty discussions.
2. Pursue a balanced strategy that integrates domestic and global manufacturing.
3. Work towards more predictable Health Canada approval timelines.
4. Promote supplier diversity rather than concentration.
5. Leverage trade and international regulatory cooperation.
The Central Role of Generics in Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
Generics play an essential role in Canada’s health system, delivering the majority of prescription
volumes and generating significant cost savings for public and private payers. Any strategy
aimed at pharmaceutical sovereignty must therefore place access to generics at its core.
Given their key role, generic medicines are essential to the sustainability and resilience of
Canada’s health care system. They provide affordable treatment options across a wide range of
therapeutic areas, enable provinces and territories to manage drug budgets, and serve as
critical substitutes during shortages of branded medicines.
For pharmaceutical sovereignty to be meaningful in practice, it must ensure that generic
medicines reach Canadian patients without unnecessary delay, particularly during supply
disruptions.
Domestic Manufacturing Is Important, but Not Sufficient on Its Own
With conversations around ensuring Canada’s domestic supply chains in other key industries,
ensuring Canada has sufficient and growing domestic manufacturing is a key aspect of
pharmaceutical sovereignty. While Dr. Reddy’s supports efforts to grow the domestic
pharmaceutical manufacturing sector where it is economically and operationally viable, it is also
important to ensure a resilient international supply chain.
Modern pharmaceutical supply chains are highly specialized and internationally integrated. A
strategy focused solely on domestic manufacturing risks narrowing supplier diversity, increasing
costs, and unintentionally limiting patient access to more affordable options.

A
strategy focused solely on domestic manufacturing risks narrowing supplier diversity, increasing
costs, and unintentionally limiting patient access to more affordable options.

By ensuring that global partnerships and resilient international supply chains are a key
component of the conversation around pharmaceutical sovereignty, and by expanding domestic
capacity, Canada would be well-positioned to withstand disruptions to production at home and
abroad.
Predictable Health Canada Approval Timelines Are Essential to Pharmaceutical
Sovereignty
A resilient domestic pharmaceutical supply cannot be achieved without a regulatory system that
delivers timely, predictable access to the Canadian market. While manufacturing capacity and
supply chain diversification are important components of pharmaceutical sovereignty, regulatory
delays at Health Canada remain a significant structural barrier to ensuring consistent access to
medicines in Canada.
Prolonged and unpredictable approval timelines for generic medicines reduce the viability of the
Canadian market, discourage early or parallel filings, and delay patient access to essential
therapies. For manufacturers making global allocation decisions about where to prioritize
product launches and supply, regulatory uncertainty directly undermines efforts to strengthen
domestic and near-domestic supply.
From Dr. Reddy’s perspective, pharmaceutical sovereignty must therefore include a clear focus
on regulatory efficiency. Without predictable approval timelines, even medicines manufactured
domestically can face delays in reaching Canadian patients, limiting the practical value of
domestic investment.
Dr. Reddy’s has consistently recommended targeted regulatory reforms at Health Canada to
address these challenges, including the expanded use of reliance-based pathways, greater
transparency around review timelines, and more consistent application of risk-based
approaches for generic submissions. Reliance on trusted international regulators with
comparable standards can reduce duplication, allow Health Canada to focus resources where
they add the most value, and improve overall system efficiency while maintaining Canada’s high
safety and quality standards.
Uncertainty in the approval process also exacerbates drug shortages. During periods of global
supply disruption, the ability to rapidly authorize alternate suppliers or therapeutically equivalent
generics is critical. Delays in regulatory review, even when products are already approved and
in use in peer jurisdictions, limit Canada’s flexibility to respond to shortages and constrain the
effectiveness of both domestic and international supply strategies.
Improving the predictability and timeliness of Health Canada approvals would directly support
the federal government’s objectives related to pharmaceutical sovereignty by:
•
Enabling faster access to affordable generic medicines;
•
Strengthening supplier diversity and competition;
•
Supporting domestic manufacturing investments by reducing market risk; and
•
Enhancing Canada’s ability to respond quickly to supply disruptions.
In this context, regulatory modernization should be viewed not as a separate policy objective,
but as a foundational enabler of pharmaceutical sovereignty. A more efficient and predictable
approval system would complement efforts to expand domestic capacity, leverage global

A more efficient and predictable
approval system would complement efforts to expand domestic capacity, leverage global

manufacturing networks, and ensure that Canadians benefit from both secure supply and timely
access to medicines.
The Importance of Global Partnerships and Regulatory Reliance
Global pharmaceutical companies with established manufacturing networks play a critical role in
ensuring supply resilience, and require a stable, predictable regulatory environment to truly
benefit Canadians.
Regulatory reliance frameworks, when applied in a risk-based and transparent manner, allow
Health Canada to maintain high standards of safety and quality while improving timeliness and
predictability. Faster access to approved generics directly supports affordability, competition,
and system sustainability.
Conclusion
Pharmaceutical sovereignty is ultimately about ensuring reliable access to affordable
pharmaceutical drugs for Canadian patients. As the Standing Committee on Health considers
the importance of domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories
encourages a holistic approach that also recognizes the critical role of regulatory efficiency in
enabling secure, resilient supply.
Without predictable and timely regulatory approvals, efforts to expand domestic capacity or
diversify supply chains will continue to face structural limitations. Strengthening regulatory
efficiency, alongside leveraging generics, biosimilars, and a fully integrated supply chain, is
essential to delivering meaningful pharmaceutical sovereignty in practice.
Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories stands ready to work with the Government of Canada to advance a
pragmatic, patient-centred approach to pharmaceutical sovereignty that supports access,
affordability and supply resilience.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce is pleased to contribute to the Standing Committee
on Health’s study of Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty. Ensuring a reliable supply of
essential medicines, devices and equipment is critical for health security and economic
resilience. Enhancing access to these goods is also vital for addressing health system
challenges and supporting our life sciences sector, which is a driver of innovation and
economic growth. In a less secure geopolitical climate, and as we face unprecedented
economic headwinds, a strong life sciences sector and domestic production capabilities
are valuable national assets.

However, rather than focusing on “pharmaceutical sovereignty,” the government should
instead pursue a policy of “pharmaceutical resilience.” While building domestic production
capacity is important, it is unrealistic for Canada to domestically produce all the medical
goods it needs. The best way to ensure access to critical medicines and equipment is
through a competitive life sciences sector. International trade and integration into global
supply chains is a vital precondition of our sector’s success and limiting our ability to
import the goods we need and of our domestic firms to participate in the global economy
will be counterproductive. In addition to strong domestic manufacturing capacity, risks
arising from disruptions to global supply chains can also be managed through bilateral or
multilateral mechanisms that protect the movement of medical goods during crises.

As the U.S. administration continues the overhaul of its trade policy, Canada’s life
sciences sector is faced with a new set of challenges. Chief among these is the effort of
the U.S. administration to rebalance global pharmaceutical pricing through its mostfavoured nation (MFN) policy. In light of U.S. list prices for name-brand drugs regularly
running several times higher than those abroad, the MFN policy would benchmark U.S.
prices to countries with a GDP per capita at least 60% of the U.S. Rather than face
significant losses in the U.S. market, drug manufacturers could withdraw or avoid smaller
markets like Canada, which accounts for only 2% of global pharmaceutical demand.

Rather than face
significant losses in the U.S. market, drug manufacturers could withdraw or avoid smaller
markets like Canada, which accounts for only 2% of global pharmaceutical demand.

Given the potentially profound consequences, a response that increases our support for
pharmaceutical innovation and production is needed. We have a broad range of potential
tools at our disposal, including the creation of a fund to support life sciences innovation,
reducing wait times for patients on public plans to access new drugs, building on red tape
reduction initiatives at Health Canada, and aligning our intellectual property (IP) rules with

those of key trading partners. These policies will incentivise investment in the life sciences
sector and effectively increase our support for pharmaceutical innovation.

A vision of pharmaceutical resilience must also include measures to ensure access to
medical devices and equipment, which increasingly work hand in hand with
pharmaceuticals in treating medical conditions. Currently, the U.S. administration is
conducting a Section 232 study on medical devices, PPE, and consumables. Likewise,
while building domestic manufacturing capacity is important, overly restrictive “Buy
Canadian” policies could threaten to restrict access to needed devices and equipment in
Canada. Limiting trade restrictions on medical devices must also be prioritised in trade
negotiations, including during the CUSMA review.

We submit the below recommendations for the Committee’s consideration. We would be

Recommendations
1. Continue to build on the vision of the Biomanufacturing and Life Sciences
Strategy of a strong domestic life sciences industry

Launched in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Biomanufacturing and Life
Sciences Strategy (BLSS) invested $2.2 billion into Canada’s life sciences industry. The
strategy correctly recognised that decades of decline in Canada’s domestic life sciences
capacity left us vulnerable and struggling to secure vaccines, medicines and equipment
from international partners. It also correctly concluded that the best way to ensure our
future health emergency preparedness was to reverse the decline by building a strong and
diversified domestic industry. Beyond direct investments, the BLSS identified several other
policy measures to support the sector, including developing the life sciences talent
pipeline, building public capacity, and regulatory modernisation.

Beyond direct investments, the BLSS identified several other
policy measures to support the sector, including developing the life sciences talent
pipeline, building public capacity, and regulatory modernisation.

Now that BLSS funds have been fully allocated to address pressing gaps, the focus should
be on improving the business environment for life sciences industry. Canada has several
natural advantages, including, most notably, a world-class research ecosystem. Yet limited
commercialisation pathways, lengthy approval and reimbursement timelines, and poorly
calibrated intellectual property rules continue to constrain our potential. We must not forget
the lessons of the pandemic and should proceed with a clear vision for growing Canada’s
life sciences industry.
2. Establish a Health Innovation and Resilience Fund to rapidly address
Canada’s underfunding of pharmaceutical innovation and respond to MFN
policy

A 2025 EY analysis shows that Canada spends just 0.32% of GDP per capita on
innovative medicines, compared with 0.78% in the U.S. 0.34% for EU countries. With
efforts underway to rebalance funding for global pharmaceutical innovation, this gap puts
Canada at risk. If U.S. most favoured nation policy is implemented, our access to latest
and best medicines could be severely disrupted, potentially limiting patient access to
medicines and freezing pharmaceutical investment.

Establishing a Health Innovation and Resilience Fund is a measure that can help us
quickly increase our funding of pharmaceutical innovation and close the gap with other
jurisdictions. The Fund could be used to support life sciences innovation and the
government’s goal of speeding access to new treatments by incentivising provincial and
territorial uptake of new drugs on public formularies. Additionally, investments could count
towards NATO spending targets where they align with defence objectives.

Lost or delayed access to the best treatments will mean worse health outcomes and
potentially higher overall health care spending. Less life sciences investment, which is
particularly R&D intensive, could further widen our innovation gap with peer countries and
translate to lower economic growth.

3. Better align intellectual property (IP) standards with the EU and U.S. by
extending patent term adjustments and data exclusivity

Better align intellectual property (IP) standards with the EU and U.S. by
extending patent term adjustments and data exclusivity

Canada’s IP rules are currently misaligned with those in the U.S. and European Union
(EU). Canada’s patent term adjustment system grants innovators up to two years of
additional protection due to time lost during regulatory approval processes, which is
significantly less than the five years available in both the U.S. and the EU. The two-year
cap may also not satisfy the intent of Canada’s CUSMA commitments on IP (chapter 20).
Shorter patent term adjustments are a significant source of uncertainty for innovators who
may fear insufficient compensation for time lost during regulatory review.

Data exclusivity is also shorter in Canada, lasting only eight years, whereas it lasts 12
years in the U.S., for biologics, and up to 11 years in the EU. An early version of the
CUSMA agreement included provisions requiring Canada to extend data exclusivity to 10
years. This extension should be implemented to incentivise pharmaceutical investment,
innovation, and product launches in Canada.
4. Work with provinces and territories to accelerate patient access to new
treatments

A 2023 analysis by PhRMA shows that Canadians on public drug plans currently face the
longest wait times in the G7 to access new medicines. Whereas patients in countries like
France and Germany generally face little to no wait times to access new medicines,
Canadians must wait, on average, 52 months following the first global launch. This
translates to worse health outcomes and more resources spent on emergency room visits
or extended hospital stays that could have been avoided had patients had access to the
right drugs. Given that approximately 21% of Canadians are on public drug plans,
according to Statistics Canada, these delays also disincentivise drug manufacturers from
investing and launching new treatments in Canada.

Given that approximately 21% of Canadians are on public drug plans,
according to Statistics Canada, these delays also disincentivise drug manufacturers from
investing and launching new treatments in Canada.

While the drug approval and listing process involves several complicated steps, most
delay occurs following the conclusion of pricing negotiations between drug manufacturers
and the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance, and provincial and territorial governments
listing new drugs on their formularies. The federal government should work with provinces
and territories to reduce these delays. Ontario’s Funding for Specific Treatments (FAST)
programme, which provides access to select high-priority cancer drugs immediately
following a positive recommendation from Canada’s Drug Agency, is a useful model that
could be replicated nationally and eventually expanded to other drug categories.
5. Appropriately calibrate “Buy Canadian” policies to prevent medical supply
chain disruptions

Foreign drug suppliers account for approximately 70% of Canadian demand. Similarly,
Canada depends on a globally integrated medical technology industry for critical devices
and equipment. It would therefore be unrealistic for Canada to reshore all production.
Proposed “Buy Canadian” policies, while intended to support the domestic industry, could

isolate it from the global ecosystem that supports its competitiveness. Unintended
consequences of poorly calibrated “Buy-Canadian” policies are especially concerning in
relation to medical goods because they could interfere with patient treatment and lead to
worse health outcomes. With the U.S. MFN policy and Section 232 studies threatening a
range of medical goods, we should avoid adding to harmful trade restrictions with “BuyCanadian” policies, especially given the sensitive nature of medical goods. While we
should seek to increase domestic production capabilities, incentives should remain
voluntary.
6. Work with like-minded countries to ensure access to essential medicines,
devices and equipment during crises

Life sciences supply chains are globally diversified and highly integrated. It may be wise to
produce certain vulnerable medical goods within Canada, but as a small market, we
cannot be fully self-sufficient. Risks to global supply chain disruptions are best mitigated by
upholding the rules-based international trading system, which includes working with
partners to strengthen specific frameworks relating to the trade of medical goods.
Additional agreements with like-minded countries to guarantee the continued flow of
medical goods during crises may also be worth pursuing.

Executive Summary
BioCanRx – Canada's Immunotherapy Network – respectfully submits this brief to the Standing Committee
on Health in support of its study on Canada's pharmaceutical sovereignty.

Canada's discussion of pharmaceutical sovereignty has focused predominantly on supply-chain security:
securing access to medicines manufactured elsewhere. That framing, while important, addresses only half
the question. True pharmaceutical sovereignty also requires the capacity to create novel therapies on
Canadian soil — to move Canadian discoveries from the laboratory to the clinic and into patients' hands. On
that dimension, Canada's performance is measurably poor, and the cause is structural.

In December 2025, BioCanRx commissioned the Institute on Governance (IOG) to benchmark Canada's
translational health research ecosystem against six international comparators. The finding is unambiguous:
Canada does not lack excellent science or policy effort. It lacks the governance infrastructure to convert
discovery into therapy. Advanced therapies — including the cell and gene therapies that represent the next
generation of medicine — fall structurally between federal mandates: too applied for federal health
research funding, too risky for private capital.

The consequences are visible: only 3.4% of cancer immunotherapy clinical trials conducted in Canada
between 2002 and March 2026 were based on made-in-Canada innovations. Canada is the only G7 nation
without a domestic pharmaceutical company producing novel medicines. These are not market failures.
They are governance failures.

The recent $280 million Government of Canada commitment to advance Aspect Biosystems' bioengineered
cellular medicines — a Canadian company developing therapies in partnership with a global industry leader
— illustrates precisely what is possible when translational infrastructure, industrial partnership, and
sovereign manufacturing capacity converge. It also illustrates how rare this convergence currently is in
Canada, and how dependent it remains on ad hoc co-investment rather than durable governance
architecture.

BioCanRx urges the Committee to adopt a definition of pharmaceutical sovereignty that encompasses
sovereign innovation capacity — not only supply security — and to recommend governance reforms that
will make outcomes like the Aspect Biosystems model the rule, not the exception.

It is the direct product of a milestone-driven, outcome-accountable
governance model applied to health research — a model that the broader federal system does not yet
replicate at scale.

2. Reframing Pharmaceutical Sovereignty: Supply Security Is Necessary but Not
Sufficient
The conventional framing of pharmaceutical sovereignty focuses on resilience: ensuring Canadians can
access medicines when global supply chains are disrupted, when geopolitical pressures alter trade flows, or
when foreign manufacturers reallocate supply to larger markets. These are legitimate and urgent concerns,
and Canada must address them.

But sovereignty defined only as supply security is, by definition, a dependent condition. It accepts that
Canada will continue to rely on innovations created elsewhere and asks only that access to those
innovations remain stable. That framing forecloses the more important question: why is Canada not creating
more of these therapies itself?

Canada's position on this dimension is documented and troubling:
• Only 3.4% of cancer immunotherapy clinical trials conducted in Canada between 2002 and March
2026 were based on made-in-Canada innovations — despite world-class Canadian researchers,
hospitals, and publicly funded science infrastructure.¹
• Canada is the only G7 nation without a domestic pharmaceutical company producing novel medicines.
• Canada invests only 1.5% of total health expenditures in research — well below international peers
who have already built dedicated national translational infrastructure.²

These are not market failures. Canada has excellent discovery science. The problem, as the IOG's December
2025 analysis makes clear, is that Canada systematically fails to convert that science into products. The fault
lies in governance architecture, not scientific capacity.

True pharmaceutical sovereignty — the kind that generates economic returns, secures patient access to
novel therapies, and insulates Canada from supply dependence — requires the capacity to create, not
merely to procure.

3. The Structural Failure: A Governance Gap, Not a Science Gap
In December 2025, BioCanRx commissioned the Institute on Governance (IOG) to assess Canada's
translational health research ecosystem against six international comparators — the United States, United
Kingdom, European Union, Japan, Australia, and China. The IOG's central finding is unambiguous:
"Canada faces a persistent institutional valley of death that signifies a gap, not of policy
effort, but of structural design."

The IOG's central finding is unambiguous:
"Canada faces a persistent institutional valley of death that signifies a gap, not of policy
effort, but of structural design."

The IOG identifies a "risk-governance deficit": Canada's two key federal portfolios — Health Canada (health,
regulatory, health research) and ISED (innovation, economic development, granting agencies) — are
intrinsically complementary but operate without mandated synchronization. Neither portfolio possesses an
adaptive mechanism for coordinating risk-based decision-making across the translational continuum.

The practical result is a structural funding gap — a "valley of death" with two distinct valleys:
• The Translation Gap: from bench-to-bedside. Translational work — GMP manufacturing, toxicology,
assay development, regulatory dossier preparation required for a Health Canada Clinical Trial
Application — is too applied for federal health research funding and too risky for private capital. No
federal funding mechanism is designed to bridge this gap.
• The Health System Adoption Gap: from regulatory approval to patient access. Therapies that have
obtained regulatory approval may remain inaccessible to patients for years due to reimbursement and
procurement delays across provincial health systems.

3.1 The CIHR Funding Gap: An Illustrative Case

In the 2023 and 2024 federal clinical trial competitions, three BioCanRx portfolio projects were selected to
receive clinical trial funding. None could proceed: they were unable to file a Clinical Trial Application to
Health Canada because the regulatory readiness work — considered too "applied" for health research
funding — had never been supported. These projects sat idle for at least one year. No federal funding
mechanism existed to bridge this gap.

All three subsequently received BioCanRx Enabling Studies or Clinical Trial funding through the Strategic
Science Fund. One has since opened a clinical trial offering a novel CAR-T therapy for pediatric and adult
blood cancer patients — a therapy that did not exist in Canada before.

This is not an isolated failure. It is structurally reproducible across any advanced therapy development
program in Canada. It is invisible to any single federal accountability framework because no single
framework has visibility across the full pipeline.

It is invisible to any single federal accountability framework because no single
framework has visibility across the full pipeline.

The pattern is consistent: peer nations that outperform Canada in translating health research to patient
benefit have not simply spent more — they have built coordinating institutions that reconcile the logic of
health research with the logic of health innovation. Canada has not.

4. Advanced Therapies as the Frontier of Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
Advanced therapies — cell therapies, gene therapies, and tissue-engineered products — represent the next
generation of medicine. They are not incremental improvements to existing pharmaceutical products. They
are disease-modifying and, in some cases, potentially curative. They are also uniquely demanding in their

development and manufacturing requirements: highly personalized, biologics-based, and dependent on
specialized GMP biomanufacturing infrastructure.

Canada has the scientific foundations to be a global leader in this field. The recent federal commitment to
advance Aspect Biosystems' pipeline of bioengineered cellular medicines — representing a $280 million
multi-year project building on prior federal and provincial co-investment — demonstrates the potential
when translational infrastructure, industrial partnership, and sovereign manufacturing capacity converge.
Aspect's collaboration with a global industry partner has integrated advanced cell therapy technologies into
a Canadian platform now targeting functional cures for metabolic and endocrine diseases, including Type 1
diabetes. This is exactly the model of pharmaceutical sovereignty that Canada should be building
systematically — not on a case-by-case basis.³

This is exactly the model of pharmaceutical sovereignty that Canada should be building
systematically — not on a case-by-case basis.³

BioCanRx's own CAR-T program illustrates the same potential at the cancer end of the spectrum. Canada has
the researchers, the hospitals, the patients, and the public investment to be a maker of these therapies —
not merely a buyer of them. The governance architecture to achieve this at scale does not yet exist.
The consequences of inaction compound over time. Advanced therapies are not yet fully globalized
commodities. The countries that build sovereign manufacturing and development capacity now will
determine access, pricing, and supply conditions for the next generation of medicine. Canada's window to
participate as a creator, not only a consumer, is open — but it will not remain open indefinitely.

5. Recommendations
BioCanRx respectfully urges the Committee to include the following in its report to the House:

Recommendation 1 — Redefine Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
Direct the government to adopt a definition of pharmaceutical sovereignty that encompasses both supplychain security and the sovereign capacity to develop, manufacture, and deploy novel therapies originating
from Canadian science. Policy recommendations and investment frameworks should be evaluated against
both dimensions.

Recommendation 2 — Establish a Dedicated Translational Health Research Program
Create a permanent, milestone-driven Translational Health Research Program within the federal research
funding architecture, scalable across disease areas, explicitly designed to bridge the gap between discovery
research and clinic-ready advanced therapy development. This program should operate with outcome
accountability metrics tied to patient access and Canadian manufacturing capacity — not only academic
publication outputs.

Recommendation 3 — Align Regulatory Readiness with Clinical Funding
Direct Health Canada and ISED to co-develop a regulatory readiness framework for advanced therapies that
funds the GMP manufacturing, toxicology, and CTA preparation activities currently falling between federal
mandates. Eligibility criteria for clinical trial funding should require or support a credible regulatory pathway,
not presuppose one already completed.

Recommendation 4 — Publish an Advanced Therapy Sovereignty Strategy with a Cross-Departmental
Coordination Mechanism
Direct the government to publish a sector-based Advanced Therapy Sovereignty Strategy with transparent
milestones, aligned accountability across Health Canada, ISED, and federal research bodies, and implement
the cross-departmental coordination mechanism recommended by the IOG — a translational research
concierge function to guide innovators through the full development pipeline. Canada currently has no
published framework coordinating federal action in this field.
