Strengthening Canada’s Pharmaceutical Resilience
Building Capacity Along the Value Chain in a Context of Strategic
Interdependence
Introduction
Recent disruptions in supply chains have reignited discussions about the resilience of health
care systems. The COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions and the concentration of
certain industrial capacities have exposed how vulnerable many countries are to disruptions
in the supply of drugs and health products.
The conclusion is clear: Canada must take action to strengthen its position in this strategic
sector. This means enhancing its research and development capacity, better capturing and
retaining the value of domestically developed innovation and supporting robust industrial
capacities. At the same time, it is essential to improve the conditions for accessing drugs to
ensure that the health care system operates smoothly.
In an environment marked by increasing geopolitical tension, a systemic approach is needed
to strengthen pharmaceutical resilience in the long term. Part of the solution lies in
developing local production capacities in several components of the pharmaceutical value
chain. Several countries have taken steps in this direction to better secure their supply of
health care products.1
However, the pharmaceutical industry is extremely globalized. The various stages of
research, development and production are spread across multiple countries, and this
international organization of value chains is now a structural characteristic of the sector.
Pharmaceutical resilience does not rely solely on the self-sufficiency of certain products, but
on a balance between developing local capacity and integrating into diversified and reliable
international supply chains. Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty is expressed through its
ability to choose, secure and diversify its interdependencies.
Canada has significant strengths at multiple stages of the pharmaceutical value chain. It has
recognized capacities in basic, preclinical and clinical research, drug formulation, and a
large network of contract research and pharmaceutical development organizations. In

The life sciences sector contributes to access to care, improved treatments for patients and

Background and key facts
Health security is now widely recognized as a national security issue. Canada is part of this
evolution. In its Defence Industrial Strategy, Canada notes that several allies explicitly link
biodefence and medical countermeasure readiness to their economic and national security,
and indicates having taken similar steps including the creation of Health Emergency
Readiness Canada.3 In that vein, drugs and their supply chains should be more widely
recognized as strategic components of national security.
As highlighted in the Québec Strategy 2025-2028, the price of generic drugs has driven
production abroad to emerging countries, compromising the reliability of supply.4 This trend
is reflected specifically in the production of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), which
is now highly concentrated in Asia, particularly in China and India.5
In terms of innovative drugs, a significant portion of API production is in North America and
Europe.6
This production model has helped reduce the costs of many drugs, but it has also led to a
concentration of certain capacities, which can weaken supply chains.

In several jurisdictions, drug shortages have been on the rise in recent years. International
analyses indicate that these shortages are generally the result of a combination of factors,
including dependence on a limited number of suppliers, the complexity of industrial
processes, price pressures and demand volatility. More than half of the reported shortages
are attributed to manufacturing and quality issues.7
Recent international trade policies are increasing the complexity of global supply chains, in
particular, tariffs, the CUSMA negotiation and the Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN) pricing
principle, impacting the transborder environment and introducing new uncertainty.
These factors call for a balanced approach that considers innovation, industrial capacity,
access to drugs and Canada’s integration into global value chains.
1. A shared objective: strengthening pharmaceutical resilience
Strengthening pharmaceutical resilience is a shared objective, in an environment
characterized by the interdependence of its value chains and the diversity of the levers
employed.
Capacity development should be considered in a holistic manner, covering all components
of the drug’s life cycle, including research, development, clinical trials and production.
This approach relies on mobilizing these levers in a complementary manner, to support
access to drugs, security of supply and the capacity for innovation of the health care system.
Recommendation 1 |
Adopt a national pharmaceutical resilience strategy based on strategic interdependence,
aimed at developing local capabilities, securing the supply chain through reliable and
complementary partnerships, and fostering the integration of innovation.

The production of drugs relies on a complex industrial value chain that includes several
distinct steps.
This industrial value chain includes:

•

•
Production of excipients required for drug formulation

3. Industrial capacity in Canada
Canada has certain industrial capacities in different aspects of the pharmaceutical value
chain. It has several pharmaceutical manufacturing sites and a limited number of
manufacturers of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) and finished products. Quebec is
home to an API manufacturer, demonstrating the presence industrial expertise in this
strategic area.
Although these capacities are real, they remain too limited in terms of the needs and
vulnerabilities that have been identified. This situation weakens supply, particularly in a
context of health, geopolitical or commercial disruptions.
Pharmaceutical manufacturing is both an economic and strategic issue. Increasing these
capacities is therefore critical to improving Canada’s pharmaceutical resilience. It
contributes to industrial activity, employment and exports, while also playing a role in the
country’s ability to ensure a stable supply of health care products that are essential to public
health.
Several jurisdictions are implementing industrial policies to attract and develop production

5. Business environment and market access
Canada's ability to attract investment in pharmaceutical research, development and
manufacturing relies in large part on a predictable, consistent and competitive business
environment. In a context of international competition and the reconfiguration of value
chains, these elements influence decisions to invest, locate and launch new products.
Market access is a key factor. The time lag between regulatory approval and actual access
to drugs, which are related to processes that are still too sequential, among other things,
influences the prioritization of launches, the carrying out of clinical trials and investments in
Canada. On average, it takes almost two years from approval to access for patients covered
by public plans.10 These delays have a direct impact on patients and limit the treatment
options available. Recent pressures on Health Canada’s resources are exacerbating some
operational challenges.
Innovations contribute to the efficiency of the health care system and complement the other
levers that are necessary for its performance. By reducing hospitalizations, improving
prevention and promoting a return to productivity, innovations generate benefits that exceed
their initial cost. Better recognition of this value would allow for greater alignment of
economic and health objectives.

type of policy has implications when it comes to the availability of certain treatments in

The intellectual property framework plays an important role in the competitiveness of the life
sciences sector and the development of innovation in Canada. The 2025 federal budget
highlights the importance of better protecting and enhancing intellectual property in order to
support the competitiveness and growth of Canada's knowledge-based economy.11 A
significant portion of the value related to intellectual property developed in Canada is still
being harnessed outside the country, which limits the growth of companies here and the
anchoring of activities. Better support for commercialization in Canada would further retain
this value and generate economic benefits.
In an environment of highly globalized pharmaceutical value chains, open and predictable
markets support the competitiveness of the Canadian sector, exports and the attraction of
investments. For developing companies, access to international markets is essential,
especially for building partnerships and supporting their growth.
Increasing the market share of local firms can strengthen Canada’s economy and industrial
capacity. Canadian value-added includes capacities that support the quality, continuity and
resilience of public services. These choices can promote local value-added, while supporting
an industrial ecosystem open to global innovation.

Conclusion
Strengthening Canada’s pharmaceutical resilience is a public health, national security and
economic development issue. Recent disruptions have highlighted the limitations of a model
based on highly concentrated supply chains. Despite this awareness, concrete actions
remain limited. Several jurisdictions have already taken initiatives to strengthen their
industrial capacities and secure their supply. Canada must be part of this dynamic.
Resilience is founded on an approach of strategic interdependence, combining the
development of targeted local capacities with diversified and reliable international
partnerships and strong measures to accelerate access to innovations. Canada’s
pharmaceutical sovereignty must be understood as the ability to act in this interconnected
environment. It is therefore a systemic approach: increasing competitiveness, reducing
vulnerabilities, strengthening industrial capacities and collaborating with reliable partners.
Public policy choices will be crucial. A clear strategy, based on well-defined priorities, a
predictable business environment and close collaboration between public and private actors
will not only secure supply, but also position Canada as a leading partner in the global life
sciences ecosystem.

Introduction
Tackling the topic of Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty necessitates recognizing that Canada
is affected by events beyond its borders over which it does not have full control, whether the
emergence and spread of a new disease that makes Canadians ill, or access to the medicines
that can make them better. Similarly, decisions made in Canada, such as the recent cuts to
global health under the federal international assistance budget, can have impacts on both the
spread of disease and access to medicines abroad. As a medical humanitarian organization
operating in over 70 countries, MSF witnesses firsthand the impact of outbreaks and epidemics
as they transcend national borders, as well as the deadly consequences of inequities in access
to medicines, vaccines and other health tools. The submission below emphasizes the fact
addressing Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty must look outward as well as inward to
effectively address Canada’s place within the larger world.

In making this submission, MSF expresses concern that the Government of Canada has
increasingly framed pharmaceutical development and production as an economic driver rather
than as a means to benefit society across numerous metrics by keeping people healthy. Canada
has also made substantial cuts to international assistance with an emphasis on cuts to global
health; these cuts have misleadingly been framed as “savings” rather than accurately reflecting
that, in an interconnected world, investment in global health is also an investment in Canada’s
health. In conducting this study, it is important that HESA reject a narrow economic framing of
pharmaceutical sovereignty focusing on commercial returns within the health innovation and
biomanufacturing sectors, and consider the full scope of the issue both within and beyond
Canada’s borders, from mitigating global health threats like pandemics, to avoiding disruptions
to supply chains and travel, to soft-power global leadership – all of which are furthered by
ensuring that vital health products reach all those who need them, both in Canada and around
the world.

The Legacy of Vaccine (In)Equity
The issue of Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty was brought to the forefront by the COVID19 pandemic, which saw Canada facing both shortages of existing drugs and lack of access to
novel vaccines. While these challenges implicated many factors, including major disruptions to
supply chains and trade caused by the pandemic, one core issue was that Canada had limited
capacity to produce any of these products domestically. An immediate consequence was that
Canada competed directly with other countries for a limited supply of vaccines, undermining
the government’s efforts to position itself as a leader in global health. While Canada’s
government rightly and repeatedly recognized that “the pandemic is not over anywhere until
it’s over everywhere”, in practice there were massive global inequities in access to vaccines.
This was fueled by Canada’s own approach that put narrow commercial interests first and
broader access second, despite the impacts, including on the wider economy, caused by the

ongoing pandemic. MSF has previously expressed concerns around Canada’s outsize role in
perpetuating global vaccine inequity; those will not be reiterated at length here, as this topic
has been explored in detail elsewhere.1 However, MSF would point HESA towards the previous
work of their colleagues on the FAAE Committee on the issue of global vaccine equity, and the
continued relevance of multiple recommendations made in the resulting FAAE report to the
broader issue of pharmaceutical sovereignty.2

Domestic Pharmaceutical R&D – Public Funding Must Prioritize Public Benefits
While boosting public investment in domestic pharmaceutical research and development (R&D)
is one important consideration around developing Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty, it is
also crucial to ensure that these public investments are structured in a way to ensure that the
benefits flow primarily to the public, rather than primarily serving to enrich private parties at
public expense. As MSF has repeatedly emphasized, including in a petition signed by over
91,000 Canadians3, such investments of public funds must prioritize lives over profits.

As MSF has repeatedly emphasized, including in a petition signed by over
91,000 Canadians3, such investments of public funds must prioritize lives over profits.

Without public investment, many medical breakthroughs would not exist. This is because much
of the research underpinning new pharmaceuticals occurs at institutions such as universities,
rather than within the private sector; this publicly funded research in effect subsidizes private
interests by de-risking early-stage research. Nevertheless, in Canada the return on public
investment often accrues to profit-motivated entities (e.g., pharmaceutical companies),
without fairly recognizing the contributions made by taxpayers and without fair access and
pricing provisions. Canada’s health systems have continued to pay high prices for health
products whose development was dependent, in whole or in part, on Canadian funding.
Furthermore, despite being urgently needed by patients, these products have frequently not
been made affordable, or even available, in other jurisdictions, either by the producer directly
or via licensing agreements with other producers. Part of exerting pharmaceutical sovereignty
is ensuring that the government steers its investments of public money towards products with
the greatest utility; another is that it maintains some ability to ensure the final products are
available and accessible, rather than leaving those decisions entirely to the private interests
who have benefitted from public investment.

Capitalizing on Canadian Expertise with End-to-End Innovation
Canadian researchers, including those working directly for the Government of Canada, have
been responsible for breakthrough research into diseases of global importance. However,
Canada needs a better strategy for getting important Canadian innovations out of the lab and
to the patients who need them. To ensure rapid access to patients and to health systems,
Canada needs to establish clear funding and resource pathways to guide Canadian research
from discovery through development and clinical trials to final approval, particularly where the
product is of high public health importance but considered to be of comparatively low
commercial value. Supporting an end to-end R&D and manufacturing strategy would also be a
logical extension of Canada’s Biomanufacturing and Life Sciences Strategy.

Reliance on private industry to bring research to market creates a number of problems, even
before issues of accessibility and affordability for the final product. One is that it disadvantages
vitally important research into diseases that exert a major impact on health, but are not viewed
as a lucrative commercial market, and thus do not receive adequate investment from the
private sector. This includes diseases that disproportionately impact some of the countries and
populations with whom MSF works; it also includes diseases that continue to have a serious and
sustained impact on marginalized groups in Canada, such as tuberculosis. MSF is aware of a
number of products in development that would respond to urgent health needs, including in
Canada, but do not currently have the resources to move through the clinical trials stage. In
situations such as this, reliance on the private sector is not an effective solution.

Consider the work done on viral haemorrhagic fevers at the National Microbiology Laboratory
(NML) in Winnipeg. The first successful Ebola vaccine originates at the NML; so too have
promising candidates for a range of other serious diseases, from a less common form of Ebola

have faced barriers getting from “bench to bedside”. As discussed above, a transparent,
accessible database of innovations receiving Canadian funding for R&D would promote both
accountability and further innovation, including by facilitating licensing. However, such
licensing must also be carried out responsibly, with conditions to ensure that licensed
technologies are acted upon, especially when the licensed technology is owned by the
Government of Canada itself. In the case of the Ebola vaccine, progress was delayed by poor
licensing decisions, with the vaccine initially licensed to a private company that had never

before brought a product to market.10 That company did not move the vaccine forward; it was
not until the major outbreak of Ebola in West Africa that this company sublicensed the vaccine
– making a considerable amount of money in the process – to another company, who
ultimately did bring the vaccine to market (albeit with a high price-tag). The unnecessary delay
demonstrates the folly of relying completely on the private sector, particularly when the
partner chosen had no track record of success, and did not act to move the innovation forward.

The Government of Canada has since made improvements to its licensing strategy, at least for

Publicly Owned Biomanufacturing Facilities and the Exercise of Sovereignty
The COVID-19 pandemic also catalyzed major public investments into biomanufacturing in
Canada, with funding recipients ranging from wholly publicly owned facilities, to facilities
connected to public universities, to profitable privately owned pharmaceutical companies.11
While such funding has often been accompanied by broad claims that these investments will
result in improved access, particularly during a future pandemic, there has been a lack of
transparency in demonstrating whether public funding is accompanied by any legally binding
conditions to ensure this is actually the case.

One immediate step Canada can take in exercising its pharmaceutical sovereignty is to use its
publicly owned pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities for public benefit. In response to
COVID-19, Canada built the publicly owned Biologics Manufacturing Centre (BMC) in Montreal.
The completion of construction, and of Health Canada certification, in a very short timeframe is
a noteworthy achievement in developing biomanufacturing capacity. Not only does the BMC
have capacity to produce certain vaccines, it can produce other important products like
monoclonal antibody treatments (mAbs). However, since opening in 2022, the BMC has
manufactured no end-use commercial products at all; a well-publicized deal with Novavax to
produce the Nuvaxovid COVID-19 vaccine was ultimately terminated without any doses
produced. Reports indicate the BMC costs roughly $17 million per year just to keep the lights
on; for only slightly more money, Canada could be identifying key access gaps, and using the
BMC to fill those gaps itself.

Win-Win Investments for Domestic and Global Access to Medicines
It cannot be said that Canada is effectively asserting pharmaceutical sovereignty when not all
the medicines needed by Canadian patients are marketed in Canada, especially medicines long
recognized as the appropriate standard of care both in Canada and internationally. Instead,
they have to be accessed through mechanisms like the Special Access Program (SAP),
mechanisms that were not designed or intended as a permanent means to access longstanding
standard of care medicines. Some of these medicines have never been marketed in Canada,
while others have been discontinued as the result of business decisions. In both instances,
these decisions are too often driven by the financial interests of private companies rather than
by the health needs of the public. The absence of these medicines from markets where they
constitute the recommended standard of care for patients is quite simply a market failure.

will likely hear more about the recent proposal for Canada to make increased use of approvals
by foreign regulatory authorities12 from other stakeholders. While there have been concerns
raised around preserving appropriate standards for safety, efficacy and quality, there have also
been suggestions that this new proposal could improve access to existing medicines of
established utility for diseases like tuberculosis, and expand access to product formulations,
such as pediatric formulations, that would help address unmet needs in key populations. While
MSF does not take an official position on this specific proposal, it does note that the issue of
ensuring access to existing as well as future medicines addressing unmet health needs is an
important one that deserves government attention, and that international coherence between
regulatory regimes can be a useful component of improving access to medicines at home and
abroad.

MSF does not take an official position on this specific proposal, it does note that the issue of ensuring access to existing as well as future medicines addressing unmet health needs is an important one that deserves government attention, and that international coherence between regulatory regimes can be a useful component of improving access to medicines at home and abroad.

Even with increased domestic biomanufacturing capacity, it is simply unrealistic to expect that
Canada can produce every medicine that is needed by Canadian patients, including the
production of underlying active pharmaceutical ingredients (API), particularly for drugs used in
small quantities. As a consequence, any efforts at on-shoring pharmaceutical production need
to be undertaken rationally. This issue underscores how investing in global health can be a winwin situation, including for drugs to which Canadians currently face access other barriers, like
absence from the Canadian market. Canada was a founding donor to the Global Drug Facility
(GDF), a global mechanism that facilitates access to quality-assured supplies of tuberculosis
medicines for all countries. However, despite being a founding donor, Canada has never itself
accessed drugs from the GDF, despite the fact the GDF offers medicines recommended in
Canada’s Tuberculosis Standards13, but which pharmaceutical companies are not making efforts
to actually sell in Canada. The GDF’s value in improving domestic access in higher-income
countries is increasingly recognized in Europe.14 PHAC recently indicated that Canada was
exploring the possibility of using the GDF15, but more concrete action is needed to turn this
exploration into reality. Canada should take steps both to adequately fund the GDF, and to
itself use the GDF to access drugs that are currently not marketed in Canada. This is a very clear
win-win situation for Canada investing in global health.
12 Canada Gazette, Part I, Volume 159, Number 51: Order Providing for Reliance on Decisions of, or Documents
Produced by, Foreign Regulatory Authorities in Respect of Certain Drugs (December 20, 2025)
https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-12-20/html/reg4-eng.html
13 Public Health Agency of Canada, Canadian Tuberculosis Standards, 8th Edition (2022)
https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/tuberculosis/health-professionals/canadiantuberculosis-standards.html
14 Médecins Sans Frontières, “Bridging the gap: Securing access to essential TB medicines in the EU and EEA” (July
2, 2025) https://msfaccess.org/bridging-gap-securing-access-essential-tb-medicines-eu-and-eea

Tuberculosis Elimination” (2025) https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseasesconditions/government-tuberculosis-response-2025-working-towards-tuberculosis-elimination.html

of Certain Drugs (December 20, 2025) https://gazette.gc.ca/rp-pr/p1/2025/2025-12-20/html/reg4-eng.html 13 Public Health Agency of Canada, Canadian Tuberculosis Standards, 8th Edition (2022) https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/diseases/tuberculosis/health-professionals/canadiantuberculosis-standards.html 14 Médecins Sans Frontières, “Bridging the gap: Securing access to essential TB medicines in the EU and EEA” (July 2, 2025) https://msfaccess.org/bridging-gap-securing-access-essential-tb-medicines-eu-and-eea 15 Public Health Agency of Canada, “Government of Canada’s Tuberculosis Response (2025): Working towards Tuberculosis Elimination” (2025) https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/diseasesconditions/government-tuberculosis-response-2025-working-towards-tuberculosis-elimination.html

Trade, Intellectual Property, and Sovereignty
It is also striking that Canada has in recent years strongly opposed measures at the
international level that would assist countries in achieving pharmaceutical sovereignty. For
instance, Canada was notably reluctant to support a temporary waiver of intellectual property
(IP) protections to combat the COVID-19 pandemic (the “TRIPS Waiver”) at the World Trade
Organization. This was the case even after the United States, a firm proponent of strong IP
protections, declared support for a limited waiver. Similarly, during negotiations of the WHO
Pandemic Agreement, Canada was particularly vocal in pushing for technology transfer for new
medicines and health products to take place only on a voluntary and mutually agreed basis.
Where such transfers do in fact occur voluntarily, it is a positive thing that is to be encouraged;
however, history offers numerous examples where technology holders have not voluntarily
agreed, impeding lifesaving access. During the Government of Canada’s consultations on the
Pandemic Agreement, MSF repeatedly requested that the Government of Canada provide
justifications for its position, and that it address the scenario where transfer on voluntary and
mutually agreed terms did not occur. These requests were never satisfactorily addressed.

It is not too late for Canada to course-correct, however. It is in Canada’s interest to protect
existing legal means for countries to avail themselves of tools such as compulsory licensing
when needed to protect the health of the public, such as the flexibilities that exist under the
WTO TRIPS Agreement. Indeed, Canada considered availing itself of such flexibilities via
temporary measures expanding compulsory licensing under the COVID-19 Emergency Response
Act. Furthermore, Canada should not weaken existing international protections, for itself or
others, by accepting agreements with more extensive intellectual property protections (socalled “TRIPS+”) measures that could impact access to medicines. This includes the upcoming
review of the CUSMA trade agreement, and other such agreements Canada may enter into.

This includes the upcoming
review of the CUSMA trade agreement, and other such agreements Canada may enter into.

Emergency Readiness and Pharmaceuticals: Development, Stockpiling and Deployment
Canada now has a new agency, Health Emergency Readiness Canada (HERC), dedicated to
preparing for health emergencies, although thus far HERC’s activities have been relatively
subdued. If prioritizing domestic access to medical countermeasures (MCMs) is what gets
Canadian innovations like the haemorrhagic fever vaccines discussed earlier to the finish line,
then it is a positive step. However, that investment would pay off more effectively if those tools
were also made available where they are needed, when they are needed. In addition to issues
like affordable pricing, intellectual property licensing and tech transfer discussed earlier,
physical supplies of vaccines and treatments for diseases posing biosecurity threats are too
frequently found gathering dust in the stockpiles of wealthy countries rather than being used to
tackle outbreaks at the source, before they can spread.

Here, it is worth noting that Canada’s history of being reticent to share its stockpiles of vaccines
in a timely manner is not unique to COVID-19. This was true of H1N1 vaccine in 2009, and more
recently of mpox vaccine. Canada needs better, faster mechanisms to assess how to meet its
own realistic domestic needs while also advancing biosecurity both globally and domestically by
tackling outbreaks where they emerge elsewhere in the world, rather than allowing vaccines
and other vital tools that are desperately needed elsewhere to expire on shelves unused.

MSF Recommendations – Canada’s Pharmaceutical Sovereignty
1) Increase public funding for R&D, with conditions to prioritize public benefit: That Canada
increase federal funding for health R&D with an emphasis on addressing unmet health needs,
and that all Canadian federal funding of health R&D include binding access conditions that
explicitly encompass intellectual property and technology transfer, as well as demonstrated
best efforts to obtain market approval, to ensure products developed with public funds are
affordable and accessible, domestically and in low- and middle-income countries.

2) Public registry of publicly funded innovations: That Canada establish a public registry of all
innovations developed with public funding, providing information on development status,
regulatory status and licensing. This should include, but absolutely not be limited to,
innovations developed at government facilities such as the National Microbiology Laboratory.

This should include, but absolutely not be limited to,
innovations developed at government facilities such as the National Microbiology Laboratory.

3) Establish end-to-end R&D pathways prioritizing health needs over commercial appeal: That
Canada develop effective, adequately funded end-to-end, “bench-to-bedside” pathways for
Canadian R&D, prioritizing R&D that addresses major public health needs but lacks support
from the commercial pharmaceutical sector. This includes using public funds and publicly
owned facilities such as the Clinical Trial Material Facility to advance clinical trials.

4) Use publicly owned pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities to fill access gaps: That Canada
should ensure that Canadian federal funding of all biomanufacturing facilities include binding
access conditions and that those conditions be made public; should proactively identify access
gaps not met by commercial producers; should use public funds and publicly owned
manufacturing facilities such as the Biologics Manufacturing Centre to produce product in
adequate quantities to address domestic and key international access gaps.

5) Reverse global health funding cuts and invest in win-win tools like the Global Drug Facility:
That Canada reverse its budget cuts to global health, and that it take further steps to actively
fund and participate in mechanisms such as the Global Drug Facility to improve access to
quality-assured medicines both domestically and internationally.

6) Avoid access restrictions, including around intellectual property, in trade agreements: That
Canada ensure that it does not promote or enter into bilateral or multilateral trade
arrangements that would limit the ability of itself or other countries to use all tools available to
ensure pharmaceuticals and other health tools are affordable and available to all who need
them. In particular, Canada must not restrict the use of such tools, particularly around
intellectual property, such as by entering into trade agreements with “TRIPS+” provisions.

7) Ensure Canada’s emergency readiness strategies consider global contexts: That Canada
ensure its strategies for both development and stockpiling of pharmaceuticals for emergency
readiness must effectively account for the global context, including the value of ensuring that
domestic stockpiles are deployed abroad when necessary to prevent the spread of disease.

About MSF: Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is a medical humanitarian
organization operating in more than 70 countries.

text:
Pharmaceutical Sovereignty and Insulin Supply in Canada
Submission to the Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
by
Independent Voices for Safe & Effective Drugs
March 13, 2026
Executive Summary
Insulin is one of the most important medicines in modern healthcare. For the 640,000
Canadians living with diabetes who need it, uninterrupted access to insulin is essential for
survival. For those with Type 1 diabetes, an auto-immune disease, there are no substitutes for
insulin and without it they will die within days or weeks.

Despite insulin’s importance—and its discovery in Canada—we currently have no domestic
manufacturing capacity for this medicine. Instead, Canadians rely entirely on three foreign
corporations that control 95% of the global supply of insulin.

Recent developments in the global insulin market, including the discontinuation of multiple
insulin products for commercial reasons, illustrate the dangers of relying exclusively on
global pharmaceutical supply chains for essential medicines. The World Health Organisation
estimates that half of the world’s population who need insulin either cannot afford it or have
no access to supplies.

Other jurisdictions have begun responding to these risks by strengthening domestic
pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity and treating certain medicines, including insulin, as
strategic assets. Canada is not currently among these.

Until the mid-1980s, however, Canada did maintain domestic production of insulin and other
biologics through publicly owned Connaught Laboratories. Re-establishing domestic insulin
manufacturing capacity—preferably under public ownership and accountability—would
strengthen Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty while ensuring secure access to one of the
country’s most important medicines.
Insulin as a Strategic Medicine
Insulin is unique among medicines because of its indispensable clinical role. Individuals
living with Type 1 diabetes depend on insulin therapy every day to survive, while some with
advanced Type 2 diabetes require insulin to effectively manage their condition. Interruptions
in insulin supply can rapidly lead to serious complications such as ketoacidosis and certain
death if access is not possible.

The global insulin market is also highly concentrated. The vast majority of the world’s insulin
is produced in three countries – Denmark, France and Germany – by three multinational
companies – Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi – which control the global supply chain.

This concentration creates systemic vulnerability for people who live in countries that lack
domestic manufacturing capacity.

org: Independent Voices for Safe and Effective Drugs
text:
This concentration creates systemic vulnerability for people who live in countries that lack
domestic manufacturing capacity.

At the same time, the global insulin market is chronically unstable. Over the past two decades
more than sixty human, analogue and animal insulin products have been discontinued by
manufacturers. Without exception, these discontinuations were driven by commercial

considerations rather than safety concerns. Studies have consistently shown that newer
replacements for these withdrawn insulin options provided little to no therapeutic advantage
over older versions.

A recent example is the discontinuation of the popular insulin detemir, marketed as Levemir
by Novo Nordisk. Prior to its withdrawal, detemir was used by an estimated one million
patients in the United States and was a commonly used insulin in Canada as well. Its
discontinuation has increased the risk of harm among affected patients who require an often
stressful, clinical re-evaluation while confronting reduced options and flexibility.

These developments illustrate how corporate portfolio decisions can affect access to clinically
necessary medicines. Such decisions are beyond the control of the regulator.
Lessons From Market Withdrawal: Animal Insulin
The discontinuation of animal-derived insulin occurred in the aftermath of the privatisation
and sale of Connaught Laboratories and provides another example of how market forces can
eliminate necessary medicines. Since the mid-1990s, there have been 62 different animal,
human and analogue insulins withdrawn from the global market, not a single one for reasons
of safety or effectiveness.

Since the 1980s, when recombinant human and analogue insulins were first introduced, some
patients continued to rely on porcine or bovine insulin because they either maintained greater
stability or experienced fewer side effects. Today the world’s only remaining porcine insulin
brand is Hypurin, produced by Wockhardt in the U.K.

The range of options available to those who need insulin has also narrowed considerably.
This is harmful for those who cannot safely or effectively use what the market has to offer.
There are different reasons that may be the case, including auto-immune responses / allergies,
individual pharmacokinetics, or injection site reactions. Some people are also better able to
detect hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) on animal-sourced insulins, an issue which triggered
an outcry in Europe and North America during the 1980s and 1990s.

org: Independent Voices for Safe and Effective Drugs
text:
Some people are also better able to
detect hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) on animal-sourced insulins, an issue which triggered
an outcry in Europe and North America during the 1980s and 1990s.

The decreasing number of options in the insulin market resulted in a study conducted by the
House Standing Committee on Health in 2003, including two days of hearings. HESA urged
Health Canada to assure ongoing access to animal-sourced insulin products because of the
serious, sometimes life-threatening reactions reported by patients and some of their doctors.

As a public interest producer, Connaught Laboratories included more than a dozen speciality
insulins vital to a small number of Canadians but amounting to less than one half percent of
the company’s production by volume. Today, the population relying on animal insulin is
small and the sole supplier, Wockhardt, has announced it will be discontinued in Canada. This
situation illustrates a broader policy problem: when domestic manufacturing capacity
disappears for essential medicines, patients are vulnerable to the decisions of a single global
supplier.
International Responses to Insulin Supply Vulnerability
Several jurisdictions have begun responding to challenges posed by what is referred to as the
insulin oligopoly by strengthening domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity.

In January 2025 the European Parliament adopted the Critical Medicines Act, which seeks to
strengthen secure access to essential medicines by encouraging domestic production and
reducing reliance on external supply chains. One of the medicines that prompted the
legislation was insulin. While this move is probably good for Europeans, it may have
negative repercussions for Canadians because Germany, Denmark and France collectively
export between 85% to 96% of global retail insulin (by value).

In the United States, governments have also begun exploring public or nonprofit insulin
manufacturing initiatives in an effort to gain some control over the world’s highest insulin
prices. A 10ml vial of one popular brand, for example, sells for over $380 in the United
States, compared to $35 in Canada. The State of California has launched a partnership with
the nonprofit manufacturer Civica Rx to produce low-cost generic insulin.

Other states—including New York and Michigan—have passed legislation enabling the
development of state-supported insulin manufacturing programs.

org: Independent Voices for Safe and Effective Drugs
text:
Other states—including New York and Michigan—have passed legislation enabling the
development of state-supported insulin manufacturing programs.

Brazil, too, has taken steps to regain control over the manufacture and distribution of insulin
more than 20 years after the acquisition of Biobras by Novo Nordisk in 2003. Biobras,
Brazil’s only domestic producer of animal and human insulin products, was the world’s
fourth largest insulin producer and an increasingly important supplier of low-cost human,
bovine, and porcine insulins to the countries in the global south. Today, Brazil’s ministry of
health has entered into a partnership with two private companies for the manufacture and
distribution of insulin to Brazilians and others across Latin Americans.

These initiatives reflect growing recognition that essential medicines such as insulin may
require public-interest manufacturing models in order to ensure reliable access.
Canada’s Experience with Public Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
Canada has a long history of domestic public pharmaceutical production through the work
of Connaught Laboratories.

Established in 1913 at the University of Toronto, Connaught Laboratories was created to
ensure reliable access to vaccines and biologics at a time when commercial supply was
limited and often unaffordable.

The “fundamental idea” underpinning these early beginnings of Connaught Laboratories,
“was the production of all sera and vaccines of value in public health work and their
distribution at cost” to provinces. This idea underpinned the principle articulated by JJR
Macleod and embraced by his co-discoverers, as well as the University and Connaught: “the
best Insulin…at the lowest cost.”

But today, Canada doesn’t produce a drop of insulin and instead relies on three global
corporations that dominate the supply of all the insulin used. Human and analogue insulins
cost an average of $2-$6 per 10ml vial to produce, but in Canada sell for between $35 and
$80 per vial, or 1500% above the cost of production.

For more than seventy years Connaught played a central role in producing vaccines, insulin,
and other biologics for Canadians and the country’s public drug plans. Because it operated as
a publicly owned institution, Connaught was able to prioritize affordability and reliability of
supply rather than shareholder returns.

org: Independent Voices for Safe and Effective Drugs
text:
Because it operated as
a publicly owned institution, Connaught was able to prioritize affordability and reliability of
supply rather than shareholder returns.

This experience demonstrates that public pharmaceutical manufacturing can function as an
effective public health instrument.
Recommendations
1. Re-establish domestic insulin manufacturing capacity.
The Government of Canada should support the development of domestic insulin
production as part of a national pharmaceutical sovereignty strategy.
2. Recognize that a broad range of animal, human and analogue insulin options are
essential for the diverse population of Canadians who need them.
Insulin – both natural and biosynthetic – should be designated as a critical medicine
within Canada’s pharmaceutical supply resilience framework.
3. Create an Essential Medicines Manufacturing Program.
Canada should identify medicines that are clinically indispensable but vulnerable to
supply disruption and ensure domestic production capacity for those products.
4. Support public-interest pharmaceutical manufacturing.
Canada should explore public or nonprofit manufacturing models similar to initiatives
in other countries such as Brazil and the United States.
Conclusion
Insulin was discovered in 1921 at the University of Toronto through the work of Frederick
Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and JJR Macleod. It was manufactured by Connaught
and distributed at cost to Canadians across the country. Today, however, Canada relies
entirely on imported insulin produced by multinational pharmaceutical companies. At a time
when approximately 640,000 Canadians depend on insulin therapy, rebuilding domestic
manufacturing capacity would strengthen Canada’s pharmaceutical sovereignty while
reaffirming the public-health principles that guided the discovery and early production of
insulin in Canada.

Establishing a domestic supply chain for critical
immunoglobulin therapy in Canada
Canadian Blood Services operates the blood supply system in all provinces and territories
except Quebec. Through an arm’s-length governance model, it is accountable to provincial and
territorial ministers of health, who are its corporate members, and who provide operational
funding. Canadian Blood Services is regulated by Health Canada. Within this framework, the
organization is responsible and accountable to act in the best interests of the country by
ensuring the safety and security of the supply of blood and blood products. As part of these
responsibilities, the organization also manages a pan-Canadian formulary of about 50 plasma
protein and related products, or PPRP, including immunoglobulin therapy made from human
plasma.
Human plasma carries immune-supporting proteins that specialized pharmaceutical companies
manufacture into immunoglobulins through a process called fractionation. When someone's
immune system fails, doctors turn to immunoglobulin therapy to provide antibodies to treat
infections and immune-related conditions like primary immunodeficiencies, autoimmune
diseases, and others. It is estimated that more than half (50 to 60 per cent) of patients in
Canada prescribed immunoglobulins must take them to live, with no other treatment option
available for their care.
At a time when Canada’s governments and residents are focused on greater self-reliance —
securing essential supply chains, building manufacturing capacity, and reaffirming the country’s
sovereignty — Canadian Blood Services is implementing a comprehensive plan in keeping with
these goals to ensure patients continue to have long-term access to immunoglobulins. The plan
has multiple components and was informed by a robust risk analysis. It includes establishing an
end-to-end domestic supply chain for immunoglobulins in Canada through a strategic
agreement with Grifols, a global healthcare company and leader in producing plasma
medicines.
With this context in mind, and as outlined below, key aspects of Canadian Blood Services’ panCanadian approach, deep supply chain and system expertise, and commitment to patients in
Canada contribute to greater pharmaceutical sovereignty for the country.
Plasma protein and related products (PPRP) formulary
The PPRP formulary is comprised both of treatments made from plasma which Canadian Blood
Services collects, and other finished products (medicines) purchased on the global market.
Regarding PPRP purchased on the global market, Canadian Blood Services applies a panCanadian approach which gives provincial and territorial health systems (excluding Quebec)
bulk-buying power. This helps to manage PPRP costs and support the sustainability of the
formulary, and it provides an opportunity to negotiate a lower price per product for Canadians.
Over the years, Canadian Blood Services’ contract negotiations with manufacturers have totaled
approximately $1 billion in savings and cost avoidance based on annual national demand
forecasts.

Over the years, Canadian Blood Services’ contract negotiations with manufacturers have totaled
approximately $1 billion in savings and cost avoidance based on annual national demand
forecasts.

As part of its formulary management, Canadian Blood Services also stores, ships and delivers
PPRP to hospitals and health-care organizations across the country, leveraging the distribution
network already in place and funded as part of its national blood supply responsibilities. In
addition to bulk purchasing, this national system ensures traceability, equity, an integrated
supply chain, and expertise in transfusable and plasma products.
Canadian Blood Services also employs a robust shortages management approach within its
formulary operations, including centralized inventory management, the ability to leverage wellestablished relationships with suppliers, and a process with provincial and territorial
governments and hospitals to activate a national shortage plan for immunoglobulins in times of
need. Further, all supply contracts for PPRP require the manufacturers to maintain a minimum
inventory of 8 weeks in Canada. This is in addition to the inventory that Canadian Blood
Services carries, which varies from 4-10 weeks depending on the product.
Ensuring long-term access to immunoglobulins: the most
widely used class of PPRP
Global demand for immunoglobulins is rising quickly. In Canada, it’s expected to grow by more
than 50 per cent over the next five years, driven by medical advances and an aging population.
This pressure is made more challenging by the fact that, today, approximately 70 per cent of the
immunoglobulins Canadian patients require is imported and made largely from plasma collected
in the U.S.
One of the lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic is that nations which do not produce their own
essential products are exposed to risk. This is greatly underscored by the current resurgence of
protectionist strategies internationally. In keeping with the overall goals of Canada’s
Biomanufacturing and Life Sciences Strategy, and other similar federal and provincial
approaches, Canadian Blood Services announced a plan to further secure domestic sufficiency
for immunoglobulins in 2022.
The plan was informed by a robust risk analysis on plasma and immunoglobulin security of
supply. The analysis recommended Canadian Blood Services increase plasma sufficiency to
reach a minimum target of at least 50 per cent in the quickest time possible. This would reduce
mounting supply chain risks so that at least half of Canada’s demand for immunoglobulins
would be met using products made from plasma collected domestically. It would also strengthen
security of supply for patients who rely on immunoglobulins to live, and for whom there are no
alterative therapies. The remaining domestic demand would continue to be met through bulk
purchasing of immunoglobulins on the global market, thereby maintaining important diversity of
supply of these life-saving medicines for patients in Canada.
To increase plasma sufficiency with urgency, Canadian Blood Services has significantly added
plasma donation sites and opportunities across the country, with plans for more.
Agreement with Grifols: To further accelerate at the scale and speed necessary to meet the
sufficiency target as quickly as possible, Canadian Blood Services has also entered an
agreement with Grifols, a specialized commercial pharmaceutical company and global leader in
plasma collection and manufacturing. This agreement was reached following a comprehensive
request for proposal (RFP) process. The RFP assessed whether the growing commercial

The RFP assessed whether the growing commercial

plasma sector in Canada could help increase plasma collection, and manufacture that plasma
into immunoglobulins, all in Canada, thereby delivering the first ever end-to-end, domestic
supply chain of immunoglobulins, while still safeguarding the nation’s existing integrated blood
and plasma supply chain. The RFP also addressed a key recommendation from the 2018
Health Canada expert panel on sufficiency of immunoglobulin report, which called for creative
options to ensure that plasma collected in Canada from Canadian donors (whether paid or
volunteer) be made available for the needs of Canadian patients.
Grifols operates a compensated model and is now collecting plasma in Canada as per its
agreement with Canadian Blood Services. Prior to this agreement, plasma collected by
commercial companies in Canada was sold on the global market and did not contribute to
Canadian sufficiency targets, as commercial collectors were in no way compelled to ensure their
products serve patients in Canada.
Canada’s new end-to-end domestic supply chain for immunoglobulins: Beyond plasma
collection, a major aspect of the agreement is that all plasma collected by Grifols in Canada is to
be manufactured into immunoglobulins exclusively for Canadian Blood Services for Canadian
patients at a large-scale biologics manufacturing facility Grifols is building in Montreal. The
facility will be the first of its kind in Canada (manufacturing of immunoglobulin currently takes
place largely the U.S.), creating a domestic supply chain that is both groundbreaking and
essential. This will reduce reliance on the U.S. market, ensure resilience to global shocks, and
enhance domestic biologics manufacturing capabilities. Construction is well underway on
Grifols’ facility in Montreal, with anticipated completion and license by Health Canada to
manufacture immunoglobulins by the end of 2027.
Use of byproducts from manufacturing immunoglobulins: Manufacturing plasma into
immunoglobulins results in leftover byproducts containing proteins and other substances that
were present in the plasma. These byproducts can be used to produce other medicine, such as
albumin. When these byproducts are not used to make medicine, they are discarded as
biological waste. Canadian Blood Services has been meeting Canada’s demand for albumin
with plasma collected in Canada. As a result, it agreed that Grifols can use the byproducts from
the plasma they collect in Canada to manufacture albumin.
Not only is this an ethical, responsible choice that reduces waste and benefits patients globally,
in exchange, Canada benefits, as this arrangement also offsets the substantial cost of
immunoglobulins. This is good for Canadians and for provincial and territorial blood system
funders. Of note, donors at Grifols’ centres sign a consent form before their plasma is taken
which communicates that Grifols may use their donations as best needed. It also makes clear
that this plasma is used to make immunoglobulins for Canadian Blood Services exclusively, for
patients in Canada.
Canadian Blood Services’ plan is working
Canadian Blood Services’ broader plan to strengthen domestic supply chain resilience has been
informed by patients, clinicians, industry and market analysts, health economists, specialists in
ethics and law, as well as other blood operators — and it is working.

Canadian Blood Services’ plan is working
Canadian Blood Services’ broader plan to strengthen domestic supply chain resilience has been
informed by patients, clinicians, industry and market analysts, health economists, specialists in
ethics and law, as well as other blood operators — and it is working.

From the time of entering into the agreement with Grifols, Canadian Blood Services has
reported an increase in domestic immunoglobulin sufficiency from approximately 15 per cent to
33 per cent, as of the end of 2025. More importantly, Canadian Blood Services is creating
Canada’s first-ever domestic supply chain for immunoglobulins, exclusively for patients in this
country.
This is a stabilizing factor in keeping with federal and provincial goals to reduce international
dependencies in a volatile geopolitical environment. In this way, Canadian Blood Services’ panCanadian approach, deep supply chain and system expertise, and commitment to patients in
Canada contributes to greater pharmaceutical sovereignty for the country.

Association des collèges et universités de la francophonie canadienne ▼
The Association des collèges et universités de la francophonie canadienne (ACUFC) is an association of
22 French-language and bilingual post-secondary institutions outside Quebec. The ACUFC represents the
collective interests of its members and leads initiatives that bring about structural and lasting change.
More specifically, it works to strengthen the continuum of French-language education by expanding
access to post-secondary education in francophone minority communities (FMCs). The Consortium
national de formation en santé (CNFS), a national health training consortium housed at the ACUFC and
funded by Health Canada under the Official Languages Health Program, plays a key role in providing
access to French-language health services in FMCs. The CNFS supports the recruitment and training of
additional students in health programs, the integration of graduates into FMCs, and health-related
research in FMCs. In short, the CNFS increases the number of health professionals able to deliver health
services in French, thereby supporting the vitality of FMCs.
Recently, the CNFS national secretariat commissioned a study on possible solutions to support the
integration of internationally trained health professionals (ITHPs) into FMCs.1 This brief summarizes the
study’s main findings and outlines the challenges and needs of ITHPs in francophone communities. This
study is directly related to the one currently being conducted by the Standing Committee on Health.
Internationally trained minority francophone health professionals ▼
While French-language health services are not always accessible, as this depends on the availability of
health workers with French-language skills, francophone ITHPs make up a skilled pool of workers who
can bolster the health care workforce. Even though there are francophone ITHPs in FMCs, integrating
them into the health sector remains a challenge due to various factors related to professional
certification and professional, social and cultural integration.
Representativity and access to employment by francophone ITHPs
There are several barriers, some of them attributable to training location, hindering access to health
sector employment in FMCs. Outside Quebec, a significant number of francophone ITHPs are not
working in the health sector. There are 58,246 francophone health professionals in Canada outside
Quebec, including 53,691 trained in Canada and 4,555 trained internationally. Among those who are
employed, 65% of francophone professionals trained in Canada work in the health sector, compared to
only 56.7% for francophone ITHPs, a difference of 8.3%. A similar but less pronounced difference (4.5%)
can also be observed between non-francophone professionals trained in Canada and those trained
internationally. This is therefore a common challenge for ITHPs.

formé(e)s à l'étranger (PSFÉ) dans les communautés francophones en situation minoritaire (CFSM) grâce à la mise en œuvre de
projets de formation [Final Report: Providing solutions to promote the integration of internationally trained health professionals
(ITHPs) into francophone minority communities (FMCs) through the implementation of training projects], research project conducted
for the Association des collèges et universités de la francophonie canadienne and the Consortium national de formation en
santé, Ottawa, 62 pp. Available upon request.

org: Association des collèges et universités de la francophonie canadienne
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Available upon request.

In addition, the number of francophone ITHPs across Canada outside Quebec is limited and unevenly
distributed. As mentioned, there are 4,555 francophone ITHPs living outside Quebec. However, of the
1,952 francophone ITHPs employed in the health sector, the majority, or 1,570, are in Ontario.
Francophone immigration policy should more effectively address this interprovincial disparity to
facilitate access to care in FMCs.
Various approaches can be considered to implement measures, including recruitment, skills
development, and professional and language training, to increase the availability of French-language
services through francophone ITHPs. However, in addition to the barriers related to the location of
training also faced by their non-francophone counterparts, these measures must take into account the
FMC-specific challenges faced by francophone ITHPs.
Challenges and needs of francophone ITHPs ▼
ITHPs, whether francophone or not, face employment challenges and barriers that Canadian-trained
health professionals do not. Among these common challenges is the location of training in the health
sector. However, francophone ITHPs in Canada outside Quebec face additional barriers specific to
francophone minority contexts. We will therefore address the professional certification and
professional, social and cultural integration challenges based on their structural, institutional and
individual factors.
Structural and institutional factors
1.
Credential recognition and licensing
One of the main challenges facing francophone ITHPs is getting their credentials recognized and
obtaining a licence to practise. Canadian regulators rigorously assess the skills of francophone ITHPs to
ensure that they meet standards. However, the current process, which is long, complex and costly, often
significantly delays the integration of ITHPs into the labour market. Many ITHPs have to repeat a
significant portion of their training. Because their qualifications are not recognized or due to delays,
initial employment generally occurs outside the health field.
In addition, the lack of support during the accreditation process is seen as a barrier by francophone
ITHPs. Given the complexity of this process, support services, particularly those provided by professional
associations, should provide francophone ITHPs with tailored support to assist them in the process. For
example, better dissemination of information on the accreditation process and the steps to follow for
francophone ITHPs undergoing immigration would provide them with better support and would allow
them to access clear information and start the process earlier.
2.
Limited access to residency positions or clerkships
Another challenge is accessing residency positions or clerkships to complete their training. Due to direct
competition with Canadian university graduates and Canadians who have studied abroad, opportunities
for francophone ITHPs to gain the clinical experience required to be licensed to practice are sometimes
more limited. So even when francophone ITHPs meet the licensing requirements and pass their exams,
the scarcity of available positions is a barrier to integration into Canadian health care systems.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
So even when francophone ITHPs meet the licensing requirements and pass their exams,
the scarcity of available positions is a barrier to integration into Canadian health care systems.

3.
Limited programs and services
Nationally and provincially (outside Quebec), there is a limited range of programs and services that meet
the needs of francophone ITHPs. Among current initiatives, there are at least 95 programs and services
geared to ITHPs. However, only 23 initiatives are specifically designed for francophone ITHPs or include
a French-language option. Similarly, most of these initiatives, including francophone ones, are
implemented in Ontario. In order to address gaps in services, training and professional integration,
creating programs and services that meet the specific needs of francophone ITHPs across the country
would help integrate them into the health sector and FMCs.
Individual factors
1.
Language and cultural barriers
Despite efforts to attract qualified francophone workers in order to increase the availability of Frenchlanguage services, the linguistic and cultural dynamics are different from what francophone ITHPs were
prepared for. First, English proficiency is often a requirement to enter the labour market in FMCs.
Several professional associations require francophone ITHPs to learn English in order to pass
certification exams, and employers also value bilingual workers to meet market needs. Without
language training tailored to their needs in certain provinces, these language barriers hinder their
integration into the workforce. Second, ITHPs find it difficult to adapt to the social, cultural and
organizational norms of Canadian workplaces. In addition to different dialects, accents and cultural
practices within FMCs, these difficulties can jeopardize the integration of francophone ITHPs into the
labour market.
2.
Barriers to social and professional integration
In FMCs, the lack of French-language services, resources and information is an additional barrier to the
social and professional integration of francophone ITHPs. In addition to public services in French,
integration services tailored to francophone ITHPs are sometimes lacking or inadequate. These kinds of
services offered in French are essential for integrating francophone immigrants into their communities
and the workplace. In addition, certain sociocultural factors, such as discrimination based on origin or
accent, can make things more difficult. Lastly, the lack of coordination between governments,
community organizations and employers in certain communities can make it harder to attract and retain
ITHPs in FMCs. All these factors negatively affect francophone ITHPs and their professional integration
into the community and, more broadly, into Canadian society. Our francophone immigration policy and
related services should take these challenges and needs into account in order to better support
francophone ITHPs.
In short, the integration of francophone ITHPs into the health sector in Canada outside Quebec can be
improved by introducing measures that address their specific needs, such as education and training
programs. A combination of integrated recruitment, training and support measures will help overcome
the challenges faced by francophone ITHPs.

Policy brief for --Reducing pressures on Canada’s healthcare
industry
Lok Bhattarai, PhD
A stark mismatch in demand and supply of Canadian health-services is visible and
is an ‘experiential reality’ rather than an ‘uncommon experience’. There is a
complex relation between the augmenting healthcare demand, Canada’s
immigration policy and integration of internationally trained professionals into
the workforce. To address this problem, Canada can undertake several smaller
fixes which altogether can produce greater impact in the long run. Below, I have
discussed some of the cost-effective fixes which I believe can yield impressive
results.
Regulating doctor appointments and walk-ins: It is often reported that
many family doctors or the doctors offering walk-ins often ask their patients to
limit on only one health issue to consult per visit. In other words, doctors are
reluctant to discuss more than one issue with the patients in one visit regardless
of how minor or interconnected those issues are. This is one of the practices that
instead of resolving healthcare burden is contributing to escalating artificial
burden in the industry. Consequently, number of visits multiplies as patients may
need to visit doctors more than once (maybe several times) where the issues
could have been consulted in the first visit in a matter of an additional few more
minutes. A strict regulatory instruction can effectively resolve this malpractice so
that doctors, except in reasonable cases, will overview all relevant issues a patient
wants to discuss in one visit. There will be no additional cost for the doctor or the
patients in so doing. This will also reduce patients’ time and resources to
commute for several visits and their exposure to public space (this is also
important for vulnerable patients). Consequently, number of doctor-visits can be
expected to go noticeably down nationwide and fewer number of doctors may be
able to serve higher population than before.
Promote non-prescription drugs: One recent report estimates that around
2,000 non-prescription / OTC-classified medicines are approved for sale in
Canada. Compared to other G7 Countries including Italy, France and Japan,
Canada appears to have broader spectrum of medicines available in this category.
This is one of the favorable factors towards reducing workloads and demands of
diagnostic and healthcare services. However, there are much more that can be
