text:
However, there are much more that can be

done in utilizing this regulatory ease and reducing workload for diagnostic and
healthcare workforce and facilities. However, despite the number of nonprescription medicines is massive in Canada, general public are often unaware in
what is available and what works when. Consequently, there is a tendency in
general population to rush to the ‘hospital emergency’ even in a situation which
could have been mitigated by non-prescription medicines. Firstly, community
organizations can be supported to run ‘self-care campaign’ in the community with
elements of educating non-prescription drugs. Secondly, collaboration with retail
pharmacy chain and encourage local pharmacist for disseminating about OTC
drugs can be one other supplementary approach.
Promotion of ‘traditional medicines and NHP: Canada boasts and
celebrates its multicultural assets and diversities. Every year 100’s of thousands of
new immigrants arrives to Canada from across the globe with their physical and
intellectual assets with them. In many of those countries that a huge number of
immigrants came from may have a rich heritage of ‘traditional medicines’ and
overspread practices of using natural health products (NHP). That means those
immigrants must have been brought up in a context where ‘traditional medicines’
and NHP had a huge role in their cultural life. Canada can review its existing
regulatory arrangement relates to the designation of ‘traditional medicines’ and
entry of NHP in Canadian market provided that any changes will not put Canadian
to heightened health-risks. As communities in the remote hinterland are often
customarily inherited of the knowledge of ‘traditional medicines’ and NHP, their
production process may not be in Canada’s required scientific standard. This is
something an acceptable and reasonable discounts could accelerate the entry of
‘traditional medicines’ and NHP into Canadian market and that would ultimately
offer alternatives for Canadian. Newcomers and immigrants can be encouraged
for introducing traditional medicines, NHP and related knowledge from their
country of origin to their new home. This way Canada’s access to global
knowledgebase will be enhanced and many immigrants can also feel home at
Canada when they have access to medicines they are used to. This could open an
avenue for some entrepreneurship as well for newcomers. Among other things,
this could be one of the effective fixes of over-burdened healthcare industry in
Canada by ways of reducing potential demands for diagnostic and healthcare
services and utilizing alternatives of western medicines.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Impact of Immigration Policy on Health Care in Canada, with a Focus on Nurse
Practitioners
Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Submitted by: Nurse Practitioner Association of Canada (NPAC-AIIPC)
Dr. Laura Housden, PhD, MN-NP(F), President
 Dr. Stan Marchuk, DNP, MN-NP(F), Chief Executive Officer
Date: December 8, 2025
1. Introduction
The Nurse Practitioner Association of Canada (NPAC-AIIPC) submits this brief to inform the
Standing Committee on Health’s study on the impact of immigration policy on Canada’s
health care system, with specific attention to nurse practitioners (NPs).
Canada is experiencing sustained health workforce shortages and growing unmet needs in
primary care, mental health, chronic disease management, and rural and remote services.
Nurse practitioners, advanced practice nurses who independently assess, diagnose, order
and interpret tests, prescribe, and manage care across the life span, are a proven way to
expand access and improve quality.
Federal immigration policy increasingly recognizes health workers, including NPs, as a
priority occupation. However, misalignment between immigration pathways, credential
recognition, and the availability of funded NP positions contributes to underutilization of
internationally educated health professionals (IEHPs) and missed opportunities to improve
access to care.
2. Background: Nurse Practitioners in Canada
2.1 Historical development
The NP role was introduced in Canada in the 1960s to respond to provider shortages and
improve access in northern, rural, and remote communities. Early programs prepared
experienced nurses to provide comprehensive primary care in settings where no other
providers were available.
By the 1970s, NP programs expanded across several provinces but many initiatives were
discontinued in the 1980s because of perceived physician oversupply, lack of stable funding,
and uncertainty about regulation and remuneration.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
By the 1970s, NP programs expanded across several provinces but many initiatives were
discontinued in the 1980s because of perceived physician oversupply, lack of stable funding,
and uncertainty about regulation and remuneration.

From the late 1980s onward, population aging, rising chronic disease, and renewed
emphasis on primary health care led to a second wave of NP role development. Provinces
and territories gradually created NP legislation, standards, and education programs, and NPs
were integrated into primary and specialized care.
A major federal milestone was the Canadian Nurse Practitioner Initiative (CNPI, 2004–2006),
funded by Health Canada. CNPI produced a pan-Canadian framework for NP role
integration, including harmonized competency frameworks and education standards, and
helped support a substantial increase in NP numbers.
2.2 Current NP workforce
According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), in 2024 there were 9,891
NPs in Canada, and 7,477 were employed in direct patient care, an increase of 651 (9.5%)
from 2023. Per 10,000 population, the number of NPs in direct patient care rose from 1.6 in
2020 to 2.2 in 2024.
NPs now work across the continuum: primary care, emergency and acute care, long-term
care, mental health and addictions, Indigenous health services, and specialized programs
such as oncology, cardiology, endocrinology, and palliative care. About two-thirds of NPs in
direct care work in hospitals or community health agencies.
Despite strong evidence of effectiveness and rapid growth, NP supply remains modest
relative to need and NPs continue to be described as an “untapped resource” in the
Canadian health system.
3. The Nurse Practitioner Association of Canada (NPAC-AIIPC)
NPAC-AIIPC is the national professional association representing NPs and NP students
across Canada. Established in 2016, NPAC advocates for NPs, reduces barriers to NP
practice, and supports NP leadership and education in collaboration with provincial and
territorial NP associations, regulators, governments, and other partners.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Established in 2016, NPAC advocates for NPs, reduces barriers to NP
practice, and supports NP leadership and education in collaboration with provincial and
territorial NP associations, regulators, governments, and other partners.

4. Immigration, Health Workforce and Nurse Practitioners
4.1 Internationally educated health professionals in Canada
Internationally educated health professionals (IEHPs), including internationally educated
nurses and NPs, are an important part of Canada’s health workforce. In 2021, 259,695
IEHPs aged 18–64 were living in Canada, representing 13% of Canadians in that age group
with post-secondary education in a health field.
Many IEHPs are not employed in roles that fully utilize their skills. Only about 58% of
employed IEHPs worked in health occupations in 2021, and even among those in health
jobs, positions are often not commensurate with their training and education.
Internationally educated NPs accounted for 4.5% of the NP workforce in 2024, a small but
important minority. Internationally educated nurses (IENs) make up a growing share of newly
licensed nurses overall, rising from about 8% of new nurses in 2017 to 12% in 2022.
However, evidence shows that IEHPs face persistent barriers to workforce integration,
including complex, expensive, and lengthy credential recognition processes and delays in
licensure even after passing exams. These challenges contribute to underemployment in
roles below their qualifications or outside health care altogether.
4.2 Immigration policy and health worker recruitment
Federal immigration policy has increasingly prioritized health occupations. In 2023,
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) introduced category-based selection
under Express Entry, including a specific category for healthcare and social services
occupations. NPs (NOC 31302) are explicitly listed among the eligible occupations.
In parallel, Health Canada’s Ethical Framework for the Recruitment and Retention of
Internationally Educated Health Professionals in Canada (2024) emphasizes reducing
underutilization of IEHPs, aligning foreign credential recognition and licensure with ethical
recruitment, and enhancing domestic training capacity and data-informed workforce planning.
These federal initiatives are important but do not, on their own, resolve mismatches between
how immigration programs select health professionals and how regulators and employers
recognize credentials, issue NP licences, and fund NP positions.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
These federal initiatives are important but do not, on their own, resolve mismatches between
how immigration programs select health professionals and how regulators and employers
recognize credentials, issue NP licences, and fund NP positions.

5. Impacts of Immigration Policy on Health Care and Nurse Practitioners
5.1 Underutilization of internationally educated NPs and nurses
When immigration streams identify nursing and NP occupations as priority sectors, but
licensure pathways and funded positions are limited or slow, internationally educated NPs
often work in lower-skilled roles, experience prolonged underemployment, or leave the health
sector entirely. Canada is therefore attracting highly skilled health professionals without fully
leveraging their expertise during a time of critical health workforce shortages.
5.2 Misalignment of timelines and processes
Immigration, licensure, and employment operate largely in silos. Immigration decisions bring
nurses and potential NPs to Canada based on education and experience abroad. Regulatory
processes can involve lengthy document verification, bridging requirements, and exams,
often taking years and significant personal cost. Employment then depends on provincial and
territorial funding, NP remuneration models, and the creation of NP positions.
IEHPs often lack integrated, transparent information about these steps. Misaligned timelines
and fragmented processes contribute to unmet expectations, financial stress, and delayed
entry into practice.
5.3 Geographic and sectoral distribution
Immigration programs may encourage settlement in large urban centres where newcomer
services are concentrated, while health system needs are often greatest in rural, remote, and
Indigenous communities. Some immigration or return-of-service arrangements tie IEHPs to
specific locations or employers without sufficient professional and community supports, which
can undermine retention.
Targeted NP residency or fellowship models, especially in rural, remote, and specialized
areas, could help both domestically educated and internationally educated NPs transition into
practice and integrate into communities. Funding and scale for such programs remain limited.
5.4 Equity, ethics, and global responsibility
Canada’s reliance on immigrant health workers must be balanced with global responsibilities
to avoid exacerbating shortages in lower- and middle-income countries. The Health Canada
ethical framework, aligned with the WHO Global Code of Practice, calls for prioritizing

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
The Health Canada
ethical framework, aligned with the WHO Global Code of Practice, calls for prioritizing

reduction of underutilization of IEHPs already in Canada, investing in domestic education,
training, and retention, and ensuring equitable treatment and working conditions for both
IEHPs and domestically educated health professionals.
For NPs, immigration policy should therefore be paired with clear, funded pathways to NP
practice and robust domestic NP training capacity so that immigration complements, rather
than replaces, investments in Canada’s own health workforce.
6. Policy Recommendations to the Standing Committee on Health
NPAC-AIIPC respectfully offers the following recommendations.
Recommendation 1 – Align immigration selection with realistic NP licensure pathways
Work with IRCC, Health Canada, provincial and territorial regulators, and Health Workforce
Canada to:
•
Ensure that when NPs (NOC 31302) and related nursing occupations are targeted in
immigration programs, there are realistic pathways to licensure and employment in NP
roles.
•
Provide clear, pre-arrival information about NP licensure requirements, timelines, and
costs that is explicitly distinguished from immigration processes.
Recommendation 2 – Create NP-focused bridging, residency and fellowship initiatives
for IEHPs
Support Health Canada, provinces and territories, and academic partners to:
•
Develop and fund NP-specific bridging programs for internationally educated nurses
and NPs who meet baseline criteria, aligned with national NP competencies.
•
Expand mentorship, and NP residency and fellowship programs open to both
domestically educated and internationally educated NPs, with federal co-funding
where appropriate.
Recommendation 3 – Reduce underutilization of IEHPs already in Canada
In keeping with the Health Canada ethical framework, prioritize actions that enable IEHPs
currently residing in Canada to work at their full scope:
•
Support initiatives that streamline credential recognition, reduce unnecessary
duplication in assessment, and shorten licensure timelines for qualified IEHPs.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Recommendation 3 – Reduce underutilization of IEHPs already in Canada
In keeping with the Health Canada ethical framework, prioritize actions that enable IEHPs
currently residing in Canada to work at their full scope:
•
Support initiatives that streamline credential recognition, reduce unnecessary
duplication in assessment, and shorten licensure timelines for qualified IEHPs.

•
Incentivize employers to create NP roles designed to integrate IEHPs, including
targeted orientation, mentorship, and cultural safety supports.
•
Monitor and publicly report on the proportion of IEHPs working in health occupations
at a level commensurate with their education, including disaggregated data for NPs
and nurses.
Recommendation 4 – Strengthen domestic NP education and retention alongside
immigration
To ensure immigration is part of a balanced strategy, NPAC recommends that the federal
government:
•
Continue to invest in domestic NP education seats, including targeted funding
agreements with provinces and territories and academic institutions.
•
Support NP residency and fellowship programs as a standard component to meet
Canadians health care needs, NP transition to practice, improving retention and
distribution in high-need areas.
•
Link federal health transfers and bilateral workforce agreements to transparent plans
for NP integration in primary care, emergency care, long-term care, and rural and
remote health.
Recommendation 5 – Improve pan-Canadian data on NPs, immigration and IEHPs
Leverage Health Workforce Canada, CIHI, and Statistics Canada to:
•
Integrate immigration and workforce datasets so policy-makers can track the journey
of internationally educated nurses and NPs from immigration to licensure to
employment.
•
Produce regular, publicly accessible reports on NP supply, distribution, international
education status, sector of employment, and practice setting.
•
Include NP and IEHP indicators in health human resource planning tools used for
bilateral and pan-Canadian health agreements.
Recommendation 6 – Ensure fairness, ethical recruitment and global responsibility
Consistent with Canada’s commitments under the WHO Global Code of Practice and Health
Canada’s ethical framework, NPAC recommends that:
•
Federal and provincial governments avoid aggressive recruitment from countries with
critical health workforce shortages unless reciprocal, ethically designed agreements
are in place.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Recommendation 6 – Ensure fairness, ethical recruitment and global responsibility
Consistent with Canada’s commitments under the WHO Global Code of Practice and Health
Canada’s ethical framework, NPAC recommends that:
•
Federal and provincial governments avoid aggressive recruitment from countries with
critical health workforce shortages unless reciprocal, ethically designed agreements
are in place.

•
Return-of-service and location-restriction policies apply equitably to domestically
educated and internationally educated health workers, with appropriate professional
and community supports.
•
International recruitment strategies be balanced by robust domestic NP training and
retention plans.
7. Summary
Immigration policy is a powerful lever to support Canada’s health workforce, but without
alignment with licensure, funding, and ethical recruitment, it can leave IEHPs underutilized
and communities underserviced. By aligning immigration selection with realistic NP licensure
pathways, supporting NP-focused bridging and residency programs, reducing underutilization
of IEHPs already in Canada, strengthening domestic NP education, improving pan-Canadian
data, and upholding ethical recruitment principles, the federal government can ensure that
immigration policy supports a sustainable, equitable, and effective NP workforce.
These actions will improve access to timely, high-quality care for people across Canada while
honouring Canada’s global responsibilities.
8. Organizational Profile – Nurse Practitioner Association of Canada (NPAC-AIIPC)
The Nurse Practitioner Association of Canada (NPAC-AIIPC) is the national voice for nurse
practitioners and NP students in Canada. Established in 2016, NPAC represents more than
10,000 NPs and NP students from a wide range of clinical specialties and all provinces and
territories. NPAC advocates for high-quality, equitable access to care, reduces policy and
funding barriers to NP practice, supports NP leadership, education, research, and innovation,
and collaborates with stakeholders to advance pan-Canadian NP regulation and health
human resource planning.
NPAC appreciates the opportunity to provide this brief to the Standing Committee on Health
and would be pleased to appear as a witness to elaborate on these recommendations.

text:
Brief on Addressing Workforce Challenges in Respiratory Therapy
Written Submission to the Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Submitted by the Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists (CSRT)
November 2025
[CONTACT] www.csrt.com

Introduction
Respiratory therapists are regulated health professionals who are essential in Canada’s
acute care, critical care, primary care, and community-based health systems. They support
disease management in primary care for conditions such as asthma and chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), provide critical care in Canadian hospitals, and
deliver ongoing care in the community for patients requiring complex respiratory disease
management including home oxygen and mechanical ventilation.
There are approximately 12,000 respiratory therapists working in Canada.1 Even before the
COVID pandemic, and increasingly in its aftermath, Canada’s Occupational Projection
System (COPS) Occupational Outlook identified a “Strong Risk of Shortage” of respiratory
therapists between 2024-2033 at a national level. This shortage is likely to intensify: As
frontline care providers to critically ill patients, the COVID pandemic has taken its toll on
respiratory therapists. Alarmingly, respiratory therapists are showing worryingly high rates
or signs of PTSD, symptoms of depression, and anxiety or stress. During the pandemic,
more than 25% of respiratory therapists in Canada who were surveyed reported that they
were considering leaving healthcare.12 Respiratory therapists are essential for addressing
backlogs and access challenges across Canadian health systems. A shortage in the
respiratory therapist workforce threatens Canadians’ access to essential healthcare,
particularly lifesaving emergency and critical care, and chronic disease management.
Ensuring people living in Canada have timely access to these experts is essential for
improving access to the management of acute and chronic cardiopulpmary disease in
primary care, acute care, critical care and community settings
As the national body representing Canada’s respiratory therapists, the Canadian Society of
Respiratory Therapists (CSRT) urges Canada’s policymakers to strengthen federal analyses
of the respiratory therapist workforce and the factors leading to recruitment and retention
issues for respiratory therapists across Canada.3 We view the current study as a natural
extension of existing and ongoing discussions about addressing Canada’s health workforce
crisis, and offer the following recommendations as they relate to the Committee’s study on
immigration.
Support A Standardization of the International Respiratory Therapist
Workforce
Respiratory therapists are integral to delivering care and relieving pressures throughout
Canada’s health systems. The profession originated in Canada and the United States
leading to a consolidation of expertise and training in North America. There are, however,
sizable and growing professional communities of respiratory therapists in multiple

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
There are, however,
sizable and growing professional communities of respiratory therapists in multiple

countries including in the Philippines, India, and Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab
Emirates, among others.a The growth and diversification of the profession is a positive
development, with the potential to support Canada’s health workforce, should
internationally educated respiratory therapists choose to immigrate here and enter clinical
practice. However, the international respiratory therapy profession lacks harmonization of
occupational and educational standards, resulting in a heterogeneous global workforce
that is challenging to integrate into the Canadian health workforce.
The International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO), maintained by the
International Labour Organization (ILO), serves as a global framework for classifying and
aggregating workforce data, distinguishing health workers by skill level and specialization.
The respiratory therapy profession is currently excluded from ISCO and from the World
Health Organization (WHO) international classification of health workers. These omissions
hinder global workforce data collection, international reporting, international recruitment
and retention initiatives, and professional recognition in several jurisdictions. The absence
of respiratory therapy in the ISCO and in the WHO classification also creates challenges for
Canadian regulators and health systems to assess internationally trained respiratory
therapists and integrate suitable and capable clinicians into the Canadian workforce who
meet Canada’s national standard of competence.
The CSRT does not propose that international recruitment of respiratory therapists be used
as the sole or even an adequate mechanism for addressing the health workforce crisis.
However, given that respiratory therapists are integral to the delivery of care in Canadian
health systems, Canada is in a unique position to serve as a leader in advancing the
standardization of the international classification for respiratory therapists. Pursuing this
registration would be one step toward establishing global common standards for the
respiratory therapy profession, leading to more standardized and consistent training. This
could improve the ability of Canadian regulators to assess internationally educated
respiratory therapists and, if deemed qualified, allow them to enter the Canadian health
workforce.
The Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists is prepared to work with the Canadian
government and other national respiratory therapy societies to pursue ISCO and WHO
occupational designations. We make this recommendation out of a recognition of the
positive impacts and contributions that immigrants to Canada have had on the Canadian
health system and the reality that the sustainability and effectiveness of the Canadian
health system necessitate an increase in the health workforce, some of which may be
a A list of members of the International Council for Respiratory Care is available at:
https://irccouncil.org/about/member-countries-and-areas/

text:
a recognition of the positive impacts and contributions that immigrants to Canada have had on the Canadian health system and the reality that the sustainability and effectiveness of the Canadian health system necessitate an increase in the health workforce, some of which may be a A list of members of the International Council for Respiratory Care is available at: https://irccouncil.org/about/member-countries-and-areas/

provided through immigration. As such, ensuring the international respiratory therapist
workforce is aligned with the Canadian occupational profile, training, and competencies is
necessary to ensure the complementarity of global respiratory therapy training programs
and professional profiles with the needs of the Canadian health system.
Recommendation 1: Canada should endorse and support a submission to the
International Labour Organization to establish an International Standard Classification of
Occupations (ISCO) for the respiratory therapy profession and the inclusion of respiratory
therapists in the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of health workers.
Canada should lead and support efforts to include respiratory therapists in the ISCO and
WHO classifications, to harmonize global standards. This will improve credential
recognition and facilitate workforce mobility, including for internationally trained
respiratory therapists who wish to seek licensure and employment in Canada, by
harmonizing international training standards and competencies, increasing the likelihood
that internationally trained respiratory therapists meet Canadian standards. The CSRT is
prepared to work with our international partners and the Canadian government to develop
this submission.
Recommendation 2: Canada should establish impactful pathways to get internationally
educated respiratory therapists and other healthcare providers working.
Canada faces a strong risk of shortage for respiratory therapists between 2024-2033.
Immigration could potentially help alleviate some of these shortages, but current pathways
for internationally educated respiratory therapists and other health professionals are slow
and fragmented. Canada should fund and establish expedited, competency-based
assessment processes for internationally trained respiratory therapists, and fund and
implement bridging programs and mentorship opportunities across Canada.
Support Canada’s Current Respiratory Therapist Workforce
Canadians need access to timely respiratory therapy. Respiratory therapists have a role in
addressing long and often frustrating wait times in Canadian clinics and hospitals for
patients needing access to healthcare for the management of their acute and chronic
cardiorespiratory illnesses. Respiratory therapists possess an in-depth knowledge and
understanding of cardiorespiratory physiology, assessment, oxygenation, ventilation, and
pharmacology and perform case management, patient education, and the management
and care of complex patients and are integral to improving timely access to high-quality
health care for Canadians.4

text:
Respiratory therapists possess an in-depth knowledge and
understanding of cardiorespiratory physiology, assessment, oxygenation, ventilation, and
pharmacology and perform case management, patient education, and the management
and care of complex patients and are integral to improving timely access to high-quality
health care for Canadians.4

Growing demands for respiratory care are contributing to high, often unrealistic, workloads
for respiratory therapists. For example, in the critical care environment, the staffing
patterns of respiratory therapists in intensive care units – in particular, the ratio of
respiratory therapists to patients requiring mechanical ventilation (i.e. patients needing a
ventilator) – is variable across Canada, with no agreed-upon standard to guide staffing
decisions, and some respiratory therapists responsible for large caseloads of critically ill
and medically complex patients.5
The CSRT encourages Canadian governments to engage immediately in actions that
support the current respiratory therapist workforce in Canada to ensure that Canadians
and newcomers to Canada are guaranteed access to the highest quality care available.
Recommendation 3: Engage respiratory therapists in integrated health workforce planning.
Ensuring that respiratory therapists are available in sufficient numbers across all care
settings where patients with cardiorespiratory illnesses are receiving care strengthens
Canadian health systems and improves patient safety. Governments, health systems, and
health leaders must address respiratory therapy staffing needs and engage respiratory
therapists in integrated health workforce planning across Canada, ensuring that the
respiratory therapist workforce is planned and integrated into health systems to meet the
needs of Canada’s growing and aging population. Health workforce planning should align
population respiratory health needs, including planning that is informed by Canada’s
immigration policies and targets, with health workforce development to address health
care inequities and access gaps.
Recommendation 4: Strengthen and deepen the data on the respiratory therapy workforce
in Canada.
The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) collects high-level, standardized
information on the respiratory therapist workforce. The CSRT encourages decision-makers
to leverage data on respiratory therapists in health workforce and health services planning
to meet the respiratory therapy needs of the growing and aging Canadian population. We
recommend that Canadian health workforce planning include more sophisticated models
integrating demographic data, health care utilization trends, workforce training outputs,
and policy impacts.
Recommendation 5: Establish recruitment and retention strategies that equitably support
respiratory therapists across all areas of practice, and that document and address issues of
high workload and respiratory therapists’ wellbeing.
Health workforce planning and Canadian immigration policy must consider how new
approaches, population demographic changes (e.g. aging populations), and population

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Health workforce planning and Canadian immigration policy must consider how new
approaches, population demographic changes (e.g. aging populations), and population

growth, may affect respiratory therapists’ and all other healthcare professionals’ practice
environments, roles, wellness, and workloads. Recruitment and retention strategies should
include a focus on supporting interprofessional team-based care that allows respiratory
therapists to work at their full scope of practice, as well as initiatives to address respiratory
therapists’ workload and reduce administrative burdens.
We encourage the federal government to establish national guidelines and standards on
the ratio of respiratory therapists to high need patients (e.g. respiratory therapist to
ventilated patient ratios) like those that exist for other professions, based on rigorously
collected and analyzed evidence to ensure patient safety and respiratory therapist
wellbeing.
Recommendation 6: Establish a national strategy to support the mental health of
respiratory therapists and all healthcare providers.
The federal government, along with provincial and territorial governments and Canadian
health systems, should develop a more robust mental health and wellness strategy to
inform health human resources planning, and as part of recruitment and retention efforts.
This mental health and wellness strategy needs to specifically address the needs of
respiratory therapists, along with other frontline care providers, who experience high
workloads, traumatizing events in the clinical environment, and who are at risk of burnout
and other mental health problems because of their work. This could include funding
wellness programs to better protect health care providers from burnout and promoting
resilience, and to enhance respiratory therapists’ physical, psychological, and cultural
safety across primary care, acute care, critical care, and community/home care practice
settings.
Conclusion
The Canadian Society of Respiratory Therapists (CSRT) is Canada’s national voice for
respiratory therapists. We encourage decision makers to include respiratory therapists in
all aspects of health workforce planning and to take steps that strengthen the work that
respiratory therapists do in Canada and internationally, to meet the needs of patients with
cardiorespiratory diseases and in the promotion of respiratory health.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Submission to the Standing Committee on
Health for the Study on the Impact of
Immigration on Health Care

November 28, 2025

Section 1: Introduction

A strong and sustainable healthcare workforce is essential to delivering high-quality
cancer care in Canada. Healthcare providers – including those on the frontlines and in
supportive roles – bring a range of skills and expertise that directly impact access, quality
and continuity of care. With over 80 professions involved in cancer care, ensuring an
adequate, well-trained and well-distributed workforce is a critical priority which can be
aided by strategic immigration policy.

Canada’s healthcare system is facing unprecedented pressures due to an aging
population, rising cancer incidence and persistent gaps in workforce distribution. These
challenges are especially acute in rural and remote communities, where access to timely
and specialized care is often limited. As the demand for cancer services grows, it
becomes increasingly important to ensure that our healthcare workforce is not only
sufficient in number but also equipped with the diverse skills and professional
competencies needed to serve everyone in Canada. Strategic immigration policy,
alongside federal investments in training and workforce mobility, is essential to building
a resilient system that can adapt to evolving healthcare needs.

Section 2: Strategic Immigration Alleviates
Healthcare Workforce Challenges

While Canada’s overall supply of doctors has been growing, the increase in those
providing primary care is not keeping pace.1 6.5 million Canadians do not have access to
a primary care provider. Within 5 years, Canada needs 7,500 net new family physicians;
15,000 within 10 years. The supply of other primary care providers, including nurses,
nurse practitioners and physician assistants, needs to increase in tandem.

According to a new report developed in partnership with the Angus Reid Institute and
Canadian Cancer Society (CCS), one-quarter (26%) of Canadians report chronic difficulty
accessing the health-care system, while one-third (33%) face some challenges.
Furthermore, 26% of people with cancer had to leave their community for treatment,
often impacting mental health and finances.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Furthermore, 26% of people with cancer had to leave their community for treatment,
often impacting mental health and finances.

A strong and sustainable healthcare workforce is essential to delivering high-quality
cancer care in Canada. Healthcare providers – including those on the frontlines and in
supportive roles – there is a whole a range of skills and expertise that we need that
directly impact access, quality and continuity of care.

Addressing system capacity challenges involves attracting healthcare workers from
abroad and making it easier to recognize their credentials. It also means enabling
healthcare workers in Canada to work where they are needed most, while ensuring they
have supportive work environments. A coordinated, collaborative approach can enhance
system capacity, resilience and support equitable cancer care across Canada.

To strengthen pathways for internationally educated health professionals (IEHPs), CCS
also calls upon the federal government, in partnership with provinces, territories and
regulators to:
• Invest in streamlined, timely, fair and transparent processes to assess and
recognize international credentials and experience.
• Increase access to residency positions and bridging programs for international
medical graduates and other IEHPs.
• Expand fast-track pathways for IEHPs that better connect immigration,
credentialing, and training systems.
• Provide dedicated system navigators with expertise in IEHP licensure to guide
professionals through the right pathways to practise.
1 Canadian Partnership Against Cancer and the Canadian Association of Provincial Cancer Agencies, March
2010. The Cancer Workforce Scoping Study: A Report from the Front Lines of Canada’s Cancer Control
Workforce. https://s22457.pcdn.co/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Cancer-workforce-study-technicalreport-EN.pdf

• Offer mentorship, peer support, settlement support and mental health services to
help IEHPs transition smoothly into the Canadian healthcare system.

All efforts to recruit IEHPs should mitigate impacts on the health systems of their home
countries.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
All efforts to recruit IEHPs should mitigate impacts on the health systems of their home
countries.

Furthermore, to support the attraction of trained professionals to the healthcare
workforce, CCS calls upon all levels of government to:
• Provide financial and non-financial incentives to attract and retain healthcare
providers in rural and remote communities.
• Target recruiting and incentivize efforts to those who want to practice in Canada,
particularly those living in the US, prioritizing the healthcare workers we need
most and the needs of respective provinces and territories.
• Develop a national pool of temporary and mobile healthcare workers to fill
staffing gaps and provide relief in areas facing shortages based on local needs.
• Ensure healthcare workers can fully use their training and licenses by performing
all the procedures and practices that they are qualified for while maintaining high
standard and quality care (called scope of practice).

Moreover, many populations in Canada, especially in rural and remote communities,
continue to experience staffing shortages and workforce imbalances. Healthcare
workers already living in Canada often face challenges when moving between provinces
or territories and those trained in other countries often must wait a long time to get their
qualifications recognized in Canada. These factors impact timely care delivery, increase
workloads for staff, and limit the system’s ability to respond to emerging needs.

To improve workforce mobility so healthcare professionals can work and provide care
where they are needed most across Canada, CCS calls upon federal, provincial and
territorial governments, in collaboration with regulatory bodies, to:
• Implement pan-Canadian licensure through coordinated credential recognition,
beginning with doctors and nurses.
• Introduce legislation to remove federal barriers to workforce mobility for
healthcare professionals, including cancer care professionals.
• Develop streamlined, portable licensure mechanisms to allow qualified healthcare
professionals to work across provinces and territories without unnecessary
delays, extra costs or repeated steps.

• Align and review scope of practice policies across provinces and territories, where
possible, so providers can use their full training and licensure.
• Invest in shared digital systems to securely and quickly transfer licensing and
credential information between provinces and territories.
• Implement competitive, transparent and equitable pay to attract and retain
healthcare providers to meet the need of each jurisdiction, regardless of where
they choose to practice.

provinces and territories, where possible, so providers can use their full training and licensure. • Invest in shared digital systems to securely and quickly transfer licensing and credential information between provinces and territories. • Implement competitive, transparent and equitable pay to attract and retain healthcare providers to meet the need of each jurisdiction, regardless of where they choose to practice.

All efforts to improve workforce mobility must protect patient safety and maintain high
standards of cancer care.

Section 3: Pan-Canadian Strategic Oncology
Workforce

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Section 3: Pan-Canadian Strategic Oncology
Workforce

CCS provided seed funding to the Canadian Association of Provincial Cancer Agencies
(CAPCA), to develop a Pan-Canadian strategy on the oncology workforce. The strategy
identified several challenges, such as a lack of data, that hamper the ability of
professionals to deliver the high-quality cancer care patients need. Along with the rest of
the population, the oncology workforce is aging, leading to an expected increase in the
gap between professionals needed to deliver oncology services and those that are
available to do so. Furthermore, newer generations of oncology professionals are less
likely to adapt to the strenuous work hours we expect of our medical professionals to
keep our system operational - leading to issues in recruitment and retention further
exacerbating the lack of sufficient personnel in the oncology workforce.
These issues have a grave and pressing impact on patients who, without adequate care
from oncology professionals, suffer worse outcomes and worse quality of life. In this
context, immigration is not just a demographic factor, but a vital part of the solution. By
strengthening and streamlining pathways for IEHPs—including fair and timely recognition
of international credentials, expanded access to training and residency opportunities, and
comprehensive support for integration—Canada can attract and retain the skilled
professionals needed to deliver high-quality care. These efforts will help ensure that all
communities, regardless of location, have access to the oncology expertise they need. It
is incumbent upon this Committee to ensure that in its study on the impact of
immigration on healthcare, the ability of internationally educated oncology professionals
to practice to Canada is a high priority.
A pan-Canadian healthcare workforce strategy is needed to prioritize retaining an
adequate number of healthcare professionals who are sufficiently trained, provide
culturally safer care and workforce safety, and meet the evolving needs of cancer care
delivery across provinces and territories. Such a strategy should:
o Strengthen recruitment, retention, and training.
o Promote equity, diversity, and inclusion in our healthcare system by
addressing systemic discrimination and barriers that disproportionately
affect underserved and underrepresented populations, including rural and
remote communities.
o Ensure that we have the capacity to train and support healthcare providers
in the full continuum of cancer care, including a palliative approach to care.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
o Strengthen recruitment, retention, and training. o Promote equity, diversity, and inclusion in our healthcare system by addressing systemic discrimination and barriers that disproportionately affect underserved and underrepresented populations, including rural and remote communities. o Ensure that we have the capacity to train and support healthcare providers in the full continuum of cancer care, including a palliative approach to care.

o Ensure healthcare providers are available where they are needed most, and
that their services are aligned with the cultural expectations and
experiences of the communities they are working in to foster trust.
o Include the voices of people with cancer, caregivers and those at risk of
cancer when making decisions around the healthcare workforce.

Addressing Canada’s healthcare workforce crisis will ultimately result in a more resilient
and effective healthcare system, one that will ensure people with cancer can access
healthcare when they need to, close to home.

Section 4: Lack Of Health Workforce Data

Addressing system capacity issues caused by understaffing requires that we have an
adequate understanding of the staffing numbers is needed and an accurate assessment
of where that need most greatly lies.

As is stated in CAPCA’s report on the oncology workforce:
“A key challenge uncovered in this work is the limited pan-Canadian oncology
workforce data. Within provincial jurisdictions, available data supports local oncology
workforce planning, allowing provinces to develop strategies that address their specific
oncology workforce challenges, though some variation may exist across jurisdictions.
However, system partners agree that, given the realities of the current state and the
evolving innovations and trends in cancer care, a provincial workforce view is no longer
sufficient. A pan-Canadian view of the workforce must be established, not only to
strengthen provincial planning, but also drive transformation in pan-Canadian
workforce approaches, such as models of care, education and training, and workforce
distribution.”

For these reasons, a pan-Canadian healthcare workforce strategy should also require
enhanced workforce data collection and analysis including establishing a minimum data
standard and encouraging transparent data sharing to support healthcare workforce
planning and evaluation across regions and training programs.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
For these reasons, a pan-Canadian healthcare workforce strategy should also require
enhanced workforce data collection and analysis including establishing a minimum data
standard and encouraging transparent data sharing to support healthcare workforce
planning and evaluation across regions and training programs.

CCS calls on the federal government to:
• Determine national minimum data standards, annual reporting, and
interjurisdictional data sharing to inform planning, evaluation and accountability
for all healthcare professionals.
• Support internationally trained healthcare workers to enter the Canadian
workforce by addressing barriers in immigration, credential recognition, licensing
and employment.
• Invest in safe, fair and supportive work environments that protect the mental
health and well-being of healthcare providers in all healthcare settings.
• Harness new technologies by investing in digital tools, data connectivity and AI
solutions for a more modern, efficient healthcare system.
• Provide funding to increase training positions for health professionals in areas of
need by coordinating efforts between federal ministries responsible for health
and post-secondary education.

• Include First Nations, Inuit and Métis leadership in the development of the
strategy to ensure it reflects their needs and priorities.

Section 5: Why it Matters

CCS urges the Standing Committee on Health to prioritize these solutions in its study
and to champion policies that will build a resilient, equitable, and sustainable cancer care
workforce for the benefit of all Canadians.
A strong and resilient healthcare workforce is the backbone of high-quality cancer care
in Canada. Yet, the country faces critical shortages, uneven distribution of professionals,
and persistent barriers for IEHPs. These challenges threaten timely access to care,
especially in rural and remote communities, and increase pressure on existing staff.
Immigration is not just a demographic factor—it is a vital part of the solution. By
streamlining credential recognition, expanding training opportunities, and providing
comprehensive support for IEHPs, Canada can attract and retain the skilled professionals
needed to deliver equitable, high-quality care. This approach ensures that all
communities, regardless of location, have access to the oncology expertise they need.
Moreover, a coordinated, pan-Canadian strategy that includes robust data collection, fair
workforce mobility, and ethical recruitment practices will help build a sustainable system.
Such efforts not only improve outcomes for patients but also foster trust, inclusion, and
cultural safety within the healthcare system.
Ultimately, addressing these workforce challenges is essential for ensuring that people
with cancer can access care when and where they need it—now and in the future.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Sonography Canada submits this brief to the Standing Committee on Health to highlight
the importance of sonographers in the Canadian healthcare system and the barriers to
internationally trained professionals.

Executive Summary:
Diagnostic medicine is a vital but often less recognized component of the Canadian
healthcare system, which has been increasingly under strain for the last five years. One
important aspect of the diagnostic ecosystem in Canada is sonography.

Sonography is the practice of using ultrasound as a medical investigation to assess organs,
tissues, and blood flow inside the body. Diagnostic medical sonographers perform at least
10 million ultrasound scans in Canada each year. These highly skilled professionals are a
vital part of the care economy and consistently enable improved health outcomes for
Canadians, from diagnosis through patient care.

Sonographers have been bearing the brunt of a medical system under strain, resulting in a
shortage of Canadian-trained sonographers who are ready to enter active practice.
However, there is a solution to this issue in supporting and funding programs for
internationally trained medical professionals to transition into Canadian sonography
practice.

Current Situation:
Sonography is practiced differently around the world. In most countries, sonography is
performed by physicians who have the essential skills to become sonographers in Canada,
should they wish to do so. With fundamental medical skills in place, most only need to
familiarize themselves with Canadian practice norms and standards and acclimate to the
Canadian health care system to succeed. These candidates do not require the same level
of education and upskilling for practice as would a Canadian accredited program student
and could be transitioned to practice quickly.

There are established pathways for these internationally trained health professionals to
obtain credentials and/or licenses to practice in Canada. However, there are still
significant barriers to success within the Canadian health care system. These barriers
include:

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
These barriers
include:

 Sonographers are regulated health professionals in only Ontario, Nova
Scotia, Saskatchewan, and Quebec. Most other provinces are pursuing
regulation, but the timeline is unknown. Requirements for practice in all
jurisdictions, even for those that are regulated, vary. This can be very
confusing and challenging for both domestic and international
professionals.
 There are an increasing number of requests for various documents and
letters to assist those wishing to move to Canada with the immigration
process. This includes requests for dates and process updates for Visa
applications, letters of invitation, and so on.
 Even though there is currently a pathway to practice, there are very few
supports in place to transition into Canadian practice and gain
experience in this country. In many cases, these individuals end up taking
an accredited sonography education program designed for students with
very different entrance prerequisites or find unaccredited “prep
programs” that take advantage of internationally trained professionals.
 Even if international candidates earn credentials or get a license to
practice without taking an accredited educational program, they often
struggle to find employment because they have no Canadian work
experience. Workplaces are already overwhelmed and are unable to take
on the burden of supporting their transition to practice.

If early experiences in Canada for a newcomer are not positive, including
the ability to work and becoming employed, it can impact the retention of
these skill workers in the country. 1
Data and Insight
• There were more than 300 international applicants in 2024 to the two practice
pathways. This number has been steadily increasing over the last few years.2
• The current timeline for individuals from application to practice varies from:
 Quickest ~ 6 months
 Average currently 1 to 1.5 years
1 https://forcitizenship.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/print_the-leaky-bucket_2023.pdf
2 Annual Reports · CMRITO Portal. https://www.cmrito.org/static-resources/publications/Annual-Reports/.
Accessed 1 Dec. 2025.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Accessed 1 Dec. 2025.

 The completion time varies based on the application process
(Sonography Canada vs. Regulatory College, where applicable),
candidate motivation, and the location of the applicant.
 Many approved applicants, once approved, never move forward with the
credentialing process. This is strongly influenced by whether the
candidate has already relocated to Canada.
• Certification Exam Statistics
o International applicants have at least a 20% lower pass rate than
Canadian-accredited program graduates (on the written exam).
o The pass rate for the clinical skills assessment is 70%. However, many
candidates never get past the written examinations or choose not to
pursue this assessment.
 There is so much attrition. Many candidates exhaust the five-year
eligibility timeline and do not complete the process due to personal
obligations and cost.

However, despite the barriers, there is an example of a successful clinical bridging
program in the country that has been an asset to internationally trained professionals to
familiarize themselves with Canadian practice. The only drawback is that it has mostly
served the greater Toronto area, to date, and class size is limited.

Case Study of Successful Bridging To Canadian Practice:
The Michener Institute of Education offers a Continuing Education Bridging Course in
Generalist Ultrasound, that has been successful in bridging previously trained,
international medical professionals and integrating them into the Canadian practice
context. It has enabled internationally trained sonographers to overcome the challenges
outlined in the statistics above, and we believe this approach could be replicated across
Canada.

Since 2019, the Michener Continuing Education Bridging Course in Generalist Ultrasound
has seen many of its students pass program assessments, and those who have
successfully completed the program report that they have found work in diagnostic
imaging clinics in Ontario. Students have stated that the course either helped them feel
confident in their next steps or they have identified gaps in their knowledge and skills with
respect to aspects of Canadian sonography practice. The Michener Institute’s program
hosts expert instructors who are engaged with their students and their successes.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
The Michener Institute’s program
hosts expert instructors who are engaged with their students and their successes.

Despite this program's success, there are also other notable barriers that potential new
sonographers may face. Some are financial, as there are no bursaries available to help
fund their training. Students can only turn to Windmill Microlending or the Accelerating
Career Advancement program for small-interest loans. Potential students may be applying
from their home countries and are unable to get visas.

The Michener program is offered in Toronto only. While the program accepts out-ofprovince students, many struggle to relocate to Ontario for the course. Therefore, the
program mostly sees applicants from Ottawa, Belleville, Barrie, Milton, Richmond Hill,
Brampton, Vaughan, and Oakville.

Conclusion:
Sonography Canada has observed an increasing demand for additional educational seats
and support for international students, and it is evident that the current programs are
successful. International medical professionals can thrive in the Canadian medical
landscape, especially as sonographers; we need the funding and programs to train them.

While the federal government is projecting that 200 sonographers will retire per year,
Sonography Canada data indicates that this number is may be low. Current member
research indicates that 43.2 % of 7500 members are over the age of 45, and 14.75% say
they will be retiring within five years.3

Additionally, the vacancy rate within hospitals and clinical sites is at least 12 percent at
any given time. Training new sonographers domestically cannot be the only strategy used
to address staffing shortages. Investment in bridging programs for international candidates
is needed to identify and address gaps in candidates’ professional knowledge and
experience to expedite the recognition of their skills and experience. This would enhance
capacity and maximize the benefits of our immigration system to grow the number of welltrained, experienced sonographers in the workforce.

Reputable bridging programs that support the successful integration of internationally
trained sonographers are almost non-existent in Canada today. Adequate funding and
availability of bridging seats is critical to support new health professionals, including
3 Institute For Canadian Citizenship. “ A Study of Immigrant Retention Trends in Canada.” 2023,
https://forcitizenship.ca/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/print_the-leaky-bucket_2023.pdf.

sonographers, in Canada. This is an important consideration in the development of a
holistic bridging strategy for internationally trained healthcare providers who are looking to
come to Canada as well as those who may already be here and not able to work.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
This is an important consideration in the development of a
holistic bridging strategy for internationally trained healthcare providers who are looking to
come to Canada as well as those who may already be here and not able to work.

Sonography Canada has the resources, expertise and connections to create a
standardized framework for a more expansive bridging supports nationwide. However, this
requires government support and the inclusion of sonography as a discrete profession in
the foreign credential recognition program.

Diagnostics are fundamental to a patient’s healthcare journey and a positive outcome.
Sonography is one of the most accessible, cost-effective and widely-used diagnostic
examinations, more than MRI and CT combined. Canada needs well-trained sonographers
who are competent and comfortable within the Canadian context.

About Us:
Sonography Canada represents over 7,500 practicing diagnostic medical sonographers
across Canada. These highly skilled professionals perform over 10 million ultrasound
examinations per year and are vital to the care economy, delivering improved health
outcomes for Canadians. Sonography Canada is the national credentialing body and
professional association for sonographers across the country, ensuring practitioners who
hold a credential in sonography have met high, nationally consistent standards of patient
care. Sonography Canada advocates on behalf of its members to ensure they have the
supports necessary to deliver the high standard of diagnostic imaging care that Canadians
expect and deserve.

text:
From registration to retention: Supporting
Internationally Educated Nurses through quality
bridging education and integration support
Submitted to
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Parliament of Canada
Submitted by
Dr. Jean Daniel Jacob
Executive Director
Canadian Association of Schools of Nursing
Contact Information
Email: [CONTACT]
Phone: [CONTACT]
Website: www.casn.ca
Address: 200-[CONTACT]., Ottawa, ON, [CONTACT]
Submitted on
December 2, 2025

A Note on Terminology
This briefing note refers to the nursing professions in Canada, which include licensed practical nurses
(LPNs), registered psychiatric nurses (RPNs), registered nurses (RNs), and nurse practitioners (NPs).
In Ontario, the designation for diploma-prepared nurses is registered practical nurse. In this note, we use
LPNs when referring to practical nurses across Canada.
Background
Concerns surrounding the domestic production of nurses are not new. In 2018, forecasting models
predicted that Canada would face a shortage of 117,600 nurses by 2030 (Scheffler & Arnold, 2019). The
COVID-19 pandemic introduced conditions that accelerated retirements and other attrition from the
nursing workforce.
Nursing programs have increased seats in response to the rising demand for LPNs, RNs, and NPs. For
example, from 2009–2020, program seats in entry-to-practice programs for RNs remained stable,
admitting an average of 15,696 students annually (Canadian Association of Schools of Nursing [CASN], in
press). A notable 12% increase occurred between 2021 and 2024, with programs admitting 18,389
students (see Figure 1). During this period, seats in NP programs increased by 41%. The Canadian
Institute for Health Information (CIHI) reported growth in the supply of both LPNs and RPNs in 2023 and
2024 (CIHI, 2025a, 2025b).
Recent projections of health workforce supply to 2034 identified a persistent gap, with the largest
shortage expected among RNs (Health Canada, 2025). Although expanding the domestic production of
nurses is a sustainable and ethical strategy, it must be considered alongside the broader potential
workforce, including IENs.

Since well before the pandemic, Canada has been a destination for IENs. While the immigration system
has made it easier for this highly skilled workforce to enter the country, fewer resources have been
dedicated to ensuring they are able to transition into employment that matches their education (Covell
et al., 2017; OECD, 2019). Over half of recently immigrated IENs work as orderlies, nurse’s aides or LPNs,
despite holding a bachelor’s degree or higher. (Bernard & Seddiki, 2025). This underutilization of IENs
represents “brain drain,” the loss of nurses from a country’s health system due to migration, and “brain
waste,” the underuse of nursing skills after migration. This is misaligned with international guidance for
ethical immigration of health professionals (Walton-Roberts et al., 2014).
To practise nursing in Canada, IENs must obtain licensure from a provincial or territorial regulatory body
for nursing. Historically, the pathway from application to registration and licensure was challenging
costly, leading to attrition of IENs from the process (Blythe & Baumann, 2009; Lee & Wojtiuk, 2021).
When the nursing shortage rapidly escalated during the COVID-19 pandemic, the nursing regulatory
bodies streamlined the processes surrounding the application and registration of IENs (Chui et al., 2025).
These reforms have led to growth in IEN registrations across jurisdictions and in all categories of nursing.
The proportion of IENs in Canada grew from 8% of the nursing workforce in 2017 to 12% in 2022 (CIHI,
2024).
An increase in IEN applicants and faster application processing has increased demand for bridging
education. Research supports bridging education that is flexible and accounts for the IEN learners’ needs
and their previous nursing experience, with an emphasis on clinical practice opportunities (Neiterman et
al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2025). Provincial governments, regulatory colleges, and post-secondary

org: Canadian Association of Schools of Nursing
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Provincial governments, regulatory colleges, and post-secondary

institutions have responded to the increased demand and challenges associated with the rigidity of
existing bridging education by developing targeted, expedited bridging education (e.g., accelerated
pathways for IENs at Saskatchewan Polytechnic; the Ontario Colleges IEN Upgrade Courses).Changes to
bridging education have varied across the country and reflect the availability of resources provincially.
Attrition of the nursing workforce remains a reality that must be considered alongside IEN integration
and retention. 4 in 10 nurses intend to leave the profession within the next year (Canadian Federation of
Nurses Unions, 2024) and 40% of nurses are leaving the profession before the age of 35 (Faubert, 2025).
In Ontario, IENs were less likely to renew their registration and be employed in nursing compared to
graduates educated in Ontario (CNO, 2024). Reasons for this higher rate of attrition are not well
understood.
Considerations for the Committee
Recent streamlining of the IEN application and registration reflects the implementation of long-overdue
reforms (Crea-Arsenio et al., 2023). Research is needed to understand the impacts of reforms to identify
best practices in IEN application and registration. Further harmonization across provinces in these
processes could also reduce confusion and create a more equitable process for all IENs seeking nursing
registration in Canada (Chiu et al., 2025).
IEN bridging education is beneficial for preparing IENs for nursing practice in Canada and supports their
long-term retention (Covell et al., 2018). Evaluating the outcomes of reformed targeted bridging
education of IENs is necessary to understand best practices and future directions. These best practices
should be integrated into standards for program approval and accreditation processes to ensure quality
and lessen variable outcomes.
Health care institutions require access to reliable and accessible transition support programming,
particularly for IENs who transition directly from another country into nursing practice in Canada.
Common learning needs include communication barriers, unfamiliarity with the Canadian health care
culture and the autonomous yet interprofessional nature of Canadian nursing practice (McGillis Hall et
al., 2015; Ramji & Etowa, 2018). IENs encounter interpersonal and systemic racism that affects their
transition and work experience. Nurses that are made aware of these experiences and are trained in
culturally safe mentorship contribute to inclusive workplaces (Cruz et al., 2025). Given that there is a
lower rate of registration renewal amongst IENs, it is important to ensure investments in improving
registration processes and bridging education pathways are not wasted.
Recommendations
CASN respectfully requests that the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health consider the
following actions:
1. Create a national joint commission on IENs to further optimize registration, bridging,
and transition supports for IENs.

org: Canadian Association of Schools of Nursing
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Create a national joint commission on IENs to further optimize registration, bridging,
and transition supports for IENs.

That a joint commission be established between provincial and territorial nursing regulatory
bodies, CASN, the Canadian Nurses Association, Chief Nurses Officers/Executives, and Canada’s
Chief Nursing Officer to work in a coordinated, pan-Canadian effort to strength IEN registration,
bridging education, and integration.
This joint commission could work to:
•
coordinate actions between systems that support IENs from application through to
employment to further streamline entry to practice;
•
evaluate the outcomes of recent reforms to identify best practices and strive towards
implementation across jurisdictions where feasible; and
•
explore innovative solutions, such as IEN residency or accreditation of international schools.
2. Support continued improvement of IEN bridging education.
That the Foreign Credential Recognition Program (FCRP) support regulatory authorities and
schools of nursing in building flexible and targeted bridging education for IENs that recognizes
the competencies the IENs already possess. The outcomes of these programs should be
evaluated and support approval and accreditation processes of IEN bridging education.
3. Support integration programming for IENs.
That the FCRP support institutions in strengthening their capacity to effectively integrate IENs
through structured, accessible programs, such as CASN’s IEN Mentorship Program.
Conclusion
The World Health Organization (2025) predicts a global nursing shortage of 4.5 million nurses by 2030.
Canada must implement ethical and sustainable solutions now to meet our domestic needs. The support
of IEN integration should be seen as one element of a broader necessary HHR strategy for nursing that
includes domestic production, providing transition supports for new graduates, cultivating healthy work
environments, and enabling nurses to practise to their full scope.

INTEGRAL TO HEALTH FOR CANADA
December 2, 2025
WRITTEN SUBMISSION TO THE HOUSE OF COMMONS STANDING COMMITTEE
ON HEALTH (HESA) STUDY: IMPACT OF IMMIGRATION POLICY ON

Dr. Gillian Muir, DVM, PhD
Professor and Dean,

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Gillian Muir, DVM, PhD
Professor and Dean,
Western College of Veterinary Medicine,
University of Saskatchewan

SUMMARY
Veterinarians are a key component in Canada’s public health and food systems, serving many essential roles
in keeping Canada safe from disease.
The current and future shortage of veterinarians in Canada poses a critical risk to Canadians’ health.
Canada needs a dedicated national clinical proficiency testing centre for internationally trained veterinarians
to ensure the country has a sufficient workforce to meet our needs now and into the future.
BRINGING TOGETHER HUMAN, ANIMAL, AND ECOSYSTEM HEALTH
The health of humans, domestic and wild animals, plants, and the wider environment (including ecosystems)
are closely linked and interdependent.
Collaborating across sectors and disciplines to protect health, address health challenges such as the
emergence of infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance, and food safety and promote the health and
integrity of our ecosystems is called a "One Health" approach.i
Because of that interdependence, Canada's veterinarians form the foundation of full spectrum of disease
control from prevention to detection, preparedness, response and management. They are a critical link in
protecting public health in Canada and providing Canada's contribution to global health security.
VETERINARIANS FULFILL KEY ROLES
Protecting public health: Veterinarians are responsible for animal health and welfare and also for public
health.
Veterinarians identify and report zoonotic diseases. Three out of every 4 new or emerging infectious
diseases in people come from animals, and more than 6 out of every 10 known infectious diseases in
people can be spread from animals, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and
Preventionii.
Veterinarians provide disease surveillance, and address wildlife health.
Protecting Canada's food system: Food animal veterinarians, including aquaculture veterinarians, focus on
the health and well-being of livestock and other food animals raised for human consumption, such as cattle,
poultry, seafood and swine.
Veterinarians are the ‘boots on the ground’, identifying emerging diseases, and providing disease
prevention, herd health management, reproductive assistance, oversight to protect food animal
safety and supply security.
Veterinarians provide diagnostic/inspection services, ensuring the health and safety of commercial
food products.
Veterinarians ensure the safety of the food supply by regulating the import and export of livestock and
food products and the control of infectious diseases among livestock and wildlife.
Protecting Canadians via research and innovation: Research and Industry veterinarians work in research
institutions, pharmaceutical companies, and various industries related to animal health:
improving animal disease prevention, diagnostic tests and treatment, and

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Protecting Canadians via research and innovation: Research and Industry veterinarians work in research
institutions, pharmaceutical companies, and various industries related to animal health:
improving animal disease prevention, diagnostic tests and treatment, and

providing translational medicine where animal models are used to research and improve diagnosis
and treatment of conditions in humans, as well as studying disease transmissible between animals
and humans.
A NATIONAL VETERINARIAN SHORTAGE
There will be consistently less than one unemployed worker per job vacancy. Employers will be unable to fill
vacancies, and job seekers will be insufficient to fill all the openings.
According to the Canadian Occupational Projection System, from 2022-2031iii:
Number of vet job vacancies: 5,000.
Number of new vets coming online from new graduates and immigrants, combined: 4,300.
WHY NOT JUST TRAIN MORE VETS IN CANADA?
There is no capacity to train any additional veterinarians in Canada—Canada's five vet schools are already
full. Even with the expansions of vet schools being contemplated, the potential expanded capacity will not
close the gap.
A significant growth in supply of veterinarians must come from certification of internationally trained vets.
Currently, 43 per cent of veterinarians working in Canada were trained internationally. The population of
internationally trained is a combination of Canadians going abroad to seek veterinary training because of
significant capacity limitations in Canadian vet schools and non-Canadians seeking to bring their talents and
their knowledge to Canada via immigration.
ENSURING INTERNATIONALLY TRAINED VETS ARE READY
Before they are qualified to practise in Canada, internationally trained veterinarians who studied in a program
not accredited by the AVMA/CVMA Council on Education must pass both a series of written exams and a sixpart Clinical Proficiency Examination (CPE) that assesses their hands-on clinical skills in a basic set of
veterinary competencies. The pass rate depends upon the experience and level of preparation of the
candidate and annually averages between 30 - 55 per cent.
The University of Saskatchewan's Western College of Veterinary Medicine (WCVM) is the only place in
Canada for veterinarians to take this exam in English.
THE BOTTLENECK
WCVM can currently only provide 108 testing spots annually for nearly 1,000 potential internationally
educated veterinary candidates who have passed all the requisite written exams.
The waiting time is currently 8 – 12 months to take the exam. This results in a substantial backlog
of veterinarians who are waiting to take the test, working in unrelated, or tangential fields.
Exam testing events require substantial resources and commandeer existing WCVM hospital clinical and
laboratory spaces. WCVM provides Saskatchewan’s only 24/7 tertiary care veterinary hospital; during exam

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
WCVM provides Saskatchewan’s only 24/7 tertiary care veterinary hospital; during exam

events, the public cannot access the hospital, as the exam requires redirecting resources from regular clinic
operations.
The current physical space at WCVM limits exam enrolment, the frequency of testing events, and thus, the
number of qualified internationally trained vets entering the workforce.
RECOMMENDATION:
ESTABLISH A DEDICATED NATIONAL CLINICAL PROFICIENCY EXAM TESTING CENTRE AT
UNIVERSITY OF SASKATCHEWAN’S WESTERN COLLEGE OF VETERINARY MEDICINE (WCVM).
The University of Saskatchewan requests that the Government of Canada support the construction of a
dedicated space for testing internationally educated veterinarians at the University of Saskatchewan’s
Western College of Veterinary Medicine.
At a cost of approximately $50 million, this space would leverage the existing expertise, systems, personnel,
experience, and space at WCVM to maximize value for Canadians at minimum cost.
Having a dedicated space will triple the frequency of testing events and number of potential qualified vets
being tested.
A dedicated space for retraining/upskilling unsuccessful candidates will also increase the passing rate and
cut down the backlog, while ensuring vets enter the Canadian market with the highest proficiency in minimal
time.
The multi-purpose facility will include:
Multiple stations to assess candidates’ clinical proficiency in medical examination,
Multi-user surgical suite,
Veterinary pathology suite,
Basic medical imaging facilities,
Anesthesia induction and recovery areas, and
Housing for live animals.

Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers
