Submitted by 369 Global

About 369 Global
369 Global is a group of companies with business interests in skills training and workforce
development, media and communications, and global market facilitation.
Our vision is to inform, educate and activate global citizens to make a worldwide impact. We
do this by providing our clients with innovative, inclusive, and scalable training, business and
communications solutions that prepare our clients to address global challenges.

Recommendations:
Key federal departments, including Health Canada, Employment and Social Development
Canada, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, Global Affairs Canada, and Export
Development Canada, should begin exploring to support a shift towards the use of
international TVET to address the shortage of PSWs and other key technical and vocational
key healthcare professions, including by:
• engaging with experts and potential GSC operators,
• examining opportunities to provide both financial and diplomatic support, and
• evaluating possible changes to Canada’s immigration system to ensure alignment
with the concept of international TVET and the GSC model.

of international TVET to address the shortage of PSWs and other key technical and vocational key healthcare professions, including by: • engaging with experts and potential GSC operators, • examining opportunities to provide both financial and diplomatic support, and • evaluating possible changes to Canada’s immigration system to ensure alignment with the concept of international TVET and the GSC model.

Overview
Canada is at a pivotal moment. Our country is facing critical shortages of health care
professionals and other skilled workers. These gaps are only expected to grow in the coming
years as a result of Canada’s aging population, significant reductions in temporary foreign
workers, and growing competition for skilled immigration across the Global North. Canada
must take action to address these challenges.
Current approaches to correcting these labour shortages are not sufficient. Canadian
education institutions are not training the volume of people necessary to meet current
labour demands. Furthermore, Canada’s recent overreliance on temporary foreign workers
and international students put strain on the country’s housing, infrastructure, and health
care. For the first time since the turn of the century, a majority of Canadians now think that
there is too much immigration.1 Newcomers are also struggling — 42 per cent of newcomers
would consider leaving Canada2 and immigrants who landed since 1982 are leaving at an
annual rate of almost one per cent per year.3
The Growing PSW Shortage
While shortages of physicians and nurses often generate headlines, Canada is also facing a
significant shortages for Personal Support Workers (PSWs), which is only expected to worsen
in coming years as Canada’s population ages.4 Research from McMaster University found
that the home care sector will require an additional 39,000 PSWs by 2043 (for a total of
115,000) while the hospital sector will require an additional 100,000 (for a total of 200,000).5
The Government of Canada recognizes how critical it is to attract and retain PSWs: Budget
2025 introduced a temporary Personal Support Workers Tax Credit under which workers can
claim a tax credit equal to five per cent of their wage.6
PSWs are a key example of the crisis caused by the technical and vocational skills gap in
Canada. While skills gaps exist across education levels, nearly two-thirds of Canadian job
vacancies that require post-secondary training require non-university credentials.7 These
skills shortages are not just costly – for both governments and for those paying out of pocket
– but they also lead to lower standards of care and often put additional burdens on family
members in caring for their loved ones. This skills gap is likely to intensify further given
planned reductions to immigration levels and to international student permits. Canada
heavily relies on newcomers to fill the roles as PSWs: approximately 35 per cent of PSWs in

and Future Skills Centre.

Canada are immigrants.8 Furthermore, the success of efforts to accelerate the credentialling
of internationally-trained nurses – many of whom work as PSWs while waiting – would also
reduce a potential source of PSWs.
The Path Forward
This is the moment for Canada to consider innovative approaches to addressing skills and
labour shortages through tactical immigration and labour mobility policy. While addressing
Canada’s long-term health workforce needs will require a comprehensive, long-term,
approach, opportunities exist to address shortages of technical and vocational professions
in the interim - particularly those which are not regulated by professional bodies, such as
PSWs. These professions are in high demand, require less training time, and do not entail the
complexities related to industry recognition and regulation that are a persistent challenge
for credentialled newcomers. As a result, they present an opportunity for people to more
quickly and effectively enter the Canadian labour market.
A forthcoming 369 Global policy paper entitled Global Skilling Centres: Building Canada’s
Talent Pipelines Abroad, planned for release in early 2026, will explore how Canada can
leverage international technical and vocational education and training (TVET) to respond to
these shortages. Based on approach used to greater effect by peer countries – such as
Australia, Germany, and the United Kingdom – Canada – we lay out the potential for new
Global Skilling Centres (GSCs) to provide high-quality Canadian training abroad to those
seeking to immigrate to Canada.
GSCs would be physical centres in key international locations that offer technical and
vocational education and training (TVET), broader pre-arrival training, and integration with
Canadian employers to trainees in specific in-demand professions, including PSWs. They
would be run by Canadian educational institutions in close collaboration with immigrant
service providers and employers. Along with greater predictability, support, and job
connections for newcomers, international training would provide both a more targeted and
more effective way to help fill domestic labour market gaps through immigration.
Government support will be key to the establishment of Canada’s first Global Skilling
Centres, as well as to the eventual scale-up of the model. That is why we recommend that
key federal departments, including Health Canada, Employment and Social Development
Canada, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, Global Affairs Canada, and
Export Development Canada begin exploring how they can support a shift towards the use
of international TVET to address the shortage of PSWs and other key healthcare workers.
This would include engaging with experts and potential GSC operators, examining
opportunities to provide both financial and diplomatic support, and evaluating possible
changes to Canada’s immigration system to ensure alignment with the concept of
international TVET and the GSC model.
8

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Immigration, IEHP Integration, and Solutions to Accelerate
Workforce Entry
Submitted by
Canadian Medical Foundation (CMF) and PEGASUS Institute
November 2025

Executive Summary
Canada is facing one of the most significant health human resource (HHR) shortages in its history. At the
same time, nearly 260,000 internationally educated health professionals (IEHPs) currently reside in
Canada—yet only 58% are working in health-related occupations. Although Canada’s immigration
system successfully attracts highly skilled health professionals, our regulatory, licensure, and workforce
systems do not integrate them efficiently or effectively. This represents a profound missed opportunity
at a time when Canada urgently needs physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, and other essential
providers.
Evidence from the Canadian Medical Foundation (CMF) and its partners, including the PEGASUS
Institute, shows that IEHPs experience fragmented licensure pathways, outdated or inaccurate
information, reduced newcomer supports due to federal program cuts, and limited access to mentoring
or professional networks. These challenges delay their entry into the workforce, erode clinical skills, and
create financial and emotional strain for newcomers and their families.
While reforms to immigration, regulatory, and licensing systems are underway, IEHPs who are already in
Canada—and those who have begun their immigration journey—require targeted support to navigate
the system, progress toward licensure, and optimize their contributions to Canada’s health workforce.
This submission outlines key barriers and presents three evidence-based recommendations:
1.
Expand wrap-around supports such as mentoring, capacity-building, and social capital
development for IEHPs already living in Canada.
2.
Establish and fund a centralized, continuously updated national IEHP Resource Hub, ideally
hosted by a nimble NGO embedded within IEHP communities.
3.
Invest in one-on-one human navigation supports to ensure IEHPs have clear, accurate guidance
on pathways to licensure and alternative health careers.
Implementing these measures will streamline access to information, accelerate workforce entry,
improve newcomer outcomes, and strengthen Canada’s health workforce and ultimately improve
population health.
Background and Context
Canada’s HHR Crisis and the Underutilized IEHP Workforce
Canada’s health system is under unprecedented strain. Millions of Canadians are unable to access a
family doctor; emergency departments face recurring closures; and nurse retention remains one of the
greatest challenges facing provincial health systems. Meanwhile, Canada is home to a large, diverse, and
highly trained IEHP population—physicians, nurses, pharmacists, dentists, medical laboratory
technologists, and others—whose skills remain underutilized.
Recent national data underscores the issue:

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Recent national data underscores the issue:

259,695 IEHPs live in Canada, many as permanent residents or citizens.
76% are employed, but
Only 58% work in health occupations, leaving tens of thousands in unrelated employment,
unemployment, or precarious roles.
It is common to meet refugee doctors driving taxis, internationally trained dentists working in retail, or
pharmacists unable to access exam dates or obtain credential assessments. These individuals arrive
highly skilled and motivated, yet encounter licensing and integration systems that are confusing,
inconsistent, and often impenetrable.
Immigration Success Meets Regulatory Bottlenecks
Canada excels at recruiting health professionals through the Federal Skilled Worker Program, Provincial
Nominee Programs, and targeted draws. But upon arrival, newcomers must navigate decentralized
provincial regulatory systems without structured support. The assumption that IEHPs can decipher these
complex processes alone is inaccurate and harmful.
IEHPs report consistent barriers:
Fragmented licensure pathways varying by province, regulator, and profession.
Outdated or contradictory information across uncoordinated websites.
Reductions in settlement and employment supports due to IRCC funding cuts.
Loss of “recency of practice” as they wait months or years for exams or assessments.
Limited social capital, including the absence of mentors, peers, and professional networks.
While important reforms are emerging—such as increased residency seats for internationally trained
physicians, supervised practice pathways for nurses, and expanded Practice Ready Assessments—IEHPs
cannot benefit if they are unaware of these opportunities or unable to access them.
Simply creating more pathways is insufficient if IEHPs lack the support to find and navigate them.
Current Challenges and System Gaps
1. Fragmented and Complex Licensure Pathways
Licensure requirements differ significantly across provinces and professions. Navigating them demands:
advanced English or French proficiency
knowledge of regulatory processes
substantial financial resources for exams and assessments
flexibility for supervised practice or bridging programs
comfort with digital tools and online systems
For many refugees and disadvantaged newcomers, these requirements create prohibitive barriers
without personalized support.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Navigating them demands:
advanced English or French proficiency
knowledge of regulatory processes
substantial financial resources for exams and assessments
flexibility for supervised practice or bridging programs
comfort with digital tools and online systems
For many refugees and disadvantaged newcomers, these requirements create prohibitive barriers
without personalized support.

2. Inaccurate, Outdated, or Unreliable Information
IEHPs often rely on scattered resources—including unregulated websites and informal community
groups—many of which are outdated, contradictory, or incorrect. Misinformation leads to wasted time,
unnecessary costs, and delayed workforce entry.
3. Reduced Settlement and Navigation Supports
Recent IRCC funding reductions have scaled back employment counselling, navigation services,
community orientation, and sector-specific supports. For IEHPs—whose pathways are among the most
complex—this loss is particularly damaging. IEHPs often describe being left to “figure it out alone.”
Many accumulate debt, support extended families on low-wage jobs, or abandon the licensure process
entirely.
4. Lack of Social Capital and Professional Networks
Newcomers arrive without local professional networks. Without mentors and connectors, IEHPs struggle
to:
access bridging programs
prepare competitive applications
secure supervised practice or residency placements
understand Canadian workplace norms
identify alternative health roles
IEHPs who receive mentoring and networking support are substantially more likely to advance toward
licensure.
5. Loss of Recency of Practice
Lengthy licensing timelines mean many IEHPs lose their recency of practice—an essential requirement
for many health professions. Some IEHPs make the decision to return home on a regular basis in order
to main clinical practice, but many cannot afford this option and refugees or IEHPs from conflict zones
simply cannot return home, making this barrier particularly inequitable.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Some IEHPs make the decision to return home on a regular basis in order
to main clinical practice, but many cannot afford this option and refugees or IEHPs from conflict zones
simply cannot return home, making this barrier particularly inequitable.

Recommendations
Recommendation 1: Expand Wrap-Around Supports Including Mentorship
and Social Capital Development
IEHPs consistently identify the absence of mentorship and professional networks as one of their greatest
barriers. Wrap-around supports are not a luxury; they are foundational to licensing success and
workforce integration.
Key supports should include:
one-to-one and group mentoring with licensed Canadian professionals
networking opportunities with employers, regulators, and peers
professional readiness and orientation workshops
mental health, financial, and family supports
peer-led communities of practice
Recommended Action:
Expand federal funding for IEHP-specific wrap-around programs delivered by NGOs, community
organizations, and settlement agencies with proven expertise and cultural competency.
Recommendation 2: Establish a Centralized, Continuously Updated IEHP
Resource and Information Hub Hosted by an NGO
Canada lacks a single, authoritative national platform that consolidates all IEHP-related information. A
centralized resource hub would deliver consistent, credible, bilingual (EN/FR) information about:
licensure pathways by profession and province
exam schedules and preparation resources
bridging programs and supervised practice opportunities
financial supports and bursaries
alternative health careers
regulatory updates and policy changes
settlement and employment services
Government platforms often face limitations in real-time updating, user-centred design, and sector
responsiveness. NGOs, including CMF and PEGASUS, are well positioned to host such a hub due to their
agility, deep community relationships, multilingual reach, and credibility with IEHPs.
Recommended Action:
Fund a national IEHP Resource Hub, maintained through quarterly updates, stakeholder partnerships,
and user testing. Ensure long-term sustainability through co-funding models and partnerships with
philanthropic and community organizations.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Ensure long-term sustainability through co-funding models and partnerships with
philanthropic and community organizations.

Recommendation 3: Invest in One-on-One Human Navigation Supports
for IEHPs
Information alone does not eliminate structural barriers. IEHPs require personalized human navigation—
trained navigators who understand both regulatory complexity and the lived experiences of newcomers.
Navigators help IEHPs:
map licensure options across provinces
choose between PRA, residency, bridging programs, or alternative roles
prepare applications and documentation
access financial and settlement supports
maintain progress toward licensure over months or years
avoid misinformation or predatory intermediaries
Recommended Action:
Create a funded national network of professional navigators integrated into settlement agencies,
professional associations, and NGO-led IEHP hubs. Support digital tracking systems to monitor progress
and outcomes.
Conclusion
Canada urgently needs the expertise and cultural diversity that internationally educated health
professionals bring. Yet for decades, IEHPs have encountered systemic barriers that prevent them from
contributing fully to the country’s health workforce. While immigration policies succeed in attracting
talent, Canada’s integration systems fall short—creating inefficiencies, inequities, and lost opportunities.
To address Canada’s health workforce crisis, we strongly urge the federal government to invest in three
essential pillars:
wrap-around supports, mentorship, and social capital development
a centralized and continuously updated national IEHP Resource Hub
direct one-on-one human navigation support
These interventions will accelerate IEHP workforce entry, reduce bottlenecks across health professions,
support newcomers and their families, and strengthen health services for Canadians.
The time to act is now. Canada cannot meet its health workforce needs without fully harnessing the
potential of the IEHPs who are already here.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Written Submission to the Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Study: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating
Internationally Trained Professionals
Systemic Barriers Facing Internationally Trained Dentists (ITDs) in Canada and the
Need for Federal Oversight of the National Dental Examining Board (NDEB)
Submitted by Seyedeh Fereshteh Morsali
Internationally Trained Dentist (ITD)
November 2025

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Internationally Trained Dentists (ITDs) in Canada face severe and well-documented
barriers in their attempts to enter the dental workforce, despite Canada’s urgent need
for qualified health-care professionals. The National Dental Examining Board of Canada
(NDEB), which oversees the equivalency and licensing process, has created a system
that is widely perceived by candidates as inconsistent, subjective, and lacking the
transparency expected of a national regulatory body. These issues are particularly
evident in the NDECC (Skills Exam), where candidates report unpredictable scoring,
unrealistic clinical conditions, and an exam structure that does not reflect real-world
dentistry.
The consequences are significant: highly trained, experienced dentists—many with over
a decade of clinical practice—are repeatedly failing an exam that often appears to
reward inexperience rather than competence. Candidates face financial strain,
emotional distress, career instability, and prolonged under-employment, frequently
being forced into low-skill or low-wage jobs despite possessing advanced professional
qualifications. These systemic issues affect thousands of internationally trained
professionals across Canada and directly undermine federal goals related to
immigration, labour market integration, and health-care capacity.
This brief urges the Standing Committee on Health to examine the NDEB’s practices,
oversight structure, and evaluation standards, and to consider the need for federal
involvement to ensure fairness, transparency, and accessibility in the licensing pathway
for ITDs.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
This brief urges the Standing Committee on Health to examine the NDEB’s practices,
oversight structure, and evaluation standards, and to consider the need for federal
involvement to ensure fairness, transparency, and accessibility in the licensing pathway
for ITDs.

INTRODUCTION
My name is Seyedeh Fereshteh Morsali, and I am an Internationally Trained Dentist
(ITD) who immigrated to Canada with the hope of contributing to the health-care system
and building a stable future for my family. I earned my Doctor of Dental Surgery (DDS)
degree outside Canada, practiced for many years, and entered the NDEB equivalency
process with the expectation that a clear, fair, and standardized pathway existed for
qualified internationally trained dentists to integrate into the Canadian workforce.
Like thousands of other ITDs, I have devoted years of my life to this process and have
invested substantial financial resources, time, and effort to meet the requirements
established by the National Dental Examining Board of Canada (NDEB). However, my
experience—particularly with the NDECC (Skills Exam)—has revealed deep structural
flaws that make this pathway far more uncertain and punitive than necessary.
Through repeated attempts at the NDECC, I have witnessed firsthand the exam’s
inconsistency, unrealistic clinical expectations, lack of transparency, and scoring
patterns that appear disconnected from real-world practice. My experience is not
unique. The concerns I raise in this brief reflect a widespread crisis documented by
thousands of candidates across multiple platforms, petitions, online discussions, and
even legal cases.
I am submitting this brief to share the urgent challenges faced by ITDs and to
respectfully request that the Standing Committee on Health include the NDEB’s
practices in its study on barriers to integrating internationally trained health-care
professionals. Canada needs dentists, patients need care, and ITDs want to serve. A
dysfunctional licensing system should not stand in the way.
Canada is facing a widespread and well-documented shortage of dental professionals.
Millions of residents struggle to access timely dental care, especially in rural, remote,
and underserved urban communities. Federal and provincial governments have
acknowledged these shortages, and recent initiatives — including the Canadian Dental
Care Plan (CDCP) — have further increased the demand for qualified dentists across
the country.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Federal and provincial governments have
acknowledged these shortages, and recent initiatives — including the Canadian Dental
Care Plan (CDCP) — have further increased the demand for qualified dentists across
the country.

At the same time, Canada continues to welcome internationally trained health
professionals, including dentists, under immigration streams that explicitly frame their
skills as an asset to the Canadian economy. Many ITDs arrive in Canada with years —
sometimes decades — of clinical experience, specialized training, and a proven
commitment to patient care.
However, the pathway to licensure for internationally trained dentists depends entirely
on the National Dental Examining Board of Canada (NDEB), an independent body
whose equivalency and licensing examinations determine whether a dentist may
practice in Canada. While licensing exams are necessary for public safety, serious
concerns have been raised about the fairness, transparency, and reliability of the
NDEB’s processes.
Over recent years, thousands of internationally trained dentists have described the
same recurring problems with the NDEB process: unpredictable exam results,
non-standardized scoring, vague evaluation criteria, unrealistic clinical conditions in the
NDECC, and repeated failures even among highly experienced clinicians. Candidates
consistently report receiving no meaningful feedback and facing unexplained
discrepancies that sometimes feel discriminatory or inconsistent.
These concerns appear everywhere—large public petitions, Reddit communities and
candidate groups, testimonies delivered outside regulatory bodies, legal challenges,
and media coverage. Collectively, they reveal a licensing system that blocks qualified
dentists from entering the profession while Canada simultaneously faces major
shortages in oral-health care.
For many ITDs, this process becomes a multi-year cycle of financial strain, emotional
distress, and professional stagnation, forcing them into survival jobs unrelated to their
expertise.
Because immigration policy is federal and the integration of internationally trained health
professionals has national implications, the NDEB’s practices fall squarely within the
mandate of the Standing Committee on Health. The challenges facing ITDs are not
individual failures — they reflect deep systemic issues in the NDEB’s equivalency and
licensing system, repeatedly documented by thousands of candidates across the
country.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
The challenges facing ITDs are not
individual failures — they reflect deep systemic issues in the NDEB’s equivalency and
licensing system, repeatedly documented by thousands of candidates across the
country.

● The NDECC NDEB skills exam suffers from serious systemic problems. The scoring is
completely opaque—candidates only receive a pass or fail with no breakdown,
comments, or documentation. This prevents meaningful improvement, makes
preparation guesswork, and allows evaluator inconsistency to go unchecked.
Unsurprisingly, grading appears unreliable: highly experienced dentists often fail while
less-experienced candidates pass, suggesting subjective, non-standardized evaluation.
● There is also no appeal system. Candidates cannot request re-evaluation, access
examiner notes, or challenge potential errors. This lack of due process is almost unheard
of in a high-stakes professional exam.
● The exam itself is built on unrealistic clinical conditions. Plastic teeth, inaccurate tactile
feedback, and artificial requirements (especially in endodontics) push candidates to
perform procedures that don’t match real anatomy, rewarding mannequin “perfection”
instead of clinical judgement.
● Financial pressure adds another layer. Each attempt costs thousands in exam fees,
thousands more in prep courses, and lost income during preparation — leading many
ITDs to accumulate tens of thousands in expenses while being unable to work in their
profession.
● The emotional toll is severe: chronic stress, anxiety, loss of identity, damaged
confidence, and strained family life. Many candidates feel stuck in survival jobs despite
years of training.
● Most importantly, these issues are not isolated complaints. They are echoed across
petitions, online communities, public testimonies, legal challenges, media coverage, and
video statements before regulatory bodies — showing clear, widespread systemic failure
in the current NDECC system
This demonstrates a system-wide problem requiring federal attention.
The challenges described in this brief are fully supported by numerous sources of public
evidence. These include candidate testimonies, petitions, media coverage, online discussions,
legal cases, and community actions. While the specific documents are too numerous to attach
individually, the examples below reflect the breadth and seriousness of the systemic issues
surrounding the NDEB’s licensing process.
EVIDENCE & EXAMPLES
Multiple sources of evidence show that the problems within the NDEB system are widespread,
consistent, and structural. Large public petitions with hundreds or thousands of signatures
document shared concerns about transparency, unpredictable scoring, the lack of an appeal

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Large public petitions with hundreds or thousands of signatures
document shared concerns about transparency, unpredictable scoring, the lack of an appeal

process, and the heavy financial and emotional burden placed on candidates. Video
testimonies—such as the widely circulated recording outside the RCDSO—feature dozens of
ITDs describing repeated unexplained failures, examiner bias, and the unrealistic nature of
performing clinical tasks on plastic teeth.
Online discussions on Reddit echo the same themes: inconsistent examiners, unpredictable
outcomes between candidates with similar performance, and the severe psychological and
financial toll of repeated attempts. These issues are reinforced by multiple legal actions,
including human rights complaints and challenges alleging unfair or discriminatory assessment
practices. Media reports across Canada further highlight the barriers ITDs face, the long delays
in the licensing pathway, and the contradiction between Canada’s dental-care shortages and the
underutilization of highly trained immigrant dentists.
The consistency of these reports across different provinces, backgrounds, and exam cycles
shows that these concerns are not isolated incidents but symptoms of deep systemic issues
within the NDEB. The scale of the problem — and its impact on both internationally trained
dentists and national access to care — makes federal review and reform essential.
This brief respectfully recommends that the Standing Committee on Health take the following
actions:
The Committee should launch a federal review of the NDEB’s examination practices, focusing
on transparency, reliability, examiner training, and internal oversight. A key reform is the creation
of a clear, independent appeal system that provides candidates with scoring details,
re-evaluation options, and transparent criteria. Greater transparency is also needed overall,
including detailed performance breakdowns and meaningful examiner feedback.
The clinical validity of the NDECC should be examined to determine whether its plastic-tooth
testing conditions fairly reflect real dentistry or impose unrealistic standards that disadvantage
experienced clinicians. The Committee should also explore alternative pathways used in other
countries—such as bridging programs, supervised practice, and competency-based
assessments—to better integrate skilled ITDs into Canada’s workforce.
Because the NDEB functions as a federal examining body, stronger federal oversight is
necessary to ensure fairness, accountability, and alignment with national immigration and
health-care goals. Given the significant emotional toll of the licensing process, ITDs should also
receive mental-health supports and clearer guidance throughout. Finally, ITDs must be included
as stakeholders in any review or reform effort, as their lived experiences are essential for
identifying systemic problems and building meaningful solutions

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Finally, ITDs must be included
as stakeholders in any review or reform effort, as their lived experiences are essential for
identifying systemic problems and building meaningful solutions

These recommendations seek to make Canada’s dental licensing system fair, transparent, and
clinically relevant, while also supporting the federal goal of integrating skilled internationally
trained health professionals into the workforce. Thousands of internationally trained dentists are
qualified and ready to help address Canada’s growing dental-care needs, yet the current NDEB
pathway—especially the NDECC—has become a major barrier. Its inconsistent, opaque, and
clinically unrealistic evaluation system has pushed many experienced clinicians into survival
jobs, financial hardship, and emotional strain.
The issues raised by ITDs are not isolated; they are backed by petitions, legal challenges,
media reports, online communities, and public testimonies across the country. This widespread
evidence shows a systemic problem that requires immediate federal attention. By reviewing the
NDEB’s practices and enforcing higher standards of transparency, fairness, and accountability,
the Standing Committee on Health can help remove unnecessary barriers and ensure that
skilled dentists are able to contribute fully to Canada’s health-care system.
Canada has already invested in attracting talented immigrant professionals. Ensuring that the
assessment system is fair, reasonable, and reflective of real clinical practice is the essential next
step. ITDs are not seeking exceptions — only a licensing process that is transparent, consistent,
and aligned with Canadian professional standards.
The following materials provide additional context, evidence, and firsthand testimony regarding
the systemic challenges faced by internationally trained dentists in the NDEB licensing process.
These examples represent only a small portion of the extensive public documentation available
online.
Appendix A — Petitions Regarding NDEB Practices
These petitions reflect the collective concerns of hundreds to thousands of ITDs across Canada
and document widespread dissatisfaction with the transparency, fairness, and consistency of the
NDEB examinations.
● Petition created by the author:
https://c.org/4GWnyzgXsg

● Additional petition with over 2,000 signatures:

https://www.change.org/p/canadian-dental-association-justice-for-discrimination-against-f
oreign-trained-dentists-by-ndeb
These petitions demonstrate the scale of the concern within the community.
Appendix B — Public Testimony from ITDs
Video footage of internationally trained dentists speaking publicly about their experiences
reveals the emotional and professional toll of the licensing process.
● YouTube video: ITDs speaking outside the RCDSO

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Briefing Note to the Standing Committee on Health
(HESA)
Topic: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating
Internationally Trained Health Professionals
Submitted by: Society of Rural Physicians of Canada (SRPC)
Executive Summary
Rural, remote, northern, and Indigenous communities continue to face significant
physician shortages that limit access to primary care, emergency services, and ongoing
management of chronic illness. Internationally trained physicians (ITPs) could help meet
these needs, but federal immigration pathways and credential-recognition processes are
not consistently aligned with provincial licensure or rural workforce requirements.
Streamlining federal pathways for licensure-ready physicians and strengthening
assessment and rural readiness supports would improve timely access to care for
communities in need. The recommendations that follow focus on practical federal levers
that support equitable healthcare access while respecting provincial jurisdiction.
1. Issue
Rural and remote communities experience recurring gaps in physician services, including
limited primary care access, temporary emergency department closures, and reduced
continuity of care. The Globe and Mail reported that Canada saw 47,500 ER closure days
between 2019 and June 2025, almost all of which were in rural communities and many of
which were related to physician shortages. These challenges undermine patient outcomes
and place additional strain on local health systems and impact community wellbeing.
ITPS are essential to addressing these gaps. Many ITPs arrive with extensive experience
and are ready to practice broad‑scope generalist medicine—the foundation of rural
healthcare. Yet federal immigration pathways and federal funding programs remain
misaligned with rural workforce needs. Physicians who have already demonstrated
eligibility for licensure with provincial regulatory authorities still encounter federal delays,
unclear pathways, and administrative barriers, all of which slow rural recruitment.
The federal government holds primary responsibility for immigration policy and foreign
credential recognition funding, giving it a direct role in shaping how quickly licensure-ready
physicians can enter the workforce. Federal immigration policy and Health Canada
programs can be better aligned to support the timely entry of licensure‑ready physicians
into rural practice while respecting provincial jurisdiction over licensure. By improving how
these federal levers are designed and applied, Canada can strengthen the rural physician
workforce and support more equitable access to care across the country.

org: Society of Rural Physicians of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
By improving how
these federal levers are designed and applied, Canada can strengthen the rural physician
workforce and support more equitable access to care across the country.

2. Background and Context
2.1 Canada’s National Physician Shortage
National shortages in family medicine and generalist specialties disproportionately affect
rural, remote, and Indigenous communities. These shortages contribute to reduced
continuity of care, greater reliance on emergency departments, avoidable transfers, and
widening health inequities.
2.2 Role of Internationally Trained Physicians
ITPs have historically filled critical service gaps, particularly in rural generalist practice.
However, navigation of immigration pathways, Practice Ready Assessment (PRA)
programs, and licensure processes is complex, and assessment capacity has not kept
pace with need.
2.3 Federal Responsibility
The federal government influences physician supply through immigration legislation
(IRPA/IRPR), Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) and LMIA-exempt pathways,
permanent residence streams, Foreign Credential Recognition Program (FCRP) funding,
federal–provincial agreements, and investments that support regulatory and assessment
capacity. Better alignment of these federal tools with rural workforce needs would
accelerate ITP integration.
3. Federal Immigration and Credentialing Pathways: Current State
Temporary and permanent immigration pathways, including LMIA‑based work permits,
LMIA‑exempt permits, and Express Entry programs, provide routes for ITPs to enter
Canada. While useful, these pathways are not designed specifically for physicians and do
not consistently reflect licensure readiness or rural workforce needs. Assessments funded
through the FCRP support some integration activities, but PRA capacity remains limited
relative to demand.
4. Barriers to Integration of Internationally Trained Physicians
4.1 Immigration Barriers
ITPs encounter several barriers that slow or limit their ability to enter rural practice. At the
immigration stage, federal pathways remain complex and are not tailored to physicians
who have already demonstrated eligibility for provincial licensure. Processing delays and
the absence of mechanisms to recognize licensure readiness contribute to avoidable
waiting periods. The administrative requirements placed on rural employers can also be
difficult for small clinics or hospitals to manage.

org: Society of Rural Physicians of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
The administrative requirements placed on rural employers can also be
difficult for small clinics or hospitals to manage.

4.2 Credentialing and Assessment Barriers
Credentialing and assessment challenges further delay integration. PRA programs do not
have sufficient capacity to meet the needs of provinces or the volume of qualified
applicants, and rural placements within PRA pathways remain limited. For many ITPs, the
sequencing of immigration steps and licensure requirements is misaligned, leading to
periods in which physicians are unable to progress despite meeting regulatory
expectations.
4.3 System Coordination Challenges
System coordination issues also contribute to delays. Immigration, credential recognition,
and licensure involve multiple federal and provincial actors, and the absence of a
coordinated approach means that information, timelines, and program design can vary
significantly. This creates uncertainty for ITPs and contributes to inefficiencies.
4.4 Rural, Remote, and Indigenous Context
Rural and remote contexts introduce additional barriers such as limited housing
availability, childcare gaps, spousal employment challenges, and fewer mentorship or
team supports. For Indigenous communities, the need for culturally safe and contextually
relevant care adds further considerations that are not consistently supported through
existing federal programs.
5. Consequences for Rural, Remote, and Indigenous Communities.
Physician shortages drive service disruptions, reduce access to preventive care, delay
diagnosis, increase avoidable transfers, and worsen health outcomes. These impacts are
amplified in Indigenous communities already facing systemic inequities. Without timely
physician recruitment and retention, community stability, economic viability, and trust in
the health system continue to deteriorate.
6. Recommendations. Recommendations
1. Strengthen federal immigration pathways for internationally trained physicians
by creating expedited, streamlined LMIA-exempt and permanent residence
routes for ITPs who are eligible for licensure with a provincial medical
regulatory authority.
2. Improve clarity, accessibility, and coordination of federal immigration
programs for ITPs seeking to practice in underserved communities.
3. Invest in rural skills enhancement programs for ITPs preparing for rural
generalist practice in Canada.
4. Enhance federal incentives and supports that strengthen retention of ITPs in
rural and remote communities.
5. Support Indigenous-led physician pathways, recruitment, and retention
initiatives.

org: Society of Rural Physicians of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Support Indigenous-led physician pathways, recruitment, and retention
initiatives.

6. Provide funding to expand national rural-ready Practice Ready Assessment
(PRA) capacity.
7. Improve federal data systems to track the immigration → licensure → rural
practice trajectory of ITPs.
7. Conclusion.
Rural, remote, northern, and Indigenous communities deserve equitable access to timely,
comprehensive physician care. Federal immigration policy—supported by targeted
financial investments—can play a decisive role in strengthening the rural physician
workforce. By streamlining immigration pathways for licensure‑ready physicians,
expanding rural PRA capacity, supporting Indigenous‑led initiatives, improving retention
tools, and investing in rural skills development, the federal government can directly
address barriers that fall within its jurisdiction.
The SRPC urges HESA to consider how federal immigration and related policy levers can be
used more effectively to support rural health equity. With coordinated federal action, ITPs
can transition more efficiently into practice, remain supported in rural communities, and
contribute fully to improving health outcomes across Canada.
The SRPC stands ready to collaborate with federal partners to help advance these
solutions.

text:
Written Submission

To:

House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Topic:
Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating
Internationally Trained Professionals
Date:
November 28, 2025.
I.
Introduction
The Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada (AFMC) represents all 19 medical schools
in the country and was pleased to provide testimony at the House of Commons Standing
Committee on Health hearings on November 20, 2025. The purpose of this written submission
is to build upon the important topics and questions raised at that hearing, and to provide the
Committee with:
-
Key definitions and data points
-
Insights into the lack of capacity in undergraduate medical education
-
Ways to integrate more IMGs and FTPs into Canada’s existing training system

II.
Key Definitions
Canadian Medical Graduates (CMGs):
• Canadian citizens and permanent residents are eligible to apply for undergraduate
medical seats in Canada’s 18 (soon to be 19)1 medical schools. Approximately one in
five applicants (19.2%) gets in.2 Students who complete medical school here are known
as Canadian Medical Graduates (CMGs). CMGs must complete residency training
before entering practice.

• Over and above student-paid tuition fees, it costs the taxpayer approximately $430,000
to educate one Canadian Medical Graduate at the undergraduate level.3 These funds
primarily flow through Provincial allocations to the universities.
1 Simon Fraser University will welcome its inaugural class in September 2026
2 Table F-13; 2024 CMES
3 2002 Senate Report – adjusted for inflation.

• Because medical school seats are heavily subsidized by Canadian taxpayers, less than
2% of these seats go to international students.4 International students must apply
through separate streams and they cannot access residency positions in Canada unless
they have obtained permanent resident status.5 Although small in number, international
students bring diversity to the learning environment that improves education and patient
care over the long term.

• CMGs apply for residency positions through the annual resident match process, which
is overseen by the Canadian Resident Matching Service (CaRMS).

org: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
• CMGs apply for residency positions through the annual resident match process, which
is overseen by the Canadian Resident Matching Service (CaRMS).

• Because CMGs have consistent levels of training, and because part of the cost to
educate a CMG is borne by the Canadian taxpayer, CMGs get priority over medical
graduates applying from elsewhere in the world to compete for residency positions in
Canada (except in some cases in Quebec and Ontario).

• It is important to remember that Canadian tax dollars only support Canadians and
permanent residents to pursue medical school and residency. They are not used to fund
international students or visa trainees.
International Medical Graduates (IMGs):
• A student who graduates from a medical school anywhere outside Canada and wants to
complete residency in Canada is called an International Medical Graduate (IMG).

• On average, one in three IMGs are Canadian citizens or permanent residents who
pursued medical school abroad and are looking to return to Canada for their residency
training. In 2025, 2,073 of 5,987 IMGs were Canadian citizens or permanent residents,
or 34.6% of all IMGs.

• Most IMGs compete for residency positions in the second round of the CaRMS match,
with some exceptions in Québec and, recently, in Ontario.
Visa Trainees:
• The topic of “visa trainees” is widely misunderstood and easily subverted into antiimmigrant rhetoric. Care must be taken when using this term and related data to inform
policy decisions.

• Foreign-born trainees can pay medical schools to access residual residency positions
in Canada, or to obtain post-graduate training in very specific subspecialties. These
4 Table F-13; 2024 CMES
5 2025 CaRMS Forum

positions can only be allocated once all residency positions funded by the provincial
ministries have been allocated, and if there is remaining capacity for training.

• On average, each trainee pays $117,000/year to attend a Canadian medical school.6
Some trainees pay their own way, while in other cases, foreign governments pay their
fees. The latter are called “sponsored trainees”.

• In 2023/2024, there were 3,140 visa trainees working and learning in the Canadian
healthcare system.7 Most come from Saudi Arabia, Ireland, India, Kuwait, United
Kingdom, Israel, Australia, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates.8

org: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
• In 2023/2024, there were 3,140 visa trainees working and learning in the Canadian
healthcare system.7 Most come from Saudi Arabia, Ireland, India, Kuwait, United
Kingdom, Israel, Australia, Oman, and the United Arab Emirates.8

• These trainees are a quadruple win for Canada:
 They provide millions of hours of clinical care in the healthcare system;
 They contribute to more diverse learning and clinical environments;
 They bring important foreign investment into Canadian universities, and;
 They help bolster Canada’s reputation and impact worldwide.
• These trainees access residual and/or highly specialized spots, and do not take places
away from CMGs or new doctors. They are never offered positions until all funded
positions have been filled.

• While some visa trainees elect to remain in Canada, 90% of sponsored trainees return
to their country with Canadian training to practice.
The “Visa Trainee” group should be examined as two distinct segments: Visa Resident
Trainees and Visa Fellow Trainees.

Visa Resident Trainees (smaller segment):
• After the residency match process is completed each year, about 3% of residency
positions remain unclaimed across Canada.9 Following the 2025 resident match, 118
out of a possible 3,942 residency positions remained unfilled in Canada and were
available to visa trainees.10

• Provinces can elect to pay to fill these positions but typically do not.

• If residency positions remain unfilled, universities can accept fees from foreign
governments to allow non-Canadian IMGs to fill the vacant positions, where capacity
permits.
6 Personal correspondence.
7 Table B10; 2024 National IMG Database Report
8 Table B4ii; 2024 National IMG Database Report
9 Tables 8, 48, 55; 2025 CaRMS Data Tables
10 Table 55; 2025 CaRMS Data Tables

• In 2023/2024, there were a total of 738 visa resident trainees working and learning in the
Canadian health care system.11 Of these, only eight were sponsored trainees (1.1%),12
whose fees were being paid by a foreign government.
Visa Fellow Trainees (larger segment):
• A visa fellow trainee is a trained international physician who has already completed
residency training elsewhere, and who comes to Canada to gain additional training in a
highly specialized area of medicine.

• In 2023/2024, there were 2,402 visa fellow trainees providing high-level clinical care and
learning in the Canadian health care system.13 Of these, 976 (40%) were sponsored
trainees, whose fees were being paid by a foreign government.

org: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
• In 2023/2024, there were 2,402 visa fellow trainees providing high-level clinical care and
learning in the Canadian health care system.13 Of these, 976 (40%) were sponsored
trainees, whose fees were being paid by a foreign government.

• Visa fellow trainees do not occupy undergraduate seats in Canadian medical schools,
nor do they participate in the resident match process. Therefore, they do not take spots
away from Canadian medical students or Canadian resident doctors.

• Visa fellow trainees are trained by sub-specialists who would not otherwise be teaching
in a medical school or training new medical graduates in a regular residency program.
They do not pull from the teaching pool required to make new doctors in Canada; they
provide education for students and residents in their focused area of expertise.

• Visa fellow trainees provide approximately 8 million hours of specialized clinical care to
Canadians each year, at very little cost to taxpayers. To train an equivalent cohort of
expertise in Canada would cost over $2.4B every year.
Internationally Trained Physicians (ITPs) and Foreign Trained Physicians (FTPs):
• Physicians who are fully certified to practice medicine in other countries, and who
satisfy immigration and licensing requirements to practice in Canada, are referred to
interchangeably as Internationally Trained Physicians (ITPs) or Foreign Trained
Physicians (FTPs).

• This group consists of immigrants to Canada, who have chosen to come here for various
reasons. It is important to note that for ethical reasons, Canada does not recruit
physicians from low- and middle-income countries, where their expertise is essential.
11 Table B10; 2024 National IMG Database Report
12 Table D-1i; 2023-24 CAPER Census
13 Table B10; 2024 National IMG Database Report

• In total, there are 26,169 FTPs practicing medicine in Canada: family doctors as well as
specialists. This represents 27.4% of the overall physician workforce and helps address
our doctor shortage.14

• FTPs bring a wealth of knowledge, skills, and diverse perspectives to our physician
workforce. However, credentialing remains a challenge for many.

• A 2023 report estimates that there are 13,000 FTPs in Canada who are not practicing
medicine.15 There are many reasons these doctors may not be practicing medicine,
including the possibility that their foreign training does not satisfy Canadian standards.
Better data is required to understand this group and what would be needed to upskill as
necessary.

III.
Canada Lacks Capacity in Undergraduate Medical Education
Why doesn’t Canada have enough doctors?

org: Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Canada Lacks Capacity in Undergraduate Medical Education
Why doesn’t Canada have enough doctors?

In the 1980s, provincial governments began cutting undergraduate medical school seats
across the country, resulting in a low point in first year enrolments around 1998.16 Meanwhile,
Canada’s population kept growing, creating a gap between the number of medical school
graduate seats and the number of Canadians needing care.

For the past 20+ years, provincial governments and medical schools have been working to
correct this phenomenon. They have increased the number of undergraduate medical seats
by 43.6%17 and the number of residency positions by 66.9%18 – bringing us up to training levels
slightly higher than in the 1970s. In 2024, Canadian medical schools produced 3,055 new
doctors, ready for practice.19

This has not been enough to keep up with population demands, and medical schools are now
at – or beyond – capacity at the undergraduate training level. Presently, Canada relies heavily
on international medical graduates (IMGs) and foreign trained physicians (FTPs) to fill the gap
– both in family medicine and other specialties.

IV.
Canada has Capacity at Post-Graduate Level (Residency)
Currently, Canada has more residency positions available than there are CMGs to fill them. On
average, there is only one CMG at the ready to fill every 1.12 residency positions in Canada20 –
for a capacity surplus of 12%.
Figure 4: PGME Training Capacity since 2008
Figure 5: Ratio of residency seats to CMG graduates, by region
Following the 2025 resident match, 118 out of a possible 3,942 residency positions remained
unfilled in Canada.21 These positions went to visa resident trainees.

The fact that Canadian medical schools can accommodate these externally funded trainees
shows that there is further training capacity in the health system, but that the provinces are not
funding this capacity.
20 CaRMS Forum 2025; Slide 13
21 Table 55; 2025 CaRMS Data Tables

Until such time as Canadian medical schools are funded to produce more CMGs, this 12%
capacity surplus in residency positions is a prime opportunity to bring in more
international medical graduates (IMGs) – but governments must be ready to fund these
positions.
V.
Manitoba Case Study
Manitoba experienced the same reduction in medical school seats as the rest of Canada in
the 1980’s, reaching a low point of 60 seats/millions in 1994, resulting in a shortfall of doctors.
Although funding was steadily restored, it was not enough to offset population growth. Since
1985, Manitoba has lost the opportunity to train over 800 physicians. It is very difficult to come
back from this deficit position.

In 1999, Manitoba stood up a formal program to integrate FTPs, focused on family medicine.
This program allows FTPs to complete a practice ready assessment (PRA) or a one-year
training program to get them ready to practice in Canada. This program has been highly
successful, enabling >300 FTPs to enter practice in Canada since inception, with 75%
remaining in Manitoba long-term.

More recently, Manitoba has funded additional residency spots to repatriate IMGs. This has
shown early and encouraging results.

AFMC encourages the Committee to look at these examples as possible ways forward in
solving Canada’s doctor shortage.
VI.
Contact
Canadian medical schools are world-renowned and are ready to work with government to
address the doctor shortage.

text:
Submission to The Standing Committee on Health Study: Impact of
Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating
Internationally Trained Professionals
Submitted by the Pediatric Chairs of Canada
November 24, 2025
Introduction
Canada’s ability to deliver timely, high-quality healthcare to children and youth increasingly
depends on the strength of its highly specialized pediatric workforce. Today, that workforce is atrisk. Across the country, pediatricians and pediatric subspecialists—whose expertise is essential
when children require preventive care, specialized treatments, or coordinated diagnosis and
management of complex conditions—are in short supply. In addition to our important national
focus on primary care, we must also recognize increasing subspecialty shortages which are
directly limiting access to medically necessary care and compromising long-term health
outcomes for Canadian infants, children and teenagers.
This challenge is not abstract. More than 8 million children and youth currently live in Canada, a
number expected to grow by 24% over the next fifty years. Yet across many jurisdictions,
children now wait longer than adults for essential care, not because their needs are less urgent,
but because the workforce trained to meet those needs is too small, aging, and increasingly
stretched to meet the needs of an increasingly complex population of kids.
Why Pediatric Workforce Sustainability Matters
Children are not tiny adults. Children have unique physiological, developmental, and social
needs that require dedicated training and coordinated care. Pediatric subspecialties—such as
neonatology, pediatric neurology, gastroenterology, cardiology, oncology, and developmental
pediatrics—form highly interdependent systems and are not inter-changeable with
subspecialists who care for adults.
When even one pediatric sub-specialist position sits vacant, the impacts are widespread:
clinical services are reduced or delayed across a jurisdiction
training capacity shrinks
regional models of coordinated care can weaken or collapse
research and innovation programs are disrupted
These risks are evident across Canada and are especially acute in smaller provinces and
academic health centres serving large geographic areas that include rural and remote
communities. In addition, for pediatric subspecialists with highly specialized expertise (eg
pediatric bone marrow transplant or interventional cardiologists) there is much less resiliency in

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
In addition, for pediatric subspecialists with highly specialized expertise (eg
pediatric bone marrow transplant or interventional cardiologists) there is much less resiliency in

the system given their scarcity, in comparison to the larger pool of internal medicine
subspecialists who care for adult patients.
Evidence of a System Under Strain
To better understand the scope of the issue, the Pediatric Chairs of Canada (PCC) conducted a
national data collection exercise in 2024 focused on the academic pediatric subspecialty
workforce (hospital-based providers) and trainees (graduates of medical school) currently
preparing to enter these fields (summary in appendix). The majority of pediatric subspecialists
are affiliated with one of the 17 academic health science centers and affiliated medical schools
represented by the PCC.
The findings painted a clear picture:
Shortages are causing delays in access to essential pediatric care, jeopardizing longterm outcomes.
Fewer trainees are choosing pediatrics, resulting in a shrinking workforce attempting
to serve a growing, increasingly medically complex pediatric population.
Insufficient provincial residency spots in general pediatrics and subspecialties to
train sufficient numbers of Canadian pediatricians and pediatric subspecialists to meet
current demand.
Delays in hiring internationally trained pediatric subspecialists—including
Canadians trained abroad—are threatening service delivery, clinical teaching, capacity
building, and research continuity.
Taken together, these trends signal an approaching inflection point. Without timely intervention,
Canada risks a progressive service deterioration that will undermine child health outcomes,
family wellbeing, and system performance for decades to come. A 2024 publication from
Children’s Healthcare Canada and the Conference Board of Canada outlines social and
economic impacts associated with delays in access to care for children and youth.
The Case for a Multi-Pronged Workforce Strategy
Addressing pediatric workforce shortages requires coordinated, national-level action. No single
lever will be sufficient. Canada must adopt a strategy that strengthens domestic training
pathways while modernizing immigration, credentialing, and retention processes.
This includes:
Training more pediatricians and subspecialists in Canada;
Reducing barriers and delays for Canadians trained at accredited medical schools
abroad to practice in Canada;
Improving pathways for foreign medical school graduates who successfully complete
their pediatric subspecialty training in Canada to remain and practice;

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
This includes:
Training more pediatricians and subspecialists in Canada;
Reducing barriers and delays for Canadians trained at accredited medical schools
abroad to practice in Canada;
Improving pathways for foreign medical school graduates who successfully complete
their pediatric subspecialty training in Canada to remain and practice;

Expediting and simplifying processes for highly-qualified internationally trained pediatric
subspecialists who want to make Canada home.
Today, highly trained pediatric subspecialists—many urgently needed to maintain essential
services—face unnecessary delays in immigration processing, protracted licensure timelines,
and systemic obstacles that prevent them from joining the workforce in a timely manner. These
barriers are not only administrative; they translate directly into longer waits for children,
increased pressures on hospitals, and lost opportunities to build the pediatric workforce Canada
urgently requires.
Three Case Studies
1. Canadians who completed their medical school degree abroad and want to return to
Canada for postgraduate medical education (residency) and/or subspecialty training.
Their return would be a win for our workforce.
Barriers include limited residency spots for international medical graduates (IMGs),
inconsistent recognition of foreign training, and complex licensure requirements that
differ by province, even though these individuals represent “high-potential” candidates
for integration and retention.
2. International medical graduates who completed their medical degree abroad but
completed their specialty (general pediatrics) or subspecialty training (eg pediatric
cardiology) in Canada. These clinicians have already been trained in the Canadian
system, almost exclusively within pediatric academic centers for 1-3 years or more, and
represent a significant potential workforce, available now when many gaps exist.
Current immigration rules make it difficult for these subspeciality pediatricians to stay
after training.
They face complex and lengthy processes to secure permanent residency, work permits,
or pathways to remain in Canada—despite being already integrated into Canadian
teams.
Those who completed subspeciality training (eg pediatric cardiology, oncology, or
gastroenterology) in Canada, but not their core general pediatric training, also face
complex licensure requirements that unnecessarily limit recruitment opportunities.
3. Highly qualified international pediatric subspecialists who completed all of their
medical training outside Canada (e.g., U.S. or other high-performing systems) and
wish to relocate and practice here.
These individuals may have trained at world-leading institutions (e.g., Harvard), and
would significantly strengthen subspecialty pediatric capacity in Canada.
These clinicians face complicated and inconsistent provincial licensing requirements,
lengthy assessment processes, and a lack of coordinated pathways to bring them into
academic centers.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
These clinicians face complicated and inconsistent provincial licensing requirements,
lengthy assessment processes, and a lack of coordinated pathways to bring them into
academic centers.

Academic hospitals often lose these candidates with highly specialized clinical expertise
because the time, complexity, potential need to do additional training or exams in
Canada, and uncertainty of licensure and immigration are simply too high.
Many current pathways to licensure are restricted to pediatric subspecialists applying for
positions that include both clinical work and research. Recruitment of full-time clinical
subspecialists currently is more challenging in most provinces.
Recommendations to support workforce sustainability (across all subspecialties).
1. Streamline immigration processes.
Streamline paperwork for work authorizations and visas.
Create faster, clearer pathways for permanent residency for pediatric specialists and
subspecialists.
Prioritize pediatric subspecialists in existing federal health-related immigration streams,
like Express Entry.
2. Harmonize and coordinate licensure requirements across provinces and territories.
Reduce variability in assessment processes for internationally trained pediatricians.
Develop national standards for recognizing training from reputable international
institutions.
Create an expedited and consistent licensure pathway for pediatric subspecialists
recruited into academic health science centres.
3. Support joint federal–provincial initiatives.
Encourage collaboration between Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada
(IRCC), provincial ministries of health, and medical regulatory authorities.
Ensure workforce planning for pediatrics is aligned with immigration and licensure
processes.
Include and prioritize pediatric workforce needs as part of the broader health human
resources strategy that addresses gaps in specialist /subspecialist care. This should
apply to pediatric physician groups but also to other health care professions (eg nursing,
physiotherapy, psychology) that focus on children and youth.
About the Pediatric Chairs of Canada:
Pediatric Chairs of Canada (PCC) is a national network of leaders in pediatric medicine, focused
on building and leading the next generation of the specialized workforce to deliver excellent care
for children, youth and families. Membership includes all seventeen department heads of
pediatrics across Canada’s medical schools. Most of the Department chairs are also the Chiefs
of Pediatrics at the majority of pediatric hospitals in Canada.

SE Health: Submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare
Nov 25, 2025
Executive Summary
Recent changes to immigration policy are beginning to impact SE Health’s ability to sustain care delivery. With
over 8,000 staff providing approximately 25,000 healthcare visits daily, SE Health has relied on more than 650
temporary foreign workers to address persistent workforce shortages and expand services in high-need areas.
However, a growing number of work permit renewal denials now threaten this critical staffing stream. If the
trend continues, it could significantly reduce SE Health’s capacity to meet rising demand - particularly as
Canada’s aging population accelerates. The potential loss of these workers would result in loss of around 1,800
health care interactions daily, impacting thousands of Canadians.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
The potential loss of these workers would result in loss of around 1,800
health care interactions daily, impacting thousands of Canadians.

SE Health urges this committee to recommend that the House of Commons address the urgent need for policy
changes to support the continued use of temporary foreign workers in the healthcare system.
Impacts of Immigration Policy Changes
Canada is experiencing a persistent health human resources shortage that is placing growing pressure on the
home and community care sector. As the population ages and demand for services rises, the limited supply of
trained healthcare professionals, particularly nurses and personal support workers, is making it increasingly
difficult to sustain high-quality care in the community. Recruitment and retention challenges, compounded by
regional disparities and workforce burnout, have led many providers to rely on temporary or internationally
trained workers to fill critical gaps.
SE Health delivers exceptional care to Canadians every day and has consistently stepped up to meet these
workforce challenges. In cases where domestic recruitment has fallen short, we have successfully brought in
international talent. For example, we were able to open a dementia care wing in a long-term care home in rural
Alberta - an area with limited housing and distance from major urban centres - thanks to the recruitment of
temporary foreign workers. These individuals, many of whom were trained as nurses or even physicians in their
home countries, are currently working in personal support or health care aide roles and are eager to build their
lives in Canada.
However, recent changes to federal immigration policy threaten this vital workforce. If current trends in work
permit denials continue, we risk losing hundreds of skilled and dedicated individuals who are essential to
maintaining care for vulnerable populations. According to the Ontario government, the province is projected to
face a shortfall of nearly 50,000 personal support workers and 33,000 nurses by 2032 - a forecast made before
the latest immigration policy shifts. It is reasonable to expect these shortages will worsen under the new rules.

SE Health Submission: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare
Without a thoughtful review of the impact of immigration policy on healthcare staffing, Canada’s already fragile
system could face further strain - resulting in reduced services and diminished access to care for those who need
it most.

SE Health Submission: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare
Without a thoughtful review of the impact of immigration policy on healthcare staffing, Canada’s already fragile
system could face further strain - resulting in reduced services and diminished access to care for those who need
it most.

Proposed Solution
Restore work permits for temporary foreign healthcare workers who were previously denied and roll back recent
changes to the Temporary Foreign Worker Program that have adversely affected the healthcare sector. These
measures will help stabilize staffing levels, alleviate burnout among Canadian healthcare professionals, and
maintain continuity of care for vulnerable populations. They also support federal commitments to expand
healthcare access and address labour shortages as outlined in Canada’s Health Workforce Strategy.

On behalf of the National Association of Pharmacy Regulatory Authorities (NAPRA), I would like to thank
HESA for this study and the opportunity to provide input in writing.

Founded in 1995, the National Association of Pharmacy Regulatory Authorities (NAPRA) is the alliance of
Canada’s pharmacy regulators – the 13 provincial and territorial pharmacy regulatory authorities (PRAs)
across the country as well as the Canadian Forces Health Services. NAPRA’s Members regulate the
practice of pharmacy in their respective jurisdictions in Canada, and their primary mandate is to protect
and serve the public interest. NAPRA facilitates collaboration and national approaches among its
Members as they address common issues in the practice of pharmacy in Canada.

The provincial and territorial PRAs govern the pharmacy professions so that they best support the public
in realizing optimal health outcomes. As part of that mandate, PRAs license pharmacy professionals
(pharmacists and pharmacy technicians), set required standards and codes of ethics for pharmacy
practice, and investigate and resolve complaints in their respective jurisdictions. In addition to their core
work of establishing and implementing licensure pathways, and ensuring adherence to professional
standards, PRAs also explore opportunities that would allow them to better serve the public interest.

Pharmacy professionals are the third largest group of health professionals in Canada, after nurses and
physicians0F1, with over 50,600 registered/licensed pharmacists and over 11,500 registered/licensed
pharmacy technicians across the country. Pharmacists apply their expertise in the appropriate use of
medications to assess patients and provide patient-centered, clinical care and advice that promotes the
optimal use of medications to achieve the patient’s health goals. They also provide preventative and
public-health care, advice, and services to promote and advocate for the health and safety of the public
in Canada. Pharmacy technicians apply their expertise in medication preparation and pharmacy
operations to ensure the safe, accurate, and efficient distribution of medications and health products,
and support pharmacists and other health professionals in the provision of patient-centered clinical care
and public-health care. Pharmacy professionals work in collaboration with other health professionals to
keep patients healthy and safe. They may work in a variety of different practice settings, including
community pharmacies, hospitals, family health teams and primary care clinics. Appropriate oversight
by the PRAs is critical to ensure safe, ethical pharmacy practice that can relieve the burden on the health
