appropriate use of medications.

While the 2025 Canadian Health Workforce Education, Training and Distribution Study1F2 identified the
current gap between the supply and demand of pharmacists to be 1,700 individuals, this number does
not include all jurisdictions, nor does it consider all services provided by pharmacists as they take on a
larger role in primary care with an evolving scope of practice; hence we believe the study
underestimates the current and expected gap. Nova Scotia alone is reporting a shortage of 260
pharmacists in 2025, with projections indicating that number could reach 500 by the end of 2026. This is
consistent with the report’s findings that the shortage is showing an upward trend and is expected to
double by 2034. In addition, several jurisdictions are observing reduced pharmacy hours, closures on the
weekends, or permanent pharmacy closures due to the shortage of pharmacy professionals. NAPRA and
its members recognize that internationally educated pharmacy professionals (IEPPs) play a role in filling
this gap and supporting the Canadian healthcare system. All 10 provincial PRAs have licensure pathways
for international pharmacy graduates (IPGs), and four provincial PRAs have licensure pathways for
internationally educated pharmacy technicians.
The PRAs also recognize that while pharmacy may be practiced and regulated similarly to Canada in
many international jurisdictions, there also remain many jurisdictions where there are significant
differences. Given these differences, regulators put processes in place to ensure that IEPPs have the
competencies required to practice safely and ethically in Canada, including experience in providing
clinical care directly to patients.
The licensure process for IEPPs in Canada vary slightly across the jurisdictions, but include, overall, steps
to ensure that IEPPs:
have completed the education and training required to acquire the base competencies
necessary to practice in Canada. This includes an assessment of credentials and, for some
candidates, an examination to assess their knowledge.
have the capacity to practice competently in the province. This may include an assessment of
competence using a national licensing examination, which is also taken by Canadian graduates,
or a programmatic assessment of competence in real life practice. In some jurisdictions,
candidates might have to complete a bridging program.
are able to understand complex medical information and communicate effectively with patients
and other health professionals in one of Canada’s official languages. This can be demonstrated
via language tests, education and/or relevant work experience in English or French.
are trusted professionals who are ethical, honest, and of good character. This is demonstrated
through letters of standing from previous regulators, criminal background checks and
references.

understand the federal and provincial laws, as well as the standards and regulations that govern
pharmacy practice in their chosen jurisdiction, by taking a jurisprudence course and/or
examination.
The licensure process can begin before IEPPs arrive in Canada. Pharmacists’ Gateway Canada is a NAPRA
service, unique to the pharmacy profession, which provides international pharmacist graduates (IPGs)
detailed information in French and English about the licensure pathway in each Canadian jurisdiction on
its webpage (https://www.pharmacistsgatewaycanada.ca/), which is accessed by 80,000 users per year
and receives 345,000 visits on average. Further, Pharmacists’ Gateway Canada has been offering client
services since 2014 and now responds to over 5,000 inquiries from IPGs every year with the goal of
clarifying processes and helping international candidates navigate the licensure process. IPGs are able to
complete their credential evaluation, their language tests, and a portion of the national licensing
examination prior to coming to Canada, giving them an opportunity to gauge whether they are likely to
be successful with the licensure process before they arrive. Through NAPRA, PRAs are also exploring the
implementation of a national practice registry, which would support the mobility of pharmacy
professionals, including IEPPs, across jurisdictions after their initial licensure.
Depending on where IPGs gained their qualifications and have practiced, they may be exempted from
completing several parts of the licensure process. For example, at the national level, IPGs who studied in
or have been licensed in Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the
United States are exempt from the evaluating examination, which assesses whether they have the
knowledge expected of a graduate of a Canadian program. This exemption was implemented because
the practice and regulation of pharmacy in these counties are deemed comparable to Canada by the
Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada.
In addition, in recent years, several PRAs have implemented streamlined licensure pathways for
countries in which the training, practice, and regulation of pharmacy is similar to Canada, such as
Australia, New Zealand, Ireland, the United Kingdom and the United States. These pathways allow
candidates to bypass steps in the licensure pathway to become licensed more quickly in Canada, such as
the national licensing examination, bridging programs, or additional practical training. Further
innovation is also underway, such as a pilot project in Nova Scotia based on the assessment of the
individual candidate's competency to practice in real-life settings rather than based on the country in
which they are licensed. Through these processes, the PRAs have identified areas where immigration,
employment and professional licensure processes should be better aligned.
Changes that could be made by the federal government to the federal immigration system to further
support IEPPs would be to:
initiate collaboration between Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada and the PRAs to
align immigration processes with regulatory processes.
provide funding to support PRA initiatives and innovation in the IEPPs licensure pathways.
work with PRAs to prioritize applications from IEPPs who are closest to being ready to practice in
Canada.

Briefly about me:
I am a Canadian citizen. I mention this because Canada is the only home I’ve known; I
understand Canadian culture and I do not require a visa. I am a healthcare provider so I am
familiar with the ethical framework, the Health Professional Act and the Canadian healthcare
system. I have experience working in remote BC communities. I understand the limitations and
increased workload required within small communities, where the need is great. As well, rural
providers have long waitlists.
I self funded my education to study a Caribbean medical school. I completed third year
hospital clerkships in USA, which is an approved jurisdiction. I am currently in my fourth year. I
completed rotations in USA as well as rural and urban Canada. I am applying to internal
medicine residency in both Canada and America, via CARMS and ERAS, respectively.
My partner works in in BC, he loves his work and his employer loves him. He is originally from
Europe, he has lived in various European countries, Australia, Caribbean, USA and Canada. I
am very familiar with the immigration process. Both of us hope that I match in Canada so we
can raise a family here and continue to call it home, but we have decided that we will settle in
whichever country I match because that will require the least amount of investment. If I match
within Canada, I will probably stay in the province I match in because of the long return of
service which I am fine with, even if it is not a rule applied to Canadian medical students. By
the way, the public fund CMGs yet they are not required to have a return of service.
My Medical Education
My medical education is a 4 year WFME-accredited MD program and education is provided in
English. The first two years are in the Caribbean third year is in affiliated US or Canadian
locations. Fourth year is in our location of interest but 12 weeks must be in the US.

Even though CARMS is a uniform, centralized process, each province has very restrictive
processes, making it apparent the federal and provincial goals are not aligned. In all of Canada,
although there are a total of 104 internal medicine residency positions available for IMGs, I will
only be eligible for 5 of them in the first iteration. Even though these are “funded” by the

during their clerkship. In addition, one resident is much more cost-effective than the cost of a
fully trained and certified physician. I notice other countries, like America, recognize this and
embrace our expertise. Patients and colleagues, alike, treat medical students and residents
with respect, despite our background.
The federal government believes highly educated immigrants provide value to Canadian
communities, that is why there is an increased number of points based on the education.
Education is a means of adaptability, resilience and decreased crime rates, but it cannot be
blindly applied to every sector and a systematic approach needs to occur so that immigrant
physicians and Canadians studying medicine are happy and are able to come back home.
Some physician members of the HESA community are biased with the Visa trainee category as
some of them are physicians and may benefit from their funds. I understand having people
from abroad adds cultural experience and it can be mutually beneficial, yet it cannot take away
from our current citizens, who are long term investments within the healthcare system.
Because after training, we will stay and work in Canada and contribute to the healthcare
system. Federal government policies need to reflect on long term investment for the benefit of
Canadians or at least, find a way to be inclusive to expand on these CARMS trainee positions.
The visa trainees range in first year residents to extreme sub-specialization. Some members of
the committee mentioned the trainees are only involved in trainee roles but in my experience in
four institutions that is not the case. The subspecialty process is the way visa-trainees are able
to immigrate to Canada. As a side note, the USA system if very streamlined, everyone has to
pass the same exams to be eligible for training and everyone competes based on merit.

CMA submission
Brief on the impact of
immigration policy on
health care
Submission to the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
November [CONTACT] Towers, suite 500, Ottawa, Ontario [CONTACT]

The Canadian Medical Association (CMA) respectfully submits this brief to the House of
Commons Standing Committee on Health for its study on the impact of immigration
policy on health care and barriers to integrating internationally trained professionals.

As the voice of physicians and medical learners across the country, the CMA has seen
the human impact of a health system under growing strain – from patients waiting too
long for care to colleagues struggling to stay in practice. This is a reality felt by more
than 6.5 million Canadians who have no family doctor to turn to. We have also seen
skilled physicians trained abroad who are eager to help, but unable because of the
barriers that stand in their way.

The CMA views this study as a natural extension of the conversation our country must
have about health workforce planning. We testified before the health committee in
2022 about solutions to the health workforce crisis. Three years later, health workforce
planning remains fragmented while demand for care continues to climb. More than
13,000 internationally trained physicians in Canada are not working in their field. We
must do more to recognize medical talent already here – and to attract, welcome and
retain more from around the world.

One physician shared that he was offered several promising hospitalist positions in
British Columbia, but they fell through due to confusing and restrictive rules around
work permits for locum physicians. Another, a UK-trained specialist with 27 years of
distinguished experience, still cannot qualify for permanent residency – a frustrating
barrier that undermines both his contributions and Canada’s healthcare capacity.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Another, a UK-trained specialist with 27 years of
distinguished experience, still cannot qualify for permanent residency – a frustrating
barrier that undermines both his contributions and Canada’s healthcare capacity.

When newcomers are included in our health workforce, staffing gaps begin to close and
patient care benefits from diverse voices and experiences, reflecting the communities
we serve. Streamlining immigration and licensing pathways for qualified physicians
would allow skilled professionals to put their training to work – instead of being held
back by months or years of red tape. We must act swiftly to simplify pathways for U.S.-
based health professionals seeking to work in Canada, seizing a strategic opportunity to
welcome skilled clinicians during a period of uncertainty south of the border.

The CMA recommends that the federal government work with provinces and territories
to make it easier for internationally trained physicians to contribute their skills here in
Canada.

Recommendation 1: Scale up proven expedited licensing pathways that help
internationally trained physicians enter practice quickly, without compromising
standards of care.

Recommendation 2: Modernize immigration policies to remove lengthy administrative
hurdles. Lifting the Labour Market Impact Assessment requirement, which requires
employers to prove a vacancy needs to be filled by a foreign worker, would remove

months of delay for physicians already in demand.

Recommendation 3: Create a new path outside of the Provincial Nominee Program for
health care professionals. The program adds further barriers and delays. Canada needs a
far more efficient, dedicated, federally-coordinated “concierge-style” pathway – one
simplified process that fast-tracks qualified health workers and helps them move quickly
from temporary to permanent residency.

Recommendation 4: Provide targeted resources to provinces and territories to expand
Practice-Ready Assessments and make them available across Canada, so all experienced
international physicians can practise sooner.

Recommendation 5: Work with provinces and territories to invest in medical schools
and training facilities. Canada lags behind other OECD countries in our number of
medical schools and training facilities, underscoring the need to invest infrastructure
funds in expanding health profession education capacity. Innovative training models are
emerging across the country, but their impact is limited by physical space and training
infrastructure.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
Innovative training models are
emerging across the country, but their impact is limited by physical space and training
infrastructure.

Recommendation 6: Collaborate with provinces and territories, alongside the
Federation of Medical Regulatory Authorities and the Medical Council of Canada, to
draw lessons from the U.S. Interstate Medical Licensure Compact and Australia’s
National Scheme. These models provide guidance for modernizing Canada’s regulatory
framework, creating a national registry of health professionals and improving workforce
mobility. A sustainable financial model will also be needed to support regulatory
infrastructure and long-term sustainability. Even as more physicians enter Canada,
current licensing models restrict where and how they can practise. The CMA continues
to advocate for pan-Canadian licensure, a practical reform that would allow providers to
move freely across jurisdictions and deliver care where it is needed most.

Recommendation 7: Foster federal leadership on integrated health workforce planning
– a national approach that connects how we train, recruit and support health care
professionals with the care Canadians need. This is critical to aligning immigration,
licensure and workforce planning into one coherent, sustainable system that serves
both patients and providers. The CMA recently released a new policy Building capacity
through integrated health workforce planning. On the basis of extensive consultations
with the public, health system leaders, health care professionals, researchers,
policymakers, government representatives, Indigenous leaders and persons with lived
experience, the policy identifies key principles and action-oriented recommendations to
guide the planning and establishment of an integrated health workforce.

Immigration policies are only one part of the solution. We cannot rely on them alone to
solve the access-to-care crisis. We also need to recognize that many internationally
trained health care professionals face systemic barriers, including racism, at every stage

– from education to practice. Addressing these inequities is essential to building a fair,
effective system and sustainable health workforce.

Canada’s physicians are ready to be partners in that effort, and we thank the health
committee for turning its attention to this critical issue.

®
Written Submission to The Standing Committee on Health Impact of Immigration Policy on
Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
Submitted by the National Dental Examining Board of Canada
November 2025

Category Based Selection: Considerations for Dentistry
Canada is currently facing a significant health human resource challenge, and the Government of Canada is
taking decisive action to attract the expertise and talent required to meet the health needs of Canadians. One
important initiative has been the prioritization of health-related occupations through the Express Entry system.

While this approach appropriately seeks to strengthen Canada’s health workforce, the inclusion of dentistry in
dedicated rounds of invitations for healthcare professionals may unintentionally create unrealistic expectations
among prospective immigrants regarding their ability to obtain licensure and practise as dentists in Canada.

Under an Act of Parliament, the National Dental Examining Board of Canada (NDEB) has a statutory obligation to
certify only those candidates who meet the established national standard of competence. All individuals—
regardless of citizenship or country of education—must successfully complete the NDEB’s Certification Process
prior to licensure in Canada.

Canada’s dental profession maintains reciprocal agreements with a limited number of countries, including the
United States, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand. These agreements recognize the equivalency of dental
education and facilitate licensure for graduates of accredited programs in those jurisdictions. However,
internationally trained dentists (ITDs) from countries without such reciprocal recognition must demonstrate
equivalency through one of two routes:
1.
Completion of an accredited Qualifying/Degree Completion Program for graduates of nonaccredited dental schools; or
2.
Successful completion of the NDEB Equivalency Process, a structured assessment pathway for
graduates of non-accredited programs.

Given the requirements of these routes, prioritizing immigration candidates based on an academic credential in
dentistry offers limited practical benefit in addressing Canada’s oral health workforce needs. In fact, it risks
generating false expectations among applicants that their degree alone will permit them to practise dentistry
upon arrival in Canada.

Examinations administered by the NDEB are essential safeguards to ensure public protection. Dentistry is a
profession in which practitioners often work independently and without supervision; therefore, a standardized and
independent assessment of competence is critical. These examinations confirm that all entrants—domestic or
international—meet the minimum threshold for safe and effective practice.

org: National Dental Examining Board of Canada
study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
These examinations confirm that all entrants—domestic or
international—meet the minimum threshold for safe and effective practice.

Global dental education varies widely in curriculum, clinical exposure, and assessment standards. Since the
establishment of the NDEB Equivalency Process in 2011, 12,208 internationally trained dentists have applied, of
whom 24.5% have completed all the examinations and achieved certification. These data highlight both the rigor
of Canada’s licensure standards and the educational disparities that exist internationally.

Recommendation

The NDEB recommends that the federal government remove dentistry from the healthcare occupations included
in dedicated immigration invitations and prioritized permanent residency pathways. This would ensure alignment
between immigration policy and professional regulatory realities, while maintaining transparency for prospective
immigrants.

Supporting Integration for Internationally Trained Dentists
To more effectively support internationally trained dentists, the federal government could consider targeted
investments in bridging and upskilling programs that align international education and experience with Canadian
standards.

The current success rate within the NDEB Equivalency Process demonstrates that many internationally trained
dentists require additional education and clinical preparation to meet Canadian entry-to-practice expectations.
Each year, the NDEB receives approximately 1,700 new applications from internationally trained dentists, yet
fewer than 500 candidates achieve certification. Furthermore, alternative qualifying programs remain limited,
with fewer than 100 seats available annually, making the NDEB pathway the only accessible option for most
candidates.

Enhanced collaboration between the federal government, provincial regulators, and academic institutions could
help create more accessible and scalable bridging opportunities, enabling qualified international candidates to
meet Canadian standards and contribute meaningfully to the oral health workforce.

text:
Submission to the House of Commons Standing
Committee on Health (HESA)
Study: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating
Internationally Trained Professionals
Submitted by:
Canadian Association for Long Term Care (CALTC)
Date: November 5th, 2025

Executive Summary
Canada’s long-term care (LTC) sector is experiencing a severe and growing workforce
crisis that directly impacts the quality of care for older adults and the overall sustainability
of the health system.
As the population ages—particularly with the number of Canadians aged 85 and older
expected to double by 2040—demand for LTC will rise dramatically. Yet, according to
Statistics Canada (2024), there are already over 25,000 vacant LTC positions across the
country1.
Domestic recruitment and training initiatives remain essential but will take time to have an
effect. Immediate workforce stabilization requires federal leadership through targeted
immigration policy, enhanced settlement supports and streamlined administrative
processes.
CALTC recommends:
1. Include LTC homes in federal settlement funding programs to ensure that employers,
newcomers and their families have the support needed to successfully integrate,
further supporting their retention.

2. Expand and simplify immigration pathways—for example, by creating a healthcarespecific pilot for LTC. This could build on strengths and lessons learned from the
Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot and the Atlantic Immigration Program to attract
and retain internationally educated health professionals specifically interested in
working in LTC .
3. Create a healthcare-specific work permit that is Labour Market Impact Assessment
(LMIA) exempt. The Francophone Mobility work permit is a proven model, as it
addresses the significant Canadian interest in supporting official language minority
communities. That same regulatory authority can be applied to healthcare — another
sector of national interest. Permits would be occupation- specific and employerrestricted, helping reduce administrative burden while maintaining oversight and
worker protections.
4. Prioritize immigration processing in all programs for individuals already working or
committed to working in the LTC sector, while reducing the administrative burden for
LTC employers. As the next step, the government should prioritize pathways to
permanent residency for individuals working in LTC.

pressures in the years ahead6.

The LTC workforce crisis requires immediate solutions.

Immigration and the LTC Workforce
Supporting Ethical Recruitment
CALTC fully supports ethical recruitment practices, consistent with Canada’s Code of
Practice for the Recruitment of Internationally Educated Health Professionals8.
This includes ensuring fair employment, recognizing international qualifications, and
supporting integration into the workplace.
Many internationally educated healthcare providers begin their Canadian careers as
personal support workers (PSWs) in LTC while navigating credential recognition processes.
Employers often provide extensive settlement supports—such as housing, transportation,
and childcare assistance—largely at their own expense.
However, formal settlement supports remain limited, particularly in rural and remote
areas, where workforce needs are greatest.
Challenges in Current Immigration Pathways
Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot (EMPP)
There is strong interest among LTC providers in the Economic Mobility Pathways Pilot,
which allows skilled refugees to fill critical roles. However, processing delays and
administrative costs make this program difficult for many LTC employers to use
effectively.
Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) Program
The Temporary Foreign Worker Program continues to play an essential role in LTC staffing.
Despite this success, recent changes—including new LMIA requirements and annual
renewal limits—have created administrative and financial burdens for LTC employers.
Many must now repeat the same process every 12 months simply to retain existing
workers.
These challenges make it increasingly difficult for LTC homes to maintain stable staffing
levels.
8 Ethical Framework for the Recruitment and Retention of Internationally Educated Health Professionals in
Canada. July 2025. https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/publications/health-systemservices/ethical-framework-recruitment-retention-internationally-educated-health-professionals.html

text:
July 2025. https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/publications/health-systemservices/ethical-framework-recruitment-retention-internationally-educated-health-professionals.html

Opportunities for Action
To build a sustainable LTC workforce, CALTC recommends that the federal government:
1. Integrate Long-Term Care into Federal Settlement Funding Programs
● Enable LTC homes to access federally funded settlement supports for workers and
their families.
● Strengthen retention and community integration, particularly in rural and remote
areas where support services are limited.
2. Expand and Simplify Immigration Pathways
● Create a healthcare-specific immigration pilot for LTC , building on lessons from
the Home Care Worker Immigration Pilot and the Atlantic Immigration Program.
● Streamline eligibility and credential recognition processes for internationally
educated professionals seeking to work in LTC.
3. Introduce a Healthcare-Specific Work Permit (LMIA-Exempt)
● Develop a sector-specific work permit modeled after the Francophone Mobility
Program, recognizing healthcare as a sector of national interest.
● Make permits occupation-specific and employer-restricted to reduce
administrative burden while maintaining oversight and worker protections.
4. Prioritize Immigration Processing and Permanent Residency Pathways
● Fast-track applications for individuals already working, or committed to working, in
LTC .
● Reduce administrative barriers, including repetitive LMIA renewals, for LTC
employers.
● Prioritize pathways to permanent residency for LTC workers to strengthen
workforce stability and retention.
Current Example of a Real Life Situation
An internationally trained care provider with six years of experience in the Philippines
began working at an LTC home in Prince Edward Island in November 2024 under an open
work permit.

When her permit expired in July 2025—while her Atlantic Immigration Program application
was still in process—it was not renewed. She is now preparing to return home, despite
holding a full-time position and being fully integrated into her community.
This is precisely the kind of situation that Canada must avoid. The system should support,
not hinder, the ability of LTC homes to retain qualified and dedicated staff.
Conclusion
Canada’s LTC sector is at a pivotal moment. Without immediate and coordinated federal
action, workforce shortages will continue to strain care capacity and undermine quality.
Immigration policy can and should be a strategic tool to stabilize the sector, support
ethical recruitment, and ensure that every older Canadian receives the care they deserve.
CALTC stands ready to work with the federal government and partners across Canada to
advance these solutions.

Written submission to the Standing Committee on Health
Addressing Workforce Challenges in Dermatology
Submitted by the Canadian Dermatology Association
November 4, 2025

Introduction
Canada's dermatologist community issued early warnings in the 2000s regarding a critical
shortage of dermatologists1. The profession aimed to pre-empt the significant
demographic shifts now evident in 2025, specifically a rapidly increasing aging population
alongside a dermatology workforce shortage2. Despite these warnings, proactive solutions
were not implemented, leaving us in a far more difficult position today.
The health human resource (HHR) shortage is one that is prevalent throughout the entire
Canadian health care system and extends globally. HHR recruitment and retention
challenges have been building for years and were significantly intensified by the pressures
of COVID-193. Across the system, gaps in workforce planning, training capacity, and
provider well-being are straining the delivery of timely care.
Dermatology is a critical component of an effective health care system and has been
directly affected by these system pressures. The skin is the body’s largest organ and plays
a vital role in overall health, providing a first line of defense against infection and
environmental hazards. When skin is diseased, the impacts can be severe. Conditions like
skin cancer require rapid diagnosis and treatment to prevent death, while non-lifethreatening conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, or severe acne can lead to chronic pain,
physical discomfort, and serious mental health and systemic consequences4.
The State of the Shortages
Current State:
Canada is experiencing a critical and climbing shortage of dermatologists. In 2023,
according to the Canadian Institute of Health Information (CIHI), there were 750
dermatologists registered within Canada5, responsible for providing care for a population

of Canadian dermatology--who will be your skin expert? Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery, 8(3), 141–147.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10[CONTACT]-7

Association member survey. Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery, 14(2), 71–79. https://doi.org/10.2310/7750.2010.09025

The shortages have been longstanding, a factor of which has been the relatively stable

population (Table 2). Over the past 10 years, the average growth in supply has been about

To better quantify the shortage, an optimal dermatologist-to-population ratio of 3:100,000
was identified in a recent study7. Based on this ratio, there would ideally be 1,215
dermatologists practicing in Canada, meaning there is a shortage of 465 dermatologists
across the country.

When comparing Canada directly to Germany, the comparator country with the highest
dermatologist-to-population ratio, in 2023 Canada would have needed an additional 2,338
dermatologists to reach their current dermatologist to patient ratio of 7.7:100,000.
Compared to Australia, the comparator country with the lowest, albeit still higher than
Canada, dermatologist-to-population ratio, in 2023 Canada would need an additional 252
dermatologists for a total of 1,002 to reach their ratio of 2.5:100,000.
It is important to note that these results are indicative rather than conclusive due to the
complicated nature of international comparison, as the characteristics of both the
populations and the physicians differ, as well as the delivery and payment modalities of
each country’s health care system. These findings should be interpreted within the context
of identifying and learning from high-performing countries, with the goal of examining
their achievements to help identify potential pathways for improvement.
Impact of the shortages
The shortage of dermatologists has implications for providers, patients and the health
care system at large.
Patient wait times are a direct way to demonstrate and understand the shortage of
dermatologists8. Most patients wait for months9 to meet with a dermatologist, leading to
the worsening of conditions and missed opportunities for early diagnosis. This is
particularly concerning when the early detection of diseases such as skin cancer is critical
for effective treatment10. Waiting for medically necessary care can mean the worsening of
a condition, potentially requiring more complex care and possibly poorer outcomes from
care11.

For dermatologists, the shortages have resulted in an increased workload and increased
pressure to manage a high volume of referrals. These demands can result in a risk of
burnout and can compromise the quality of care delivered. A study looking at burnout in
Canadian dermatology residents found that 54% of residents experience high rates of
emotional exhaustion, one of the signs of burnout12.
Solutions
To alleviate the dermatologist shortage in Canada, three areas for improvement were
identified through the literature and through discussions with system leaders.
Dermatologists, as the leading skin health expert, must lead and actively contribute to the
development and implementation of solutions.
1. Bolster System Capacity
• Prioritize pan-Canadian health workforce planning
• Expand training capacity amongst the dermatology workforce to enable
expansion of existing programs
• Create supportive programs to train international dermatologists
• Emphasize and Incentivize Medical Dermatology
• Implement national licensure
2. Develop efficient and effective team base care models
3. Integrate technology
Create supportive programs to train international dermatologists
Immigration policies and creating supportive programs to train and integrate international
dermatologists is one of the solutions supported by the CDA. There needs to be improved
processes in place to welcome qualified internationally trained dermatologists into the
medical system, including prioritizing Canadian International Medical Graduates. This is
especially paramount to better support the current workforce and provide the timely care
that patients need and deserve.
Internationally trained dermatologists face many barriers when trying to practice in the
Canadian health care system. These safeguards are in place to protect patients, however,

obstacles are sometimes so burdensome that dermatologists and other physicians living in
Canada end up working in a different field altogether13. A review of these processes and
programs must be undertaken to identify areas where we can expedite certifications and
leverage the talent and skill that is already available. That being said, it is especially
important not to compromise on the training quality. Internationally trained
dermatologists must be equivalent in training to Canadian dermatologists prior to
licensing.
Recommendations:
1. Immigration policies impact health care capacity. As such Health care
organizations such as the CDA should be consulted on capacity and demand issues
when developing these policies.

2. Supportive program should be developed to support international dermatologist,
prioritizing Canadian International Medical Graduates.

3. There should be no compromise on the training quality. Programs must be
developed to expedite pathways for certification while maintaining Canadian
quality standards as developed by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Conclusion
Canada’s longstanding shortage of dermatologists has reached an unsustainable point.
The Canadian Dermatology Association has identified three solutions:
• Bolster System Capacity
• Develop efficient and effective team base care models
• Integrate technology
Immigration policies and creating supportive programs to train and integrate international
dermatologists is one way of bolstering system capacity supported by the CDA. It is a
shorter-term solution while we build our internal capacity.
The Canadian Dermatology Association is ready to be part of the solution working with
government and key stakeholders, steadfast in the knowledge that dermatologists are, and

How the Government of Canada can increase the supply of family doctors

Overview
Canada has a primary care crisis. Some 6.5 million Canadians do not have a family doctor. The federal
government can rapidly and cost-effectively help mitigate this crisis by funding Practice Ready Assessment
(PRA) programs across Canada. PRA programs provide an accelerated pathway to licensure for
internationally-trained physicians (ITPs), thousands of whom are currently living in Canada as permanent
residents and citizens. ITPs have completed their medical school and residency and have practiced medicine
abroad. They have met all Canadian medical licensing requirements except for one: a competency
assessment. This can be provided through a PRA which can be completed in 12 weeks or less. Successful
completion of a PRA indicates that the ITP has demonstrated the ability to provide medical care at Canadian
standards.

Proposal
We propose the federal government fund 4,500 PRA spots across Canada over a 4-year period. Given the
average family physician sees 1,500 patients per year, this would give each currently waiting Canadian access
to a family doctor by the end of the 4-year period. The proposal is efficient, since becoming licensed through a
PRA is much quicker than the 2-year period to complete a medical residency. The proposal is also more costeffective than funding residencies–which cost about $340,000 per spot. The average cost for each 12-week
PRA is only $35,000. We also propose that the federal government directly fund the Medical Council of
Canada to continue to provide standardized assessor/assessment training and evaluation as well as a single
point of entry for ITPs applying for a PRA (estimated about $12 million over 4 years).

Cost
The total cost of our proposal would be $169.5 million. This expenditure would represent just 0.3% of what the

significant. ITPs would now be paying income and consumption taxes on an average annual salary of

and spending time with their families. Moreover, offering more preventative care through this workforce

text:
World Education Services
Submission to the
Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Study: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to
Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
October 2025

Underutilized Health Care Skills in Canada
Health care systems across Canada are in crisis, facing critical shortages of qualified health
professionals to respond to increased demands for care, particularly in small and mid-sized
communities. The federal government anticipates a shortage of 117,600 nurses by 2030 and 20,000
family doctors by 2031.
Meanwhile, thousands of internationally educated health professionals (IEHPs) living in Canada are
ready and qualified to help. Many are Canadian citizens and permanent residents. However,
systemic barriers to licensure, certification, and workforce integration continue to limit their ability
to contribute to their full potential.
Statistics Canada data suggest that roughly 47% of internationally educated health professionals
are either unemployed or working outside their field. The reasons for this are well understood and
well-documented. They include insufficient access to training positions (for example, medical
residency training), barriers to maintaining recent practice experience, high fees associated with
assessments and licensing processes, insufficient access to bridging or laddering pathways, lengthy
timelines, and the complexity of information about licensing pathways.
Canada invites health care professionals to the country through our immigration system and
invests in programs to support their integration through federal and provincial immigration
dollars, as well as health care, employment and education funds. Allowing skills underutilization of
IEHPs to continue is costing Canada—both economically and in patient outcomes.
There is a clear and urgent need to advance ongoing efforts to remove systemic barriers that
prevent IEHPs from becoming licensed to practice and to ensure that their skills can be fully applied
in the Canadian health care sector.
The Need for Federal Leadership and Pan-Canadian Strategy
The complexity of systems and stakeholders involved in this issue at the federal and provincial
levels, and across federal, provincial, and territorial (FPT) ministries, demands pan-Canadian,
cross-departmental, and multi-stakeholder approaches.
Successful solutions that have a positive impact are already being implemented across the country
and across health care professions. However, these initiatives are unaligned and contribute to an
increasingly fragmented patchwork of licensure processes, criteria, and supports for IEHPs. This
fragmentation, in turn, leads to wasted federal and provincial investments and deeply disrupted
lives for IEHPs looking to contribute their skills to our health care system. Additionally, the federal
immigration pathways for health professionals remain entirely disconnected from the provincial
regulatory processes that IEHP need to navigate.
As Canada moves to break down barriers to interprovincial labour mobility, we have a crucial
opportunity to leverage the momentum towards pan-Canadian solutions and address these long-

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
As Canada moves to break down barriers to interprovincial labour mobility, we have a crucial
opportunity to leverage the momentum towards pan-Canadian solutions and address these long-

standing and costly problems. The effort to find and align solutions must include collaboration
across federal departments and between levels of government, as well as with regulatory bodies,
the health education system, health care employers, IEHP organizations, and non-governmental
partners.
Federal leadership is critical to ensuring that the criteria and processes to determine whether
IEHPs are competent to practice in Canada are evidence based and standardized across the
country. Federal leadership can help move provinces and territories and regulatory bodies to align
standards and best practices, reduce duplication, and provide necessary supports to IEHPs
consistently and effectively across jurisdictions.
While the federal government funds a range of initiatives through Health Canada, IRCC, and
Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), this funding is not coordinated and aligned.
Equally importantly, the federal government has not yet fully engaged its convening power to bring
stakeholders together to find solutions, nor has it explored the potential for a national legislative
framework for licensure that would include pathways to licensure for internationally trained health
professionals who have made Canada their home.
One promising example of a federal convening effort was the IEHP task group brought together by
Health Canada in 2021. The group included leaders from national physician and nursing regulatory
bodies and professional associations, as well as other key players, to develop collaborative
solutions which were supported by federal funding. However, this effort was not sustained. The
work of Health Workforce Canada, a national data centre established in 2023, also has tremendous
potential to provide robust health workforce data inclusive of IEHPs. This type of multi-stakeholder
collaboration is key to developing sustainable, system-level strategies and solutions going forward.
Scaling Solutions that Work
Solutions to the barriers that keep IEHPs from practicing in our health care system already exist.
Spurred by the pandemic, many important initiatives have been developed or expanded in the last
several years. Some key examples include:
•
Registration modernization initiatives: Some provincial regulatory bodies have begun
proactively examining types of licenses available to IEHPs as well as IEHP entry-to-practice
processes.
o The Nova Scotia College of Physicians and Surgeons introduced Defined licensing for
internationally trained physicians (ITPs), enabling some ITPs to work under
supervision for a period of 6-24 months and to then apply for an independent license.
o Some provincial regulators, including in Alberta, Nova Scotia, British Columbia, and
others, have expanded approved jurisdiction pathways for internationally educated
nurses (IENs) and ITPs, increasing access to streamlined registration processes for
IEHPs from a designated list of countries where education regimes have been deemed
substantially equivalent to Canada’s.

study_or_consultation_title: Impact of Immigration Policy on Healthcare and Barriers to Integrating Internationally Trained Professionals
text:
of 6-24 months and to then apply for an independent license. o Some provincial regulators, including in Alberta, Nova Scotia, British Columbia, and others, have expanded approved jurisdiction pathways for internationally educated nurses (IENs) and ITPs, increasing access to streamlined registration processes for IEHPs from a designated list of countries where education regimes have been deemed substantially equivalent to Canada’s.

o Several nursing regulators have made significant changes to their requirements and
processes. The College of Nurses of Ontario has undertaken a comprehensive
modernization exercise leading to changes in requirements. As a result of these changes,
the number of IENs registered annually has almost quadrupled, rising from 1,500 in
2019 to nearly 6,000 in 2024.
•
Programs that allow IEHPs to meet recent practice requirements without leaving
Canada: A common requirement across licensure and assessment processes is that candidates
trained abroad must have recent active clinical experience—defined as practice within a
specific timeframe and for a specific duration. However, there is considerable variation in how
this recency period is defined within the same profession across provinces. Programs which
allow IEHPs to maintain or update their practice hours in Canada are essential.
o Ontario’s Supervised Practice Experience Partnership (SPEP) launched in 2022. This
partnership between the College of Nurses of Ontario and Ontario Health enables
qualified IENs to meet recent practice experience requirements and demonstrate
language proficiency by working under supervision in a hospital or long-term care
setting for three months. Since the inception of SPEP, over 4,500 IENs have obtained
licensure in Ontario through the program. The model has since been replicated in other
provinces, including Newfoundland and Labrador.

•
Supervised practice and assessment models: For health professionals who have already
completed clinical training and practiced in other countries, in-practice clinical assessments by
qualified assessors are a “best practice” that can be widely replicated across professions and
jurisdictions.
o Practice Ready Assessment (PRA) is a model that creates a licensure pathway for ITPs
who have already completed postgraduate residency training abroad and have
practiced independently for a defined period of time in another country. This pathway
eliminates the need for experienced physicians to redo residency training. PRA
programs exist in nine provinces, primarily for family medicine. While the Medical
Council of Canada oversees a national PRA assessment framework, many essential
elements of the program—including eligibility requirements regarding previous
postgraduate training and recency of practice requirements—vary widely by province.
The length of “Return of Service” requirements following a successful assessment also
varies, as does the scale of various PRA programs.

text:
The length of “Return of Service” requirements following a successful assessment also
varies, as does the scale of various PRA programs.

•
Occupation-specific navigation assistance is a proven best practice for ensuring IEHPs can
access pertinent information in a timely manner. Examples include the “Ally” tool for ITPs from
the Alberta International Medical Graduates Association and case-management models such as
the CARE Centre for IENs.

•
Financial supports are a vital element in ensuring IEHPs can obtain licensure and employment
in their fields. Several provinces have introduced bursaries, loans, or subsidies for costs
associated with examinations, applications, and registrations, for instance, the IEN Bursary
Program available through Health Match BC.
Recommendations
1. Establish a pan-Canadian body with cross-departmental, cross-jurisdictional
representation. This body would guide strategy, planning, and coordination of an IEHP
strategy inclusive of immigration, licensure, integration, and other necessary supports.
Effective solutions demand the participation of multiple stakeholders: federal and
provincial ministries governing immigration, health care, clinical education, and labour,
alongside IEHP organizations whose lived experience perspectives are essential to
developing practical approaches.
2. Streamline and harmonize licensing pathways for IEHPs across provinces and
territories. This strategy would establish pan-Canadian mechanisms to create consistent
eligibility criteria, requirements, and licensure pathways across jurisdictions, with a focus
on evidence-based, competency-driven standards that are equitably implemented.
3. Provide leadership and financial resources to develop a comprehensive health
workforce data strategy, ensuring policy decisions on IEHP integration are grounded
in evidence. Significant gaps in health workforce data make it nearly impossible to
determine how many IEHPs are in Canada, where they are in the process of obtaining
licensure, and whether they are working in their professions. Health Canada should
continue to fund Health Workforce Canada, the Canadian Institute for Health Information
(CIHI), and other health workforce bodies to strengthen robust data collection and data
linkage initiatives that include IEHP information. Similarly, IRCC should systematically
collect “field of study” and “intended occupation” for both temporary and permanent
immigration streams, and link to the data collected by provincial licensing bodies.

4. Ensure that IEHPs invited to immigrate through category-based selection (CBS) have
a viable pathway to licensure. The CBS program should include outcome metrics that
assess whether individuals selected based on their health care background are able to
obtain licensure and employment in their profession in Canada.

5. Establish federal frameworks and provide funding to provincial stakeholders to
implement and/or expand proven practices, including modernized registration
processes, supervised clinical experience and assessment models, and career navigation
supports tailored to specific occupations, as outlined above.

text:
Establish federal frameworks and provide funding to provincial stakeholders to
implement and/or expand proven practices, including modernized registration
processes, supervised clinical experience and assessment models, and career navigation
supports tailored to specific occupations, as outlined above.

6. Ensure alignment with principles outlined in Health Canada’s Ethical framework for the
recruitment and retention of internationally educated health professionals in Canada. This
new framework, based on the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Code of Practice on
the International Recruitment of Health Personnel, provides practical guidance for
stakeholders to ensure that practices in recruitment and retention of IEHPs: adopt a
reciprocal benefit approach for source countries and support health workforce
sustainability globally; ensure accurate and accessible information for IEHPs; and function
according to best practices in fairness, anti-racism, diversity, equity, inclusion, and
collaboration.
7. Investigate the extent to which "visa trainees" occupy medical training spaces in
Canada, and assess whether public investment could repurpose this capacity to
provide residency opportunities for ITPs who are permanent residents and citizens.
At present, a significant proportion of Canada’s postgraduate medical residency and
fellowship training seats are designated for visa trainees who are funded by governments
and entities outside of Canada to train here before returning to their home country. In
Ontario in 2024, 44.9% of all new training positions at Ontario medical schools (1,126 out
of 2,506 positions) went to visa residents and fellows. There should be a critical analysis of
the impact of such a large proportion of medical training positions allocated to individuals
who do not intend to remain in the country.
About WES: World Education Services (WES) is a non-profit social enterprise that supports the
educational, economic, and social inclusion of immigrants, refugees, and international students.
Since 2013, WES has been a designated provider of Educational Credential Assessments for IRCC,
providing over 240,000 ECAs to applicants for the Express Entry system in 2024.
For over 50 years, WES has set the standard for international academic credential evaluation. From
evaluating academic credentials to shaping policy, designing programs, and providing philanthropic
funding, we partner with a diverse set of organizations, leaders, and networks to uplift individuals
and drive systems change. Together with its partners, WES enables people to learn, work, and
thrive in new places.
WES works closely with system stakeholders and organizations representing IEHPs to advocate for
comprehensive, sustainable policy reforms that enable equitable access to licensure so that IEHPs
can support Canada’s health care system.

Addressing Workforce Challenges in the Oral Health Workforce
Submitted by the Canadian Dental Association
October 2025

Addressing Workforce Challenges in the Oral Health Sector
Across Canada, the oral healthcare sector is grappling with serious human resources
challenges, similar to those seen across the broader healthcare system. Dental clinics
are struggling to hire and retain dental assistants and dental hygienists.
Even prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, dentists were reporting significant concerns
regarding their ability to recruit and retain well-qualified staff, particularly dental
assistants. By 2019, roughly one-third of dental offices had vacant dental assistant
positions, and this issue was exacerbated by the pandemic. Further, as Canada’s
population continues to age, there will be an increase in demand and added pressures
for dental offices.
According to a recent Statistics Canada survey, 80% of dental offices in Canada are
reporting staffing challenges. 46.5% of dental offices are having difficulties in recruiting
dental assistants and 50.% are having difficulties in recruiting dental hygienists. In 2023
alone, over 7,200 job vacancies (dental assistants and dental hygienists) went unfilled
across Canada.
The Canadian Dental Care Plan (CDCP), which fully launched for all eligible populations
earlier this year, will add to these staffing pressures on dental offices. CDA estimates
that there will be a need for 2,300 additional dental assistants and 1,500 additional
dental hygienists due to the CDCP alone. Ensuring that the dental workforce has the
capacity to respond to the increase in patient volumes is critical.
One way the federal government can support the oral health sector in addressing
critical workforce challenges is by better supporting and attracting global
international talent. Currently, the federal post-graduation work permit (PGWP),
allows international students who have graduated from eligible Canadian schools to
remain in Canada and gain valuable Canadian work experience. However, due to the
immigration reforms introduced by the federal government in 2024, new eligibility
criteria were implemented to the PGWP which made many college programs
ineligible. While the PGWP is still available to dentists and dental hygienists, it is no
longer available to dental assistants. These changes are unintentionally worsening
workforce challenges by excluding graduates from dental assisting programs. Unless
addressed, these combined pressures will undermine access to timely, high-quality
oral health care for Canadians.
This means that international students who complete a dental assisting program, and
who could help address shortages immediately, cannot or face significant barriers to

text:
This means that international students who complete a dental assisting program, and
who could help address shortages immediately, cannot or face significant barriers to

work in Canada after graduation. This is happening while the country is experiencing
an acute shortage of dental assistants, a vital member of the oral healthcare team.
Recommendation
• Given the urgent need for dental assistants and the anticipated pressures
created by the CDCP, CDA urges the federal government to expand PGWP
eligibility to once again include dental assisting.
This targeted, evidence-based policy change would help address proven shortages of
dental assistants and would also make immigration policies better align with the federal
government’s own criteria for PGWP eligibility. According to Immigration, Refugees
and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), fields of study linked to jobs facing long-term shortages
in Canada should be prioritized for PGWP eligibility. Dental assisting clearly meets this
test given the demonstrated, widespread shortages across Canada, the thousands of
unfilled positions and its essential role in providing oral health care for all people living
in Canada.
Ensuring that Canada’s dental workforce can meet rising patient needs requires
immediate and targeted action. Expanding PGWP eligibility to include international
students studying dental assisting in Canada is a practical, timely step toward
strengthening oral healthcare access in Canada.
Background on Dentist Workforce - Internationally Trained Dentists
The report “Characteristics and Labour Market Outcomes of Internationally Educated
Health Care Professionals in Canada” (Statistics Canada, 2024) stated that about 7.8%
of all internationally educated health professionals in Canada (~20,000 individuals)
were educated in dentistry.
The most frequent occupations for those who studied dentistry outside of Canada were
dentists (25%), dental assistants and dental laboratory assistants (13%), dental
hygienists and dental therapists (7%), dental technologists and technicians (7%), and
receptionists (2%).

Brief to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health (HESA)
Topic: How Agricultural Chemicals and Clinical Coding Gaps are Fueling
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR)
Executive Summary
Canada's strategy to fight Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) has two major blind
spots. First, agricultural chemicals like glyphosate and neonicotinoids act as lowdose antimicrobials in the human gut. They force bacteria to adapt and become
resistant to life-saving medical treatments. Health Canada's safety models miss
this entirely because they evaluate systemic organ damage rather than localized
gut bacteria disruption.
Second, national data on AMR is fundamentally flawed. Tracking AMR carrier
status (like MRSA) in hospitals is weighed down by administrative burdens and
outdated records. We cannot fight an AMR crisis if our chemical safety laws
ignore environmental root causes and our clinical data is incomplete.
Part 1: The Chemical Blind Spot in the Gut
Health Canada and the Pest Management Regulatory Agency (PMRA) calculate
safety limits, such as the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI), based on systemic
toxicity—meaning they look for measurable damage to organs.
This model ignores the human microbiome. Glyphosate is poorly absorbed by the
human body; the vast majority remains in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
The Target: Glyphosate targets the "shikimate pathway". Human cells do
not have this pathway, but our essential gut bacteria do.
The "Dilution Fallacy": PMRA calculates safety limits based on the weight
of an entire human body. However, because the chemical pools in the gut,
the concentration against the 200–500g microbiome is exponentially
higher, meaning the calculation is flawed.
The Biomass Illusion: When regulatory studies claim these chemicals have
limited interaction with the gut microbiome, they often measure the total
weight or amount of bacteria. This fails to measure the drastic shift in the
composition and type of bacteria surviving in the gut.
The Bacterial Divide (Class I vs. Class II):
o Friendly Bacteria (Defenseless): Specialized, beneficial gut bacteria
are adapted to the safe environment of the human digestive tract.
They are highly specialized for tasks like creating amino acids and

They are highly specialized for tasks like creating amino acids and

lack robust defenses against harsh agricultural chemicals. When
exposed, these specific taxa decrease and die off.
o Wild-Type Pathogens (Adaptable): Opportunistic "wild-type"
pathogens evolved to survive harsh environments. They possess
non-specific built-in defense systems.
The Defense Mechanism: When friendly bacteria die, wild-type pathogens
multiply to fill the empty space. To survive the chemical exposure, these
wild-type bacteria activate defense systems called "efflux pumps".
These biological pumps act as a defense to spit out the agricultural chemicals,
but they also spit out clinical antibiotics. The pesticide exposure effectively
primes the harmful bacteria to fight human medicine.
Part 2: The Administration Route Matters (Pharmacokinetics)
How a patient receives an antibiotic dictates how much damage is done to the
gut's "resistome" (the collection of resistance genes).
Oral Route: Pills go directly through the GI tract, creating a highconcentration selective environment that clears out sensitive bacteria and
allows resistant strains to multiply.
IV Route: Intravenous antibiotics bypass the gut initially. However, drugs
that are excreted through the biliary tract dump directly back into the
intestines in active form.
When a patient with a gut already stressed by dietary pesticide residues is given
oral or biliary-excreted antibiotics, it creates a compounding effect that amplifies
AMR.
Part 3: "Leaky Gut" and How Resistant Bacteria Enter the Bloodstream
The danger of agricultural chemicals is not just that they create antibioticresistant bacteria inside the digestive tract. It is that they also destroy the
physical barrier keeping those dangerous bacteria out of the rest of the body.
Breaking the Barrier: A healthy microbiome maintains a tight, secure seal
along the intestinal lining. Chronic exposure to pesticides alters microbial
composition and triggers subtle shifts in barrier function.
The "Leaky Gut" Effect: Ongoing dysregulation compromises the
paracellular permeability of the intestinal epithelium, creating a "leaky gut".
The physical seal fails, leaving gaps in the defense system.

The physical seal fails, leaving gaps in the defense system.

Escaping into the Bloodstream: Once the gut barrier is compromised, the
antibiotic-resistant bacteria created by the pesticide exposure do not stay
contained in the digestive tract. They cross the damaged lining directly into
the bloodstream.
Systemic Infection: What started as localized microbial disruption becomes
a severe, multi-organ threat. This escape route is how resistant gut bacteria
lead to life-threatening blood infections (bacteremia) and sepsis.
Part 4: The Clinical Data Gap
The committee relies on national surveillance data to track AMR. Frontline clinical
coding highlights massive blind spots within this data.
The Coding Burden: It is mandatory to code for an AMR carrier status.
However, this information is rarely prioritized in the current patient visit
record.
Missing Data: Coders do not have the time to hunt through years of
historical records for every patient. Unless an active infection triggers a
manual search, historical carrier status is skipped. This leads to systemic
underreporting.
Outdated Data: When a carrier status is found, it is often years old. While
regions like Alberta track the date of the last swab, there is no national
standard defining when a carrier status expires.
Recommendations for the Committee
1. Update the "One Health" Framework: The PMRA must be mandated to
include microbiome disruption as a formal "adverse effect" when
calculating the safety limits of agricultural chemicals.
2. Fix the Data Pipeline: AMR carrier status must be mandated as a "priority
status" in electronic health records, identical to chronic conditions like
diabetes.
3. Establish Data Expiry: Create a national clinical coding standard that
defines the exact clinical lifespan of an AMR carrier flag to ensure national
surveillance data is accurate and current.
4. Call Independent Expert Witnesses: The Committee should invite
independent toxicologists, medical researchers, and microbiome
specialists (from organizations such as the Canadian Association of
Physicians for the Environment (CAPE), Environmental Defence, or
university digestive health institutes) to testify on the specific mechanisms

Call Independent Expert Witnesses: The Committee should invite
independent toxicologists, medical researchers, and microbiome
specialists (from organizations such as the Canadian Association of
Physicians for the Environment (CAPE), Environmental Defence, or
university digestive health institutes) to testify on the specific mechanisms

of pesticide-induced antimicrobial resistance and the current flaws in the
PMRA's safety models.
4. Call Independent Expert Witnesses: The Committee should invite independent
toxicologists, medical researchers, and microbiome specialists (from
organizations such as the Canadian Association of Physicians for the

Mémoire présenté au Comité permanent de la santé de la Chambre des
communes (HESA)
Sujet : Comment les produits chimiques agricoles et les lacunes en matière de
codage clinique alimentent la résistance aux antimicrobiens (RAM)
Résumé analytique
La stratégie du Canada pour lutter contre la résistance aux antimicrobiens (RAM)
comporte deux angles morts majeurs. Premièrement, les produits chimiques
agricoles tels que le glyphosate et les néonicotinoïdes agissent comme des
antimicrobiens à faible dose dans l'intestin humain. Ils forcent les bactéries à
s'adapter et à devenir résistantes aux traitements médicaux essentiels. Les
modèles de sécurité de Santé Canada omettent complètement ce fait, car ils
évaluent les dommages systémiques aux organes plutôt que la perturbation
localisée des bactéries intestinales.
Deuxièmement, les données nationales sur la RAM sont fondamentalement
erronées. Le suivi du statut de porteur de la RAM (comme le SARM) dans les
hôpitaux est alourdi par des fardeaux administratifs et des dossiers obsolètes.
Nous ne pouvons pas lutter contre une crise de la RAM si nos lois sur la sécurité
chimique ignorent les causes environnementales profondes et si nos données
cliniques sont incomplètes.
Partie 1 : L'angle mort chimique dans l'intestin
Santé Canada et l'Agence de réglementation de la lutte antiparasitaire (ARLA)
calculent les limites de sécurité, telles que la dose journalière admissible (DJA),
en fonction de la toxicité systémique — c'est-à-dire qu'ils recherchent des
dommages mesurables aux organes.
Ce modèle ignore le microbiome humain. Le glyphosate est mal absorbé par le
corps humain ; la grande majorité reste dans le tractus gastro-intestinal (GI).
La cible : Le glyphosate cible la "voie du shikimate". Les cellules humaines
ne possèdent pas cette voie, mais nos bactéries intestinales essentielles
l'ont.
L'erreur de dilution : L'ARLA calcule les limites de sécurité en se basant
sur le poids d'un corps humain entier. Cependant, comme le produit

Cependant, comme le produit

chimique s'accumule dans l'intestin, la concentration contre le microbiome
de 200 à 500 g est exponentiellement plus élevée, ce qui signifie que le
calcul est erroné.
L'illusion de la biomasse : Lorsque les études réglementaires affirment que
ces produits chimiques ont une interaction limitée avec le microbiome
intestinal, elles mesurent souvent le poids ou la quantité totale de
bactéries. Cela ne permet pas de mesurer le changement radical dans la
composition et le type de bactéries qui survivent dans l'intestin.
La division bactérienne (Classe I vs Classe II) : * Bactéries amicales (sans
défense) : Les bactéries intestinales bénéfiques et spécialisées sont
adaptées à l'environnement sûr du tube digestif humain. Elles sont
hautement spécialisées pour des tâches telles que la création d'acides
aminés et manquent de défenses robustes contre les produits chimiques
agricoles agressifs. Lorsqu'ils sont exposés, ces taxons spécifiques
diminuent et meurent.
o Agents pathogènes de type sauvage (adaptables) : Les agents
pathogènes opportunistes de "type sauvage" ont évolué pour
survivre dans des environnements difficiles. Ils possèdent des
systèmes de défense intégrés non spécifiques.
Le mécanisme de défense : Lorsque les bactéries amicales meurent, les
agents pathogènes de type sauvage se multiplient pour combler l'espace
vide. Pour survivre à l'exposition chimique, ces bactéries de type sauvage
activent des systèmes de défense appelés "pompes à efflux".
Ces pompes biologiques agissent comme une défense pour recracher les
produits chimiques agricoles, mais elles recrachent également les antibiotiques
cliniques. L'exposition aux pesticides prépare efficacement les bactéries nocives
à combattre la médecine humaine.
Partie 2 : La voie d'administration est importante (Pharmacocinétique)
La façon dont un patient reçoit un antibiotique dicte l'étendue des dommages
causés au "résistome" de l'intestin (la collection de gènes de résistance).
Voie orale : Les pilules passent directement par le tractus gastro-intestinal,
créant un environnement sélectif à forte concentration qui élimine les
bactéries sensibles et permet aux souches résistantes de se multiplier.
Voie IV (intraveineuse) : Les antibiotiques intraveineux contournent
initialement l'intestin. Cependant, les médicaments excrétés par les voies
biliaires se déversent directement dans les intestins sous forme active.

Cependant, les médicaments excrétés par les voies
biliaires se déversent directement dans les intestins sous forme active.

Lorsqu'un patient dont l'intestin est déjà stressé par des résidus de pesticides
alimentaires reçoit des antibiotiques par voie orale ou à excrétion biliaire, cela
crée un effet cumulatif qui amplifie la RAM.
Partie 3 : L'hyperperméabilité intestinale ("Leaky Gut") et comment les bactéries
résistantes pénètrent dans la circulation sanguine
Le danger des produits chimiques agricoles n'est pas seulement qu'ils créent des
bactéries résistantes aux antibiotiques à l'intérieur du tube digestif. C'est qu'ils
détruisent également la barrière physique empêchant ces bactéries dangereuses
de se propager dans le reste du corps.
Briser la barrière : Un microbiome sain maintient une étanchéité sûre le
long de la muqueuse intestinale. L'exposition chronique aux pesticides
altère la composition microbienne et déclenche des changements subtils
dans la fonction de barrière.
L'effet d'hyperperméabilité intestinale : La dérégulation continue
compromet la perméabilité paracellulaire de l'épithélium intestinal, créant
un "intestin perméable". L'étanchéité physique échoue, laissant des
brèches dans le système de défense.
S'échapper dans la circulation sanguine : Une fois la barrière intestinale
compromise, les bactéries résistantes aux antibiotiques créées par
l'exposition aux pesticides ne restent pas confinées dans le tube digestif.
Elles traversent la muqueuse endommagée directement dans la circulation
sanguine.
Infection systémique : Ce qui a commencé comme une perturbation
microbienne localisée devient une menace grave et multi-organique. Cette
voie de fuite est la façon dont les bactéries intestinales résistantes
entraînent des infections sanguines potentiellement mortelles (bactériémie)
et des septicémies.
Partie 4 : La lacune des données cliniques
Le comité s'appuie sur des données de surveillance nationale pour suivre la
RAM. Le codage clinique de première ligne met en évidence des angles morts
massifs dans ces données.
Le fardeau du codage : Il est obligatoire de coder pour un statut de porteur
de la RAM. Cependant, ces informations sont rarement priorisées dans le
dossier de visite actuel du patient.

Cependant, ces informations sont rarement priorisées dans le
dossier de visite actuel du patient.

Données manquantes : Les codeurs n'ont pas le temps de fouiller dans des
années de dossiers historiques pour chaque patient. À moins qu'une
infection active ne déclenche une recherche manuelle, le statut de porteur
historique est ignoré. Cela conduit à une sous-déclaration systémique.
Données obsolètes : Lorsqu'un statut de porteur est trouvé, il date souvent
de plusieurs années. Bien que des régions comme l'Alberta suivent la date
du dernier écouvillonnage, il n'existe aucune norme nationale définissant
l'expiration d'un statut de porteur.
Recommandations pour le Comité
1. Mettre à jour le cadre "Une seule santé" : L'ARLA doit être mandatée pour
inclure la perturbation du microbiome comme "effet indésirable" formel
lors du calcul des limites de sécurité des produits chimiques agricoles.
2. Corriger le pipeline de données : Le statut de porteur de la RAM doit être
mandaté comme "statut prioritaire" dans les dossiers de santé
électroniques, au même titre que les maladies chroniques comme le
diabète.
3. Établir l'expiration des données : Créer une norme nationale de codage
clinique qui définit la durée de vie clinique exacte d'un indicateur de
porteur de la RAM pour s'assurer que les données de surveillance
nationale sont précises et actuelles.
4. Convoquer des témoins experts indépendants : Le Comité devrait inviter
des toxicologues indépendants, des chercheurs en médecine et des
spécialistes du microbiome (provenant d'organisations telles que
l'Association canadienne des médecins pour l'environnement (ACME),
Environmental Defence, ou des instituts universitaires de recherche en
santé digestive) à témoigner sur les mécanismes spécifiques de la
résistance aux antimicrobiens induite par les pesticides et sur les failles
actuelles des modèles de sécurité de l'ARLA.Bibliographie et références
