Introduction
The Canadian Antimicrobial Innovation Coalition (CAIC) applauds the House of Commons
Standing Committee on Health for initiating a study on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in
Canada, pursuant to Standing Order 108(3)(i). This study—examining resistant organisms,
the drivers of rising resistance, the clinical and economic impacts in Canada, and the
research needed to advance new antimicrobial agents, non-pharmacological strategies,
novel drug-identification methods, and approaches to neutralize virulence factors—
represents a critical step forward. We commend the committee for dedicating a minimum
of four meetings to this issue and for committing to report its findings to the House.
I serve as Chief Scientific Officer of Fedora Pharmaceuticals, an Edmonton-based
antibiotic drug discovery company. Our team was responsible for the discovery and
development of several antibacterial and antifungal agents. Our flagship drug,
Tazobactam—discovered in the early 1980s by our founder, Dr. R.G. Micetich—is sold
globally by Pfizer to treat difficult-to-treat pneumonia and hospital-acquired infections and
saves millions of lives every year. Our second flagship product, Nacubactam, is now in
phase 3 clinical trials being conducted by our partner, Meiji Seika of Japan. We also have
antibiotics in preclinical development.
I am also Chair of CAIC. As a non-profit coalition of life science companies and
organizations dedicated to combating AMR, we believe this committee has a vital
opportunity to underscore both the urgency of AMR and the need to strengthen Canada’s
R&D infrastructure to better prepare for this growing threat. Beyond advancing the research
pipeline, it is equally important to address the market barriers that stifle domestic
innovation—since without a viable market, these essential products will never reach
patients.
According to the Council of Canadian Academies, approximately 26% of infections in
Canada were resistant to the drugs generally used to treat them in 2018. This figure is
projected to rise to 40% by 2050, resulting in a cumulative loss of 396,000 Canadian lives,
$120 billion in hospital costs, and $388 billion in GDP.
Antimicrobial resistance is a far greater threat than many Canadians realize. Without
effective antibiotics and other antimicrobials, routine medical procedures—such as organ
transplants, cancer chemotherapy, or even treatment for something as common as a

Without
effective antibiotics and other antimicrobials, routine medical procedures—such as organ
transplants, cancer chemotherapy, or even treatment for something as common as a

throat infection—could become life-threatening. We are already seeing AMR undermine the
effectiveness of emergency and intensive care, where infections are harder to treat and
risks to patients—and the broader population—are increasing.
As the committee undertakes this study, the need to champion domestic AMR innovation
has never been more urgent.
Canada’s Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR: From Missed Implementation to Action
Plan 2.0
Canada released its Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR in June 2023, outlining a
comprehensive framework structured around four pillars—surveillance, infection
prevention and control, stewardship, and research and innovation. While the plan set out a
strong conceptual foundation, it has not yet been implemented, resourced, or
operationalized. Without a funded national program and clear governance structure, the
plan cannot drive change across health systems, research institutions, or industry.
Canada must now look ahead to developing Action Plan 2.0, informed by lessons from the
past two years. A core design principle of the next action plan must be the recognition that
innovation is not simply one pillar among four—it is the backbone supporting all pillars.
•
Surveillance requires innovative diagnostics, sequencing tools, and data
platforms.
•
Stewardship requires access to novel antimicrobials and precision diagnostics to
ensure the right drug is used for the right patient at the right time.
•
Infection prevention and control (IPAC) is strengthened by innovations across
vaccines, therapeutics, materials science, and environmental decontamination.
•
R&D cannot advance without market conditions that support clinical development,
commercialization, and manufacturing.
Innovation must therefore be treated as a cross-cutting enabler—embedded into every
aspect of Canada’s AMR strategy, not siloed as a standalone workstream.
To ensure this next phase succeeds, the federal government must also establish formal,
ongoing consultation and coordination with industry. Biotech SMEs, diagnostics
developers, multinational firms, and domestic manufacturers understand firsthand the
structural barriers that prevent new antimicrobials and technologies from reaching the
Canadian market. A modernized Action Plan 2.0 should include mechanisms for regular
industry engagement to ensure policy solutions are feasible, aligned to real-world
innovation pathways, and capable of producing measurable public health impact.
A strengthened Action Plan 2.0 should therefore include:
•
Dedicated programmatic funding for each pillar, with innovation embedded
throughout;

A strengthened Action Plan 2.0 should therefore include:
•
Dedicated programmatic funding for each pillar, with innovation embedded
throughout;

•
Clear leadership and accountability mechanisms across federal, provincial, and
territorial jurisdictions;
•
Structured consultation with industry to identify and address innovation
bottlenecks;
•
A national AMR innovation strategy that spans R&D, clinical development,
procurement, and manufacturing;
•
Explicit links to health and national security frameworks, given the foundational role
antibiotics play in modern medicine.
Canada has the scientific talent, the companies, and the research infrastructure. What is
missing is the national, funded framework to convert these capabilities into impact.
The Importance of Innovation in AMR
Canada’s ability to respond to rising rates of AMR will not be possible without a vibrant
innovation network that supports end-to-end development and adoption of novel
therapeutics, diagnostics, vaccines, and antibiotic alternatives.
Currently, Canada can boast of having an array of exciting companies performing R&D and
commercialization to address AMR. However, the lack of new antibiotics developed
globally—and the even further lack of new antibiotics launched in Canada—represents a
failure of the market that can only be resolved through the collaboration and partnership of
government, industry, academia, and the broader health care sector.
We have and can realize an opportunity for Canada to create an environment that supports
continued discovery, development, and commercialization of novel, innovative antibiotics,
while preserving these critical therapies that underpin many medical procedures
performed today.
•
With respect to biomedical innovation to combat antimicrobial resistance, our
country’s strengths lie in the diversity of biomedical innovation that exists in
Canada: traditional antibiotics in early-stage and clinical development, antifungal
treatments, diagnostic technologies, antimicrobial therapies, vaccines, phage
therapy, and information technology systems.

•
Similar to other biopharmaceutical development areas, our weaknesses in the
AMR domain lie in access to capital and commercialization: preclinical
development through to licensure and GMP manufacturing.

•
With respect to antibiotics in particular, Canada faces a vulnerability as all active
pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) for antibiotics are produced overseas,
predominantly in Asia. Given that antibiotics underpin all modern medicine, this
presents a national security concern in addition to an innovation ecosystem

Given that antibiotics underpin all modern medicine, this
presents a national security concern in addition to an innovation ecosystem

concern. As Canada looks to increase defence innovation spending to meet its
obligations under NATO, investments in AMR R&D should be counted as
contributing to both national and global health security.
Full implementation of the Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR—supported by Action Plan
2.0—requires dedicated programmatic funding, structured engagement with industry, and
innovation embedded across all pillars.
Incentivizing Domestic Innovation
Canada has strong AMR research capacity in universities, government, and private labs,
but retaining scientific talent is difficult as researchers move toward better-funded fields
like oncology. Early-stage government funding is critical to sustain this pipeline, and
programs such as IRAP should dedicate more resources specifically to AMR. Continued
support is also needed to bridge the “valley of death” in clinical development and
manufacturing, alongside consideration of sustainable business models and governance
structures.
Push Incentives
Canada should expand push incentives—grants, tax credits, and public-private
partnerships—to fund early-stage AMR R&D, create opportunities for young scientists, and
support SMEs as well as larger pharmaceutical firms. Crucially, when Canadian companies
apply to international or global AMR funding programs, they are often required to provide a
cost share. Canadian government support could help meet a company’s cost share
obligation for international grants, reducing the burden on companies while ensuring they
remain competitive in securing international funding.
Examples abroad include U.S. BARDA’s antibiotic portfolio partnerships, CARB-X’s global
early-stage accelerator, the NIH/NIAID translational support programs, the EU’s ND4BB,
the UK’s GAMRIF, and the AMR Action Fund’s $1B investment program. Canada’s new
Health Emergency Readiness Canada program offers a potential opportunity to prioritize
advanced domestic R&D on antimicrobial resistance (AMR), strengthening the
development of cutting-edge biomedical solutions to address this urgent threat.
Canada can take inspiration from these while tailoring domestic programs such as IRAP
and Health Emergency Readiness Canada to include this kind of cost-share support.
Pull Incentives
To stabilize the fragile antibiotic market, Canada also needs robust pull policies—such as
reimbursement reform, market assurance contracts, and stewardship-linked procurement.
International experience is now demonstrating that predictable, de-linked payments are
essential to sustain antibiotic development:

International experience is now demonstrating that predictable, de-linked payments are
essential to sustain antibiotic development:

•
The United Kingdom has implemented the world’s first subscription-style pull
incentive, providing manufacturers with fixed annual payments for high-value
antibiotics regardless of sales volume.
•
Sweden has piloted a guaranteed-payment model that ensures availability of
critical antibiotics by guaranteeing manufacturers a minimum revenue floor.
•
The European Union is actively discussing continent-wide pull incentives,
including a Transferable Exclusivity Voucher (TEV), which would extend market
exclusivity for a qualifying antibiotic or allow the developer to transfer that
exclusivity to another product. This reflects the EU’s recognition that bold economic
incentives are necessary to restore viability to the antibiotic market.
These international models demonstrate that pull incentives are now becoming standard
practice among high-income countries seeking to rebuild the antibiotic pipeline.
The recent Lancet EClinicalMedicine paper, Bridging the fair share gap for antibacterial
innovation, provides updated “fair share” estimates that take into account domestic
revenues and R&D incentives. According to this analysis, Canada’s fair share is 2.5% of
global antibacterial revenues (about 3.7% of the G7+EU27 total), translating into a
contribution range of $11 million to $21 million annually.
This benchmarking makes two points clear:
1. Canada must incentivize and reward domestic R&D if it is to meet its fair share
as part of the G7, especially as peer countries adopt increasingly sophisticated pull
mechanisms.
2. Domestic pull incentives are directly relevant for Canadian companies like
Fedora, ensuring they are rewarded for innovation in a manner aligned with
emerging international expectations and competitive global market standards.
Concluding Remarks
Canada is uniquely positioned to demonstrate leadership on antimicrobial resistance. With
world-class research institutions, a vibrant biotechnology sector, and a track record of
global health engagement, Canada has both the capacity and responsibility to act. By
implementing targeted push incentives and aligning pull incentives with updated fair-share
benchmarks, Canada can safeguard its domestic innovation ecosystem, ensure
sustainable access to lifesaving antimicrobials, and set an example for other G7 nations.
Full implementation of the Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR—and the development of a
strengthened, fully funded Action Plan 2.0—will enable Canada to turn commitments into
action. With innovation embedded across all pillars and structured consultation with
industry, Canada can lead globally in safeguarding health and readiness.

With innovation embedded across all pillars and structured consultation with
industry, Canada can lead globally in safeguarding health and readiness.

As Canada prepares to assume a greater role on the international stage, stepping up in this
area will not only protect Canadians but also reinforce Canada’s reputation as a trusted
leader in addressing one of the most urgent health and economic security challenges of our
time.

Antimicrobial Resistance
Results Canada & Stop TB Canada
February 2026

Overview
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most urgent threats to global and Canadian
health, undermining the effectiveness of life-saving medicines and straining health
systems. Drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) is a major driver of this crisis, causing
substantial mortality worldwide. Although Canada’s TB burden is relatively low, cases have
surged sharply, with DR-TB rising by 233% over the last 14 years, exposing vulnerabilities in
surveillance, diagnostics, and treatment systems and amplifying domestic risk from global
transmission. TB and AMR are deeply interconnected: both require robust infrastructure
for detection, stewardship, and treatment. Tackling TB is therefore essential not only to
control this deadly disease but also to strengthen Canada’s broader response to AMR and
reinforce overall health system resilience.
Key recommendations:
1. Integrate TB into the National AMR Framework
Integrating TB will help leverage existing systems, prevent duplication, and promote faster,
more effective antibiotic use.
2. Invest in Research and Development for TB and AMR
Funding vaccines, diagnostics, and better treatments will reduce resistance and strengthen
health systems and AMR preparedness globally and domestically.
3. Strengthen Global Health Partnerships and Investments
Investing and aligning TB and AMR efforts will reduce international transmission of
resistant strains while reinforcing domestic resilience.
4. Build resilient diagnostic, surveillance, and stewardship systems
Using TB systems as a tracer for AMR to expand diagnostics, surveillance, stewardship, and
equitable access, will create a model for a resilient and effective AMR response.
5. Promote health equity

Promote health equity

Ensuring equitable, culturally safe, and accessible care will address the structural barriers
that drive resistance.
Introduction
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the most serious and complex public health
threats facing the world and Canada. Resistant pathogens undermine the effectiveness of
medicines, increase health-care costs, strain health systems, hinder progress toward
sustainable development, and threaten Canada’s health security. As the tuberculosis (TB)
crisis illustrates, AMR is fundamentally a systems challenge, in which failures in
surveillance, diagnosis, treatment and stewardship – anywhere in the world – have direct
consequences at home.
TB remains the world’s deadliest infectious disease, causing an estimated 1.23 million
deaths globally in 2024. Drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) is among the most dangerous and costly
forms of AMR, accounting for approximately one third of all deaths associated with AMR.
The World Health Organization has identified TB bacteria as one of the most threatening
drug-resistant pathogens, underscoring its central role in the global AMR crisis.
Although Canada has a relatively low TB burden, global TB transmission and resistance -
often driven by the spread of resistant TB in settings with weaker health infrastructure -
have direct implications for domestic health security. Resistant strains circulate through
travel, migration, and trade. Indeed, the majority of new TB cases in Canada are found
among migrants in the population. Additionally domestic outbreaks – such as those
recently reported in Edmonton and Nunavik – highlight how global trends intersect with
local realities and vulnerabilities in surveillance, diagnosis, and continuity of care,
particularly in settings and populations that are most vulnerable to the severe risks these
especially virulent pathogens pose. The number of people who fell sick with TB in Canada
increased by more than 80%, rising from 1,385 reported cases in 2010 to 2,508 in 2024. As
more people are affected by TB, the AMR threat intensifies during the same period, the
number of people with DR-TB in Canada increased by 233%, signalling a growing domestic
risk linked directly to rising pathogen circulation. Global efforts to end TB underscore the
immense challenge that AMR presents. Gaps in access to quality healthcare continue to
drive the emergence and spread of drug resistance, eroding decades of hard-won progress
against the disease. It is evident that efforts to end TB cannot succeed without a strong
AMR response – and that no AMR strategy will be complete without tackling TB.

It is evident that efforts to end TB cannot succeed without a strong
AMR response – and that no AMR strategy will be complete without tackling TB.

TB and AMR are inextricably linked, and addressing them together strengthens Canada’s
domestic and global health security:
•
Monitoring and responding to TB requires the same infrastructure, surveillance,
stewardship - coordinated strategies and interventions to optimize medicine use -,
diagnostics and treatment-completion systems as broader AMR responses. TB
offers a vital entry point into the AMR agenda.

•
Health-system failures that drive TB drug-resistance, such as delayed diagnosis, subprescribing, are classic drivers of AMR across pathogens.
•
Embedding TB within the AMR framework strengthens the case for research,
diagnostics, vaccines, and health-system resilience that benefits multiple diseases
simultaneously.
•
Investments that reduce TB and drug resistance abroad directly safeguard
Canadians, while reinforcing Canada’s research ecosystem, global leadership, and
preparedness for future infectious disease threats.
To protect Canadians and advance global health, Canada must explicitly integrate TB into
its AMR strategy, aligning domestic policies with international efforts and investing
strategically to fight TB and AMR together – at home and abroad.
Recommendations for Canada’s AMR strategy
1. Explicitly integrate TB into the national AMR framework
TB is one of the world’s leading drug-resistant infections, yet it remains siloed from broader
AMR policy. Canada’s AMR action plan should include TB as a core pillar rather than a
parallel program. This means setting measurable targets for preventing, diagnosing, and
treating DR-TB, and aligning surveillance systems so that TB and other AMR pathogens
share diagnostic, laboratory, reporting, and data platforms. Integrating AMR stewardship
efforts with TB programming, such as ensuring rapid identification of TB cases and
minimizing unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotic use, will reduce resistance and improve
treatment outcomes. Since TB already has advanced systems for drug susceptibility testing,
surveillance, and treatment stewardship, integrating it into the AMR framework avoids
duplication, supports faster and more appropriate antibiotic use, and ensures the national
plan addresses this major driver of resistance.
2. Invest in research and development for TB and AMR

Invest in research and development for TB and AMR

Investing in TB research delivers substantial returns for AMR prevention and control.
Dedicated funding for vaccines, rapid diagnostics, shorter and more effective treatments,
and implementation science not only reduces antibiotic use and prevents resistance from
emerging but also strengthens health systems, AMR stewardship, and outbreak
preparedness. Supporting both global R&D partnerships and domestic research capacity
provides a platform for innovation that strengthens Canada’s health security while
generating tools directly relevant to high-risk populations at home and abroad.
Canada should support needs-driven global product development partnerships (PDPs)
such as the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI), which is advancing new and
promising TB vaccine candidates; the TB Alliance, which is developing faster, simpler, and
more effective cures for all forms of TB; and FIND, which is improving access to accurate
and rapid TB diagnostics in underserved settings. These partnerships accelerate innovation
that benefits high-burden countries while simultaneously strengthening the global
knowledge base, product pipelines, and tools available to Canadian health systems. By
working with Canadian researchers and institutions or creating opportunities to do so,
these PDPs also reinforce Canada’s research excellence and innovation leadership.
Domestically, Canada should invest in comprehensive TB and AMR research that spans
vaccines, diagnostics, treatments, and implementation science. Priority areas include
improving preventive strategies for high-risk populations, such as immigrants from regions
with high rates of DR-TB, where current screening and referral programs reach only a
fraction of those who could benefit. Strengthening in-country prevention and early
intervention for latent TB infection, particularly for individuals exposed to drug-resistant
strains, is a critical implementation challenge that can reduce reactivation and
transmission. In parallel, Canada should continue to support discovery and clinical
research, leveraging existing infrastructure and investments in preparedness to accelerate
the development of next-generation vaccines, rapid diagnostics, and novel therapeutics
that reinforce national health security and contribute to broader AMR stewardship efforts.
3. Strengthen global health partnerships and investments
Recognizing AMR as a shared global public health security issue, Canada’s domestic health
security depends on strong systems abroad. Canada’s AMR response should be anchored
in strong global health investments and partnerships that strengthen both global and
domestic resilience. Through mechanisms such as the Global Fund to Fight AIDS,
Tuberculosis and Malaria, and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI),

Through mechanisms such as the Global Fund to Fight AIDS,
Tuberculosis and Malaria, and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI),

Canada can advocate for alignment of TB, AMR, and broader health-system strengthening
in partner countries, ensuring every dollar yields multiple global and domestic returns.
Partnerships with organizations such as Unitaid are essential to ensure that innovations
reach countries with the highest TB burden and the weakest health systems – reducing
global transmission and the likelihood that resistant strains will spread to Canada. These
investments are direct contributions to AMR resilience: new vaccines reduce reliance on
broad-spectrum antibiotics, improved diagnostics enable appropriate treatment, and
shorter, more effective regimens reduce the risk of resistance emerging or spreading both
abroad and at home.
4. Build resilient diagnostic, surveillance, and stewardship systems
To reinforce Canada’s AMR response, TB should serve as a tracer condition for building
resilient diagnostic, surveillance, and stewardship systems. Strengthening TB laboratory
networks, including drug-susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance, creates
infrastructure that benefits all AMR pathogens. Expanding access to rapid and point-of-care
diagnostics will improve TB case detection, while enhanced stewardship – ensuring correct
regimens, supporting adherence, reducing off-label antibiotic use, and addressing
equitable access to both marketed and unmarketed TB medications – can serve as a model
for a unified AMR stewardship approach. Addressing medication shortages and regulatory
barriers will further strengthen system resilience and effectiveness.
5. Promote health equity
Finally, Canada must ensure equitable access and strengthen global health equity as a core
part of its AMR response, recognizing that global inequities directly affect domestic health
security. Inequities in access to diagnostics, treatment, and culturally safe care - including
persistent challenges in obtaining key TB medications at home - directly contribute to
delayed diagnosis, incomplete treatment, and the emergence and spread of resistance.
Innovations supported by Canadian investments should be affordable, accessible, and
deployed where they are needed most. Canada can help shape global markets through
procurement and regulatory support to lower costs and expand access in high-burden
regions. Ongoing monitoring and evaluation, supported by implementation science and
data sharing, will ensure that interventions deliver impact across diverse contexts. To
succeed, Canada’s AMR strategy should promote multi-sectoral coordination, bridging TB,
One Health, nutrition, WASH, and social determinants to build a comprehensive, equitable,
and sustainable approach to combating AMR.

To
succeed, Canada’s AMR strategy should promote multi-sectoral coordination, bridging TB,
One Health, nutrition, WASH, and social determinants to build a comprehensive, equitable,
and sustainable approach to combating AMR.

Domestically, access to TB medications - including some of the most important drugs for
treating resistant TB – remains a significant challenge. Ensuring timely access to the full
range of TB diagnostics and treatments, particularly for populations most affected, is
critical. Canada can support this through measures such as strategic national stockpiles,
consolidated expertise via a formal DR-TB consilium - a team of experts from different
fields to guide the management of complex drug-resistant TB cases - and streamlined
access to evidence-based drugs approved by international regulatory authorities. Equally
important is delivering care that is culturally safe, community-led, and tailored to local
needs, with investments in outreach, education, and the healthcare workforce to ensure
services are trusted, accessible, and acceptable. By addressing both structural and social
barriers, Canada can reduce health disparities while strengthening domestic resilience
against TB and AMR.
Conclusion
For Canada, an AMR strategy that does not explicitly address TB is incomplete. TB is both a
major driver of AMR and a practical tracer for building integrated surveillance, diagnostics,
treatment-completion systems, and stewardship frameworks. By embedding TB as a core
pillar of its national AMR strategy and investing strategically in research, innovation, and
global partnerships, Canada can strengthen domestic health security, reduce the risk of
resistant pathogens reaching Canadians, and support equitable global health outcomes. A
coordinated approach to TB and AMR will advance Canada’s leadership in health security,
maximize the impact of investments in research and health systems, and accelerate
progress toward ending TB and curbing antimicrobial resistance worldwide.

Leveraging Economics and the One Health Approach to Unlock the Full Potential of the
Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance
Prepared by: François Arès,1 Caroline Raymond,2 Nicolas Macia3 and François M. Castonguay4
For: The House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Presented by: François M. Castonguay
Executive Summary
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a major threat to Canada’s health and economy. It is already the cause
of thousands of deaths each year, and without stronger action, its health burden could more than double by
2050. The economic costs could rise from a few billion dollars today to tens of billions in 2050, which would
be increasingly borne by sectors outside the health care system. The Pan-Canadian Action Plan on
Antimicrobial Resistance provides a solid foundation, but to be fully effective, it must be part of an integrated
framework such as the “One Health” approach, which links human, animal and environmental health.
Combined with economics tools, this framework becomes a powerful lever for targeting efficient
interventions, strengthening intersectoral cooperation, and directing investments based on their
expected health and economic benefits.
The Driver of Antimicrobial Resistance
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a cross-sectoral issue affecting human and animal health. It results from
the widespread use of antimicrobials in human medicine and agriculture (livestock production, dairy farming
and aquaculture), with possible dissemination via wastewater, soil, the food chain, wildlife or vectors [1].
Any use can promote the emergence of resistant pathogens, a well-documented phenomenon. While AMR is
not a new issue, it is currently occurring at an unprecedented scale: between 2000 and 2015, global
antimicrobial use increased by 65% [2]. The incidence of AMR is growing, as is the speed at which it is
developing [2], which means that it is taking less time for bacteria to develop resistance once a new antibiotic
is introduced [3], and these resistant bacteria are spreading at increasing speed [4]. Given this accelerating
trend, it is vitally important to promote the cautious and rational use of antimicrobials in order to preserve
their effectiveness, ensure their sustainability and prevent a major health crisis.
The Health and Economic Impact of Antimicrobial Resistance in Canada
In Canada, antimicrobial resistant microbes are linked to more than 21,000 deaths each year [5], of which
5,400 are directly caused by AMR [6]. This already makes it one of the leading causes of death in the country,
comparable to COVID-19 (7,900 deaths in 2023) and influenza (6,300 deaths in 2023) [7]. Without effective
public intervention, this burden could more than double by 2050, exceeding 13,700 deaths directly caused
by AMR each year [6]. Global projections are even more concerning: by 2050, AMR could be linked to more
than 10 million deaths annually, making it the leading cause of death worldwide [8].
AMR already imposes a heavy economic burden on Canada. According to an expert panel at the Council of
Canadian Academies, its impact on health care systems was $1.4 billion in 2018 and could reach $7.6 billion
by 2050 [6] due to the loss of antimicrobial effectiveness, making certain common procedures—dialysis,

systems: gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated to have been reduced by more than $2 billion in 2018,
with losses potentially exceeding $21 billion per year in 2050 [6]. The share of costs outside health care
systems, already 30% in 2018, could reach nearly 65% in 2050, affecting sectors such as agriculture, utilities,
transportation, livestock production, construction and retail [6], illustrating the increasingly multisectoral
nature of AMR.
The Contribution of Economics to Combating Antimicrobial Resistance
The economics literature provides concrete tools for assessing the trade-offs between health objectives and
economic considerations, as well as for measuring the social impacts of integrated approaches to combating
AMR [9]. The Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance [10] follows this approach by
proposing a framework structured around five pillars of action: (i) Research and innovation, (ii) Surveillance,
(iii) Stewardship, (iv) Infection prevention and control, and (v) Leadership. However, one major challenge
remains: determining the pillars in which to invest in order to maximize return on investment. AMR
is a multidimensional problem at the intersection of human, animal and environmental health, making
optimal resource allocation particularly complex. Siloed interventions often yield limited gains, as AMR
transcends sectoral and geographic boundaries. However, enhanced cross-sectoral cooperation—based on
the pooling of effort, knowledge and resources between health, agriculture, fisheries, the environment and
research—can generate significant benefits, often without major additional costs. Economics tools can
be used to quantify these benefits, compare investment scenarios, prioritize interventions and direct resources
toward those offering the best health, economic and social returns. They make it possible not only to identify
efficient interventions within each pillar, but also to target the pillars offering the best overall return
on investment.
Operationalization of the Pillars: Examples of Economically Efficient Interventions
These analyses are reflected in each of the strategic pillars of the Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial
Resistance [10], illustrating how targeted interventions can generate a high health and economic return on
investment. Pillar 1 – Research and innovation: Funding the development of new antibiotics or alternative
treatments, such as bacteriophages, is a cost-effective option for combating AMR [11,12]. Pillar 2 –
Surveillance: Strengthening surveillance, particularly through whole genome sequencing, helps track the
evolution of resistant strains and limit their spread. A quick estimate based on the literature suggests that this
alone could generate more than $70 million in benefits per year for Canada [13]. Pillar 3 – Stewardship:
Promoting responsible prescribing in primary care—such as requiring justification for certain prescriptions,
public commitment to responsible prescribing, and peer comparison—reduces inappropriate antimicrobial
use by changing prescriber behaviour [14]. Pillar 4 – Infection prevention and control: Vaccines and nonpharmaceutical interventions, such as rapid PCR testing for MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus
aureus), play a key role in preventing bacterial and viral infections, thereby reducing antimicrobial use and,
consequently, the occurrence of subsequent complications that can promote the emergence of resistant strains
[15,16]. Pillar 5 – Leadership: Lastly, strengthening intergovernmental and interministerial cooperation,
particularly through the “One Health” approach, very often generates positive returns on investment in the
fight against AMR [17].
Mobilizing the “One Economic Health” Approach
The integrated One Health approach—which recognizes the interdependence between human, animal and
environmental health—presents Canada with a major strategic opportunity. The effectiveness of
antimicrobials is a true “public good”: it benefits society as a whole, but preserving it requires collaboration,

sector and communities. Partial or compartmentalized regulations risk being ineffective, while an integrated
approach helps design policies that are better suited to collective needs and the missions of each
department and government. The vast majority of One Health initiatives (80%) generate a positive economic
return [17], with many of them relying primarily on enhanced cooperation rather than new financial
investments. Combining the One Health approach with economics tools provides a powerful
interdepartmental and intergovernmental framework for equitably distributing costs and benefits and
prioritizing the pillars and interventions that offer the best return on investment.
AMR threatens Canada’s public health, economic vitality, and food and health safety. Considering this
systemic challenge, the Pan-Canadian Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance [10], which is already
pivotal and inclusive, would benefit from incorporating the One Health approach and economics tools to
identify key interventions, strengthen intersectoral cooperation, and direct investments toward actions with
the highest social return. Using this approach, Canada would be able to (i) save lives; (ii) preserve
antimicrobial effectiveness; (iii) protect the sustainability of provincial health systems; and (iv) increase
its economic resilience to future health crises, including AMR. It also provides an opportunity for Canada
to optimize its public spending, prevent health crises, and strengthen its role as an international leader in
integrated health governance, in partnership with the provinces and territories.

School of Public Health, Université de Montréal
Department of Health Management, Evaluation and Policy
The Socio-economic Impacts of Antimicrobial Resistance in Quebec by 2050
Prepared by: François Arès,1 Caroline Raymond2 and François M. Castonguay3
For: House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, at the request of Mr. Maxime BlanchetteJoncas4
Executive Summary
We have adapted the results of a Canadian study on the socio-economic impacts of antimicrobial resistance
(AMR) to the Quebec context, while incorporating the demographic and economic differences between
provinces. Without enhanced action, AMR could lead to 1,500 to 3,000 deaths per year by 2050,
resulting in annual losses of $2.6 to $4.2 billion to Quebec’s gross domestic product (GDP), including
$1.2 to $1.7 billion in additional costs for the health care system. Quebec would be more negatively
affected than the Canadian average, underscoring the pressing need for concerted action to reduce the
inappropriate use of antimicrobials.
Summary of the Canadian report “When Antibiotics Fail”
Commissioned by the Public Health Agency of Canada and published in 2019, the Council of Canadian
Academies’ report When Antibiotics Fail [1] was produced amid growing concern about antimicrobial
resistance (AMR). It is intended to inform public decisions with estimates adapted to the Canadian context.
Using a One Health [2] approach—linking human, animal and environmental health—the report
quantifies the health and economic impacts of AMR: mortality, costs to the health care system, and
economic losses measured by a decline in gross domestic product (GDP). These estimates make it possible
to anticipate the evolution of the burden if the status quo is maintained without further measures.
1.1.
Methodological overview of the report
Approximately one in four infections (26%) in Canada are already resistant to antimicrobials
recommended as first-line treatment in clinical guidelines. These infections therefore require alternative
treatments, which are often longer, more expensive and less effective. According to the report’s
projections, this proportion could reach 40% by 2050 if nothing is done to curb the spread of resistance.
To estimate the impacts of AMR on mortality and hospital costs, the report focuses on 10 important clinical
syndromes (for example, pneumonia) and examines different microbial resistance scenarios. Deaths and
days spent in hospital are projected by applying these resistance rates
to infection volumes and the Canadian population. To assess the economic impacts of AMR on GDP, the
report uses a computational general equilibrium model—an economic simulation tool that analyzes how

sectors of the economy—translating these human and health losses into a decline in GDP.
Projected impact of AMR in Quebec
According to Canadian projections, AMR could increase from 26% (status quo) today to 40% by 2050
(likely scenario). Applying these results to the Quebec context, taking into account its demographic weight
(21.75% of Canada’s population [3]) and age structure, AMR could lead to between 1,500 and 3,000
deaths per year in the province by 2050. Assuming a case profile and hospital unit costs comparable to
the Canadian average, this would represent annual expenditures of approximately $1.2 to $1.7 billion
for Quebec’s health care system by 2050. In terms of the overall economic impact, adjusting GDP losses
according to Quebec’s demographic weight and the Quebec/Canada GDP per capita ratio (0.89 [4]), the
annual loss to Quebec’s GDP could be between $2.6 and $4.2 billion per year in 2050 (see Table 1).

Potential impact of mitigation measures for Quebec
The report notes that several measures can be implemented to save lives and reduce the economic impact
of AMR. In particular, it quantifies the potential savings generated by two key measures: (i) an infection
prevention and control (IPC) program,5 which could save between $23.5 and $35.5 billion in Quebec’s
GDP between 2020 and 2050 depending on the extent of resistance; and (ii) the introduction of a
hypothetical C. difficile (CDI) vaccine, which could generate savings of between $1.4 and $7.5 billion
for Quebec’s GDP by 2050, also depending on the AMR level (see Table 2).

and remote areas, and individual accountability measures such as staying home when sick.

Factors specific to Quebec that may increase its vulnerability
Quebec has a number of factors that make it vulnerable to AMR. Its population, which is older than the
Canadian average (20% aged 65 and over, a proportion that is expected to reach 26% by 2041 [5]), is
therefore more exposed to resistant infections, the burden of which—hospital stays, mortality, costs—
increases significantly with age. Canadian hospital analyses show that the majority of deaths attributable
to AMR occur among seniors, for whom the costs per case are also higher [6]. A simple demographic
adjustment suggests that Quebec could face additional costs of approximately 3.4% compared to the
Canadian average.
Quebec is also a key player in Canadian pork production (nearly 30% of Canadian production), a sector
with the highest use of veterinary antimicrobials. In 2023, approximately 450,000 kg of medically
important antimicrobials were used in the pork industry, significantly more than in other animal production
sectors—for example, 285,000 kg for beef cattle—out of a national total of approximately 970,000 kg for
all species [7]. This industry-specific reality suggests that Quebec is particularly vulnerable to selection
pressures in the food chain.
Findings and levers for action in Quebec
The results adapted to the Quebec context are based on Canadian data and therefore do not perfectly reflect
the provincial reality. In the absence of Quebec-specific data, these estimates nevertheless provide an order
of magnitude of potential impacts. They suggest that Quebec could be more severely affected by AMR
than the rest of Canada, highlighting the urgent need to take action and implement a national cross-sector
policy aimed at limiting inappropriate antimicrobial use, in line with Quebec’s 2025– 2035 National
Health Prevention Strategy, which calls for preserving the efficacy of antibiotics to protect the safety of
care and public health.

Re: Input for study on antimicrobial resistance
Dear Members of the Standing Committee on Health,
On behalf of the National Cattle Feeders’ Association (NCFA), thank you for the opportunity to provide input
into your study on antimicrobial resistance. NCFA represents cattle feeders across Canada and advocates for
policies that support animal health and welfare, food safety, and the long-term sustainability of the Canadian
beef sector.
As the Committee examines the drivers of antimicrobial use and resistance in Canada, it is important that the
role of cattle feedlots is accurately understood and appropriately reflected in your analysis and
recommendations. Canadian feedlots operate within a robust regulatory and stewardship framework and are
subject to oversight by Health Canada and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency. Medically important
antimicrobials are available by prescription only and are used under veterinary oversight through established
veterinary-client-patient relationships, supported by record-keeping requirements and mandatory withdrawal
periods to protect public health.
Feedlots provide a highly controlled environment that enables close monitoring of cattle health, early disease
detection, and targeted treatment when animals become ill. This structure supports responsible antimicrobial use
by ensuring treatments are timely, precise, and based on veterinary guidance. Prompt treatment of sick animals
is essential to maintaining animal welfare and reducing the spread of disease within a population, and should
not be characterized as routine or indiscriminate antimicrobial use.
Canadian cattle feeders have made significant investments in prevention-focused practices that reduce reliance
on antimicrobials. These include comprehensive vaccination programs, optimized nutrition, enhanced
biosecurity measures, facility design that minimizes stress and disease transmission, and the adoption of lowstress cattle handling practices. Together, these measures align closely with Canada’s One Health approach by
addressing antimicrobial resistance through integrated human, animal, and animal-health-focused strategies.

Together, these measures align closely with Canada’s One Health approach by
addressing antimicrobial resistance through integrated human, animal, and animal-health-focused strategies.

Several challenges facing the cattle feeding sector relate to the development of, and access to, new antimicrobial
products intended for livestock production. There is an opportunity for government to support targeted research
in this area to broaden the range of antimicrobials available, while also informing optimal antimicrobial
stewardship and animal welfare outcomes.
The Canadian livestock sector would also benefit from more efficient approval processes for veterinary
products, including timely assessment and review of new products and greater recognition of approval decisions
from trusted international jurisdictions. Compared to some countries, Canada is a relatively small market for
large-animal veterinary products, and as a result, some manufacturers may be reluctant to pursue lengthy and
costly registration processes for products with potentially limited return on investment.
As the Committee considers policy responses to antimicrobial resistance, NCFA encourages the adoption of
science-based, risk-proportionate approaches that recognize both the progress made and the practical realities of
animal agriculture. Policies that unnecessarily restrict access to essential animal health tools risk unintended
consequences, including compromised animal welfare, increased disease incidence, and potentially leading to
greater antimicrobial use over time.
NCFA believes that Canadian feedlots are an important part of the solution to antimicrobial resistance and
should be recognized as active partners in antimicrobial stewardship. Continued collaboration among
policymakers, regulators, veterinarians, producers, and researchers will be critical to ensuring effective,
balanced, and sustainable outcomes.
Thank you for your consideration of these perspectives. NCFA would welcome the opportunity to continue
engaging with the Committee as your study progresses.

Canadian Veterinary Medical Association
The Essential Role of Veterinarians in Antimicrobial Stewardship in Canada
For the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
January 2025
The Canadian Veterinary Medical Association (CVMA) respectfully submits this brief to the
House of Commons Standing Committee on Health for its study on antimicrobial
resistance (AMR). The aim is to inform the Committee about the role of veterinarians in
antimicrobial stewardship (AMS), the system-level challenges they face, and opportunities
to strengthen Canada’s public health response.
Public Health Context: AMR and One Health
AMR threatens human and animal health, food systems, and economic stability. In
Canada, approximately 26% of human infections are resistant to commonly used
treatments, with projections indicating rising resistance and increasing mortality and costs
if additional action is not taken.
AMR arises from complex interactions among humans, animals, and the environment.
While antimicrobial use in both human and veterinary medicine contributes, transmission
pathways vary by pathogen and setting. Evidence shows that a coordinated, cross-sectoral
One Health1 approach is effective to reduce AMR while protecting animal welfare, public
health, and the environment.
Canada has established foundations through the Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR
(PCAP) and integrated surveillance programs. However, assessments by the Auditor
General of Canada and the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences identify gaps in
coordination, coverage, and sustained investment. Veterinarians are essential partners in
ensuring antimicrobial stewardship and protecting public health.
Veterinary Role in Antimicrobial Stewardship
The CVMA represents veterinarians and allied professionals nationally. CVMA provides
guidance and decision-making tools to support veterinary antimicrobial stewardship2 in a
One Health approach to reduce the threat of AMR.
Veterinarians oversee antimicrobial use in animals, including diagnosis, prescription,
appropriate use, and preventive strategies such as vaccination, biosecurity, and improved
management. Since 2018, all medically important antimicrobials used in animals in

Since 2018, all medically important antimicrobials used in animals in

Canada require a veterinary prescription under a valid Veterinary–Client–Patient
Relationship (VCPR)3, positioning veterinarians as gatekeepers of antimicrobial access.
The VCPR is the basis for interaction among veterinarians, their clients and their patients,
and is defined by provincial veterinary licensing bodies. Prescribing of veterinary
medications including antimicrobials requires a VCPR.
Veterinary antimicrobial stewardship uses a precautionary framework emphasizing
responsible use, reduction, refinement, replacement, and review of antimicrobial use.
These practices reduce selection pressure for resistance while safeguarding animal health
and welfare.
System-Level Challenges
Limited integration of veterinary expertise into policy and regulation
Veterinary input is essential to ensure antimicrobial policies achieve stewardship
objectives without unintended consequences. Inconsistent engagement of veterinary
experts can result in reduced treatment options and counterproductive shifts in
antimicrobial use.
Declining access to veterinary medicines and alternatives
Access to effective veterinary antimicrobials and alternatives, is essential for animal health
and welfare, public health and food security. Between 2017 and 2022, the number of
licensed veterinary medicines available in Canada declined by approximately 40%4. Health
Canada recently proposed changes5 to the categorization of antimicrobials that could
reduce access to important veterinary antimicrobials and inadvertently contribute to
increased veterinary use of antimicrobials that are important in human medicine. Limited
access to antimicrobials and preventive alternatives such as vaccines constrains
appropriate treatment and stewardship efforts.
Gaps in research, data, and surveillance
Canada lacks comprehensive data on antimicrobial use and resistance in animals.
Integrated systems like CIPARS provide insights but have geographic and species coverage
gaps due to funding constraints. Reports from the Auditor General of Canada and the
Canadian Academy of Health Sciences found much room for improvement in existing
systems.
Stewardship capacity and workforce support
Veterinarians are central to surveillance, research, and AMS implementation. Limited
investment in stewardship tools, guidelines, and continuing education reduces overall
system effectiveness.

Limited
investment in stewardship tools, guidelines, and continuing education reduces overall
system effectiveness.

CVMA Recommendations
1. Improve the integration of veterinary expertise into antimicrobial policy and
drug regulatory development
Ensure veterinarians and animal health experts are systematically involved in
developing and revising antimicrobial regulations, classifications, and guidelines.
Consider the importance of ensuring the continued availability of less medically
important antimicrobials for veterinary use, such as antimicrobials used in
veterinary medicine that were recently affected by changes in Health Canada
regulations.
2. Maintain and improve access to veterinary medicines and alternatives
Streamline regulatory pathways and incentivize manufacturers to supply approved
products in Canada, including alternatives to antimicrobials, such as vaccines,
probiotics, phages and other medicines.
3. Invest in One Health research and surveillance
Strengthen integrated human–animal–environment AMR surveillance and research
in Canada to support evidence-based disease prevention and control and enhanced
AMS. Recent investments by the federal government are a step in the right direction
but more is needed according to the Canadian Academy of Health Sciences 2025
Report.
4. Support veterinary stewardship capacity and tools
Sustain investment in national stewardship initiatives, clinical guidelines, and
decision-support tools, such as the CVMA’s Firstline AMR Stewardship App.
Additional funding is needed to update and expand these resources.
Conclusion
Antimicrobial resistance is a complex, cross-sectoral challenge that requires coordinated,
sustained action. Veterinarians play a leading role in stewardship, surveillance, and
prevention, protecting both public health and animal welfare. Supporting veterinarians
through inclusive policy development, access to essential medicines, and investment in
stewardship tools strengthens Canada’s capacity to manage AMR effectively. The CVMA
provides leadership, guidance, and collaboration across One Health initiatives, making
veterinarians a key national resource in the fight against AMR. Continued investment in
collaborative, multisectoral antimicrobial use and resistance surveillance, and veterinary
stewardship will ensure responsible antimicrobial use today and for future generations.

collaborative, multisectoral antimicrobial use and resistance surveillance, and veterinary

AMR: Burden, Sources, and Role of Animal AMU

AMR threatens human and animal health, food systems, and economic stability
globally.

AMR emerges from complex interactions among humans, animals, and the

Canada categorizes drug-resistant pathogens to focus stewardship and response

Canada relies on systems such as CIPARS, Canada Animal Health Surveillance

•
Systems are underfunded, geographically limited, and focus on certain foods or
pathogens.
•
Equity-related factors (gender, Indigeneity, disability, socio-economic status)
affecting AMR risk are poorly understood.

Veterinary oversight

Submission to the House of Commons Standing Committee
on Health
Written Testimony by Leanne McConnachie
World Animal Protection Canada

Thank you, Madame Chair, and House Committee members, for the opportunity
to submit the following brief. The information in this brief was also shared with
the Standing Committee on Science and Research in October 2025 during their
AMR study.

I will address the overuse of antimicrobials in intensive animal agriculture.

I am representing World Animal Protection Canada, a global animal welfare
organization that, for decades, has advocated for better farmed animal welfare
standards. World Animal Protection is also a member of Animal Health Canada’s
National Farm Animal Care Council (NFACC). I personally have been involved in farm
animal welfare issues for the past 20 years.

Seventy percent (70%) of the world’s antibiotics are used in animal agriculture1, often
administered prophylactically, and daily in-feed, to prevent disease.2

Prophylactic use refers to the administration of antimicrobials even when illness and
harmful bacteria are not present. This is unlike metaphylactic use where bacteria or
infection is nearby and disease spread is likely, or therapeutic use when infection is
present and treatment of the animal is necessary. We fully support the use of
antimicrobials for metaphylactic or therapeutic treatment, but not for prophylactic
purposes. This principle has been put into effect in a number of jurisdictions which I will
discuss shortly.

When it comes to human health, we know we can help prevent disease and infection if
we practice good hygiene, live in sanitary conditions, eat a healthy diet, exercise, avoid
crowded areas, and don’t use antibiotics unless necessary.

As you can imagine, many of these conditions are not met on today’s intensive livestock
operations where antimicrobials are routinely used to compensate for systems that
prioritize production goals over good animal welfare.

These intensive systems are the most common methods for raising food animals today,
yet a 2023 literature review3 of hundreds of peer-reviewed scientific research papers
shows how poor animal welfare from poor management practices are linked to high
levels of AMU, and how AMU can be reduced when improvements to housing
conditions and management practices are implemented. I will table a copy of the 2023
report with the Committee.

I will table a copy of the 2023
report with the Committee.

Practices most affiliated with prophylactic AMU include high stocking densities,
confinement of animals in cages and crates, unsanitary conditions, early and abrupt
weaning, comingling of unfamiliar animals, unnatural diets, high rates of reproduction
1 Van Boeckel TP, Pires J, Silvester R. et al. Global trends in antimicrobial resistance in animals in low-and middleincome countries. Science 2019; 365: eaaw1944. [DOI] [PubMed] [Google Scholar]
2 https://cahs-acss.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CAHS-AMU-Report_EN_Final-1.pdf
3 https://www.worldanimalprotection.ca/our-work/reports-library/the-overuse-of-antibiotics-in-farm-animals-is-a-byproduct-of-poor-animal-welfare/

and protein output, and generally barren, stressful or otherwise inadequate
environments.

Jurisdictions which have demonstrated leadership in policies to reduce AMU in animal
agriculture include:
o the EU’s 2022 ban of all prophylactic antibiotic use;4
o Denmark’s yellow-card system implemented in 2010 in the pig industry with
sector-specific antimicrobial use targets and penalties for non-compliance;5
o Quebec’s provincial policy adopted in 2019 to immediately prohibit the
prophylactic use of Category 1 antibiotics in farm animals.6,7

The updated 2023 Pan Canadian Action Plan and its 5 pillars are commendable, and
the 2018 Health Canada policy requiring a veterinary prescription for sales of all
medically important antimicrobials to farm animals8 is helpful in reducing prophylactic
AMU.

However, while PCAP does include a commitment to collect better data on AMU, to
date, there’s no indication it will track all AMU on farms. This means the amount and
type of antibiotics used, along with the reasons for doing so, are not fully known.
Without this data, the most effective policy decisions to support therapeutic and
metaphylactic use, and restrict prophylactic use, cannot be made.

Furthermore, while PCAP has a primary focus on root cause infection prevention in
human health environments, the focus in farm animal settings is not on root cause
prevention, but rather on regulating and tracking drug prescriptions and use. The
omission of addressing the management and living environments of farm animals must
equally be addressed to responsibly reduce unnecessary antimicrobial use.

The
omission of addressing the management and living environments of farm animals must
equally be addressed to responsibly reduce unnecessary antimicrobial use.

Specifically, we recommend Canada:
o phase-out the prophylactic use of antimicrobials in farming in all but exceptional
cases (such as outbreaks or surgical prophylaxis).
o phase out animal management practices that compromise animal welfare
(possibly through the National Farm Animal Care Council’s Codes of Practice).
o Implement a national mandatory reporting system of antimicrobial sales by
pharmacies and on-farm use by veterinarians, feed mills and farmers.
o Integrate the sector-specific reporting systems already in use.

We recognize the above concerns and requests fall outside the mandate of any one
ministerial portfolio. We are thus asking for a central figure or body (perhaps via the
Privy Council’s Office) to lead a coalition of human, animal and environmental health
ministries and agencies to coordinate and fund a sustainable and actionable response
4 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/MEMO_18_6562
5 https://www.nature.com/articles/486465a
6 https://zonemembre.omvq.qc.ca/DATA/media/2024/12/Use%20of%20Category%201%20Antibiotics.pdf
7 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6973201/
8 https://www.cvbc.ca/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Changes-to-Health-Canada-Regulations-Mar.-2018.pdf

to PCAP, with concrete deliverables and timelines, in order to achieve the
necessary changes outlined today and throughout these hearings. Thank you.

Evidence Brief: Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) in Canada, with a focus on
infection control and surveillance needs in human healthcare systems.
Prepared by Dr. Kevin J. Stinson, PhD CIC, on behalf of Infection Prevention and Control
Canada
Submission to House of Commons Standing Committee on Health
Study on Antimicrobial Resistance
Meeting Date 02 December 2025
Submitted 16 December 2025

Executive Summary
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health concern already associated with
significant mortality and financial impacts in Canada and abroad. AMR has been described as a
“silent pandemic”, as cases and transmission often go unnoticed. Antimicrobial resistant
organisms (AROs) have an ability to transfer resistance genes to bacteria of the human
microbiota, thereby driving persistent colonization. Today, nearly one in 10 acute care patients in
Canada is colonized with an ARO.
Infection control, surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship are three of the core pillars
required to effectively combat AMR. Yet there are inconsistencies with the implementation of
these programs across Canada, especially in underserved communities or healthcare sectors.
Current surveillance programs in Canada act as sentinels to identify broad AMR trends but lack
the depth or breadth needed to effectively map transmission, and current practices lack the
granularity needed to inform local practices.
Opportunities to address these challenges include building infection control capacities
within the healthcare workforce, through training and capacity-building initiatives such as the
IPAC Hub program currently operating across Ontario. As a long-term strategy, Canada must
improve our AMR surveillance programs. We need an integrated, multi-sector approach, with a
specific focus on understanding transmission dynamics and identifying control measures, both in
and out of healthcare. Canada must also continue to support broad public health initiatives aimed
at preventing infectious diseases, as these measures do indirectly support antimicrobial
stewardship efforts.

Canada must also continue to support broad public health initiatives aimed
at preventing infectious diseases, as these measures do indirectly support antimicrobial
stewardship efforts.

AMR as a silent pandemic
In 2019, the World Health Organization (WHO) released a list of the top 10 threats to
global health, including antimicrobial resistance (AMR). AMR is when microorganisms,
including bacteria, viruses, parasites, and fungi, become resistant to one or more classes of
antimicrobial agents used to treat them. A 2019 study estimated that, globally, bacterial AMR
directly contributed to 1.27 million deaths1. This is projected to rise to 1.91 million deaths per
year by 2050, with a cumulative 39 million deaths over the next 25 years2. In Canada, a 2018
study commissioned by the Public Health Agency of Canada estimated that AMR was directly
associated with 5,400 deaths per year, with figures projected to grow to 13,700 deaths per year
by 2050, and a cumulative 396,000 deaths over that period. Economically, AMR is already
associated with $1.4 billion in costs to the Canadian healthcare system annually, and an
additional $2 billion in GDP losses per annum, projected to rise to $7.6 billion and $21 billion
respectively by 20503.
Despite these figures, AMR is often referred to as a “silent pandemic”, because
transmission often goes unchecked and without notice. When we think about an epidemic or
pandemic, we tend to picture respiratory viruses or other pathogens that cause symptomatic
disease which is either self-limiting or treatable. However, the mechanisms governing AMR
transmission are far more nuanced, and this directly contributes to its ability to rapidly spread
undetected.
1 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators. (2022). Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019:
A systematic analysis. The Lancet, 399(10325), 629–655.
2 GBD 2021 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators. (2024). Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial
resistance 1990–2021: A systematic analysis with forecasts to 2050. The Lancet, 404(10459), 1199–1226.
3 Council of Canadian Academies. (2019). When antibiotics fail: The Expert Panel on the Potential SocioEconomic Impacts of Antimicrobial Resistance in Canada. Ottawa, ON: Council of Canadian Academies.

Ottawa, ON: Council of Canadian Academies.

The term “iceberg phenomenon” is often used to describe this challenge, meaning that for
every clinical infection with an antimicrobial-resistant organism (ARO), there are many more
patients silently colonized with the organism. Colonization is a major driver of transmission and
risk from an infection prevention and control (IPAC) perspective; colonized patients can act as
reservoirs within a healthcare facility and their community, and seed AROs into the environment,
exposing others. A publication from the Canadian Nosocomial Infection Surveillance Program
(CNISP) in 2016 identified that 8.9% of acute care patients in participating hospitals were
colonized with at least one ARO4.
In many cases, colonization is transient, and the ARO can be cleared by the immune
system. However, many AMR genes are encoded on mobile genetic elements, which can be
readily transferred from one bacterium to another. This “horizontal gene transfer” poses a unique
challenge as it can transfer the genes which confer resistance into bacteria of the microbiota, the
natural bacteria which live in or on a person. This leads to persistent colonization and
significantly increases the risk of subsequent clinical infections and ongoing spread.
Beyond human health, AMR is influenced by animal health, agriculture, and
environmental reservoirs. The term “One Health” is often used to describe the multi-sector
approach required to address AMR. Moreover, AMR is a global challenge; low- and middleincome countries bear a disproportionate burden of AMR, with particularly high burdens in
Africa, South Asia, and Latin America. Thus, even if Canada performs well domestically, success
in controlling this pandemic depends on global progress and collaboration. In keeping with the
4 Martin, P., Abou Chakra, C. N., Williams, V., Bush, K., Dyck, M., Hirji, Z., Kiss, A., Larios, O. E., McGeer, A.,
Moore, C., Weiss, K., & Simor, A. E. (2019). Prevalence of antibiotic-resistant organisms in Canadian
hospitals: Comparison of point-prevalence survey results from 2010, 2012, and 2016. Infection Control &
Hospital Epidemiology, 40(1), 53–59.

Infection Control &
Hospital Epidemiology, 40(1), 53–59.

2024 Pan-Canadian Action Plan on AMR, this requires research, surveillance, stewardship,
IPAC, and multi-sector leadership5. The focus of this brief is on current needs and gaps in
infection control and surveillance programs in Canada’s human healthcare system, as it pertains
to AMR.
Challenges and Knowledge Gaps
As noted in the Pan-Canadian Action Plan, three core pillars of the response to AMR
include infection prevention and control, surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship. Together,
these three pillars respectively allow for a response to prevent transmission of AMR, identify
epidemiological trends, and safeguard current antimicrobial agents to reduce further emergence
of resistance. Within healthcare systems across Canada, Infection Control Professionals (ICPs),
and Infection Prevention and Control (IPAC) programs, form a core component of the
infrastructure responsible for establishing monitoring these practices. Where these programs are
established, AMR is frequently a primary area of focus, due to the widespread impact of the
issue. However, we see inconsistencies across Canada in the implementation of these programs
and access to trained and certified ICPs in all healthcare settings. These gaps are especially
prevalent in rural communities and sectors outside of acute care, for example long-term care
facilities.
ICPs are tasked with developing AMR surveillance and control measures within their
facilities to ensure the safety of patients or residents. ICPs are reliant on epidemiological data to
inform their program development, to create policies and processes that appropriately match the
needs of their communities, and to balance clinical operational needs, and financial stewardship.
5 Public Health Agency of Canada. (2023). Pan-Canadian action plan on antimicrobial resistance (HP40337/2024E-PDF).

Pan-Canadian action plan on antimicrobial resistance (HP40337/2024E-PDF).

This highlights the importance of accurate and reliable surveillance data which reflects AMR
trends. However, AMR surveillance programs across Canada are instead built as sentinels to
identify broad AMR trends, with data often aggregated to a Provincial or National level. These
data lack the granularity to be effectively translated to inform local practice. Moreover, when
looking at the utility of this data to inform control strategies, current surveillance programs lack
the depth and breadth to effectively map transmission, especially outside of healthcare settings,
which limits the ability to identify effective control strategies to prevent transmission. Again,
these challenges are heightened when looking at under-resourced settings, such as rural facilities,
or healthcare sectors outside of acute care.
Opportunities and Recommendations
To begin addressing these challenges, Canada must look to better invest in building the
infection control, surveillance, and antimicrobial stewardship infrastructure in all healthcare
settings. One solution is to invest in training and capacity building initiatives aimed at growing
the IPAC workforce. One example of this is the IPAC Hub program currently operating across
Ontario, which is an initiative developed during the COVID-19 pandemic aimed at establishing a
network of trained ICPs to provide education, coaching, and mentoring to frontline staff and
those responsible for IPAC programming in long-term care and congregate living organizations
across the province. It is also important to grow the skillset of those professionals currently
working in infection control. ICPs come from a diverse background, with a significant number
being nurses. Many do not have formal training in epidemiology, statistics, or quality
improvement. Training grants to develop these important skills in ICPs would build capacity in
the healthcare workforce and support a unified approach to AMR research and management.

Training grants to develop these important skills in ICPs would build capacity in
the healthcare workforce and support a unified approach to AMR research and management.

Looking more broadly at our surveillance infrastructure, Canada’s current surveillance
efforts lack a unifying framework, particularly for tracking transmission outside large acute care
facilities. As a long-term strategy, Canada must invest in an integrated, cross-sector surveillance
system to close these gaps. Integrated surveillance should link real-time whole-genome
sequencing with clinical, epidemiologic and geospatial data, incorporate environmental and agrifood/animal-health AMR monitoring, and operate under coordinated national and provincial
governance to map transmission and identify control measures.
Lastly, it is important to highlight the impacts of effective science-based public health
leadership in combatting AMR. Initiatives such as vaccination campaigns aimed at reducing
overall burden of infectious disease have direct and indirect impacts on reducing antimicrobial
utilization in the Canadian population, supporting antimicrobial stewardship goals. Canada has a
strong history of supporting public health initiatives. However, in an era where vaccine hesitancy
and skepticism in science are on the rise, we are seeing challenges such as the re-emergence of
measles and the recent loss of the measles elimination status. We need our government to
continue to back evidence-based policy that supports strong public health initiatives and
strengthen health security for Canadians.

Brief and Speaking notes for Dec 11, 2025 HESA meeting. Prepared by Kim Neudorf patient and family
partner with Patients for Patient Safety Canada (PFPSC).
Madam Chair and committee members thank you for this opportunity to share our recommendations. I
represent Patients for Patient Safety Canada.
We are a non-for-profit volunteer-driven organization representing patients and families, who have
experienced harm within our publicly funded healthcare system. Our mission is Every Patient Safe. We view
AMR, sepsis and healthcare associated infections, as a key patient safety issues.
We collaborate on AMR research, help develop standards and resources, raise public and professional
awareness, present to health professionals, and participate in policy discussions. Appendix A, outlines the
breadth of our work over the past 12 months.
With the family’s permission, I would like to share an experience that illustrates the profound human tragedy
behind the science, and the clinical, economic and social burden of AMR.
A healthy 70-year-old sustained a simple foot fracture. Within two days she developed severe pain
beneath the cast, accompanied by concerning changes in her vital signs and cognition. When the cast
was removed, her foot was gravely infected. Sepsis was eventually diagnosed. MRSA, the most common
HCA AMR pathogen, was identified.
What followed was 419 consecutive days of hospital care. She lost her foot, and averted amputation of
her arm by two hours. Sepsis returned, as it does, and ultimately MRSA and sepsis claimed her life.
The estimated healthcare costs incurred exceeded $750,000. She never received a prosthesis, but a
prosthetic foot can cost $15k and potentially $250k for a hand.1
Her husband was at her side each of those 419 days incurring hotel, food, and fuel costs.
We hear these stories of harm and we see the opportunities for improved patient safety. PFPSC holds that
unique perspective. Our recommendations will benefit the public, mitigate the moral distress and burnout
experienced by health care workers and reduce healthcare costs.
PFPSC is a strong ally in advancing AMR efforts nationally and globally. We accept 100% of every AMR related
invitation to do work.
Yet, Canada, like many civil society organizations dedicated to AMR, struggle financially. Our long term
sustainability is now in jeopardy.
1) Therefore, in our first recommendation we call on the Government of Canada to establish dedicated
grants for patient organizations like PFPSC enabling us to continue collaborative work.
The remaining recommendations focus on people-centred engagement and empowerment2.
2) Strengthen Health Promotion, Infection Prevention, and Patients’ Early Recognition of Serious
Infection (Health Canada and PHAC and CIHR):
a. Promote healthy lifestyle choices rather than a “take a pill’ mentality, including the importance
of oral and gut microbiome health and optimized chronic disease management to reduce
infection risk.

Promote healthy lifestyle choices rather than a “take a pill’ mentality, including the importance
of oral and gut microbiome health and optimized chronic disease management to reduce
infection risk.

b. Encourage personal agency in our communities and healthcare facilities3 – supporting individuals
to practice effective infection prevention and self-management of acute symptoms.
c. Improve Patient-Provider interactions. We trust providers.4 Listen to our concerns, clearly explain
treatment decisions, avoid dismissal of symptoms, and ensure compassionate follow-up care.
d. Ensure healthcare accountability for adherence to standards developed by CSA, HSO and IPAC
Canada.
e. Accelerate research for rapid diagnostic tests and consumer wearables that can potentially
detect early infection or symptom progression (CIHR).
f. Given the rising rates of STBBIs and the increasing reliance on presumptive antibiotic therapy
more needs to be done upstream and downstream.
g. Include demographic data in AMR surveillance to better understand the social burden and
disparities related to AMR5
3) Develop Resources For Patients Living with AMR (Health Canada and PHAC)
a) Provide accessible, high-quality self-management resources for patients who feel dismissed,
bewildered and uninformed6, 7
4) Expand Public Health Literacy on AMR (Health Canada and PHAC)
a) Build on the public’s understanding of ‘infection,’ which is familiar, to improve understanding of
AMR and sepsis.8, 9
b) Focus literacy efforts on target groups, such as expecting parents, older adults, people with noncommunicable diseases or cancer, and socially or racially marginalized communities.
c) Recognize the role of hygiene inaccessibility on infection risk.
d) Engage youth in AMR science and innovation (e.g. Canada-Wide Science Fair, a One Health network
of stewards, video competitions to raise health promotion awareness).
e) Expand the role of pharmacists in stewardship and public education.10
f) Incentivize community pharmacies and medical clinics to disseminate Health Canada materials on
appropriate antibiotic use.

5) Integrate Patient Voices in National AMR Strategies
The current national AMR action plan does not adequately incorporate patient and family perspectives.
HESA can play a pivotal role in ensuring that patient and family voices are embedded in policy
development, implementation and evaluation.

HESA can play a pivotal role in ensuring that patient and family voices are embedded in policy
development, implementation and evaluation.
