Government Response
Second Report of the Standing Committee on Health "Women's Health in Canada:
Closing the Gender Gap"
This Government Response addresses the committee's recommendations using the following four
stages of the health care continuum:
5.
Knowledge development, including research, data collection, surveillance, and
implementation science
6.
Health promotion, including prevention, risk reduction, health education, and awareness
raising
7.
Diagnosis, including screening
8.
Treatment, including non-medical services
The Government implemented a Women's Health Strategy in 1999, and overall has delivered on the
strategy through a broad number of initiatives, programs and policies, as detailed in this
government response. This work is conducted by many federal departments, agencies, and third­
party organizations that are wholly or partially funded by the Government. This includes Health
Canada, CIHR, Indigenous Services Canada, Justice Canada, PHAC, Public Safety, Statistics
Canada, and WAGE among federal departments and agencies. As well, arm's length organizations
like the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer provide important services to address the needs of
Canadians, including with respect to women's health.
As a whole, these initiatives, programs, and policies demonstrate how the Government has
addressed wholly or in part the recommendations of this committee. But as your report
demonstrates, there is more to do.
Some initiatives cut across multiple health conditions and aspects of the health care continuum.
For that reason, they may be referenced in multiple sections of the response.
The Government also recognizes the health of women, girls and gender-diverse people as a cross­
cutting priority that intersects with health equity, anti-racism, Indigenous health, 2SLGBTQI+
health, mental health, socioeconomic status, disability, geography, language, and gender-based
violence. Further, the Government is committed to advancing gender equity in health for Indigenous
women and Two-Spirit people, including through continued engagement with Indigenous partners.
Knowledge development, including resear9h, data collection, surveillance, and
implementation science (Recommendations 2, 6, 7, 11, 12, 15, 16)
The Government is investing in research, data collection, and surveillance on various women's
health issues, including endometriosis, gynecological cancers, and mental health. Below is a
description of current policies, programs and other measures.
CIHR is Canada's health research investment agency and is recognized internationally as a leader
in the appropriate integration of sex, gender and intersectionality in health research. CIHR invests
directly in women's health research, based on internationally accepted standards of excellence, to
advance science to help close the gender health gap, improve health outcomes, and strengthen
health care across Canada. CIHR requires all research applicants to integrate sex and gender into

their research design and practices, when appropriate, meaning all Cl HR-funded research
accounts for sex, gender and other identity factors, when relevant. This approach makes health
research more rigorous and more applicable to everyone.
Endometriosis research:
Supporting Recommendation 2, from 2020-21 to 2024-25, CIHR invested $4.9 million in new
endometriosis research, ranging from studies on the efficacy of cannabinoids as a therapeutic
intervention to endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer. This includes multiple investments
through the National Women's Health Research Initiative. For example, a research team led by Dr.
Tania Di Renna at the Women's College Hospital aims to decrease delays in diagnosis for young
adults and to advance access to high-quality care through the validation of a screening measure for
the early detection of endometriosis and the development of a toolkit to support early screening
and early intervention in primary care. Additionally, research led by Dr. Chandrakant Tayade at
Queen's University aims to develop both non-invasive diagnostic methods and new treatments to
target lesion growth and pain.
Additionally, Health Canada established the Sexual and Reproductive Health Fund in 2021 to help
Canadians access the sexual and reproductive health services they need. Since then, the
Government has invested $91 million to support a range of third-party projects to improve access to
needed services, including supporting research activities related to endometriosis, polycystic ovary
syndrome, and other gynecological conditions.
Research and knowledge transfer on gynecological cancers:
Aligned with Recommendations 6 and 7, CIHR is one of the leading cancer research funders in
Canada. CIHR funds a wide range of cancer research, including on preventing and treating cancer
and on improving the health and quality of life of cancer patients. Over the past five years, CIHR has
invested over $1.1 billion in cancer research and knowledge mobilization, inclusive of gynecological
cancers such as ovarian, endometrial and cervical cancers. For example, Dr. Gina Ogilvie and her
team at the University of British Columbia are advancing cervical cancer research, including how to
prevent, detect, and treat it. Dr. Ogilvie and her team demonstrated that Human Papillomavirus
(HPV) tests are a more reliable method for detecting at-risk cases than the Pap test. As a result, all
Canadian provinces and territories have or are in the process of changing organized cervical cancer
screening programs to make HPVtesting their primary screening method. Cl HR-funded research on
cervical cancer prevention and screening is helping to eliminate cervical cancer, an almost entirely
preventable cancer.
CIHR also supports critical research to improve the diagnosis and treatment of ovarian and
endometrial cancers. For example, Dr. Michele Ardolino from the Ottawa Hospital Research
Institute is leading research to help understand why ovarian cancer patients have, to date,
responded poorly to immunotherapy and to better understand how to harness cells within the
ovaries to make them better effectors of anti-cancer responses.
In 2024, CIHR launched an opportunity on Bringing Biology to Cancer Prevention, which included a
Cancer in Women funding pool to support research on cancers among women and gender-diverse
individuals aimed at identifying new targets and approaches for cancer prevention, risk reduction,
and early detection. As a result, CIHR and partners are investing over $41 million in ground-

breaking cancer prevention research, including eight research teams developing prevention
strategies for women at risk of breast, cervical or ovarian cancer.
Statistics Canada collects and disseminates data on cancer incidence, prevalence, mortality, and
survival, including cervical, uterine and ovarian cancers. Further, the cancer microsimulation
model, OncoSim, led and supported by the Health Canada-funded Canadian Partnership Against
Cancer, with model development by Statistics Canada, provides future projections of incidence
and mortality of 32 cancer types, including several gynecological cancers. The model allows for
evaluation of the impact of screening program changes and innovations on future disease and
mortality patterns.
Further, Statistics Canada, PHAC, and the Canadian Cancer Society currently produce the
Canadian Cancer Statistics report. In addition to providing comprehensive surveillance statistics
on cancer, the report informs the development and evaluation of prevention strategies, health
policy, research priorities, and resource allocation. The full publication is produced biennially and
includes detailed statistics on incidence, mortality, and survival by sex, age group, geographic
region, and time period for more than 20 cancer types, including female breast and gynecological
cancers. In alternate years, a special report is released and current-year projected estimates of
incidence and mortality are published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.
PHAC also independently publishes cancer products (e.g., manuscripts, reports, infographics, data
tools) that integrate cancer information from multiple data sources to provide comprehensive
information on the status of specific cancers (e.g., progress against cervical cancer).
Related to the implementation of knowledge on gynecological cancers, PHAC currently provides
funding, as well as scientific, methodological, and secretariat support to the Canadian Task Force
on Preventive Health Care. The Task Force is an independent arms-length body of clinicians and
methodologists that develops clinical practice guidelines to support primary care providers on
various health topics, including gynecological cancers such as cervical cancer.
In October 2024, PHAC announced the launch of the External Expert Review to study the structure,
governance and processes of the Task Force. The External Expert Review Panel was required to
prepare a report with recommendations for a renewed Task Force. In March 2025, the work of the
Task Force was paused until the Panel finalized its work and their recommendations could be
assessed. The Panel's report, publicly available since June 2025, outlines key recommendations
and system-wide actions to strengthen preventive health guidelines in Canada. A renewed Task
Force, to be established as an External Advisory Body to PHAC, will be launched in April 2026, after
which it will select topics for guideline development.
In 2007, the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer (CPAC) was formed to provide a pan-Canadian
perspective to cancer control. Fully funded with ongoing federal funding of $47.5 million per year,
CPAC's mandate is to accelerate the implementation of the Canadian Strategy for Cancer Control.
The strategy's objective, and by extension CPAC's, is to mobilize partners including provinces and
territories, Indigenous organizations, academics, patients, survivors, policy makers and others from
across the country to reduce the burden of cancer through coordinated, system-level practice and
policy change. Providing governments, non-government organizations and Canadians access to
research, information and decision-making tools in a coordinated fashion reduces fragmentation in
knowledge and service delivery and enhances cancer control.

Although CPAC does not directly fund cancer research, research is an enabler of the Canadian
Strategy for Cancer Control and CPAC funds the Canadian Cancer Research Alliance and its
conference to advance collaboration and coordination in the research sector. The alliance works
strategically to coordinate and collaborate on most cancer research in Canada, including research
focused on factors that may cause cancer and treatments to improve patient and survivor
outcomes. The alliance fosters partnerships among cancer research funders and promotes the
development of national research priorities. These initiatives will benefit women by supporting
equitable access to cancer services, including for gynecological cancers, which, as pointed out in
your report, account for ten percent of cancer deaths in women.
CPAC and the Canadian Cancer Society worked with provincial cancer agencies and partners to
develop the Pan-Canadian Cancer Data Strategy in 2023, to strengthen the quality, timeliness,
integration, and accessibility of cancer data. This data will help better understand the experiences
of equity-deserving populations, including diverse groups of women. The strategy supports First
Nations, Inuit, and Metis-governed data systems. CPAC invested $14 million in 2024-25 in initiatives
to improve how cancer data is collected, integrated and used to support decision-making. CPAC
accelerated data modernization, equity-focused reporting and First Nations, Inuit and Metis­
specific data and data governance.
In Budget 2019, the Government committed up to $150 million over five years to the Terry Fox
Research Institute to establish a Marathon of Hope Cancer Centres Network. The network's
research includes gynecological cancers. The network unites cancer centres around a shared
strategy for precision medicine research. It will develop skilled personnel and generate, analyze,
and share diagnostic, molecular, genomic, imaging, clinical and health outcomes data on a cohort
of 15,000 cancer patients. Budget 2025 announced $80 million over four years, starting in 2026-27,
to support a second phase of the network.
The Government also committed $1 O million over five years in Budget 2019 to Ovarian Cancer
Canada (OCC) for Advancing New Treatments to Improve the Survival of Women with Ovarian
Cancer (OvCAN}. The project contributed to an increased knowledge of effective treatment options
for ovarian cancer and improvements in quality and responsiveness of the health care system and
care received by women at risk or affected by ovarian cancer. The project has developed better
experimental models to test novel treatments, identified and evaluated novel treatments, and
advanced clinical trials. The Government invested a further $3 million over two years, starting in
2024-25, through Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's Strategic Science
Fund for the OCC-led initiative Beyond OvCAN.
Research on women's mental health:
Addressing Recommendations 11, 12and 15, CIHR has invested over$700 million over the past
five years in research on mental health and behavioural conditions, including research on perinatal
mental health and women's mental health. For example, CIHR is investing over $1.5 million in
MOVIN, a randomized controlled trial of a collaborative care model for perinatal mental health care
delivery. Led by Dr. Simone Vigod and Dr. Noah Ivers at the Women's College Hospital, MOVIN
enables patients to screen themselves for symptoms, access tailored educational resources, and
collaborate with a care coordinator to develop personalized treatment plans, in collaboration with
primary care practitioners or perinatal psychiatrists. The research will evaluate the efficacy of the

approach which, if proven successful, could be scaled across Ontario, and potentially across
Canada, to improve perinatal mental health care.
Through the National Women's Health Research Initiative, CIHR is supporting Dr. Sarasthwathi
Vedam and her team to lead the Justice and Equity in Perinatal Services Hub at the University of
British Columbia, which aims to improve pregnancy and birthing services and experiences for
pregnant and perinatal people, including for Indigenous, Black, other racialized people, gender
diverse, queer, trans, newcomers to Canada, and people with disabilities, which links directly to
perinatal mental health. CIHR is also investing in the next generation of researchers to advance
perinatal health through targeted training programs, including the Empowering Next-generation
Researchers in Perinatal and Child Health and the Mother-Child Collaborative training platforms.
These platforms ensure that Canada has the capacity to advance and mobilize knowledge on
perinatal mental health in the years to come.
Despite these advancements in research and practice, there remains a need for an integrated,
equitable system for timely access to perinatal mental health services. This is why, in April 2025,
CIHR committed up to $6 million to support the development of a pan-Canadian learning health
system network in perinatal mental health. Building on past successes with learning health system
approaches, where data and evidence are generated and fed back into the system to improve
service delivery, the objective of this initiative is to enable the rapid translation of research findings
into clinical and care practice. Ultimately, the funding opportunity aims to support research that
will enhance equitable and timely access to specialized, perinatal mental health services to
improve the quality of life for affected individuals and to better reach underserved populations.
Statistics Canada's 2024 Parental Experiences Survey, the 2018/2019 Survey on Maternal Health,
and the 2006 Maternity Experiences Survey collected information on symptoms of perinatal
depression and anxiety. These data informed research on screening. The 2024 Parental Experiences
Survey, funded by PHAC, collected data from parents on experiences during pregnancy and the
postpartum period, including on perinatal mental health and access to mental health services. The
survey data, released in February 2026, contribute to the evidence base informing perinatal mental
health screening and other policies and programs.
Statistics Canada collects data that could inform research and improve the experience of care for
women with mental illness. This includes data on met and unmet health care needs in the 2022
Mental Health and Access to Care Survey, the 2025 and 2026 Canadian Community Health
Surveys, as well as in the Canadian Health Survey on Children and Youth.
PHAC conducts surveillance activities related to mental illness, including mood disorders, anxiety
disorders, and post-traumatic stress disorder and reports statistics by sex and/or gender. Statistics
Canada and PHAC developed the Survey on Mental Health and Stressful Events, a national survey
to collect data on traumatic events in 2021 and 2023, which can be broken down by gender.
In March 2022, the then Minister of Mental Health and Addictions and Associate Minister of Health
held a roundtable discussion, bringing together leading research and advocacy organizations
focused on perinatal and maternal mental health. In response to the roundtable's advice, Health
Canada provided $372,000 to Women's College Hospital in Spring 2023 to develop a clinical
guideline for the treatment of perinatal mood disorders, the first of its kind internationally. In
February 2025, the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments released the peer.reviewed

Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Perinatal Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders,
and Seeds of Hope: A Patient and Family Guide. The guideline has been downloaded more than
42,000 times. It was presented to the Federal-Provincial-Territorial Assistant Deputy Minister
Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use in June 2025 to encourage implementation in
provinces and territories.
The Government is investing more than $14 million per year, through PHAC, to support multi-year
health promotion projects that prevent family and gender-based violence and improve health
outcomes for people impacted by violence. These projects incorporate intervention research to
build needed evidence of what works, for whom and in what settings. Specific to recommendation
15, this includes 21 projects aiming to provide youth with the knowledge and skills to develop and
maintain future healthy relationships, prevent sexual violence, and prevent the long-lasting health
and social consequences of violence, including mental health impacts.
Mental illness is linked with dementia as both a risk factor and a common co-morbidity. Dementia
disproportionately impacts women who have a higher risk of developing the disease. In addition,
depression has been identified as a risk factor for dementia in later life. PHAC leads Canada's
national dementia strategy, which identifies research and innovation as well as public health
surveillance as pillars of implementation. The strategy's national objective on prevention focuses
on advancing research to identify and assess modifiable risk and protective factors, building the
evidence base to inform and promote the adoption of effective interventions, expanding awareness
of modifiable risk and protective factors and effective interventions, and supporting measures that
increase the contribution of social and built environments to healthy living and adoption of healthy
living behaviours. The national objective to advance therapies and find a cure focuses on
establishing dementia research priorities, increasing dementia research, developing therapeutic
approaches, and increasing the adoption of research findings. Within the objective to improve
quality of life, several areas of focus relate to care (i.e., promoting early diagnosis, addressing the
importance of access to quality care, building the capacity of care providers, improving support for
family and friend caregivers). PHAC's Dementia Community Investment helps implement the
strategy by supporting community-based intervention research to evaluate the effectiveness of
interventions.
Investments in Indigenous midwifery influences on research, health promotion, diagnosis, and
treatment:
Regarding Recommendations 7, 11, 12, 15, 16, the Government invested $6 million over five years
in Budget 2017 to increase access to midwifery services in First Nations and Inuit communities.
Budget 2021 committed $26.5 million over three years to expand midwifery and doula/birth support
worker services, as a key component of the government's initiative for addressing anti-Indigenous
racism. Budget 2024 continued funding for Indigenous midwifery through to 2029. These
investments are supporting the regrowth of Indigenous midwifery. Indigenous midwives provide
primary care to life-givers in the perinatal period, and often throughout the life-course. Thanks to
the strong bonds they form with their clients, Indigenous midwives can provide education, health
promotion, screenings, and referrals for a wide range of conditions, including perinatal mood and
anxiety disorders, as well as screening for cervical and breast cancers. Indigenous midwives also
lead and contribute to research; provide support and referrals around healthy
relationships/intimate partner violence; provide or facilitate access to abortions; and provide
advice, referrals and advocacy for women experiencing various health concerns such as

endometriosis, fibroids, or pelvic pain. In short, Indigenous midwives are a key pathway to ensuring
Indigenous women can access care, education, support, and advocacy from a known and trusted
provider.
Funding women's health research:
Contributing to Recommendation 16, through CIHR, the Government supports research to
address the biological, social, and systemic factors shaping women's health across the life-course.
From 2020-21 to 2024-25, CIHR invested over $353 million in women's health research, including
over $86 million last year.
This includes investments through the National Women's Health Research Initiative (NWHRI),
which, in partnership with WAGE, is advancing a coordinated research program that addresses
under-researched and high-priority areas of women's health. The NWHRI promotes an
intersectional lens to research to reflect the diversity of women in Canada, aiming to ensure new
evidence improves women's and gender-diverse people's care and health outcome$ across the life
course. Launched in 2022 with funding announced in the 2021 federal budget, the NWHRI has
supported 58 research grants across the country, investing $26.5 million across its two streams: the
Pan-Canadian Women's Health Coalition and the Innovation Fund.
The coalition consists of 10 virtual hubs across Canada linked through a coordinating centre, which
lead research and knowledge mobilization activities in several high-priority areas, including
reproductive health, cardiovascular health, and gender-based violence. The Innovation Fund
supports research in high-risk and high-reward areas of women's health that have been traditionally
underfunded, including a focus on biomedical, translational and implementation research.
Together, these projects span basic science discoveries, clinical, population health, and health
system research to address implementation gaps and improve the equitable uptake of evidence­
informed interventions. This research aims to improve access to quality health care and, ultimately,
to improve health outcomes for women and gender diverse peoples. The Government remains
committed to advancing research on women's health, including through the NWHRI, that will
improve our understanding of women's health and make progress on closing the gender health gap.
Starting in 2025-26, Statistics Canada will develop a survey on female gynecological health to
collect data on symptoms, age-based prevalence, the impact on daily living, and access to health
care. Currently there is no national level data on symptoms related to menstruation, menopausal
transition, and female gynecological health. Women experiencing these symptoms can be
overlooked, underdiagnosed, misdiagnosed, or receive inadequate or inappropriate treatment. The
data could inform the identification of gender-based health needs, clinical practice, programming,
research and other related areas such as education and employment.
Statistics Canada conducted the Canadian Sexual and Reproductive Health Survey in 2024 to
collect information on sexual health and behaviours, birth control, pregnancy intentions, as well as
on access and barriers to care for miscarriage, stillbirth, ectopic pregnancy and abortion. Statistics
Canada will release survey results in May 2026.
PHAC's Canadian Perinatal Surveillance System monitors maternal health outcomes, such as
severe maternal morbidity and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. PHAC monitors outcomes
across pregnancy and the postpartum period and reports trends, disparities, and emerging issues

through the Perinatal Health Indicators Data Tool, as well as through peer-reviewed publications
that provide more in-depth examination of specific issues.
PHAC also commissioned public opinion research to better understand barriers and facilitators to
breast cancer screening participation in women aged 40 and older, with targeted recruitment of
Indigenous women, Black women, and newcomers to Canada. PHAC, in collaboration with
Statistics Canada, also supported the analysis of national cancer trends, including disparities in
breast cancer incidence based on geography, age, and ethnicity, and data on access to and
participation in mammography. These analyses, including some that were extended to other types
of cancer screening (e.g., colorectal and cervical screening), could inform policy and programming.
Health promotion, including prevention, risk reduction, health education, awareness
raising (Recommendations 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 13)
The Government is undertaking a broad range of measures to promote women's awareness of and
reduce their risks related to various health issues, including the use of substances, gynecological
cancers, and perinatal anxiety.
Actions on substance use, including alcohol. vaping, and tobacco use:
Responding to Recommendations 3, 4 and 5, Statistics Canada and Health Canada annually
collect information on alcohol consumption, the use of a-cigarettes or vaping devices, and smoking
through a range of surveys such as the Canadian Community Health Survey, the Canadian Health
Survey on Children and Youth, and Canadian Substance Use Survey. Data on alcohol and tobacco
could be used to evaluate the impact of different messaging strategies. For example, Health
Canada assesses evidence on use of vaping products, including from these surveys, and from
international practices and stakeholder input, towards the objective of reducing vaping prevalence.
The department applies GBA Plus to research and analysis.
Addressing the risks of alcohol use:
Addressing Recommendation 3, through the Health Portfolio, the Government continues to review
evidence, including international best practices to inform its communications and the development
of public education resources around the risks and harms of alcohol use. Health Canada
communicates the health risks of alcohol use, including through its webpage on alcohol use, social
media (Healthy Canadians, Facebook account), as well as polysubstance use campaigns, such as
the "Reduce Your Risks of Substance Use" for young adults in post-secondary institutions. Health
Canada has also conducted public opinion research (e.g., 2023 Public Awareness of Alcohol­
related Harms Survey) to assess the level of awareness of alcohol-related harms and support for
alcohol health messaging. PHAC supported the Students Commission of Canada to develop the
"Before You Mix, Know the Risk" campaign targeting polysubstance use amongst 2SLGBTQI+ young
adults.
The Government also supports Pan-Canadian Health Organizations that conduct research aimed at
providing the latest evidence-based information about alcohol-relateË harms and disseminate
information about the health risks of alcohol use. For example, the Canadian Centre on Substance
Use and Addiction updated Canada's Guidance on Alcohol and Health in 2023, which provides
information to consumers about the level of health risk associated with their alcohol use and

recommends limiting alcohol consumption to reduce cancer risk. The Government invested $1.5
million towards its development. It also committed an additional $2 million to the Canadian Centre
on Substance Use and Addiction to conduct regional roundtables to inform the development of
tailored knowledge mobilization and dissemination tools that communicate the risks and harms of
alcohol consumption to diverse populations.
The Government supports work by the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer (CPAC), which
includes information on its webpage, Alcohol policy and cancer. The website includes
recommended policy actions and offers a webinar series in collaboration with the Canadian
Cancer Society, the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction, and the Canadian Public
Health Association. In 2021, CPAC released a report examining the effectiveness of policies for
reducing alcohol consumption and marketing of alcohol.
Health Canada's Substance Use and Addictions Program provides contribution funding to other
orders of government and to community-led, Indigenous, and not-for-profit organizations for
innovative and evidence-informed projects across the continuum of care, including substance use
prevention, harm reduction, treatment, and recovery. Projects target a range of substances
including alcohol and tobacco at the community, regional, and national levels. Since 2017, the
program has provided more than $17 million to 12 projects addressing alcohol use and related
harms.
Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder is one of many health impacts associated with alcohol use.
Through its maternal and child health policy and programming initiatives, PHAC promotes healthy
pregnancies, for example through development of guidance and resources to prevent and raise
awareness of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder. Similarly, Indigenous Services Canada's Healthy
Child Development suite of programs supports First Nations and Inuit communities to deliver
culturally appropriate programming, including education and awareness and about the impacts of
Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder, supporting women to stop or reduce alcohol use while pregnant,
and helping families and caregivers connect with provincial and territorial health services, including
multi-disciplinary diagnostic teams.
As alcohol consumption and smoking are risks for dementia, the Dementia Community Investment
supports community-based projects that seek to increase knowledge, including for women, about
dementia and its risk and protective factors.
Reducing vaping and tobacco use:
Related to Recommendations 4 and 5, Health Canada monitors the impact of measures to
address vaping among young people, including through cyclical reviews of the Tobacco and Vaping
Products Act. Health Canada has invested close to $15 million in public education campaigns
geared towards youth since 2018. Vaping prevention advertising campaigns are updated annually to
reflect insights from performance measurement, public opinion research, and focus testing. This
Legislation and investments benefit girls and young women by reducing their risk, for example of
lung cancer, which your report noted is a leading cause of cancer death in females.
Through Canada's Tobacco Strategy, the Government invests approximately $17 million annually in
contribution funding to support smoking prevention and cessation initiatives delivered through
Health Canada, PHAC, and Indigenous Services Canada. The strategy allocates $1 million annually

to tobacco and vaping prevention and cessation public education campaigns. Previous tobacco
cessation advertising campaigns, digital toolkit, and social media campaigns were successful in
reaching target audiences. The department measures the performance of campaigns and leverages
insight from public opinion research and focus testing to reflect GBA Plus considerations in the key
messaging, creative design, and talent selection to the extent possible.
Under Canada's Tobacco Strategy, Indigenous Services Canada provides approximately $9.1
million annually to fund the development and implementation of community-led, distinctions­
based approaches to reduce high prevalence rates of commercial tobacco use among First
Nations, Inuit, and Matis populations, including youth. Many First Nations, Inuit, and Matis
communities and organizations are leading innovative, strengths-based, wholistic and culturally
grounded programming, strategies, and initiatives that strategically address both commercial
tobacco use and the rising rates of vaping, while tailored to community needs. As well, Indigenous
Services Canada's Non-Insured Health Benefits Program covers a range of smoking cessation
treatments for eligible First Nations and Inuit, including prescription medications and nicotine
replacement products.

annually to support community-based tobacco prevention and cessation projects for populations
that face health inequalities, including women, and have higher rates of tobacco use.
Further, the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care's 2025 guideline on tobacco smoking in
adults includes recommendations and resources for clinicians and patients on ways to quit
smoking. The Task Force also published a 2017 guideline on tobacco smoking in children and

Through Health Canada's Substance Use and Addictions Program, the Government has funded 19
projects focused on tobacco cessation since 2019, valued at a combined $30 million. For example,
