project Youth vaping: nicotine dependence, cessation, and the evolving vaping market, which
assessed the tobacco and vaping use patterns of young women and men to inform vaping policies.
CIHR invests in a broad array of research related to substance use. For example, CIHR has invested
in research to understand the health effects of vaping in response to the unknown effects and rapid
increase in vaping in Canada, which includes research looking at sex-based differences related to
nicotine reward and withdrawal. Further, Dr. Laura Struik and her team at the University of British
Columbia are working with youth to co-produce a digital e-cigarette intervention. Other CIHR­
funded research examines the impacts of alcohol and tobacco use during pregnancy, which could
inform targeted public health messaging and interventions.
Promoting awareness of gynecological cancers. including vaccination uptake:
Responding to Recommendations 8 and 9, in December 2025, PHAC launched the Human
Papillomavirus Indicator Framework dashboard outlining HPVvaccination coverage and
HPV-associated cancers, with breakdowns including by sex, gender, and other aspects. PHAC is
collaborating with provinces and territories to develop a new surveillance system for vaccination
coverage, the Standardized Reporting on Immunization, which uses immunization registry data
applying standardized methods to produce comparable results that can be combined. Additionally,

national HPV vaccination coverage among adults is reported from the Adult National Immunization
Coverage Survey. To close disaggregated data gaps among specific populations, PHAC launched
the Key Adult Populations Immunization Coverage Survey, which focuses on systemically
marginalized populations and underserved adults (e.g., people living on low incomes and those
living in remote areas), and the Childhood Immunization Coverage Survey in Key Populations which
reports on coverage among children of key populations (e.g., children of recent immigrant and
2SLGBTQI+ parents). This surveillance data can inform innovations in cancer prevention.
Further, Statistics Canada's Canadian Community Health Survey periodically collects information
on cervical cancer screening that could inform public awareness initiatives.
Indigenous Services Canada provides flexible funding to First Nations and Inuit communities for
community-led health promotion and primary prevention programming aimed at addressing
common behavioural risk factors, including healthy eating, that have direct links to cancer
prevention. The types of services and activities offered are wide-ranging and varied based on self­
determined local needs, priorities and capacity.
Raising awareness of perinatal anxiety:
Corresponding to Recommendation 13, information collected by Statistics Canada in the 2024
Parental Experiences Survey and the 2018/2019 Survey on Maternal Health on symptoms of
anxiety, and used by PHAC for national surveillance reporting, could inform public awareness on
anxiety in the perinatal or postpartum periods.
The Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments' Clinical Practice Guideline for the
Management of Perinatal Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders, and associated Patient and Family
Guide, funded by Health Canada could inform public awareness initiatives.
Diagnosis, including screening (Recommendations 1, 9, 10)
The Government is acting to help women receive earlier and effective screening and diagnosis of
health issues, including endometriosis, cervical cancers, and perinatal depression. The following
summarizes related initiatives.
Diagnosing endometriosis:
In support of Recommendation 1, Statistics Canada will conduct the Canadian Gynecological
Health Survey in 2026, which will collect information on endometriosis and other gynecological
conditions. Data, for example on symptoms, length of time to diagnosis, impacts on daily living,
medication use, and fertility consultations, could inform innovations in diagnosis.
Cervical cancer screening:
Contributing to Recommendation 9, the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer (CPAC) worked with
partners to develop an Action Plan to Eliminate Cervical Cancer in Canada by 2040, in response to
the World Health Organization's goal and the Government's commitment to eliminate cervical
cancer. The action plan prioritizes improving HPVvaccination rates, transitioning from Pap
screening to primary HPV screening, and enhancing follow-up for abnormal results. As part of the

implementation of the action plan, CPAC and its partners are engaging underserviced populations
who experience inequities to overcome and dismantle barriers to immunization, screening and
follow-up of abnormal screening results. This includes Indigenous Peoples, who have experienced
three times more diagnoses and four times more deaths from cervical cancer than the population
overall; youth at increased risk; 2SLGBTQI+ individuals; and rural individuals. PHAC is working with
federal, provincial, and territorial partners and experts to renew Canada's National Vaccination
Coverage Goals for 2025 to 2030. This will inform implementation of the action plan by addressing
priority 1 - the target required to improve HPV vaccination rates in Canada. PHAC tracks progress
towards achieving the vaccination coverage goals among boys and girls through the childhood
National Immunization Coverage Survey. PHAC integrates GBA Plus into scientific publications to
inform evidence-based decision making and support implementation of the action plan.
PHAC's National Microbiology Laboratory provides national reference and diagnostic testing,
including comprehensive HPV molecular genotyping. The National Microbiology Laboratory
contributes to the national and international HPV cancer monitoring programs, providing broad
coverage genotyping for cancer specimens to monitor HPV genotype distribution, vaccination
impact and guide cervical cancer prevention messaging. The National Microbiology Laboratory will
also contribute to development and pre-clinical evaluation of HPV detection methods that support
more accessible and acceptable screening approaches for diverse and difficult to reach
populations. It also participates in research collaborations that generate evidence on HPV
infection dynamics, risk factors, and disease progression, informing public education materials
aimed at increasing screening and vaccination uptake. The National Microbiology Laboratory will
further support provinces and territories by providing controls, validation materials, and technical
expertise, strengthening local screening capacity and enabling consistent national messaging.
The Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care published a cervical cancer screening
guideline in 2013 that includes questions and answers, a decision aid for patients and a one-page
recommendation summary for providers. In 2025, the Task Force commissioned a systematic
evidence review of updated evidence on cervical screening, including a question on primary care­
based interventions to increase cervical screening rates for under- and never-screened individuals.
The current Task Force will not complete an update to the cervical cancer screening guideline. The
renewed Task Force will determine topic selection for guideline development after April 2026.
Perinatal depression screening:
Regarding Recommendation 10, in February 2025, the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety
Treatments released the peer-reviewed Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Perinatal
Mood, Anxiety, and Related Disorders, and associated Patient and Family Guide, funded by Health
Canada.
In addition, the Canadian Task Force on Preventive Health Care;s 2022 guideline on depression
during the pregnancy and postpartum period includes a section outlining knowledge gaps. As part
of the guideline's development process, fifteen external stakeholders and experts reviewed the
guideline, and their input as well as the Task Force's responses are publicly available on the Task
Force's website. For each guideline, the Task Force also develops and disseminates knowledge
mobilization tools and resources to support primary care providers and patients.

Statistics Canada's 2024 Parental Experiences Survey collected information on symptoms of
perinatal depression and anxiety, including data on whether the parent was asked by a health care
provider about their emotional and mental health during the perinatal period. The survey data,
released in February 2026, could inform a future evaluation of the guideline.
Treatment, including non-medical services (Recommendations 1, 7, 14)
The Government is taking action to increase women's access to treatment, care, and other services
to address endometriosis, gynecological cancers, and gender-based violence. A summary of
current policies, programs, and other measures is presented below.
Treatment and care for endometriosis:
In broad alignment with Recommendation 1, Health Canada's Sexual and Reproductive Health
Fund has funded projects related to endometriosis. The Society of Obstetricians and
Gynaecologists of Canada's project ($1.4M) raised awareness on endometriosis care through the
development and distribution of educational resources. It also supported underserved patient
populations, including Indigenous, racialized and 2SLGBTQI+ people, by improving access to health
resources through their website Sex and U. An Endometriosis Network Canada project ($1.3M)
supported the development of patient-focused educational resources for people living with
endometriosis. Key resources specific to patients and youth were co-developed with health care
providers. The project raised public awareness of endometriosis through a targeted national
marketing campaign. In September 2025, Health Canada announced the funding of a new project
($SOOK) by the Canadian Society for the Advancement of Gynaecologic Excellence that aims to
build the awareness, knowledge, and clinical skills of health care professionals on endometriosis
diagnosis, diagnostic imaging, and surgical management. Project activities will also include social
media awareness activities and interdisciplinary educational resources for health care providers
that will be evidence-based.
In addition, the Government continues to support efforts responding to the Canadian Pain Task
Force recommendations, including those recommendations specific to addressing the needs of
women living with chronic pain. For instance, the Government has invested $4.6 million towards
Pain Canada -an initiative dedicated to support national coordination and mobilization of pain
management resources -to support people living with chronic pain, including women living with
painful health conditions, like endometriosis and chronic pelvic pain. The Government also
provided more than $1.4 million through Health Canada's Substance Use and Addictions Program
for the Ottawa Hospital Research lnstitute's development of the Power Over Pain Portal, which
provides free evidence-based virtual pain management resources. Through this portal, a chronic
pelvic pain webpage directs women living with this condition towards evidence-based pain
management resources, including workshops, virtual courses and peer support groups.
Treatinggynecological cancers:
Supporting Recommendation 7, Health Canada's number one priority is the health and safety of
Canadians. As a result, all therapeutic products marketed in Canada must undergo rigorous drug
approval via a sponsor's drug submission, where experts evaluate safety, efficacy, and quality to
determine whether the risks associated with the product are acceptable considering its potential
benefits. Health Canada has pathways to expedite access to innovative treatments, such as the

Notice of Compliance with Conditions policy and the Priority Review policy. Through international
collaborations such as Project Orbis, Health Canada accelerates the availability of new cancer
treatments, including for gynecological cancers, by encouraging timely submission and concurrent
reviews with global partners.
Health Canada implements its Sex- and Gender-Based Analysis Plus Action Plan, in part, by
integrating intersectional factors - such as age, sex, race, and ethnicity- into its approach to drug
regulation. The objective of this work is to enhance representation in clinical trials and promote the
inclusion of historically underrepresented groups including women, pregnant and breastfeeding
individuals, minority and remote communities, Indigenous populations, and 2SLGBTQI+
communities.
Health Canada's disaggregated data regulatory requirement, which came into effect in December
2024, supports the submission of clinical trial data broken down by factors such as sex, age, race
and ethnicity. This requirement is intended to strengthen the evaluation of safety and efficacy of
drugs across diverse populations and improve understanding of drug risks for specific subgroups
within the Canadian population.
Additionally, as part of the Clinical Trials Regulatory Modernization initiative, Health Canada has
also proposed additional regulatory requirements to improve access to new and innovative
therapies while maintaining strong safety participant protections. The associated consultation also
includes draft guidance documents that provide direction to sponsors and encourage more
inclusive clinical trial practices.
Services to address gender-based violence:
Gender-based violence is one of the most pervasive, deadly, and deeply rooted criminal violations
of our time. It can take many forms, including physical, sexual, psychological, emotional, and
financial abuse, as well as technology-facilitated violence.
In broad alignment with Recommendation 14, in Budget 2022, the Government committed $539.3
million over five years to support provinces and territories to supplement and enhance services and
supports within their jurisdictions, including sexual assault centres, to prevent gender-based
violence and support victims, survivors and their families.
Since the National Action Plan to End Gender-Based Violence was launched in November 2022,
WAGE has developed and signed 13 bilateral agreements with provinces and territories. The
bilateral agreements are flexible in addressing each jurisdiction's challenges, needs, and priorities
under the five pillars and foundation of the action plan. Each pillar and foundation provides
opportunity for action that relate to sexual assault centres.
In Budget 2025, the Government also committed:
•
$223.4 million over five years, starting in 2026-27, with $44.7 million ongoing, to strengthen
federal action on gender-based violence.
•
$54.6 million over five years, starting in 2026-27, with $10.9 million ongoing, to support the
2SLGBTQI+ community sector. This includes $7.5 million over five years, with $1.5 million
ongoing, for pride security.

•
$382.5 million over five years, starting in 2026-27, with $76.5 million ongoing, to revitalise
and stabilise efforts to advance women's equality.
As part of the commitment to strengthen federal action on gender-based violence, continued
funding supports crisis hotlines across Canada, which helps to provide robust services, resources,
and supports to serve the urgent needs of all victims and survivors of gender-based violence and
their families, no matter where they live.
The Criminal Code of Canada provides a robust framework to address gender-based violence,
including sexual violence. For instance, all non-consensual sexual activity is prohibited through the
offences of sexual assault, with escalating penalties based on the degree of harm and
circumstances. Other offences of general application such as assault, kidnapping, extortion,
criminal harassment, nonconsensual distribution of intimate images and voyeurism also contribute
to protecting the public from gender-based violence. The Criminal Code further contains
procedural safeguards for victims. including testimonial aids, publication bans, and limits on the
use of evidence of the complainant's sexual history and the complainant's private records in sexual
offence proceedings, and requires courts to consider the context of intimate partner violence at
bail and sentencing to better reflect the risks posed by repeat or escalating abuse.
In fall 2025, the Government introduced bills to strengthen these protections. In particular, the bail
changes proposed in Bill C-14, An Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act
and the National Defence Act (bail and sentencing), aim to better protect victims of intimate
partner violence, which is a prevalent form of gender-based violence, by making bail more difficult
to obtain for those charged with assault and sexual assault involving choking, and human
trafficking, which are offences that disproportionately impact women and girls. Further, it would
address repeat violent offending by expressly codifying repeat violent conduct, which is a well­
established predictor of serious harm in intimate partner relationships, as an aggravating factor at
sentencing.
Bill C-16, An Act to amend certain Acts in relation to criminal and correctional matters (child
protection, gender-based violence, delays and other measures), would complement these changes
by criminalizing engaging in a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct in intimate relationships to
ensure that the criminal law is able to recognize and address these patterns of abuse that are far
too often present in intimate relationships. It would amend the Criminal Code's homicide
provisions to treat murders that disproportionately impact females as murders in the first degree,
specifically, murders that are motivated by hate, including based on gender, murders of intimate
partners who have been subjected to coercive and controlling conduct, murders that occur during
the commission of any sexual offence, and murders that occur during exploitative conduct. The
amendment would also ensure that these murders are labelled as "femicide" when the victim is
female. Bill C-16 would further modernize the criminal law to better address sexual and gender­
based violence, including harms such as sexual deepfakes and sexual extortion and criminal
harassment. It would also strengthen victim protection and participation in the criminal justice
system, including through improved access to testimonial aids, enhanced firearms-related
safeguards in domestic violence contexts, and reforms to the private records regime that would
better protect victims' therapeutic records in sexual offence trials, while streamlining procedures to
reduce delay and the risk of stays. Together, these proposals are intended to reduce re­
traumatization of victims, improve access to justice, and ensure fairer outcomes.

Since 2010-11, Justice Canada has funded the development and enhancement of Child Advocacy
Centres through the Federal Victims Strategy. A Child Advocacy Centre/Child & Youth Advocacy
Centre (CAC/CYAC) is a collaboration of law enforcement, child protection, medical and mental
health professionals, and victim advocates in a child-friendly facility to provide an individualized
response for children and youth who have experienced child abuse and their families. Services
include prevention, intervention, prosecution, treatment and support services. Most Canadian
CACs/CYACs serve child and youth clients who have experienced sexual abuse, physical abuse,
serious neglect or who have been exposed to family violence, and their families. CACs/CYACs are
regarded as a leading practice in responding to child abuse cases. They can contribute to
reductions in trauma, improved outcomes, and support long-term healing in children and youth.
Justice Canada provided $6 million in funding for 65 CAC/CYAC projects in 2023-2024 and $7
million in 2024-2025 for 66 projects.
Justice Canada has also provided funding to support initiatives addressing sexual assault and
sexual violence through the Federal Victims Strategy. These initiatives aim to improve services for
victims and survivors, enhance access to justice, and strengthen community-based responses.
Funded projects often involve collaboration among law enforcement, victim services, health
professionals, and community organizations to ensure a trauma-informed and victim-centered
approach. Services supported include prevention, intervention, counseling, and long-term healing
programs. Many projects focus on reducing barriers for underserved populations, including
Indigenous communities, racialized groups, and persons with disabilities. These initiatives are
regarded as leading practices in addressing sexual violence, as they contribute to reducing re­
traumatization, improving justice outcomes, and supporting recovery and empowerment for
survivors.
Justice Canada has funded numerous projects, including specialized sexual assault response
teams, training for justice professionals, and programs that integrate restorative justice
approaches. In 2023-2024, Justice Canada provided almost $800,000 for seven projects, and in
2024-2025, $2 million for 29 projects. Recent data indicate that more than 10,000 survivors and
front-line workers have accessed services through the funded projects.
Further, Indigenous Services Canada funds mental health services, in particular crisis lines that
provide culturally grounded emotional support and crisis intervention to Indigenous Peoples. This
includes the Hope for Wellness Helpline, the National Indian Residential School Crisis Line, and the
Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls Crisis Line. The department also provides
eligible First Nations and Inuit with coverage for mental health counselling services through its Non­
Insured Health Benefits Program.
PHAC's Preventing Family Violence Program supports projects that equip service providers to
detect and safely respond to family and gender-based violence, contributing to national capacity
for trauma and violence-informed services. For example, McMaster University partnered with 22
national organizations to create free, publicly available evidence-based guidance and resources in
both official languages for health care and social service providers, with a focus on recognizing and
responding to child maltreatment and intimate partner violence.
Finally, women's health outcomes can be linked with their economic prosperity. To increase
women's economic security and prosperity, WAGE funds projects led by organizations working to
break down barriers impeding women's participation in Canadian economic, social, and political

life. For instance, through the Women's Program, WAGE supports organizations working to advance
economic security and prosperity for women and girls at the local, regional, and national level,
including those experiencing additional barriers such as Black and Indigenous women and girls,
and women and girls in rural, remote, and northern areas. WAGE supports a range of activities
undertaken by not-for-profit organizations, including from funding organizations aiming to improve
women's representation in male-dominated sectors and efforts to change policies and practices to
increase workplace inclusiveness and opportunities for women's advancement.
In addition, to make life more affordable for women and girls, WAGE is improving access to
essential menstrual products for households living on low income and increasing access to
menstrual health education through the Menstrual Equity Fund National Pilot. Since September
2023, Food Banks Canada has been leading the pilot to address the barriers related to menstrual
equity and period poverty. As of June 2025, Food Banks Canada had procured and distributed more
than 84 million menstrual products, reaching approximately 4.2 million individuals. Additionally,
education and awareness activities have resulted in over 300 resources being scaled and directly
impacting over 50,000 Canadians through various workshops and event. Thanks to its success, the
Government committed a further investment in December 2024 to extend the pilot.
Many people are unable to access menstrual products due to financial limitations or other barriers.
Marginalized populations such as refugees, those who are experiencing homelessness, sex
workers, trans and non-binary people, Indigenous communities, people with disabilities, and
people living in rural, remote, and Northern communities face additional barriers to accessing
menstrual supplies and are at greater risk of period poverty.
The Government is committed to advancing health equity through trauma- and violence-informed
approaches, recognizing the links between gender-based violence, family violence, mental health,
sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections, chronic disease, and long-term health outcomes,
and the need for coordinated responses across the health and social systems.
The Government is also committed to monitoring emerging health equity considerations related to
innovation and technology, including the use of artificial intelligence in health research,
surveillance, screening, and care delivery, to mitigate bias and ensure equitable benefits for diverse
groups of women and girls.
Conclusion
Since the Government implemented a Women's Health Strategy in 1999, there has been a
concerted federal action to address gaps and challenges related to improving women's health. The
Government is committed, in collaboration with provincial, territorial, and Indigenous partners and
other stakeholders, to fostering the health, well-being, and economic achievement of women in
Canada, including by strengthening health, social, and justice systems.
While there has been much progress since 1999, it is clear that more needs to be done by
governments, stakeholders, and others. Women and girls continue to face barriers to accessing the
health services they need, particularly for issues related to reproductive and sexual health.
Systemic gender bias in health research, data, diagnosis, and treatment persists, particularly for
conditions affecting diverse groups of women. A continued focus on women's health, in partnership
with research, public health, and health system partners at the federal, provincial, territorial, and

municipal levels, remains critical if Canada is to work towards improving equitable access to
culturally relevant and trauma-informed treatment, supports, and services to improve health
outcomes and reduce health inequities for women.

Government Response to the First Report of the Standing Committee on Health: Saving More
Lives: Improving Guidance, Increasing Access and Achieving Better Outcomes in Breast Cancer
Screening
The Government of Canada agrees with the 13 recommendations outlined in HESA’s first report
titled, “Saving More Lives: Improving Guidance, Increasing Access and Achieving Better
Outcomes in Breast Cancer Screening”. This response addresses HESA’s recommendations using
the following themes:
1. Structure, governance and accountability of the Canadian Task Force on Preventive
Health Care;
2. Reviewing, developing and updating breast cancer screening guidelines;
3. Delivery of breast cancer screening services;
4. Cancer research, data collection and modelling; and
5. Public education and awareness raising of breast cancer screening.
Theme 1: Structure, governance and accountability of the Canadian Task Force on Preventive
Health Care (Recommendations 1, 2, 3 and 5)
The Government of Canada recognizes the importance of staying at the forefront of preventive
health care guideline development, which includes ensuring that the Canadian Task Force on
Preventive Health Care (Task Force) has the appropriate membership, governance and
accountability structure to develop recommendations; is robust and transparent in its methods;
and responds to the emerging needs and expectations of people in Canada in a timely manner.
The activities outlined below will also support provincial and territorial health sectors, policy
and decision makers, researchers and health professionals to gain a better understanding of the
current state of breast cancer in Canada and support the development and implementation of
better, more inclusive breast cancer screening.
With regard to Recommendations 1 and 2, the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) provides
scientific, methodological and secretariat support to the Task Force. In addition, PHAC’s
epidemiologists that work with the Task Force undergo the International Guideline Training and
Certification Program (INGUIDE) certification process to become certified guideline
methodologists and are INGUIDE Level 1 or Level 2 certified. They also regularly undergo
additional training from contracted specialists in the Grading of Recommendations Assessment,
Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach for rating the quality of evidence syntheses
and for translating evidence and contextual considerations to recommendations.
In 2022, PHAC conducted an internal evaluation of the Task Force. Areas for improvement
noted in the evaluation’s final report included addressing funding challenges; clarifying the
roles for supporting teams (e.g., PHAC Science Team and the Evidence Review and Synthesis
Centres); and decreasing the time required to develop guidelines. PHAC has worked with the
Task Force to address the recommendations from this evaluation.
On October 9, 2024, PHAC announced the launch of the External Expert Review (EER) of the
Task Force. The EER Panel was composed of 13 experts from various fields relevant to
preventive health care, including clinical practice, bioethics and methodology. It was designed
to reflect a broad range of knowledge, expertise and experience, as well as being
representative of the diversity of Canada, which included having two Indigenous physicians as
panel members.

The EER Panel was tasked with studying the structure, governance and processes of the Task
Force. This included assessing the rigour, agility, inclusiveness and timeliness of the scientific
review processes of the evidence and data sources that are used to develop well rounded,
useful, and timely guidelines. As part of its work, the EER Panel reviewed approaches and best
practices to preventive health care guidelines and engaged with experts and stakeholders
domestically and internationally. The EER Panel also considered the outcomes of ancillary
reviews, consultations and evaluations to the extent that they provide relevant evidence for
panel consideration.

As part of the research and information gathering phases of the EER, the EER Panel collected
evidence through verbal and written submissions from specialists, international comparisons of
established and emerging best practices, as well as a month-long open consultation process
that was launched on November 21, 2024, during which 74 written submissions were received.
Organizations (e.g., health professional associations, non-governmental organizations,
provincial and territorial health authorities, Indigenous health organizations, and academic
institutions) and individuals (e.g., family physicians, medical specialists, non-medical experts
and the general public) from across Canada who participated in the consultation responded to
three questions:
1. Which practices should be maintained or what changes to the Task Force governance or
structure could further support transparency, accountability, independence and
leadership, towards scientifically rigorous, timely, agile and inclusive guidelines?
2. Considering the broader preventive health care landscape, what should be the mandate
of the Task Force of the future and how can it collaborate with other entities involved in
guideline development nationally and internationally?
3. How can the Task Force strengthen interest holder engagement including subjectmatter experts and equity-deserving groups?

Additionally, the EER Panel received advice from experts to advance their understanding of
topics such as governance, guideline development process, knowledge translation and ethics.

Provinces and territories (PTs) were also engaged in the EER through the Pan-Canadian Public
Health Network’s Communications Working Group.

On March 4, 2025, the former Minister of Health announced a temporary pause of the work of
the Task Force until the EER Panel finalized its work and the recommendations could be fully
assessed.

The EER Panel’s final report, titled “Modernizing Preventive Health Care Guideline Development
in Canada: A Way Forward” was submitted to PHAC on April 25, 2025, and made publicly
available on June 13, 2025. The report presented the findings of the EER and provided 12
recommendations which aim to modernize the development of preventive health care
guidelines by better aligning the Task Force with current health care system realities and
ensuring its long-term effectiveness. The report also provided three supplementary
recommendations aimed at addressing broader system-wide challenges and advancing national
coordination in preventive health guideline development.

In July 2025, PHAC established an Implementation Advisory Panel (IAP) composed of 14
members, excluding the Chair, to offer expert advice to inform the launch of a renewed Task
Force by April 2026. The IAP’s advice will be instrumental in reforming the Task Force’s
approach to be more inclusive, transparent and responsive to preventive health services and
guideline development in Canada. The implementation of EER recommendations and launch of
a renewed Task Force will continue to demonstrate the Government of Canada’s commitment
to addressing HESA’s recommendations specific to the Task Force and the development of
preventive health guidelines.

In addition to the EER of the Task Force, PHAC has also developed a separate “Scientific
Framework for Guidance Development”, which is intended to provide a common scientific
baseline to guidance developed or funded by PHAC. This framework will be publicly available in
2025 and shared with external experts funded by PHAC to inform the development of future
guidance.

The EER explored the topics of Task Force member selection, the inclusion of specialists, and
transparency and accountability of the Task Force as part of its mandate and through its open
consultation process. The EER final report includes a summary of the consultation and
actionable recommendations specific to Recommendation 3, such as clarifying the Task Force’s
role; evolving the Task Force’s methodological framework; building a competency-based and

inclusive membership nomination framework; formalizing subject matter expert engagement
so they can contribute to guideline development without compromising the Task Force’s
independence; and reconstituting the Task Force as an External Advisory Body, supported by
transparent governance and accountable decision-making processes. PHAC, with support from
the IAP, began to implement the recommendations from the EER report, which includes
developing an implementation plan that will be released for public consultation in Fall 2025.

In regard to Recommendation 5, it is important to note that guidelines produced by the Task
Force are one of several factors that impact health outcomes. Under its current mandate, Task
Force guidelines are developed to support primary care providers in delivering preventive
health care and their use is voluntary. In addition, while many PTs consider guidelines
developed by the Task Force when designing and implementing screening programs, they are
often one of several factors being considered. As use of guidelines developed by the Task Force
is voluntary, it would be challenging to measure and directly attribute changes in health
outcomes to guidelines developed by the Task Force.

The Government of Canada has undertaken several activities that demonstrate its commitment
to implementing measures to audit outcomes associated with the recommendations of the
Task Force. The Task Force receives annual funding from PHAC through a contribution
agreement, which includes a clause for performance measurement and evaluation. This clause
outlines that the Task Force is required to carry out performance measurement and/or
evaluation activities and to participate in any performance measurement and/or evaluation
activities at the regional, provincial/territorial and/or national scale as directed, led by or on
behalf of the Government of Canada. As a result, the Task Force conducts an annual evaluation
measuring awareness, engagement, and use of their clinical practice guidelines and related
knowledge translation tools and resources. The annual evaluation report is published on their
website and provides feedback on the Task Force’s activities, highlights their strengths,
identifies areas for improvement and includes recommendations to enhance the Task Force’s
activities.

Additionally, the EER Panel’s final report provides recommendations for improving the
transparency and accountability of the Task Force, including through clear performance
expectations and reporting requirements, which will be considered as part of the
implementation plan to renew the Task Force.

PHAC is working closely with Statistics Canada to conduct an analysis of national breast cancer
trends by location, age, race, ethnicity and stage at diagnosis; and examine data on
participation in breast cancer screening mammography programs in Canada. PHAC also
provided $295,000 to the Canadian Partnership for Tomorrow’s Health (CanPath) to examine
differences in breast cancer screening participation, treatments and outcomes by race and
ethnicity using existing Canadian cohort and administrative data.

Additionally, PHAC collaborates with Statistics Canada and the Canadian Cancer Society to
produce regular cancer surveillance reports. The Canadian Cancer Statistics biennial full reports
provide information on breast cancer incidence, mortality and survival over time. Brief reports
are published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal in alternating years. Special topic

reports provide information on breast cancer stage at diagnosis, prevalence, and cost to the
health care system, patients and caregivers. This information can be used to observe changes in
breast cancer outcomes over time.

Theme 2: Reviewing, developing, and updating breast cancer screening guidelines
(Recommendations 4, 6 and 8)

Improving the processes to review, develop and update breast cancer screening guidelines is
the focus of three recommendations in HESA’s Report and requires several considerations. The
Government of Canada is addressing these recommendations through engagement and
collaboration with relevant partners and stakeholders, the consideration of breast cancer
detection and treatment technologies, mechanisms for periodic review of new evidence and
even the consideration of socioeconomic factors that contribute to health inequities, including
individual preferences and values.

Corresponding to Recommendation 4, as directed by the former Minister of Health in his May
30, 2024 statement on breast cancer screening and prevention, Canada’s former Chief Public
Health Officer engaged with key experts, including provincial and territorial officials from the
Canadian Partnership Against Cancer (CPAC)’s Canadian Breast Cancer Screening Network
(CBCSN), members of the Task Force and members of the United States Preventive Services
Task Force to generate and share knowledge, lessons learned and best practices related to
breast cancer screening.

PHAC, in collaboration with key partners, also convened two stakeholder events related to
breast cancer screening and prevention. On September 26 and 27, 2023, PHAC convened a twoday Knowledge Exchange Event to discuss the current state of the science, including knowledge
gaps related to breast cancer screening. Planning for the event was supported by an Advisory
Planning Committee (APC) consisting of representatives from Health Canada, the Canadian
Institutes of Health Research (CIHR), CPAC, CPAC’s CBCSN, the Canadian Cancer Society, and the
University of Toronto. Approximately 70 participants attended both days of the Event, including
people with lived experience, Canadian and international experts, health professionals,
academics and researchers, representatives from patient advocacy groups, Indigenous and
racialized communities, non-governmental organizations and provincial and territorial officials.
Topics covered during the Knowledge Exchange Event included domestic and international
breast cancer screening guidelines; perspectives of patient and health care providers; and
research and innovation opportunities for advancing breast cancer screening practices, such as
shared decision-making and artificial intelligence. A “What We Heard” Report from the event
was published online and shared with the Task Force to support the development of the draft
updated Breast Cancer Screening Guideline.

PHAC convened another event on February 26, 2025, with support from the APC, titled “Closing
the Gap: Action for Equity in Breast Cancer Screening”. This event welcomed 57 participants
and focused on equitable implementation of breast cancer screening services, including
increasing awareness and educating partners and stakeholders on systemic and social barriers
that prevent equitable access to breast cancer screening services for underserved groups;
sharing knowledge and best practices that highlight evidence-based approaches, research
findings and case studies of successful breast cancer screening programs and tools; and
fostering collaboration through open dialogue. A resource that outlines key partners identified
by participants, areas of potential action, best practices, lessons learned, and successful
programs was shared with event participants and their organizations to help improve equitable
implementation of breast cancer screening in Canada.

In regard to Recommendation 6, PHAC has worked with the Task Force to develop a process to
monitor emerging evidence for guideline topics to determine when updates are required. The
Task Force’s process of monitoring evidence to update guidelines is outlined in their methods
manual, which states that published guidelines undergo continuous surveillance via an evidence
alert service, review of clinical trials and ongoing feedback from clinical experts and
stakeholders to alert the Task Force of any significant new evidence that may lead to a decision

to update a guideline earlier than anticipated. The threshold for “significant” new evidence
varies by guideline, as strong recommendations based on multiple trials with high certainty
data may require substantive new contrary evidence compared to guidelines with conditional
recommendations and/or those with low certainty or limited data.

As part of the scientific support that PHAC provides to the Task Force, PHAC also reviews
evidence and prepares summaries for the Task Force on a monthly basis to determine if a
guideline should be considered for early update or continue ongoing surveillance. Once a
guideline is five years old, PHAC prepares an in-depth evidence report for the Task Force’s
consideration to decide if a guideline topic should be updated, reaffirmed or sunset.

One of the recommendations resulting from PHAC’s formal evaluation of the Task Force in 2022
was for PHAC to explore ways to improve the timeliness of the guideline development process.
In response to this recommendation, PHAC worked with the Task Force to review, revise and
streamline processes and roles; supported the development of a project management process;
and identified and addressed common factors in the guideline development process that
impede the timeliness of guideline publication.

Lastly, the EER Panel assessed the rigour, agility, inclusiveness and timeliness of the scientific
review process of the Task Force. The EER final report provides insights into opportunities to
develop more frequent updates to guidelines that would be more responsive to the evolving
scientific landscape. This includes the recommendation for PHAC to enable and support the
Task Force to implement a phased approach to maintaining and updating high priority
guidelines using living methods, including continuous evidence monitoring, the use of emerging
technologies, and collaboration with international partners. As mentioned previously, PHAC is
currently working with an IAP to review recommendations presented in the EER final report and
inform the launch of a renewed Task Force in April 2026.

The following initiatives highlight the Government of Canada’s commitment to addressing
Recommendation 8, noting that full implementation of this recommendation requires ongoing
collaboration with PTs.

The Government of Canada plays an active convenor role in bringing together key experts,
including provincial and territorial officials from the CBCSN, to generate and share knowledge,
discuss lessons learned and share best practices related to breast cancer screening services,
especially for women who are underserved or at higher risk for developing breast cancer.

PHAC is working with Statistics Canada and CanPath to enhance the analysis of disaggregated
breast cancer screening data by geographic location, age, race, ethnicity, stage at diagnosis, and
participation in breast cancer screening mammography. Statistics Canada completed drafts of
these articles in Spring 2025 with publications recently released in August 2025, and
forthcoming. CanPath anticipates submitting its findings for publication in 2025. The findings of
these analyses will be available to inform the potential development of recommendations for
women who are underserved and at higher risk for developing breast cancer in future breast
cancer screening guidelines.

Further, Budget 2024 outlined the Government of Canada’s investment of close to $200 billion
over 10 years, including $44 billion in new funding for PTs and Indigenous partners, to support
the health care system. The Canada Health Transfer will increase by $2.6 billion in 2025-26 to
bring it to a total investment of $54.7 billion. This funding will be used by PTs to support overall
health care for people in Canada, which may include further designing and implementing
jurisdictional breast cancer screening programs for those at higher risk of developing breast
cancer, should PTs choose to allocate funding to this priority health issue.

Theme 3: Delivery of breast cancer screening services (Recommendations 12 and 13)

The Government of Canada is committed to working with PTs, Indigenous partners and other
relevant partners and stakeholders to strengthen Canada’s publicly funded health care system,
including enhancing and expanding breast cancer screening programs and services and
investing in health human resources.

In regard to Recommendation 12, the Canada Health Act Diagnostic Services Policy (effective
2020) confirms the federal position that all medically necessary diagnostic services are insured
services, regardless of the venue where the services are delivered (i.e., hospital or clinic).
Health Canada continues to work with PTs to ensure that patients can access medically
necessary diagnostic services free from barriers, including patient charges.

Additionally, ISC’s Non-Insured Health Benefits Program provides medical transportation
coverage, including travel, meals and accommodations to registered First Nations and
recognized Inuit to access publicly funded screening services, such as breast cancer screening,
when not available locally.

The Government of Canada recognizes the importance of investing in health human resources,
as outlined in Recommendation 13. In regard to this recommendation, Budget 2024 included
the Government of Canada’s plan to provide close to $200 billion over 10 years, including $44.4
billion in new funding to PTs and Indigenous partners, to support the health care system. This
investment included:
• An immediate $2 billion top up to the Canada Health Transfer to address immediate
pressures on the health care system, including health human resources;
• A guarantee of five per cent annual growth for the Canada Health Transfer for five years
(2023-24 to 2027-28), which is estimated to provide an additional $15.3 billion;
• $25 billion over 10 years to advance shared health priorities through tailored bilateral
agreements that will support the needs of people in each province and territory in four
areas of shared priority: family health services; health workers and backlogs; mental
health and substance use; and a modernized health system;
• $2 billion over 10 years to address the unique challenges faced by Indigenous people
related to fair and equitable access to quality and culturally safe health care services;
and
• $505 million over five years to the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI),
Canada Health Infoway and federal data partners to work with the PTs on developing
new health data indicators, supporting the creation of Health Workforce Canada,
advancing digital health tools, and enhancing efforts to use data to improve safety and
quality of care.

In addition, Budget 2021 announced an investment of $354 million over five years, beginning in
2021-22, to increase the number of nurses and other medical professionals in remote and
isolated First Nations communities.

To further highlight the Government of Canada’s successful efforts to invest in Health Human
Resources, CIHI released a report titled, “Taking the pulse: Measuring shared priorities for
Canadian health care” in October 2024. This report stated that almost all PTs have seen a net
increase in the number of family physicians, nurse practitioners and nurses.

Theme 4: Cancer research, data collection and modelling (Recommendations 7, 9 and 11)

The Government of Canada is committed to supporting advancements in breast cancer
prevention, detection and treatment and has demonstrated an active role in implementing
Recommendation 7 through ongoing work between PHAC, CPAC and Statistics Canada.

CPAC was established in 2007 by the Government of Canada to provide a pan-Canadian
perspective to cancer control. CPAC receives $47.5 million in federal funding per year to
accelerate the implementation of the Canadian Strategy for Cancer Control (Strategy). This

Strategy aims to provide governments, non-government organizations and people in Canada
access to research, information and decision-making tools to reduce the burden of cancer
through coordinated and system-level practice and policy change.

In line with the priorities of the Strategy, the OncoSim model was developed by Statistics
Canada with leadership and support from CPAC. OncoSim is a free, web-based simulation tool
that evaluates cancer control strategies. OncoSim is calibrated to simulate the Canadian
population according to observed and projected demographic characteristics by combining data
from the real world, expert opinion and published literature to project health and economic
outcomes. These outcomes are then attributed to 19 cancer risk factors, such as smoking and
physical inactivity. It currently models four cancer sites (breast, colorectal, lung and cervical)
and related screening programs in detail and provides high-level projections for 25 cancer sites.
This unique tool is used by decision-makers across Canada, including the Task Force, to better
understand the impact and value of cancer control interventions and develop cancer screening
guidelines.

CPAC and Statistics Canada are undertaking a project to improve the performance of the
OncoSim-Breast microsimulation model by refining its inputs and projections related to breast
density. Updating and refining the OncoSim-Breast microsimulation model will ensure that the
most accurate and relevant outputs are produced and used when developing future breast
cancer screening guidelines.

The Government of Canada is also undertaking initiatives that are in support of
Recommendation 9. PHAC is supporting Statistics Canada with four projects launched in 20242025 to enhance the analysis of ongoing population-level assessments and disaggregate data by
race and ethnicity. These projects explore insights from the Canadian Cancer Registry, the
Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohorts and the Canadian Community Health Survey:
breast cancer outcomes by race and ethnicity; temporal trends of breast cancer by race and
ethnicity; participation in breast cancer screening mammography; and geographic variation in
breast cancer incidence, stage at diagnosis and survival. As previously noted, Statistics Canada
completed drafts of these articles in Spring 2025 that highlight the results of their analyses,
with publications recently released in August 2025, and forthcoming, including one specifically
examining breast cancer characteristics and outcomes in Canadian Black women by ancestry.

To date, Statistics Canada has enhanced the data linkage that allows for the identification of
race and ethnicity information for breast cancer cases in the Canadian Cancer Registry and
breast cancer deaths in the Canadian Vital Statistics Deaths Database. The availability of this
information has been improved with better coverage of the population, as it now includes more
cases from Quebec as well as more recent years of data available (up to 2021 for cancer and up
to 2023 for deaths).

With support from PHAC and Women and Gender Equality Canada in 2023-2024, Statistics
Canada also conducted and published five studies on breast cancer that explored incidence
trends in younger women; impact of organized screening programs on stage at diagnosis in
younger women; impact of breast cancer screening on 10-year net survival in younger women;
molecular and histological subtypes of breast cancer in Canada; and breast cancer incidence
and mortality by age, stage, and molecular subtypes by race/ethnicity in Canada. The purpose
of these studies was to provide insight into risk factors for early onset breast cancer for women
in Canada.

As mentioned previously, PHAC collaborates with Statistics Canada and the Canadian Cancer
Society to produce regular biennial cancer surveillance reports, with alternating brief summary
reports published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. These reports are the most upto-date statistics on breast cancer incidence, mortality and survival over time, while special
topic reports may include information on breast cancer stage at diagnosis and the cost of breast
cancer on the health care system, patients and caregivers.

In Fall 2024, PHAC provided $295,000 to CanPath to examine differences in breast cancer
screening participation, cancer treatments and outcomes by race and ethnicity using existing
Canadian cohort and administrative data.

Lastly, the Government of Canada is supportive of Indigenous-led data collection efforts and
data sovereignty in this area. This includes the work of the First Nations Information
Governance Centre (FNIGC). The FNIGC is an independent, non-profit organization that collects
relevant information related to First Nations living on reserve and analyzes and manages the
health data they collect in alignment with First Nations data sovereignty principles. One
questionnaire funded by the Government of Canada and administered to First Nations adults
aged 18 and over included questions about health conditions, including breast cancer. These
questions included the age at diagnosis and whether the respondent has undergone treatment.

In regard to Recommendation 11, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) has
invested over $1.1 billion in priority-driven and investigator-led cancer research between 20192020 and 2023-2024, including through its dedicated Institute of Cancer Research.
Approximately $147 million of this total supported research related to breast cancer, such as
research that aims to create a rapid evaluation framework to help PTs quickly assess and
update cancer screening guidelines; identify barriers to cancer screening participation and
improve screening uptake; and to better identify individuals at higher risk of breast cancer to
guide earlier and fairer screening. In 2024, CIHR’s Institute of Cancer Research also launched
the Team Grants: Bringing Biology to Cancer Prevention funding opportunity, which includes a
dedicated Breast Cancer Pool to advance prevention and early detection of breast cancer.

CIHR led the development of a roadmap that summarized research gaps relating to breast
cancer screening in consultation with federal partners, oncologists, health organizations,
researchers and people with lived and living experience in 2024. The research roadmap
identified gaps in two key areas: social determinants of health and technology strategies.
Further research is needed regarding breast cancer screening practices in diverse populations
and the impact of information and personal values on individual decision-making about testing.
Likewise, more data is required to better understand the relationship between different
screening technologies and health outcomes, as well as the efficiency of various screening
strategies at a population level.

CIHR’s research roadmap was shared with key experts, federal partners and stakeholders, and
will be used to inform future research priorities and potential investments in this area.

Theme 5: Public education and awareness raising of breast cancer screening
(Recommendation 10)

The Government of Canada recognizes the importance of ensuring that accurate, evidencebased and accessible information on breast cancer screening and prevention is available for all
people in Canada. The Government of Canada also recognizes the importance of public health
education to reduce knowledge barriers. Many current initiatives are supportive of
Recommendation 10, as they support public education and awareness raising to ensure that
diverse groups of women can access and make informed decisions about their breast health.

Ministerial messages and social media content were publicly shared for Breast Cancer
Awareness Month in October 2024 and 2025. These messages highlighted the importance of
breast cancer awareness and early detection and reiterated that the Government of Canada is
committed to advancing women’s health through comprehensive breast cancer screening and
prevention efforts.

PHAC continues to develop and implement ongoing social media campaigns that highlight the
importance of cancer screening, including breast cancer. Social media content was created for
National Cancer Wellness Awareness Day in June 2024, and Cancer Awareness Month in
September 2024 and 2025.

The Government of Canada also continues to inform the public about new initiatives and
investments related to breast cancer screening and prevention. For example, on November 29,
2024, PHAC issued a news release and supporting social media content, to announce an
investment of $545,000 in breast cancer screening and research for CanPath and the Canadian
Cancer Society. CanPath received $295,000 for a project that aims to generate better
disaggregated data to inform best cancer screening practices in Canada.

The Canadian Cancer Society received $250,000 to scale-up their successful Memo-mamo
public awareness and social media campaign in Quebec to reach women across Canada,
especially those at higher risk of developing breast cancer who have never been screened or
have not been getting screened regularly.

The Canadian Cancer Society’s awareness campaign ran from February 10, 2025, to March 31,
2025, and included a new webpage providing information on getting a mammogram in Canada.
The campaign was positively received, with the majority of respondents to the campaign
evaluation finding it effective in encouraging mammogram uptake, seeking information and
discussing screening with healthcare providers. The campaign evaluation also identified several
barriers to breast cancer screening, including lack of a medical recommendation, unawareness
of age-based guidelines and lack of access to a family doctor. Additional concerns included fear
of pain, cost misconceptions and uncertainty about how to access breast cancer screening. The
strongest motivators for breast cancer screening were a doctor’s recommendation,
personalized reminders, and mobile clinic availability. Women aged 40–49, those without a
family doctor, and residents of Quebec were highlighted as priority groups for targeted
outreach due to lower awareness, engagement and intention to be screened.

PHAC also issued a news release and supporting social media content on February 26, 2025, to
highlight progress on breast cancer screening research and implementation efforts in Canada.
The update spoke to the Government of Canada’s commitment to supporting the health of
women by addressing knowledge gaps in breast cancer screening and prevention.

Additionally, PHAC commissioned public opinion research (POR) on the barriers to equitably
accessing breast cancer screening services between January and February 2025. The POR,
administered to 1,800 Canadian women, aged 40 and older, has been useful in gaining a better
understanding of awareness, participation and perceived barriers to breast cancer screening
across different breast cancer screening programs and population subgroups, including
Indigenous, Black, racialized and newcomer women. Findings from the POR indicate that
awareness of routine breast cancer screening programs is relatively high, with 76% of women
reporting familiarity with services available in their area. Similarly, 71% of women self-reported
awareness of the screening recommendations applicable to women aged 40 and older who are
not at increased risk. However, only 60% of women feel well-informed about the associated risk
factors, highlighting an ongoing need for public education and engagement. The results from
this POR were shared with stakeholders to help inform potential future policy and
programmatic work and are publicly available on the Government of Canada’s Publications
database.

Conclusion

The Government of Canada is committed to improving the health and well-being of all people in
Canada. As noted in this Government Response, the Government of Canada agrees with the
committee’s recommendations, and continues to demonstrate leadership to address issues
related to breast cancer screening and prevention by actively engaging and investing in
initiatives with PTs and other key non-governmental partners and stakeholders. This work has
also been catalyzed across the federal government by the former Minister of Health’s
statement on breast cancer screening and prevention in May 2024. Many of these initiatives
are addressing and responding to the unique needs of women in Canada, with an emphasis on
improving breast cancer screening to respond to the realities of Canada’s diverse population
and how women in Canada interact with the health care system. The approach taken by the
Government of Canada allows it to create tailored solutions that are not only inclusive but also

respond to the various experiences faced by women from diverse backgrounds. The
Government of Canada’s demonstrated commitment to advancing women’s health reflects a
holistic and innovative approach to achieving better outcomes in breast cancer screening, while
empowering women in Canada to make informed decisions about their health supported by the
best available science and evidence.
